AGENCY:
National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), Department of Transportation (DOT).
ACTION:
Extension of comment period.
SUMMARY:
In response to a request from the Alliance for Automotive Innovation (Auto Innovators), NHTSA is announcing a 30-day extension of the public comment period for the Supplemental Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (SNPRM) published on September 22, 2026. The SNPRM supplements NHTSA's September 2023 notice of proposed rulemaking to amend NHTSA's regulations to include an advanced crash test dummy (the Test Device for Human Occupant Restraint (THOR) 50th percentile adult male) by requesting comment on specifying an additional spine configuration and an alternative to the face foam, and announcing the availability of additional documents. The comment period for the SNPRM was originally scheduled to end on October 22, 2026. It will now end on November 21, 2026.
DATES:
The comment period for the SNPRM published on September 22, 2026 at
91 FR 60068
is extended to November 21, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments to the docket number identified in the heading of this document by one of the following methods:
Federal Rulemaking Portal:
http://www.regulations.gov
. Follow the online instructions for submitting comments.
Mail:
Docket Management Facility, U.S. Department of Transportation, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, West Building, Room W58-213, Washington, DC 20590-0001.
Hand Delivery:
1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, West Building, Room W58-213, Washington, DC, between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. ET, Monday through Friday, except Federal Holidays. To be sure someone is there to help you, please call (202) 366-9826 or (202) 366-9317 before coming.

For information on DOT's compliance with the Privacy Act, see
https://www.transportation.gov/​privacy
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
For technical issues, you may contact Garry Brock at
garry.brock@dot.gov
. For legal issues, you may contact John Piazza at
John.Piazza@dot.gov
. You can reach these officials by phone at 202-366-1810. Address: National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, U.S. Department of Transportation, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, West Building, Washington, DC 20590.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
On September 7, 2023, NHTSA published a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) to amend NHTSA's regulations to include an advanced crash test dummy, the THOR-50M.
[
1
]
The dummy represents an adult male of roughly average height and weight and is designed for use in frontal crash tests. The documentation for the dummy, including engineering drawings, qualification procedures and specifications, and procedures for assembly, disassembly, and inspection (PADI), would be incorporated by reference in
49 CFR part 572
, Anthropomorphic Test Devices. Since the NPRM, and in response to the NPRM comments, NHTSA has evaluated additional modifications to the dummy.
On September 22, 2026, NHTSA published an SNPRM specifying alternative designs to the proposed drawing package for the spine and the face insert.
[
2
]
For the spine, an alternative design referred to as the “four-position spine” is proposed, which allows integration of in-dummy data acquisition systems from different vendors while maintaining equivalent inertial properties and performance to the spine proposed in the NPRM. For the face insert, an alternative insert was developed to address the limitations of the face foam proposed in the NPRM in response to both comments received and operational concerns. Research reports were also placed in the THOR-50M research docket.
[
3
]
NHTSA also proposed a minor modification to the upper arm to address a durability concern.
On September 28, 2026, NHTSA received a request from the Alliance for Automotive Innovation (Auto Innovators) for a 30-day extension of the comment period. Auto Innovators stated that the 30-day comment period was
(
printed page 66828)
insufficient for stakeholders to review and provide comments to the notice, research reports, and technical drawing packages. Auto Innovators noted that there were more than 1,700 pages of highly detailed technical information provided with the SNPRM. Auto Innovators stated that a 30-day extension of the comment period would provide stakeholders with sufficient opportunity to complete the necessary technical analyses, coordinate across member companies, and submit more detailed comments to help better inform any changes to the final rule.
NHTSA is granting the request to extend the comment period by 30 days. We have determined that the requestors have shown good cause for an extension and that the extension is consistent with the public interest. A 30-day extension appropriately balances NHTSA's interest in providing the public with sufficient time to comment on the SNPRM and the associated technical updates to the THOR-50M design, with its interest in obtaining specific feedback from stakeholders in a timely manner. Accordingly, NHTSA is extending the comment period until November 21, 2026.

4
]

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Change in Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) Approval for Information Returns
Under the PRA, the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) assigned a control number to each “collection of information” that it reviews and approves for use by an agency. A single information collection may consist of one or more forms, recordkeeping requirements, and/or third-party disclosure requirements. Under the PRA and OMB regulations, agencies have the discretion to seek separate OMB approvals for forms, recordkeeping requirements, and third-party reporting requirements or to combine any number of forms, recordkeeping requirements, and/or third-party disclosure requirements (usually related in subject matter) under one OMB Control Number. Agency decisions on whether to group individual requirements under a single OMB Control Number or to disaggregate them and request separate OMB Control Numbers are based largely on considerations of administrative practicality.
The PRA also requires agencies to estimate the burden for each collection of information. Accordingly, each OMB Control Number has an associated burden estimate. The burden estimates for each control number are displayed in (1) the PRA notices that accompany collections of information, (2)
Federal Register
notices such as this one, and (3) OMB's database of approved information collections. If more than one form, recordkeeping requirement, and/or third-party disclosure is approved under a single OMB Control Number, the burden estimate for that OMB Control Number reflects the burden associated with all the approved forms, recordkeeping requirements, and/or third-party disclosure requirements.
As described below under the heading “Updated Burden Estimate Methodology,” the Internal Revenue Service's (IRS) currently accepted burden estimate methodology, referred to as the RAAS Taxpayer Burden Model, is based on taxpayers' tax reporting experience taking into account, among other things, the forms and schedules used by those taxpayers and the recordkeeping and other activities needed to complete those forms. The transition of the information return
[
1
]
reporting burden represents the IRS's continued effort to improve the ability of IRS to measure the burden imposed on various groups of taxpayers by the Federal tax system. While the RAAS Taxpayer Burden Model methodology provides a more accurate and comprehensive description of information return reporting burden, it will not provide burden estimates on a form-by-form basis, as has been done under the previous methodology. When the prior model, known as the legacy Arthur D. Little (ADL) model was developed in the mid-1980s, almost all tax returns were prepared manually, either by the taxpayer or a paid preparer. In this context, it was determined that estimating burden on a form-by-form, line-by-line basis was an appropriate methodology. Information returns are increasingly being prepared
(
printed page 66943)
using software or with preparer assistance. In this current reporting environment, in which many taxpayers' activities are no longer directly associated with particular forms, estimating burden on a form-by-form basis is not an appropriate method of estimating taxpayer burden. The RAAS Taxpayer Burden Model methodology, which takes into account broader and more comprehensive taxpayer characteristics and activities, provides a much more accurate and useful estimate of taxpayer burden.
Currently, there are 51 forms used by information return issuers when complying with Federal tax laws. These include Forms 1098, 1099-B, 1099-DA, 1099-DIV, 1099-INT, 1099-MISC, 1099-NEC, 1099-R, 5498, W-9 and their schedules. For most of these forms, IRS has in the past obtained separate OMB approval under unique OMB Control Numbers and separate burden estimates.
The RAAS Taxpayer Burden Model methodology estimates the aggregate burden imposed for information reporting, based upon the reporting-related characteristics and activities of the issuers. IRS therefore will seek OMB approval of all 51 information reporting tax forms as a single “collection of information.” The aggregate burden of these tax forms will be accounted for under OMB Control Number 1545-0108, which is currently assigned to Form 1096. OMB Control Number 1545-0108 will be displayed on all information returns and related information collections. As a result of this change, burden estimates for information returns will now be displayed differently in PRA Notices on tax forms and other information collections, and in
Federal Register
notices. This new way of displaying burden is presented below under the heading “Proposed PRA Submission to OMB.”
Updated Burden Estimate Methodology
The RAAS Taxpayer Burden Model for Information Returns revises the estimates of the levels of burden experienced by information return issuers when complying with their federal reporting requirements related to information return reporting. It replaces the legacy ADL model methodology developed in the mid-1980s. Since that time, improved technology and modeling sophistication have enabled the IRS to improve the burden estimates. The RAAS Taxpayer Burden Model methodology provides taxpayers and the IRS with a more comprehensive understanding of the current levels of taxpayer burden. It reflects major changes over the past two decades in the way taxpayers prepare and file their returns. The RAAS Taxpayer Burden Model methodology also represents a substantial step forward in the IRS's ability to assess likely impacts of administrative and legislation changes on information reporting.
The RAAS Taxpayer Burden Model methodology focuses on the characteristics and activities of information return issuers rather than solely focusing on the forms they file. Key determinates of taxpayer burden in the model are the type of forms issued, number of forms issued, and whether the issuer is newly issuing that form. Indicators of tax law and administrative complexity, as reflected in the tax forms and instructions, are incorporated into the model. The legacy ADL model methodology primarily focused on the number of line items on each tax form. The changes between the old and new burden estimates are due to the improved ability of the RAAS Taxpayer Burden Model to measure burden and the expanded scope of what is measured. These changes create a one-time shift in the estimate of imposed burden. It is important to note that the difference between the legacy and revised estimates does not reflect any change in the actual burden imposed on taxpayers.
Tax Compliance Burden
Tax compliance burden is defined as the time and money taxpayers spend to comply with their tax filing responsibilities. Time-related activities include recordkeeping, tax planning, gathering tax materials, learning about the law, and completing and submitting the return. Out-of-pocket costs include expenses such as purchasing tax software, paying a third-party preparer, and printing and postage. Tax compliance burden does not include a taxpayer's tax liability, economic inefficiencies caused by sub-optimal choices related to tax deductions or credits, or psychological costs.
As has been done for individual taxpayer burden since 2005, business entity burden since 2014, tax-exempt organization burden since 2018, employer reporting burden since 2023, and trust and estate burden since 2024, both the time expended and the out-of-pocket costs for information return issuers are estimated. The RAAS Taxpayer Burden Model methodology relies on surveys that gather data about time spent and out-of-pocket costs incurred for pre-issuing and issuing activities for information return issuers. The methodology establishes econometric relationships between tax return characteristics and reported compliance costs. The methodology controls for the substitution of time and money by monetizing time and reporting total compliance costs in dollars. The RAAS Taxpayer Burden Model methodology better reflects taxpayer compliance burden because, in a world of electronic tax preparation, time and out-of-pockets costs are governed by the information required rather than the form on which it is ultimately reported. Importantly, even where various information return issuers complete the same tax form lines, the RAAS Taxpayer Burden Model methodology differentiates the cost incurred to complete those forms based on characteristics of those issuers. Key characteristics that serve as coefficients in the information return burden model are:
Type of form issued
Number of forms issued
Whether the issuer is newly issuing the form type

Form Numbers and Published Guidance:
Forms include but are not limited to Forms 1098, 1099-B, 1099-DA, 1099-DIV, 1099-INT, 1099-MISC, 1099-NEC, 1099-R, 5498, W-9 and all related forms, schedules, and attachments.
Abstract:
These forms, schedules and attachments are used by information return issuers when complying with Federal tax laws. This information collection covers the burden associated with preparing and issuing information returns and related forms, schedules, and attachments, and complying with published guidance.
Current Actions:
The burden estimation methodology for information returns is being transitioned from the legacy Arthur D. Little (ADL) model to the RAAS Taxpayer Burden Model. The changes discussed above result in a burden hour estimate of 140,987,248, a decrease in total estimated time burden of 2,420,759,231 hours. The newly reported total out-of-pocket cost estimate is $6,179,662,122 and total monetized burden is $13,962,431,740. The change related to the transition of the burden estimate from the legacy ADL methodology to the RAAS Taxpayer Burden Model is a one-time change. In addition, changes are being made to forms included in this estimate to be current with enacted legislation.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Under the PRA (
44 U.S.C. 3501-3521
), Federal Agencies must obtain approval from the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for each collection of information they conduct or sponsor. “Collection of information” is defined in
44 U.S.C. 3502(3)
and
5 CFR 1320.3(c)
and includes Agency requests
(
printed page 66849)
or requirements that members of the public submit reports, keep records, or provide information to a third party. Section 3506(c)(2)(A) of the PRA (
44 U.S.C. 3506(c)(2)(A)
) requires Federal Agencies to provide a 60-day notice in the
Federal Register
concerning each proposed collection of information, including each proposed extension of an existing collection of information, before submitting the collection to OMB for approval. To comply with this requirement, FDA is publishing notice of the proposed collection of information set forth in this document.
With respect to the following collection of information, FDA invites comments on these topics: (1) whether the proposed collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of FDA's functions, including whether the information will have practical utility; (2) the accuracy of FDA's estimate of the burden of the proposed collection of information, including the validity of the methodology and assumptions used; (3) ways to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected; and (4) ways to minimize the burden of the collection of information on respondents, including through the use of automated collection techniques, when appropriate, and other forms of information technology.
Export Certificates for FDA Regulated Products
OMB Control Number 0910-0498—Revision
This information collection supports the implementation of FDA statutory and regulatory provisions and related forms. Sections 801(e) and 802 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) (
21 U.S.C. 381(e)
and
382
) pertain to the export of FDA-regulated products and are intended to ease restrictions on exportation. Section 801(e)(4) of the FD&C Act provides that persons exporting FDA-regulated products may request FDA to certify that the product meets the requirements of the FD&C Act. The provisions also require the Agency to issue written export certifications within 20 days of any request. To offset Agency resource expenditures for processing certifications requests, the statute provides that FDA may charge firms a fee not to exceed $175.
The information collection contains seven FDA forms (Form FDA 3613, 3613a, 3613b, 3613c, and 3613g) related to exporting FDA-regulated products. A description of each form is provided below. To obtain a fillable PDF file of each form, visit
https://www.fda.gov/​about-fda/​reports-manuals-forms/​forms
,
and type “3613” in the search field. We accept online applications for export certificates for specific product areas through web-based application systems. To access these web-based application systems, visit the FDA Industry Systems web page,
http://www.access.fda.gov
.
The Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER) and The Center for Veterinary Medicine (CVM) are transitioning to a requirement for electronic submission of the forms related to biological products and medical devices, as well as food, drugs, and devices for animals. Therefore, we are in the process of revising FDA Forms 3613, 3613a, and 3613b to remove the paper submission instructions related to biological products and medical devices, as well as food, drugs, and devices for animals.
The forms are also being updated to align with those of the other FDA Centers for conformity and to help improve clarity and accuracy. Proposed revisions include, but are not limited to the following:
CVM intends to include a field for insertion of the National Drug Code, which is the product listing number that identifies the drug and is legally required for animal drugs.
CBER is revising the exporter's certification statement of FDA Form 3613 (for Human Cells, Tissues, and Cellular and Tissue-Based Products (HCT/Ps) Regulated Solely under Section 361 of the Public Health Service Act) to more closely align the with the exporter's certification statement used for CBER's Certificate to Foreign Government, as applicable for the requirements of
Title 21, Code of Federal Regulations
Part 1271. In addition, these revisions will provide more clear examples of how establishments and products identified in the FDA Form 3613
Supplementary Information
must be in compliance with Part 1271.
Additionally, CVM is adding two new forms. FDA Form 3613h
Supplementary Information; Certificate of Free Sale
and FDA Form 3613i
Supplementary Information; Current Good Manufacturing Practice Certificate.
These forms were created for improved clarity as previously the Certificate to Foreign Government FDA Form 3613 was used to apply for both these certificate types, which can lead to confusion.
The scope of the collection includes provisions introduced under the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security Act (CARES Act) that may require supplemental information for exported product certificates. The data elements have been incorporated into our current form versions. The fact that FDA has issued an export certificate does not preclude FDA from taking appropriate regulatory action against a product covered by the certificate.
We developed the guidance document entitled, “
Exports Under the FDA Export Reform and Enhancement Act of 1996”
(December 1996) to assist respondents to the information collection. The guidance summarizes and explains the basic requirements and procedures under the FDA Export Reform and Enhancement Act of 1996 (
Public Law 104-134
, as amended by
Public Law 104-180
) for exporting human drugs, animal drugs, biological products, devices, food, food additives, color additives, and dietary supplements that may not be sold or distributed in the United States. The 1996 law amended sections 801 and 802 of the FD&C Act, as well as section 351(h) of the Public Health Service Act, simplifying the requirements for exporting unapproved human drugs, biological products, and devices. In addition, the FDA Export Reform and Enhancement Act substantially reduced the requirements for exporting unapproved new animal drugs and provided a new option for exporting unapproved devices. The guidance document is available from our website at:
https://www.fda.gov/​regulatory-information/​search-fda-guidance-documents/​guidance-industry-exports-under-fda-export-reform-and-enhancement-act-1996
.
https://www.fda.gov/​media/​138075/​download
.
In addition, we developed the guidance document “
FDA Export Certification”
(August 2021) which is intended to provide a general description of FDA export certification to industry and foreign governments. The guidance document is available from our website at:
http://www.fda.gov/​RegulatoryInformation/​Guidances/​ucm125789.htm
.
To learn more about how to complete these forms and general information for specific product areas, visit:
https://www.fda.gov/​vaccines-blood-biologics/​exporting-cber-regulated-products/​fda-forms-certificates-exporting
and
https://www.fda.gov/​vaccines-blood-biologics/​exporting-cber-regulated-products/​how-complete-fda-export-certificate-forms
(CBER);
https://www.fda.gov/​drugs/​human-drug-exports/​electronic-certificates-pharmaceutical-product-general-information
(CDER); and
https://www.fda.gov/​medical-devices/​importing-and-exporting-medical-devices/​exporting-medical-devices
(CDRH). In addition, the CVM web-
(
printed page 66850)
based application offers a guide on how to fill out the forms, entitled: “Center for Veterinary Medicine Export Certification Application and Tracking System (CVM eCATS) Step-by-Step Instructions for Industry Applicants.”

Product Jurisdiction and Combination Products—
21 CFR Parts 3
and
4
OMB Control Number 0910-0523—Extension
This information collection helps support implementation of statutory requirements that govern product jurisdiction and combination products. Congress expressly directed FDA to
(
printed page 66854)
assign combination products to the appropriate Agency component for regulation as set forth in section 503(g) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) (
21 U.S.C. 353(g)
). Congress also expressly directed FDA to determine the classification of a product as a drug, biological product, device, or combination product, or the component of the Agency that will regulate the product, as applicable, in response to a request submitted under section 563 of the FD&C Act (
21 U.S.C. 360bbb-2
). Regulations in
21 CFR part 3
provide for product classification determinations and FDA designation on which Agency component will have primary jurisdiction for any drug, device, biological, or combination product, where such jurisdiction is unclear or in dispute. These determinations are made by our Office of Combination Products (OCP) upon receiving Requests for Designation (RFDs). We maintain a web page that includes contact and resource information pertaining to the RFDs process at
https://www.fda.gov/​combination-products/​jurisdictional-information
.
As communicated on our web page, FDA welcomes comments from interested stakeholders on issues pertaining to OCP and encourages medical product developers to contact us if they are uncertain about the classification or assignment of their products and with questions regarding premarket or postmarket considerations for combination products. A dedicated mailbox is established at
combination@fda.gov
.
Similar to the RFD process, we have established the Pre-RFD process for sponsors to obtain preliminary, nonbinding feedback regarding medical product classification and assignment. Forms FDA 5003 and 5004 (RFD and Pre-RFD forms) have been developed to facilitate information collection for RFDs and Pre-RFDs, we expect to explore implementing the forms as resources become available. At the same time, we have more recently issued the following Agency guidance documents to provide instruction and recommendations to respondents regarding the submission of RFDs and Pre-RFDs.
The guidance document entitled, “How to Write a Request for Designation” (April 2011), provides instruction regarding the information that needs to be submitted to OCP in an RFD as described in
21 CFR 3.7
. The guidance is available at
http://www.fda.gov/​regulatory-information/​search-fda-guidance-documents/​how-write-request-designation-rfd
.
The guidance document entitled “How to Prepare a Pre-Request for Designation,” (revised November 2025) assists sponsors in obtaining a preliminary, non-binding assessment regarding the classification and assignment of products from OCP through the Pre-RFD process. The guidance explains the Pre-RFD process and helps a sponsor understand the type of information to provide in a Pre-RFD submission. The guidance is available at
https://www.fda.gov/​regulatory-information/​search-fda-guidance-documents/​how-prepare-pre-request-designation-pre-rfd
.
This information collection also includes burden associated with Combination Product Agreement Meetings (CPAM) requests. The guidance document entitled, “Requesting FDA Feedback on Combination Products,” (issued December 2020) addresses ways in which combination product sponsors can obtain feedback from FDA on scientific and regulatory questions and describes best practices for FDA and sponsors when interacting on these topics. The guidance is available at
http://www.fda.gov/​regulatory-information/​search-fda-guidance-documents/​requesting-fda-feedback-combination-products
.
The guidance documents were issued consistent with sections 503(g) and 563 of the FD&C Act and with our good guidance practice regulations in
21 CFR 10.115
, which provide for public comment at any time.
The information collection also includes regulations in
21 CFR part 4
that govern current good manufacturing practice requirements and postmarketing safety requirements for combination products. We expect, however, that burden attendant to the associated recordkeeping, reporting, and/or disclosure activities is already accounted for in approved information collections that apply to drug, device, and/or biologic products specifically and respectively. Therefore, we do not ascribe separate burden in this information collection request for the activities generated by these requirements.
Respondents to the information collection are sponsors of medical products, including combination products. Based on submissions received by OCP during fiscal years 2022, 2023, and 2024, we account for 149 respondents annually.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
In compliance with
44 U.S.C. 3507
, FDA has submitted the following proposed collection of information to OMB for review and clearance.
Accreditation Scheme for Conformity Assessment Program
OMB Control Number 0910-0889—Reinstatement
The FDA Reauthorization Act of 2017 (FDARA), enacted as part of the Medical Device User Fee Amendments of 2017 (MDUFA IV), amended section 514 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) by adding Section 514(d). Section 514(d) directed FDA to establish a pilot program under which testing laboratories may be accredited by accreditation bodies meeting criteria specified by FDA to assess whether a device conforms with certain FDA-recognized consensus standards. The FDA User Fee Reauthorization Act of 2022 (FUFRA), enacted as part of the Medical Device User Fee Amendments of 2022 (MDUFA V), subsequently directed FDA to conclude the pilot phase and continue the Accreditation Scheme for Conformity Assessment (ASCA) as an ongoing program.
FDA generally accepts determinations by ASCA-accredited testing laboratories that a device conforms with an eligible standard unless FDA determines that a particular conformity determination should not be accepted.
The statute provides that FDA may review determinations made by accredited testing laboratories, including by conducting periodic audits of such determinations or reviewing the processes of accreditation bodies or testing laboratories.
Following such a review, or if FDA becomes aware of information materially bearing on safety or effectiveness of a device assessed by an ASCA-accredited testing laboratory, FDA may take additional measures as determined appropriate. Such measures may include suspension or withdrawal of a testing laboratory's ASCA Accreditation, withdrawal of an accreditation body's ASCA Recognition, or a request for additional information regarding a specific device.
FDA issued the final guidance “The Accreditation Scheme for Conformity Assessment (ASCA) Pilot Program” in September 2020 to discuss the goals and implementation of the voluntary ASCA Pilot Program. In September 2024, FDA issued three draft guidance documents intended to update the ASCA Program based on lessons learned during the pilot phase and support its continued operation as an ongoing program.
The establishment of the goals, scope, procedures, and a suitable framework for the voluntary ASCA Program supports the Agency's continued efforts to use its scientific resources effectively
(
printed page 66846)
and efficiently to protect and promote public health. FDA believes the voluntary ASCA Program may further encourage international harmonization of medical device regulation because it incorporates elements, where appropriate, from a well-established set of international conformity assessment practices and standards (
e.g.,
ISO/IEC 17000 series). The voluntary ASCA Program does not supplant or alter any other existing statutory or regulatory requirements governing the decision-making process for premarket submissions.
Under the ASCA Program's conformity assessment scheme, ASCA-recognized accreditation bodies accredit testing laboratories using ASCA program specifications associated with each eligible standard and ISO/IEC 17025:2017: General requirements for the competence of testing and calibration laboratories. ASCA-accredited testing laboratories may conduct testing to determine conformance of a device with at least one of the standards eligible for inclusion in the ASCA Program. When an ASCA-accredited testing laboratory conducts such testing, it may provide a complete test report to the device manufacturer. A device manufacturer who utilizes an ASCA-accredited testing laboratory to perform testing in accordance with the provisions of the ASCA Program can then include a declaration of conformity with supplemental documentation (including a summary test report) as part of a premarket submission to FDA. Testing performed by an ASCA-accredited testing laboratory can be used to support a premarket submission for any device if the testing was conducted using a standard eligible for inclusion in the ASCA Program and in accordance with the ASCA program specifications for that standard.
The ASCA Program includes participation from accreditation bodies, testing laboratories, device manufacturers, and FDA staff. Each of these entities plays a critical role in the ASCA Program to ensure that patients and healthcare providers have timely and continued access to safe, effective, and high-quality medical devices.
To participate in the ASCA Program, accreditation bodies request ASCA Recognition from FDA. Testing laboratories first obtain accreditation from an ASCA-recognized accreditation body and then request ASCA Accreditation from FDA. Each application includes an agreement to comply with the applicable terms of participation. For example, a participating accreditation body or testing laboratory agrees to attend training, regularly communicate with FDA, and support periodic FDA audits. FDA recognizes qualified applicants as participants. In its recognition, FDA will identify the scope of recognition of specific standards and test methods to which each participant may accredit or test as part of the ASCA Program.
After recognizing a testing laboratory as a participant in the ASCA Program, FDA will generally grant the testing laboratory ASCA Accreditation. During the ASCA Program, FDA generally will accept determinations from ASCA-accredited testing laboratories that a medical device is in conformity with the specified testing to a particular standard and does not intend to review complete test reports from ASCA-accredited testing laboratories in support of a declaration of conformity submitted with a premarket submission except in certain circumstances. The ASCA Declaration of Conformity, including any ASCA-specific content required therein, is submitted as part of a premarket submission and is therefore not covered under this ICR.
ASCA Accreditation is separate from any accreditation that an accreditation body may provide to a testing laboratory for purposes other than the ASCA Program. FDA's decision to recognize the accreditation for purposes of the ASCA Program is separate and distinct from any independent decision by the accreditation body with respect to a testing laboratory for purposes outside of the ASCA Program.
The ASCA Program does not address all specific content for a particular premarket submission. Specifically, the ASCA Declaration of Conformity and its ASCA-specific content are submitted in connection with a premarket submission and are subject to the information collection requirements applicable to premarket submissions, which have been previously approved. Information collections associated with premarket submissions are therefore not included in this ICR.
Respondents are accreditation bodies (ABs) and testing laboratories (TLs). In tables 1 through 3, these abbreviations are used.
In the
Federal Register
of July 17, 2026 (
91 FR 44854
) FDA published a 60-day notice requesting public comment on the proposed collection of information. Two comments were received. Both comments were determined to be PRA-related.
The first comment was submitted by an ASCA-recognized accreditation body. The commentor commented on the extension process for currently recognized accreditation bodies under Section X, Subsection C (Extension of ASCA Recognition) of the ASCA Pilot Program Final Guidance (September 25, 2020). The commentor recommended that FDA streamline the process by limiting submission requirements to information directly relevant to the requested extension and any information that has materially changed since the accreditation body's most recent recognition or renewal, rather than requiring resubmission of documentation FDA has recently reviewed.
FDA appreciates the commentor's comment and acknowledges the concern that the current extension process may generate duplicative administrative burden for accreditation bodies and FDA staff. FDA is currently preparing the final version of the ASCA Program Guidance (draft September 20, 2024) that will replace the ASCA Pilot Program Guidance of September 25, 2020, which we believe will address concerns like these. FDA will continue to evaluate opportunities to reduce unnecessary burden while preserving the integrity of the ASCA Program's oversight framework.
The second comment was received from a patient, the commenter addressed two PRA-related topics: the practical utility of the information collected, and three (3) ways to enhance its quality, utility, and clarity. On practical utility, the commenter observed that the collection captures scopes only within the program's existing two standards families and therefore produces no data on where accredited testing would be most useful next. On quality and clarity, the commenter recommended adding two items to the existing feedback questionnaire: (1) ask respondents which FDA-recognized consensus standards or test methods outside the current ASCA categories they would use an accredited laboratory for if the program were extended; and (2) ask respondents whether the information generated under the program is available to and usable by a clinician or patient reviewing a device after implantation. The commenter also suggested that audit outcomes and the basis for withdrawal of ASCA accreditation be captured in the collection in a form that can be counted and compared.
FDA appreciates the commenter's observations regarding the utility and quality of the ASCA Program information collection. FDA notes that the PRA burden estimates for the ASCA Program do not represent an existing or ongoing questionnaire. Rather, the estimated burden reflects: (a) the time
(
printed page 66847)
accreditation bodies and testing laboratories spend applying to and maintaining their status in the ASCA Program; and (b) the time testing laboratories spend completing the summary test report format for testing conducted under the program.
Regarding the commenter's observations on program scope, FDA notes that the ASCA Program launched as a pilot, which limited the number of standards eligible for inclusion. The program transitioned from a pilot to an ongoing program in 2023, and since that time, FDA has held workshops and engaged regularly with program participants on the topic of expanding the program's scope. Expansion of the standards contained in the ASCA Program is an ongoing priority for FDA.

Federal Register
, and no comments were received. NSF is forwarding the proposed submission to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for clearance simultaneously with the publication of this second notice.

.

splimpto@nsf.gov
.

Title:
Improving Customer Experience (OMB Circular A-11, Section 280 Implementation).
OMB Clearance Number:
3145-0254.
Abstract:
A modern, streamlined and responsive customer experience means raising government-wide customer experience to the average of the private sector service industry; developing indicators for high-impact Federal programs to monitor progress towards excellent customer experience and mature digital services; and providing the structure (including increasing transparency) and resources to ensure customer experience is a focal point for agency leadership.
This proposed information collection activity provides a means to garner customer and stakeholder feedback in an efficient, timely manner in accordance with the Administration's commitment to improving customer service delivery as discussed in Section 280 of OMB Circular A-11 at
https://www.performance.gov/​cx/​a11-280.pdf
.
As discussed in OMB guidance, agencies should identify their highest-impact customer journeys (using customer volume, annual program cost, and/or knowledge of customer priority as weighting factors) and select touchpoints/transactions within those journeys to collect feedback.
These results will be used to improve the delivery of Federal services and programs. It will also provide government-wide data on customer experience that can be displayed on
www.performance.gov
to help build transparency and accountability of Federal programs to the customers they serve.
As a general matter, these information collections will not result in any new system of records containing privacy information and will not ask questions of a sensitive nature, such as sexual behavior and attitudes, religious beliefs, and other matters that are commonly considered private.
NSF will only submit collections if they meet the following criteria.
The collections are voluntary;
The collections are low-burden for respondents (based on considerations of total burden hours or burden-hours per respondent) and are low-cost for both the respondents and the Federal Government;
The collections are non-controversial and do not raise issues of concern to other Federal agencies;
Any collection is targeted to the solicitation of opinions from respondents who have experience with the program or may have experience with the program in the near future;
Personally identifiable information (PII) is collected only to the extent necessary and is not retained;
Information gathered is intended to be used for general service improvement and program management purposes
Upon agreement between OMB and the agency all or a subset of information may be released as part of A-11, Section 280 requirements only on
performance.gov
. Summaries of customer research and user testing activities may be included in public-facing customer journey maps or summaries.
Additional release of data must be done coordinated with OMB.
These collections will allow for ongoing, collaborative and actionable communications between the Agency, its customers and stakeholders, and OMB as it monitors agency compliance on Section 280. These responses will inform efforts to improve or maintain the quality of service offered to the public. If this information is not collected, vital feedback from customers and stakeholders on services will be unavailable.

(
printed page 67000)
AGENCY:
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, Treasury.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) is issuing regulations implementing the Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins Act regarding the issuance of payment stablecoins and certain related activities by entities subject to the OCC's jurisdiction.
DATES:
The final rule is effective on January 18, 2027.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Sarah Turney, Assistant Director, Henry Barkhausen, Special Counsel, Kevin Korzeniewski, Special Counsel, Mark O'Horo, Special Counsel, Daniel Borman, Counsel, or Collin Berger, Attorney, Chief Counsel's Office, 202-649-5490, Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, 400 7th Street SW, Washington, DC 20219. If you are deaf, hard of hearing, or have a speech disability, please dial 7-1-1 to access telecommunications relay services.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background and Summary of the Final Rule
The Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins Act (
12 U.S.C. 5901
et seq.
) (GENIUS Act or the Act) was enacted on July 18, 2025. The Act establishes a regulatory framework for payment stablecoin activities.
[
1
]
Stablecoins are digital assets,
i.e.,
digital representations of value recorded on a cryptographically secured distributed ledger,
[
2
]
such as a blockchain.
[
3
]
The Act sets forth various regulatory and licensing requirements for permitted payment stablecoin issuers and foreign payment stablecoin issuers. In many instances, the Act states that the specific requirements applicable to these entities (
e.g.,
those related to capital, liquidity, or operational risk management) will be established by regulations issued by the relevant primary Federal payment stablecoin regulator, in coordination with other relevant agencies, as appropriate.
[
4
]
On March 2, 2026, the OCC issued a notice of proposed rulemaking (proposal or proposed rule) proposing, and seeking comment on, the regulations that would apply to permitted payment stablecoin issuers and foreign payment stablecoin issuers under the OCC's jurisdiction (including subsidiaries of insured national banks or Federal savings associations, Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuers, certain nonbank State qualified payment stablecoin issuers, and foreign payment stablecoin issuers) as well as certain custody activities conducted by OCC-supervised entities.
[
5
]
The OCC received approximately 328 comments in response to the proposal from a wide variety of commenters, including crypto-focused companies, trade groups, banks, non-profit organizations, academics, and individuals.
[
6
]
Commenters had diverging views on several of the proposal's key provisions. The final rule addresses these comments, as discussed below. However, as discussed in the proposal, the OCC anticipates that these implementing regulations will be updated, as necessary, in the years following the effective date of the GENIUS Act as the business practices of permitted payment stablecoin issuers and foreign payment stablecoin issuers continue to evolve and develop and the OCC gains experience regulating and supervising permitted payment stablecoin issuers. Likewise, the OCC will supplement this final rule with guidance documents, as appropriate. As is its practice in other areas, the OCC will continue to track market developments and meet with interested parties to discuss the regulation and supervision of permitted payment stablecoin issuers, foreign payment stablecoin issuers, national banks, Federal savings associations, and Federal branches under the final rule in the coming years to understand the application of the rule in practice. At a high level, many commenters held differing views with respect to the proposal's approach concerning reserve asset management, liquidity, and diversification; the prohibition against a permitted payment stablecoin issuer paying interest or yield to a payment stablecoin holder solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of such payment stablecoin (yield prohibition); redemption; and the proposal's capital requirements.
With respect to reserve asset management, liquidity, and diversification, commenters differed as to how prescriptive the final rule should be. Several commenters advocated setting principles-based requirements, either with or without a quantitative safe harbor concerning diversification requirements, and making certain changes to the proposed quantitative diversification safe harbor. Other commenters advocated for more prescriptive and quantitative reserve asset management, liquidity, and diversification requirements.
Many commenters opposed the proposal's approach with respect to the yield prohibition. The proposal included a rebuttable presumption that would have presumed certain transactions with affiliates and related third parties violated the prohibition. Many commenters generally favored a strong prohibition that would address a permitted payment stablecoin issuer using a third party to pay interest or yield. Of these commenters, several favored broadening the rebuttable presumption. Others said that a presumption was inadequate, and certain transactions that implicated indirect payments should be
(
printed page 67001)
conclusively prohibited. In contrast, many commenters advocated for a narrow prohibition and either eliminating or narrowing the rebuttable presumption. Many of these commenters voiced concerns that the proposed rebuttable presumption could capture certain payments to related third parties that were not made solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of payment stablecoin.
Concerning redemption, many commenters argued against imposing a freeze on (or extension of) redemption when there is a spike in redemption requests. Commenters argued that including these types of provisions could accelerate a run. With respect to capital, many commenters generally favored the flexible approach afforded by the proposed rule. Nevertheless, other commenters advocated a more quantitative and standardized approach. Commenters also addressed several other issues, including definitions; permitted activities; redemption; risk management; audits, reports, and supervision; State issuers; custody; foreign issuers; applications and registration requirements, among other issues. Each of these subjects is addressed in greater detail below.
Commenters also provided input concerning requirements relating to Bank Secrecy Act/Anti-Money Laundering (BSA/AML) and sanctions evasion. These comments will be addressed in a separate rulemaking.
[
7
]
Likewise, some comments on that separate rulemaking are best addressed in this final rule. Some commenters stated that the OCC should delay finalizing the rule due to uncertainties in stablecoin markets, ongoing legislative efforts, the complexity of the Act and rule, or to facilitate issuance of a joint rule.
[
8
]
Some commenters requested that the OCC re-propose any aspects that are inconsistent with the proposals of other agencies that issue rules under the GENIUS Act. The GENIUS Act will be effective on January 18, 2027, and it is important that the OCC's implementing regulations be effective as of that date. With respect to legislation, the OCC will revise the final rule, as appropriate, in response to any enacted legislation impacting the OCC's implementation of the GENIUS Act.
In addition, several commenters requested an extension of the comment period or to avoid finalizing the rule until certain legislative clarity was provided or to ensure that the effective date of the Act would be no sooner than January 18, 2027. Commenters also raised concerns regarding interagency coordination and advocated for ensuring that there is alignment among the rules issued by the agencies tasked with implementing the GENIUS Act. Balancing the need to have final rules implementing the GENIUS Act in advance of the statutory effective date against commenters' desire for additional time to comment on the proposal, the OCC elected not to extend the comment period but did accept and consider comments submitted after the close of the formal comment period. With respect to interagency coordination, the OCC has coordinated closely with the other Federal agencies consistent with section 13 of the GENIUS Act. The OCC has taken seriously its obligation to coordinate with other agencies, as appropriate, and does not believe that it is necessary to do so through a joint rule. The OCC will continue to coordinate appropriately.
Commenters provided suggestions on amendments to regulations that should be made in coordination with the GENIUS Act rulemaking. For example, a few commenters noted that the OCC should coordinate with the other Federal banking agencies to amend the standardized bank capital and liquidity requirements to provide for appropriate treatment for payment stablecoins and reserve assets, including that because reserve assets are not available to meet the obligations of a parent entity of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer, they should not be included in parent-level capital and liquidity requirements. Other commenters stated that the agencies implementing the GENIUS Act should revise their liquidity rules to accommodate the GENIUS Act framework, including the liquidity coverage ratio and net stable funding ratio. These comments are beyond the scope of this rulemaking, and the final rule therefore does not revise existing regulations to address them.
Several commenters raised other issues that are also beyond the scope of this rulemaking. Some commenters requested that the OCC apply certain other statutes to permitted payment stablecoin issuers by rule. The OCC has not done so in this final rule. The scope of statutes that apply to permitted payment stablecoin issuers cannot change by regulation. Thus, the final rule neither subjects permitted payment stablecoin issuers to statutes that would not otherwise apply nor excludes them from the scope of statutes that do apply to their activities. Some commenters stated that the OCC should coordinate with the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (Federal Reserve) concerning designation of certain permitted payment stablecoin issuers as systemically important. Such designation is beyond the scope of this rulemaking, and therefore the final rule does not address such designations. In addition, one commenter requested that the OCC address the tax treatment of payment stablecoins. This issue is outside the scope of this rule and the OCC's authority and is not addressed in the final rule. Likewise, some commenters brought up antitrust concerns that are outside the scope of this rulemaking. Some commenters raised issues concerning non-payment stablecoins, decentralized finance (DeFi),
[
9
]
and crypto-assets more broadly that also fall outside the scope of this rulemaking.
Many commenters suggested that the OCC apply various existing consumer protection laws and regulations to permitted payment stablecoin issuers. For example, several commenters pointed to Unfair, Deceptive, or Abusive Acts or Practices (UDAAP) pursuant to section 1031 of the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act (
12 U.S.C. 5531
), Unfair or Deceptive Acts or Practices (UDAP) under section 5 of the Federal Trade
(
printed page 67002)
Commission Act (
15 U.S.C. 45
), the Electronic Fund Transfer Act of 1978 (
15 U.S.C. 1693
et seq.
) (EFTA), the Truth in Lending Act of 1968 (
15 U.S.C. 1601
et seq.
) (TILA), and the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (
15 U.S.C. 6801
et seq.
) (GLBA) as existing consumer protection laws that should apply to permitted payment stablecoin issuers. Commenters argued that consumers should not receive different protections based solely on the technological form of a payment instrument. Some commenters suggested that new consumer protection requirements for permitted payment stablecoin issuers should be drafted rather than simply applying existing statutes and regulations. For example, a few commenters suggested that consumer protection should be addressed in the application and supervisory framework under the GENIUS Act. A few commenters suggested that permitted payment stablecoin issuers should be required to maintain frameworks for managing risks arising from redemption failures, misleading disclosures, or inadequate customer communication. Other commenters suggested that, in addition to traditional fraud risks, specific operational risks such as transaction delays, rejections, and account restrictions should be addressed in the case of permitted payment stablecoin issuers. In contrast, a few commenters argued that consumer protection currently has its own regulatory framework and should not be duplicated. It would be outside the scope of this rulemaking to opine on all the statutes that may be applicable to permitted payment stablecoin issuers. The OCC's final rule does not alter the scope of the consumer protection laws that apply to permitted payment stablecoin issuers.
Several commenters also requested that the OCC take additional action to clarify the treatment of reserve assets upon an issuer's insolvency. For example, commenters suggested that the rule clarify that reserve assets are held for the benefit of the holders of the issuer's payment stablecoin or that the assets are not assets of the issuer's estate. Another commenter suggested that the OCC rely on its fiduciary rulemaking powers to require that reserve assets be held in a statutory trust or other equivalent legal structure. As discussed in greater detail below, the OCC has made changes in the final rule to accommodate certain structures, including the use of special purpose vehicle (SPV) issuers designed to protect the rights of payment stablecoin holders.
One commenter emphasized that it is appropriate to recognize the United States Federal framework already applicable to foreign banks' United States presence when operationalizing the permitted payment stablecoin framework. Although the International Banking Act of 1978 (
12 U.S.C. 3101
et seq.
) applies to the United States operations of foreign banks, the GENIUS Act includes additional, specific requirements related to foreign issuers of payment stablecoins in the United States.
The OCC is adopting this final rule with certain modifications from the proposal in light of the comments received. At a high level, the final rule makes several changes to the provisions concerning reserve asset management. These changes provide more flexibility to permitted payment stablecoin issuers while still maintaining core liquidity, diversification, and concentration requirements to ensure that permitted payment stablecoin issuers remain sufficiently reserved and capable of meeting redemption requests in a timely manner. The final rule provides additional clarity with respect to a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's permitted activities, redemption requirements, and risk management obligations. It also includes clarifications concerning the OCC's supervision of permitted payment stablecoin issuers, custody, and licensing and registration. In addition, the final rule includes capital and operational backstop requirements that are more detailed than, but consistent with, the proposal. The capital elements have also been simplified relative to the proposal. The final rule, like the proposal, imposes requirements consistent with the GENIUS Act that are tailored to the business model and risk profile of permitted payment stablecoin issuers. For example, as described below, the agency is implementing flexible risk management standards in § 15.13 that scale based on the nature, scope, and risk of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's activities. Consistent with certain comments received on the proposal, the final rule facilitates an approach to supervision that focuses on activities over institution type.
In addition, other regulations beyond those addressed in this rulemaking may need to be updated in light of the passage of the GENIUS Act. For example, the OCC intends to incorporate references to permitted payment stablecoin issuers and foreign payment stablecoin issuers, as appropriate, into
12 CFR part 4
[
10
]
and is considering updates to
12 CFR part 28
.
These implementing regulations will be effective on January 18, 2027.
A. Self-Executing Provisions
The proposal discussed certain self-executing provisions of the GENIUS Act but did not propose rule text for these self-executing provisions.
[
11
]
For example, the Act includes several provisions addressing the applicability of State law to permitted payment stablecoin issuers. Specifically, section 4(b)(1) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(b)(1)
) states that, notwithstanding certain Federal law addressing preemption standards for OCC-regulated institutions,
[
12
]
and certain State laws, a Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuer “shall be licensed, regulated, examined, and supervised exclusively by the Comptroller.” This provision provides the OCC with the exclusive authority to exercise visitorial powers with respect to Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuers, consistent with the agency's authority in
12 U.S.C. 484
.
[
13
]
This exclusivity generally prevents other regulators from subjecting these entities to additional oversight, which can be unduly burdensome, duplicative, or inconsistent.
[
14
]
In addition, based on the exclusivity granted to the OCC, section 4(b) of the Act preempts certain State laws with respect to Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuers.
Section 5(h) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5904(h)
) expressly preempts “any State requirement for a charter, license, or other authorization to do business with respect to a Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuer or [a] subsidiary of an [OCC-regulated] insured depository institution . . . that is approved . . . to be a permitted payment stablecoin issuer.” As a result, these entities are only required to obtain authorization to do business from the OCC, which reduces the complexity that
(
printed page 67003)
would result from requiring these entities to also obtain a charter, license, or other authorization from one or more States.
[
15
]
Finally, section 7(f)(4) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5906(f)(4)
) provides that nothing in the GENIUS Act preempts State consumer protection laws.
[
16
]
Together, these GENIUS Act provisions establish a framework for assessing the applicability of State law to a Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuer or a subsidiary of an OCC-regulated insured depository institution approved to be a permitted payment stablecoin issuer.
[
17
]
The OCC received several comments on these self-executing provisions. Some commenters requested that the OCC more specifically address whether the GENIUS Act preempts licensing requirements in certain circumstances (
e.g.,
when third parties provide services to certain permitted payment stablecoin issuers, when a foreign payment stablecoin issuer is authorized to issue stablecoins in the U.S., or when a Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuer or subsidiary of an OCC-regulated insured depository institution engages in activities other than those addressed in section 4(a)(7)(A) (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(7)(A)
). Commenters also recommended that the OCC state that it has exclusive visitorial powers over subsidiaries of insured national banks that are permitted payment stablecoin issuers, similar to the proposal's statement regarding the OCC's exclusive visitorial powers for Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuers. With respect to State consumer protection laws, commenters had several suggestions, including that the OCC specifically address compliance with applicable State consumer protection laws in its final regulation. Commenters also recommended that the OCC further explain how it will approach certain preemption issues.
After carefully considering the comments received, the OCC determined that the issues raised by commenters do not require regulatory changes, are outside the scope of this rulemaking, or are better evaluated on an individualized basis. The section of the preamble to the proposal discussing these self-executing provisions was intended to provide stakeholders with a general understanding of the GENIUS Act's preemption and visitation framework. Because this framework is self-executing, however, the OCC did not propose any implementing regulation text, nor is it including any in the final rule. While commenters raised several interpretive issues that may warrant clarification at the appropriate time, the OCC has concluded that the agency should retain the flexibility to address such issues as they arise. This will ensure that the OCC's analysis is appropriately informed by, and tailored to, the relevant facts and circumstances. Stakeholders may contact the OCC with questions as they arise, and the OCC will provide additional clarification if appropriate.
[
18
]
Among other self-executing provisions, section 4(g) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(g)
) provides that a Federal savings association established under the Home Owners' Loan Act (
12 U.S.C. 1461
et seq.
) that holds a reserve that satisfies the requirements of section 4(a)(1) of the GENIUS Act shall not be required to satisfy the qualified thrift lender test under section 10(m) of the Home Owners' Loan Act (
12 U.S.C. 1467a(m)
)
[
19
]
with respect to such reserve assets. Because this provision is self-executing, the OCC did not propose regulatory text to implement section 4(g). The OCC received no comments on this aspect of the Act and, consistent with the proposal, is not including any regulatory text to implement section 4(g) of the Act.
II. Description of the Final Rule
The final rule, like the proposal, addresses the majority of the OCC's implementation of the GENIUS Act through new
12 CFR part 15
. In addition, like the proposal, the final rule makes updates to
12 CFR parts 3
(Capital Adequacy Standards), 6 (Prompt Corrective Action), 8 (Assessment of Fees), and 19 (Rules of Practice and Procedure). For each subpart, or substantive subsection, of
12 CFR part 15
, an overview of the changes from the proposed rule to the final rule is provided, followed by a detailed description of the proposed rule, relevant comments, and final rule.
A. Subpart A—Purpose, Scope, Definitions, Severability, and Reservation of Authority
Consistent with the proposal, subpart A of
12 CFR part 15
provides the purpose and scope and defines terms used throughout the final rule.
1. Overview of Changes From Proposed Rule to Final Rule for Subpart A
As described below, the OCC is adopting § 15.1, which provides the scope and purpose of part 15, as proposed.
The OCC is adopting many of the part 15 definitions in § 15.2 as proposed, but several definitions are being added, removed, or changed. The agency is adopting the following definitions as proposed: affiliate, Bank Secrecy Act, control, deposit, digital asset, director, distributed ledger, executive officer, fair value, FDIC, Federal branch, Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuer, Federal Reserve, foreign payment stablecoin issuer, GAAP, immediate family, insider, insured credit union, insured depository institution, monetary value, money, national currency, nonbank entity, OCC, payment stablecoin, permitted payment stablecoin issuer, person, principal shareholder, publicly available information, registered public accounting firm, related interest, reserve asset, Stablecoin Certification Review Committee, State, State payment stablecoin regulator, and subsidiary. The agency is adding to § 15.2 new definitions for business day, payment stablecoin holder, reserve asset value, sensitive customer information, share account, and tokenized form. Additionally, the agency is removing from § 15.2 the definitions of distributed ledger protocol, State-chartered depository institution, and trading volume.
The agency is finalizing the following § 15.2 definitions with differences from the proposed definitions: board of directors, customer, depository institution, eligible financial institution, nonpublic personal information, outstanding issuance value, private key, State qualified payment stablecoin issuer, and United States customer.
As described below, the OCC is adopting § 15.3, providing for the severability of part 15 provisions, as proposed.
(
printed page 67004)
The OCC is adding § 15.4 on the reservation of authority that was not in the proposed rule.
2. Purpose and Scope (§ 15.1)
Proposed § 15.1 set forth the purpose and scope of the stablecoin-related regulations. Paragraph (a) described the purpose, which is to implement the GENIUS Act,
12 U.S.C. 5901
et seq.,
with respect to entities for which the OCC is authorized to issue regulations or exercise its enforcement authority under the Act. These entities were listed in the proposed scope provision in paragraph (b), which provided that proposed part 15 would apply to activities related to payment stablecoins and certain custody activities of (1) national banks and their subsidiaries; (2) Federal savings associations and their subsidiaries; (3) Federal branches and their subsidiaries; (4) foreign payment stablecoin issuers; (5) nonbank entities that seek to be or are approved as Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuers; and (6) State qualified payment stablecoin issuers for whom the OCC has regulatory or enforcement authority pursuant to proposed § 15.15 or § 15.16. Thus, except where otherwise noted, references in part 15 to permitted payment stablecoin issuers would only apply to these types of listed entities despite the broader scope of the term in the GENIUS Act.
As described in the section-by-section analysis below, proposed subparts B and E would apply to permitted payment stablecoin issuers that are subsidiaries of insured national banks, subsidiaries of Federal savings associations, uninsured national banks, Federal branches or subsidiaries thereof, nonbank entities that are not State qualified payment stablecoin issuers, and State qualified payment stablecoin issuers for which the OCC has regulatory or enforcement authority. Proposed subpart C would apply to national banks, Federal savings associations, Federal branches, Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuers, and State qualified payment stablecoin issuers with a total consolidated outstanding issuance value of more than $10 billion subject to supervision and regulation by the OCC that provide custodial or safekeeping services for payment stablecoins, reserve assets, and other “covered assets” (described in detail in subpart C). The application and registration sections in proposed subpart D would apply to insured national banks, Federal savings associations, or Federal branches that seek to issue payment stablecoins through a subsidiary; nonbank entities that seek to be Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuers, uninsured national banks, and uninsured Federal branches that seek to be Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuers; and entities that seek to register as foreign payment stablecoin issuers. The capital requirements detailed in proposed subpart E would apply to subsidiaries of insured national banks, subsidiaries of Federal savings associations, uninsured national banks, Federal branches or subsidiaries thereof, nonbank entities that are not State qualified payment stablecoin issuers, and State qualified payment stablecoin issuers for which the OCC has regulatory authority.
Several commenters sought greater clarity about which entities would become subject to the proposed regulation because of their activities. These commenters were concerned that a broad scoping of stablecoin issuer activities and digital asset service provider activities might result in an overly broad set of entities becoming subject to the OCC's regulations, including entities engaged in blockchain infrastructure, technology-service providers, vendor support function providers, and companies that facilitate businesses' adoption of stablecoin technology. Related to this scope issue, one commenter suggested that the rule should require a standardized certification under Federal oversight for core service providers, which would alter the scope of entities affected by the rule. Several commenters suggested the OCC follow a regulatory approach based on the activity type and not the institution type. Commenters suggested such an approach increases fair competition and decreases the risk of regulatory arbitrage.
The scope of the final rule is consistent with the text of the GENIUS Act and the OCC's jurisdiction. The OCC's part 15 applies to national banks and their subsidiaries, Federal savings associations and their subsidiaries, Federal branches and their subsidiaries, foreign payment stablecoin issuers, nonbank entities that seek to be or are approved as Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuers, and State qualified payment stablecoin issuers over which the OCC has regulatory or enforcement authority. To the extent that an entity falls under one of these categories, it is subject to part 15. Otherwise, the entity is not captured by the rule. Therefore, to the extent a blockchain infrastructure or technology service-provider issues a payment stablecoin and is a type of entity subject to the OCC's jurisdiction, it is covered under part 15. Additionally, entities that are covered custodians as that term is defined in subpart C of part 15 are also subject to part 15. Otherwise, part 15 does not apply.
The OCC received no additional comments concerning proposed § 15.1 and is adopting § 15.1, with one technical change. Paragraph (b)(6) of the proposed rule referred to State qualified payment stablecoin issuers for whom the OCC has regulatory or enforcement authority. The final rule replaces “for whom” with “for which.”

The OCC proposed to define the term “customer” to mean a person that purchases (through any consideration) the products or services of another person. Among other provisions, the definition of “customer” was relevant to certain information protection and notification requirements.
The OCC received several comments addressing the definition of “customer.” Several commenters regarded the proposed definition of “customer” as
(

These commenters generally argued in favor of requiring a contractual relationship between a permitted payment stablecoin issuer and a counterparty for the counterparty to be covered by the definition of customer. The final rule modifies the definition by defining customer (except in the context of the custody provisions, where the term “covered customer” is used) to mean a person that purchases (through any consideration) the products or services of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer or foreign payment stablecoin issuer directly from the issuer or that makes a request directly to the issuer that the issuer convert, redeem, or repurchase a payment stablecoin. This definition focuses on the relationship between the issuer and its direct counterparties. Thus, for example, if a payment stablecoin holder acquired its payment stablecoin from a third-party distributor (including a distributor that is associated with the payment stablecoin, for example, as part of a white-label arrangement) that did not act as agent for the permitted payment stablecoin issuer, the payment stablecoin holder would not be a customer of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer unless and until the holder sought to redeem the payment stablecoin from the permitted payment stablecoin issuer (or otherwise purchased products or services directly from the permitted payment stablecoin issuer).
The OCC believes that this narrower definition is appropriate in light of additional changes, described below, including adopting a definition of “payment stablecoin holder” and clarifying how certain notification requirements in the final rule apply to customers. The OCC believes that these changes will help ensure that the term is neither overly broad nor overly narrow. The OCC believes that this revised definition will result in a set of customers that is easily identifiable by permitted payment stablecoin issuers. This definition does not affect the definition of customer for purposes of other laws and regulations, including privacy laws and the Bank Secrecy Act and its implementing regulations.

The statute uses both terms, and it is appropriate to regard each term as having a separate meaning. Thus, for example, under proposed § 15.11(c) a permitted payment stablecoin issuer could hold reserves as deposits at a national bank regardless of whether the national bank acted as custodian for the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's other reserve assets.
To meet the proposed definition, a financial institution would have also needed to comply with the applicable requirements of section 10 of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5909

The OCC recognized that multiple agencies will regulate permitted payment stablecoin issuers and the entities that may permissibly custody reserve assets. The proposed rule would have imposed requirements on where and how OCC-regulated permitted payment stablecoin issuers may hold reserve assets in § 15.11. Proposed subpart C would have separately imposed the requirements of section 10 of the GENIUS Act (

Accordingly, the proposal acknowledged that there could be overlap between the requirements imposed by different regulators with different requirements implementing section 10 of the GENIUS Act. The OCC invited comment on the best ways to manage potentially overlapping requirements. The proposed rule would have required that an “eligible financial institution” comply with the requirements in section 10(b), (c), and (d) of the GENIUS Act, including applicable implementing regulations. Accordingly, even if different types of eligible financial institutions were subject to different regulations on the safe handling of stablecoin reserve assets, an OCC-regulated permitted payment stablecoin issuer could still custody reserve assets at any entity that met the requirements in the definition of “eligible financial institution.”
The proposed rule would have required a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to enter into a custody agreement with an eligible financial institution, which would have required that the eligible financial institution adhere to the requirements in section 10(b), (c), and (d), along with any applicable implementing regulations. This requirement would have helped ensure that the eligible financial institution knows that it is subject to the requirements of the GENIUS Act and would have provided permitted payment stablecoin issuers a contractual means of enforcing compliance with applicable provisions of the Act.

Rather than updating the list every time a new entity type becomes eligible, the OCC believes that a definition that relates back to the statutory requirements in section 10 (
12 U.S.C. 5909

12 U.S.C. 5909

(

The OCC received a few comments recommending the OCC define “excessive” both for purposes of affiliate transactions and for purposes of relevant capital requirements. The OCC is not adding a definition of “excessive” because the final rule does not use the term. The OCC has revised the provisions of the rule that used the word “excessive” in the proposal to provide additional clarity.
Executive officer.
The OCC proposed a definition for the term “executive officer,” which is used in connection with the proposed application process in § 15.30. Under the proposal, the term “executive officer” would have been defined to mean the president, chairman, chief executive officer, chief operating officer, chief financial officer, chief investment officer, chief risk officer, chief technology officer, and Bank Secrecy Act officer. The term would have included any individual serving in the functional capacity of the listed titles or their equivalent, without regard to title, salary, or compensation. The OCC based the proposed “executive officer” definition on the definition of “Senior executive officer” in
12 CFR 5.51(c)(4)
with certain modifications to conform the language and format to apply to the relevant individuals and entities under this part and to streamline the definition to the positions most likely to be relevant for permitted payment stablecoin issuers. The OCC received no comments addressing the definition of “executive officer.” The OCC is adopting the definition as proposed.
Fair value.
The OCC proposed to include a definition of the term “fair value” in the rule. As proposed, the term “fair value” would mean the fair value as determined under GAAP.
[
28
]
Fair value is used in the definition of “reserve asset value,” which pertains to the reserve asset requirements in § 15.11. The OCC received no comments addressing the definition of “fair value.” The OCC is adopting the definition as proposed.
FDIC.

12 U.S.C. 5901(5)
). The OCC opted not to use the term “Corporation” to describe the FDIC because that term is used more broadly in the definition of person, discussed below. The OCC received no comments addressing the definition of “FDIC.” The OCC is adopting the definition as proposed.

12 U.S.C. 5901(10)
. Specifically, the proposed rule provided that the term “Federal branch” would have the meaning set forth in section 3 of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act (
12 U.S.C. 1813(s)(2)
). The OCC received no comments addressing the definition of “Federal branch.” The OCC is adopting the definition as proposed.
Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuer.
The OCC proposed to define the term “Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuer” consistent with the definition of that term in the GENIUS Act,
12 U.S.C. 5901(11)
, with certain technical and conforming changes. Specifically, the proposed rule defined the term “Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuer” to mean the following entities that are approved by the OCC, pursuant to proposed § 15.30, to issue payment stablecoins: (1) a nonbank entity, other than a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer; (2) an uninsured national bank that is chartered by the OCC, pursuant to title LXII of the Revised Statutes; or (3) a
(
printed page 67010)
Federal branch.
