b. Description of Proposed Rule, Comments, and Final Rule
Enumerated Permissible Activities in § 15.10(a)(1) Through (4): Core Statutory Activities
Consistent with the statute, the OCC proposed to mirror the permitted activities set forth in section 4(a)(7)(A) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(7)(A)
) in proposed § 15.10(a)(1) through (4), which include: (1) issuing payment stablecoins; (2) redeeming payment stablecoins; (3) managing reserves related to the issuance or redemption of payment stablecoins, including purchasing, selling, and holding reserve assets or providing custodial services for reserve assets, consistent with applicable State and Federal law; and (4) providing custodial or safekeeping services for payment stablecoins, required reserves, or private keys of stablecoins consistent with the GENIUS Act, as implemented in proposed subpart C. Additionally, consistent with section 4(a)(7)(A)(v) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(7)(A)(v)
), proposed § 15.10(a)(8) provided that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer may undertake any other activities that directly support any of the activities in proposed § 15.10(a)(1) through (4).
With respect to the activities enumerated in proposed § 15.10(a)(1) through (4) as implementations of section 4(a)(7)(A)(i) through (iv), commenters did not express substantive concerns. Two commenters offered suggestions about how the agency should list or otherwise recognize additional permissible activities, including integration with payment networks and development of compliance tools. One comment suggested the regulation remain narrowly focused such that stablecoin issuers may engage in necessary activities, but any additional activities should be closely connected to stablecoin issuance.
With respect to integration with payment networks and development of compliance tools, without more information, the OCC cannot determine whether such activities are permissible. While these activities might qualify as directly supporting activities pursuant to final § 15.10(a)(11), the OCC would need to assess the facts underlying these activities prior to making such a determination. The OCC invites permitted payment stablecoin issuers to seek clarification from the OCC as to whether a particular activity is permissible. For the list of enumerated permissible activities in § 15.10(a)(1) through (4), the agency declines to focus only on necessary activities and activities closely connected to stablecoin issuance. The commenter's requirement of a close connection to stablecoin issuance alters the statutory test and does not account for activities that are authorized, such as redemption of payment stablecoins, managing related reserves, and providing custodial or safekeeping services. Accordingly, the OCC is adopting § 15.10(a)(1) through (4) as proposed, with a clarifying edit in paragraph (a) to replace the word “only” with “not engage in any activity other than the following:” to make clear that the list of activities in final § 15.10(a) is an exclusive list of activities that permitted payment stablecoin issuers may engage in.
Activities that Directly Support: Proposed § 15.10(a)(8), Renumbered as Final § 15.10(a)(11)
In proposed § 15.10(a)(8), consistent with section 4(a)(7)(A)(v) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(7)(A)(v)
), the OCC included a provision that would have provided that permitted payment stablecoin issuers may undertake any other activities that directly support the issuance of payment stablecoins, redemption of payment stablecoins, managing reserves related to the issuance or redemption of payment stablecoins, or providing custodial or safekeeping services for payment stablecoins. One such example of an activity that would qualify under proposed § 15.10(a)(8) because it directly supports both issuance and redemption of payment stablecoins would be the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's holding of non-payment stablecoin digital assets as principal necessary for testing a distributed ledger, whether internally developed or acquired from a third party. Such an activity may be necessary to ensure that the permitted payment stablecoin issuer may operate safely and effectively on a distributed ledger.
[
42
]
Several commenters suggested the OCC provide additional examples of activities that directly support such activities or otherwise indicate that such activities are broader than what the proposed rule illustrated. Among these commenters, one argued that the above example (holding non-payment stablecoin digital assets as principal for testing a distributed ledger) could imply the agency would limit permissible activities that directly support to those that are necessary. This commenter suggested a broader definition. Various commenters suggested the agency provide specific examples of directly supporting activities, and some commenters offered examples. Such examples included, among other things, the operation of distributed ledger nodes, smart contract deployment, wallet infrastructure and key management, blockchain transaction monitoring, and settlement and liquidity services.
As an alternative to listing examples, one commenter suggested that the agency publish separate interpretive guidance specifically on the scope of proposed § 15.10(a)(8) activities. Several commenters suggested the agency take a narrow understanding of “directly support” in section 4(a)(7)(A)(v) of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(7)(A)(v)
). These commenters suggested a broad interpretation could allow such activities to expand over time or overlap with activities that generally require State licensing. One commenter recommended that activities permissible under the “directly support” prong should only be those that materially facilitate certain other permitted activities or are operationally necessary for those activities.
Congress's use of “directly support” demonstrates the statute does not limit permitted activities to those that are necessary for one of the statute's enumerated activities.
[
43
]
Such a reading would add a substantive limitation—namely, that the activities be strictly necessary—that is absent from the text of the statute. Given the innovation in the payment stablecoin industry, a limitation of “directly support” to what
(
printed page 67020)
is strictly necessary for one current operational model could also stifle innovation. The above example of holding crypto-assets as principal for testing does not necessarily illustrate the outer perimeter of activities that fit under the “directly support” prong; it is only intended to be a clarifying example.
With respect to the examples for which commenters requested clarification, the OCC declines to opine on the permissibility of such activities in the final rule without additional information. The OCC encourages permitted payment stablecoin issuers to seek clarification from the OCC regarding the permissibility of such activities.
One commenter suggested the agency adopt a brand- and technology-neutral interpretation of the Act's “directly support” language. As indicated above, the agency is aware technology and business models may change substantially. To avoid locking industry participants into the current standards that may quickly become outdated and run counter to the Act's goals, the OCC plans to, consistent with its general technology-neutral approach, follow a brand- and technology-neutral understanding of the “directly support” language in the statute and rule.
Some comments combined discussion of the scope of proposed § 15.10(a)(8) permissible activities with discussion of the appropriate risk management practices. One such commenter stated that some of the activities under proposed § 15.10(a)(8) may entail novel risks. Refer to the discussion below on § 15.13 for more about appropriate risk management practices.
One commenter stated that the list of enumerated activities in proposed § 15.10(a) is incomplete and risks being read as an exclusive list. The commenter suggested other activities that should qualify, including the facilitation of independently provided customer rewards and benefits, liquidity management, and interaction with third-party protocols or distributed ledger infrastructure.
Without additional information, the OCC declines to add the facilitation of independently provided customer rewards as an enumerated activity. The OCC expects liquidity management generally to be permissible as an activity that directly supports issuance, redemption, and the management of reserves. With respect to interaction with third-party protocols or distributed ledger infrastructure, without additional information, the OCC cannot categorically determine whether such activities are permissible in the final rule. However, permitted payment stablecoin issuers may seek additional clarity from the OCC to the extent issuers have questions on the permissibility of an activity. With respect to the list in § 15.10(a) being incomplete, the OCC may amend these regulations over time, including the list of enumerated activities.
As discussed in more detail below, in the final rule, the OCC is adopting proposed § 15.10(a)(8), renumbered as § 15.10(a)(11), with a change to explicitly permit the hiring of third parties to engage in certain activities.
Third-Party Investment Advisers, Asset Managers, and Separately Managed Accounts
Several comments spoke to the permissibility of permitted payment stablecoin issuers hiring third-party investment advisers or asset managers of separately managed accounts, where a custodian controls investment decisions within parameters set by the owner. Some commenters stated that separately managed accounts can be an operationally prudent tool because they allow reserve assets to remain legally owned and controlled by the issuer while improving transparency and reducing operational risk. Some of these commenters argued these investment advisers and asset managers would directly support the management of reserves and reserves' liquidity under § 15.10(a)(3) of the proposed rule. Thus, these commenters argued that a stablecoin issuer may hire investment advisers or asset managers under proposed § 15.10(a)(8). One prospective stablecoin issuer asked for confirmation that its particular structure with a third-party reserve manager would be permissible.
The OCC agrees that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer may use an investment adviser or asset manager and may use a separately managed account for reserve assets because such arrangements directly support stablecoin issuance and reserve management. Accordingly, the OCC is clarifying in final § 15.10(a)(11) that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer may undertake any other activities, including the hiring of third parties, that directly support any of the activities described in § 15.10(a)(1) through (a)(4). The hiring of third-party investment advisers or asset managers is an example of an activity that is permissible under § 15.10(a)(11) of the final rule. However, such activities should be designed to ensure compliance with the GENIUS Act,
12 CFR part 15
, and other applicable laws and regulations.
Collateral Trustee Arrangements
A few commenters addressed the topic of collateral trustee arrangements. As explained in the preamble to the proposed rule, a collateral trustee arrangement involves a permitted payment stablecoin issuer granting a first-priority security interest in reserve assets to the collateral trustee for the benefit of stablecoin holders. The proposal asked for comments on whether collateral trustee arrangements would protect the reserve assets.
Many commenters responded that the OCC should expressly permit collateral trustee arrangements used solely for the benefit of stablecoin holders. Several of those commenters stated that the rehypothecation prohibition applies to issuer self-dealing in which issuers exploit reserve assets for their own benefit. Those commenters noted that a collateral trustee arrangement is intended to further the purposes behind the prohibition against rehypothecation, in that it exists to ensure that reserves remain available to back outstanding payment stablecoins, protect stablecoin holders, and promote financial stability. Several commenters supported requirements for permitted payment stablecoin issuers to include disclosures for holders related to a collateral trustee arrangement. Commenters advocated for disclosures involving the identity and regulatory status of the trustee, the nature and scope of the security interest, the circumstances in which the trustee may enforce its rights, and any limitations on the issuer's ability to access or substitute reserve assets. Some commenters also advocated for requirements that issuers obtain express and affirmative consent from holders regarding the collateral trustee structure before purchasing to ensure holders can understand and evaluate the arrangement.
The OCC agrees that permitted payment stablecoin issuers may establish such collateral trustee arrangements. These arrangements may have the benefit of protecting payment stablecoin holders by providing a potential mechanism for administration of the reserve assets prior to bankruptcy or receivership. It is possible that such arrangements can facilitate redemptions more quickly than would occur in insolvency or bankruptcy. The OCC plans to continue to evaluate such arrangements to ensure they are serving their intended purpose of protecting payment stablecoin holders. To the extent it becomes clear that such arrangements add uncertainty or do not adequately protect payment stablecoin holders, the OCC will consider whether
(
printed page 67021)
such arrangements should continue to be permissible.
To effectuate the use of collateral trustee arrangements, the OCC is adding a new § 15.10(a)(9) clarifying that it is permissible for a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to establish a trust arrangement under applicable law for reserve assets, including the granting of a security interest in reserve assets, provided that: (i) any security interest in reserve assets granted to the trustee is for the sole benefit of payment stablecoin holders; (ii) the arrangement with the trustee does not impair the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's ability to timely redeem payment stablecoins in the normal course of business prior to default; (iii) the arrangement does not introduce claims that would compete with the claims of payment stablecoin holders of payment stablecoins issued by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer in the event of the insolvency of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer; and (iv) the arrangement with the trustee does not impair the ability of a receiver of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer to direct the prompt transfer or liquidation of the reserve assets in order to pay claims to payment stablecoin holders.
[
44
]
These conditions are designed to ensure that such arrangements do not compete with the claims of payment stablecoin holders both prior to default as well as following default and that such arrangements are not used to grant security interests on behalf of parties that are not payment stablecoin holders. The OCC is considering whether to issue a separate rulemaking providing further clarity regarding this activity. As part of such a rulemaking, the OCC may consider including additional conditions, such as conditions to clarify the rights that the trust agreement must expressly provide to the receiver of, or bankruptcy trustee for, an insolvent permitted payment stablecoin issuer.
With respect to the payment of the trustee in collateral trustee arrangements, it would be a violation of the condition in § 15.10(a)(9)(i) if the trustee were paid from the proceeds of the reserve asset collateral because the trustee holds a security interest in such collateral.
The OCC declines to require a disclosure regime for collateral trustee arrangements at this time. Mandating a disclosure regime will not be effective at this point as the practice is nascent and the arrangements may vary extensively, such that mandatory disclosure may not capture the important aspects of such arrangements and could lead to customer confusion or a lack of relevant information. The OCC is also not requiring permitted payment stablecoin issuers to obtain express consent from payment stablecoin holders prior to entering into such arrangements. The OCC believes that the conditions set forth in § 15.10(a)(9)(i) through (iii) are designed to protect payment stablecoin holders and obviate the need to require affirmative consent.

12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(7)

With respect to the commenter's suggestion about the inclusion of fees, the OCC does not believe further elucidation of this provision is necessary as it is intended to encompass a broad set of fees. The OCC addresses the assessment of fees in non-payment stablecoin digital assets in more detail below. To the extent an issuer has questions regarding whether a fee structure is permissible, it may reach out to the OCC. With respect to the commenter's concern regarding disclosure of fee arrangements, as discussed below, final § 15.12(e)(1)(iv) requires disclosure of all fees associated with purchasing or redeeming payment stablecoins. 12 U.S.C. 5915(b)

One commenter suggested addressing these examples in the preamble as published guidance. The commenter's suggestion therefore conflates two related but distinct inquiries: whether an activity is permissible for permitted payment stablecoin issuers; and whether and how the permitted payment stablecoin issuer may conduct the activity safely in accordance with the relevant risk management-related requirements.

Managing Foreign Exchange Risk
Several commenters recommended that the OCC recognize that permitted payment stablecoin issuers that issue non-U.S. dollar-denominated stablecoins may engage in foreign exchange risk management as a permitted activity. Some of those commenters characterized the permissible foreign exchange risk management activities as conditional upon or related to the issuance of non-U.S. dollar-denominated stablecoins, while one commenter recommended the OCC allow broader powers related to foreign exchange risk management if the final rule permits non-U.S. dollar-denominated stablecoins and narrower powers if the final rule does not permit non-U.S. dollar-denominated stablecoins. Several commenters distinguished these foreign exchange management activities from purely speculative trading activities, while two such commenters recommended explicit prohibitions on speculative activities and regulatory controls to discourage speculation.
One commenter recommended against rigid supervisory rules or capital add-ons for foreign exchange risk in favor of expectations of safe and sound controls including board-approved risk appetites and independent risk oversight. One commenter recommended that foreign exchange risk management be understood as a tool to meet permitted payment stablecoin issuer reserve and redemption requirements, rather than insulating payment stablecoin holders from fundamental currency risk and recommended that any requirements imposed by the OCC focus on such reserve and redemption requirements rather than rigid limits or capital add-ons that constrain legitimate hedging activities.
The OCC agrees with commenters that engaging in foreign exchange risk management should be a permissible activity. Specifically, the definition of payment stablecoin in section 2(22) of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5901(22)
) specifies that a payment stablecoin is a digital asset that the issuer “is obligated to convert, redeem, or repurchase for a fixed amount of monetary value.” Additionally, under section 2(17) of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5901(17)
), “monetary value” means “a national currency or deposit . . . denominated in a national currency.” These provisions may reasonably be read to indicate that payment stablecoins are not necessarily limited to U.S. dollar-denominated stablecoins because it suggests that issuers may issue payment stablecoins backed by other types of national currencies. However, the list of permissible reserve assets that issuers may hold are generally U.S. dollar- or U.S. government-based reserve assets. Accordingly, to the extent that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer seeks to issue a non-U.S. dollar-denominated payment stablecoin, it could incur substantial foreign exchange risk or else be limited to using a very narrow subset of reserve assets.
Such foreign exchange risk would make it difficult for the issuer to ensure that it is able to meet the requirements of § 15.11 and § 15.13. The OCC therefore believes that managing foreign exchange risk is a permissible activity under managing reserves related to the issuance or redemption of payment stablecoins under § 15.10(a)(3) and is permissible under final § 15.10(a)(11) as an activity that directly supports the activities in § 15.10(a)(1) through (a)(3).
The OCC is providing in new § 15.10(a)(10) of the final rule that permitted payment stablecoin issuers
(
printed page 67024)
may manage foreign exchange risk. However, permitted payment stablecoin issuers that manage foreign exchange risk are subject to the risk management requirements in § 15.13(a)(10) of the final rule. Those requirements impose conditions on foreign exchange risk management such as requiring that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer must not use foreign exchange risk management as a means to speculate, including with respect to the appreciation or depreciation of any national currency.
Other Suggested Activities or Requests for Interpretations
Separate from the specific activities enumerated in proposed § 15.10(a)(1) through (7), several commenters suggested additional activities that should be considered permissible activities. For example, one commenter recommended that the enumerated list include treasury management functions, including short-term investment-optimization among permissible reserve assets subject to diversification and concentration limits. Another commenter recommended that the OCC recognize treasury management activities for reserve asset management within a non-exhaustive list of examples of activities that qualify under proposed § 15.10(a)(8) as directly supporting core activities.
At this time, the agency is not adding treasury management to the list of permissible activities enumerated in § 15.10(a). The OCC notes that aspects of treasury management, including short-term investment optimization, are already included under § 15.10(a)(3), which allows permitted payment stablecoin issuers to manage reserves related to the issuance or redemption of payment stablecoins. Additionally, with respect to treasury management functions that are not encompassed by that provision, such functions may qualify under final § 15.10(a)(11) as activities that directly support the activities in § 15.10(a)(1) through (a)(4).
The OCC declines to specifically add “treasury management” to the enumerated list of activities because that term is not clearly defined and could be read broadly, and therefore, the OCC would need to evaluate the specific treasury management functions a permitted payment stablecoin issuer proposes to engage in to determine whether they are permissible under the final rule. For example, treasury management activities conducted to ensure liquidity to meet payroll demands and to pay business expenses incurred as a result of conducting payment stablecoin activities directly support core permitted payment stablecoin issuer activities and are permissible. The OCC invites permitted payment stablecoin issuers to seek clarification from the OCC as to whether a particular activity is permissible.
One commenter recommended that the OCC add to the enumerated permissible activities list customer onboarding, identity verification and compliance functions reasonably necessary to support permitted payment stablecoin issuer operations. Another commenter recommended that the OCC recognize onboarding processes as an item in a non-exhaustive list of examples of activities that qualify under § 15.10 as directly supporting core activities.
The agency declines to include customer onboarding, identity verification, and compliance functions in the list of permissible activities enumerated in § 15.10(a) at this time. As explained below, § 15.12 provides that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's obligation to redeem does not begin until, among other things, the customer has been successfully onboarded. Accordingly, because the OCC addresses onboarding in § 15.12 of the final rule, the OCC does not believe it needs to specifically include onboarding as an enumerated activity. Permitted payment stablecoin issuers may onboard customers, so long as the onboarding complies with the Act,
12 CFR part 15
, and other applicable laws, including AML/CFT laws and regulations and economic sanctions obligations.
Several commenters recommended the OCC add various specific interpretations to the final rule. One commenter recommended that the OCC clarify whether non-hosted or external wallets are permissible for a permitted payment stablecoin issuer and to set clear boundaries to keep payment control within regulated entities. Another commenter recommended that the OCC prohibit regulated entities from hosting or transacting with self-custody wallets due to money laundering concerns.
[
50
]
The Act does not specifically prohibit self-custody or non-hosted wallets. The OCC declines to explicitly prohibit the use of such wallets by permitted payment stablecoin issuers but notes that the use of such wallets must comply with the requirements of the Act,
12 CFR part 15
, and other applicable laws. For example, permitted payment stablecoin issuers that use such wallets still must comply with section 4(a)(6) of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(6)
), which provides that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer may issue payment stablecoins only if the issuer has the technological capability to comply, and will comply, with the terms of any lawful order. Additionally, permitted payment stablecoin issuers must comply with all applicable AML/CFT laws and regulations and economic sanctions obligations.
One commenter recommended that the OCC require permitted payment stablecoin issuers to use a formally defined wallet credential state machine describing the status of the wallet, explicit permitted and prohibited transactions, cryptographic wallet binding, compliance-gated activation preconditions, automatic cascading orders to force wallet compliance and freezing, and regulated credential expiration.
The OCC declines to mandate particular technical requirements for permitted payment stablecoin issuers that are not required under the Act, consistent with
12 CFR part 15
's generally technology-neutral approach. The OCC will not mandate the specific technical requirements in light of the continued evolution of the stablecoin industry and the likelihood that any technical requirements may become obsolete and potentially stifle innovation. However, the final rule in § 15.13 contains risk management requirements, including those related to information technology and security, which could implicate some of the commenter's suggestions. The OCC will continue to assess permitted payment stablecoin issuers' compliance with such risk management requirements against the potential risks posed to issuers throughout the supervisory process.

Two commenters recommended that the OCC explicitly codify that payment stablecoin holders are not eligible for deposit insurance, including on a pass-through basis. One commenter noted that this clarification would prevent issuers from implying “insured-like” status that could foster false confidence and increase run risk.

The OCC declines to opine on pass-through insurance in this rulemaking as that topic is subject to the FDIC's notice of proposed rulemaking that has not yet been finalized.

Yield
Consistent with section 4(a)(11) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(11)
), proposed § 15.10(c)(4) provided that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer must not pay the holder of any payment stablecoin any form of interest or yield (whether in cash, tokens, or other consideration) solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of such payment stablecoin. The OCC noted that issuers might attempt to make prohibited payments of interest or yield to payment stablecoin holders through arrangements with third parties. The OCC also noted that there would likely be a large and changing variety of arrangements with third parties in which issuers could achieve the payment of yield to payment stablecoin holders. The OCC stated that it would not be possible to identify in detail all, or even most, of the potential arrangements between permitted payment stablecoin issuers and third parties that the OCC may prohibit under section 4(a)(11) of the GENIUS Act and the OCC's rulemaking authority under section 4(h) of the GENIUS Act,

53
]
particularly as such arrangements may evolve over time. On the other hand, the OCC noted that a rule with only a general prohibition on the payment of yield could create uncertainty within the payment stablecoin market.
The OCC therefore proposed to include a presumption in paragraph (c)(4)(i) that certain types of arrangements with certain types of persons would be prohibited payments of yield or interest by the issuer. Specifically, the OCC would have presumed that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer is paying the holder of any payment stablecoin any form of interest or yield (whether in cash, tokens, or other consideration) solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of such payment stablecoin if: (A) the permitted payment stablecoin issuer has a contract, agreement, or other arrangement with an affiliate or a related third party to pay interest or yield to the affiliate or related third party; and (B) the affiliate

or related third party (or affiliate of such related third party) has a contract, agreement, or other arrangement to pay interest or yield (whether in cash, tokens, or other consideration) to a holder of any payment stablecoin issued by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of such payment stablecoin. To the extent that the person, or an affiliate of the person with whom the permitted payment stablecoin issuer had a contract, agreement, or other arrangement to pay interest or yield was a related third party of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer because the permitted payment stablecoin issuer issues payment stablecoins on the related third party's behalf or under the related third party's branding, the arrangement between the related third party and the holder of the payment stablecoin would have considered the holder of the payment stablecoin to be the holder of the payment stablecoin issued by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer on the related third party's behalf or under the related third party's branding. With respect to a white-label relationship, the rebuttable presumption would have been triggered only to the extent the payment stablecoin holder was a holder of the related third party's white-labeled stablecoin (as opposed to other payment stablecoins issued by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer).
Related third parties were defined to include any person offering to pay interest or yield to payment stablecoin holders as a service (
i.e.,
on behalf of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer) and any person that the issuer issues payment stablecoins on behalf of or under the branding of (
i.e.,
persons that have entered into a white-label relationship with the issuer).

The OCC received many comments concerning the prohibition against a permitted payment stablecoin issuer or foreign payment stablecoin issuer paying the holder of any payment stablecoin any form of interest or yield (whether in cash, tokens, or other consideration) solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of such payment stablecoin (“the yield prohibition”). As discussed in greater detail below, after reviewing the comments, the OCC has determined to eliminate the rebuttable presumption from the final rule.
Commenters held diverging views on the proposal's implementation of the yield prohibition and associated rebuttable presumption. Many advocated eliminating the rebuttable presumption. A large number advocated interpreting the yield prohibition narrowly and not applying the prohibition or associated rebuttable presumption to certain indirect payments, to payments based on transactions, or to payments to intermediaries (rather than payment stablecoin holders) made not solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of a payment stablecoin. On the other hand, a substantial number of commenters advocated for a broadly applicable yield prohibition that captured indirect payments, transaction-based payments, and payments where holding, using, or retaining a payment stablecoin was a necessary condition of receiving payment. Many of these commenters advocated expanding the scope of the rebuttable presumption. Additional detail on these comments and other comments received is below.
Several commenters stated that the statutory yield prohibition is not yet settled, noting ongoing legislation that could interact with the GENIUS Act's prohibition. Unless and until such legislation passes, the OCC must implement the GENIUS Act's yield prohibition, as enacted. If the GENIUS Act is amended, or legislation that clearly relates to the GENIUS Act's yield prohibition passes, the OCC will evaluate whether any amendments to the final rule are necessary and appropriate to give effect to such legislation.
A few commenters advocated eliminating the yield prohibition from the final rule altogether. One commenter advocated allowing issuers to peg payment stablecoins to a fixed amount of purchasing power, arguing that doing so would not amount to paying any form of interest or yield (whether in cash, tokens, or other consideration).
Eliminating the prohibition would be inconsistent with the requirements of section 4(a)(11) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(11)
), and the definition of payment stablecoin in section 2(22) of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5901(22)
), which hinges on an issuer being obligated to convert, redeem, or repurchase a payment stablecoin for a fixed amount of monetary value (rather than a fixed amount of purchasing power). The OCC therefore is not revising the rule in response to these comments.
One commenter requested that the OCC confirm that the yield prohibition does not capture interest paid on deposits, including tokenized deposits. The OCC confirms that the GENIUS Act's yield prohibition does not apply to deposits. The definition of payment stablecoin in section 2(22) of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5901(22)
) explicitly excludes deposits, regardless of whether the deposit is recorded using distributed ledger technology. Because the yield prohibition in section 4(a)(11) of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(11)
) applies to holders of payment stablecoins solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of payment stablecoins, the prohibition does not extend to paying interest on deposits, including deposits in tokenized form.
Several commenters stated that the proposed yield prohibition and associated rebuttable presumption were too broad and exceeded the OCC's authority. One stated that the rebuttable presumption could raise issues under the major questions doctrine. One commenter stated that disclosures revealing the economic substance of arrangements between issuers, affiliates, and third parties would be more effective than the rebuttable presumption. Commenters also stated that the rebuttable presumption would invert the burden of proof, chill competition, and discriminate against savers in favor of borrowers. Commenters stated that the statutory prohibition applies to permitted payment stablecoin issuers and foreign payment stablecoin issuers and does not speak to payments from other entities or payments made by other persons in the secondary market. Several of these commenters noted that, unlike the prohibition against pledging, rehypothecating, or reusing reserve assets in section 4(a)(2) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(2)
), the prohibition in section 4(a)(11) of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(11)
) does not contain language explicitly prohibiting a permitted payment stablecoin issuer or foreign payment stablecoin issuer from
indirectly
engaging in activities that are proscribed for the issuer.
Many of these commenters stated that the yield prohibition was intensely debated by Congress and that the final text of the Act reflects a considered decision not to prohibit indirect payments. Some of these commenters argued that any indirect payments should be permitted while others took a narrower view, arguing that payments made at the direction of, or on behalf of, the issuer should be prohibited while payments made by third parties that are not controlled by, or made pursuant to an agreement with, the issuer should be permitted. Some commenters stated that independently funded rewards paid by affiliates or third parties should be permitted under certain circumstances.

]
Many of the commenters that advocated for a narrow prohibition stated that the OCC could not use its anti-evasion authority under section 4(h)(1) of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(h)(1)
) to adopt a rebuttable presumption. These commenters argued that, since the statutory prohibition does not apply to indirect payments, some or all indirect payments should not be considered evasion. These commenters stated that the anti-evasion provisions of the Act should capture bad-faith arrangements, including arrangements where an issuer actually directs a third party to make a payment on the issuer's behalf.

Some commenters also stated that the anti-evasion language appears in section 4(h)(1) of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(h)(1)
) and should be read to prevent the evasion of section 4's (
12 U.S.C. 5903

12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(11)
) yield prohibition.
With respect to this last point, section 4(h)(1) of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(h)(1)
) states that “the primary Federal
(
printed page 67027)
payment stablecoin regulators shall . . . issue such regulations relating to permitted payment stablecoin issuers as may be necessary to establish a payment stablecoin regulatory framework necessary to administer and carry out the requirements of this section [(section 4)], including to establish conditions, and to prevent evasion thereof.” The yield prohibition in section 4(a)(11) (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(11)

Although the OCC is eliminating the rebuttable presumption from the final rule, the OCC emphasizes that the OCC retains its authority to address evasion of section 4 of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903
), including the yield prohibition.
Many commenters advocated a broad prohibition that would capture indirect payments as well as direct payments. Some of these commenters advocated capturing additional types of transactions through the rebuttable presumption, including transactions involving indirect payments through persons with whom the issuer has a financial interest, contractual relationship, or business arrangement. Others advocated for a flat prohibition on direct and indirect payments, rather than employing a rebuttable presumption. These commenters stated that preventative measures, such as a broad prohibition, would be preferable to reactive measures, like the rebuttable presumption. Several of these commenters characterized indirect payments as a loophole that must be closed, either by regulatory action or Congressional action.
Many of the commenters favoring a broad prohibition stated that permitting indirect payments could lead to deposit flight that would disproportionately affect community banks and reduce lending. One commenter stated that clear and enforceable treatment of the yield prohibition could reduce uncertainty around asset-liability dynamics and help preserve the intended protection provided by 1 to 1 reserve backing and the timely redemption obligation.
The statutory yield prohibition can capture certain payments that commenters characterized as indirect payments. A person may pay another person through someone else and thus be within the scope of the yield prohibition. For example, interest or yield payments to payment stablecoin holders made by an agent of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer or foreign payment stablecoin issuer on the issuer's behalf solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of a payment stablecoin would be within the scope of the prohibition. In these instances, the agent acts for the issuer. The issuer pays interest or yield to a payment stablecoin holder. Even if the issuer were not considered to be the payor, it would clearly evade the statutory prohibition on yield for an issuer to merely pay another entity to make an interest or yield payment that the issuer could not make directly. As discussed below, other scenarios may present closer questions. For example, indirect payments that are not made solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of a payment stablecoin are outside the scope of the prohibition by the Act's own terms. Depending on the facts and circumstances, a payment to payment stablecoin holders through an intermediary might be made solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of a payment stablecoin or might be made, at least in part, for other reasons.
One commenter stated that issuers should be permitted to pass yield from reserves through to institutional payment stablecoin holders but not to retail payment stablecoin holders. The GENIUS Act does not distinguish between retail and institutional payment stablecoin holders. Accordingly, the final rule applies the yield prohibition equally to payments by an issuer to institutional and retail payment stablecoin holders. One commenter requested that the OCC provide a cure period for violations of the yield prohibition. The final rule does not include such a cure period but, as discussed below, does not include the rebuttable presumption. The OCC will exercise its enforcement discretion appropriately, based on the given facts and circumstances.
Commenters requested clarification about the various prongs of the rebuttable presumption, the process for rebutting the presumption (including standardized rebuttal language), and the particular wording of the presumption (
e.g.,
the definition of “related third party”). Commenters also requested a list of illustrative examples of arrangements that would not violate the prohibition. Because the final rule does not include the rebuttable presumption, the OCC is not further clarifying the terms of the presumption or the process for rebuttal. In response to requests for examples of activities that would violate or be permitted under the yield prohibition or that would be captured by the presumption or constitute evasion, the OCC is not including a list of prohibited or permitted arrangements. Rather, the OCC will apply the language of the statute to the facts and circumstances of any particular arrangement so that any such arrangement can be evaluated based on all relevant facts and circumstances.
Commenters addressed a number of potential safe harbors or exclusions for certain activities. Some commenters stated that there should be a de minimis exemption for small payments or incidental payments that do not scale with the amount of payment stablecoins held by the payee. These commenters stated that such small payments pose no credible risk of evasion of the GENIUS Act and that subjecting these small payments to the rebuttable presumption would impose disproportionate burdens. Other commenters disagreed, stating that such a safe harbor or exclusion would be unnecessary and unsupported by the statute. The OCC is not adopting a safe harbor for de minimis payments because the statutory yield prohibition, by its terms, does not contemplate an exemption for such payments.
Some commenters argued that the GENIUS Act was not intended to prohibit existing rewards programs and that rewards programs that were in existence as of the enactment of the GENIUS Act should be excluded from the statutory yield prohibition. Many commenters argued for an explicit safe harbor for these indirect payments or for excluding them from the scope of the rebuttable presumption. The OCC declines to presume that rewards programs that predated the GENIUS Act comply with the GENIUS Act. The fact that Congress may have had notice of these rewards programs does not necessarily imply that Congress endorsed them as permissible. Indeed, Congress could have provided a safe harbor for such programs but did not do so. Accordingly, rewards programs that predate the enactment of the GENIUS Act will be evaluated the same as rewards programs that are established after the enactment or effective date of the GENIUS Act.
Many commenters argued that the prohibition and associated rebuttable presumption should not capture payments that the issuer does not control and that are not funded directly by the issuer. Commenters requested specific exclusions or safe harbors for fiduciary income earned by trust entities, certain DeFi arrangements, payments in connection with the promotion or distribution of payment stablecoins, rewards from staking, and interest from lending. Several commenters advocated for specific exclusions or safe harbors for various types of white-label arrangements. Commenters also requested exclusions
(
printed page 67028)
or safe harbors for certain arrangements subject to Federal securities laws, customer loyalty or rewards programs structured in good faith, and payments for services (including compliance, technological, operational, marketing, or distributional services).
In response to comments, the OCC has not provided a general safe harbor. With respect to DeFi arrangements, the facts of each DeFi arrangement may bear significantly on whether such an arrangement is entered into to evade the yield prohibition. The OCC is also not adopting an explicit safe harbor for payments made for services. Absent additional facts to the contrary, payments for bona fide services generally would not be prohibited because such payments generally are not interest or yield paid solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of a payment stablecoin.
The OCC also has not adopted a safe harbor for arrangements subject to the Federal securities laws. Although payment stablecoins are excluded from the definition of security, an arrangement where an issuer pays interest or yield solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of payment stablecoins could be a security, depending on the facts and circumstances. The statute does not provide a clear safe harbor from the yield prohibition for securities. Accordingly, the OCC declines to adopt a safe harbor for arrangements that are securities.
The OCC also is not adopting a safe harbor for white-label partners. Payments to and from white-label partners may be more likely to be made on behalf of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer or foreign payment stablecoin issuer than other types of payments. Accordingly, the OCC believes that a broadly applicable safe harbor would be inappropriate.
Many commenters stated that the key terms used in the prohibition and associated rebuttable presumption must be defined or clarified. Some argued that failing to include definitions for these terms violated the OCC's notice-and-comment obligations under the Administrative Procedure Act. Others stated that the terms were sufficiently clear and did not require further definition. As discussed below, the OCC has decided not to include additional regulation text defining certain terms used in the yield prohibition, with the exception of the term “payment stablecoin holder,” discussed elsewhere. The OCC believes that it is not necessary to do so and that including definitions for certain terms could encourage the adoption of arrangements that are intended to evade the prohibition.
A large number of commenters stated that “interest” and “yield” should be defined. Several commenters favoring a broad yield prohibition stated that these terms should be interpreted broadly. Commenters noted that the prohibition in section 4(a)(11) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(11)
) applies to the payment of “any form of interest or yield, whether in cash, tokens, or other consideration” and stated that this language suggests that the terms “interest” and “yield” should be interpreted broadly. Several commenters stated that “interest” should include all scenarios where an issuer provides economic value to a partner or affiliate who then delivers yield-like benefits to payment stablecoin holders. Many commenters stated that the definitions of “interest” and “yield” should hinge on economic substance and not on how the term is labeled (
e.g.,
as rewards). Many commenters stated that interest should be defined to mean economic benefits that scale with the amount of payment stablecoins that a stablecoin holder holds or the duration that the stablecoin holder holds the payment stablecoins. Some commenters stated that the terms interest and yield should include payments by an issuer based on the passive holding of a payment stablecoin. Some commenters noted that interest has long been interpreted to refer to a wide range of types of compensation and that the Supreme Court has rejected the notion that interest must be time- or rate-based. Commenters stated that, since the GENIUS Act prohibits yield, in addition to interest, the OCC should interpret the prohibition broadly.
Several commenters stated that a broad definition of interest and yield, as part of a broad prohibition, would help maintain the distinction between payment instruments, like payment stablecoins, and investment instruments. In contrast, many commenters that favored a narrow yield prohibition advocated excluding certain types of payments from the definitions of interest and yield. One stated that the OCC should not prohibit arrangements that are the economic equivalent of paying any form of interest or yield (whether in cash, tokens, or other consideration), arguing that, if the OCC commits to regulating economic equivalents, rather than statutory categories, there is no principled stopping point. The OCC disagrees. Interest and yield are broad terms under their generally understood meanings. Interest does not stop being interest merely because it is given a different name. An approach that looked to labels rather than economic substance would render the yield prohibition meaningless.
Other commenters requested carveouts (either from the definition of interest or yield, the scope of the prohibition, or through the implementation of a safe harbor) for certain commercial transactions, fee waivers, promotional or loyalty payments, merchant discounts and rebates (subject to certain requirements), white-label profit sharing, and transaction-based payments. Many of these comments focused on the idea that transaction-based rewards should not be considered interest or yield. Commenters disagreed as to whether customer rewards should be included within the definition and thus be subject to the yield prohibition. Commenters advocating a broad yield prohibition stated that rewards programs could act as an evasion of the prohibition, rewards would blur the line between payment and investment instruments, and excluding rewards from the scope of the prohibition could negatively impact competition between highly regulated banks and less regulated entities. Others stated that certain types of rewards (
e.g.,
transaction-based rewards or independently funded third-party rewards, discussed above) should not be considered interest or yield.
After considering the comments received, the OCC has decided not to define the terms “interest” or “yield.” The OCC will apply principles of statutory interpretation to the terms in light of the facts and circumstances before it. The OCC therefore declines to adopt a definition of these terms.
Several commenters stated that “pay” should be interpreted broadly and that the OCC should look to the economic substance of a transaction to determine whether a payment has occurred. In contrast, in the context of the rebuttable presumption, one commenter said that the OCC should not interpret the term to capture any transfer of economic value, arguing that doing so would expand the OCC's authority and would cover general commercial relationships. The OCC is not defining the term in the final rule. The OCC will apply principles of statutory interpretation to the term “pay” in light of the facts and circumstances before it. Commenters had diverging views on whether and how to define “holding,” “use,” and “retention” for the purpose of implementing the statutory yield prohibition. Many commenters advocated for excluding transactional activities from the scope of “use”
(
printed page 67029)
altogether, stating that the prohibition should apply to passive holding of payment stablecoins rather than active use of payment stablecoins. These commenters argued that the use of the terms “interest” and “yield” suggest that the prohibition applies to passive holdings and that the word “use” is intended merely to ensure that an issuer cannot evade the prohibition by mislabeling payments for passive holdings. Several commenters requested that the OCC clarify that “use” refers to bona fide customer-facing activity rather than ministerial issuance, redemption, settlement, or internal asset-transfer functions. Other commenters stated that the terms should be read broadly, such that payments that are conditioned on holding, using, or retaining a stablecoin are captured.
The statutory yield prohibition applies to payments of interest or yield solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of a payment stablecoin. Thus, the statute contemplates that certain payments made in connection with the use of a payment stablecoin may be prohibited. Specifically, a payment would need to (a) be interest or yield and (b) be made solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of a payment stablecoin to be within the scope of the prohibition. Transaction-based payments that did not amount to interest or yield or that were not made solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of a payment stablecoin would not be prohibited. Whether a transaction-based payment meets those criteria is a fact-specific inquiry, and the OCC will address the facts presented by particular arrangements as they arise.
Commenters had diverging views as to the meaning of the term “solely” in the yield prohibition. Several commenters stated that the term must remain in the prohibition, should be included in the rebuttable presumption, if retained, and should be given the effect of excluding payments made even in part based on factors other than the holding, use, or retention of payment stablecoins. Commenters stated, for example, that payments made for commercial purposes, including marketing payments, payments for liquidity provision, and the posting of collateral should be outside the scope of the prohibition because they are not made solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of a payment stablecoin. Commenters also stated that payments made in connection with serving as a node, validating transactions, and staking are not made solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of payment stablecoins. Some commenters stated that giving effect to the term “solely” would help distinguish payment instruments and investment products.
A large number of other commenters stated that the term “solely” should be read narrowly to prevent evasion of the yield prohibition. These commenters emphasized that the term should be read in the broader context of the prohibition, which prohibits a permitted payment stablecoin issuer or foreign payment stablecoin issuer from paying any form of interest or yield (whether in cash, tokens, or other consideration) solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of such payment stablecoin. Some commenters stated that the yield prohibition should capture the transfer of economic benefit to a payment stablecoin holder unless the person providing the benefit can demonstrate by clear and convincing evidence that the purpose of the payment is for a substantial business purpose other than incentivizing, or otherwise making payments in connection with, the holding, use, or retention of a payment stablecoin. Similarly, another commenter stated that an economic benefit provided to a holder or user of a payment stablecoin should be presumed to be provided solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of that stablecoin if holding, using, or retaining the stablecoin is a necessary condition to receiving the benefit or is the reason the benefit is provided.
The word “solely” in the statutory yield prohibition is best read under its plain terms to exclude payments made in connection with reasons other than holding, using, or retaining a payment stablecoin. Thus, payments made for other purposes are not barred by the GENIUS Act. To the extent that there are concerns that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer pays interest or yield only nominally for another purpose in an attempt to evade the statute, the OCC will look to the substance of the transaction to determine whether the permitted payment stablecoin issuer was truly paying solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of a payment stablecoin or whether the transaction was structured for the purpose of evading the yield prohibition.
Commenters had widely varying views on the economic impact of the yield prohibition. A large number of commenters stated that the economic impact of a prohibition that allowed for indirect payments would be significant. These commenters stated that the promise of interest- or yield-bearing payment stablecoins could divert funds away from bank deposits (particularly at community banks) and diminish lending and the provision of financial services and investments within communities. Several of these commenters noted that community banks are important sources of loans, particularly for smaller communities and for farmers. These commenters stated that the scale of deposit flight would depend on the strength of the yield prohibition and the growth of the payment stablecoin industry. Specific estimates varied, but many of these commenters cited to reports that deposits could be reduced by trillions of dollars and that lending could decrease by hundreds of billions of dollars, with certain States being more impacted than others.
[
57
]
Several commenters favoring a narrow prohibition criticized these estimates, including by arguing that some of these estimates represented advocacy, rather than research, stating that some of the estimates were inconsistent with past statements of the organizations that produced the estimates, and by questioning the applicability of the assumptions or models used to create these estimates. Many of these commenters stated that deposits would likely be recycled back into community banks in the form of reserve assets. A number of commenters favoring a broad prohibition disagreed, stating that reserve assets would likely be concentrated in large financial institutions (as opposed to in community banks) and that deposits held as reserves would be wholesale deposits, rather than retail deposits. These commenters stated that wholesale deposits serving as reserve assets would be less able to support credit creation than retail deposits.
A large number of commenters favoring a narrow prohibition stated that the economic impact of permitting third parties to pay interest or yield on payment stablecoins was likely to be insignificant. Many of these expressed skepticism that widespread adoption of
(
printed page 67030)
payment stablecoins, including yield-bearing payment stablecoins, would lead to widespread deposit flight. One commenter noted that the introduction of money market mutual funds did not lead to widespread deposit flight. This commenter argued that competition between bank deposits and payment stablecoins may affect bank profits but would not necessarily affect credit creation. Many commenters cited to a report by the White House Council of Economic Advisers (CEA Report) concluding that a yield prohibition would have relatively little impact on deposits or lending but would cause consumers to forgo the benefits of competitive returns on stablecoin holdings.
[
58
]
Commenters favoring a broad prohibition criticized the conclusions of the CEA Report and reports reaching similar findings, stating that these reports were based on flawed assumptions and addressed the wrong question (
i.e.,
the policy concern is not whether prohibiting yield on payment stablecoins would constrain bank lending; rather, it is whether allowing yield on payment stablecoins would encourage deposit flight, especially from community banks, raise funding costs, and reduce local credit availability). Commenters favoring a narrow prohibition also stated that a broad prohibition could stifle competition and innovation, distort markets, exacerbate concentration risks, and make stablecoin activity more likely to migrate outside of the United States financial system. Some commenters also stated that the threat to community bank deposits does not arise from payment stablecoins but rather from concentration among global systemically important banks.
A small number of commenters stated that the economic impact of a broad or narrow prohibition is uncertain. Of these, some advocated delaying finalization of certain aspects of the rule until after completing a study on the impact of stablecoin adoption on deposits. One commenter stated that the OCC has indicated that it will monitor for deposit flight but has not stated how it would address deposit flight. One commenter stated that the OCC should clearly articulate any concerns about the similarities between payment stablecoins and deposits, so that commenters could provide meaningful input.
Congress created a new regulatory framework through the GENIUS Act, and the payment stablecoin and banking industries may change as a result of this new framework. The scale and character of these changes may depend substantially on market developments, customer demand, and implementation of the GENIUS Act. For example, any estimate as to the impact of payment stablecoins on bank deposits or on the broader economy will depend, in part, on how much the payment stablecoin industry grows, where issuers hold their deposits, and whether those deposits are stable. While the OCC can estimate the economic impacts of the rule, there is necessarily a degree of uncertainty with respect to key variables. The OCC intends to monitor the impacts of the final rule as well as developments in the market. The OCC may consider revising the final rule, to the extent necessary and to the extent consistent with the text and purpose of the GENIUS Act.
After carefully considering the comments concerning the yield prohibition, the OCC has eliminated the rebuttable presumption from the final rule. Because payment stablecoins are a nascent market, the OCC does not believe that it is appropriate to impose a rebuttable presumption with respect to the yield prohibition at this time. The rebuttable presumption could have been both overinclusive and underinclusive, capturing permissible arrangements that would have been subject to the rebuttable presumption and allowing the inference that impermissible arrangements not triggering the presumption are consistent with the yield prohibition. Requiring such arrangements to go through the rebuttal process risks imposing burden without a commensurate benefit.
Instead of finalizing the proposed rebuttable presumption or otherwise providing guidance on the types of potentially prohibited transactions, the OCC will initially monitor arrangements with permitted payment stablecoin issuers and foreign payment stablecoin issuers as part of its review of issuers' applications and ongoing supervision of such entities. Where it identifies transactions that violate or evade the yield prohibition, the OCC will take action and provide the public with additional guidance regarding such actions and interpretations, as appropriate. As the payment stablecoin market develops, the OCC anticipates that it will gain sufficient experience with identifying prohibited transactions to allow it to propose a rulemaking clarifying the yield prohibition that does not have the disadvantages noted above.
Prohibition on Rehypothecation
Proposed § 15.10(c)(5) included the language from section 4(a)(2) of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(2)
) that prohibits permitted payment stablecoin issuers from pledging, rehypothecating, or reusing any reserve assets required under
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)
, except for the purposes listed in section 4(a)(2) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(2)

The OCC anticipates that these implementing regulations will be updated, as necessary, in the years following the effective date of the Act as the business practices of issuers continue to evolve and develop.

As a result, the agency is not defining a timeframe for responses at this time, but the OCC may revisit this matter in the future as it reviews requests and the industry develops.

One such commenter stated that white-label arrangements create risks such as obscuring actual reserves and implicit step-in risk for the sponsoring institution to prop up a distressed permitted payment stablecoin issuer. Another commenter mentioned potential de-pegging, run, and contagion risks and noted that appropriate reserve allocation does not necessarily protect against issues related to cyberattacks and money laundering.
Many commenters opposed a requirement that would only allow a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to issue one brand of payment stablecoin. Commenters stated several reasons for their opposition to this requirement, including that requiring a separate affiliate to issue a different brand of payment stablecoin would create additional regulatory burden, make white-labeling economically unviable for all but the largest partners, and add complexity without a corresponding benefit. One commenter stated that costs of a one-brand requirement were not considered in the proposal's economic analysis. One commenter stated that the OCC did not identify evidence that a single brand restriction would meaningfully reduce risk and that it was not adequately explained, arguing that it would be arbitrary and capricious for the OCC to include such a limitation. Another commenter stated that a single brand restriction would impose asymmetric costs on nonbank fintech issuers, for which the white-label distribution model is a primary mechanism of market adoption. One commenter stated that the final rule should clarify that the supervisory focus is on the issuer and not on the branding.
Some commenters also suggested that a single brand requirement was not consistent with the GENIUS Act. Commenters stated that the term “outstanding issuance value” and Congress's use of the term “consolidated total outstanding issuance” suggests that Congress did not intend to require product or brand-level segregation of reserves. A few commenters stated that language in section 5(g) of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5904(g)
) provides that regulators “may not impose requirements in addition to the requirements specified under section 4,” which militates against a single brand restriction. One commenter suggested that any insolvency concerns are better addressed by the statutory provisions of the GENIUS Act. A different commenter stated that even if a one-brand model were adopted, it would not be clear that a bankruptcy court would respect the separate structure because the court could potentially consolidate the assets and liabilities of affiliates.
A few commenters acknowledged that a run on payment stablecoin reserves could be a concern in the event a single permitted payment stablecoin issuer issues multiple brands of payment stablecoins but suggested that a single brand restriction was a disproportionate response. Another commenter stated that in times of stress, payment stablecoin holders are unlikely to parse legal entity structures or differentiate between affiliated issuing entities.
The OCC is not implementing a one-brand-per-issuer requirement. While the OCC agrees with certain commenters that such a requirement could help mitigate contagion risks and protect the rights of payment stablecoin holders in the event of insolvency, the OCC acknowledges that such a restriction would also impose burden and is not clearly mandated by the statute. By not implementing such a requirement, the OCC is being responsive to the vast majority of commenters that stated that such a requirement would increase regulatory burden on permitted payment stablecoin issuers. The OCC understands commenters' concerns that a categorical one-brand restriction could lead to duplication of supervisory obligations and could potentially make it harder for smaller issuers to issue multiple brands of payment stablecoins.
While the OCC is not mandating a one-brand-per-issuer requirement, a one-brand-per-issuer structure may better protect the rights of payment stablecoin holders than other models as discussed in more detail below. Accordingly, the final rule accommodates business models that employ multiple SPV issuers and reduces the burden of using such business models, including by making certain technical changes. For example, while each SPV would require a license to operate as a permitted payment stablecoin issuer, the OCC anticipates that the burden of seeking out a new license for an SPV will be limited compared to seeking or receiving the initial license, as the applicant could leverage information contained in previous applications for other related SPVs. Similarly, an SPV could rely on a risk management framework developed by its parent entity, provided that the framework met the requirements of § 15.13.
Many commenters suggested potential alternatives to a single brand restriction, including that the OCC could require potential disclosures to ensure transparency with respect to branding. Specifically, one commenter stated that such disclosures should capture same-branded issuance across affiliates. One commenter suggested a monthly reserve composition disclosure, examined by a registered public accounting firm and that includes: (i) the par value of outstanding stablecoins of that brand; (ii) the composition of reserve assets attributable to that brand; (iii) the legal segregation mechanism applicable to that brand's reserves; (iv) operational controls preventing cross-brand encumbrance; and (v) the holder claim priority rules applicable in the event of issuer distress. Another commenter recommended that the OCC require disclosure of the legal identity of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer that is behind each brand. One commenter mentioned that the disclosures should be prominent to payment stablecoin purchasers and holders and explain which permitted payment stablecoin issuer is responsible for reserves, redemption, and regulatory compliance. The same commenter also stated that issuers should disclose whether the co-branded payment stablecoins are backed by the same reserve pool, the aggregate outstanding issuance across all brands backed by that pool, and the co-branding arrangements in the issuer's regulatory filings and reserve disclosures.
The OCC is not adopting additional disclosure requirements with respect to branding. The final rule, in § 15.11(e), requires that permitted payment stablecoin issuers publish a monthly composition report that lists the different classes or brands of payment stablecoins separately if reserve assets are segregated by brand. Accordingly, the monthly report may already contain the number of total outstanding payment stablecoins by class or brand and the composition of reserves for each brand. The OCC does not believe that additional disclosures related to the legal segregation mechanism, operational controls, or holder priority are necessary to include in rule text. The OCC is not mandating a legal segregation mechanism in the final rule, and a description of operational controls could potentially be complex, which could confuse payment stablecoin holders. Additionally, because of the current inherent uncertainty associated with resolving white-label issuers, there is a risk that disclosures about a payment stablecoin holder's claim in the event of insolvency could misstate the legal protection that will ultimately be afforded to payment stablecoin holders.
Moreover, the redemption disclosures in § 15.12(e) of the final rule will require
