Such disclosures are required to be conspicuous and readily noticeable under § 15.12(e)(1) of the final rule, so no further requirements related to prominence are necessary. Permitted payment stablecoin issuers may include additional disclosures regarding their co-branding arrangements and whether co-branded payment stablecoins are backed by the same reserve pool so long as the disclosures comply with the Act,
12 CFR part 15
, and other applicable laws.
One commenter stated that issuers should be required to disclose to the OCC the internal policies and controls by which they achieve legal segregation. Another commenter stated that the OCC should prohibit any co-branding arrangement in which the distribution partner represents to holders that it, rather than the licensed issuer, is responsible for reserves, redemption, or regulatory compliance. Another commenter stated that reserve reporting should align with the statute and be at the entity level with the option for issuers to report reserves at the individual brand level. One commenter stated that there should be express disclosures to each brand's holders concerning the multi-brand structure and the cross-brand non-encumbrance regime. One commenter stated that the OCC should permit and encourage layered, technology-enabled disclosure approaches.
The OCC may review a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's internal policies and controls during the supervisory process, and therefore, no specific disclosure requirement to the OCC is expressly required. Additionally, if a distribution partner that is not a permitted payment stablecoin issuer falsely represents that it is the issuer, the permitted payment stablecoin issuer responsible for redemption may not be in conformance with the disclosure requirements in § 15.12(e). For the entities under its jurisdiction, the OCC would ensure that any such misrepresentations, at a minimum, are handled through the supervisory process. Additionally, the monthly composition report in § 15.11(e) of the final rule limits the need for additional disclosures around a multi-brand structure because issuers will already be required to publish the reserves on a per-brand basis if the brands are secured by distinct pools of reserve assets. The monthly composition report specifically requires that, to the extent that different classes or brands of payment stablecoins are secured by distinct pools of reserve assets, permitted payment stablecoin issuers should publish a composition table for each class or brand of payment stablecoin and describe the legal and operational mechanisms, as applicable, for how the assets are separately secured. The final rule further specifies that if different classes or brands of payment stablecoins are issued by distinct issuers, including SPV issuers, a separate report must be provided for each issuer.
Moreover, the final rule does not require that reserves of each branded stablecoin be legally separate, and therefore, the OCC is not requiring disclosures related to cross-brand encumbrance. Of course, reserve assets may not be pledged, rehypothecated, or reused as provided in the Act and in § 15.10(c)(5), and every permitted payment stablecoin issuer must maintain reserve assets that at all times have a reserve asset value that equals or exceeds the outstanding issuance value of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer in accordance with § 15.11(a)(1)(iii). As discussed in more detail below, the OCC is not prescribing a specific format for disclosures beyond the reports required in § 15.14, but technology-enabled disclosures are acceptable as long as they conform with the requirements of the Act and this final rule.
In addition to disclosures, many commenters suggested that as an alternative to a single brand restriction, permitted payment stablecoin issuers should segregate reserves based on brand. Another commenter suggested specific regulatory text that would allow for permitted payment stablecoin issuers and foreign payment stablecoin issuers to issue one or more distinctly branded payment stablecoins, provided that the issuer satisfies certain brand-level segregation and disclosure requirements, including that the issuers maintain reserves in segregated account structures, SPVs, or other legally recognized segregation mechanisms approved by the OCC. The commenter suggested that the OCC could consider on a facts-and-circumstances basis whether the issuer's segregation mechanism provides adequate protection for reserves. Another commenter stated that the OCC should recognize certain statutory cell structures established in other jurisdictions as satisfying the legal separateness objective and that not doing so would disadvantage issuers operating in jurisdictions whose corporate law specifically addresses the segregation issue. One commenter suggested that the OCC should address any concerns regarding branded stablecoins through its authority in section 4(h)(1) of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(h)(1)
) by imposing conditions, including maintenance of segregated reserves at the issuer level, brand-level attestations that reconcile to the issuer's reserves. The same commenter suggested that the OCC should condition certain arrangements where there is an evasion of the reserve requirements in the Act.
In the proposed rule, the OCC also asked whether it should require a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to hold reserves in a SPV that is fully capitalized by the issuer and has no liabilities. While one commenter stated that the OCC has the authority to require the use of SPVs when warranted, a few commenters stated that the OCC should permit, but not mandate, the use of SPVs to hold different reserves. Commenters stated that SPVs should not be mandatory as they would impose substantial structural and operational costs, particularly for smaller issuers and would not provide meaningful additional protection to stablecoin holders. The commenter stated that while SPVs are not prohibited under the GENIUS Act, the regulators should work through resolution options for permitted payment stablecoin issuers and clarify how SPVs would fit into the bankruptcy protections of the GENIUS Act. A different commenter stated that if appropriate, issuers should provide a legal opinion or third-party attestation confirming that each brand's reserve pool is held in a bankruptcy-remote structure. Another commenter opposed requiring SPVs for each brand, stating that legal separateness would not prevent risk. One commenter stated that certain protections apply to the bankruptcy of an issuer, which would raise questions about the status of a SPV and how it would manage liquidity. One commenter stated that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer should only be able to issue more than one brand of payment stablecoin if the reserves are in a SPV, each program's reserves are managed, valued, and reported on a stand-alone basis, and each brand has its own redemption arrangements under which redemptions are payable solely from the brand's reserves. One commenter stated that such SPVs must have documented controls preventing cross-brand reserve encumbrance.

The final rule does not require a specific per-brand reserve segregation requirement, but reserve assets must comply with the requirements of § 15.11, including that they are identifiable and segregated from and not commingled with other assets owned or held by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer. The OCC retains discretion to impose conditions through the licensing process and will consider any segregation mechanisms proposed by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer or foreign issuer as well as any alternative approaches and determine whether such a mechanism or approach provides adequate protection for payment stablecoin holders, which will include consideration of whether reserves are adequately protected. With respect to statutory cell structures, the OCC will evaluate any particular proposed legal segregation mechanism at the time of licensing or registration as well as during ongoing supervision. However, the OCC declines in this rulemaking to make a categorical determination that a particular legal segregation mechanism is sufficient or required. With respect to the commenter's concern regarding evasion, to the extent that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer evades the reserve requirements of the Act, the OCC would consider whether the issuer was violating the Act, § 15.11, or any other requirements in part 15.
As discussed previously, the one-brand-per-issuer structure may better protect the rights of payment stablecoin holders than other models. Specifically, such a structure could help to ensure that the reserves of each brand of payment stablecoin are legally separate, reducing the risk that a run on one brand of payment stablecoin causes a run on other brands of a related payment stablecoin. Accordingly, while the final rule does not require the use of SPVs, the OCC is making changes to the final rule to accommodate the use of multiple SPV issuers and reduce the burden of using such a business model, including by making certain technical changes.
Commenters stated that the OCC should focus on establishing clear regulatory expectations for segregation, clear titling, recordkeeping, and labeling of reserve assets to ensure transparency and that the OCC should allow issuers to present specific mechanisms for separating and tracking reserves across differently branded stablecoins. One commenter suggested segregated account structures, including segregated custodial sub-accounts at eligible financial institutions, customer-property segregation regimes, or other segregation mechanisms approved by the OCC. The commenter further stated that the selected mechanism must have documented controls preventing the encumbrance, pledging, rehypothecation, or commingling of reserves. A few commenters suggested that permitted payment stablecoin issuers can set up separate trusts to otherwise manage reserve assets. Another commenter suggested token-level ring-fencing and compliance controls as well as sub-ledgering of reserves to address concerns.
While the OCC is not requiring a particular reserve segregation method, permitted payment stablecoin issuers are subject to the recordkeeping requirements in § 15.14(f) of the final rule. Accordingly, the OCC believes that the final rule sets clear regulatory expectations for recordkeeping and labeling of reserves. The OCC agrees that issuers should be allowed to present specific mechanisms for separating and tracking reserves and will allow issuers to present a specific mechanism during the licensing or registration process and as part of ongoing supervision. The OCC will consider the use of custodial sub-accounts and other customer segregation mechanisms when making a facts-and-circumstances determination as to whether payment stablecoin holders are adequately protected, including in the event of insolvency. Any custodial sub-accounts must comply with the requirements in final § 15.22(c). The OCC agrees that documented controls can help to strengthen a particular segregation mechanism, which will factor into the OCC's evaluation of whether the mechanism protects payment stablecoin holders. With respect to the use of separate trusts, the OCC again will consider such a mechanism as part of the application process, rather than making a categorical determination as part of this final rule that such a mechanism adequately protects payment stablecoin holders, to ensure a more detailed review of the trusts. Similarly, the OCC will need to evaluate in each instance how an issuer seeks to achieve token-level ring-fencing to better understand its utility. For issuers that use segregation mechanisms, the monthly composition report will already require the sub-ledgering of reserve assets.
In addition to suggestions regarding disclosures and segregation of reserves, many commenters suggested other alternatives to a single brand restriction. For example, a few commenters suggested redemption rights, internal controls, and operational allocation as ways to mitigate concerns regarding uncertainty of reserve assets for permitted payment stablecoin issuers with multiple brands of payment stablecoins.
The OCC will consider an applicant's internal controls and operational allocation when evaluating the permitted payment stablecoin issuer or foreign issuer during the licensing or registration process. An issuer's redemption policies must comply with the Act and, among other things, the requirements for redemption in § 15.12. However, the OCC expects that there may be some situations where redemption rights alone will be insufficient to protect the rights of payment stablecoin holders in the event of insolvency.
A different commenter suggested brand-level CPA examinations and explicit operational controls preventing cross-brand reserve encumbrance. One commenter suggested that the OCC use its supervisory tools to address any issues regarding reserve uncertainty in white-label arrangements.
With respect to the suggestion regarding brand-level CPA examinations, the monthly reserve composition report required under § 15.11(e), which requires reporting of reserve assets by brand, if applicable, must be examined by a registered public accounting firm, and therefore, no further CPA examination is necessary as an across-the-board requirement. Additionally, the OCC will use its supervisory tools to ensure that any concerns regarding white-label arrangements are being managed adequately.
One commenter stated that the OCC should focus on ensuring that there is supervisory coordination and service provider/affiliate risk management to cover bank and nonbank consortium members, including distribution platforms. Another commenter stated that consistent treatment of comparable claimants and operational planning could help mitigate risks related to the issuance of multiple brands of payment stablecoins.
The final rule includes risk management requirements related to affiliate transactions as well as service provider arrangements. Accordingly, permitted payment stablecoin issuers are already expected to ensure sufficient oversight of such arrangements. To the extent that members of a white-label arrangement are regulated by another entity, the OCC will strive to ensure there is supervisory coordination between agencies. With respect to treating comparable claimants consistently, a permitted payment stablecoin issuer must comply with the
(

Act and the redemption requirements in
12 CFR part 15
. Additionally, the OCC encourages operational planning and expects it would be prudent for most issuers to engage in such planning in the ordinary course of business.
One commenter suggested that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer should be required to submit a brand-level stress-period redemption plan setting forth: (i) the threshold conditions that will trigger stress-period mechanisms for the branded payment stablecoins it issues or may issue in the future; (ii) the redemption queue, prioritization, and processing protocols applicable during stress; (iii) the communication and disclosure protocols for that brand's holders; and (iv) the operational steps to ensure that brand-level stress does not propagate to other brands.
The OCC is adding monetization and stress-testing requirements for all permitted payment stablecoin issuers in § 15.13(a)(9) of the final rule. In addition, final § 15.11 requires that permitted payment stablecoin issuers must demonstrate the operational capability to access and monetize identifiable reserve assets to meet redemptions, in both normal and adverse economic, liquidity, market, and interest rate conditions. Accordingly, the OCC is not instituting any white-label specific stress testing because a permitted payment stablecoin issuer that issues multiple brands of payment stablecoins must ensure that it can access and monetize reserve assets to meet redemption requests for all brands of payment stablecoins. As discussed above, the OCC is not instituting additional communication and disclosure protocols. The OCC will consider the operational steps an issuer takes to ensure that brand-level stress does not propagate to other brands as part of the licensing, registration, and ongoing supervisory process.
A few commenters stated that the OCC should align with the FDIC's notice of proposed rulemaking implementing the GENIUS Act and manage brand-level obligations through mandating disclosures and ensuring that required reserves can be separately identified as backing a particular brand of payment stablecoin. A few commenters suggested that if the OCC were not to align with the FDIC, it would create regulatory divergence and favor FDIC-regulated issuers. Similarly, one commenter suggested coordination with the other Federal regulators to ensure consistent requirements for white-label arrangements.
The OCC declines to take the same approach as the FDIC did in its notice of proposed rulemaking, which requires multi-brand issuers to have a segregated pool of reserves that are recorded separately, unless the FDIC approves in writing that the permitted payment stablecoin issuer may commingle reserves. Instead, the OCC is taking a case-by-case approach during the licensing or registration process and will evaluate whether payment stablecoin holders are adequately protected when the issuer issues multiple brands of payment stablecoins. The OCC believes this approach allows issuers flexibility to explain to the OCC how it can adequately protect payment stablecoin holders when issuing multiple brands of payment stablecoins. The OCC will coordinate with other primary Federal payment stablecoin regulators and will continually evaluate its treatment of white-label arrangements to strive for consistent treatment.
A few commenters stated some conditions they would favor if the OCC were to impose a single brand restriction. One commenter stated that if the OCC does require a separate issuer for each brand of payment stablecoin, the OCC would need to clarify how capital, liquidity, and other risk management requirements and governance arrangements would be applied across each separate issuer. Another commenter stated that if the OCC adopts such a restriction, it should clarify that the restriction applies to issuer and custodian functions and does not require highly duplicative per-brand separation of infrastructure.
Although the OCC is not imposing a single brand restriction, the OCC is clarifying how capital, liquidity, and other risk management requirements and governance arrangements would be applied if a permitted payment stablecoin issuer makes use of an SPV during the licensing or registration process. The OCC is committed to ensuring that the use of an SPV would not cause unnecessary duplication of supervisory obligations.
A few commenters remarked on the language in the proposal that suggested that the OCC was considering streamlining the licensing process for affiliates if it were to impose a single brand restriction. A few commenters stated that if the OCC decides that separate legal entities are required for each brand, the OCC should adopt a streamlined approval process. One commenter suggested a notification-based process, under which the OCC confirms approval within a defined timeframe. One commenter stated that the OCC should clarify that a license for a permitted payment stablecoin issuer should extend to cover any consolidated affiliates of the issuer that issue the same token under the same brand and reserve framework, without requiring a separate license application for each affiliate entity. Another commenter stated that any requirements relating to multi-brand issuance should be applied consistently across all OCC-regulated entities. One commenter stated that State regulatory agencies would need to review applications for a new entity and a streamlined process for affiliates of already-approved issuers would be antithetical to how State regulatory agencies operate and would not enhance safety and soundness.
The OCC is not revising the application process for affiliates because it is not imposing a one-brand restriction and the final application process is sufficiently streamlined to limit burden for SPV issuers. To the extent that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer makes use of an SPV, the OCC will ensure that the process is streamlined if the SPV is a separate issuer. If an affiliate is issuing the same token under the same brand and reserve framework but is a different issuer, the issuer would need to apply separately to the OCC through the licensing or registration process; a license to issue payment stablecoins is not a group-wide authorization that automatically extends to affiliates.
Multi-Jurisdictional Stablecoin Issuance
In the proposal, the OCC asked whether it should address permitted payment stablecoin issuers that also issue or redeem the same or similar stablecoins in one or more foreign jurisdictions, sometimes referred to as multi-jurisdictional stablecoin issuance.
Many commenters stated that the OCC should clarify that permitted payment stablecoin issuers may engage in multi-jurisdictional issuance, emphasizing that fungibility, transferability, and global circulation are central features of payment stablecoins. Commenters stated that, absent OCC guidance, multi-jurisdictional issuance could be subject to uncertainty and barriers that impede cross-border adoption and prevent payment stablecoins from circulating on a global basis. One commenter specifically advocated for a safe harbor for such arrangements. One commenter stated that section 4(a)(1)(A)(ii) of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(A)(ii)
) explicitly permits reserves at correspondents and foreign agents of insured depository institutions, reflecting that permitted payment stablecoin issuers will conduct issuance and redemption activity outside of the
(

United States as a matter of ordinary operations.
Commenters identified several issues that would result from the OCC not addressing multi-jurisdictional issuance, including duplicative or conflicting supervisory expectations, inefficient reserve allocation, inconsistent redemption architecture, and technical design mandates that fragment liquidity and undermine interoperability. One commenter stated that the OCC should ensure permitted payment stablecoin issuer licenses include like-branded stablecoins issued by consolidated affiliates to ensure OCC visibility and accountability for all like-branded stablecoins. One commenter requested that the final rules enable a permitted payment stablecoin issuer and its foreign affiliate to rebalance reserve assets to meet their redemption needs, provided that the permitted payment stablecoin issuer and its affiliate at all times hold reserves on a 1 to 1 basis against the total outstanding issuance of their aggregate payment stablecoins.
Many commenters mentioned coordination with the United States Department of the Treasury or other regulators with respect to multi-jurisdictional stablecoin issuance. Specifically, a few commenters urged coordination between the OCC and Treasury with respect to Treasury's obligations under section 18 of the Act regarding making determinations that foreign countries have comparable regulatory and supervisory regimes. A few commenters stated that multi-jurisdictional stablecoin issuance should be permissible when Treasury has made a comparability determination or entered into certain reciprocal arrangements.
Another commenter stated that the OCC should not push stablecoin issuers to create multiple licensed entities in different jurisdictions to achieve multi-jurisdictional stablecoin issuance. One commenter stated that even if such a push would have short-term benefits, separate licensing for separate entities in separate jurisdictions would be inconsistent with the GENIUS Act, including with respect to reciprocal arrangements under section 18(d) of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5916(d)
). A different commenter stated that foreign jurisdictions seeking reciprocity should not be permitted to impose fundamentally different prudential requirements on permitted payment stablecoin issuers. One commenter stated that the OCC should provide a safe harbor for foreign affiliates that operate under a comparable regime, including guidance that addresses reserve location, reserve rebalancing, disclosures, customer segregation, redemption routing, operational controls, and examination expectations for the relevant permitted payment stablecoin issuers. Another commenter stated that the OCC should clarify that the operations of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer are subject to compliance with applicable requirements under the laws of other jurisdictions in which it issues stablecoins. One commenter stated that the OCC should engage with relevant electronic money institution regulators in the European Union to further support global acceptance of multi-jurisdictional issuance. The commenter further stated that the OCC should prioritize functional coordination with foreign regulators whenever an OCC-supervised permitted payment stablecoin issuer operates through foreign regulated issuing affiliates, including through memoranda of understanding and information sharing protocols.
As explained below, the OCC is not specifically addressing multi-jurisdictional issuance in the regulatory text of the final rule. The OCC agrees with the numerous commenters that stated that the OCC should coordinate with the Department of the Treasury and foreign regulators. Under section 18 of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5916
), the Secretary of the Treasury may determine whether a foreign country has a comparable regulatory and supervisory regime upon a recommendation from the other members of the Stablecoin Certification Review Committee. Additionally, the Secretary of the Treasury may also create and implement reciprocal arrangements or other bilateral agreements between the United States and jurisdictions with comparable payment stablecoin regulatory regimes. Accordingly, the OCC declines to provide any guidance on such determinations or reciprocal arrangements, as they are within the authority of the Department of the Treasury. Similarly, the OCC is not providing a safe harbor for foreign affiliates that operate under a comparable regime because these are determinations of the Department of the Treasury that have yet to be made, and as noted, the OCC plans to coordinate with the Department of the Treasury as appropriate on the continuing implementation of section 18 of the Act. Additionally, the OCC will not opine on the applicability of foreign laws because doing so is outside the scope of this rulemaking, which focuses on implementing the GENIUS Act.

As stated, the OCC is declining to provide specific guidance on multi-jurisdictional issuance beyond the fact that such arrangements must comply with the Act and part 15. provide an exception allowing cross-border redemptions to be completed on a longer redemption timeframe than domestic redemptions. All redemptions must comply with the requirements in § 15.12 of the final rule, including that timely redemptions may not exceed two business days following the date of the requested redemption. As explained below in response to comments about § 15.12, the final rule clarifies the beginning and end of the redemption timeline while retaining the baseline for timely redemption. Under § 15.12(a)(1) of the final rule, the obligation to redeem begins with the receipt of a redemption order from a customer and the satisfaction of conditions necessary to permit redemption (such as customer onboarding). Under § 15.12(a)(2) of the final rule, a redemption that involves an outgoing transfer of monetary value is deemed to occur when the permitted payment stablecoin issuer has fully processed and initiated the outgoing transfer of monetary value to the customer or customer's financial institution as directed by the customer. Given the changes to § 15.12, a longer redemption timeframe for cross-border redemption is unnecessary as certain processes that could take longer in a cross-border context (
e.g.,
the time required for funds to be received or credited to an account) are outside the redemption timeframe. The OCC is not specifically addressing reserve rebalancing in the final rule, except to state that such arrangements must comply with the Act and this final rule, including the requirement that reserve assets must fully back outstanding payment stablecoins at all times.

The OCC agrees that clear reporting, disclosures, and transparency could be helpful in promoting clarity with respect to multi-jurisdictional arrangements, but the OCC needs more information before it can specifically provide clarity on how these topics apply to such arrangements. Similarly, the OCC is not setting any technical mandates for such arrangements for the same reason. To the extent a permitted payment stablecoin issuer engages in multi-jurisdictional issuance, any risk management requirements in the final rule will still apply.
A few commenters urged the OCC to avoid prescriptive requirements, rigid segregation requirements, or a categorical ban that would disfavor multi-jurisdictional issuance. Commenters cautioned that such requirements could impair liquidity management, increase operational complexity, undermine fungibility, and worsen redemption risk. Commenters also stated that the OCC should permit shared infrastructure, compliance services, and personnel; allow holders to redeem through any participating permitted payment stablecoin issuer within a network, subject to BSA checks and OCC timely-redemption standards; and consider allowing a unified reserve pool for all outstanding tokens, provided United States holders retain clear redemption rights. One commenter stated that permitted payment stablecoin issuer licenses should include like-branded stablecoins issued by consolidated affiliates. The commenter further stated that permitted payment stablecoin issuer licenses should encompass the issuer and any consolidated affiliates issuing the same token.
The OCC is neither imposing prescriptive requirements nor a categorical ban on multi-jurisdictional issuance as it believes further coordination and experience would be useful to ensure any potential guidance on such arrangements is responsive and fully informed. For these reasons, the OCC declines to provide further guidance on shared infrastructure, redemption rights specific to such arrangements, and the idea of a unified reserve pool. As previously stated, any such arrangements must comply with the Act and the requirements in this final rule, including those related to redemption.
2. Reserve Assets (§ 15.11)
a. Overview of Changes From Proposed Rule to Final Rule for § 15.11
In both the proposed rule and the final rule, § 15.11(a) contains reserve requirements for permitted payment stablecoin issuers. The OCC is adopting § 15.11(a)(1) largely as proposed except for a substitution of “reserve asset value” where the proposed rule had used “total fair value” in § 15.11(a)(1)(iii). As in the proposal, final § 15.11(a)(2) requires permitted payment stablecoin issuers to demonstrate the operational capability to access and monetize the identifiable reserve assets, but the final rule further explains that such operational capability is to meet redemptions under various conditions after taking into account several relevant factors, which had been raised in the preamble of the proposed rule and are now being codified in the regulatory text itself. New § 15.11(a)(3) requires a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to ensure that reserve asset value will continue to equal or exceed outstanding issuance value at all times and that the reserve asset portfolio will be capable of supporting timely redemption under both normal conditions and adverse economic, liquidity, market, and interest rate conditions, including, to the extent necessary, maintaining a buffer of reserve assets in excess of outstanding issuance value. The agency is adopting proposed § 15.11(a)(3), renumbered as § 15.11(a)(4) and revised, to address when a permitted payment stablecoin issuer may withdraw reserve assets in excess of outstanding issuance value. While the proposed version of this paragraph permitted withdrawals of surplus reserve assets only once per month and explained how a permitted payment stablecoin issuer must make such a withdrawal, the final version permits withdrawals of reserve assets at any time following appropriate due diligence and confirmation that the withdrawal would not cause reserve asset value to fall below outstanding issuance value. Final § 15.11(a)(4) also deletes the phrase “any surplus” as superfluous because the phrase “reserve assets in excess of outstanding issuance value” sufficiently identifies what constitutes surplus reserve assets. Final § 15.11(a)(4) does not subject income earned from reserve assets to due diligence and confirmation requirements for withdrawal, as long as a permitted payment stablecoin issuer otherwise complies with the requirements of the final rule necessary to ensure that reserve asset value at all
(
printed page 67042)
times equals or exceeds outstanding issuance value.
Final § 15.11(b) describes the composition of reserve assets much as the proposed § 15.11(b) did. The OCC is finalizing § 15.11(b)(1), (3), and (4) as proposed. In § 15.11(b)(2), the OCC has modified the description of deposits and insured shares to more closely align with the Act. In adopting the phrasing used by the Act (“funds held as demand deposits”), the OCC is clarifying that reserve assets held as deposits must be deposits payable on demand (
i.e.,
without features that would delay or condition withdrawals), notwithstanding interpretations of the phrase “demand deposits” from other contexts.

b. Reserve Requirements (§ 15.11(a))
Section 4(a)(1)(A) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(A)
) requires a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to maintain identifiable reserves backing the outstanding payment stablecoins of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer on at least a 1 to 1 basis with reserves comprising certain high-quality assets specified in the Act. Section 4(a)(4)(A) of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(4)(A)
) requires the OCC, among other regulators, to issue regulations to implement certain liquidity standards as well as reserve asset diversification and interest rate risk management standards that are tailored to the business model and risk profile of permitted payment stablecoin issuers and do not exceed the standards that are sufficient to ensure the ongoing operations of permitted payment stablecoin issuers. Section 10 of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5909
) also imposes requirements on the “Custody of Payment Stablecoin Reserve and Collateral,” including restrictions on commingling certain assets. Consistent with these various sources of authority, the proposed rule included requirements related to reserve assets in several sections, including proposed § 15.11 (“Reserve Assets”), § 15.13 (“Risk Management”), and subpart C (“Custody”). Proposed subpart C's custody requirements would have applied to OCC-regulated custodians while proposed § 15.11's reserve asset requirements would have applied to OCC-regulated permitted payment stablecoin issuers. These requirements mirror each other but apply to distinct sets of entities (the permitted payment stablecoin issuers placing the reserve assets and the custodians holding them).
Proposed § 15.11 set forth (a) requirements relating to ensuring that there are sufficient reserves backing a payment stablecoin, (b) the assets eligible to serve as reserve assets, (c) diversification and concentration requirements, (d) minimum insured deposit requirements, (e) monthly reporting requirements, (f) monthly certification requirements, and (g) requirements relating to the failure to maintain the required minimum amount of reserve assets. With respect to diversification and concentration risk, the proposed rule presented two options: Option A (a principles-based general requirement coupled with a quantitative safe harbor) and Option B (mandatory quantitative minimums). The proposed rule also included risk management requirements related to reserve assets, including liquidity and interest rate risk management.
Many commenters offered general comments on the proposed liquidity, diversification, and concentration requirements. Several of these commenters recommended that reserve and redemption requirements should be clear or strict to protect consumers and reduce run risk, and these commenters generally recommended that liquidity requirements should be in line with
(
printed page 67043)
those that apply to banks. One commenter stated that the proposed rule's emphasis on high-quality reserves, segregation of assets, defined redemption timelines, and operational backstops is directionally supportive of credit stability.
A few commenters stated that the proposed liquidity and diversification requirements were overly strict or inflexible. One of these commenters also argued that the GENIUS Act grants the OCC authority to require reserve asset diversification but not diversification across reserve asset custodians. One commenter stated that liquidity, diversification, and concentration requirements are not adequate to prevent the risk of stablecoins “breaking the buck” and that only capital protections are adequate to address those losses.
One commenter stated that liquidity requirements should focus on the speed and reliability of monetizing assets since the relevant stress scenario for permitted payment stablecoin issuers is a surge in redemption rather than deterioration in asset quality. Another commenter recommended that liquidity requirements be tiered based on issuer size. One commenter stated that reserve composition requirements do not address the liquidity-during-receivership gap demonstrated by the failure of Silicon Valley Bank.
A few commenters stated that concentration requirements should be calibrated to existing supervisory expectations to avoid duplicative burdens. One commenter argued that concentration risk should be assessed together with the quality and operational reliability of the counterparty, as it may be safer for large-scale issuers to rely on concentrated exposure to a stronger, better integrated institution that can provide operational liquidity at sufficient scale to satisfy timely redemption. One commenter favored a principles-based approach to concentration and diversification in lieu of fixed limits, and this commenter cautioned that concentration and diversification requirements could push reserve assets to institutions with less operational capability to manage and deploy reserve assets. One commenter recommended addressing concentration risk by requiring larger issuers to report sector-level concentrations. A few commenters recommended against adding additional categories of risk to be considered beyond credit, liquidity, interest rate, and price risk. One of these commenters stated that counterparty risks can be better addressed through the examination process than with quantitative limits.
After carefully considering the comments received, the OCC is revising § 15.11 to provide additional flexibility while still including certain core requirements intended to ensure that payment stablecoins remain appropriately reserved at all times and available to meet redemptions. A detailed description of the proposed rule and changes to it, including the OCC's reasoning for any changes, follows. At a high level, the OCC is adopting a principles-based approach with respect to reserve asset diversification and concentration requirements supplemented by two quantitative requirements designed to ensure a minimum amount of daily liquidity and avoid excessive concentration with respect to a single counterparty (
e.g.,
to address the possibility of operational disruptions at certain counterparties and to mitigate potential credit risk posed by certain counterparties). The final rule also includes additional provisions designed to ensure that permitted payment stablecoin issuers are able to monetize reserve assets in stressed conditions, including new stress-testing provisions in § 15.13, and provisions relating to the use of custodians.
i. Description of Proposed Rule
Proposed § 15.11(a)(1) would have required that permitted payment stablecoin issuers maintain reserve assets that: (i) are identifiable; (ii) are segregated from and not commingled with other assets owned or held by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer; (iii) at all times have a total fair value that equals or exceeds the outstanding issuance value of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer; and (iv) are either held directly by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer or within the custody of an eligible financial institution. To maintain reserve assets that are “identifiable” and comply with proposed § 15.11(a)(1)(i), permitted payment stablecoin issuers would have needed to maintain appropriate records to ensure documented ownership and legal entitlement to individual reserve assets. Similarly, any ownership arrangements, including ownership of assets held via custodians, must comply with applicable laws and regulations, for example, requirements applicable to customer securities owned through the Fedwire Securities Service. An issuer would have been required to maintain the appropriate operational capabilities, internal controls, policies, and safeguards to ensure that stablecoins are always backed by reserves on an at least 1 to 1 basis. Among other things, safeguards could include mechanisms to prevent the issuance of abnormally large amounts of new payment stablecoins without additional approvals.
To comply with the requirement in proposed § 15.11(a)(1)(ii), a permitted payment stablecoin issuer would have needed to ensure that reserve assets were appropriately segregated from and not commingled with other assets owned or held by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer.
To comply with the requirement in proposed § 15.11(a)(1)(iii), a permitted payment stablecoin issuer would have needed to ensure that the fair value of reserve assets equaled or exceeded the outstanding issuance value of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer.
Proposed § 15.11(a)(1)(iv) would have required that the reserve assets must either be held directly by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer or within the custody of an eligible financial institution, which is defined in proposed § 15.2.
Proposed § 15.11(a)(2) would have required that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer demonstrate the operational capability to access and monetize the identifiable reserve assets, commensurate with the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's risk profile and business model. The issuer would have needed to be able to monetize the reserve assets, potentially quickly and at short notice, in order to meet redemption requests.
To comply with proposed § 15.11(a)(2), a permitted payment stablecoin issuer would have needed to be able to demonstrate the ability to monetize all types of reserve assets it maintains.
Proposed § 15.11(a)(3) included requirements for when permitted payment stablecoin issuers could withdraw reserve assets in excess of outstanding issuance value. In order to ensure that, at all times, sufficient reserve assets are maintained to back outstanding stablecoin issuance, permitted payment stablecoin issuers would have been permitted to withdraw excess reserve assets only after the monthly examination and certification required by section 4(a)(1) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)
) and provided for in proposed § 15.11(e) and (f). Specifically, permitted payment stablecoin issuers would have been able to withdraw any surplus reserve assets in excess of outstanding issuance value, calculated and reported as of the last day of the previous month, only upon the publication of that month's public disclosure, due at the end of the subsequent month. Proposed
(
printed page 67044)
§ 15.11(a)(3) would have also required that, while withdrawals would be based on calculations as of the end of the previous month, a permitted payment stablecoin issuer could only make withdrawals if the remaining reserve assets remained at least equal to the current outstanding issuance value, calculated as of the day of withdrawal.
ii. Description of Comments and the Final Rule
Commenters expressed different views regarding proposed § 15.11(a)(1)(iii)'s requirement that permitted payment stablecoin issuers maintain reserves that “[a]t all times have a total fair value that equals or exceeds the outstanding issuance value of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer,” both regarding the “at all times” standard and the potential propriety of alternative valuation methodologies.
Regarding the “at all times” standard, some commenters supported a real-time valuation standard, noting that proof of reserves technologies can provide near-real-time information regarding reserves. Some of the commenters further noted that the OCC should allow permitted payment stablecoin issuers to rely on continuous, cryptographically verifiable on-chain attestations provided by eligible custodians to fulfill this requirement. However, other commenters believed that the language was ambiguous, that a strictly real-time valuation standard would introduce unnecessary complexity, be impractical and, in some cases, may be impossible, based on underlying technology, intra-day asset value fluctuations, and settlement or clearing timing differences, and would be out of step with how other assets are valued. These commenters instead supported an end-of-day standard as more practical and effective.
Regarding the valuation of reserve assets, some commenters noted that fair value may not be applicable in all cases. These commenters noted examples such as money market mutual funds, which are measured at their net asset value, and reverse repo agreements, which may be carried at cost less impairment. Some commenters recommended allowing valuation using amortized cost.
The OCC requested comment on whether “the proposed rule [should] include additional measures to ensure that reserve assets are appropriately traceable and linked to their corresponding stablecoin so as to avoid any difficulties in resolving claims to reserve assets.” One commenter responded that such traceability would be operationally impractical and would not have a commensurate risk management benefit. The OCC agrees and has not adopted any additional regulation text requiring that reserve assets be traceable and linked to their corresponding payment stablecoin for these reasons. The OCC notes, however, that permitted payment stablecoin issuers must maintain identifiable reserves backing the outstanding value of payment stablecoins.
[
75
]
One commenter requested that the OCC clarify the permissibility of automated reserve asset management systems, including those executed via smart contracts.
After careful consideration of the comments, the OCC is finalizing § 15.11(a)(1) with one minor change. The final rule replaces a reference to “total fair value” with the new defined term “reserve asset value.” The final rule continues to require an issuer to maintain reserve assets, the value of which equals or exceeds the outstanding issuance value of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer at all times. This requirement follows directly from section 4(a)(1)(A) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(A)
). The final rule also continues to require reserve assets to be valued at fair value (with the exception of United States coins and currency, which must be valued at par) as a result of the new defined term “reserve asset value.” Valuing reserve assets at fair value (
i.e.,
market value) will help ensure that the reserve assets maintained by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer reflect current prices and will be monetizable at a value sufficient to meet any redemption requests at par value. The OCC notes that “outstanding issuance value” is based on the total par value of all of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's payment stablecoins rather than on the fair value of the outstanding issued payment stablecoin. Thus, if the fair value of the payment stablecoin decreased (
i.e.,
if the payment stablecoin de-pegged in the secondary market), the permitted payment stablecoin issuer would nevertheless be obligated to retain a stock of reserve assets, the fair value of which equals or exceeds the par value of outstanding payment stablecoins.
Taking a contrary approach (
e.g.,
basing the outstanding issuance value on the fair value of payment stablecoins) would be inconsistent with the plain text and goals of the GENIUS Act.
[
76
]
Moreover, such an approach could allow permitted payment stablecoin issuers to inappropriately remove assets from the required stock of reserve assets when stablecoins de-peg (as reserve asset requirements decline, along with the secondary market price of the stablecoin), rather than maintaining the reserve assets on behalf of stablecoin holders, which may in turn exacerbate run risk for a permitted payment stablecoin issuer. In response to certain comments, the OCC confirms that permitted payment stablecoin issuers may use automated reserve asset management systems provided that the systems used conform to the requirements of §§ 15.11, 15.13, and 15.14 as well as any other applicable requirements in part 15.
The OCC notes that it anticipates that reserve assets generally will be recorded on the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's balance sheet under GAAP and be included in the quarterly reports required under proposed § 15.14(i) and on Call Report Schedule RC, Balance Sheet, for a parent insured national bank or Federal savings association.
Several commenters addressed the requirement in proposed § 15.11(a)(3) that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer may only “withdraw any surplus reserve assets in excess of outstanding issuance value once per month, upon publication of the composition report required.” Many commenters requested clarifications or amendments to this proposed requirement. Some commenters noted that the requirement may have unintended consequences—for example, it may disincentivize issuers holding excess reserves since the rule would impose a significant delay should the issuer decide to withdraw some amount of such excess. Other commenters suggested that the end-of-month timing may incentivize issuers to increase their reserves at month's end. One commenter argued that surplus reserve withdrawals should be calculated based on the present value of the reserves, rather than the value reported for the prior month. The commenter stated that this approach would decrease risk that withdrawals cause the reserve assets to fall below the 1 to 1 ratio. Still another commenter requested clarification as to whether withdrawals may only occur on the actual day of the specified report in § 15.11(e) (discussed below).
Some commenters requested clarity on when an asset becomes a reserve asset and recommended adding requirements concerning the handling of funds prior to the point at which they become reserve assets. Some commenters advocated for requiring reserve principal, earnings, and interest to remain identifiable and traceable until the issuer verifies the existence of excess and completes an authorized
(
printed page 67045)
withdrawal procedure. Others opposed treating interest generated from reserve assets as reserve assets, stating that such treatment is not mandated by statute. Some argued in favor of treating customer funds as reserve assets immediately on receipt of such funds.
Relatedly, several commenters expressed views on the propriety of charging expenses related to management of the reserve assets against the reserve assets. Many commenters stated that, as a general matter, such expenses should not be chargeable against the reserve assets. However, several commenters offered exceptions, for example, one commenter noted that transaction-related expenses, such as interest on repurchase agreements or investment management fees, should be chargeable against the reserve assets. Another commenter stated that management should have discretion as to the use of excess reserves if the use of such excess reserve assets is subject to an appropriate policy or agreement.
Several commenters noted the importance of liquidity planning regarding reserve assets in addition to an issuer's broader risk management obligations. Several commenters, for example, suggested that permitted payment stablecoin issuers should be required to adopt written plans, policies, and procedures related to liquidity planning, noting the importance of formal documentation in forcing an issuer to identify risks in advance, assign responsibility, and assess contingency options prior to stress arising. Other commenters discussed specific contingency planning issues, such as Federal Reserve discount window or Federal Home Loan Bank lending access for certain issuers or mandated recovery and resolution plans. Still other commenters noted that liquidity and contingency plans should be tailored to an issuer's operational and risk profile or should take into account any related liquidity planning that an issuer may already be subject to under other regulations.
Other commenters noted that it is also important for permitted payment stablecoin issuers to plan for interest rate and credit risk regarding reserve assets. For example, commenters suggested that the OCC require written interest rate and credit risk management plans, policies, and procedures. However, other commenters stated that the asset diversification and concentration expectations in the proposal are sufficient to address interest rate and liquidity risk.
Commenters also suggested that the OCC provide guidance on liquidity, interest rate, and credit risk management, including, for example, expectations regarding liquidity depth, redemption flow, measurement methodologies, risk appetites, counterparty due diligence, the unique risks posed by custodians and other intermediaries, and other topics related to reserve asset risk management.
In addition to the reserve asset risk management requirements included in the proposed regulation itself, the proposed rule requested comment on two specific potential requirements: stress testing and buffers. The OCC requested comment on whether permitted payment stablecoin issuers should be required to conduct stress tests, including as to their management of liquidity and interest rate risk. Commenters largely supported the use of stress tests as a risk management tool, though commenters differed on their views as to how any stress-testing expectations should be implemented in the regulation. Numerous commenters stated that the OCC should expressly require permitted payment stablecoin issuers to undertake liquidity and interest rate risk stress tests, with some commenters providing proposed standards (
e.g.,
documentation requirements, thresholds issuers would be expected to meet, consequences for failing to meet such thresholds) or scenarios. One commenter suggested that a stress testing requirement could substitute for the weighted average maturity requirement (or safe harbor) in proposed § 15.11(c). Relatedly, several commenters suggested broader “monetization testing” to ensure that issuers' channels for converting reserve assets into liquid funds are operational and reliable under normal and stressed circumstances. Finally, one commenter suggested that the OCC design and conduct multi-issuer stress tests prior to the effective date of the GENIUS Act and publish the results.
Other commenters noted the utility of stress testing but stated that the OCC should not impose prescriptive requirements but rather adhere to a principles-based approach, under which stress testing may be an appropriate risk-based approach for an issuer depending on its characteristics. One commenter stated that any stress testing requirements would be better issued at a later date after the OCC gains experience supervising permitted payment stablecoin issuers and an understanding of the potential utility of such stress tests.
The proposed rule noted that it “includes robust liquidity requirements but does not include capital-based overcollateralization or reserve asset buffer requirements. An alternative possibility would be to remove some of the proposed liquidity requirements, though this may warrant increased capital or buffer requirements.” Additionally, the OCC posed several questions to commenters on how such an approach might be handled.

]
Several commenters requested that the OCC require a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to hold a “buffer” of reserve assets—that is, to overcollateralize its reserves or apply haircuts against the values of certain reserve assets—such as a standardized across-the-board 1 percent buffer or a codification of the Fixed Income Clearing Corporation Government Securities Division Clearing Fund haircut schedule published by the Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation for United States Treasuries. Others rejected standardized approaches, arguing that they are inconsistent with the GENIUS Act's tailoring requirement. These commenters instead suggested that any buffers be specific to an issuer based on the facts and circumstances or else discussed the relative benefits of buffers in the GENIUS Act reserve asset context since such assets are generally low-risk assets.
Some commenters also recommended that the OCC explicitly address in guidance that both the monetization capability standard and the diversification framework are intended to be jointly satisfiable, and that supervisory assessments will take into account the operational constraints that diversification arrangements may place on monetization capability.
After careful review of the comments, the OCC has made several changes to § 15.11(a)(2) and (3) and added new paragraph (a)(4) to the final rule. As discussed below, the final rule reduces the number of quantitative requirements relating to reserve asset liquidity, diversification, and concentration from the number that were included in Option B of the proposed rule. To ensure that permitted payment stablecoin issuers remain adequately reserved, the OCC is balancing these reduced quantitative requirements with new provisions emphasizing the ability of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to maintain the appropriate level of reserve assets and to monetize those assets. Some of those provisions, including those relating to stress testing, are also addressed in the final rule's risk management provisions. Paragraphs
(
printed page 67046)
(a)(2) through (4) also provide certain clarifications in response to comments.
Paragraph (a)(2) of the final rule's § 15.11 requires a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to demonstrate the operational capability to access and monetize the identifiable reserve assets to meet redemptions, in both normal and adverse economic, liquidity, market, and interest rate conditions, commensurate with the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's risk profile and business model, taking into account, among other relevant factors, market access, financing channels, haircut assumptions, and operational readiness. Depending on a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's size, risk profile, business model, activities, and operations, a permitted payment stablecoin issuer may be able to demonstrate monetization in different ways. For example, it may be sufficient for some permitted payment stablecoin issuers to demonstrate the ability to monetize Treasury bills they hold as reserve assets by establishing that they maintain appropriate repurchase arrangements through which they can quickly sell Treasury bills and receive liquid funds with which they can satisfy redemption requests.
For other permitted payment stablecoin issuers, for example, larger permitted payment stablecoin issuers or permitted payment stablecoin issuers with more complicated operations, additional measures may be appropriate to demonstrate the operational capability to monetize. It may be appropriate for such permitted payment stablecoin issuers to maintain multiple alternative methods of monetization (for example, multiple repurchase agreement lines or repurchase agreement lines plus arrangements allowing outright sales of Treasury securities) to satisfactorily demonstrate the ability to monetize their reserve assets. Such redundant arrangements may be necessary if a permitted payment stablecoin issuer maintains a sufficiently large Treasury position that it could be difficult to monetize the entire position through transactions with a single repo counterparty or if a permitted payment stablecoin issuer maintains concentrated positions in particular types of reserve assets. The availability of multiple monetization channels is intended to help ensure that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer is not required to monetize assets at reduced or “fire sale” prices. Having alternative monetization channels reduces the risk that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer would be obliged to accept unfavorable pricing when monetizing reserve assets under stress.
For certain permitted payment stablecoin issuers, it may be appropriate to periodically conduct actual monetization transactions (that is, actual outright sales or repurchase transactions) in order to demonstrate the ability to monetize. Actual transactions can more fully confirm that monetization capabilities exist. In the absence of actual test transactions, potential barriers to monetization may still exist. Permitted payment stablecoin issuers may be unfamiliar with or lack the procedures and systems to monetize assets at any time in accordance with standard settlement periods and processes. For example, internal staff may be unprepared to execute procedures, or borrowing agreements may name authorizing officials who are unavailable or inappropriate. Actual monetization transactions may be appropriate, for example, for permitted payment stablecoin issuers with unusually complicated operations or organizational structures, or for permitted payment stablecoin issuers that are particularly dependent on certain monetization channels or the ability to monetize particular assets. Periodic actual monetization transactions can minimize the risk of negative signaling during financial stress and help prepare the issuer to move quickly if necessary to acquire additional liquidity.
If a permitted payment stablecoin issuer begins using a monetization channel that it has not regularly used in the past, that may spark concerns about the financial health of the issuer. For example, if a permitted payment stablecoin issuer has pre-established a repurchase agreement with a bilateral counterparty but never utilized it, sudden utilization of the repurchase agreement may generate concerns that the issuer is experiencing a run on its stablecoins. Periodic test transactions using multiple monetization channels can mitigate such concerns and may be particularly important for large, systemically important issuers where concerns about financial distress are more likely to contribute to contagion. Permitted payment stablecoin issuers may be able to demonstrate the ability to execute actual monetization transactions in the ordinary course of their business (for example, redeeming stablecoins) and would not necessarily be required to engage in additional test transactions.
Paragraph (a)(3) of the final rule's § 15.11 requires a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to ensure that reserve asset value will continue to equal or exceed outstanding issuance value at all times and that the reserve asset portfolio will be capable of supporting timely redemption under both normal conditions and adverse economic, liquidity, market, and interest rate conditions, including, to the extent necessary, maintaining a buffer of reserve assets in excess of outstanding issuance value. This requirement will provide permitted payment stablecoin issuers flexibility in composing their reserve asset portfolio while ensuring that permitted payment stablecoin issuers are able to maintain 1 to 1 backing at all times. The final rule does not mandate a particular buffer level but makes clear that such a buffer may be appropriate, depending on the makeup of the reserve asset portfolio of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer. Permitted payment stablecoin issuers with certain reserve asset portfolios may not be required to maintain any buffer, or only a small buffer, in order to comply with paragraph (a)(3), for example, reserve asset portfolios consisting entirely of reserve assets that represent immediately available liquidity, such as deposits payable upon demand. In contrast, it may be necessary for permitted payment stablecoin issuers with longer-duration reserve asset portfolios to maintain a more substantial buffer.

12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(A)(ii)

In determining whether a potential reserve asset qualifies as “any other similarly liquid Federal Government-issued asset,” under proposed § 15.11(b)(7) the OCC would have considered, among other relevant factors, whether: (i) the asset has liquidity characteristics, including during times of stress, comparable to the other reserve assets allowed under proposed § 15.11(b); (ii) permitted payment stablecoin issuers will be operationally capable of monetizing the asset to meet redemption requests, including sudden and high-volume requests; (iii) the asset poses levels of risk comparable to the assets allowed under proposed § 15.11(b), including interest rate risk and counterparty credit risk; and (iv) the asset introduces additional risks that may be difficult for permitted payment stablecoin issuers to manage.
ii. Description of Comments and the Final Rule
A few commenters generally favored the reserve asset composition set forth in the OCC's proposed rule. One commenter recommended that issuer reserves should be permitted to be composed entirely of Treasuries, overnight Treasury repurchase agreements, and their equivalents, considering their low credit risk. Another commenter recommended that all permitted payment stablecoin issuers should be required to hold a majority of their reserves as deposits in insured depository institutions and Treasuries with a remaining maturity of no longer than 93 days.
Physical Currency
Overall, commenters supported limited recognition of physical currency, subject to basic safeguards rather than detailed prescriptive requirements. A few commenters addressed physical currency and generally suggested that the OCC adopt a simple, principles-based approach because physical currency is unlikely to serve as a significant reserve asset in
(
printed page 67048)
practice. One commenter stated that any physical currency held as a reserve asset should be valued at par. Another commenter noted that physical currency should be permitted only within defined limits, such as a small percentage of total reserves and potentially subject to geographic distribution requirements, while recognizing that some operating balance in physical currency may be practical for smaller issuers.
The final rule does not impose direct limits on the use of physical currency in § 15.11(b)(1) or elsewhere, but, as discussed above, physical currency must be valued at face value (rather than fair market value). In addition, risk management considerations, in particular operational risk, will likely discourage the extensive use of physical currency as reserve assets.

Reserve Bank Balances
Overall, commenters generally supported greater clarity on the treatment of reserve bank balances but differed on whether such balances should receive preferential treatment or be subject to concentration safeguards. Several commenters suggested that reserve bank balances be exempt from concentration limits and argued that balances at Federal Reserve Banks do not present credit risk and that treating reserve banks like insured depository institutions would impose unnecessary operational constraints without corresponding safety benefits. A few commenters stated that the OCC should work with the Federal Reserve to permit an operating subsidiary of an insured depository institution to open a master account directly or maintain a designated sub-account of its parent institution's Federal Reserve master account. In contrast, one commenter stated that exempting Federal Reserve master accounts from concentration limits could confer a competitive advantage on banks and urged the OCC to revisit the issue after the Federal Reserve further addresses payment account implementation or clarifies master account eligibility. Another commenter stated that, if a permitted payment stablecoin issuer were to obtain master account access, the OCC should limit the share of reserve assets that may be held at a Reserve Bank.
As discussed below, the final rule, like the proposed rule, imposes a 40 percent single counterparty limit with respect to money standing to the credit of a Federal Reserve Bank. The OCC determined that, although Federal Reserve Banks do not present counterparty credit risk, providing preferential treatment for the placement of reserve assets at Federal Reserve Banks could implicate financial stability risks. In times of stress, permitted payment stablecoin issuers may generally have an incentive to move reserve assets out of commercial banks and into Federal Reserve Banks. Imposing a 40 percent single counterparty limit on commercial banks but not Federal Reserve Banks could exacerbate this dynamic. This flight could also lead to increased money market volatility and potentially impede the transmission of monetary policy. Thus, consistent with the OCC's authority and mandate under section 4(b) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(b)
) to ensure financial stability, the final rule applies a 40 percent single counterparty limit with respect to money standing to the credit of a Federal Reserve Bank.
Although the OCC has coordinated and will continue to coordinate with the Federal Reserve in the agencies' implementation of the GENIUS Act, the OCC declines to provide guidance on Federal Reserve master account structures, consistent with its approach to national banks, as master account access is outside the OCC's statutory authorities.
Deposits
Some commenters suggested that permissible reserve assets should include a broader range of deposit arrangements, including ordinary deposit and settlement accounts. To emphasize that settlement accounts are a routine and important part of reserve operations, some commenters stated that reserves should not be limited to custody account arrangements. Other commenters stated that the term “demand deposit” should be interpreted to include money market deposit accounts and similar deposits that may not formally qualify as demand deposits, so long as the permitted payment stablecoin issuer can withdraw the funds at any time. One commenter stated that this interpretation is necessary to give effect to the concept of funds being “payable on demand” and would broaden the range of depository institutions permitted to hold reserve assets, including industrial loan companies that may not accept demand deposits. A few commenters opposed requiring or encouraging reserve assets to be held as insured deposits or shares, arguing that: (i) deposit insurance resources are not designed to support stablecoin volumes, (ii) increased coverage could raise unfair assessment burdens on banks, (iii) payment stablecoins are not deposits, and (iv) diversification into bank deposits could increase risks to the banking system. One commenter also cautioned that uninsured deposits are neither risk-free nor always highly liquid.
A few commenters addressed insurance-related issues for reserve assets and generally urged greater clarity regarding the treatment and risks of insured and uninsured deposits. One commenter recommended that the OCC explore a supplemental excess deposit insurance or guarantee mechanism for stablecoin reserve deposits held in trust for payment stablecoin holders. Some commenters argued against permitting uninsured deposits because they would leave stablecoins highly vulnerable to runs. One commenter noted that disclosures should clearly explain the level of protection available for insured and uninsured deposits, including whether tokenized deposits qualify for deposit insurance or whether insurance does not pass through to token holders. One commenter also referenced the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants' (AICPA) stablecoin criteria as supporting explicit disclosure where deposit insurance does not pass through to the token holder.
A few commenters urged the OCC not to categorically limit reserve deposits to United States insured depository institutions and instead to permit deposits held through foreign banking organizations, foreign branches, or correspondent banking arrangements under appropriate conditions. Some commenters stated that the statute permits deposits to be maintained at foreign banking organizations, including where those institutions maintain correspondent accounts with United States insured depository institutions. Some commenters stated that foreign banks operating in the United States should receive national treatment and thus should be allowed to conduct the same activities as United States financial institutions. Other commenters stated that permitted payment stablecoin issuers may have legitimate operational needs for reserves in non-U.S. locations, including to meet requirements established under reciprocal arrangements. Several commenters stated that restricting U.S. dollar-denominated payment stablecoins to demand deposits at United States-based depository institutions would be disproportionate, commercially harmful, and inconsistent with a competitive and accessible

stablecoin framework. Some commenters argued that the rule should avoid blanket haircuts or capital charges on reserve assets held at foreign branches or correspondent banks and instead require issuers to maintain documented risk management frameworks addressing the risks of such arrangements. One commenter urged the OCC to specify the conditions under which Eurodollar deposits would be appropriate in a manner that minimizes interference with free competition and to apply any restrictions on foreign branches, agents, or correspondent banks equally to U.S.- and foreign-headquartered firms.
As discussed above, section 4(a)(1)(A)(ii) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(A)(ii)

12 U.S.C. 5901(15)

Accordingly, deposits that are not held at insured depository institutions (regardless of whether the deposits themselves are insured) are not eligible reserve assets.
Some commenters also suggested that the OCC clarify that deposit placement networks may be used to hold reserve assets through eligible financial institutions. These commenters argued that such networks can improve diversification, operational efficiency, liquidity, and timely redemptions while also channeling deposits to community banks. One commenter stated that deposit placement networks are unlikely to increase run risk because deposits would be spread across institutions and stablecoins may be less likely to experience concentrated redemptions than some other liabilities. The OCC confirms that permitted payment stablecoin issuers may use deposit placement networks provided that the issuer does so in compliance with applicable requirements, including those in §§ 15.11 and 15.13. For example, if a network's agreements included limitations on withdrawals that rendered the issuer unable to meet the liquidity demands of customers and to timely redeem tendered payment stablecoins, it would be inappropriate for the permitted payment stablecoin issuer to place amounts of its reserve assets through that deposit placement network that rendered the permitted payment stablecoin issuer unable to comply with the final rule.
The final rule does not substantively change the description of funds held as deposits or insured shares payable on demand at an insured depository institution in § 15.11(b)(2). The final rule does, however, more closely match the language of section 4(a)(1)(A)(ii) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(A)(ii)

12 CFR part 204
and section 2 of the BHC Act; as other laws and regulations do not use the same phrasing as the GENIUS Act, may not be within the OCC's jurisdiction, and are based on different policy purposes, applying definitions, interpretations, or market practices based on other law for purposes of this provision of the Act is not appropriate. In addition, the OCC confirms that a deposit account that allows the bank to require prior notice of withdrawal or limits the number of withdrawals within a period of time would not be a demand deposit or other deposit that may be withdrawn upon request at any time under the GENIUS Act regardless of whether the deposit was treated as a demand deposit under other law. As discussed in greater detail below, the OCC is also eliminating the proposed requirement that certain permitted payment stablecoin issuers hold a set amount of reserves as insured deposits. Permitted payment stablecoin issuers continue to be expected to manage credit and concentration risks, including those regarding insured deposits and insured depository institutions. With respect to deposit insurance, the OCC notes that the FDIC has issued a notice of proposed rulemaking addressing insurance coverage rules in
12 CFR part 330
that apply to all FDIC-insured depository institutions by clarifying that deposits held as reserves backing a payment stablecoin would be insured as to the permitted payment stablecoin issuers under the FDIC's coverage rules for corporate deposits, but would not be insured to payment stablecoin holders on a pass-through basis.
