d. Reserve Asset Diversification and Concentration (§ 15.11(c))
i. Description of the Proposed Rule
Section 4(a)(4)(A)(iii) of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(4)(A)(iii)
) requires the OCC to issue regulations implementing reserve asset diversification, including deposit concentration at banking institutions and interest rate risk management standards that (1) are tailored to the business model and risk profile of permitted payment stablecoin issuers and (2) do not exceed standards that are sufficient to ensure the ongoing operations of permitted payment stablecoin issuers. The proposed rule included two alternative options to implement these diversification and concentration limits in proposed § 15.11(c). “Option A” included a principles-based general requirement with an optional safe harbor containing quantitative requirements. “Option B” would have made the quantitative requirements mandatory for all issuers. Option A's principles-based general requirement would have required a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to maintain reserve assets that are sufficiently diverse to manage potential credit, liquidity, interest rate, and price risks. In addition, the principles-based requirement in Option A in proposed § 15.11(c) would have required a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to measure and manage the risk that concentrating reserve assets at one eligible financial institution or a small number of eligible financial institutions may impair the ability of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to satisfy redemption demands if individual eligible financial institutions are unable to return, or if there is a delay in returning, reserve assets placed by a permitted payment stablecoin issuer.
[
87
]
The proposed rule's diversification and concentration requirements would have applied to custodial relationships, including sub-custodial arrangements. Permitted payment stablecoin issuers would have been expected to “look through” any sub-custodial relationships to ensure that reserve assets are custodied at a sufficiently diverse number of eligible financial institutions needed to comply with the proposed rule's requirements.
Option A contained a safe harbor under which a permitted payment stablecoin issuer would be deemed to satisfy proposed § 15.11(c) if the permitted payment stablecoin issuer maintains on each business day: (i) at least 10 percent of its required reserve assets as deposits or insured shares payable upon demand or money standing to the credit of an account with a Federal Reserve Bank; (ii) at least 30 percent of its reserve assets as deposits or insured shares payable upon demand, money standing to the credit of an account with a Federal Reserve Bank, or amounts receivable and due unconditionally within five business days on pending sales of reserve assets, maturing reserve assets, or other maturing transactions (
e.g.,
reverse repurchase agreements); (iii) no more than 40 percent of its reserve assets at any one eligible financial institution, whether as deposits or insured shares at any one insured depository institution, securities custodied at any one eligible financial institution, bilateral reverse repurchase agreements with any counterparty, or through other exposures; (iv) no more than 50 percent of the amount provided in proposed § 15.11(c)(2)(i) at any one eligible financial institution; and (v) reserve assets with a weighted average maturity of no more than 20 days.
The safe harbor would also have required that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer maintain at least 30 percent of its reserve assets as deposits or insured shares payable upon demand, money standing to the credit of an account with a Federal Reserve Bank, or amounts receivable and due unconditionally within five business days on pending sales of reserve assets, maturing reserve assets, or other maturing transactions.
The safe harbor would have also required that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer maintain no more than 40 percent of its reserve assets at any one eligible financial institution, whether as deposits or insured shares at any one insured depository institution, securities custodied at any one eligible financial institution, bilateral reverse repurchase agreements with any counterparty, or through other exposures.
The safe harbor would have also required that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer maintain no more than 50 percent of the required daily liquidity specified under proposed § 15.11(c)(2)(i) at any one eligible financial institution. This requirement was intended to guard against the risk that problems at one eligible financial institution prevent a permitted payment stablecoin issuer from accessing its reserve assets. If a permitted payment stablecoin issuer is dependent on one eligible financial institution to maintain all or a large portion of its reserve assets, the permitted payment stablecoin issuer may be excessively exposed to, for example, operational concerns at that eligible financial institution or even the risk of the institution's failure.
To qualify for the safe harbor, proposed § 15.11(c)(2)(v) would have required that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's reserve assets have a weighted average maturity of no more than 20 days.
Option B would have imposed the quantitative standards as mandatory requirements, rather than an optional safe harbor.
ii. Description of Comments and the Final Rule
Generally, more commenters expressed support for the “Option A” approach to reserve asset diversification over “Option B.” Several commenters supporting Option A stated that it appropriately balances rigor, flexibility,
(
printed page 67053)
and clarity for permitted payment stablecoin issuers and enables appropriate tailoring. Some other commenters stated that Option A provides for appropriate tailoring to different business models and risk profiles. A few commenters stated that Option A would be consistent with established custody fundamentals or existing state-level frameworks. A few commenters favored Option A because it offers predictability for new entrants and flexibility for mature issuers to demonstrate diversification through risk management practices tailored to actual operations. One commenter stated that Option B would depart from Congressional intent because the proposed reserve requirements would be excessive and not properly tailored.
A few commenters supported Option A but suggested changes. One commenter stated that weighted average maturity provisions should be changed so as not to discourage holding longer-dated Treasuries (subject to the statutory 93-day cap). One commenter suggested the OCC make clear that Option A may require a buffer of extra reserve assets. One commenter suggested that small permitted payment stablecoin issuers should be presumed to comply with Option A.
Some commenters specifically addressed the proposed safe harbor provision. A few of these commenters stated generally that the safe harbor would provide flexibility for issuers. Several commenters stated that the safe harbor is improperly calibrated and suggested changes to the quantitative limits that they argued would reduce risk or better support liquidity needs. A few other commenters argued that quantitative thresholds were unnecessary, impractical, or inadequately supported by data. One of these commenters suggested that, if retained, issuers should be able to satisfy the safe harbor by meeting board-approved diversification requirements. Several commenters stated that the safe harbor should not be treated as a minimum requirement or baseline expectation. One commenter suggested that compliance with the safe harbor should be measured as of the close of each business day, with opportunity for a cure period of one business day.
Several commenters favored “Option B” instead. Some of these commenters stated that quantitative thresholds would create more certainty and consistency for both issuers and third parties compared to a principles-based approach without specific quantitative thresholds. A few of these commenters also recommended changes to the specific requirements under Option B. One commenter stated that mandatory limits including single-custodian caps could reduce risk but suggested the OCC should clarify that reserve composition requirements do not eliminate liquidity risk in the event of a third-party custodian's insolvency. One commenter supported Option B but suggested the OCC evaluate the impact of concentration limits and 20-day weighted average maturity to ensure they do not lead to unintended consequences.
One commenter stated that neither Option A nor Option B fully addresses concerns related to deposit flight, impacts to credit creation, and potential systemic risk in light of increasing connections between stablecoin issuers and the banking system, citing the example of Silicon Valley Bank.
A few commenters supported the establishment of minimum requirements for immediately available liquidity. One commenter noted that these requirements were preferable to issuers relying on sales or repurchase agreements to generate liquidity. A few commenters supported having a weekly minimum liquidity requirement. One commenter supported the 10 percent and 30 percent thresholds for daily and weekly liquidity requirements, respectively. One commenter recommended that the 10 percent daily liquidity requirement should be adjustable based on each issuer's demonstrated redemption profile, with 5 percent being an appropriate baseline for experienced issuers. The commenter further recommended that an issuer should be permitted to propose a threshold below the 5 percent minimum if the issuer can provide support for lower daily liquidity needs. One commenter suggested that the daily requirement should be calibrated to reflect actual historical redemption patterns instead of worst-case scenarios. One commenter stated that the OCC may need to revisit the 30 percent threshold for weekly liquidity at a later date to determine whether that threshold is still appropriate. A few commenters recommended raising the daily minimum liquid asset requirement, to at least 20 percent or 25 percent. One commenter recommended raising the weekly minimum liquidity requirement to 50 percent.
A commenter recommended that the timeframe used for the weekly liquidity framework should be calibrated to redemption expectations across the agencies. One commenter stated that the proposal would require issuers to honor redemption requests within two business days from the date of the redemption request. Accordingly, the commenter stated that liquidity and operational constraints would not prevent almost all permissible reserve assets from being monetized within the redemption window. Another commenter recommended that the rule clarify how issuers should comply with the daily and weekly liquidity requirements without maintaining a significantly high cash balance that does not promote the rule's liquidity objectives.
One commenter opposed the weekly liquidity requirement, stating that the requirement would not have a meaningful effect. This commenter stated that any reserve asset can be monetized within five business days. Several commenters opposed the daily liquidity requirement. Some commenters stated that the daily liquidity requirement would create unnecessary credit risk. One commenter stated that the minimum daily requirement is unnecessary because the scope of eligible reserve assets is highly liquid, as demonstrated by the requirements of SEC Rule 2a-7 (under which Treasury securities may count towards daily and weekly liquidity requirements). One commenter asserted that the 10 percent daily liquidity requirement lacks empirical or theoretical support and is inconsistent with international prudential standards, like the Basel III liquidity standards.
A few commenters recommended that the final rule adopt a principles-based approach in which issuers would be required to demonstrate the capability to monetize at least 10 percent and 30 percent of their reserves on an overnight and weekly basis, respectively. One of these commenters asserted that an issuer should be permitted to demonstrate its monetization capability through any combination of eligible reserve assets. Other commenters stated that a principles-based approach would permit issuers to hold reserves like tokenized money market funds, which have less credit risk than bank deposits and settle no later than the next day.
Several commenters commented on which assets should be eligible to count towards the daily and weekly liquidity requirements. One commenter recommended that eligible government money market funds offering same-day redemption should count towards the daily liquidity reserves requirement. A few commenters recommended that assets eligible to count towards the daily liquidity requirement should include reverse repurchase agreements, conducted on either an open or overnight basis. One commenter recommended that same- and next-day high-quality instruments should be
(
printed page 67054)
considered eligible reserve assets for purposes of the daily liquidity requirement. Another commenter suggested that all GENIUS Act-compliant reserve assets should count towards the daily liquidity requirement.
One commenter recommended that reserves for the weekly liquidity requirement should include any eligible reserve asset convertible to cash within five business days, including GENIUS Act-eligible money market funds. Such a liquidity framework, the commenter reasoned, would be focused on functional liquidity and, in turn, better reflect how liquidity is generated in funding markets. One commenter recommended that government money market funds should count towards the weekly liquidity requirement, as redemption and settlement typically occur within one business day. A few commenters recommended that qualifying registered funds, like exchange-traded funds, should count towards the weekly liquidity requirement, considering their short settlement period and their daily price and portfolio transparency.
One commenter stated that deposits are more vulnerable than custodied securities. One commenter noted that tokenized funds under SEC Rule 2a-7 are being developed primarily as collateral instruments rather than as cash payment instruments. One commenter suggested that any offset for expected inflows should be permitted only on a conservative basis. One commenter recommended that the OCC remove or replace the requirement in proposed § 15.11(c)(2)(ii) relating to Board review of the percentage of reserve assets required to be held that must be receivable within five days.
One commenter argued that concentration limits should be limited to uninsured deposit holdings because further concentration restrictions would add little stability and could increase operational and run risk or reduce reserve yields. This commenter also stated that it is not possible to apply concentration limits to United States Treasury repurchase agreements because there is only one remaining tri-party repurchase agreement clearing bank for United States Treasury repurchase agreements and it handles virtually all of the cleared tri-party repurchase agreement market.
Several commenters specifically addressed the proposed 40 percent concentration limit under the proposed safe harbor. A few commenters stated that the 40 percent limit was well calibrated. One commenter suggested the limit should be raised to 60 percent to reflect the limited number of custodians currently willing to serve stablecoin issuers. Another commenter suggested reducing the limit to 15 percent and explicitly prohibiting the use of affiliated bank deposits as qualified reserves unless ring-fenced under separate capitalization and governance structures. One commenter stated that the 40 percent threshold was too limiting and that permitted payment stablecoin issuers should have flexibility to use one or more custodians. One commenter noted the limit could be breached due to changes in asset prices rather than redemptions or transfers. Another commenter stated that concentration restrictions should be based on gross exposures, aggregated across affiliates, custody, deposits, and bilateral transactions. This commenter further suggested that, if the OCC adopts deposit concentration caps, they should be tiered by bank credit quality, distinguish between insured and uninsured exposure, and also distinguish between deposit exposure and collateralized repo exposure. Some commenters categorically objected to the 40 percent threshold. One commenter explained that the concentration limit would still allow large exposures in the form of uninsured deposits, which highlights problems associated with a single numerical threshold without distinguishing between private credit risk and infrastructure or custodian concentration. A few commenters suggested that concentration caps should be tiered based on the issuer's size, and one of these commenters also recommended higher limits for assets collateralized by United States Treasuries or held at systemically important financial institutions.
Several commenters argued that custodians or assets held in custody should be excluded from concentration limits. Some of these commenters stated that applying concentration and diversification limits to custodial arrangements would require permitted payment stablecoin issuers to manage a larger number of transactions across custodians, which increases the risk of operational and process errors without meaningfully reducing risks. One commenter stated that few institutions currently provide custodial services to issuers. A few commenters stated that custodians are highly regulated and pose little credit risk with respect to non-cash assets held off-balance sheet that are segregated from the custodian's proprietary assets. A few of these commenters stated that custodian-level concentration limits may introduce risks for permitted payment stablecoin issuers by fragmenting reserve assets across numerous custodians and banking relationships. One commenter stated that custodian diversification requirements would be novel, as SEC-registered money market funds and similar instruments are not subject to similar requirements, and could drive issuers away from the institutions best able to provide secure custody services. A few commenters suggested that concentration caps would be ineffective at preventing failures and could contribute to instability by spreading and potentially commingling reserve assets among the same set of large asset managers.
One commenter suggested that self-custodied assets should be explicitly excluded from the 40 percent limit. Another commenter suggested excluding deposits held at an OCC-regulated affiliate if the affiliate holds an equivalent amount of cash at its Federal Reserve master account and remains well-capitalized. A few commenters stated that the 40 percent cap should not apply to Federal Reserve Bank balances, and one of these commenters also suggested eliminating the cap for global systemically important banks (G-SIB).
Several commenters raised other criticisms of concentration limits. One commenter suggested the OCC exclude ETFs from the 40 percent requirement, or at a minimum explain the benefit of imposing the limit on ETFs, since shares are generally held through a third-party custodian subject to a legal and regulatory framework that addresses asset segregation and protects the investor in the event of the custodian's insolvency. This commenter also stated the 40 percent limit should not apply to self-custodied money market funds or on a look-through basis to a government money market fund's custodian or other service providers. One commenter stated that the 40 percent limit discourages the use of local banks for remote communities and proposed a higher limit for reserves held at insured depository institutions that are located in more remote areas and meet certain other criteria. One commenter stated that the 40 percent limit should apply specifically to uninsured deposits. One commenter suggested the OCC clarify the scope of “other exposures” and in particular should address whether and how intraday credit facilities, uncommitted liquidity lines, and custodial sub-arrangements extended by or through an eligible financial institution would count toward the cap.
A few commenters criticized the proposed look-through requirement. One of these commenters stated that the
(
printed page 67055)
approach would increase compliance costs and likely impose substantial monitoring and reporting burdens, which could also reduce operational efficiency and increase the risk of settlement delays or frictions. Another commenter stated that the requirement could create significant operational challenges since reserve assets may be held through omnibus accounts, sub-custody chains, or collateral-agent structures that do not map cleanly onto a single-institution concentration calculation. One commenter recommended removing the phrase “through other exposures” so that issuers would not need to “look through” sub-custodians to satisfy diversification requirements, as issuers would need to obtain and continuously monitor information about their custodians' internal sub-custodial arrangements and may be at risk of non-compliance due to subsequent events beyond their control. One commenter suggested the look-through requirement is unnecessary with respect to Treasury securities, repurchase agreements, and securities issued by a GENIUS Act-eligible investment fund, since these types of reserve assets ultimately reside with highly regulated central counterparties or central securities depositories.
A few commenters recommended that the OCC remove the requirement limiting the amount of daily liquidity an issuer may hold at one financial institution. They reasoned that the requirement is impractical and the risks associated with cash reserves held at regulated institutions are already effectively addressed within the existing prudential framework. A few commenters noted that ordinary transaction flows could cause an issuer to routinely breach a 50 percent limit on daily liquidity at a single institution, especially when an issuer places liquidity reserves in only two financial institutions. Commenters recommended the OCC address this issue by raising the limit to 60 percent or building flexibility into the limit on liquidity reserves held at a single institution.
A few commenters objected to the limits on deposit concentration, in whole or in part. One commenter suggested that there should be no limit on deposits at a single institution, and if such a deposit limit is established, the limit should be in the 20 to 25 percent range. Another commenter recommended that limits on deposits should not apply to insured deposits, and that, for uninsured deposits, the OCC should adopt a tiered limit for uninsured deposits that reflects historical loss rates. A few commenters advocated for the establishment of a lower deposit concentration limit, including more granular limitations. One commenter suggested that an issuer should be permitted to deposit no more than 5 percent of eligible reserve assets at depository institutions and have no more than 2 percent exposure to a single institution, with additional deposit balances permissible for purposes of operational liquidity.
Several commenters requested or suggested clarifications in the final rule regarding how to calculate the weighted average maturity. A few commenters requested confirmation that the weighted average maturity calculation would be performed on a portfolio basis, allowing issuers to hold a mix of maturities so long as the overall weighted average does not exceed the 20-day limit. Another commenter suggested the 20-day requirement be paired with amortized cost valuation. A commenter recommended that issuers whose stablecoins are predominantly used as settlement infrastructure for duration-bearing tokenized instruments be permitted to maintain a higher weighted average maturity, subject to supervisory approval. One commenter recommended that the weighted average maturity be extended in response to concentration in Treasury markets. Another commenter suggested the OCC have a two-year pilot program and modify the weighted average maturity requirements based on data collected during that timeframe. A few commenters opposed the use of SEC Rule 2a-7's methodology to calculate the weighted average maturity. One of these commenters explained that the key consideration for measuring liquidity is how quickly an issuer can convert a non-cash asset to cash. The commenter stated that use of the methodology in SEC Rule 2a-7 would effectively assign a 20- or 40-day maturity to funds with shares that can be redeemed at par in much less time. Because of the speed with which reserves can be redeemed, the commenter recommended the OCC assign a weighted average maturity of zero for money market funds.
Another commenter stated that payment stablecoins represent redemption-backed liabilities, whereas money market funds are investment products that seek to maintain stability of net asset value. Accordingly, the commenter stated that the calculation methodology under SEC Rule 2a-7, which includes “maturity-shortening provisions” for securities subject to a demand feature or interest rate reset, is not the appropriate measurement for stablecoin reserves. The commenter suggested that the final rule calculate maturity as the period remaining until the date on which, in accordance with the terms of the security, the principal amount must unconditionally be paid, or in the case of a security called for redemption, the date on which the redemption payment must be made. A few commenters supported the 20-day weighted average maturity requirement. Several other commenters opposed the 20-day weighted average maturity on various grounds. Several of these commenters were concerned that the weighted average maturity requirement would limit issuers' ownership of reserve assets with longer maturities, including Treasuries, which would otherwise be permissible under the GENIUS Act. Commenters also asserted that the 20-day weighted average maturity requirement would constrain efficient reserve management, increase operational risk by requiring investment in short-term assets that mature or roll over rapidly, and would impose compliance burdens on issuers, who would need to ensure that reserve assets do not breach the 20-day weighted average maturity requirement. A few commenters stated that the proposed 20-day weighted average maturity requirement would provide little, if any, benefit to an issuer's liquidity and redemption capabilities.
Several commenters recommended that the OCC increase the length of the weighted average maturity. A few commenters recommended increasing the length to 40 days, to allow smaller issuers more flexibility and to allow more issuers to use three-month Treasuries. A few commenters recommended increasing the length to 60 days to align with money market funds and SEC Rule 2a-7, and to afford issuers greater flexibility to use Treasuries. A few commenters recommended increasing the length to 93 days, to align with permitted Treasury holdings.
Several commenters proffered their views on how the reserve requirements of the proposed rule might affect community banks. One commenter, for example, noted that payment stablecoin reserves may not be as stable as demand deposits and thus may subject community banks to a greater run risk, while another noted that community banks for that reason may not be willing to provide services to permitted payment stablecoin issuers. Another commenter argued that reserve diffusion requirements could increase the financial stability risk of a run on one permitted payment stablecoin issuer throughout a large number of community banks. However, other
(
printed page 67056)
commenters worried that payment stablecoins will shift stable funding sources away from community banks, reducing their competitiveness, and believed that reserve asset diversification should be premised in part on the funding needs of community banks. A few commenters argued that diversification should be risk-based and should not increase the risks to permitted payment stablecoin issuers or payment stablecoin holders to achieve other aims.
The final rule neither mandates that permitted payment stablecoin issuers use community banks nor requires community banks to take on permitted payment stablecoin issuers as customers. The OCC believes that this approach appropriately allows community banks to exercise their business judgment with respect to payment stablecoin activities. The OCC acknowledges that deposits that serve as reserves backing a payment stablecoin could, at this time, be less stable sources of funding than other types of deposits. It is possible that these deposits may become more stable over time (
i.e.,
as the GENIUS Act framework continues to be implemented). At this point, in light of the comments received, the OCC believes that diversification requirements that neither mandate nor discourage placement at community banks are appropriate.
The final rule makes a number of changes to § 15.11(c) in response to the comments received. Specifically, the OCC is adopting a hybrid approach using the principles-based approach from Option A and a modified and limited set of the quantitative requirements from Option B. The proposed rule included robust liquidity requirements but did not include stress testing or buffer requirements. The proposal noted that an alternative possibility would be to remove some of the proposed liquidity requirements, though this may warrant increased capital or buffer requirements. The final rule substantially lessens the quantitative liquidity, diversification, and concentration requirements that apply to permitted payment stablecoin issuers and instead imposes stress testing and buffer requirements in §§ 15.11 and 15.13. The OCC recognizes that, as a permitted payment stablecoin issuer sells more liquid assets to meet redemption requests in times of stress, it may temporarily fail to satisfy all of the terms in § 15.11(c) of the final rule. For example, a permitted payment stablecoin issuer might draw first on its deposits to timely redeem payment stablecoins, and, as a result, may temporarily fall below the 5 percent minimum while it reconfigures its reserve asset portfolio. Depending on the facts and circumstances, negative supervisory consequences for a failure to maintain that 5 percent minimum may be inappropriate, and the OCC will consider any supervisory actions for such a temporary violation in light of the totality of the circumstances causing the violation. A permitted payment stablecoin issuer should nevertheless appropriately diversify its reserve assets as soon as practicable following such an event. However, at no point can a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's reserve asset value be less than the outstanding issuance value of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer.
Consistent with the proposed rule, § 15.11(c)(1) provides that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer must maintain reserve assets that are sufficiently diverse to manage potential credit, liquidity, interest rate, and price risks. The final rule clarifies in § 15.11(c)(1)(iii) that, depending on relevant factors, including a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's risk profile, business model, and portfolio of reserve assets, a permitted payment stablecoin issuer may need to maintain an amount of reserve assets that exceeds the requirements of § 15.11(c)(2) and the reserve asset value of which exceeds outstanding issuance value. A permitted payment stablecoin issuer must measure and manage the risk that concentrating reserve assets at one eligible financial institution or a small number of eligible financial institutions may impair the ability of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to satisfy redemption demands if individual eligible financial institutions are unable to return, or if there is a delay in returning, reserve assets placed by a permitted payment stablecoin issuer.
The final rule clarifies that, depending on relevant factors, including a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's risk profile, business model, and stock of reserve assets, a permitted payment stablecoin issuer may need to maintain reserve assets in excess of the daily liquidity amounts required under paragraph (c)(2) (discussed below). The OCC believes that this baseline principles-based approach, supplemented with the quantitative requirements described below, provides permitted payment stablecoin issuers sufficient flexibility while also providing a backstop against key risks that could result from undue concentration in assets that may be difficult to monetize within a day or exposures to a single counterparty. Permitted payment stablecoin issuers with less complex business models and lower risk profiles may be able to maintain a less diverse stock of reserve assets than permitted payment stablecoin issuers with more complex business models or higher risk profiles. However, section 4(a)(4)(A)(iii) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(4)(A)(iii)
) mandates some reserve asset diversification for all permitted payment stablecoin issuers, both in types of reserve assets maintained and in the number of eligible financial institutions holding a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's reserve assets. The OCC expects that all permitted payment stablecoin issuers will need to maintain multiple reserve asset types, if only to serve as a backup to what is otherwise a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's primary reserve asset. Some permitted payment stablecoin issuers may need to maintain more robustly diverse stocks of reserve assets to satisfy § 15.11(c), depending on their business model, risk profile, and other relevant factors. For example, a large permitted payment stablecoin issuer with complex operations may need to maintain deposits with multiple eligible financial institutions, as well as a stock of Treasury bills, potentially custodied with more than one eligible financial institution in order to ensure they are capable of being monetized during periods of financial stress. Factors such as the number of parties that redeem directly with the permitted payment stablecoin issuer, the volume of redemptions (and volatility with respect to such volume), and the number and nature of the blockchains on which a payment stablecoin is traded could all increase the complexity of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's operations and weigh in favor of maintaining multiple different pools of reserve assets.
Section 15.11(c)(2) of the final rule provides a modified version of the daily liquidity and counterparty concentration requirement from the proposed rule. Section 15.11(c)(2)(i) requires a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to maintain at least 5 percent of its reserve assets as demand deposits (or other deposits that may be withdrawn upon request at any time), funds in share accounts that are payable on demand, or money standing to the credit of an account with a Federal Reserve Bank.
[
88
]
This minimum daily liquidity requirement is intended to ensure that a payment stablecoin issuer has readily
(
printed page 67057)
available funds necessary to meet redemption requests. While all of the proposed reserve assets should be liquid and easily monetizable, the requirement to have some minimum level of immediately liquid funds provides additional protection against the risk that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer would be unable to meet redemption requests in a timely manner, which is critical to maintain confidence in the permitted payment stablecoin issuer and the stablecoin industry as a whole. Including a baseline requirement to maintain a minimum percentage of liquidity that is immediately available (without the need to sell any assets, even highly liquid assets like Treasury securities) will help ensure a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's ability to meet redemption requests. In light of other changes to §§ 15.11(a) and 15.13 (
e.g.,
stress testing requirements), the final rule lowers this daily liquidity requirement from 10 percent to 5 percent of reserve assets. The requirements of §§ 15.11(a) and 15.13 are designed to ensure that permitted payment stablecoin issuers are able to timely redeem payment stablecoins, including in times of stress. Since these requirements will necessarily entail measures the permitted payment stablecoin issuer must take to maintain capacity to meet short-term redemption requests, it is appropriate to lower the quantitative requirement for daily liquidity. For example, when a permitted payment stablecoin issuer has capabilities to monetize reserve assets quickly because a large portion of their reserve assets is in the form of Treasury securities, whether held directly or by a custodian, that may obviate the need to hold a higher amount of daily liquidity.
The final rule does not include the requirement from proposed § 15.11(c)(4) requiring no more than 50 percent of daily liquidity to be held at any one eligible financial institution in light of the fact that the total requirement has been reduced to 5 percent (the total amount of required daily liquidity that could be held at a single eligible financial institution under the proposed rule). The OCC notes that, under § 15.12, a permitted payment stablecoin issuer must notify the OCC when it receives redemption requests in excess of 10 percent of its outstanding issuance value over a single 24-hour period. As discussed elsewhere, permitted payment stablecoin issuers that hold only 5 percent of their reserve assets as demand deposits or money standing to the credit of a Federal Reserve Bank should take steps to ensure that they can timely redeem tendered payment stablecoins under stressed conditions.
Section 15.11(c)(2)(ii)(A) of the final rule requires a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to limit its exposure to any one counterparty to no more than 40 percent of its reserve assets. Section 15.11(c)(2)(ii)(B) lists various exposures that are not subject to this limitation. Under the final rule, the following exposures are excluded: (1) exposures to the United States Government, (2) exposures to an appropriate custodian (as described in § 15.11(d)), resulting from reserve assets being held in the custody of the custodian, and (3) exposures resulting from centrally cleared repurchase agreements and centrally cleared reverse repurchase agreements. For clarity, reserve assets held directly by a permitted payment stablecoin issuer also are not subject to the 40 percent limit in § 15.11(c)(2)(ii)(A) because the permitted payment stablecoin issuer cannot be its own counterparty. The requirement in § 15.11(c)(2)(ii) is intended to prevent an issuer from being overly exposed to any one eligible financial institution or counterparty, including through a deposit relationship, bilateral repurchase agreement, bilateral reverse repurchase agreement, or investment company. While this requirement would not eliminate the chance of either temporarily or permanently losing reserve assets because of distress at an eligible financial institution holding reserve assets, it would ensure that permitted payment stablecoin issuers have other reserve assets available to satisfy redemption requests. The final rule modifies the counterparty limit by explicitly excluding exposures to the United States Government. As discussed above, exposures to Federal Reserve Banks would remain subject to this limit. The final rule excludes exposures resulting from centrally cleared repurchase agreements and reverse repurchase agreements due to the low credit risk associated with such transactions.
The final rule also does not apply the 40 percent limit to custodians that meet certain requirements (as discussed in greater detail below). The OCC agrees with commenters that imposing a limit on custodians that comply with the requirements of the GENIUS Act may introduce unnecessary operational risks without a corresponding benefit. At the same time, it is important that there are mechanisms in the final rule to help ensure that custodians of reserve assets comply with the terms of the GENIUS Act if they are to be exempt from the 40 percent limit. Accordingly, as discussed in the next section, the final rule imposes certain additional requirements on permitted payment stablecoin issuers with respect to custodians designed to ensure that the custodians comply with the requirements of the GENIUS Act.
Paragraph (c) of the final rule's § 15.11 does not include a weighted average maturity requirement. The OCC believes that changes to §§ 15.11(a) and 15.13 will be sufficient to ensure that the reserve asset portfolio of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer is sufficiently liquid without imposing a separate weighted average maturity requirement.
e. Custody of Reserve Assets (§ 15.11(d))
Self-Custody and Use of Affiliates
Several commenters suggested that the OCC place significant limits on, or prohibit, an issuer holding its reserve assets itself (self-custody). These commenters argued that self-custody and captive affiliate structures can undermine the independence of the custody function and create conflicts of interest inconsistent with safety and soundness. Some commenters stated that the proposed rule does not provide sufficient clarity on how self-custody would work in practice, including: (i) whether a permitted payment stablecoin issuer holding reserves directly would qualify as the covered customer or an eligible financial institution, (ii) how reserve assets would be segregated from proprietary assets, and (iii) whether the custody function would need to be separated from issuance and reserve management activities. A few commenters noted that, if self-custody is permitted, permitted payment stablecoin issuers should be required to maintain clear segregation, bankruptcy-remote protections, and operational separation. Some commenters argued that additional capital requirements should apply because the permitted payment stablecoin issuer would be assuming risks otherwise borne by an external custodian. Other commenters opposed intragroup reserve arrangements and urged the OCC to apply concentration limits across affiliated entities on a consolidated basis rather than institution by institution. In contrast, a couple of commenters stated that the OCC should not mandate fixed minimum allocations of reserve assets between affiliated and unaffiliated custodians and instead should focus on operational resilience, concentration risk, and effective segregation while allowing issuers flexibility in structuring custody arrangements.
Many commenters addressed how reserve assets should be managed when
(
printed page 67058)
a permitted payment stablecoin issuer is affiliated with, or is a subsidiary of, an insured depository institution. Some commenters stated that affiliated custody arrangements should be subject to consistent risk management standards and that reserve assets, liquidity-management functions, and control frameworks should be clearly maintained at the subsidiary level, with dedicated personnel, independent governance, and clear entity-level accountability to reduce the risk of internal commingling, competing liquidity demands, or unclear authority during stress. In contrast, one commenter stated that the OCC should not impose permitted payment stablecoin issuer-specific governance or staffing mandates on bank-subsidiary issuers and should allow them to use centralized group treasury and risk functions so long as applicable statutory standards are met. Another commenter opposed any exception from concentration caps that would allow an insured depository institution subsidiary to place all reserves at its parent or an affiliate. These commenters argued that statutory flexibility for omnibus commingling increases, rather than reduces, the need to avoid single-bank dependency and ensure strong segregation, control, and auditability.
Several commenters stated that the OCC should add additional requirements in instances in which a permitted payment stablecoin issuer custodies reserve assets or deposits cash reserve assets at an affiliate. These commenters stated that affiliate custody of reserve assets may give rise to significant risks as there is no independent custodian to provide an added layer of protection to holders of the relevant payment stablecoin. Commenters suggested, for example, either limiting the amount of reserves that may be custodied or deposited at an affiliate, imposing enhanced capital buffers, or including affiliate concentration risk as a factor that the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's independent accountant must consider.
The final rule, consistent with the proposal and the text of the GENIUS Act, does not prohibit self-custody of reserve assets or the use of an affiliate to hold reserve assets in custody. As discussed below, direct reserve asset holdings will not be subject to a counterparty limit but non-custodial exposures to affiliates will be. The OCC notes that, in the case of subsidiaries of national banks or Federal savings associations, the OCC will have clear visibility into the business of the parent and the subsidiary, through the supervisory process. The OCC agrees with commenters that reserve assets should be operationally separate from the other assets of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer. The OCC notes that § 15.11(a)(1)(ii) requires a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to maintain reserve assets that are identifiable and that are segregated and not commingled with other assets owned or held by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer. In addition, as discussed elsewhere, the final rule has been designed to permit the use of separate issuer SPVs, such that the reserve assets of each issuer would be segregated from one another. Finally, with respect to affiliate transactions, the OCC notes that insider and affiliate transactions must comply with the requirements of § 15.13 (described in greater detail below).
Fiduciary Responsibilities
Commenters expressed differing opinions on whether fiduciary treatment should be avoided to reduce regulatory uncertainty or required to strengthen segregation and insolvency protections. A few commenters suggested that the OCC clarify whether directed custody of reserve assets constitutes a fiduciary activity under
12 CFR part 9
. Some commenters stated that directed, non-discretionary custody should not be treated as fiduciary by default unless the custodian independently performs a fiduciary function identified in part 9. In contrast, one commenter stated that reserve assets should be required to be held in a fiduciary capacity and that all institutions with custody of stablecoin reserves should hold those assets in a legally segregated manner for the exclusive benefit of stablecoin holders. That commenter also noted that fiduciary custody at a national trust bank provides stronger insolvency protections because the assets are not part of the custodian's estate, unlike ordinary deposits at a depository bank, which become general liabilities of the bank. The OCC declines to make a blanket statement that directed custody of reserve assets is a fiduciary activity. Whether a custodian is subject to
12 CFR part 9
or
12 CFR part 150
will depend, among other factors, on the charter type of the custodian and applicable law, including the agreement that the custodian has with its customer.
Some commenters stated that responsibility for determining whether assets qualify as permissible reserve assets, whether reserves are sufficient on a portfolio-wide basis, and how reserves should be classified or reported should remain with the issuer rather than the custodian. Other commenters noted that custodians often lack visibility into an issuer's full reserve portfolio, particularly where multiple custodians or intermediaries are used, and therefore should not be required to independently verify reserve composition, adequacy, sufficiency, or compliance with diversification and concentration requirements. As discussed in greater detail below, the OCC confirms that the permitted payment stablecoin issuer remains responsible for ensuring compliance with all requirements in the GENIUS Act and implementing regulations related to reserve assets and other requirements pertaining to its issuance of payment stablecoins.
[
89
]
Covered custodians under subpart C of the final rule are responsible for compliance with requirements contained within the GENIUS Act and subpart C related to appropriate custody of reserve assets and other covered assets.
Obligations of Third-Party Custodians To Ensure Compliance
Commenters addressed oversight of custodians, service providers, and counterparties, with some stating that permitted payment stablecoin issuers should conduct thorough initial due diligence and ongoing monitoring of custodians' legal status, financial condition, operational resilience, cybersecurity, and compliance programs, consistent with third-party risk management principles. In contrast, one commenter suggested that permitted payment stablecoin issuers should not be required to monitor the financial condition of all depository institutions holding reserve assets because those institutions are already subject to robust prudential regulation. Another commenter stated that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer should continuously monitor the condition of its counterparties and treat concentration risk as risk-sensitive.
One commenter suggested that the OCC clarify that third-party custodians are not responsible for ensuring that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer or foreign payment stablecoin issuer directs reserve assets to the correct account, such as a reserve account rather than a proprietary account. The commenter stated that, consistent with the futures commission merchant framework, the issuer should bear responsibility for segregation and avoiding commingling, while the custodian's role should be limited to
(
printed page 67059)
recognizing and maintaining the designated account as separate. This commenter also noted that custodians should not be required to verify the sufficiency of reserve assets held by a permitted payment stablecoin issuer at the custodian or be subject to additional requirements with respect to transaction services they provide. One commenter requested that the OCC expressly confirm that prior OCC guidance, including Interpretive Letter 1172, to the extent it required custodians to monitor 1 to 1 reserve sufficiency, has been superseded by the GENIUS Act framework. Another commenter requested additional clarity regarding reserve assets held through custodians or intermediaries, including governance, control, and access rights.
As discussed in greater detail below, the final rule has been modified to provide additional clarity and notice to custodians. With respect to Interpretive Letter 1172, the OCC notes that the letter addressed deposit-taking activity and not custody. Nevertheless, the OCC confirms that a national bank or Federal savings association that holds deposits that serve as reserves or that holds other reserve assets in custody is not under an obligation to ensure that the reserve assets equal or exceed the outstanding issuance value of the payment stablecoin unless otherwise required by contract.
Under § 15.11(d) of the final rule, reserve assets in the custody of one or more eligible financial institutions will not be subject to the 40 percent limit in § 15.11(c)(2)(ii) provided that the permitted payment stablecoin issuer: (1) identifies itself to the custodian as a permitted payment stablecoin issuer; (2) ensures that the custodian commits to adhering to the requirements of section 10 of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5909
), including applicable implementing regulations; and (3) engages in appropriate due diligence and ongoing monitoring of its custodial arrangements to ensure compliance with applicable requirements of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5901
et seq.
), including applicable implementing regulations. These changes are intended to benefit custodians by providing them notice of when their obligations under section 10 of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5909
) attach. In addition, the requirements make clear that the permitted payment stablecoin issuer has an ongoing responsibility to conduct appropriate monitoring of the custodians that it employs. The OCC believes that this ongoing monitoring requirement will be both more effective and less burdensome than imposing a hard limit on the amount of exposure that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer can have to a single custodian. The final rule's approach requires a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to take appropriate steps to ensure that its custodians comply with the GENIUS Act. This puts an emphasis on understanding and analyzing the activities of custodians, whereas the proposal could have allowed a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to meet its obligations merely by diversifying among different custodians without engaging with the substance of the custodians' activities.
