f. Minimum Insured Deposit Requirement for Large Issuers
Proposed § 15.11(d) would have required a permitted payment stablecoin issuer with an outstanding issuance value of $25 billion or more to, on each business day, maintain at least 0.5 percent of its reserve assets in the form of insured deposits or insured shares at an insured depository institution, up to a cap of $500 million.
Several commenters opposed the proposed insured-deposit minimum. These commenters explained that the insured-deposit minimum would add significant operational complexity and liquidity risk without providing a commensurate prudential benefit, especially for large operational deposit balances that do not meaningfully benefit from deposit insurance. Regarding liquidity risk, a commenter asserted that many deposit insurance schemes have tighter settlement cutoff times than traditional demand deposit accounts, which would increase operational risk if reserves would not be immediately available. Furthermore, the FDIC's proposed restrictions on insured reserve balances would further complicate operationalizing the insured-deposit minimum requirement. A few commenters asserted that the OCC lacks the statutory authority to require issuers to place a percentage of reserve assets in numerous banks through the minimum insured deposit requirement. One commenter noted that the FDIC does not insure deposits above the $250,000 corporate limit, a limit that could render the minimum insured deposit requirement operationally infeasible. A commenter stated that the minimum insured deposit requirement would confuse stablecoin holders regarding what percentage of reserve assets are insured. Another commenter asserted that the requirement would unduly restrict an issuer's ability to manage counterparty and credit risk. One commenter noted that it is expensive to open numerous deposit accounts, and the costs necessary to comply with the minimum insured deposit requirement could impede the adoption of stablecoins.
One commenter requested clarification on how the minimum insured deposit requirement interacts with FDIC deposit insurance limits and capacity constraints at insured depository institutions. A few commenters suggested that if the minimum insured deposit requirement is finalized, it should not exceed the smaller of $100 million or 0.1 percent of reserve assets. A commenter recommended the OCC calibrate the minimum insured deposit requirement to recognize the distinction between reserves held at smaller banks and other institutions.
A few commenters were in favor of establishing a minimum insured deposit requirement and asserted that the proposed $25 billion threshold for issuers to be subject to the minimum insured deposit requirement is too high to prevent runs, de-pegging, and contagion. One of these commenters recommended lowering the threshold from $25 billion to $10 billion and raising the requisite percentage of reserve assets comprising insured deposits or shares from 0.5 percent to 5 percent, with total insured deposits or shares not to exceed $500 million regardless of the size of the issuer. A commenter opined that it is too early to determine whether all reserve deposits should be required to be insured in the event deposit insurance rules change, and that the final rule should not address such a requirement.
One commenter supported permitting issuers to use deposit placement services to comply with the GENIUS Act's diversification requirements for stablecoin reserves, subject to appropriate due diligence, including independent audit reports and Federal Financial Institutions Examination Council examinations. A few commenters opposed the use of deposit placement services for compliance with the diversification requirements, as the addition of intermediaries would increase operational complexity and counterparty risk.
After careful consideration of the comments, the OCC is not adopting a requirement to have a minimum insured deposit amount. The OCC agrees with commenters that this minimum requirement may introduce additional operational risk that does not merit the
(
printed page 67060)
reduction in credit risk associated with having a minimum insured amount.
g. Composition Report, Monthly Certification, and Failure To Maintain Minimum Reserve Assets (§§ 15.11(e) Through (g))
i. Description of the Proposed Rule
Proposed § 15.11(e) would have required a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to publish on its website by noon on the last day of each month the composition of the issuer's reserves held pursuant to the GENIUS Act as of noon of the last day of the prior month, using a format substantially similar to the template provided in table 1 to proposed § 15.11(e). The report contained fields for the total number of outstanding payment stablecoins issued by the issuer and the amount (fair value) and composition of the reserves, including the average tenor and geographic location of custody of each category of reserve instruments. The information in the report, including the value of reserve assets, would have been reported as of the end of the previous month. Section 15.11(e) of the proposed rule would have implemented the requirement in section 4(a)(1)(C) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(C)
).
Proposed § 15.11(f) implemented the applicable requirements of section 4(a)(3) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(3)
). This provision requires permitted payment stablecoin issuers to, each month, have the information disclosed in the previous month-end report examined by a registered public accounting firm. Proposed § 15.11(f)(1) would have required the examination of the previous month-end report to occur by noon on the last day of each month and would have required the report to be published on the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's website at the same time as the monthly report required under proposed § 15.11(e). Consistent with the Act, proposed § 15.11(f)(2) would have required the Chief Executive Officer and Chief Financial Officer (or the persons performing the equivalent functions) of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer to submit to the OCC a certification that the monthly report is accurate. Under section 4(a)(3)(C) of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(3)(C)
), any person who submits this required certification knowing that such certification is false shall be subject to the same criminal penalties as those set forth under
18 U.S.C. 1350(c)
.
Proposed § 15.11(g) set forth the consequences and remedial measures that would have applied if a permitted payment stablecoin issuer did not comply with the requirements of proposed § 15.11. Proposed § 15.11(g)(1) would have required a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to notify the OCC through its appropriate supervisory office on any day in which its reserve asset amount has fallen below the required minimum in proposed § 15.11(a). Proposed § 15.11(g)(2) would have barred a permitted payment stablecoin issuer that falls below the required minimum from issuing new payment stablecoins until it had remediated the shortfall except as necessary to facilitate a transfer of payment stablecoins from one distributed ledger to another and provided that the net outstanding issuance value does not increase. Proposed § 15.11(g)(3) provided that, if a permitted payment stablecoin issuer fails to meet its reserve asset requirement for 15 consecutive business days, it must begin liquidation of reserve assets and redemption of outstanding payment stablecoins consistent with § 15.12 and may not charge customers a fee to redeem their payment stablecoins at any time during the liquidation. The OCC would have been able to extend the time period under proposed § 15.11(g)(3) in its sole discretion. Because of the importance of maintaining minimum reserve asset levels, the proposed rule included automatic consequences for any non-compliance intended to prevent any concerns from developing further. This provision was intended to prevent chronic non-compliance with minimum reserve asset requirements. Proposed § 15.11(g)(4) stated that if at any point the OCC determined that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer had not demonstrated that it meets the reserve asset requirements in proposed § 15.11(a), (b), (c), or (d), the OCC may require the issuer to submit a plan describing how the permitted payment stablecoin issuer will attain compliance and the timeline for the plan. If the OCC determined, either before or after the submission of a plan, that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer faces a significant risk of being unable to attain compliance with the reserve requirements in proposed § 15.11(a), (b), (c), or (d) within a reasonable period, the OCC would have been able to order the issuer to initiate redemption of all outstanding payment stablecoins. Proposed § 15.11(g)(4) also stated that the OCC's authority to require a compliance plan or order redemption did not limit the OCC's authority to pursue other measures, including enforcement actions, if appropriate.
ii. Description of Comments and the Final Rule
Commenters generally supported proposed § 15.11(e) through (g), although some had a few suggested changes. With respect to § 15.11(e) and (f), several commenters suggested that the once-a-month reporting standard be dropped in favor of enhanced reporting,
[
91
]
such as through implementing random floating day attestations or surprise examinations. The OCC is not requiring an additional random floating day attestation at this time. The OCC has broad supervisory authority and may examine permitted payment stablecoin issuers, as appropriate, including on an immediate basis. In addition, the OCC will receive detailed information from permitted payment stablecoin issuers each week and will have the ability to flag any unusual activity using this information. In light of that, the OCC believes that imposing a random floating day attestation requirement across all issuers is unnecessary at this time. Permitted payment stablecoin issuers may, nevertheless, decide to engage in random-day reporting and certification as a best practice.
One commenter suggested that the monthly certification section be made public. Under the final rule, the report required under § 15.11(f)(1) must be made public and the certification required under § 15.11(f)(2) must be submitted to the OCC. Permitted payment stablecoin issuers or the OCC may choose to publish the certification. If a permitted payment stablecoin issuer failed to provide a certification, the OCC would take appropriate supervisory action. One commenter recommended using particular criteria for the monthly composition report. The OCC believes that the proposed criteria, supplemented by the reporting that the OCC will receive under § 15.14, is sufficient.
One commenter recommended that the OCC consider the Stablecoin Presentation and Disclosure Criteria developed by the AICPA in its rulemaking, recognizing that these criteria are already in use today and will continue to serve as the basis for issuer reporting and CPA examinations. Another commenter suggested the final rule specify that § 15.11(f) examinations are to be performed in accordance with the AICPA' Statements on Standards for Attestation Engagements, which could suggest particular assurance and
(
printed page 67061)
independence standards for these examinations. The OCC recognizes that certain industry criteria have been adopted by accounting firms in evaluating disclosures by stablecoin issuers today, and the OCC recognizes the importance of suitable criteria for examination engagements that are relevant, objective, measurable, complete, and available for users of the report. However, the final rule does not mandate any particular criteria so long as the examination meets the statutory requirements under the GENIUS Act to preserve flexibility as industry standards continue to develop.
The proposed rule requested comments on the treatment of white-label arrangements or other arrangements where a single issuer issues multiple payment stablecoins. Several commenters stated that nothing in the GENIUS Act prohibits such arrangements. Other commenters noted that if such arrangements are allowed, the OCC should implement additional requirements. For example, several commenters requested clarification regarding whether proposed § 15.11(a)(1)(ii)'s requirement that reserve assets be segregated from other assets owned or held by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer applied as well to payment stablecoins issued on multiple blockchains (that is, whether the reserves backing issuances on each blockchain need to be segregated from each other or can be placed in an omnibus account). The OCC confirms that it is not necessary to separate reserve assets by blockchain for a payment stablecoin that is issued under a single brand. For example, a single brand of payment stablecoin could be available on both blockchain A and blockchain B. The payment stablecoin could be backed by a single pool of reserve assets. That pool of reserve assets would be subject to the identification and segregation requirements of § 15.11(a)(1)(ii) of the final rule. Some commenters argued against allowing issuers to commingle the reserves of each payment stablecoin or to utilize a combined report under proposed section 15.11(e), as that could increase the risk that holders of one stablecoin are affected by deficient reserves of a separately marketed payment stablecoin. One commenter suggested that risks related to multi-brand issuers are best addressed through disclosure requirements akin to the treatment of white-labeled deposit or prepaid banking products.
The final rule adopts § 15.11(e) of the proposed rule with minor changes. Specifically, the OCC is adding new paragraph (e)(1) and renumbering paragraphs (e)(1) and (e)(2) to (e)(1)(i) and (e)(1)(ii), respectively. The OCC is also making certain clarifying edits throughout.
The final rule also makes edits to Table 1 to paragraph (e). Table 1 to paragraph (e) provides a template for the monthly composition report. Table 1 has been updated to reflect the definition of reserve asset value. Footnote 1 to the table provides guidance as to how to report if an issuer issues multiple classes of payment stablecoins. The final rule revises this footnote to make clear that permitted payment stablecoin issuers should separately list different classes or brands, if applicable. The OCC has generally used these terms interchangeably and is making this revision for clarity. The footnote also states that, if a class or brand is secured by distinct pools of reserve assets, the permitted payment stablecoin issuer should describe both the operational and legal mechanisms for separately securing each brand or class (the proposal did not address operational mechanisms). Finally, consistent with other changes to the final rule, the OCC has revised footnote 1 to provide additional clarity for entities that use multiple separate issuer SPVs to issue payment stablecoins. The final rule makes clear that, if different payment stablecoins are issued by distinct issuers, such as SPV issuers, there should be a separate composition report for each class or brand. The final rule adopts § 15.11(f) as proposed with certain clarifying edits.
Regarding the consequences for failing to meet minimum reserve asset requirements in proposed § 15.11(g), commenters were largely supportive but offered various amendments or requested clarifications. Regarding the required notification in § 15.11(g)(1), one commenter requested that the OCC specify the exact format, submission mechanism, and timing window for the notification. The OCC is not revising the rule text in response to this comment. The final rule specifies that the permitted payment stablecoin issuer must provide notice through its supervisory office on any day in which the reserve asset amount falls below the required amount. The OCC believes that this is sufficient guidance and that adopting an overly formalistic submission mechanism may serve to delay prompt notification.
Regarding the prohibitions that are triggered if a permitted payment stablecoin issuer fails to satisfy the 1 to 1 reserve asset requirement at any time, several commenters asked that the OCC clarify that this does not apply to temporary and immaterial intraday shortfalls arising from normal settlement timing differences. These commenters are incorrect; the reserve asset requirement applies at all times and does not allow for shortfalls. It is important that payment stablecoin holders have confidence that their payment stablecoins are appropriately backed at all times, consistent with section 4(a)(1)(A) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(A)
), which does not require that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer only maintain 1 to 1 backing on an end-of-day basis. The OCC has, however, made one change to § 15.11(g)(2)(i) in response to comments. The final rule provides that the OCC may permit a permitted payment stablecoin issuer that is under-reserved to issue new payment stablecoins. This additional language will provide additional flexibility to address situations where it may be appropriate to allow a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to continue issuing when under-reserved while ensuring that an under-reserved permitted payment stablecoin issuer remains subject to appropriate scrutiny.
Regarding the 15-consecutive-business-day trigger period for reserve asset liquidation in proposed § 15.11(g)(3), commenters expressed views on both the length of the period and the consequences. First, one commenter stated that the 15-day threshold is too permissive and should be based on a failure for 12 days in any 15-day period. Another commenter believed the 15-day period was reasonable but stated that the OCC should retain discretion to accelerate the period for material shortfalls. Second, several commenters cautioned against automatic liquidation thresholds, arguing that this could be overly punitive and could be more likely to result in fire sales. Instead, these commenters suggested either that the issuers implement gradual remediation or wind-down plans or else that the OCC establish tailored remediation timelines based on the nature and severity of the shortfall. The OCC believes that the flexibility in paragraph (g)(4) eliminates the need for any revisions. If an issuer fails to be adequately reserved for a significant period, the OCC could require a remediation plan or order the redemption of all outstanding payment stablecoins of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer even if the issuer did not trigger the automatic redemption provisions in § 15.11(g)(3). The OCC also disagrees with the commenters who cautioned against automatic liquidation
(
printed page 67062)
thresholds. In the first instance, the OCC reiterates the importance of permitted payment stablecoin issuers meeting their required reserve levels at all times. Second, the OCC notes that the OCC has discretion to extend the 15 consecutive-business-day period. Thus, if circumstances warranted an extension, the OCC could provide one.
In § 15.11(g), the agency is finalizing the rule as proposed with certain clarifying edits throughout, including using the phrase “minimum reserve asset amount required by paragraph (a) of this section” for consistency in § 15.11(g)(1), (g)(2), and (g)(3). Additionally, in § 15.11(g)(2)(i), the OCC is clarifying that a noncompliant permitted payment stablecoin issuer may issue new payment stablecoins if permitted by the OCC. The OCC is also making technical changes to § 15.11(g)(4) and splitting that paragraph into three paragraphs (g)(4)(i) through (g)(4)(iii).
Other Comments
Exceptions for Smaller Issuers That Are Subsidiaries of OCC-Regulated Depository Institutions
Commenters had a variety of views concerning potential exceptions from the requirements of § 15.11. A commenter opposed creating an exception for smaller issuers or issuers that are subsidiaries of insured depository institutions from the proposal's concentration and diversification requirements. One commenter supported the use of narrow exceptions from the proposal's concentration and diversification requirements, subject to enhanced disclosure requirements. A few commenters recommended that the exception for a subsidiary of an insured depository institution should be limited to parent institutions that are well capitalized. One of these commenters also supported permitting subsidiaries of insured depository institutions to hold all reserve assets as deposits at the parent institution only if the parent institution holds an equivalent amount of cash in its Federal Reserve master account. The commenter also suggested permitting reserve assets to be held in a designated sub-account of the parent institution's master account or in the master account of the subsidiary issuer.
The OCC is not revising the rule in response to these comments. The OCC believes that applying the same general standards to permitted payment stablecoin issuers that are subsidiaries of insured depository institutions and those that are not will enhance the safety and soundness of permitted payment stablecoin issuers, help to ensure financial stability, and facilitate competitive equity among different types of issuers. The OCC notes, however, that several of the requirements in the final rule are principles-based and tailored based on the size and complexity of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer. Thus, certain smaller and less complex permitted payment stablecoin issuers may be able to achieve compliance with these provisions using a simpler approach than that which would be necessary for a large and complex permitted payment stablecoin issuer.
Reserve Asset Management, Mechanics, and Operations
The OCC requested comments on whether to include additional measures to address de-pegging in the secondary market. Several commenters responded that the OCC should not consider secondary market transactions owing to the risk of market manipulation or a potential lack of depth or reliability. The final rule does not include additional text concerning secondary market transactions except in the context of final § 15.16 (where such transactions are a factor the OCC may consider in determining whether unusual and exigent circumstances exist). While the OCC believes that secondary market transactions may provide important supervisory information (and the OCC intends to review such information for supervisory purposes), the requirements of the GENIUS Act do not impose requirements on permitted payment stablecoin issuers regarding reserve assets that directly bear on secondary market transactions.
3. Redemption (§ 15.12)
a. Overview of Changes From Proposed Rule to Final Rule for § 15.12
As described below, the OCC is adding new paragraph (a) (and renumbering subsequent paragraphs appropriately). This new paragraph addresses the timeline for redemption.
The OCC is adopting paragraph (a) as proposed other than renumbering it to paragraph (b), changing a reference from “customer” to “payment stablecoin holder,” adding “in the policy” before the colon, and making other conforming edits to reflect the renumbering of paragraphs in final § 15.12.
The OCC is adopting paragraph (b) as proposed other than renumbering it to paragraph (c) in the final rule and making clarifying edits. The reserved numbering for proposed § 15.12(b)(2) has been removed, which led to a renumbering and a minor clarifying edit in final § 15.12(c).
The OCC is renumbering proposed paragraph (c) to paragraph (d) and eliminating the automatic redemption provision that was contained in proposed § 15.12(c)(1) and described in proposed § 15.12(c)(2) and (c)(3). Section 15.12(d)(1) of the final rule provides that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer must provide notice to the OCC through its supervisory office within 24 hours if it receives redemption requests in excess of 10 percent of the outstanding issuance value of any brand of payment stablecoin issued by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer in a single 24-hour period. Under § 15.12(d)(2) of the final rule, a permitted payment stablecoin issuer that experiences redemption requests in excess of 10 percent of the outstanding issuance value of any brand of payment stablecoin issued by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer in a single 24-hour period may request that the OCC extend the timeframe for timely redemption. Under § 15.12(d)(3) of the final rule, the OCC may, in its discretion, grant or deny an extension request or impose discretionary limitations upon timely redemption in accordance with section 4(a)(1)(B)(i) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(B)(i)
).
The OCC is renumbering proposed paragraph (d) to paragraph (e), changing references from “customer” to “payment stablecoin holders,” and making other conforming edits to reflect the renumbering of paragraphs in final § 15.12. Where proposed § 15.12(d)(1)(iii) required disclosure of a link to the monthly composition report, final § 15.12(e)(1)(iii) requires disclosure of a web page that includes a link to the same report. The OCC is also adding new § 15.12(e)(1)(v), which would require a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to disclose that payment stablecoins are not legal tender, issued by the United States, or guaranteed or approved by the United States. The OCC is also adding new § 15.12(e)(1)(vi) which requires a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to disclose that payment stablecoins are not deposits and are not backed by the full faith and credit of the United States, subject to deposit insurance by the FDIC, or subject to share insurance by the National Credit Union Administration. The OCC is removing the surplus phrase “that it provides” from § 15.12(e)(4). Finally, the OCC is adding new § 15.12(f) to clarify that the OCC will not require a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to redeem a payment stablecoin
(
printed page 67063)
to the extent the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's actions to redeem the payment stablecoin would cause the issuer to violate other applicable law.
b. Description of the Proposed Rule
Section 15.12 of the proposed rule addressed redemption requirements imposed by section 4(a)(1)(B) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(B)
). Consistent with the statute, under proposed § 15.12(a), a permitted payment stablecoin issuer must publicly disclose its redemption policy.
[
92
]
The OCC proposed that, in disclosing its redemption policy, the issuer must include, at a minimum, certain information. Specifically, proposed § 15.12(a)(1) provided that the issuer must include a timeframe in which the issuer will redeem payment stablecoins and the timeframe under which the issuer is required to redeem payment stablecoins (which, under proposed § 15.12(b)(1)(i) may not exceed two business days following the date of the requested redemption). Proposed § 15.12(a)(2) would have required the issuer to include a statement consistent with proposed § 15.12(b)(1)(ii) that any discretionary limitations on timely redemptions can only be imposed by the OCC or, in the case of a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer, by the OCC, Federal Reserve, or the State payment stablecoin regulator, as applicable. Proposed § 15.12(a)(3) required that issuers include in their redemption disclosures a statement explaining the scenarios when the redemption period may be extended as provided for in proposed § 15.12(c). Proposed § 15.12(a)(4) provided that the issuer must provide a statement with clear instructions on how a payment stablecoin holder can redeem a payment stablecoin, including a link to the website(s) where a customer can redeem the payment stablecoin. Proposed § 15.12(a)(5) would have required the issuer to specify the minimum number of payment stablecoins, if any, that the permitted payment stablecoin issuer will redeem, provided that the issuer must redeem any number greater than or equal to one payment stablecoin, subject to appropriate customer screening and onboarding.
Proposed § 15.12(b)(1) provided that an issuer's redemption policy must provide clear and conspicuous procedures for timely redemption of outstanding payment stablecoins. In proposed § 15.12(b)(1)(i), the OCC proposed to define “timely” to mean that the permitted payment stablecoin issuer would have to redeem a payment stablecoin no later than two business days following the date of the requested redemption. The OCC proposed this two-business-day timeframe as an outer limit on when a permitted payment stablecoin issuer must redeem a payment stablecoin and understands that many issuers may choose a timeframe that is less than two business days. Proposed § 15.12(b)(1)(ii), consistent with the statute, provided that discretionary limitations on timely redemptions can only be imposed by the OCC or, in the case of a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer, by the OCC, the Federal Reserve, or the State payment stablecoin regulator, as applicable.
Proposed § 15.12(c)(1) provided that the period for timely redemption is extended to seven calendar days if a permitted payment stablecoin issuer faces redemption demands in excess of 10 percent of its outstanding issuance value in a single 24-hour period. Under proposed § 15.12(c)(2), the extended redemption period would have applied to all redemption requests that are outstanding at the time the 10 percent threshold is met as well as any subsequent redemption requests following the time the threshold is met. Proposed § 15.12(c)(3) stated that the extension is non-discretionary and that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer may only redeem any of the outstanding or subsequent redemption requests prior to the seven-calendar-day period if the OCC determines that the issuer has the ability to redeem sooner in an orderly fashion and through a fair and transparent process or the OCC otherwise provides notice to the permitted payment stablecoin issuer that the extended redemption period no longer applies. Under proposed § 15.12(c)(4), a permitted payment stablecoin issuer that exceeds that 10 percent threshold would have been required to provide notice to the OCC through its supervisory office within 24 hours. Proposed § 15.12(c)(5) provided that the OCC may, in its discretion, extend timely redemption described in proposed § 15.12(b)(1) or (c)(1), as applicable, if the OCC determines that the permitted payment stablecoin issuer poses a threat to safety and soundness, financial stability, or such an extension is otherwise in the public interest.
Proposed § 15.12(d)(1) provided that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer must also publicly, clearly, and conspicuously disclose in plain language and in a format that is readily noticeable to customers, readily understandable by customers, and segregated from other information: (i) the name of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer that issues the payment stablecoin; (ii) that the permitted payment stablecoin issuer is the entity that is obligated to convert, redeem, or repurchase the payment stablecoin for a fixed amount of monetary value; (iii) the link to the monthly composition report of the relevant permitted payment stablecoin issuer's reserves as required under proposed § 15.11(e); and (iv) all fees associated with purchasing or redeeming payment stablecoins. The OCC included a requirement that the disclosures under proposed § 15.12(d)(1) be readily noticeable by customers, readily understandable by customers, and segregated from other information to provide more certainty on what it means to “publicly, clearly, and conspicuously disclose [the information] in plain language.”
[
93
]
The OCC proposed to include the requirement that the disclosures be segregated from other information to ensure that the information in the disclosures is not combined with other nonrelevant information that could obscure the importance of these disclosures.
Proposed § 15.12(d)(2) provided that an issuer must update the disclosures in proposed § 15.12(d)(1)(iv) if there are any changes in the fees associated with purchasing or redeeming stablecoins and provide customers at least seven calendar days' prior notice of the change, including by securely delivering the notice to current customers. Proposed § 15.12(d)(3) provided that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer must publish the disclosures in proposed § 15.12(d)(1) and any updates made in accordance with proposed § 15.12(d)(2) on the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's website. Proposed § 15.12(d)(4) provided that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer must include the disclosures in proposed § 15.12(d)(1) and any updates made in accordance with proposed § 15.12(d)(2) in any customer agreements that it provides.
c. Description of Comments and Final Rule
Commenters generally supported the majority of the requirements in proposed § 15.12(a). Some commenters disagreed on whether permitted payment stablecoin issuers should be permitted to set minimum redemption amounts. One commenter argued that the OCC should not require redemption
(
printed page 67064)
of amounts greater than or equal to one stablecoin because such a low threshold would create disproportionate know-your-customer and anti-money-laundering burdens. Another commenter argued that the OCC should not impose a minimum redemption amount because redemption at par is a core feature of payment stablecoins. Commenters were also divided on whether permitted payment stablecoin issuers should be required to offer direct redemption to all payment stablecoin holders. Some commenters supported direct redemption for any holder, with no minimums, subject to compliance checks or the creation of a formal customer relationship through an onboarding process. In contrast, several commenters argued that issuers should be able to choose whether to have a fully retail redemption model or operate through institutional counterparties or authorized participants. One commenter went further by suggesting that redemptions should only be structured to take place with institutional counterparties and authorized participants, rather than through retail relationships. Similarly, another commenter indicated that permitted payment stablecoin issuers should not be required to screen and onboard any stablecoin holder who requests redemption.
In setting the requirement that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer must redeem any number greater than or equal to one payment stablecoin, the OCC looked to the structure of the Act and the relevant definitions. Notably, section 2(22) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5901(22)
), defines “payment stablecoin” as a digital asset that an issuer “is obligated to convert, redeem, or repurchase for a fixed amount of monetary value.” The statutory language indicates that, while an issuer could set a minimum redemption threshold at a fraction of a payment stablecoin, an issuer redeems any number greater than or equal to one payment stablecoin under the GENIUS Act. Otherwise, a payment stablecoin would not be redeemable for a fixed amount of monetary value.
[
94
]
More generally, the OCC has identified nothing in the other provisions or structure of the Act, including the requirement to convert, redeem, or repurchase a payment stablecoin in section 2(22) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5901(22)
) that distinguishes between retail or wholesale payment stablecoin holders.
[
95
]
Accordingly, the OCC has determined that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer must have the legal obligation to convert, redeem, or repurchase a payment stablecoin from any holder, subject to applicable law (
e.g.
, Federal laws, including BSA and economic sanctions requirements, including requirements of the customer identification program rule, certain non-U.S. laws, and State laws that are not preempted).
[
96
]
To determine that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer does not have to redeem from any holder could result in the elimination of the obligation merely through a permitted payment stablecoin issuer limiting its customer base. For example, if a permitted payment stablecoin issuer were permitted to limit itself to only one institutional customer (
e.g.
, a digital asset service provider that served as a cryptocurrency exchange), and that customer ceased operations or its legal existence, the permitted payment stablecoin issuer would no longer have an obligation to convert, redeem, or repurchase from the remaining payment stablecoin holders. Such a result would not be consistent with the text of section 2(22) (
12 U.S.C. 5901(22)
). However, a permitted payment stablecoin issuer need not have a business that focuses on retail customers. Whether or not the permitted payment stablecoin issuer focuses on retail customers, it will have the legal obligation to be able to convert, redeem, or repurchase from such customers and should have appropriate procedures in place to onboard such customers, particularly in times of stress. In light of the foregoing, the OCC is finalizing § 15.12(a) as proposed with certain renumbering changes to reflect other changes in § 15.12, discussed in greater detail below. The provisions of proposed § 15.12(a) are codified in the final rule at § 15.12(b), and references to other sections of § 15.12 have been correspondingly updated. In addition, subsection (b) of the final rule includes “in the policy” before the colon and listed items, and paragraph (b)(4) of the final rule replaces a reference to a “customer” that was in proposed § 15.12(a)(4) with a reference to a “payment stablecoin holder.” The final rule also includes technical changes, including adding “the” in front of “Federal Reserve” in paragraph (b)(2) of the final rule.
Several commenters supported retaining a two-business-day standard for onboarded holders, particularly for direct counterparties, while some recommended that the OCC encourage same-day or real-time capabilities or tie shorter issuer commitments in terms of service to compliance expectations. One commenter recommended a 24-hour standard. Other commenters urged a more flexible, risk-based standard that accounts for reserve structure, safety and soundness, cross-border and intermediary arrangements, compliance reviews, and real-world settlement constraints. Commenters stated that the OCC should provide a clear timeframe for when redemption begins and ends. Commenters urged the OCC to adopt a clear, technology-neutral definition of redemption that focuses on completion of the issuer's obligations. Commenters requested clarification on when redemption is complete for compliance purposes, including whether completion occurs on burn initiation, block confirmation, ledger finality, or fiat currency credit to the customer's bank account. Several commenters suggested that redemption should be considered complete when the issuer either initiates payment, credits the holder's account, or fully processes the outgoing transfer, or when the holder receives fiat currency funds in its account. One commenter recommended a final-settlement approach based on receipt of funds by the redeeming party. Another recommended measuring compliance from the issuer's initiation of payment rather than final settlement.
Commenters also requested clarification on what is timely in various instances, including cross-border redemptions, court-ordered redemptions, and intermediated relationships. Several commenters supported preserving the two-business-day standard but allowing flexibility for delays caused by factors outside the issuer's control, such as payment-system disruptions, correspondent bank failures, or broader financial stress. Several commenters stated that the redemption timeline should begin only after the issuer is able to satisfactorily onboard the holder consistent with applicable laws and regulations. One commenter requested clarification that custodians should not be required to commit to specific settlement or release timeframes, and that the two-business-day standard should operate as an issuer liquidity and reserve requirement rather
(
printed page 67065)
than a direct custodian obligation. One commenter requested recognition of comparable home-jurisdiction redemption standards in section 18(b) comparability determinations. One commenter requested that the OCC specify the consequences for untimely redemption.
The OCC agrees that it is important to provide a clear timeframe for when redemption begins and ends. Accordingly, the OCC is adding a new paragraph (a) (and renumbering subsequent paragraphs appropriately). This paragraph addresses the timeline for redemption and provides that, for purposes of § 15.12: (1) a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's obligation to redeem begins once: (i) the permitted payment stablecoin issuer has received a redemption order from a customer;
[
97
]
and (ii) if the permitted payment stablecoin issuer has onboarding procedures reasonably designed to not unduly delay the onboarding of retail or other customers, including in times of stress, the customer has been successfully onboarded and all other legal conditions necessary to permit redemption that complies with this part have been met. As discussed in greater detail below, permitted payment stablecoin issuers should have in place the capability to onboard new customers in times of stress. While many issuers may only interact directly with a small number of digital asset service providers in normal times, in times of stress or in the event of a failure of a digital asset service provider, payment stablecoin holders may seek to redeem directly with the permitted payment stablecoin issuer. The issuer should therefore have processes in place to address a sudden increase in customers.
Accordingly, paragraph (a)(1)(ii) is designed to ensure that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer cannot use deficiencies in its onboarding process as a pretext to artificially extend the timeline for redemption. Paragraph (a)(2) clarifies that redemption is deemed to occur when the permitted payment stablecoin issuer has fully processed and initiated the outgoing transfer of monetary value to the customer or the customer's financial institution as directed by the customer,
[
98
]
or, if requested by the customer, credited monetary value to the customer's account with the payment stablecoin issuer. This approach to the redemption timeline appropriately (1) focuses on aspects that are within the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's control (
i.e.
, the issuer sending monetary value rather than the customer receiving monetary value), (2) addresses potential complications that may arise in cross-border transactions or transactions with new customers, (3) ensures that an unduly short timeline will not conflict with a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's BSA/AML obligations and economic sanctions compliance requirements, and (4) aligns with current market practices. With this clarification concerning the redemption timeline, the OCC is retaining the baseline two-business-day timeline for timely redemption. The OCC believes this timeframe provides sufficient responsiveness to stablecoin holders who seek to redeem their stablecoins while also ensuring that issuers can appropriately manage liquidity demands. The OCC is not amending the rule to address comparable requirements of other jurisdictions, as those are best addressed through the determination that the Secretary of the Treasury makes pursuant to section 18(b) of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5916
) and any associated reciprocal arrangements. In the event a permitted payment stablecoin issuer fails to timely redeem a payment stablecoin, the OCC intends to evaluate the facts and may take an appropriate enforcement action. The two-business-day timeline for timely redemption is a ceiling, and the OCC acknowledges that in order for payment stablecoins to be considered “cash equivalents” under GAAP and qualify as margin collateral under other requirements, the payment stablecoins may need to have an on-demand contractual right. Permitted payment stablecoin issuers may redeem earlier than two business days, but they may not redeem later than two business days, absent an extension of the period for timely redemption. Whether any particular payment stablecoin may qualify as margin collateral is outside the scope of this rulemaking.
One commenter urged the OCC not to permit issuers to freeze redemptions, including in unusual and exigent circumstances. Other commenters recommended a narrow safe harbor or exception where suspensions or delays result from clearly defined circumstances outside the issuer's control, such as system-wide disruptions, fraud investigations, sanctions screening, or payment-system failures, conditioned on the issuer providing notice and disclosure when the law permits. Many commenters opposed the proposed automatic seven-day stress extension and argued that it is pro-cyclical, could reinforce panic, and may undermine confidence or contribute to de-pegging. Several commenters recommended a discretionary or multi-factored approach instead of an automatic trigger. Commenters proposed alternatives including tailoring automatic extensions around reserve liquidity, requiring OCC notification of stress events and approval for an extension, a reserve-to-circulating-token trigger, and treating seven days as an outer limit rather than a mandatory delay.
Commenters also requested clarity on operational application of the trigger, including whether it would be triggered on a brand-by-brand basis for multi-brand or white-labeled coins, how to measure requests in pull-claim architectures where holders submit redemption requests but such requests are not immediately executed, whether the OCC may object or impose conditions, whether extensions apply to outstanding and subsequent requests, and queuing and communication practices during an extension. One commenter noted possible conflict where a United States issuer suspends redemption while a foreign affiliate remains redeeming.
Commenters requested clearer operational expectations for redemption throughput, automation, contingency staffing, banking-rail dependence, and stress readiness. One commenter supported requiring clear rules for timely and orderly customer redemption.
After considering the comments, the OCC is eliminating the automatic extension provided in proposed § 15.12(c). The OCC agrees with commenters that the automatic extension could prove pro-cyclical and trigger or exacerbate runs. At the same time, the OCC believes that it is important that the OCC receive prompt notice of any sudden spike in redemption requests, which may indicate stress at a permitted payment stablecoin issuer. Accordingly, § 15.12(d)(1) of the final rule provides that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer must provide notice to the OCC through its supervisory office within 24 hours if it receives redemption requests in excess of 10 percent of the outstanding issuance value of any brand of payment stablecoin issued by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer in a single 24-hour period. Under § 15.12(d)(2) of the final rule, a permitted payment stablecoin issuer
(
printed page 67066)
that experiences redemption requests in excess of 10 percent of the outstanding issuance value of any brand of payment stablecoin issued by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer in a single 24-hour period may request that the OCC extend the timeframe for timely redemption. The OCC may, in its discretion, grant or deny the extension request or impose discretionary limitations upon timely redemption in accordance with section 4(a)(1)(B)(i) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(B)(i)
). The OCC expects to use this authority sparingly and that redemption extensions will be rare. The OCC notes that the OCC may also impose (and the permitted payment stablecoin issuer may request) discretionary limitations upon timely redemption in certain other circumstances, consistent with the statute.
[
99
]
The OCC would impose any such limit so as not to trigger or exacerbate runs or other stress events. The notification requirement in the final rule will provide the OCC with an early opportunity to assess whether such limitations may be appropriate and justified under the statute. The OCC notes that, because permitted payment stablecoin issuers may face redemption requests from payment stablecoin holders (subject to appropriate onboarding and screening), permitted payment stablecoin issuers should have in place processes to appropriately and promptly screen and onboard new customers, including in times of stress. It would be prudent for a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to provide disclosures concerning its onboarding process so that customers understand the process and how it may affect the timing of redemption (including when the permitted payment stablecoin issuer is under stress).
Commenters generally supported the proposed disclosures. Many supported including additional disclosures that payment stablecoins are not insured and, in one case, not legal tender. Several commenters requested clear disclosures regarding redemption rights, timeframes, fees, reserve composition, operational disruptions, and the identity of the legal issuer responsible for redemption.
Several commenters supported disclosure of redemption fees and fee changes, limits on hidden or abusive fees, point-of-transaction disclosure flexibility, and clarification that fee disclosure obligations apply to issuers rather than all market participants. Other commenters requested clearer allocation of disclosure responsibilities among issuers, exchanges, custodians, and intermediaries.
A few commenters supported disclosures requiring such an affirmative statement, with commenters stating that the OCC should either require such disclosure, provide sample disclosures, or require a standardized disclosure related to certain prohibitions against deceptive language in the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(9)
). One commenter stated that such a requirement should be principles-based and should emphasize prominence, timing, and customer comprehension. A different commenter opposed a requirement for such disclosure, stating that such disclosures were not required by the Act, and the prohibition itself obviates the need for disclosures. The commenter further stated that to the extent the OCC believes such additional disclosures are required, the OCC should only consider requiring them if and when actual market practices or consumer confusion demonstrate a clear need. Additionally, a few commenters stated that the OCC should require disclosures that provide that the issuer's payment stablecoins are not insured by the FDIC and not eligible for pass-through insurance.
The OCC is adopting proposed § 15.12(b) and (d) but renumbered as § 15.12(c) and (e) in the final rule, with certain additional modifications. First, the paragraph includes renumbering in light of new § 15.12(a). Second, because the OCC is no longer reserving § 15.12(b)(2), the OCC has consolidated proposed § 15.12(b)(1) into final § 15.12(c) with a clarification (adding “that state” before the colon) and appropriate renumbering.
Third, final § 15.12(e) includes certain disclosures beyond those proposed in § 15.12(d). The OCC believes that the baseline disclosures in proposed § 15.12(d) are appropriate and consistent with the statute but that certain additional disclosures would provide important additional clarity to customers and payment stablecoin holders. New § 15.12(e)(1)(v) would require a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to disclose that payment stablecoins are not legal tender, issued by the United States, or guaranteed or approved by the United States. This requirement would align with the prohibition against deceptive names in section 4(a)(9) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(9)
) and § 15.10(c) of the final rule. New § 15.12(e)(1)(vi) would require a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to disclose that payment stablecoins are not deposits, not backed by the full faith and credit of the United States, not subject to deposit insurance by the FDIC, and not subject to share insurance by the National Credit Union Administration. This would align with the prohibition against misrepresentation of insured status in section 4(e) of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(e)
) and the definition of payment stablecoin (which excludes deposits) in section 2(22) of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5901(22)
). The OCC has legal authority to require the disclosures under sections 4(a)(1)(B)(ii), 4(a)(9), and 4(e) of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(B)(ii)
, (a)(9), and (e)). Waiting for market practices to develop prior to requiring such disclosures does not appear prudent, given that the benefit of disclosing this information to payment stablecoin holders outweighs the minimal burden of including these statements in disclosures to payment stablecoin holders. This burden appears particularly minimal since such redemption disclosures are mandatory regardless of whether the OCC chose to add these additional requirements.
The final rule also replaces certain references to “customers” with “payment stablecoin holders” to be clear that disclosures should be readily noticeable and understandable to payment stablecoin holders, including those who have not yet become customers (
i.e.,
payment stablecoin holders who have not interacted directly with the permitted payment stablecoin issuer, including by requesting redemption from the permitted payment stablecoin issuer). Certain requirements would, however, apply only to customers with whom the issuer has a current relationship. These changes are appropriate in light of the change to the definition of “customer” described above. For a similar clarifying purpose, the OCC is replacing the phrase “The link to the monthly composition report” in proposed § 15.12(d)(1)(iii) with “The website that contains a link to the monthly composition report” in final § 15.12(e)(1)(iii). Final § 15.12(e)(4) does not include “that it provides,” which was included in proposed § 15.12(d)(4), because the phrase introduced a risk of ambiguity while adding no substantive description of the relevant disclosures.
A few commenters provided suggestions for the format of disclosures, including that they should be on the issuer's website, provided at the point of issuance or sale, and in a standalone format before the transaction is completed. Commenters also stated that disclosures should be prominent and obvious on the issuer's website, application interface, and in any promotional materials. Another commenter stated that the OCC should adopt a specific standardized data
(
printed page 67067)
format for stablecoin-related disclosures and that on-chain disclosure has its advantages. One commenter stated that the OCC should not impose technically infeasible disclosure obligations at every downstream transaction touchpoint and that there should be issuer-level disclosures rather than at the point of sale. Moreover, one commenter stated that disclosures should not be made through terms of service while another commenter stated that permitted payment stablecoin issuers should provide a fuller set of disclosures on their primary user interfaces and web pages. One commenter stated that any such disclosures should be continuously available, prominent, and linked with the issuer's core redemption, reserve, and product-risk disclosures. A few commenters suggested that the OCC should establish safe harbors or standardized disclosure templates for payment stablecoin disclosures that emphasize clarity and brevity.
The OCC declines to provide sample disclosures or a standardized format for such disclosures but notes that the disclosures must meet the requirements of § 15.12(e)(1). That section requires that the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's disclosures must publicly, clearly, and conspicuously disclose the required information in plain language and in a format that is readily noticeable to payment stablecoin holders, readily understandable by payment stablecoin holders, and segregated from other information. Such sample disclosures are not necessary because the disclosure requirements are simple and clear. The OCC is not instituting a principles-based requirement because it believes that disclosing this limited additional information does not impose significant burden on permitted payment stablecoin issuers.
The OCC does not believe it is prudent to pick a specific format for disclosures, given that a Federal disclosure regime specific to stablecoins did not exist prior to the passage of the Act. Therefore, the market needs to develop prior to the OCC considering whether there should be a specific format for disclosures. The OCC is not opposed to on-chain disclosures, so long as such disclosures meet the requirements in § 15.12(e). Similarly, the OCC takes no view on whether disclosures should be at the issuer level or at the point-of-sale, so long as they meet the requirements of the Act and this final rule. To the extent the disclosures are made through the terms of service, but the disclosures are not conspicuous and readily noticeable to payment stablecoin holders, such disclosures would not comply with the requirement in § 15.12(e)(1) of the final rule. The OCC is not establishing safe harbors or standardized disclosures because there may be different formats of disclosures that can satisfy the requirements in § 15.12(e), and the OCC believes the disclosure requirements are straightforward and do not necessitate further clarification beyond what is in the final rule.
While the OCC agrees with commenters that stated that permitted payment stablecoin issuers should have to disclose that payment stablecoins are not insured by the FDIC, the OCC did not include any requirements related to pass-through insurance as the FDIC's notice of proposed rulemaking addresses the applicability of pass-through insurance, and the FDIC's proposal has not yet been finalized. Once the FDIC finalizes its rulemaking, the OCC will consider whether any revisions to
12 CFR part 15
are necessary.
Many commenters also made suggestions of other categories of disclosures the OCC should consider. One commenter stated that there should be clear disclosure requirements for permitted payment stablecoin issuers and intermediaries regarding the timing, content, and roles of each party so consumers understand the relevant risks. Commenters also suggested that permitted payment stablecoin issuers should disclose the redemption rights of payment stablecoin holders, the nature of the issuing entity, that the payment stablecoin is issued by a permitted payment stablecoin issuer, the identity of the primary Federal regulator, and a warning, if applicable, that all transactions using the payment stablecoin are not reversible. One commenter also suggested disclosures related to operational risk, including disclosures regarding blockchain network participation, all blockchain activities, risks from a network disruption, and third-party details. Another commenter stated that the OCC should work with the FDIC to require disclosures regarding how customer funds are protected by reserve requirements,
[
100
]
how customers can convert their payment stablecoins back to dollars, and information about insured and uninsured balances. Commenters also suggested prohibitions on nonbank permitted payment stablecoin issuers using the word “bank” in their names, marketing materials, websites, application interfaces, and any other communications targeted at customers.
The OCC is not adopting any additional disclosure requirements in the final rule beyond the changes already discussed to § 15.12(e). With respect to disclosures surrounding intermediaries, the OCC believes that disclosing the name of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer that issued the payment stablecoin under § 15.12(e)(1)(i) is sufficient to help customers understand the entity they can redeem from. Additionally, disclosing the primary Federal regulator might cause confusion because several Federal agencies have different responsibilities under the Act. The OCC also believes that disclosing that transactions using a payment stablecoin are not reversible, which may not always be the case, is unnecessary and could similarly cause confusion. The OCC also believes disclosure regarding blockchain activities need not be mandatory, but, to the extent issuers believe they would be helpful, they may provide this information to customers. While a nonbank permitted payment stablecoin issuer referring to itself as a “bank” is not explicitly prohibited by the Act, such representations might raise concerns under other applicable laws. Moreover, the OCC already requires public disclosure of reserve assets in the monthly composition report required under § 15.11(e) of the final rule. The OCC is not adding a disclosure requirement for the token asset identifier, but issuers may disseminate this information if it would be helpful to customers.
A few other commenters asked for additional clarity related to disclosures. One commenter stated that the OCC should articulate a more defined reasonableness standard based on the net impression of the communication and provide examples of likely violations and compliant communications. One commenter asked for clarity on the responsibility allocation and stated that issuers should remain responsible for their marketing materials while digital asset service providers should be responsible for their own customer-facing representations. The commenter further stated that both should be expected to maintain controls designed to prevent misrepresentation. Another commenter stated that it would be helpful to understand which factors the OCC would consider in evaluating such disclosures. Another commenter stated that the OCC should clarify how it will implement prohibitions on deceptive
(
printed page 67068)
marketing practices, provide clarity around marketing practices, and strengthen the customer protection objectives of the prohibition. The commenter further stated that the OCC should clarify the factors it would consider relevant to finding a disclaimer sufficiently clear and specific and provide examples of disclaimers that would be acceptable. Another commenter stated that the OCC should establish disclosure safe harbors for clarity and brevity.
Section 15.12(e)(1) provides sufficient clarity regarding the requirements for the disclosures required by the final rule. The disclosure requirements under § 15.12(e) apply to permitted payment stablecoin issuers, and therefore issuers are responsible for those particular disclosures. The OCC agrees that permitted payment stablecoin issuers should have controls designed to prevent misrepresentation, which would generally be part of an effective risk management program required under § 15.13 of the final rule. Permitted payment stablecoin issuers are also responsible for overseeing service provider arrangements under § 15.13(a)(7), which means that their service providers should have appropriate measures in place designed to meet the requirements of this final rule.
Permitted payment stablecoin issuers may include additional disclosures as best practices. For example, depending on a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's business model, it may be important to provide disclosures relating to the timeframe for onboarding new customers (including in times of stress). As market practices develop and the OCC gains additional experience supervising permitted payment stablecoin issuers, the OCC may consider proposing additional or revised disclosures, as appropriate.
The final rule includes new § 15.12(f), which confirms that the OCC will not require a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to redeem a payment stablecoin to the extent the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's actions to redeem the payment stablecoin would cause the issuer to violate other applicable law.
[
101
]
The OCC is adding this provision to make clear that the OCC would not consider it a violation of the Act or part 15 if a permitted payment stablecoin issuer failed to redeem a payment stablecoin due to, for example, its obligations under applicable BSA and economic sanctions requirements because the OCC would not require such a redemption. As another example, if a foreign jurisdiction required that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer be licensed or registered to redeem a payment stablecoin in a foreign country and the issuer did not have such a license or registration, the OCC would not require the issuer to redeem a payment stablecoin from a payment stablecoin holder who is in a foreign country in which the issuer was not licensed or registered. The OCC may consider revising § 15.12(f) over time based on, among other things, the nature of the conflicting laws that arise.
[
102
]
Relationship of Redemption Requirements to Liquidity and Reserve Requirements
Several commenters stated that liquidity requirements should be calibrated to the issuer's actual redemption obligations or contractual redemption period. Some commenters requested clarification on how issuers are expected to satisfy redemption obligations under the proposed liquidity thresholds and settlement mechanics. Other commenters supported strict reserve, stress-testing, and prompt par redemption requirements to protect consumers and reduce run risk.
One commenter argued that credit risk management should focus on actual counterparty and redemption risk rather than temporary fair-value fluctuations, particularly for reserves held at supervised insured depository institutions. Commenters also requested flexibility for affiliate and cross-border reserve structures, including reserve rebalancing across regulated affiliates and recognition of on-chain reserves under reciprocity arrangements. Comments related to liquidity and risk management requirements are addressed in the sections of the preamble discussing § 15.11 and § 15.13, respectively.
Fees
Commenters were divided on whether redemption fees should be permitted. Some commenters supported allowing fees if they are market-driven, transparent, proportionate, and tied to genuine processing costs. One commenter also argued that minting and burning fees are ordinary in commercial transactions and may provide needed revenue in low-rate environments. Other commenters supported prohibiting redemption fees that reduce the value received below par, while distinguishing ancillary service charges such as foreign exchange conversion or expedited settlement. The GENIUS Act clearly contemplates that permitted payment stablecoin issuers may charge fees, subject to appropriate disclosures.
See, e.g.,
section 4(a)(1)(B)(ii) of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(B)(ii)
). Accordingly, the OCC is not limiting permitted payment stablecoin issuers from charging properly disclosed fees except in the event of liquidation for failure to meet liquidity, capital, or operational backstop requirements, or pursuant to an enforcement action, as appropriate.
[
103
]
Foreign Jurisdictions
One commenter requested that the OCC address issuers operating in foreign jurisdictions and the risk that economically similar instruments issued under different regimes could confuse holders about reserve backing and redemption rights. Disclosure requirements applicable to permitted payment stablecoin issuers and the requirements of section 18 of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5916
), its implementing regulations, and any conditions imposed thereunder should help to address potential issues relating to confusion.
Multiple Chains
Commenters requested clarification on how reserve requirements, redemption timelines, reporting obligations, and the 10 percent threshold apply when issuance is distributed across multiple chains with different finality characteristics. Commenters also requested clarification that cross-chain and cross-network interoperability activities directly support issuance and redemption and that the OCC address the operational, settlement, interoperability, and control risks of cross-chain transfers used to meet redemption demands. The final rule applies in a technology-neutral manner and thus its application does not change based on the particular blockchain on which a payment stablecoin operates. The 10 percent threshold applies on a per-brand basis. With respect to interoperability, section 12 of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5912
) provides that the Federal payment stablecoin regulators, in consultation with the National Institute of Standards and Technology, other relevant standard-setting organizations, and State bank and credit union regulators, shall
(
printed page 67069)
assess and, if necessary, may prescribe standards to promote interoperability. The OCC is actively engaging in assessing issues relating to interoperability, in consultation with other regulators. The OCC is not, however, imposing interoperability standards in this rulemaking.
Civil Recovery
One commenter recommended tolling the ordinary two-business-day redemption timeframe upon receipt of a qualifying civil recovery order until the order is satisfied, requiring the issuer to satisfy order-related redemptions before ordinary requests and notify the OCC within 24 hours. The commenter stated that qualifying orders should include pre-judgment restraining orders under
18 U.S.C. 983(j)
, civil forfeiture orders under
18 U.S.C. 981
or
21 U.S.C. 881
, restitution orders in Federal criminal proceedings, and writs of execution or judgment liens. This comment addresses an issue that is generally outside the scope of this rulemaking. Accordingly, the OCC is not revising the rule to address the issue at this time but may consider it as part of future rulemakings addressing part 15. The OCC may, in the interim, use its reservation of authority to toll the two-business-day redemption timeframe in connection with a civil order, as appropriate.
Finally, the OCC notes that the requirements of § 15.12 apply only to the redemption of a payment stablecoin by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer (including any entity acting as agent on behalf of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer) and do not apply to secondary market trading.
4. Risk Management (§ 15.13)
Section 4(a)(4)(A)(iv) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(4)(A)(iv)
) provides that the OCC must issue regulations implementing appropriate operational, compliance, and information technology risk management principles-based requirements and standards that are tailored to the business model and risk profile of permitted payment stablecoin issuers and are consistent with applicable law. This provision also requires that Bank Secrecy Act and sanctions compliance standards be implemented. The Bank Secrecy Act and sanctions compliance requirements are addressed in a different proposed rule.

Proposed § 15.13 addressed the remaining requirements and standards required under section 4(a)(4)(A)(iv) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(4)(A)(iv)

a. Overview of Changes From Proposed Rule to Final Rule for § 15.13
The OCC is adopting § 15.13(a)(1) through (a)(5) as proposed except for changes to four provisions. In final § 15.13(a)(1)(i) on internal controls and information systems, the description of the organizational structure no longer includes an internal control structure. The final version of this paragraph also has a new phrase at the end; the OCC moved the proposed segregation of duties to this phrase and added a reference to dual controls. In final § 15.13(a)(2)(i), the phrase “size, complexity, or scope of operations” has been moved before “permitted payment stablecoin issuer” for clarity. In final § 15.13(a)(3)(ii), the phrase “adequate” is changed to “sufficient” and moved after the term information, and “to an extent commensurate with their duties” now qualifies the information sufficient for management and the board of directors to assess the level of interest rate exposure risk. Both of these changes are meant to clarify the expectations related to the information provided in periodic reporting to management. Additionally, other technical edits were made to final § 15.13(a)(4) to enhance readability of the provision.
The agency is adopting § 15.13(a)(6) on insider and affiliate transactions with several revisions. Additionally, the OCC has replaced proposed § 15.13(a)(6)(i)(A), which addressed transactions that would be excessive or pose significant risks of material financial loss, with § 15.13(a)(6)(i)(A) and (B). The final § 15.13(a)(6)(i)(A) addresses transactions that are quantitatively detrimental in light of the business model of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer. The OCC is adopting proposed § 15.13(a)(6)(i)(B) and (C), renumbered as § 15.13(a)(6)(i)(C) and (D), as proposed with technical edits to add commas and replace “or” with “and” when referring to transactions with, or involving, non-insiders and non-affiliates.

The final rule includes new § 15.13(a)(9) and (a)(10).
