b. Description of Comments and General Overview of Final Rule Approach
The GENIUS Act requires that the regulation's requirements and standards be “principles-based.” Accordingly, the OCC proposed flexible standards in § 15.13 that scaled based on the nature, scope, and risk of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's activities. Most of the standards in proposed § 15.13 were adapted from relevant provisions of
12 CFR part 30
, appendices A and B, which in turn implement
12 U.S.C. 1831p-1
.
[
105
]
The OCC identified standards from appendices A and B of
12 CFR part 30
that fit the requirements of section 4(a)(4)(A)(iii) or 4(a)(4)(A)(iv) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(4)(A)(iii)
or
(a)(4)(A)(iv)
) and then, consistent with the statute, adapted and tailored those standards to the business models of permitted payment stablecoin issuers, as appropriate. In addition, on July 14, 2025, the OCC issued a joint statement, together with the Federal Reserve and FDIC, on Risk Management Considerations for Crypto-Asset Safekeeping,
[
106
]
and the standards in proposed § 15.13 were consistent with the considerations described in the joint statement.
[
107
]
The OCC is adopting proposed § 15.13 with targeted changes. The final rule retains the principles-based and technology-neutral approach of the proposed rule, but the final rule has been modified to provide additional clarity, include stress test requirements, and address foreign exchange risk management. A description of the general comments received pertaining to proposed § 15.13 and the OCC's responses is below, followed by a description of specific comments relevant to proposed § 15.13 and changes made in the final rule.
Many commenters opined on whether § 15.13 should be principles-based as opposed to prescribing specific requirements. For example, a few commenters suggested that principles-based requirements and standards allow for needed flexibility while maintaining strong governance, operational resilience, and financial controls. Other commenters recommended principles-based requirements and standards accompanied by clear supervisory guidance. One commenter noted the importance of providing sufficient detail to enable consistent compliance and examination if maintaining a principles-based approach. A few commenters indicated that a principles-based approach allows for better scaling to an institution's size, complexity, and risk profile.
Additionally, many commenters discussed whether the rule should remain technology-neutral. For example, several commenters suggested that in order to remain principles-based, § 15.13 should not impose specific requirements around the use of particular technical elements of stablecoins due to rapid technological changes occurring in the industry. Other commenters, however, suggested that while requirements in general should be principles-based, the framework should focus on technology-specific risks given the technological nature of the industry. In particular, these commenters recommended addressing the risks or benefits associated with distributed ledger technology in greater detail.
Section 4(a)(4)(A)(iv) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(4)(A)(iv)
) provides that risk management standards and requirements must be “principles-based.” In addition, the nature of many of the areas covered by the § 15.13 risk management provisions is such that implementation will depend on the business model, activities, and circumstances of each institution. Because of this nature, principles-based requirements are appropriate as a matter of policy as well as required by law. Additionally, the OCC has historically taken a technology-neutral approach to rulemaking, which it intends to continue. Employing a technology-neutral approach will help ensure that the requirements of
12 CFR part 15
adequately address the core risks applicable to permitted payment stablecoin issuers even as technology changes. Thus, while the final rule includes certain references to concepts that generally apply to distributed ledger technology (
e.g.,
private keys), the final rule does not favor one particular technological solution over another.
Several commenters suggested requiring real-time monitoring of smart contract activity, distributed ledger activity, reserve management, and redemption activity. A few commenters suggested requiring real-time and API-based reporting for regulators. The above discussion of § 15.11(a) considers these and similar comments with respect to how permitted payment stablecoin issuers satisfy their reserve requirements under the GENIUS Act, and the below discussion of § 15.14 relates to audits, reports, and supervision. The final rule does not include a real-time monitoring requirement for permitted payment stablecoin issuers (consistent with the technology-neutral and principles-based approach that the OCC has taken with respect to § 15.13). The OCC notes, however, that the final rule requires permitted payment stablecoin issuers to back payment stablecoins with reserve assets on at least a 1 to 1 basis at all times. Refer to the discussions of § 15.11 and § 15.14 for more about how permitted payment stablecoin issuers satisfy this requirement.
Several commenters suggested allowing a permitted payment stablecoin issuer that is an insured depository institution subsidiary to satisfy risk management requirements through the insured depository institution's risk management framework. Commenters making this recommendation argued that doing so would reduce duplication of requirements. Some commenters made this recommendation specifically in situations where the parent insured depository institution's framework explicitly encompasses the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's specific activities and risk profile. Other commenters suggested that compliance may be based on a parent's risk management framework where the parent's framework already addresses the risks covered in § 15.13 in a manner that is at least equivalent in outcomes. A few commenters recommended that any compliance based on a parent's framework be subject to supervisory confirmation, rather than automatically and conclusively determining that the subsidiary is in compliance, and that the OCC retain discretion to require additional or standalone risk management for risks that are not adequately addressed by the parent's framework. Alternatively, one commenter argued that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer that is a subsidiary of an insured depository institution should not be allowed to satisfy risk management requirements
(
printed page 67071)
by reference to the parent institution's existing framework and that in all cases compliance should be demonstrated by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer.
A parent insured depository institution will separately be subject to the requirements of
12 CFR part 30
, Appendices A and B, and other applicable requirements, and the OCC will separately supervise the insured depository institution parent's risk management. A permitted payment stablecoin issuer that is a subsidiary of an insured depository institution may rely on the parent's risk management framework to the extent that the parent's risk management framework addresses the requirements of the GENIUS Act and
12 CFR part 15
and to the extent the management of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer plays a meaningful role in the risk management framework related to the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's activities. Similarly, a permitted payment stablecoin issuer that is an SPV may rely on the risk management framework of its parent entity, provided that the parent entity's risk management framework complies with and adequately addresses § 15.13. The OCC will reduce duplicative regulatory requirements to the fullest extent possible.
Many commenters discussed whether the rule should include additional tailoring of risk management requirements and standards across permitted payment stablecoin issuers. Several commenters called for consistent standards for all permitted payment stablecoin issuers regardless of size, which they asserted would establish a common safety and soundness baseline and promote regulatory clarity. Many other commenters supported a tailored framework to allow community banks better access to the stablecoin market. A few commenters advocated for a combination of standardized and tailored frameworks. For example, one commenter suggested that there be baseline risk management standards across permitted payment stablecoin issuers with tailoring that takes into account other regulatory requirements with which the permitted payment stablecoin issuer is already required to comply. One commenter advocated for tailored requirements based on specific risk profile and complexity rather than simply by size.
The Act requires “risk management principles-based requirements and standards . . . that are tailored to the business model and risk profile of permitted payment stablecoin issuers.”
[
108
]
Consistent with the statutory requirement, it is appropriate to require risk management requirements and standards appropriate to the size and complexity of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer and the nature, scope, and risk of its activities. Accordingly, the final rule includes broad principles-based language that accounts for the size and complexity of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer.
Some commenters suggested strategies to address challenges posed by interoperability in payment stablecoin transactions. The above discussion of § 15.12 addresses commenters who referred to interoperability in the context of certain payment stablecoin transactions (issuance and redemption). Some commenters advocated for developing mandatory interoperability standards in coordination with the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). Other commenters opposed including interoperability standards in the final rule. Some favored including high-level principles-based standards. The final rule does not mandate interoperability standards in recognition of the relative novelty of the payment stablecoin industry. The OCC notes, however, that under section 12 of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5912
), the primary Federal payment stablecoin regulators, in consultation with NIST, other relevant standard-setting organizations, and State bank and credit union regulators, shall assess and, if necessary, may prescribe standards for permitted payment stablecoin issuers to promote compatibility and interoperability. As the industry develops, the OCC will continue to work with the other regulators to assess whether it is necessary to prescribe standards for permitted payment stablecoin issuers to promote compatibility and interoperability.
A few commenters suggested that permitted payment stablecoin issuers should be required to acquire insurance against certain risks, for example, cyber, crime, or professional liability insurance. A few commenters suggested that there should be minimum coverage requirements, potentially tailored based on size and complexity of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer. A few commenters suggested that disclosure of insurance coverage should be required to regulators but not the public. A few commenters argued that a potential problem posed by requiring insurance coverage may be the lack of availability of particular types of insurance.
The OCC recognizes insurance as a piece of risk management but does not prescribe particular private insurance requirements. This approach is consistent with the OCC's treatment of other OCC-supervised entities.
c. Description of Proposed Rule, Comments, and Final Rule
Proposed § 15.13(a)(1) would have required that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer have internal controls and information systems that are appropriate for the size and complexity of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer and the nature, scope, and risk of its activities and that provide for: (i) an organizational structure with appropriate segregation of duties and an internal control structure that establishes clear lines of authority and responsibility for monitoring adherence to established policies; (ii) effective risk assessment; (iii) timely and accurate financial, operational, and regulatory reporting, including with respect to reports required under proposed part 15; (iv) adequate procedures to safeguard, manage, control, and monetize assets, including reserve assets; and (v) compliance with applicable laws and regulations. Internal controls refer to the systems, policies, procedures, and processes effected by the board of directors and other personnel to safeguard permitted payment stablecoin issuer assets, limit or control risks, achieve permitted payment stablecoin issuer objectives, and ensure compliance with applicable laws and regulations. The internal controls standards in proposed § 15.13(a)(1) were modeled on the internal controls standards in
12 CFR part 30
, with some adjustments to accommodate the particular activities and risks of permitted payment stablecoin issuers.
A few commenters discussed requirements relating to the risk assessments under § 15.13(a)(1). One commenter suggested taking an open-methodology approach where OCC examiners could audit the risk assessment methodology rather than only its output and the OCC could establish principles for what constitutes an acceptable approach rather than needing to endorse any specific methodology. Several commenters discussed the benefits of real-time or continuous risk monitoring and reporting. One commenter opined that adequate risk assessment requires continuous monitoring of the full cycle of stablecoin activity, including both on- and off-chain activity. Another commenter suggested that risk assessment frameworks should be
(
printed page 67072)
assessed against a baseline standard for all permitted payment stablecoin issuers. Some commenters supported strong internal controls, including segregation of duties, independent validation, dual or multi-party approvals, and strong governance over issuance systems. Another commenter noted that, with respect to reserve asset management, while assets should be appropriately segregated and independently controlled, any personnel or governance requirements should be proportional to the size and complexity of the issuer and implemented through broader reserve asset and risk management standards rather than as a separate standalone requirement. In contrast, some commenters suggested more specific direction concerning the appropriate organizational structure and responsibilities, such as greater clarity on the oversight role of the board of directors and requiring boards of directors to approve and implement a risk appetite statement.
The OCC is adopting paragraph (a)(1) as proposed with a change in § 15.13(a)(1)(i). Section 15.13(a)(1)(i) has been modified to delete “with appropriate segregation of duties and an internal control structure” and add “, including appropriate segregation of duties and dual controls.” These modifications are not substantive but instead clarify that segregation of duties and dual controls may be elements of an organizational structure that facilitates internal controls. In response to commenters, the OCC is not mandating any particular method for risk assessment, and the OCC expects that different permitted payment stablecoin issuers may take different approaches based on the size and complexity of the issuer and the nature, scope, and risk of its activities. This approach is most consistent with the statutory requirement to provide tailored and principles-based risk management standards. Effective risk management depends on an effective risk assessment since a permitted payment stablecoin issuer cannot effectively manage its risks without an understanding of its risk profile. Procedures to safeguard, manage, control, and monetize assets will be expected to include measures to monitor and ensure the deposit concentration and diversification requirements are met. Likewise, procedures will be expected to address potential risks related to fraud and the theft of payment stablecoins or other assets.
The OCC proposed that § 15.13(a)(2) require permitted payment stablecoin issuers to have an internal audit system that is appropriate to the size and complexity of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer and the nature, scope, and risk of its activities and that provides for (i) adequate monitoring of the system of internal controls through an internal audit function, or for a permitted payment stablecoin issuer whose size, complexity, or scope of operations does not warrant a full-scale internal audit function, a system of independent reviews of key internal controls; (ii) independence and objectivity; (iii) qualified persons responsible for the audit function; (iv) adequate independent testing and review of internal controls and information systems, verification of published information available to customers, calculations for required reserves, and regulatory filings; (v) adequate documentation of tests and findings and any corrective actions; (vi) verification and review of management actions to address deficiencies; and (vii) review by the institution's audit committee or board of directors of the effectiveness of the internal audit systems.
A few commenters discussed requirements related to internal audit systems in proposed § 15.13(a)(2). A commenter suggested specific requirements to guide internal audit structure. Specific suggestions related to revising the rule to reference specific proprietary internal audit practice frameworks and clarifying who constitutes a qualified person by requiring that such persons possess appropriate education, relevant experience, and certain professional certifications that demonstrate competency in internal auditing or other relevant expertise. A few commenters suggested that the OCC clarify structural independence expectations. One commenter suggested that the OCC address governance as a distinct area of internal audit coverage; require that procedures be developed, implemented, and adhered to; ground internal audit monitoring in a risk-based approach; require clear ownership and timelines in management action plans; clarify internal audit's purview over all material risk areas in § 15.13; require all permitted payment stablecoin issuers to establish an internal audit function; and rely on internal audit work in carrying out its supervision activities. A few commenters recommended that the rule require third-party or independent audits, or at least that systems have the records or ability to be audited by an independent party.
After careful consideration of the comments, the OCC is adopting paragraph (a)(2) as proposed except for a clarifying edit to § 15.13(a)(2)(i). Internal audit systems are intended to provide objective, independent reviews of permitted payment stablecoin issuer activities, internal controls, and information systems to help the board of directors and management monitor and evaluate internal control adequacy and effectiveness. An internal audit system, among other items, is expected to independently test and review systems, as appropriate, related to (1) a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's compliance with the GENIUS Act and requirements in any final rules implementing the GENIUS Act; (2) payment systems;
[
109
]
and (3) third-party risk management. Well-planned, properly structured audit programs are essential to effective risk management and internal control systems. Effective internal audit programs are a critical defense against fraud and provide vital information to the board of directors about the effectiveness of internal control systems. An internal audit program's coverage includes evaluating compliance systems, safeguards around use of payment systems, and risks posed by relationships with and dependence on third parties. While it is important that internal audit functions be conducted by qualified persons with an appropriate level of independence from other business lines, the final rule does not mandate a particular organizational structure (for example, three lines of defense). Section 15.13(a)(2) does not prescribe a one-size-fits-all approach to risk management. Smaller permitted payment stablecoin issuers with a lower risk profile may be able to comply using a simpler, less delineated organizational structure, or may be able to outsource certain functions such as the internal audit function, while larger permitted payment stablecoin issuers, with higher risk profiles, may require organizational structures with more clearly delineated risk management functions, including internal audit personnel. The OCC's approach is grounded in the principles-based framework, and prescriptive requirements or references to proprietary frameworks or certifications are unnecessary for the rule text. Moreover, a permitted payment stablecoin issuer that is a subsidiary of an insured depository institution or that is a SPV may rely on the audit framework of its parent, provided the parent's framework complies with § 15.13. Final § 15.13 does not mandate
(
printed page 67073)
the use of an external audit, but such an audit may be appropriate for some permitted payment stablecoin issuers. Moreover, permitted payment stablecoin issuers must comply with the requirements of § 15.14, including applicable audit requirements.
Proposed § 15.13(a)(3) addressed interest rate risk and would have required a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to (i) manage interest rate risk in a manner that is appropriate to the size and complexity of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer and the complexity of its assets and liabilities and (ii) provide for periodic reporting to management and the board of directors regarding interest rate risk with adequate information for management and the board of directors to assess the level of risk.
[
110
]
Several commenters discussed the interest rate risk provisions in proposed § 15.13(a)(3). Some commenters suggested that the OCC replace specific requirements in other provisions of the rule (
e.g.,
weighted average maturity in proposed § 15.11) with more robust risk management capabilities for interest rate risk (
e.g.,
stress testing, haircuts). Another commenter suggested that the OCC include interest rate risk, among other items, in capital requirements.
The OCC is adopting § 15.13(a)(3) as proposed with clarifying edits. While permitted payment stablecoin issuers hold reserve assets that may, depending on their type, have limited or no duration (
e.g.,
in the case of demand deposits), it is still important for permitted payment stablecoin issuers to be mindful of this risk, particularly in light of the role of interest rate risk in the previous failures of money market funds, whose investments, like those of permitted payment stablecoin issuers, were supposed to be limited to short-duration safe assets.
[
111
]
Increases in interest rates, particularly in short time periods, can reduce the value of interest-sensitive reserve assets, potentially impacting their fair value, marketability, and the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's ability to meet redemptions. Similarly, changes in interest rates can affect the earnings and long-term viability of permitted payment stablecoin issuers since their earnings may rely in substantial part on interest earned on reserve assets. Likewise, increases in interest rates may reduce the demand for payment stablecoins, particularly since permitted payment stablecoin issuers are prohibited from paying interest to stablecoin holders solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of payment stablecoins under final § 15.10(c)(4).
Proposed § 15.13(a)(4) would have required a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's asset growth to be prudent and commensurate with a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's risk management capabilities, operational capacity, and staffing. A couple of commenters addressed this provision. One stated that the interest rate exposure, asset growth, asset quality, and earnings standards from
12 CFR part 30
should be adapted to focus on reserve composition, liquidity, redemption capacity, operational scalability, and run-risk management rather than traditional banking intermediation. Another suggested that the risk management standards should include an emphasis on growth management.
The OCC is adopting § 15.13(a)(4) as proposed with clarifying edits. While there are no hard limits to how quickly permitted payment stablecoin issuers may grow, permitted payment stablecoin issuers must ensure that growth does not undercut the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's capabilities to comply with the requirements of this rule and other applicable law. For example, rapid issuance of new payment stablecoins would require a rapid increase in reserves, and permitted payment stablecoin issuers must ensure that they maintain the capabilities to maintain these reserves in compliance with § 15.11 and maintain the ability to access and monetize the reserves in order to meet redemption requests. The approach in the final rule is sufficiently tailored to the business models of permitted payment stablecoin issuers and balances flexibility with the need to appropriately manage the risks associated with asset growth.
Proposed § 15.13(a)(5) would have required that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer establish and maintain a risk management system that is commensurate with the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's size and complexity and the nature and scope of its operations to evaluate and monitor earnings and ensure that earnings are sufficient to support operations and maintain the capital levels that would be required under subpart E of proposed part 15. Commenters generally supported requiring permitted payment stablecoin issuers to adopt risk management systems commensurate with their size and complexity and the nature and scope of their operations. Some commenters recommended including additional and more prescriptive requirements with respect to how a permitted payment stablecoin issuer monitors its earnings and other risks. Some commenters stated that the rule should include more bank-like risk management requirements.
The OCC is adopting § 15.13(a)(5) as proposed. To reflect the distinct characteristics of permitted payment stablecoin issuers, the standards on earnings in § 15.13(a)(5) do not include all the listed elements in paragraph II.H in appendix A to 12 CFR part 30, from which the earnings standard in proposed § 15.13(a)(5) was adapted. Permitted payment stablecoin issuers must nevertheless comply with the overarching requirement to evaluate and monitor earnings. It may be particularly important for permitted payment stablecoin issuers to evaluate the volatility and sustainability of earnings, since changes in short-term interest rates could have sudden impacts on permitted payment stablecoin issuer earnings. Section 15.13(a)(5) provides risk management requirements that are appropriately tailored to the business model of permitted payment stablecoin issuers. The OCC declines to include additional prescriptive requirements in the rule text in keeping with the principles-based approach to risk management under
12 CFR part 15

Under proposed paragraph (a)(6)(i), a permitted payment stablecoin issuer would have been required to ensure that transactions between the permitted payment stablecoin issuer and insiders or affiliates: (1) are not excessive and do not pose significant risks of material financial loss; (2) are conducted on terms that are the same or at least as

The final rule modifies paragraph (a)(6) to provide more clarity while maintaining a principles-based approach. First, paragraph (a)(6)(i) has been modified to include the phrase “alone or in the aggregate” to clarify the scope of transactions between the permitted payment stablecoin issuer and its affiliates or insiders to which paragraph (a)(6)(i) applies. In addition, the OCC has modified paragraph (a)(6)(i)(A) to remove the word “excessive” and provide greater specificity as to the types of transactions prohibited under the final rule. Paragraph (a)(6)(i)(A) of the final rule prohibits transactions that are quantitatively detrimental to the permitted payment stablecoin issuer in light of the business model of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer. The degree of risk and potential loss associated with one or more transactions is dependent on the business model of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer. As a result, the particular business model will be relevant to whether a particular transaction, a series of transactions, or transactions in the aggregate would be appropriate for a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to consider in the context of fulfilling its § 15.13 risk management obligations. Proposed § 15.13(a)(7) addressed requirements for overseeing third-party service provider arrangements. Specifically, a permitted payment stablecoin issuer must (i) exercise appropriate due diligence in selecting its service providers; (ii) require its service providers by contract to implement appropriate measures designed to meet the requirements of part 15; and (iii) as appropriate, monitor its service providers to confirm they have satisfied their obligations under proposed part 15.
Several commenters requested clarification on third-party risk management practices. For example, a few requests for clarification concerned whether banks may oversee stablecoin-related programs through established program-management structures. A few comments requested clarification that regulated entities are responsible for compliance outcomes even when relying on third-party providers. Other comments requested clarification that evaluating a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's service provider oversight program requires assessing performance in addition to contractual provisions. Some commenters requested robust third-party risk management expectations given community banks' reliance on third-party technology partners in the digital assets space. Other commenters requested specific reference to third-party service providers in the rule, for example, by referencing the establishment and monitoring of service level agreements as a component of the contractual and monitoring requirements in § 15.13(a)(7).
The OCC is adopting § 15.13(a)(7) as proposed with two minor changes. The final rule includes a reference to compliance with the GENIUS Act in addition to compliance with part 15. Paragraph (a)(7) provides an appropriately robust and principles-based approach with respect to third-party risk management. As part of this monitoring, a permitted payment stablecoin issuer must review audits, summaries of test results, or other equivalent evaluations of its service providers. The final rule also moves the phrase “by contract” for clarity.
Proposed § 15.13(a)(8) would have required a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to (i) appropriately monitor and validate compliance with the requirements of § 15.11 and (ii) manage liquidity and concentration risk in a manner that is appropriate to the business model and risk profile of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer.
As discussed above, several commenters recommended that the OCC use a stress testing framework in place of the prescriptive and quantitative requirements in proposed § 15.11. Consistent with this feedback, the OCC is adopting § 15.13(a)(8) as proposed but is also adopting new § 15.13(a)(9), which provides monetization and stress testing requirements. Under the new § 15.13(a)(9)(i), a permitted payment stablecoin issuer must ensure that the reserve asset portfolio, taken as a whole, is capable of supporting timely redemption under both normal and stressed conditions, including by conducting analyses considering a range of redemption scenarios.

Additionally, under § 15.13(a)(9)(iii), a permitted payment stablecoin issuer must engage in regular stress testing of the reserve asset portfolio in order to confirm that the portfolio of reserve assets will continue to equal or exceed outstanding issuance value in stressed conditions,

including in significant positive interest rate scenarios.
The OCC is also adding new § 15.13(a)(10) which addresses the risk management of foreign exchange risk. The proposal asked whether the OCC should explicitly provide that managing foreign exchange risk is a permissible activity for the issuers of stablecoins that are not denominated in the United States dollar and whether to include limitations relating to the management of foreign exchange risk. Commenters generally favored permitting foreign exchange risk management as a permitted activity. Commenters noted that permitting foreign exchange risk management would reduce risk. Some commenters emphasized that the final rule should not permit speculation.
Consistent with this feedback, the final rule requires foreign exchange risk management for issuers that issue payment stablecoins that are denominated in monetary value other than the United States dollar, subject to certain conditions designed to ensure that the foreign exchange risk is appropriately hedged and that the permitted payment stablecoin issuer does not use its foreign exchange risk management program as a means of engaging in impermissible speculation. Under the final rule, a permitted payment stablecoin issuer that issues a payment stablecoin denominated in monetary value other than the United States dollar must hedge any residual foreign exchange risk identified pursuant to the monetization and stress testing requirements of § 15.13(a)(9) in accordance with § 15.13(a)(10). Section 15.13(a)(10)(ii) states that the permitted payment stablecoin issuer: (A) may not take anticipatory positions or maintain residual positions in the instruments used to hedge the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's foreign exchange risk, except as necessary for the orderly establishment or unwinding of a hedging position; (B) must hedge to retain no more than minimal foreign exchange risk; (C) must not use foreign exchange risk management as a means to speculate, including with respect to the appreciation or depreciation of any national currency; and (D) must have in place policies and procedures that appropriately manage its foreign exchange risk and any attendant risks, including risks relating to the posting or collection of margin, foreign exchange counterparties, and basis risk. The policies and procedures must include adherence to the below-described § 15.13(a)(10)(iii) and (iv). Under § 15.13(a)(10)(iii), before a permitted payment stablecoin issuer engages in foreign exchange risk management, it must provide prior notice to the OCC through its supervisory office and receive the OCC's approval. Additionally, under § 15.13(a)(10)(iv), the permitted payment stablecoin issuer must adhere to any limit or other condition to the OCC's approval under § 15.13(a)(10)(iii). Such limits or conditions are likely to concern how the permitted payment stablecoin issuer remains both capable of meeting redemption requests in a timely manner and fully reserved.
Notably, while a permitted payment stablecoin issuer that issues a non-dollar-denominated payment stablecoin must engage in foreign exchange risk management under the final rule, foreign exchange derivatives are not permitted reserve assets under section 4(a)(1)(A) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(A)
). Accordingly, the fair value of foreign exchange derivatives used to hedge a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's foreign exchange risk is not included in the reserve asset value of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer, and a permitted payment stablecoin issuer may need to hold a buffer to ensure that its non-dollar-denominated payment stablecoins remain properly reserved. Such derivatives may, however, be relevant to the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's liquidity risk management and ability to timely redeem payment stablecoins. A permitted payment stablecoin issuer that issues a non-dollar-denominated stablecoin should consider and address the effectiveness of its hedging instruments and how such instruments may behave in times of stress. For example, the need to rapidly unwind and reapply hedges in times of stress may limit the effectiveness of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's hedging strategy. Accordingly, permitted payment stablecoin issuers should carefully consider their ability to manage foreign exchange risk before issuing a non-dollar-denominated payment stablecoin. Likewise, the OCC expects it would closely review such activities, both as proposed and on an ongoing basis.
Proposed § 15.13(b) addressed risk management requirements relating to information technology and security. Several commenters suggested addressing risk management expectations for specific technologies, such as smart contracts or super intelligence. For example, a few commenters suggested requiring smart contract controls governing activities such as minting, burning, and freezing. Other commenters suggested establishing specific requirements governing the use of super intelligence, given that, as the commenters noted, its use may become commonplace among permitted payment stablecoin issuers in their compliance programs. The final rule includes a reference to smart contracts but does not impose detailed requirements with respect to particular technologies. This level of detail is consistent with the GENIUS Act and the principles-based and technology-neutral approach that
12 CFR part 15
is taking toward risk management.
Proposed § 15.13(b)(1) provided that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer must implement a comprehensive written information security risk and control framework, including a program that assesses and manages information technology and information security risks. The OCC is finalizing § 15.13(b)(1) as proposed.
Under proposed § 15.13(b)(2), the board of directors of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer, or an appropriate board committee, would have been required to approve the information technology and security program described in paragraph (b)(1). The board would have been required to oversee the development, implementation, and maintenance of the program, including the appointment of a qualified Information Technology and Security Officer. The oversight required of the board or committee would have included assigning specific responsibility for program implementation and review of program-related reports.
A few commenters supported requiring a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to have a Chief Risk Officer or Chief Audit Executive in addition to the Information Technology and Security Officer. Some commenters suggested that it is more important for the rule to require permitted payment stablecoin issuers to have officers and employees with the responsibilities of certain roles, such as a Chief Risk Officer, rather than requiring a specific officer or role. A few commenters suggested requiring a Chief Risk Officer with explicit responsibilities distinct from the Information Technology and Security Officer, for example, requiring a Chief Risk Officer with explicit responsibility for protocol-level exposure above a materiality threshold. Another commenter suggested that a subsidiary permitted payment stablecoin issuer should be able to satisfy any requirement for a Chief Risk Officer if the subsidiary's parent has a Chief Risk Officer. Another commenter suggested that a tailored approach to requiring a Chief Risk Officer or Chief Audit Executive ought to be adopted,

where the requirements should be proportionate to the size and complexity of the issuer and consistent with standards applicable to comparable financial institutions.
The OCC is adopting § 15.13(b)(2) with a modification to refer to “a qualified individual responsible for the program” and deleting the reference to an “Information Technology and Security Officer.” The OCC agrees with some commenters that it is more important for a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to have qualified individuals with the relevant responsibilities for overseeing the information technology and security program rather than to prescribe certain required titles or role names. The OCC is not requiring permitted payment stablecoin issuers to have additional named roles at this time. Permitted payment stablecoin issuers should generally create organizational roles to appropriately manage their operations. As discussed above, a permitted payment stablecoin issuer that is a subsidiary of an insured depository institution may rely on the parent's risk management framework, including certain shared employees, provided that the parent's risk management framework addresses the requirements of part 15 and the management of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer plays a meaningful role in the risk management framework related to the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's activities.
Under proposed § 15.13(b)(3), a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's information technology and security program would have needed to include (i) an inventory and classification of assets, processes, and sensitivity of data; (ii) controls supporting and safeguarding sensitive information and processes; (iii) evaluation, validation, and reporting processes to ensure that key information technology systems and controls, including smart contracts, are operating as intended; (iv) periodic independent testing; and (v) a comprehensive and effective incident identification and assessment process and incident response program.
Several commenters suggested various specific information security requirements that, they argued, would be broadly appropriate for payment stablecoin issuers. These commenters' descriptions indicate that these reflect the current and latest standards given the existing operational models and technology related to payment stablecoins. The OCC is adopting § 15.13(b)(3) as proposed. The OCC believes that the requirements of § 15.13(b)(3) are appropriately principles-based and technology-neutral. This approach will help ensure that the requirements remain relevant as relevant technology and best practices continue to develop.
Under proposed § 15.13(b)(4), a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's information technology and security program would have had to include administrative, technical, and physical safeguards designed to (i) ensure the security and confidentiality of records containing nonpublic personal information about a customer; (ii) protect against any anticipated threats or hazards to the security or integrity of such records; (iii) protect against unauthorized access to or use of such records that could result in substantial harm or inconvenience to any customer; and (iv) ensure the proper disposal of such records.
A few commenters suggested requiring permitted payment stablecoin issuers to adopt privacy-preserving technologies to limit public disclosure of information. Some commenters suggested that demonstrating adoption of privacy-enhancing technologies should be sufficient to show compliance with risk management information security requirements. The OCC is not mandating the use of any particular privacy-enhancing technology in the final rule, consistent with the OCC's technology-neutral and principles-based approach to § 15.13. Permitted payment stablecoin issuers must ensure that their activities comply with § 15.13(b) and applicable BSA/AML-related requirements. Whether a particular privacy-enhancing architecture can comply with both provisions will depend on the facts of that particular architecture. Accordingly, the OCC is not commenting generally on whether a particular architecture is permitted or prohibited.
Because § 15.13 must be principles-based and technology-neutral, as described above, the OCC believes that imposing requirements surrounding privacy-enhancing technology would be inappropriate. The OCC notes that § 15.13(b) does include requirements concerning the security of customer information, including developing an information technology and security program, ensuring the security and confidentiality of records containing nonpublic personal information about a customer, protecting against any anticipated threats or hazards to the security or integrity of records that could result in harm or inconvenience to any customer, and ensuring the proper disposal of such records. The OCC is adopting paragraph (b)(4) with one clarifying change. The final rule includes a reference to sensitive customer information, in addition to nonpublic personal information. Sensitive customer information will generally be a subset of nonpublic personal information. The final rule clarifies that, to the extent there is sensitive customer information that is not nonpublic personal information, the permitted payment stablecoin issuer must nonetheless take appropriate steps to ensure the security and confidentiality of such information.
Proposed § 15.13(b)(5) provided that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer must develop, implement, and maintain appropriate measures to ensure secure handling of digital assets, including private key management, backup, and recovery, incorporating: (i) relevant technical, operational, strategic, market, legal, and compliance considerations relating to each digital asset and its underlying ledger; and (ii) material developments specifically related to supported digital assets and their underlying ledgers.

Proposed § 15.13(b)(7)(i) would have required a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to conduct a reasonable investigation when it became aware of an incident of unauthorized access to sensitive customer information, including a customer's private key, to determine the likelihood that the information had been or would be misused. Specifically, the final rule replaces a reference to “a group of files” with “the files of a group of customers” for additional clarity. Proposed § 15.13(b)(8) provided that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's information technology and security program must include measures to ensure continuity of operations and recover critical functions in the face of disruptions, including by business impact analyses, testing of vulnerabilities, and testing with critical service providers.
Some commenters stated that § 15.13(b)(8) should be modified to include specific additional items such as ongoing monitoring of critical service provider performance. The language of § 15.13(b)(8) is broad enough to include such monitoring to the extent necessary to ensure continuity of operations.
The OCC is adopting § 15.13(b)(8) with two modifications. First, the final rule omits the phrase “in the face of disruptions” because the phrase was not necessary to include. Recent corporate information technology system failures have demonstrated the importance of measures to maintain operational resilience. Permitted payment stablecoin issuers should ensure that they have sufficient controls to reliably address operational issues that may arise with burning and minting new stablecoins and should conduct appropriate due diligence before supporting any new distributed ledger. Operational resilience will be particularly important for permitted payment stablecoin issuers, who will depend on customer confidence in the stable value and availability of their stablecoins. Second, the final rule changes “testing of vulnerabilities” to “testing for vulnerabilities” to clarify the purpose of the testing.

b. Examinations
i. Description of the Proposed Rule
Section 6(a)(1) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5905(a)(1)
) authorizes primary Federal payment stablecoin regulators, including the OCC, to supervise permitted payment stablecoin issuers, as defined in the statute, that are not State qualified payment stablecoin issuers with an outstanding issuance of less than $10 billion in payment stablecoins. Section 6(a)(3) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5905(a)(3)
) authorizes the OCC to examine permitted payment stablecoin issuers to assess the nature of their operations and the financial condition of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer; the financial, operational, technological, compliance, and other risks associated with the permitted payment stablecoin issuer that may pose a threat to the safety and soundness of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer or the stability of the financial system of the United States; and the systems of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer for monitoring and controlling the risks. Pursuant to section 6(a)(4)(C) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5905(a)(4)(C)
), the OCC may only request examinations at a cadence and in a format that is similar to that required for similarly situated entities regulated by the OCC.
Proposed § 15.14(a) provided that the OCC will conduct a full-scope examination of every permitted payment stablecoin issuer subject to its supervision at least once during each 12-month period, unless otherwise specified in proposed § 15.14(d).
Consistent with the OCC's statutory authority to supervise permitted payment stablecoin issuers, proposed § 15.14(d) would have provided the OCC with the option to examine some permitted payment stablecoin issuers on an 18- to 36-month cycle, as determined by the OCC, in its sole discretion, if the issuers satisfied the following conditions: (1) the permitted payment stablecoin issuer currently is not subject to a formal enforcement proceeding or order; (2) no person acquired control, as specified in § 15.14(m), of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer during the preceding 12-month period in which a full-scope examination would have been required but for proposed § 15.14(d); (3) the permitted payment stablecoin issuer has an outstanding issuance value of less than $1 billion or less than $25 billion in total monthly trading volume; and (4) the permitted payment stablecoin issuer is in compliance with all of the reserve requirements set forth in proposed § 15.11 and the reporting requirements in proposed § 15.14. The proposed criteria for certain permitted payment stablecoin issuers to qualify for an 18- to 36-month examination cycle were similar to the factors the OCC considers for national banks and Federal savings associations under
12 CFR 4.6(b)
.
Consistent with the OCC's statutory authority under the GENIUS Act and the OCC's supervisory authority over national banks and Federal savings associations, proposed § 15.14(e) would have allowed the OCC to conduct examinations of permitted payment stablecoin issuers as frequently as the agency deemed necessary, including examinations of a limited scope.
[
114
]
The OCC proposed this provision to ensure the agency had a clear mechanism, consistent with its statutory authority, to conduct ad hoc examinations when emergencies or risks to the safety and soundness of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer or the financial stability of the United States required the agency to deviate from its routine 12- or 18- to 36-month examination cycle.
Proposed § 15.14(b) would have required that, upon request, permitted payment stablecoin issuers grant OCC examiners prompt and complete access to all officers, directors, employees, agents, and relevant books, records, or documents of any type. The OCC, through its examination authority over national banks and Federal savings associations, has authority to access the officers, agents, and books and records of these institutions.
[
115
]
The books and records of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer include, but are not limited to, information retained on distributed ledgers. Sections 6(a)(1), (3), and (4) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5905(a)(1)
, (3), and (4)) give the OCC similar authority to supervise and examine permitted payment stablecoin issuers. Proposed § 15.14(b) would have applied the OCC's examination authority to permitted payment stablecoin issuers in the same manner that it is applied to national banks and Federal savings associations. Additionally, proposed § 15.14(c) would have clarified that the OCC may conduct examinations either on site or remotely. Proposed § 15.14(f) would have provided that all permitted payment stablecoin issuers must maintain a complete set of books and records in English. Proposed § 15.14(g) would have required all permitted payment stablecoin issuers to develop and implement a records retention policy that ensured the permitted payment stablecoin issuer could demonstrate compliance with the GENIUS Act, this part, and all applicable laws and regulations.
ii. Description of Comments and Final Rule
Many commenters submitted general comments about the proposed examination framework and requested that the OCC modify or incorporate various concepts into the proposed examination framework. The OCC received several comments related to the imposition of uniform standards on permitted payment stablecoin issuers. Specifically, several commenters stated that banks operate in a highly regulated environment, and if permitted payment stablecoin issuers offer bank-like products, they should also be subject to the same supervisory expectations to which banks are subject. One commenter also stated that inconsistent standards or permitted payment stablecoin issuer-specific safe harbors risk creating perceived tiers of payment stablecoin quality. The commenter further added that keeping standards high and uniform protects the global “singleness” of U.S.-issued dollar stablecoins and urged the OCC to establish uniform examination, reporting, capital, and other prudential requirements. Another commenter claimed that nonbank stablecoin issuers present materially different supervisory considerations and argued that the OCC should apply more stringent, standalone audit, reporting, and transparency
(
printed page 67079)
requirements to nonbank issuers to account for the absence of consolidated supervision, ongoing examination, and access to the Federal banking safety net. The commenter further argued that applying uniform requirements across bank and nonbank issuers would fail to recognize these differences and could place community banks at a competitive disadvantage despite their significantly higher level of existing regulatory oversight.
After considering these comments, the OCC is finalizing § 15.14 as proposed with certain minor changes and clarifications. The overall framework continues to recognize the key differences between the business models of banks and permitted payment stablecoin issuers while ensuring that the OCC receives sufficient information from permitted payment stablecoin issuers to carry out its supervisory duties under the GENIUS Act.
One commenter stated that, where a technology provider has been examined by another Federal regulator in connection with stablecoin services, the OCC should consider that examination work as part of its own independent evaluation. The commenter stated that this approach would reduce duplicative burden on community banks and their technology partners without compromising OCC supervisory authority. As the OCC develops experience in examining and supervising permitted payment stablecoin issuers, it will consider whether it should revisit or revise the examination schedule and the triggers or measures for conducting limited-scope or ad hoc examinations. Further, the agency has not established general retention standards for national banks and Federal savings associations, so establishing minimum records retention standards for permitted payment stablecoin issuers would be inconsistent with the agency's supervisory approach for national banks and Federal savings associations. Section 6(a)(4) of the GENIUS Act (

Proposed § 15.14(j) implemented section 6(a)(2) of the GENIUS Act and would have required each permitted payment stablecoin issuer subject to the requirements of section 6(a)(1) of the Act to, upon request, submit to the OCC a report on: (1) the financial condition of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer; (2) the systems of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer for monitoring and controlling financial and operating risks; (3) compliance by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer (and any subsidiary thereof) with the GENIUS Act and proposed part 15; and (4) compliance of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer with the Bank Secrecy Act and with laws authorizing the imposition of sanctions and implemented by the Secretary of the Treasury. This regular data reporting would have allowed the OCC to tailor its examinations to be risk-based, which would have reduced the burden of examinations by focusing the scope of examinations. In addition, the OCC stated that this regular reporting framework would have allowed the agency to identify and respond more quickly to emerging novel risks and financial stability risks. ii. Description of Comments and Final Rule
Many commenters submitted general comments about the proposed reporting framework and requested that the OCC modify or incorporate various concepts into the proposed reporting framework. Several commenters expressed general support for the OCC's proposed reporting framework. The commenters stated that the cadence and data fields were sufficient to support the prudential regulation of permitted payment stablecoin issuers. One commenter expressed support for the reporting framework on the grounds that it may reduce the need for more intrusive or frequent on-site examinations. Another commenter expressed support for standardized reporting forms on the grounds that they are a proportionate mechanism to improve supervisory visibility into the operational, liquidity, and market risks of permitted payment stablecoin issuers.
Several commenters encouraged the OCC to coordinate stablecoin reporting requirements under the proposal with other Federal payment stablecoin regulators, stating that interagency coordination is essential to promote consistency, reduce duplication, and ensure an efficient supervisory framework for institutions subject to multiple Federal regulators. At this time, the OCC has determined that the issuance of OCC-specific reporting forms for OCC-supervised permitted payment stablecoin issuers best ensures that the weekly and quarterly reporting forms are available when the agency's stablecoin regulations become effective. In the future, the OCC will consider potentially using an interagency framework for the submission of reports to promote consistency.
Several commenters recommended additional reporting requirements to strengthen supervisory oversight of permitted payment stablecoin issuers.
(
printed page 67083)
One commenter urged the OCC to require monthly reporting of any instances in which a permitted payment stablecoin issuer extends the redemption period beyond two business days to complete compliance checks. Another commenter suggested that regulators consider collecting data on transaction rejections, delays, account closures, and geographic restrictions to improve visibility into access-related outcomes. A further commenter recommended that the OCC consider requiring an annual attestation report on management's assertions regarding the effectiveness of internal controls over stablecoin operations and reserves. Another commenter recommended that the final rule require every OCC-supervised permitted payment stablecoin issuer to file a current report with the OCC within one business day whenever the secondary market trading price of its payment stablecoin deviates downward from $1.00 by more than one quarter of one percent.
One commenter stated that new reporting obligations should leverage information already maintained in the ordinary course of business wherever possible. The commenter noted that payment stablecoins may present supervisory visibility challenges that are not fully addressed by traditional banking or payments reporting, particularly once stablecoins circulate beyond initial issuance and redemption channels. The commenter stated that the OCC should consider whether targeted, standardized, machine-readable reporting fields are appropriate to capture material secondary-market activity, concentration, operational interventions, and other risk indicators that may be observable through issuers, service providers, or private or public blockchain data. The commenter claimed that such an approach would help avoid supervisory blind spots while remaining consistent with a risk-based and operationally practicable framework.
One commenter stated that smaller institutions may lack the staffing and systems needed to support frequent or highly granular reporting, including weekly submissions, and urged the OCC to account for those operational constraints. The commenter recommended that the OCC rely on existing supervisory information and frameworks for bank-affiliated issuers wherever practicable and avoid requirements that would force new technology investments, additional staffing, or duplicative attestations without clear supervisory benefit. The commenter also urged the OCC to provide standardized reporting tools if more frequent reporting is required and supported an additional tier for small issuers to better align requirements with risk and operational capacity. The commenter further stated that nonbank permitted payment stablecoin issuers warrant more prescriptive reporting obligations, given the absence of an ongoing prudential supervisory relationship comparable to that applicable to insured depository institutions. Another commenter stated that traditional core systems are often limited to two decimal places, whereas other stablecoins require six. The commenter stated that the agency should consider the operational modernization required to support stablecoins. The OCC recognizes that some banks may currently lack the operational capacity to support certain payment stablecoin activities. Such institutions are not required to engage in payment stablecoin activities, but, to the extent that they do so, they must do so in a safe and sound manner, which may entail modernizing certain systems.
Several commenters recommended that the agency adopt a risk-based reporting framework based on a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's size, complexity, and risk profile. In general, the commenters recommended that the OCC implement reduced or streamlined reporting requirements for smaller and less complex permitted payment stablecoin issuers. The commenters claimed that these permitted payment stablecoin issuers do not present the same risk as larger, more complex permitted payment stablecoin issuers and therefore should not be subject to the same reporting requirements. Some commenters added that a reduced reporting burden would result in a reduction in operating expenses for smaller permitted payment stablecoin issuers. One commenter recommended that the OCC impose reduced reporting requirements on those permitted payment stablecoin issuers that qualify for an extended examination cycle under § 15.14(d). Upon consideration, the OCC has determined that all permitted payment stablecoin issuers should be required to submit weekly reporting and quarterly reports of condition because this information is essential to the oversight of permitted payment stablecoin issuers and the stablecoin market. The OCC has proposed reporting forms for comment and will revise those forms, as appropriate, based on the comments received. In addition, the OCC intends to evaluate the information it receives from reports from permitted payment stablecoin issuers to consider whether to revise the reporting forms to reduce burden while still providing the information necessary to the OCC's supervision.
Commenters urged the OCC to adopt a reporting framework that maintains regulatory differentiation between bank and nonbank stablecoin issuers. The commenters stated that bank-affiliated issuers should be permitted to satisfy stablecoin-specific reporting obligations through streamlined, integrated disclosures—such as supplemental schedules to Call Reports—while nonbank issuers should be subject to more robust, standalone reporting and audit requirements commensurate with their risk profile and lack of prudential supervision. Commenters stated that this approach would preserve safety and soundness, promote regulatory consistency, and support community bank participation in stablecoin activities without disadvantaging institutions that already operate under a rigorous supervisory framework.
After careful consideration of the comments, the OCC has determined that all permitted payment stablecoin issuers should be subject to uniform reporting requirements. This approach ensures that the OCC receives a consistent set of data across all permitted payment stablecoin issuers. As discussed, the OCC considered the information to be collected to be an appropriate minimum amount of data for permitted payment stablecoin issuers. The receipt of this data will also allow the OCC to calibrate its supervisory approach to each permitted payment stablecoin issuer and minimize supervisory disruptions associated with limited and full-scope examinations. Moreover, reporting consistency should help the OCC ensure comparability and better facilitate market oversight.
A few commenters urged the OCC to focus reporting on primary market data, including primary market issuance, redemption activity, and reserve composition. One commenter emphasized that the proposed weekly reporting should focus on primary market data instead of secondary market data. The commenters added that, if the OCC does require secondary market reporting, the data collected should focus on material secondary market indicators relevant to prudential supervision and market integrity. Some of the commenters also noted the challenges with reporting secondary market data since market activity occurs across multiple venues and through intermediaries where the permitted payment stablecoin issuer may lack full visibility. The agency received several comments concerning whether the agency should implement real-time reporting. A few commenters expressed support for real-time reporting. One commenter noted that some relevant data exists on-chain and can be extracted in real time. Another commenter stated that the implementation of real-time reporting could meaningfully reduce the frequency of on-site examinations.
Conversely, several commenters opposed the adoption of real-time reporting and stated that it should not be required in the final rule. The commenters generally claimed that real-time reporting would be unnecessary or overly burdensome. One commenter stated that while permitted payment stablecoin issuers may track certain data in real time, translating such data into a form ready for supervisory reporting often requires reconciliation, validation, and normalization processes that would make real-time external reporting unnecessarily burdensome. Another commenter stated that some data fields are not observable in real time and that a weekly reporting cadence is more aligned with the operational rhythm already used by issuers. Another commenter stated that a weekly reporting cadence is preferable to real-time reporting and suggested that the weekly reporting framework could be supplemented with event-driven reporting.
Upon consideration, the OCC has declined to incorporate a real-time reporting component into the reporting framework for permitted payment stablecoin issuers. The OCC has determined that a weekly and quarterly reporting cadence will provide the agency with sufficient data and supervisory visibility into the stablecoin market. Further, the agency is sensitive to the increased operational expense and burden that the implementation of real-time reporting would impose on permitted payment stablecoin issuers. For these reasons, the OCC has declined to impose a real-time reporting requirement on permitted payment stablecoin issuers. The OCC may reconsider this position in the future if, for example, effective supervision of the stablecoin market demands the implementation of real-time reporting or future technological advances mean that implementing real-time reporting would not be overly burdensome for permitted payment stablecoin issuers.

Weekly Reports
As discussed above, proposed § 15.14(h) would have required all permitted payment stablecoin issuers to submit a confidential weekly report to the OCC in the manner and form specified by the agency. Under the proposal, a permitted payment stablecoin issuer would have been required to provide information regarding stablecoin issuance and redemption, trading volume, and reserve assets for each payment stablecoin it issues. The report would have included information relating to the blockchains on which the payment stablecoin operates, outstanding issuance value, secondary market activity and price movements, redemption volume and timing, detailed information regarding reserve assets, and other relevant information. As discussed above, the agency published the weekly and quarterly reporting forms for notice and public comment on June 12, 2026. The following discussion includes comments received in response to the proposal's issuance on March 2, 2026, and the weekly reporting forms and instructions' issuance on June 12, 2026.
A few commenters expressed support for the weekly reporting cadence on the grounds that the reporting framework is generally well calibrated and directionally appropriate. However, the commenters also expressed a desire for the OCC to narrow the data fields to categories more closely tied to the statutory requirements and prudential oversight. For example, commenters recommended recalibrating the data fields to focus on liquidity, reserve management, and redemptions.
Several commenters also expressed opposition to the weekly reporting requirement. Generally, the commenters opposed the weekly reporting requirement on the grounds that it is overly burdensome, particularly for smaller issuers. In some cases, the commenters questioned the supervisory value of weekly reporting. The commenters also expressed a preference for a variety of reporting alternatives, including monthly reporting, monthly reporting accompanied by event-triggered reporting, and quarterly confidential reporting in addition to quarterly public reporting. One commenter added that if the OCC adopts weekly reporting, the data fields should be limited to the core data fields necessary to monitor a permitted payment stablecoin issuer for safety and soundness.
Under proposed § 15.14(h), the weekly reporting submitted to the OCC would have been confidential. One commenter expressed the view that stablecoin holders would benefit from having access to weekly reporting and encouraged the OCC to make the weekly reporting available to the public. Two commenters opposed the disclosure of weekly data on the grounds that it could create market distortions, reveal commercially sensitive information, and risk encouraging short-term market reactions to normal operational fluctuations that do not reflect underlying prudential concerns. Further, the commenters stated that disclosures should be focused on statutorily required disclosures such as reserve composition. One of the commenters expressed an openness to the disclosure of aggregated statistics on payment stablecoin issuance and volumes, among other things, for payment stablecoins.
One commenter stated that the weekly reporting under proposed § 15.14(h) is not designed to identify protocol-level exposure. Specifically, the commenter stated that the data fields enumerated in proposed § 15.14(h) are appropriate for entity-level reserve and redemption oversight, but do not capture the protocol deployment of stablecoin-denominated assets where systemic risk is concentrated.
Several commenters opposed the OCC's proposed weekly collection of “the 100 persons that hold or trade the stablecoin the most.” Commenters generally opposed the collection of this information on several grounds. First, commenters stated that the OCC has not articulated a clear supervisory rationale for collecting this data and that this information is not essential to understanding a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's operations. Second, commenters claimed that issuers cannot reliably produce this data because payment stablecoins frequently trade through exchanges and intermediaries, which limits permitted payment stablecoin issuers' ability to reliably identify the top 100 holders on a recurring basis. Finally, the commenters claimed that the required disclosure of top-holder information raises significant privacy concerns. Several commenters presented solutions ranging from removing the collection of this data from the weekly reporting form to focusing the collection on the top 100 wallets, which would not include any beneficial ownership information.
Upon review of the comments, the OCC intends to keep the weekly reporting confidential. The agency believes that the confidentiality of this reporting serves the interest of promoting the exchange of supervisory information between permitted payment stablecoin issuers and the OCC. In the future, the OCC may consider publishing a limited set of data if it would be useful to the public. For example, the OCC may consider publishing a limited set of aggregate statistics based on the weekly reporting. The OCC published a draft weekly reporting form for comment that requests information on the top 100 payment stablecoin wallet addresses, not information identifying the top 100 individual persons holding payment stablecoins of an issuer.

The OCC believes the collection of this information will provide important supervisory data points related to concentration risk, payment stablecoin volatility, and other payment stablecoin characteristics that are important to the OCC's supervision of permitted payment stablecoin issuers. The OCC plans to make adjustments to the reporting forms as appropriate to address comments received, as the market develops, and as the OCC gains experience supervising permitted payment stablecoin issuers.
