Many transactions that involve the merger of permitted payment stablecoin issuers will have direct or indirect changes in ownership. Thus, such transactions would be subject to the provisions of § 15.14(m). For other merger transactions that would not implicate § 15.14(m), the OCC will continue to review and supervise the permitted payment stablecoin issuers in the ordinary course and would take supervisory or other action if appropriate to address concerns related to a merger. Therefore, permitted payment stablecoin issuers are encouraged to discuss any planned merger activity with the OCC to ensure consistency with OCC requirements and supervisory expectations.
With regard to noncompliance with the change-in-control regulations, section 6(b) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5905(b)
) grants the OCC enforcement authority to pursue a variety of enforcement actions for violations of the GENIUS Act and its implementing regulations. Whether the OCC pursues an enforcement action and the type of enforcement action that the agency elects to pursue will be dictated by the facts and circumstances underlying any alleged violation of the GENIUS Act or the OCC's implementing regulations. Therefore, it is not necessary or appropriate to identify explicit consequences for noncompliance with the change-in-control regulations at this time.
f. Efficiency and Burden Reduction
Proposed § 15.14(n) provided that, in supervising and examining a permitted payment stablecoin issuer, the OCC will use existing reports and other supervisory information to the fullest extent possible. The OCC stated that this subsection was intended to reduce unnecessary burden by allowing the OCC to leverage information already available through existing reporting or supervisory channels.
Proposed § 15.14(o) provided that the OCC will, to the fullest extent possible, avoid duplication of examination activities, reporting requirements, and requests for information. The OCC stated that this subsection reflects an express effort to minimize redundant supervisory demands while preserving the OCC's ability to obtain information needed for effective oversight.
The OCC received a number of comments related to burden reduction and the avoidance of duplication. One commenter recommended that the agency explicitly recognize internal audit work product as a category of existing supervisory information that examiners may rely on where such work is relevant, current, and performed in accordance with recognized professional standards. The commenter claimed that this approach would reduce issuer compliance burden, improve supervisory efficiency, and create positive incentives for investment in high-quality internal audit programs.
Two commenters recommended that the OCC allow a permitted payment stablecoin issuer that is a subsidiary of an insured depository institution to leverage its parent's enterprise-wide risk management infrastructure, including risk appetite statements and third-party risk management programs, where appropriate, to satisfy risk-management and supervisory requirements. One of the commenters further recommended that the OCC include guidance to this effect in its commentary to the final rule and the Comptroller's Handbook. The OCC confirms that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer may leverage enterprise-wide infrastructure, provided that the permitted payment stablecoin issuer does so in compliance with the requirements of part 15.
Another commenter encouraged the OCC to develop centralized and standardized reporting mechanisms—such as a secure reporting portal—that are aligned with existing bank reporting systems and service provider capabilities. The commenter stated that new reporting requirements applicable to community banks should be limited, targeted, and designed to leverage data already maintained in the ordinary course of business. The commenter also claimed that stablecoin-related risks can be effectively evaluated by incorporating them into established examination modules. The commenter stated that stablecoin-related audit and reporting obligations for bank-affiliated issuers should be appropriately integrated into existing supervisory frameworks rather than imposed through separate or duplicative regimes. The OCC will continue to consider means of updating its reporting mechanisms, but no change in the text of the regulation is necessary at this time to address the comment.
Another commenter stated that the reporting requirements across weekly, monthly, and quarterly intervals should build on one another rather than requiring duplicative reporting. Monthly reports should, to the extent possible, draw from weekly reports, and likewise quarterly reports should draw from monthly reports. The commenter claimed that such an approach can reduce operational burden while preserving the OCC's and the public's ability to assess risk over time. The commenter also stated that to best minimize the duplication of reports, the OCC's focus should be on mitigating risk while encouraging innovation. The commenter stated that requiring duplicative reports does not provide additional risk-mitigation benefits while diverting resources and creating unnecessary burden.
Another commenter stated that the OCC can best minimize duplication by implementing a single annual audit package that satisfies overlapping requirements across § 15.14(l), monthly reserve examination outputs, and related financial-condition reporting fields, rather than requiring multiple separate submissions of the same underlying data. The commenter stated that the goal should be to collect the necessary information once, in a standardized format, and reuse it across the prudential framework where possible. For issuers, or their parents, that are already subject to Exchange Act reporting or meet the Act's $50 billion public accounting threshold, the OCC should not require additional duplicative reporting beyond what is necessary to capture stablecoin-specific fields that existing filings do not address.
Pursuant to its statutory obligations, the OCC will pursue supervisory policies that minimize duplication and maximize efficiency. The OCC notes, however, that the reports applicable to permitted payment stablecoin issuers serve distinct purposes. For example, the confidential weekly reporting is intended to provide detailed information that would be unnecessary to include in the quarterly or monthly reports. The monthly and quarterly reports are intended to provide information to the public and the OCC that may be stale or less valuable if received only on an annual basis.

After careful consideration of the comments, the OCC is finalizing § 15.14(n) and § 15.14(o) as proposed. As described above, the OCC is committed to pursuing supervisory policies that minimize duplication and maximize efficiency.
6. State Qualified Payment Stablecoin Issuers (§ 15.15)
a. Overview of Changes From Proposed Rule to Final Rule for § 15.15
The OCC proposed to issue § 15.15 to implement the GENIUS Act's transition standards for State qualified payment stablecoin issuers with an outstanding issuance value of more than $10 billion. Specifically, proposed § 15.15 would require an issuer to notify the OCC within five calendar days after the issuer triggers the transition threshold, request a waiver if the issuer seeks to remain supervised solely by the applicable State regulator, and, if applicable, provide the OCC with information necessary to evaluate an associated waiver request. Proposed § 15.15 would have also established a timeframe for the OCC's review of an issuer's waiver request. Proposed § 15.15(a) describes the scope of § 15.15 and provides that the section addresses requirements related to a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer that is a nonbank entity transitioning to the OCC's regulatory framework pursuant to section 4 of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903
).
The OCC is adopting § 15.15(a) as proposed with edits. The OCC is separating proposed § 15.15(a) into § 15.15(a)(1) and (2), with § 15.15(a)(1) including the proposed language for § 15.15(a) and § 15.15(a)(2) clarifying that, for purposes of § 15.15, the term State qualified payment stablecoin issuer refers only to those that are nonbank entities. Other edits were made in final § 15.15 to conform to this clarification in final § 15.15(a)(2).
Additionally, the OCC is adopting § 15.15(b) largely as proposed with certain technical and clarifying edits. Specifically, in §§ 15.15(b)(1), (b)(1)(ii), (b)(2), (b)(2)(ii)(C), (b)(3), and (b)(4)(ii), the OCC is adding the phrase “total consolidated” before the defined term “outstanding issuance value” or replacing the phrase “an outstanding issuance value” with “a total consolidated outstanding issuance value.” The OCC is also deleting surplus language in § 15.15(b)(1) and adding clarifying language to § 15.15(b)(1)(ii) and (b)(4)(i). Additionally, in § 15.15(b)(3)(iv), the OCC is capitalizing the word “State.” The OCC is adopting § 15.15(c) as proposed. In § 15.15(d), the OCC is separating proposed § 15.15(d)(1) into § 15.15(d)(1)(i) and (ii). Within the language proposed as the last sentence in § 15.15(d)(1), the OCC is replacing “State payment stablecoin issuer” with “State payment stablecoin regulator” as well as adding the words “total consolidated” prior to “outstanding issuance value” and adding the word “threshold” to the end of the final sentence. Similarly, in § 15.15(d)(2)(iv), the OCC is replacing the term “State qualified payment stablecoin issuer” with the term “State payment stablecoin regulator.” Otherwise, the OCC is adopting § 15.15(d) as proposed. The OCC is also adding new § 15.15(e)(1) to provide that a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer that is a nonbank entity that has transitioned to the OCC's Federal regulatory framework pursuant to § 15.15 is not generally required to comply with part 15 and will cease to be supervised by the OCC upon the OCC's determination that the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer no longer exceeds $10 billion in total consolidated outstanding issuance value. ii. Description of Comments and Final Rule
A few commenters suggested extending the 360-day transition timeline or providing case-by-case extensions (including for permitted payment stablecoin issuers that request but do not receive a waiver). The OCC is finalizing §  15.15(b)(1) as proposed with technical changes. The final rule includes the words “total consolidated” in front of “outstanding issuance value.” These revisions do not result in a substantive change but are necessary in light of the changes to the definition of outstanding issuance value. The OCC is also deleting surplus language from paragraph (b)(1) and clarifying in paragraph (b)(1)(ii) that the paragraph applies to a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer.
The 360-day transition deadline is a statutory requirement, and the OCC is not authorized to extend it. Consistent with the proposed rule, the final rule clarifies that the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer would cease issuing new payment stablecoins on a net basis. This is to permit a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer to freeze, burn, mint, and issue new payment stablecoins to the extent necessary to transfer stablecoins from one blockchain to another without increasing the total outstanding issuance of the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer.
Related to the 360-day transition requirement, question 138 of the proposed rule asked whether the $10 billion threshold should be based on a point in time or a rolling average and whether the $10 billion threshold should take into account the outstanding issuance value of any payment stablecoins issued by non-consolidated affiliates of the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer.
The OCC received several comments concerning how to calculate outstanding issuance value for purposes of the 360-day transition requirement. A few commenters generally suggested that the OCC should calculate outstanding issuance value as a point-in-time threshold. On the other hand, a few commenters generally suggested that the OCC should calculate outstanding issuance value as a rolling average.
After consideration of the comments, the OCC confirms that the transition threshold is determined through a point-in-time calculation and will not be based on a rolling average. Adopting a point-in-time calculation will safeguard against outstanding issuance value manipulation by a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer that seeks to delay or avoid complying with the 360-day transition requirement. A rolling average calculated over a meaningfully long period of time could, in effect, extend the date of transition to the Federal regulatory framework beyond what Congress intended. Moreover, the OCC generally expects that a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer's outstanding issuance value is unlikely to meaningfully fluctuate back and forth across the $10 billion threshold. Thus, there would be relatively little utility gained from using a rolling average to calculate the threshold.
Additionally, the OCC received a few comments concerning whether to include payment stablecoins issued by non-consolidated affiliates in the calculation of outstanding issuance value for purposes of the 360-day transition requirement. A few commenters generally suggested that outstanding issuance value should not automatically include non-consolidated affiliates. Another commenter generally suggested that the OCC should include non-consolidated affiliates.
After consideration of the comments, the OCC is clarifying that a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer would not be required to include payment stablecoins issued by non-consolidated affiliates in its calculation of outstanding issuance value for purposes of the 360-day transition requirements. The OCC notes, however, that in certain situations, the OCC may consider a non-consolidated affiliate's issuance. For example, if a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer treats affiliate-issued payment stablecoins as fungible with its own or appears to use affiliates solely to stay under the $10 billion threshold for transition to the Federal framework, such behavior could indicate an attempt to evade the GENIUS Act or could, depending on the facts and circumstances, indicate unusual and exigent circumstances within the meaning of section 7 of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5906
).
The OCC received several comments concerning the five-day notification requirement in proposed § 15.15(b)(2). One commenter suggested that five calendar days would be operationally feasible for issuers large enough to trigger the $10 billion outstanding issuance value threshold. The commenter further explained that five calendar days would provide the OCC with timely visibility into the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer.
A few commenters suggested that the OCC should extend the threshold notification deadline, for example, to 10 or 15 business days. One commenter suggested a five-day deadline would not provide enough time for the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer to assess compliance implications, coordinate with State regulators, and complete substantive notification requirements. Another commenter generally suggested the OCC should extend the notification deadline to better reflect the operational and governance realities of State qualified payment stablecoin issuers.

Further, the transition notification requirement would apply only after a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer exceeds $10 billion in outstanding issuance value.

State qualified payment stablecoin issuers of this size should have the capabilities to appropriately monitor issuance volume as a matter of basic risk management. Moreover, only limited information is required to be included in the initial notification.

For the reasons discussed above, the final rule includes the words “total consolidated” in front of “issuance value.” As discussed in the proposed rule, regardless of whether the OCC receives notice under §  15.15(b)(4), the OCC reserves the right to pursue appropriate action to ensure compliance with the GENIUS Act with respect to a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer that transitions to the Federal regulatory framework administered by the OCC.

A few commenters suggested the OCC should not permit State qualified payment stablecoin issuers to transition back to sole State supervision and expressed concerns such a mechanism could lead to regulatory arbitrage concerns. One of these commenters suggested that the OCC does not have authority to prevent a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer with less than $10 billion in outstanding issuance value from transitioning back to sole State supervision.
After consideration of the comments, the OCC is adding final § 15.15(e)(1) to specify that a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer that is a nonbank entity that has transitioned to the OCC's Federal regulatory framework pursuant to § 15.15 is not generally required to comply with part 15 and will cease to be supervised by the OCC upon the OCC's determination that the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer no longer exceeds $10 billion in total consolidated outstanding issuance value. Final § 15.15(e)(2) clarifies that the OCC may make this determination based on an issuer's request or issue a determination without such a request. Additionally, the OCC may review an issuer's request under section 15.15(e) to prevent evasion of section 4 of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903

12 U.S.C. 5903(h)

12 U.S.C. 5906(e)(2)
).
The OCC received a few comments on the proposed capital analysis requirement. One commenter suggested that the 270-day timeline is reasonable. Another commenter suggested that the capital analysis should be tailored to the size and operations of the applicant. After consideration of the comments, the OCC is finalizing §  15.15(b)(3) as proposed with one non-substantive change. For the reasons discussed above, the final rule includes the words “total consolidated” in front of “issuance value.” As discussed in § 15.41(a)(1), section 4(a)(4)(A)(i) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(4)(A)(i)

Consistent with this requirement, the OCC expects a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer to provide a capital analysis with information sufficient for the OCC to evaluate the issuer's current capital position and anticipated capital needs based on its business model and risk profile. The OCC expects all permitted payment stablecoin issuers, including State qualified payment stablecoin issuers, to maintain capital commensurate with the level and nature of all risks to which the permitted payment stablecoin issuer is exposed.
As discussed above, a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer that seeks to transition to the Federal regulatory framework before the end of the 360-day period must certify its compliance with part 15, including applicable capital requirements. State qualified payment stablecoin issuers that seek to transition early are therefore encouraged to submit their capital analysis to the OCC early, to ensure adequate time to address any deficiencies and raise additional capital if necessary.
A few commenters addressed the timing of the initial examination requirement for State qualified payment stablecoin issuers. One commenter suggested that the initial examination should take place prior to the issuer's transition date. Another commenter suggested that while the six-month time frame is reasonable, the OCC should consider more closely aligning the examination date with the transition waiver requirements. Another commenter expressed concerns that transitioned State issuers should be required to adhere to similar regulatory standards as Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuers.
After consideration of the comments, the OCC is finalizing the examination requirement as proposed. A State qualified payment stablecoin issuer that is required to transition to the Federal regulatory framework must do so within 360 days of exceeding the $10 billion outstanding issuance value threshold. The OCC has determined that requiring a transitioned State qualified payment stablecoin issuer to undergo an initial examination no later than six months after its transition date would facilitate the issuer's pre-transition requirements while retaining flexibility for the OCC to require an earlier examination on a case-by-case basis. Because a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer that transitions to the Federal framework will already be in operation, the OCC intends to conduct this examination well before the six-month outer limit proposed to ensure that the issuer can effectively operate under the Federal framework.

c. Waiver From Federal Supervision
i. Description of the Proposed Rule
Notwithstanding the transition requirements discussed above, under section 4(d)(3) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(d)(3)
), the OCC may permit a nonbank State qualified payment stablecoin issuer that reaches the $10 billion threshold to remain solely supervised by a State payment stablecoin regulator. In determining whether to issue a waiver from Federal supervision, proposed § 15.15(d)(2) would have implemented the requirement in the statute that provides that the OCC must consider four exclusive criteria: the capital maintained by the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer; the past operations and examination history of the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer; the experience of the State payment stablecoin regulator in supervising payment stablecoin and digital asset activities; and the supervisory framework, including regulations and guidance, of the State payment stablecoin regulator with respect to payment stablecoins and digital assets.
Proposed § 15.15(d)(1) would have required a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer seeking a waiver to submit a written waiver request to the OCC within 240 days of reaching the $10 billion outstanding issuance value threshold.

The request would have needed to include information necessary for the OCC to evaluate the waiver criteria enumerated in proposed § 15.15(d)(2) and (3), discussed below. The preamble to the proposed rule specified that such information may have included the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer's reports of condition and examination, financial statements, investor statements, reports that detail significant examination findings, business activities, existence of past or current enforcement orders, and disclosure of any violations of law, as well as other information as requested by the OCC. Additionally, the waiver request would have described whether the State payment stablecoin regulator has experience regulating entities that have a similar risk profile. 12 U.S.C. 5903(d)(3)(C)

12 U.S.C. 5903(c)

If an issuer believed it qualified for the waiver presumption, it would have needed to indicate so in the waiver request and provide information sufficient for the OCC to evaluate the waiver presumption standards.
ii. Description of Comments and Final Rule
The OCC received several comments concerning the criteria the OCC should consider when evaluating a waiver request in proposed § 15.15(d). A few commenters suggested that the OCC should require waiver applicants to submit specific information, such as reports of examination, or demonstrate that the issuer would not present financial stability and safety and soundness risks. A few commenters suggested that the OCC should establish benchmarks, explicit standards, or other guidelines for when an issuer would satisfy the waiver approval criteria. A few commenters suggested that the OCC should not adopt bright-line rules or require issuers to provide additional information in connection with a waiver request. One commenter suggested that the OCC should subject waiver requests from large issuers to heightened scrutiny and require issuers to demonstrate that waiver approval would not introduce financial stability risks, have an anti-competitive effect, or create a heightened risk of illicit finance. Finally, one commenter noted that § 15.15(d) included two references to State qualified payment stablecoin issuers that should have referred to State payment stablecoin regulators.
The OCC is finalizing the waiver approval criteria as proposed with a technical fix to change a reference to “State qualified payment stablecoin regulator” in § 15.15(d)(2)(iv) to “State payment stablecoin regulator.” The GENIUS Act requires the OCC to consider four exclusive criteria when reviewing a waiver request. The OCC is not authorized to consider additional criteria and, accordingly, is finalizing the four criteria as proposed. Adopting bright-line requirements or presumptive standards would not facilitate the fact-specific nature of waiver requests, as State qualified payment stablecoin issuers may have varying business models, risk tolerances, scale of operations, and regulatory backgrounds. The OCC will review the issuer's waiver request and any associated information in relation to the waiver criteria.
Under § 15.15(d)(1) of the final rule, a waiver applicant must submit to the OCC a written waiver request containing information necessary to evaluate such request under paragraphs (d)(2) and (3) of that section. Such information may include the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer's reports of condition and examination, financial statements, investor statements, reports that detail significant examination findings, business activities, existence of past or current enforcement orders, and disclosure of any violations of law, as well as other information as requested by the OCC. Additionally, the waiver request may describe whether the State payment stablecoin regulator has experience regulating entities that have a similar risk profile. The waiver request may also include information regarding the frequency and depth of the State payment stablecoin regulator's examinations. The OCC is adopting § 15.15(d)(1) with a technical fix to change a reference to a “State payment stablecoin issuer” to “State payment stablecoin regulator.” In addition, for the reasons discussed above, the final rule includes the words “total consolidated” in front of “issuance value.” The OCC is also making a technical change to add the word “threshold” at the end of paragraph (d)(1).
Finally, a few commenters expressed concerns that the proposal did not specify standards for determining whether a State regulatory framework is “substantially similar” to the Federal regulatory framework for Federal

One of these commenters expressed concerns that the OCC's proposed rule did not provide standards governing the application and approval of State qualified payment stablecoin issuers by State regulators. While the OCC will evaluate the experience and supervisory framework of a State payment stablecoin regulator when reviewing a waiver request, the Treasury Department is tasked with establishing broad-based principles for determining whether a State-level regulatory regime is substantially similar to the Federal regulatory framework under § 4(c) of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(c)

The OCC received one comment that suggests the OCC does not have authority to re-examine the status of a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer that receives a waiver. Another commenter suggested the OCC should limit waiver discontinuance to circumstances where the relevant State payment stablecoin regulator has been decertified under § 4(c) of the GENIUS Act.
After consideration of the comments, the OCC is finalizing the rule as proposed with clarifying edits. The OCC is clarifying that a waiver request approved under § 15.15 may include conditions related to the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer's continued compliance with the waiver approval criteria under § 15.15(d)(2) and (3). Subjecting waivers to conditional approval will facilitate the OCC's statutory mandate to ensure it provides transition waivers for State qualified payment stablecoin issuers that satisfy the waiver criteria. Conditional waiver approvals will also provide the OCC with an explicit mechanism for addressing potential evasion of the GENIUS Act's requirements, such as where a waiver determination is made based on materially inaccurate or misleading information.
The OCC received a few comments concerning the timing requirement for submitting a waiver request under proposed § 15.15(d)(1). One commenter suggested that the OCC should extend the 240-day waiver request deadline to the maximum extent provided by law. Another commenter suggested the OCC should permit a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer to submit a waiver request prior to exceeding the $10 billion outstanding issuance value threshold.
To facilitate an orderly waiver process, the OCC is finalizing the 240-day waiver request deadline as proposed in final § 15.15(d)(1)(ii) with some additional clarifications. The GENIUS Act requires a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer to transition to the Federal regulatory framework within 360 days after exceeding the $10 billion outstanding issuance value threshold unless it ceases issuing payment stablecoins immediately or receives a waiver from the OCC. Requiring State qualified payment stablecoin issuers to request a waiver within 240 days after exceeding the $10 billion outstanding issuance value threshold will provide 120 days for the OCC to review and respond to the waiver request.
[
146
]
Nothing would prohibit a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer that exceeds the $10 billion threshold from seeking a waiver earlier, and State qualified payment stablecoin issuers are encouraged to submit waiver requests early to ensure adequate time and address any deficiencies.
[
147
]
The OCC is also clarifying that a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer may submit a waiver request prior to exceeding the $10 billion outstanding issuance value threshold. The OCC will generally accept waiver requests where the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer makes a good faith determination to the OCC that it is likely to exceed the $10 billion outstanding issuance value threshold in the next 30 days. However, the OCC reserves the right to request that a waiver applicant revise, update, or provide further information related to any waiver request.
One commenter suggested that the OCC should clarify that a waiver request that meets presumption criteria will be considered approved as of the filing of such request, unless and until the OCC finds grounds to affirmatively deny the request based on the criteria contained in section 4(d)(3)(C)(ii) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(d)(3)(C)(ii)
). The OCC is finalizing the waiver presumption standard as proposed. Under the final rule, a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer that submits a waiver request must receive OCC approval, even if the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer believes it qualifies for the presumption criteria. Requiring a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer to receive affirmative waiver approval from the OCC will promote consistent application of the waiver presumption standards and avoid potential confusion related to an issuer's transition obligations.
7. Unusual and Exigent Circumstances (§ 15.16)
a. Description of the Proposed Rule
The OCC proposed to issue § 15.16 to clarify the scope of the agency's enforcement authority over nonbank State qualified payment stablecoin issuers during unusual and exigent circumstances, including the review of OCC enforcement actions imposed pursuant to this authority.
[
148
]
Proposed § 15.16(a) would have addressed the scope of § 15.16 and the OCC's authority to impose restrictions on a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer that is a nonbank entity during unusual and exigent circumstances, pursuant to section 7 of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5906
).
Section 7(e)(2)(B) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5906(e)(2)(B)
) requires the OCC to issue rules to set forth the unusual and exigent circumstances in which the OCC would exercise its enforcement authority against nonbank State qualified payment stablecoin issuers. Section 7(e)(2) of the GENIUS Act provides that, during “unusual and
(
printed page 67096)
exigent circumstances,” the OCC must take an enforcement action against a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer that is a nonbank entity for violations of the GENIUS Act, provided that the agency makes two determinations.
[
149
]
First, under the Act, the OCC must determine that “unusual and exigent circumstances” exist. Second, under the Act, the OCC must determine that there is reasonable cause to believe that the continuation of any activity by an issuer constitutes a serious risk to the financial safety, soundness, or stability of the issuer. Under the Act, if the OCC determines that both conditions are met, the OCC must impose such restrictions as the OCC determines to be necessary to address the serious risks to the issuer during the unusual and exigent circumstances. For example, under the Act, the OCC can limit a nonbank State qualified payment stablecoin issuer's affiliate transactions. The OCC may also limit nonbank State qualified payment stablecoin issuer activities that might create a serious risk that the liabilities of the issuer's holding company and its affiliates will be imposed on the issuer. The restrictions must be issued in the form of a directive, with the effect of a cease-and-desist order that has become final, to the nonbank State qualified payment stablecoin issuer and any of its affiliates.
Proposed § 15.16(b) would have incorporated the GENIUS Act's unusual and exigent circumstances requirement. Under proposed § 15.16(b), if the OCC determined that unusual and exigent circumstances existed, based on the information available to the OCC, and that there was reasonable cause to believe that the continuation of any activity, including failure to act,
[
150
]
by a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer that is a nonbank entity would have constituted a serious risk to the financial safety, soundness, or stability of the nonbank entity, the OCC would have imposed such restrictions as the OCC determined to be necessary to address such risk in the form of a directive. The Act provides three examples of the limitations that the OCC may impose, which were incorporated into proposed § 15.16(b). Such restrictions may include limitations on: (1) redemptions of payment stablecoins; (2) transactions between the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer, a holding company, and the subsidiaries or affiliates of either the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer or the holding company; and (3) any activities of the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer that might create a serious risk that the liabilities of a holding company and the affiliates of the holding company may be imposed on the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer.
Proposed § 15.16(c) set forth the criteria the OCC would have considered when determining whether unusual and exigent circumstances exist. Specifically, under the proposed rule, the OCC would have considered: (1) whether the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer is, or is expected to imminently be, engaging in an activity (including any act, practice, or omission) that poses an immediate risk to the financial safety, soundness, or stability of the issuer or the financial system of the United States; (2) the actions of the relevant State payment stablecoin regulator to promptly address the risk to the issuer or the financial system of the United States; (3) risks presented to payment stablecoin holders; and (4) any other factors the OCC deems appropriate in light of the particular circumstances, consistent with the purposes of the GENIUS Act.
The OCC's proposed criteria were intended to capture circumstances that involve an immediate financial risk that cannot be sufficiently addressed through normal supervisory channels. Accordingly, the OCC's proposed criteria focused on the immediacy of the financial risks, whether to the issuer, the stablecoin holders, or the financial system, and the actions of the relevant State payment stablecoin regulator to respond to those risks. The OCC preliminarily determined that adopting flexible criteria focused on these considerations, as opposed to a limited set of specific circumstances, would establish an appropriate balance between providing stakeholders with clarity on when the OCC would act pursuant to this authority while implementing the GENIUS Act's clear intention to permit the OCC to respond to evolving and unforeseeable circumstances. The OCC asked whether to include additional factors including (1) whether a State payment stablecoin regulator or a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer has made a request for the OCC to exercise its unusual and exigent circumstances authority; (2) significant price fluctuations in the secondary market for the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer's payment stablecoin; (3) whether the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer has been, or will imminently be, unable to timely redeem its payment stablecoin; (4) whether the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer has incurred significant unanticipated losses; and (5) whether the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer has deployed nonstandard liquidity management tools.
Finally, proposed § 15.16(d) would have clarified that the administrative review procedures described in section 7(e)(2)(D) of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5906(e)(2)(D)
) are applicable to a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer or any institution-affiliated party subject to an unusual and exigent circumstances directive.
b. Description of Comments and Final Rule
The OCC did not receive comments specific to implementing the GENIUS Act's statutory criteria in proposed § 15.16(b). Accordingly, the OCC is finalizing § 15.16(b), with one minor clarification and a technical correction. The final rule clarifies that the list of limitations that the OCC may impose in § 15.16(b)(1) through (3) is not exhaustive. This is consistent with the language in the proposed rule. The final rule, however, adds the phrase, “but not limited to” for the avoidance of doubt.
Several commenters suggested the OCC should provide examples or additional guidance concerning when the OCC would invoke its unusual and exigent circumstances authority in proposed § 15.16(c). One of these commenters suggested that the OCC should consider a broad and flexible set of criteria for assessing unusual and exigent circumstances, including secondary market price fluctuations. Two of these commenters suggested that secondary market price fluctuations should carry little to no weight independently, as market prices can reflect localized trading conditions, fragmented liquidity, or external sentiment. One of these commenters suggested that the OCC should consider whether a state regulator has requested Federal assistance.
After consideration of the comments, the OCC is finalizing the unusual and exigent circumstances factors with certain additions and clarifications. The final rule includes certain additional factors for which the OCC requested comment. Under the final rule, the OCC will consider: (1) whether the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer is, or is expected to imminently be, engaging in an activity (including any act, practice, or omission) that poses an immediate risk to the financial safety,
(
printed page 67097)
soundness, or stability of the issuer or the financial system of the United States; (2) the actions of the relevant State payment stablecoin regulator to promptly address the risk to the issuer or the financial system of the United States; (3) risks presented to payment stablecoin holders; (4) any request from the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer or State payment stablecoin regulator for the OCC to exercise its authority under section 7(e)(2) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5906(e)(2)
); (5) significant fluctuations in the secondary market price of payment stablecoins issued by the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer; (6) whether the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer has been, or will imminently be, unable to timely redeem payment stablecoins issued by the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer; (7) whether the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer has incurred significant unanticipated losses; and (8) any other factor the OCC deems appropriate in light of the particular circumstances and consistent with the purposes of the GENIUS Act. The OCC has added these additional factors to provide additional clarity on the indicia that the OCC believes could warrant exercising the OCC's authority under section 7(e)(2) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5906(e)(2)
).
The OCC's finalized unusual and exigent circumstances factors are intended to capture circumstances that involve or could indicate an immediate financial risk that cannot be sufficiently addressed through normal supervisory channels. Accordingly, the final factors focus on the immediacy of the financial risks and factors likely to correlate with such risks, whether to the issuer, the stablecoin holders, or the financial system, and the actions of the relevant State payment stablecoin regulator to respond to those risks. The OCC determined that adopting flexible criteria focused on these considerations, as opposed to a limited set of specific circumstances, would establish an appropriate balance between providing stakeholders with clarity on when the OCC would act pursuant to this authority while implementing the GENIUS Act's clear intention to permit the OCC to respond to evolving and unforeseeable circumstances.
The proposed rule also asked whether the OCC should publicly disclose when it determines that unusual and exigent circumstances exist. Several commenters suggested that the OCC should not automatically disclose directives made pursuant to the OCC's unusual and exigent circumstances authority. Most of these commenters suggested that the OCC should avoid disclosure of confidential materials but retain discretion to make public disclosures as necessary to prevent future harm to the issuer or consumers. After consideration of the comments, the OCC is not adopting an automatic disclosure process for directives made pursuant to the OCC's unusual and exigent circumstances authority. Disclosures may be appropriate in certain circumstances, but an automatic process could pose significant risks to safety and soundness and financial stability. For example, a process that compelled immediate disclosures might cause or exacerbate a run while facts were still being developed and confirmed. The OCC may impose such restrictions as the OCC determines to be necessary to address serious risks to the issuer during the unusual and exigent circumstances.
Additionally, a few commenters provided suggestions related to coordinating with State regulators. A few commenters suggested the OCC should explicitly codify the statutory 48-hour notice requirement. One commenter suggested the OCC should consult with the State regulator prior to invoking its unusual and exigent circumstances authority. After consideration of the comments, the OCC is finalizing the rule as proposed. The GENIUS Act requires the OCC to comply with the 48-hour notice requirement and does not impose any requirements on State qualified payment stablecoin issuers. Although the OCC may consult with a State regulator, adopting a mandatory consultation requirement in addition to the 48-hour notice requirement could hinder the OCC's ability to quickly respond when there is a serious risk to the financial safety, soundness, or stability of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer.
The OCC did not receive comments specific to proposed § 15.16(d) and is finalizing the section as proposed.
C. Subpart C—Custody
1. Overview of Changes From Proposed Rule to Final Rule for Subpart C
The OCC is generally adopting subpart C as proposed with some modifications to enhance clarity described in more detail below.
The OCC is modifying the definition of “covered assets” in § 15.20 to make two clarifications. First, the covered assets definition in final § 15.20 is modified to clarify that the term “covered assets” only applies with respect to payment stablecoins that are offered, sold, or otherwise made available to persons in the United States. Second, the definition is modified to clarify that it includes only payment stablecoins used as collateral, where a covered custodian has actual knowledge that such payment stablecoins are being used as collateral. The OCC is also making non-substantive edits to the definition of sub-custodian.
In addition to a technical correction, the OCC is modifying § 15.21(a) to clarify that a covered custodian must separately record and account for the covered assets of a covered customer. The OCC is modifying § 15.21(b)(1) to clarify that taking appropriate steps to protect the covered assets of covered customers from the claims of creditors includes adopting, implementing, and maintaining written custody agreements. The OCC is making non-substantive edits to § 15.21(b)(2)(i). The OCC is modifying § 15.21(b)(2)(ii) to clarify that it applies to a private key used to issue a payment stablecoin held in safekeeping under subpart C and to delete an unnecessary reference to using a distributed ledger. The OCC is making non-substantive edits to § 15.21(c). The OCC is modifying § 15.21(d) to use the term covered custodian.
The OCC is modifying § 15.22(a) to add a reference to § 15.22(c). The OCC is modifying § 15.22(b) to clarify that steps to protect, possess, or control covered assets include appropriate recordkeeping.
The OCC is adding new § 15.22(c), which provides that notwithstanding any other provision of part 15 to the contrary, part 15 does not prevent a covered custodian from custodying its own assets and the covered assets of a covered customer at a sub-custodian where the sub-custodian may, for convenience, commingle the covered custodian's assets with the covered assets of its covered customers in one or more omnibus accounts of the sub-custodian; provided that the covered custodian maintains adequate safeguards and internal controls reasonably designed to ensure that the sub-custodian segregates all covered assets of the covered custodian's covered customers from, and does not commingle such covered assets with, the assets of the sub-custodian.
The OCC is modifying § 15.23 to clarify its application to covered assets and that the provision applies only to national banks, Federal savings associations, Federal branches, or permitted payment stablecoin issuers when these entities neither control nor hold themselves out as controlling the relevant private keys associated with covered assets nor provide or hold themselves out as providing safekeeping and custodial services for such assets.
(

2. Overview of Proposed Rule
Section 10 of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5909
) imposes requirements on any person seeking to provide custodial or safekeeping services for payment stablecoin reserve, payment stablecoins used as collateral, or the private keys used to issue permitted payment stablecoins. Among other things, section 10 of the Act requires such persons to be subject to supervision or regulation by a primary Federal payment stablecoin regulator, primary financial regulatory agency, or State bank supervisor, to treat covered assets as customer property, to separately account for and not commingle covered assets unless permitted under a listed exception, and to provide their regulator or supervisor with certain information as determined by that regulator or supervisor. Section 10 also provides a priority regime elevating the claims of payment stablecoin holders over other claims on persons providing custody and exempting certain persons providing hardware or software services from the requirements of section 10.
The OCC proposed to (1) establish relevant defined terms for purposes of subpart C to clarify the scope of custodial services to which subpart C would apply; (2) set minimum principles-based requirements for OCC-supervised institutions related to their provision of custodial or safekeeping services for the assets described in section 10 of the GENIUS Act that are appropriate to protect such custodied assets from the claims of creditors of the institution; and (3) implement other requirements and exclusions of the Act.
3. General Comments
The OCC received 54 comments on this subpart. Many commenters generally supported the OCC's objective of establishing a clear and prudentially sound regulatory framework for GENIUS Act custodial activities and urged the OCC generally to adopt an approach recognizing the particular legal and operational characteristics of custody arrangements while preserving necessary flexibility for regulated institutions.
4. Definitions (§ 15.20)
Broadly speaking, commenters were supportive of the proposed definitions in subpart C of the proposal. At a high level, several commenters stated that custody definitions should ensure technology neutrality and not codify practices, standards, or technologies that might quickly become outdated or impractical. The OCC agrees that its definitions are designed to be technology-neutral and functional, capable of being used without repeated amendment as technology changes.
The OCC proposed to define “applicable law” as “the law of a State or other jurisdiction governing a covered custodian's custody relationships, any applicable Federal law governing those relationships, the terms of the custody agreement, and any applicable court order.” The OCC received no material comments on this definition and finalizes it as proposed.
The OCC proposed to define “covered assets” as “payment stablecoin reserves, payment stablecoins used as collateral, and private keys used to issue payment stablecoins, as well as cash and other property received in the course of the provision of custodial or safekeeping services for such assets.”
[
151
]
In proposing this definition, the OCC asked whether it should define “covered assets” in such a way that the requirements of sections 10(a) through (c) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5909(a)
through
(c)
) would be read together to cover the same set of assets and provide a cogent and harmonized set of requirements, or whether the OCC should replicate the statutory language regarding the scope of assets covered separately in paragraphs (a), (b), and (c).
[
152
]
Commenters primarily responded that the OCC's proposal to define “covered assets” in such a way that sections 10(a) through (c) of the Act would be read together to apply to all covered assets is a correct reading of the Act. Several commenters requested clarification that territorial application of subpart C be read to be coextensive with the territorial scope established in section 3 of the GENIUS Act.
The OCC agrees that the Act is primarily focused on payment stablecoins and that there is a presumption against extraterritorial application of United States law absent specific language to the contrary. As such, the OCC has clarified in the final rule that “covered assets” are only those assets associated with payment stablecoins that are offered, sold, or otherwise made available to persons in the United States.
Several commenters also requested further clarification of certain terms used in the definition of “covered assets.” For example, the OCC sought comment on whether it is the correct approach to interpret “cash and other property” as used in the definition of “covered assets” to refer only to the cash and other property that a covered custodian may receive in connection with the provision of custodial services for the Act's three core custody assets. Commenters generally agreed with the OCC's proposed approach but requested further clarification that cash held as a deposit liability at an insured depository institution is not and cannot be a custodial asset for purposes of the segregation requirements in subpart C. While the OCC acknowledges these commenters' concerns, it believes they are best addressed in the exception in § 15.21(d) regarding deposit liabilities discussed below, rather than scoping out all cash from the requirements of subpart C, given the GENIUS Act's explicit references to “cash” in section 10. Certain protections in the GENIUS Act applicable to custodied assets are relevant to cash received from covered customers. For example, a covered custodian must properly account for cash that makes up the reserves of a payment stablecoin and treat such cash as part of the custody relationship governed by the terms of any applicable custody agreement.
Other commenters requested that the phrase “payment stablecoins used as collateral” be further clarified, noting that a covered custodian may not necessarily know whether a custodied payment stablecoin is at any given time being held as collateral. Commenters suggested various amendments to the final rule including limiting the application of subpart C to either those situations in which the covered custodian is party to a collateral agreement with respect to the stablecoin used as collateral or to situations where the covered custodian knows or should have known that the custodied payment stablecoin is being used as collateral, or else requiring the covered custodian to undertake certain due diligence regarding the use of custodied payment stablecoins. The OCC acknowledges commenters' concerns and believes that an “actual knowledge” standard best balances the foregoing against the text and purpose of the Act. The OCC expects that in most cases, a covered custodian will have actual knowledge where it is a party to a collateral agreement, but the OCC believes that limiting the term only to such
(
printed page 67099)
circumstances would be inconsistent with the Act, which does not refer to such agreements. However, including a constructive knowledge requirement may offer insufficient clarity and may incentivize covered custodians to implement burdensome due diligence requirements, which may be inconsistent with the norms of custody practices and the Act's principles-based, rather than prescriptive, approach to custody. As such, the final rule specifies that the term “covered assets” refers to “payment stablecoins used as collateral, where a covered custodian has actual knowledge that such payment stablecoins are being used as collateral.”
The OCC proposed to define “covered custodian” to mean “a national bank, Federal savings association, Federal branch, or permitted payment stablecoin issuer to the extent of such person's provision of custodial or safekeeping services for covered assets.”
[

]
The OCC proposed to define “covered customer” to mean “a person for or on whose behalf a covered custodian receives, acquires, or holds covered assets.” The OCC proposed to define “sub-custodian” to mean “a person that provides custody and safekeeping services to a covered custodian, including through a digital wallet for which such person controls the associated private keys, with respect to covered assets of a covered customer, for which the covered custodian otherwise serves as a custodian under this subpart.” One commenter recommended narrowing the definition of “covered customer” to apply only to custodial or safekeeping services provided with respect to the issuance of “payment stablecoins.” The OCC declines to narrow the definition of “covered customer” in this manner as to do so would be contrary to the statute's definition of “customer” in section 10(b)(1) of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5909(b)(1)
), which is not limited to the issuance of payment stablecoins. Other commenters asked that the OCC clarify that the terms “covered custodian” and “sub-custodian” do not include foreign entities. However, this reading appears contrary to the text of section 10 of the GENIUS Act, as well as its purpose, which largely seeks to insulate permitted payment stablecoin issuers and United States holders of payment stablecoins from potential complications related to a custodian's or sub-custodian's insolvency, failure to properly maintain and record custodied assets, or other issues. As such, the OCC is adopting these definitions as proposed, except for certain technical edits to the definition of sub-custodian, described below. The OCC notes that the changes to the definition of “covered assets,” described above, should prevent undue extraterritorial application of subpart C.
The OCC is making non-substantive changes to the definition of sub-custodian. Specifically, the final rule replaces the word “such” with “the” and eliminates an unnecessary comma.
The OCC proposed to define “custody agreement” as “a legally binding contractual agreement between a covered customer, as the principal, and the covered custodian, as the agent, that establishes the covered custodian's duties and responsibilities in providing safekeeping and ancillary services to the covered customer.” The OCC proposed to define “digital wallet” as “a software program or hardware device that stores and manages the private keys associated with a particular unit of a digital asset.” The OCC received no comments on these definitions and finalizes them as proposed.
The OCC requested comment on whether it would be helpful to define any other terms. One commenter recommended the OCC add a definition of the phrase “custodial or safekeeping services” as used in proposed subpart C. The OCC declines to define these terms as it believes the terms “custody” and “safekeeping” are well-established and well-understood terms and that adding a new definition may introduce confusion or be underinclusive or overinclusive.
5. Covered Asset Custodial Property Requirements (§ 15.21)
Proposed § 15.21 included certain minimum principles-based requirements applicable to a covered custodian's provision of custodial and safekeeping services for covered assets to ensure that such covered assets are treated and dealt with as belonging to the covered customers and protected from claims of the covered custodian's creditors, as well as the creditors of any sub-custodian, as applicable. Under proposed § 15.21(a), a covered custodian would have needed to separately account for the covered assets of each covered customer and would have had to treat and deal with those covered assets as belonging to such covered customer and not as the property of the covered custodian. Under proposed § 15.21(b), a covered custodian would have to take appropriate steps to protect the covered assets of covered customers from the claims of creditors of the covered custodian and any sub-custodian, as applicable, including through adopting, implementing, and maintaining written policies, procedures, and internal controls that are adequate to comply with applicable law and that are commensurate with the covered custodian's size, complexity, and risk profile and with the nature of the applicable covered assets for which it provides custodial or safekeeping services.
The OCC noted its belief that setting certain minimum principles-based requirements for the provision of these custody services, regardless of the use of omnibus accounts, is consistent with section 10(b)(2) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5909(b)(2)
), which requires that applicable custodians “take such steps as are appropriate to protect the [covered assets] of a customer from the claims of creditors of the [custodian]” and section 13 of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5913
), which grants the OCC broad rulemaking authority to implement the GENIUS Act.
The OCC sought comment on whether the proposed principles-based requirements accurately capture sound custodial management practices that are standard in the industry. Commenters largely supported the OCC's principles-based approach in proposed § 15.21(a) and (b) as consistent with the GENIUS Act's own principles-based approach and as setting an appropriate baseline for sound custodial practice that is also sufficiently flexible to adapt to changing circumstances. Some commenters further noted that prescriptive requirements would not keep pace with technological changes and would impose disproportionate costs on smaller banks. Several commenters, however, recommended supplementing the principles-based approach with additional protections. Examples included mandated certifications (
e.g.,
a public attestation as to compliance with subpart C); specific real-time recordkeeping standards; minimum policies, procedures, and controls, such as for key management and robust systems to authenticate customer instructions before effecting transfers; minimum technical standards, such as multi-signature architecture and requirements concerning the geographic distribution of key shards, quantum computing risk management standards, incident response and recovery, and
(
printed page 67100)
hardware specifications; special requirements related to smart contract administrative keys; mandatory contract provisions; real-time monitoring; regulatory reporting; independent audits; public disclosure; and a requirement that custody be conducted in a fiduciary capacity, among others.
Other commenters stated that the OCC should add additional requirements in instances in which an OCC-supervised permitted payment stablecoin issuer maintains any reserve assets without the use of a custodian or when a covered custodian provides safekeeping and custody services to an affiliate permitted payment stablecoin issuer or to a payment stablecoin issuer that is not supervised by the OCC. These commenters noted that so-called “self-custody” and affiliate custody of reserve assets may give rise to significant risks as there is no independent custodian to provide an added layer of protection to holders of the relevant payment stablecoin. Additionally, these commenters noted that non-OCC-supervised payment stablecoin issuers, especially foreign payment stablecoin issuers, may raise additional complications, including jurisdiction and choice of law issues. Commenters offered several examples of heightened requirements in such situations, including increased levels of capital and assessments; mandatory governance standards designed to ensure independence; disclosure obligations to payment stablecoin holders; examination standards that address intragroup conflicts of interest; and blanket prohibitions on “self-custody,” among other conditions.
A commenter suggested that as a condition to an OCC-supervised entity providing custody services to a foreign issuer, the OCC should require that the custodian's custody agreement authorize the custodian, and the custodian should be operationally prepared, to freeze, liquidate, or transfer reserve assets upon service of a final United States court order and stated that this requirement would be consistent with existing OCC requirements for custodians.
One commenter stated that a covered custodian's custody and safekeeping functions should be organizationally and functionally separate from any trading, lending, asset management, and other market-facing activities that the entity engages in, and that personnel with trading responsibilities should not participate in custody or safekeeping functions, in order to reduce conflicts of interest and protect customer assets from exposure to other business risks. Other commenters supported strong internal controls more broadly, including segregation of duties, independent validation, dual or multi-party approvals, and strong governance over issuance systems. Another commenter noted that while assets should be appropriately segregated and independently controlled, any personnel or governance requirements should be proportional to the size and complexity of the issuer and implemented through broader reserve asset and risk management standards rather than as a separate standalone requirement.
Adding additional prescriptive requirements discussed in comments to the rule would be contrary to a principles-based and technologically neutral approach. Moreover, the technical and prescriptive standards discussed in the comments may be overly burdensome and at risk of becoming outdated quickly. Covered custodians are already OCC-supervised entities subject to prudential supervision and regulation and the OCC has experience supervising crypto-asset custody. The GENIUS Act and part 15 already impose requirements on payment stablecoin issuers that would address stablecoin holder protection. A principles-based approach maintains flexibility and technology neutrality and avoids imposing undue burden. Regarding comments on self-custody and affiliate custody of payment stablecoin reserve assets, the OCC believes these concerns are best addressed in the section of the final rule applicable to reserve assets (see § 15.11). Therefore, the OCC declines to add further prescriptive requirements to §§ 15.21(a) or (b)(1).

However, the OCC is adopting §§ 15.21(a) and (b)(1) with minor changes to address certain concerns of commenters. First, some commenters requested further clarity regarding the GENIUS Act's requirement, mirrored in § 15.21(a), that a covered custodian “separately account” for the covered assets for which it provides safekeeping and custody services. Sound custodial practices would entail that a covered custodian may not rely solely on a distributed ledger and must reconcile distributed ledger data, as applicable, with its internal records. As a point of clarity, the OCC is finalizing § 15.21(a) with a reference to a covered custodian's obligation to “record,” as well as to account for, the covered assets of a covered customer. Second, other commenters noted the importance of custody agreements in ensuring the protection of customers' covered assets in line with the GENIUS Act. The OCC is finalizing § 15.21(b) to include the adoption, implementation, and maintenance of written custody agreements among the other enumerated examples in that section.
The OCC also sought comment on whether the proposal provides enough detail regarding what steps are appropriate for a covered custodian to protect the covered assets of covered customers from the claims of creditors of the covered custodian. Several commenters recommended that the OCC provide guidance to facilitate compliance with the requirements of § 15.21 or with regard to specific situations concerning covered asset custodial property requirements, including managing third-party risk and incident response and recovery planning. While the OCC may consider future requests for supervisory guidance as needed, the agency believes doing so concurrent with publication of this final rule is premature as it may interfere with the development of industry best practices, may quickly become dated due to changing technological norms, and may risk appearing to set minimum requirements that undermine a principles-based approach.
Other commenters requested that the OCC create a safe harbor for good-faith attempts at compliance. One commenter offered that such a safe harbor could be conditioned on a covered custodian (1) not recording custodied covered assets, other than cash held as deposit liabilities, on its own balance sheet; and (2) providing prompt notice to covered customers, to the extent permitted by law, upon receipt of any adverse claims asserted against covered assets. The OCC believes a safe harbor for compliance with § 15.21(b)(1) is unnecessary, as custody is a long-established business with clear norms of operation and legal frameworks. Inclusion of a safe harbor could be potentially counterproductive as the minimum conditions of a safe harbor could effectively serve as a regulatory baseline that disincentivizes more rigorous custodial standards. Therefore, the OCC declines to include a safe harbor provision in § 15.21(b)(1).

Under the proposal, with regard to any payment stablecoin or stablecoin reserve in the form of a tokenized asset held in safekeeping under proposed subpart C, a covered custodian, or sub-custodian, as applicable, would have maintained control for purposes of the proposed requirement in paragraph (b)(2)(i) if it could reasonably demonstrate, consistent with the standard of care established by applicable law, that no other party, including the covered customer, can transfer the payment stablecoin or tokenized asset using a distributed ledger without the consent of the custodian or sub-custodian, as applicable.

The final rule adopts paragraph (b)(2)(i) with non-substantive changes (adding the word “that” and replacing the word “such” with “the”).
The OCC sought comment in the proposal about whether the description in the proposed rule about how a custodian maintains control of a payment stablecoin or tokenized reserve assets is appropriately calibrated. Commenters generally supported the OCC's approach, noting the importance of a technology-neutral and functional definition of control, but requested that the OCC clarify that multi-signature, distributed key-control architectures, multiparty computation, and shareable private keys are permissible. Multi-signature approaches are consistent with the proposed regulatory text, which establishes that a custodian maintains control if “it can reasonably demonstrate, consistent with the standard of care established by applicable law, that no other party, including the covered customer, can transfer the payment stablecoin or tokenized asset using a distributed ledger without the consent of the custodian or sub-custodian, as applicable.” That is, it does not require that the custodian have the unilateral ability to transfer assets, but rather only that no other party can transfer assets without the custodian's consent, which would capture multi-party signatory systems. Therefore, changes to proposed § 15.21(b)(2)(ii) are unnecessary to clarify that multi-signature, distributed key-control architectures, multiparty computation, and shareable private keys are permissible. The OCC is, however, making three technical changes to proposed § 15.21(b)(2)(ii). First, the OCC has added “private key used to issue a payment stablecoin” as one of the types of crypto-assets to which the term “control” applies, consistent with the GENIUS Act's use of this term. Second, § 15.21(b)(2)(ii) includes a reference in the final rule to subpart C (whereas the proposal referred to § 15.21(b)(2)(i)). Finally, the final rule eliminates the phrase “using a distributed ledger” as surplusage.
Commenters also raised specific amendments or additions to the proposal's discussion of control and the use of sub-custodians. For example, one commenter recommended that the OCC clarify that for tokenized reserve assets, a covered custodian's demonstration of control should address both the on-chain custody of the token and the off-chain legal and operational arrangements ensuring the custodian can enforce the customer's rights against the underlying asset. Requiring that a covered custodian have control not only of the contractually agreed custodied asset, but also effectively of the underlying reference asset would be inconsistent with industry norms of custody and may serve to significantly impede the use of tokenized assets. As such, it is inappropriate to impose those requirements on covered custodians. The OCC notes, however, that for an asset to qualify as a reserve asset in tokenized form, a tokenized asset would need to confer rights identical to those that are conferred, or would be conferred, by a non-tokenized form of the asset under applicable law.
Other commenters recommended confirming in the final rule that cryptographic sub-ledgering (the mathematically verifiable tracking of beneficial ownership through on-chain proofs and real-time internal ledger reconciliation) inherently satisfies the adequate safeguards and internal controls standard for sub-custodian oversight under § 15.21(b). While cryptographic sub-ledgering may be an effective technological control, the OCC notes that the legal enforceability of a custodial relationship (
i.e.,
bailor-bailee vs. debtor-creditor) will depend on the facts and circumstances and that the adequacy of a covered custodian's safeguards and internal controls will ultimately depend upon the nature of its custodial business and its sub-custodial relationships. As such, it would be inappropriate to implement a safe harbor regarding cryptographic sub-ledgering.
Another commenter recommended that the OCC ensure that its principles-based framework includes clear expectations on due diligence, oversight, and contractual accountability for sub-custodian arrangements. Section 15.21 of the proposed rule provided sufficient protections regarding the use of sub-custodians, including the maintenance of “adequate safeguards and internal controls reasonably designed to provide the covered custodian with oversight of such sub-custodian's compliance with the requirements of” subpart C. The OCC also notes that covered custodians would typically consider sub-custodians as third-party relationships and manage the risks from a third-party risk perspective as well, consistent with the covered custodian's size, complexity,

The OCC also sought comment on whether certain specific issues should be incorporated into the required principles-based standards governing a covered custodian's treatment of covered customers' covered assets. First, the agency sought comment on whether it should require that any custody agreement a covered custodian enters into with a permitted payment stablecoin issuer provide for prompt release of any custodied covered assets to the covered customer's control, including whether the OCC should require a covered custodian to release covered assets within a specific timeframe or to maintain custody agreements governing such release. Several commenters opposed a requirement that any custody agreement a covered custodian enters into with a payment stablecoin issuer provide for prompt release of custodied covered assets. The commenters stated that prompt release standards should be part of the service standards determined by the covered custodian and covered customer, and that custodians are constrained by the nature of the underlying reserve assets as well as by industry-standard deadlines for processing those assets.
In contrast, a few commenters recommended the OCC require that custody agreements provide for the prompt release of custodied assets, although one such commenter also recommended that the OCC should not specify a universal timeframe and should make clear that the adequacy of a custodian's timeframes will be evaluated in the context of its overall risk management framework. The OCC believes that a regulatory requirement concerning prompt release standards would impose additional burdens on covered custodians to set up processes and procedures that are typically already addressed in contracts, contract law, and industry norms of conduct. Moreover, a prescriptive requirement could limit the development of better practices in this area. Therefore, the OCC declines to include a prescriptive requirement on prompt release and retains the proposal's principles-based approach.

One commenter, by contrast, noted that the waiver right may at times be necessary to preserve certain collateral arrangements that can provide flexibility and benefits to covered customers and covered custodians. The OCC continues to believe that the statute is clear and that additional regulatory requirements would impose burdens and not provide meaningful benefits to either covered custodians or covered customers. Furthermore, if consistent with applicable law, the OCC would not expect that section 10(c)(3) of the GENIUS Act would prohibit covered custodians from including an express waiver as a standard term in their custody agreements.

The OCC proposed to specify that any such withdrawal must be consistent with any applicable law. For example, the OCC would expect any such withdrawal to be undertaken only in compliance with the terms of a covered customer's custody agreement and that any withdrawal of funds from an omnibus account would be properly recorded so as not to implicate the custodial assets of any other covered customer.

A few commenters responded that the OCC should require covered custodians to maintain controls to ensure that fee withdrawals do not reduce reserve coverage below applicable requirements, including, for example, specified controls or mandated custody account agreement terms that address pre-arranged fee schedules, authorized withdrawal instructions, and hard-stop controls where the custodian has sufficient visibility into the full reserve pool. The OCC notes that such additional requirements would likely be impractical for many covered custodians or inconsistent with the norms of custodial practices, since the covered custodian may lack visibility into a payment stablecoin issuer's reserve assets or may only custody a portion of the reserve assets. Rather, the payment stablecoin issuer is the party better positioned to ensure that it maintains required reserve assets, and it may be reasonable to expect that such an issuer should understand any applicable fee schedules and other situations in which a covered custodian may permissibly withdraw covered assets under custody as part of its ongoing monitoring of its reserve assets. Notably, final § 15.11(d) will require a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to take certain steps with respect to custodians of reserve assets, including identifying itself as a permitted payment stablecoin issuer and engaging in due diligence to ensure that the custodian complies with applicable requirements of the GENIUS Act's implementing regulations.
