6. Use of Omnibus Accounts (§ 15.22)
Proposed § 15.22 covered the use of omnibus accounts by covered custodians. Proposed § 15.22(a) addressed the segregation of covered assets, stating that, “[a] covered custodian must segregate all covered assets of covered customers from, and not commingle them with, the assets of the covered custodian, except as permitted under § 15.21(d).” Proposed § 15.22(b) stated that “[a] covered custodian may, for convenience, commingle the covered assets of multiple covered customers, in one or more omnibus accounts,” provided the custodian has taken steps pursuant to § 15.21(b) to maintain safe and sound practices and the use of omnibus accounts is consistent with applicable law. The OCC sought comment on whether the OCC should instead implement a more detailed regulatory framework regarding a covered custodian's use of omnibus accounts.
Commenters generally supported the OCC's proposal in § 15.22(b) to permit covered custodians to utilize omnibus accounts for covered assets consistent with the principles-based approach that the OCC proposed in § 15.21. Several commenters, however, recommended that the OCC adopt more detailed expectations for omnibus account structures due to their potential to obscure entitlements and increase operational and legal risk or clarify that omnibus accounts should not refer to accounts held by a custodian on its own books.
[
158
]
The OCC believes that the principles-based approach taken in subpart C should already largely address these operational and legal risks without imposing undue burdens. As noted above, sound custodial practices would entail that a covered custodian may not rely solely on a distributed ledger and must reconcile distributed ledger data, as applicable, with its internal records. Consistent with this practice, the OCC expects a covered custodian to maintain off-chain documentation and recordkeeping to the extent that it commingles the covered assets of multiple covered customers in an omnibus account to ensure that it is able to reconcile all omnibus accounts with individual customer custodial accounts—that is, that it has “separately accounted for” the covered assets of each covered customer.

The commenter recommended explicitly allowing sub-ledgering within the same general omnibus wallet, meaning that the custodian would maintain multiple customers' assets at the same virtual address but maintain real-time internal records continuously reconciled against the blockchain showing exactly which customer owns which assets. As noted above, while cryptographic sub-ledgering may be an effective technological control, the OCC notes that the legal enforceability of a custodial relationship will depend on the facts and circumstances and that the adequacy of a covered custodian's safeguards and internal controls will ultimately depend upon the nature of its custodial business and its sub-custodial relationships. As such, the OCC believes it would be inappropriate to include a safe harbor in § 15.22 regarding the use of cryptographic sub-ledgering alone, and the agency reiterates that a covered custodian must also maintain appropriate off-chain recordkeeping.
Commenters also provided input on specific issues related to the use of omnibus accounts. First, the OCC asked whether a covered custodian may, for convenience, commingle in a single omnibus account both covered assets and other custodial assets that are not covered assets and asked whether the OCC should consider prescribing additional requirements in such situations. Several commenters supported confirming that covered custodians may hold covered assets and non-covered digital assets within the same omnibus wallet structures, provided that the custodian maintains recordkeeping sufficient to identify, at any time, which assets within the omnibus account constitute covered assets and which customers are covered customers. One such commenter recommended that the OCC should make clear that such arrangements are appropriate only where traceability, accountability, and error-resolution processes are demonstrably robust. Another commenter stated that commingling covered and non-covered assets could raise complexity and would require enhanced safeguards. The OCC agrees that commingling in a single omnibus account both covered assets and other assets that are not covered assets may be permissible, provided the custodian maintains sufficient recordkeeping to identify, at any time, which assets within the omnibus account constitute covered assets and which customers are covered customers. However, to the extent any covered assets are reserve assets, a permitted payment stablecoin issuer may not custody such assets in omnibus accounts since a permitted payment stablecoin issuer is separately required to segregate and not commingle such reserve assets with other assets owned

7. Self-Custody Hardware and Software Exclusion (§ 15.23)
Proposed § 15.23 implemented section 10(e) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5909(e)
), which provides that the requirements of section 10 of the Act do not apply to any person solely on the basis that such person engages in the business of providing hardware or software to facilitate a customer's own custody or safekeeping of the customer's payment stablecoins or private keys. In proposed § 15.23, the OCC sought to clarify that the requirements of this proposed subpart C do not apply to any national bank, Federal savings association, Federal branch, or permitted payment stablecoin issuer solely on the basis that such entity engages in the business of providing hardware or software to facilitate a person's or entity's self-custody of their payment stablecoins or private keys. The OCC sought comment on whether the OCC should consider implementing any other language to prevent the exception from being used to evade the custodial requirements of the Act, including, for example, whether the requirements of subpart C could nonetheless apply if, for example, an entity controls or holds itself out as controlling such payment stablecoins or private keys, or provides, or holds itself out as providing safekeeping or custodial services, including services that are ancillary or incidental to its custodial powers, for such payment stablecoins or private keys. In the alternative, the OCC sought comment on whether an OCC-supervised institution could provide ancillary custodial services to a user of such hardware or software while avoiding the minimum, principles-based requirements of the proposal.
Several commenters recommended that the OCC clarify that the exclusion be applied on the basis of various factors that in essence mirror the control standard proposed in § 15.21(b)(2). The OCC agrees and is clarifying § 15.23 in accordance with these comments to prevent the section from being used to evade the custodial requirements of subpart C. Third-party services may in practice resemble the types of custody arrangements that the Act intended to be performed only by covered custodians. A simple non-control requirement and a requirement that the third party not hold itself out as a custodian is a low-burden means of preventing regulatory avoidance through this provision. Therefore, the OCC is adding a requirement to the final rule that the third party also not exercise or hold itself out as exercising control over the private keys associated with covered assets or provide or hold itself out as providing custody services for covered assets. In addition, the OCC is making non-substantive changes to the language of § 15.23.
Several commenters recommended that the final rule affirm that OCC-supervised institutions may provide ancillary services to persons self-custodying covered assets without triggering the requirements of subpart C. Examples of ancillary services cited by one commenter include permitted payment stablecoin issuers providing services such as trade execution, settlement routing, recordkeeping,
(
printed page 67105)
valuation, or tax reporting to users of self-custody tools. The commenter recommended that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer be permitted to offer such services without triggering full custody rules so long as the institution never takes possession or discretionary control of the user's payment stablecoins or keys. Another commenter similarly recommended extending the safe harbor for self-custodial wallets to all self-custodial interfaces, particularly to the engagement of distributed ledger protocol developers.
The OCC believes that the “control” standard added to final § 15.23 satisfies these concerns and declines to further amend the regulation. However, if the permissibility of a national bank, Federal savings association, Federal branch, or permitted payment stablecoin issuer providing such ancillary services is premised upon such an entity's custody powers, then such an entity could only provide those services in its capacity as a custodian. In such cases, the national bank, Federal savings association, Federal branch, or permitted payment stablecoin issuer would not be covered by the self-custody hardware or software exception and would be subject to compliance with subpart C.

8. Reporting
The OCC sought comment on the extent to which Schedule RC-T of the Call Report, in the case of national banks, Federal savings associations, or Federal branches, and the portions of the reports required under proposed § 15.14 relevant to custodial activities, in the case of nonbank Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuers and applicable State qualified payment stablecoin issuers, are appropriate to ensure that the OCC possesses the information necessary to supervise covered custodians. Several commenters responded that the OCC should not impose additional, distinct reporting obligations on custodians and should instead leverage existing custody reporting mechanisms. Some commenters recommended that the OCC clarify that reporting reserve compositions by permitted-investment category is strictly an issuer obligation, noting that requiring custodians to independently verify and classify covered assets exposes them to undue liability and costs. Other commenters acknowledged that existing Call Reports and Schedule RC-T may not be sufficient on their own for GENIUS Act assessment purposes, and recommended the OCC add a stablecoin-specific supplemental reporting requirement or alter Schedule RC-T of the Call Report. The OCC currently believes that existing reporting provides sufficient insight necessary for OCC supervision and assessment calculations, but will continue to monitor whether additional reporting, including amendments to Schedule RC-T, may be necessary.
9. Miscellaneous
Bridging Arrangements
The OCC sought comment on whether there are particular circumstances for which the OCC should provide additional clarification as to the application of subpart C or the applicability of any exception. Several commenters recommended additional clarification on “bridging” or “wrapping” arrangements, which facilitate use of crypto-assets between distributed ledgers that are not interoperable. One commenter described bridging as a practical necessity for multi-chain stablecoin operations and recommended that the final rule make clear that payment stablecoins locked in a smart contract for bridging to an unsupported blockchain are not, by reason of that locking alone, subject to the custodial requirements of subpart C. Another commenter recommended the OCC clarify that a covered custodian that initiates a bridging transaction for a covered customer can still operate in compliance with subpart C, provided it maintains the ability to receive and custody the underlying asset upon unwrapping. That commenter further recommended that the OCC clarify that the covered custodian's obligations under subpart C continue with respect to the locked position, including the obligation to maintain accurate records of the customer's entitlement to the underlying asset. Other commenters stated that further clarification was unnecessary because of the exception for entities that solely provide hardware or software to facilitate a customer's own custody of payment stablecoins or private keys in section 10(e) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5909(e)
). One commenter stated that the OCC should simply confirm that issuer obligations under subpart C do not extend to activities conducted outside the issuer's control, including third-party wrapping arrangements on unsupported blockchains.
There are a number of unsettled legal questions surrounding the treatment of crypto-asset bridges. Furthermore, the mechanics of bridges can differ in important ways, and the bridge's technical design, the relevant legal contractual terms (or lack thereof), and the presence of parties exercising control over any locked assets, among other factors, may affect the analysis.
[
163
]
Additionally, there are likely to be continued technical developments in this area, which may impact that analysis in the future. Therefore, the OCC is not able to provide definitive responses to the commenters' requests at this time.
The OCC expects covered custodians to understand the mechanics, legal roles, code, contract terms, redemption rights, and other relevant features of a bridge in which covered customers' covered assets are locked in order to understand the covered custodian's legal obligations.
[
164
]
As case law and technology develop, or in response to requests involving particular bridging arrangements, the OCC may provide interpretations on the applicability of section 10 of the GENIUS Act to bridging arrangements. In the absence of definitive guidance from the OCC or clarity in relevant case law, covered custodians may rely on a well-founded legal analysis of compliance with section 10 with respect to bridging arrangements.
Valuation of Private Keys Used To Issue Payment Stablecoins
One commenter responded to the OCC's proposed approach to assign a nominal $1.00 value to private keys used to issue payment stablecoins, describing that approach as reasonable. However, that commenter noted that a nominal valuation may not fully capture the operational and control significance of private key custody, particularly where custody of the issuance keys and custody of reserve assets are held by different entities. The commenter recommended that the OCC address this potential gap without adding duplicative reporting by retaining the
(
printed page 67106)
nominal valuation framework and considering requiring limited, high-level qualitative disclosures regarding private key custody arrangements. The commenter noted that such disclosures could include whether custody of the private keys is internal or third-party, whether it is segregated from reserve asset custody, and whether appropriate internal controls, access limitations, and incident response processes are in place. The OCC does not believe that any additional reporting requirements relating to the private keys used to issue payment stablecoins are necessary to implement through part 15, but it will consider whether any applicable reporting forms should be updated.

12 U.S.C. 5904

Section 18(a) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5916(a)
) provides an exception from the prohibitions in section 3 of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5902
) for foreign payment stablecoin issuers registered with the OCC and sets forth the registration regime and other requirements for foreign payment stablecoin issuers. The OCC proposed subpart D of part 15 to implement these provisions of the GENIUS Act.
1. Overview of Changes From Proposed Rule to Final Rule for Subpart D
After carefully reviewing comments, the OCC is largely adopting subpart D as proposed. The OCC is reordering and renumbering several provisions of subpart D. The OCC is making certain targeted changes to subpart D, including adding clarifying language with respect to subsidiaries of insured depository institutions in § 15.30(a), adding the word “insured” before “Federal branch” and a reference to the Corporate Background and Financial Report in § 15.30(b)(1)(ii), moving language from § 15.30(b)(1)(iii) to § 15.30(b)(4)(i), adding new § 15.30(b)(1)(iv) providing that an applicant must certify whether section 4(a)(12) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(12)
) applies to the applicant, adding new § 15.30(b)(3)(vi) concerning abandoned applications, making technical changes to § 15.30(b)(3)(ii), (iii), and (iv), making technical changes to § 15.30(b)(4) to split it into § 15.30(b)(4)(i), (ii), and (iii), and adding clarifying language to § 15.30(b)(5).
The OCC is adding a new § 15.30(c), which provides that the OCC may approve, conditionally approve, or deny a substantially complete application based on the factors specified under paragraph (d). The OCC is renumbering § 15.30 in light of this new paragraph.
The OCC is also adding new § 15.30(d)(5), which provides that the OCC will consider the ability of the applicant (or in the case of an applicant that is an insured national bank, Federal savings association, or insured Federal branch, of the subsidiary of the applicant) to conduct its proposed activities in a safe and sound manner, including whether the applicant's proposed structure adequately addresses run risks and adequately ensures the ability to redeem payment stablecoins.
The OCC is changing a reference to a disapproval of an application in § 15.30(e)(1) to a reference to denial. The OCC is breaking up paragraph (e)(1) into paragraph (e)(1) and (e)(2). The OCC is also moving to § 15.30(e)(3) language providing that the denial of a substantially complete application under § 15.30 does not prohibit the applicant from filing a subsequent application.
The OCC is modifying § 15.30(f)(1) to clarify that an applicant may request that a hearing be on the written record, oral testimony and oral argument, or both. The OCC is modifying § 15.30(f)(2) to clarify when the OCC will communicate the denial of a substantially complete application. The OCC is modifying § 15.30(f)(3) to clarify what an applicant must submit to be considered in an appeal. The OCC is replacing the words “de novo” with “anew” in § 15.30(f)(4). The OCC is breaking up paragraphs (f)(4) and (f)(5) into subparagraphs. The OCC is adding language in new paragraph (f)(6) concerning the procedures for appeals. The OCC is making minor technical changes to § 15.30(g) and clarifying that the OCC may waive application of the GENIUS Act or part 15 pursuant to section 5(f) of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5904(f)
), rather than only waiving application of section 4 of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903
). The OCC is deleting the word “thereunder” from § 15.30(h).
The OCC is making non-substantive changes to § 15.31(a)(1) and modifying proposed § 15.31(a)(3) to provide various options for when a foreign payment stablecoin issuer's reserves will be deemed sufficient to meet the liquidity demands of United States customers. Specifically, the OCC is adding new § 15.31(a)(3)(i) to clarify that a foreign payment stablecoin issuer must hold reserves in eligible financial institutions incorporated or organized under the laws of the United States or any State that are sufficient to meet the liquidity demands of United States customers, unless otherwise permitted under a reciprocal arrangement created and implemented by the Secretary of the Treasury under section 18(d) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5916(d)
). The OCC is also adding § 15.31(a)(3)(ii) to set forth the relevant options for compliance and describe when reserves of foreign payment stablecoin issuers will be deemed sufficient to meet the liquidity demands of United States customers. New § 15.31(a)(3)(iii) provides that a foreign payment stablecoin issuer may withdraw only reserves in excess of the required amount after due diligence confirms the remaining reserves still meet the required minimum at the time of withdrawal.
The OCC is making a technical change to § 15.31(b)(1) to clarify that foreign issuers are subject to reporting, supervision, and examination requirements as determined by the OCC.
The OCC is revising § 15.31(c) to mirror the prohibition on interest or yield that applies to permitted payment stablecoin issuers under § 15.10(c)(4).
The OCC is making a technical revision to § 15.32(b)(1)(ii) to add “a” before “regulatory and supervisory regime.” The OCC is also adding a reference to compliance with part 15 in § 15.32(b)(1)(iii) and moving language from proposed § 15.32(b)(1)(v) to § 15.32(b)(3) (which is now broken into two subparagraphs).
The OCC is adding new § 15.32(b)(1)(vi) to require foreign payment stablecoin issuers to certify whether section 4(a)(12) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(12)
) applies to the applicant. This addition mirrors requirements applicable to permitted payment stablecoin issuer applicants under § 15.30.
The OCC is also adding new § 15.32(c) to provide that the OCC may approve, conditionally approve, or reject an application based on review of the factors listed in renumbered paragraph (d) of this section of the final rule. The OCC is renumbering § 15.32 in light of this new paragraph in the final rule.
The OCC is adding new § 15.32(d)(6) to clarify that the OCC may assess whether an applicant can operate safely and soundly, including managing run risk and adequately ensuring its ability to redeem payment stablecoins. This addition mirrors the new safety and soundness factor for permitted payment stablecoin issuers under § 15.30.

2. General Applications Framework
Several commenters either made general comments or requested that the OCC make certain revisions to the general proposed application framework. A few commenters suggested the final rule provide confirmation that applicants for a national trust bank charter that plan to custody stablecoin reserves for an affiliated issuer are required, as a condition of charter approval, to provide custody services to unaffiliated clients. This comment concerns the chartering of a national bank, rather than the licensing of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer, and is thus outside the scope of this rulemaking. One commenter recommended creating a public registry of authorized issuers so that downstream participants would know whether they are interacting with a legitimate issuer. The commenter suggested this registry be designed in a manner that incorporates fields for standardized data (
e.g.,
entity's legal name, charter or license identifier, specific product and jurisdictional scope of authorization, and any specific conditions or limitations on the issuer's authorization), and includes near-real-time refresh of authorization status, a machine-readable interface so that downstream participants could consume registry data programmatically, and interoperability with State-level regulators to provide a comprehensive source of authorized issuers and prevent market fragmentation. The commenter suggested that reliance on the registry should act as a safe harbor for downstream participants. The statute does not mandate the creation of a registry like the one described by the commenter. The OCC does intend to publish the determination for when an applicant is licensed as a permitted payment stablecoin issuer but is not including additional regulation text concerning the publication of a registry. In addition, the OCC, consistent with its approach to all matters, plans to operate transparently with regard to its application and registration decisions, including complying with its reporting obligations pursuant to section 15 of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5914
).
Several commenters requested that the final rule expressly provide for a prefiling consultation or application checklist to promote certainty around the information an applicant should include in an application. One commenter suggested the OCC map the checklist to the statutory factors for completeness, while another commenter recommended against including a prescriptive checklist of safety and soundness criteria in the final rule. Two commenters recommended that the OCC publish an application guide, analogous to those available for organizers of de novo institutions, explaining how the OCC will assess the statutory and regulatory review factors under proposed § 15.30(c). One of the commenters also suggested that the guidance commit the OCC to transparently engaging with applicants on any filing concerns before deciding whether to approve or deny an application. The GENIUS Act does not require the OCC to offer a prefiling meeting or publish an application checklist. The OCC historically has not published checklists for applications, but it does provide significant guidance about the filing process in the
Comptroller's Licensing Manual.
The OCC anticipates issuing similar guidance with respect to filings for OCC-supervised permitted payment stablecoin issuers. Accordingly, the final rule does not require a prefiling meeting or incorporate an application checklist. Nevertheless, applicants may request a prefiling meeting with OCC staff. The OCC plans to update the
Comptroller's Licensing Manual
in the near future to incorporate its chartering policy and procedural requirements for applicants seeking to become permitted payment stablecoin issuers. Applicants are encouraged to review these materials and any related publications prior to requesting a prefiling meeting. Further, pursuant to section 5(d)(1)(B)(ii) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5904(d)(1)(B)(ii)
), which requires a primary Federal payment stablecoin regulator to notify an applicant whether its application is considered substantially complete not later than 30 days after receipt, as incorporated under § 15.30(b)(3)(ii), the OCC will notify the applicant, within 30 days of receipt of the application, of the information required in order for the application to be considered substantially complete. The OCC believes this notification along with updates to the
Comptroller's Licensing Manual
will provide sufficient transparency regarding any filing concerns.
Two commenters suggested that the OCC provide guidance confirming that registration as a money services business (MSB) with FinCEN would not disqualify a nonbank entity from making a filing under § 15.30 and that such registration would be treated as affirmative evidence of BSA/AML compliance. The GENIUS Act provides that permitted payment stablecoin issuers shall be treated as financial institutions for purposes of the Bank Secrecy Act. MSBs, like other nonbank entities seeking OCC approval to become Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuers, must make a filing with the OCC and comply with applicable laws and regulations including those relating to BSA/AML compliance. Registration as an MSB alone does not provide conclusive evidence of compliance.
Commenters sought clarification on when the OCC will begin accepting applications pursuant to § 15.30. As discussed in more detail below, proposed paragraph (f)(3) provided that the OCC may grant a waiver of the Act's requirements for up to 12 months beginning on the effective date of the GENIUS Act if it finds the waiver to be in the public interest or extraordinary circumstances justify the waiver. Accepting applications before the effective date of the Act and final rule is appropriate in light of section 5(f) of

b. Description of Comments and Final Rule
Application Process
A few commenters suggested the OCC integrate the licensing of issuers into Federal bank oversight, particularly with respect to subsidiaries of national banks and Federal savings associations because national banks and Federal savings associations may engage in stablecoin activities including issuance and because these entities are already subject to consolidated supervision. Several commenters suggested that to promote administrative efficiency, the OCC expressly allow § 15.30 to supersede all other OCC regulations addressing filing requirements. Other commenters argued against supersession where other licensing frameworks do not displace but rather operate in parallel with the framework of § 15.30. For example, these commenters stated parallel applications for interdependent corporate transactions are necessary where a national bank seeks to establish a subsidiary through which it would issue payment stablecoins. The commenters suggested that a national bank must file both an operating subsidiary application under § 5.34 and an application under § 15.30 seeking approval to issue payment stablecoins through a subsidiary.
The substantive licensing requirements for subsidiaries of insured depository institutions, uninsured national banks, Federal branches, and nonbank entities are the same under section 5 of the GENIUS Act. The only difference is that an insured depository institution applies to establish a subsidiary while prospective Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuers apply to issue directly. Because the substantive requirements are the same, the OCC believes that it is appropriate to address licensing of all permitted payment stablecoin issuers, including subsidiaries of insured national banks and Federal savings associations, in part 15. In addition, the OCC notes that, pursuant to
12 CFR 5.36(d)(1)(iii)
, an insured national bank or Federal savings association would not need to submit a separate filing under
12 CFR part 5
to establish a subsidiary permitted payment stablecoin issuer. The OCC intends the process provided under § 15.30 to be comprehensive for stablecoin issuance and other activities described in § 15.10(a). This is consistent with the OCC's general approach of not requiring multiple filings for the same activity. For example, to the extent that stablecoin issuance would involve membership in a payment system and notice to join a payment system was provided during the filing process, no additional filing under
12 CFR 7.1026
would be required at that time. However, an applicant that wishes to establish an uninsured national trust bank that would be a permitted payment stablecoin issuer will need to apply to form a de novo national bank under
12 CFR 5.20
or convert to a national bank under
12 CFR 5.24
and apply to become a permitted payment stablecoin issuer under
12 CFR 15.30(a)
because different statutory and regulatory requirements apply to the formation of national banks and the licensing of permitted payment stablecoin issuers.

Application Standards and Additional Factors
Proposed § 15.30(c) included the statutory factors in section 5(c) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5904(c)
) that a primary Federal payment stablecoin regulator could have considered when evaluating a complete application. The OCC requested comment on whether the OCC should include additional factors necessary to ensure the safety and soundness of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer.
Several commenters supported inclusion of a principles-based safety and soundness factor based on objective benchmarks. Specifically, commenters recommended that the safety and soundness evaluation consider whether an applicant evidences operational and governance capacity to run a stablecoin business responsibly at scale, a mature compliance architecture that supports an effective control environment, and substantiated financial viability. Commenters recommended that operational capacity be assessed based on an applicant's technology infrastructure (including smart contract, private key, and cybersecurity management), exposure to third-party technology dependencies (
e.g.
, blockchain validators, oracle providers, and cloud infrastructure), and capacity for business continuity and disaster recovery to preserve redemption reliability and avoid systemic contagion. Commenters recommended that governance capacity be assessed based on an applicant's ownership chain, board and senior management responsibility for stablecoin operations, oversight of interaffiliate service arrangements and transactions, and staffing adequacy.
Commenters recommended that the maturity of an applicant's compliance architecture be evaluated based on the ability of its systems to monitor compliance with BSA/AML and OFAC requirements (including capabilities with respect to customer verification, the Travel Rule, and transaction monitoring and sanctions screening calibrated to the velocity and pseudonymity of on-chain activity), consumer compliance (including prohibitions on unfair or deceptive acts or practices, fraud prevention, and error resolution and dispute rights), and effective third-party oversight (including data privacy and security).
Commenters recommended that financial viability be assessed based on reserve integrity observable in real time (including reserve composition, transaction flows, counterparty exposure, and funding strategy), liquidity management controls, the revenue model and projected operational expenses (including adequate funding of an applicant's operational backstop at inception), and sustainability of an applicant's redemption model under various stress scenarios. One commenter also encouraged the OCC to ensure that a nonbank applicant is assessed consistent with the principle of “same risk, same regulation” and also ensure that a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer transferring to OCC jurisdiction has obtained a unanimous vote of the Stablecoin Certification Review Committee. While agreeing that a safety and soundness factor should be explicitly included in the regulatory text of the final rule, another commenter recommended against a checklist of safety and soundness criteria to avoid stifling innovation and discouraging non-traditional, low-risk business models. Other commenters opposed adding specific safety and soundness factors to the final rule as they would not be anchored in statutory requirements and would impose additional hurdles and unnecessary administrative gloss.
The OCC agrees with some of the commenters that the final rule would benefit from an explicit reference to safety and soundness in the review factors given that it is included in the statutory factors for review and denial of an application. The OCC believes that this reference should be sufficiently detailed to provide applicants guidance. Accordingly, the OCC is adopting § 15.30(c) as proposed (renumbered as § 15.30(d)) with the addition of a new review factor in subparagraph (5). Under the final rule, the OCC will also consider the ability of the applicant (or in the case of an applicant that is an insured national bank, Federal savings association, or insured Federal branch, of the subsidiary of the applicant) to conduct its proposed activities in a safe and sound manner, including whether the applicant's proposed structure adequately addresses run risks and adequately ensures the ability to redeem payment stablecoins.
Some commenters expressed concern that they believe the standards under proposed § 15.30 are weaker than those established for approvals of insured de novo banks. Specifically, commenters were concerned that the proposal did not address the convenience and needs of the community that an applicant intends to serve or require consistency of an applicant's corporate powers with the purposes of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act (
i.e.
, ensuring the safety and soundness of FDIC-insured depository institutions and consumer protection). The GENIUS Act does not apply deposit insurance requirements to payment stablecoin issuers. Section 4(e) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(e)
) explicitly states that payment stablecoins shall not be subject to deposit insurance by the FDIC. The OCC believes that the statutorily enumerated approval factors under § 15.30, combined with the additional safety and soundness requirement under the final rule, are sufficient for the OCC to make an appropriate determination under § 15.30, particularly in light of the limited activities and authorities of permitted payment stablecoin issuers relative to insured depository institutions.
One commenter recommended the OCC periodically revise application standards and processes to ensure that they remain appropriately tailored to observed risks and market developments. The OCC may engage in future rulemaking to revise this approach, as needed, as it gains additional experience and data concerning the application process.

4. General Foreign Payment Stablecoin Issuers Framework
Section 18 of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5916
) generally addresses foreign issuers and provides an exemption from the prohibitions of section 3 of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5902
) for issuers that meet certain requirements. Under section 18, for an issuer to be exempt from those prohibitions, among other conditions, the Secretary of the Treasury must determine that the issuer is subject to regulation and supervision by a foreign payment stablecoin regulator that has a regulatory and supervisory regime comparable to the GENIUS Act. In addition, the foreign payment stablecoin issuer must register with, and be subject to ongoing monitoring by, the OCC. Section 18 also contemplates that the Secretary of the Treasury may create and implement reciprocal arrangements or other bilateral agreements between the United States and jurisdictions with payment stablecoin regulatory regimes that are comparable to the requirements established under the GENIUS Act. The OCC proposed to implement the provisions of the GENIUS Act relating to foreign payment stablecoin issuers for which the OCC is responsible in §§ 15.31 through 15.33. A discussion of comments received and the changes to those particular sections follows.
Some commenters provided broad, overarching comments concerning the OCC's implementation of provisions relating to foreign payment stablecoin issuers. One commenter stated that the OCC should adhere to the principle of national treatment in its rulemaking and interpretation of the GENIUS Act, which the commenter said would support robust competition, market liquidity, and diversified sources of credit. One commenter suggested that the OCC's rulemaking authority with respect to foreign payment stablecoin issuers relates only to standards for approval of registration requests and the process for appealing denials of registration requests because the Department of the Treasury is charged more broadly with rulemaking authority to carry out section 18 of the GENIUS Act. Several comments focused on how a foreign regime is determined to be comparable to the GENIUS Act. Some commenters stated that the OCC's role does not extend to evaluating the quality of a foreign payment stablecoin issuer's home-country regulations. One commenter suggested that the OCC clarify the criteria by which state and foreign supervisory regimes are evaluated for equivalence, including objective benchmarks for reserve localization, liquidity coverage, and supervisory intensity. Another commenter suggested that the OCC should adopt a stringent comparability standard that requires foreign regimes to demonstrate substantive equivalence—not merely formal similarity—to United States reserve quality, audit standards, redemption protections, and AML/CFT requirements. The commenter asserted that U.S.-based issuers must not be placed at an economic disadvantage relative to foreign issuers operating under less rigorous regimes. The commenter also noted that the OCC should require ongoing monitoring and periodic recertification of foreign regime comparability and should establish clear triggers for the suspension or revocation of a foreign payment stablecoin issuer if that jurisdiction's standards deteriorate. The commenter also requested clarification of how the Stablecoin Certification Review Committee will evaluate foreign regimes and what specific role public input will have in that evaluation process. A commenter further stated that the OCC should not extend the regime applicable to permitted payment stablecoin issuers to foreign issuers not expressly provided for in the Act as Treasury is responsible for assessing the comparability of home-country requirements. One commenter suggested that the OCC publish guidance, interpretive materials, or supervisory statements setting out how each substantive requirement in the proposed rule applies to foreign payment stablecoin issuers, including where functional equivalence with home-jurisdiction standards will be recognized and what the process is for demonstrating that equivalence.
The final rule, like the proposed rule, does not require the OCC to evaluate the quality of a foreign payment stablecoin issuer's home-country regulations. That role is reserved for the Secretary of the Treasury. With respect to requirements of registration, the final rule, like the proposal, adheres closely to the statutory requirements with certain additional clarifications necessary to effectuate a registration process and give market participants clarity on how to register with the OCC.
A few commenters argued that the OCC should not prescribe substantive requirements for foreign payment stablecoin issuers in the United States. A commenter stated that proposed subpart D should more closely reflect the statutorily specified role of the OCC
(
printed page 67116)
regarding the substantive regulation of foreign issuers while preserving the OCC's supervisory oversight. A commenter stated that it should not be necessary for the OCC to create any new requirements in the registration process beyond what is required by the Act. One commenter suggested that foreign payment stablecoin issuers should be subject to requirements that achieve equivalent outcomes as the requirements imposed on permitted payment stablecoin issuers. Some commenters requested that there be no requirement limiting foreign payment stablecoin issuers to a single brand of payment stablecoin. Some commenters also stated that foreign payment stablecoin issuers should be required to redeem at par to provide parity with permitted payment stablecoin issuers, which must redeem at par. Commenters also asked whether foreign payment stablecoin issuers have an obligation to redeem with respect to any payment stablecoin holder. A few commenters discussed reserve requirements and the treatment of yield. One commenter suggested that the requirements addressing the interface between the issuer and United States customer and United States infrastructure, for example, reserve requirements, United States customer determination, and yield prohibition, should apply directly to foreign issuers. The commenter also suggested that the OCC should consider the Financial Action Task Force's March 2026 report on the regulation and supervision of offshore virtual asset providers in shaping its approach.
Another commenter suggested that the OCC should provide explicit guidance on managing conflict-of-law risks and cross-jurisdictional regulatory obligations. The commenter also indicated that foreign issuers should be subject to requirements proportionate to and consistent with those applied to domestic issuers where comprehensive consolidated supervision is in place. The commenter noted that more extensive requirements on foreign issuers could discourage participation without materially improving safety or consumer protection.
A few commenters suggested that the OCC not allow foreign-issued stablecoins to operate without reserve verification. The commenters argued that United States issuers should not be subject to rules that are more stringent than those for foreign issuers. Under the OCC's rule, foreign issuers are subject to the same reporting requirements as permitted payment stablecoin issuers, and monthly reporting requires providing information about reserve assets.
The Act imposes substantive requirements on foreign payment stablecoin issuers, which the final rule, like the proposed rule, implements. These requirements include the yield prohibition in section 4(a)(11) of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(11)
), the requirement to hold reserves sufficient to meet liquidity demands of United States customers in section 18(a)(3) of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5916(a)(3)
), and the requirement to be subject to ongoing monitoring in section 18(c)(2) of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5916(c)(2)
). As described in greater detail below, the final rule imposes certain requirements directly related to the statute but does not impose all of the requirements applicable to permitted payment stablecoin issuers. The OCC believes that imposing all such requirements on foreign payment stablecoin issuers would be inconsistent with the role of the Secretary of the Treasury in evaluating a foreign regime to determine if the regime is comparable to the GENIUS Act. The Secretary of the Treasury also retains the ability to enter into reciprocal arrangements that may include substantive requirements with respect to foreign payment stablecoin issuers' payment stablecoin activities. Moreover, the OCC may impose, as a condition of registration, certain requirements applicable to permitted payment stablecoin issuers on foreign payment stablecoin issuers, if the OCC determines necessary based on the facts relevant to a prospective foreign payment stablecoin issuer's registration. The OCC intends to use such conditions, as appropriate, based on the particular facts, including the degree to which the payment stablecoin circulates in the United States. With respect to a limitation on issuing more than one brand of payment stablecoin, as discussed more extensively in the portion of this supplementary information addressing subpart B of part 15, the OCC is not adopting any such requirement in regulation text for permitted payment stablecoin issuers or foreign payment stablecoin issuers. The OCC may, however, impose conditions concerning the issuance of multiple brands, as appropriate, based on the facts of a particular applicant. The OCC also confirms that foreign payment stablecoin issuers, like permitted payment stablecoin issuers, must redeem payment stablecoins at par. This requirement follows from the definition of payment stablecoin in section 2(22) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5901(22)
), which provides that the issuer is obligated to convert, redeem, or repurchase the payment stablecoin for a fixed amount of monetary value, not including a digital asset denominated in a fixed amount of monetary value. As with a permitted payment stablecoin issuer, a foreign payment stablecoin issuer would likewise be required to redeem from any payment stablecoin holder, subject to appropriate onboarding. Although foreign payment stablecoin issuers might generally interact with a small number of customers (
e.g.,
exchanges), they should ensure that they have the capacity to onboard and redeem from other payment stablecoin holders. This approach is consistent with the definition of payment stablecoin and helps ensure parity between permitted payment stablecoin issuers and foreign payment stablecoin issuers.

The final rule, like the proposal, imposes no direct requirement on foreign payment stablecoin issuers related to capital. As discussed in greater detail below, the OCC anticipates that comparability determinations and reciprocal arrangements will be generally sufficient to ensure that the United States operations of foreign payment stablecoin issuers are appropriately capitalized. In addition, the OCC may, to the extent not sufficiently addressed by the home-jurisdiction or reciprocal arrangement, impose capital requirements as a condition of registration.

One commenter asserted that the proposed rule imposes asymmetric regulatory burdens that disadvantage permitted payment stablecoin issuers while leaving foreign competitors largely unaffected. The commenter suggested that the OCC should compare the effective regulatory burden against the benefits actually received for foreign payment stablecoin issuers. The OCC notes that, under section 18, a foreign issuer is only exempt from the prohibitions of section 3 if, among other conditions, the Secretary of the Treasury determines that the foreign payment stablecoin issuer is subject to a regulatory and supervisory regime that is comparable to the requirements established under the GENIUS Act. Thus, these issuers will be subject to certain requirements outside of this final rule. In addition, foreign payment stablecoin issuers may be subject to additional requirements pursuant to reciprocal arrangements or individualized conditions imposed under the registration process.
5. Foreign Payment Stablecoin Issuers (§ 15.31)
Section 18(a) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5916(a)
) exempts a foreign payment stablecoin issuer from the prohibitions of section 3 of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5902
) if it meets all of the following requirements: (1) the foreign payment stablecoin issuer is subject to regulation and supervision by a foreign payment stablecoin regulator that has a regulatory and supervisory regime comparable to the GENIUS Act with respect to payment stablecoins, as determined by the Secretary of the Treasury under section 18(b) of the GENIUS Act; (2) the foreign payment stablecoin issuer is registered with the OCC pursuant to § 15.32; (3) the foreign payment stablecoin issuer holds reserves in a United States financial institution sufficient to meet liquidity demands of United States customers, unless otherwise permitted under a reciprocal arrangement created and implemented by the Secretary of the Treasury under section 18(d) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5916(d)
); and (4) the foreign country in which the foreign payment stablecoin issuer is domiciled and regulated is not subject to comprehensive economic sanctions by the United States or in a jurisdiction that the Secretary of the Treasury has determined to be a jurisdiction of primary money laundering concern. The OCC proposed § 15.31(a) to implement this exemption.
Commenters requested additional clarity both as to what constitutes a United States customer and as to what would be sufficient to meet the liquidity demands of United States customers. In particular, commenters requested clarity on how to determine if liquidity was sufficient (
e.g.,
what measures should be used, what thresholds a foreign payment stablecoin issuer must meet). One commenter suggested that the OCC adopt a flexible, principles-based approach to estimating United States customer liquidity demands for foreign payment stablecoin issuers. One commenter suggested that the OCC should confirm how residency for purposes of “United States customer” will be determined in practice. In particular, the commenter suggested that United States customers should be limited to persons with direct contractual or onboarding relationships with the issuer. The commenter also requested that the OCC confirm that the residence information from KYC checks of direct customers would be sufficient to determine whether a customer is a resident of the United States. One commenter stated that foreign issuers
(
printed page 67118)
will not always be able to precisely determine whether every holder is a United States customer, and that the rule should not require a single rigid methodology or rely on proxies for the estimated number of United States holders. This commenter further stated that foreign issuers may be able to identify United States nexus through a combination of indicators such as onboarding information for direct customers, IP data, wallet analytics, transaction patterns, and other reasonably available information.
One commenter raised concerns regarding how a foreign issuer will be able to identify where its tokens circulate, where the payment stablecoin holders reside or are located, as well as the nationality of payment stablecoin holders. Some commenters advocated for a flexible, principles-based approach to requirements for foreign issuers. One commenter noted that employing a flexible approach would be particularly important until more data becomes available regarding the operations of foreign issuers. A number of commenters opposed requiring a fixed percentage of reserves to be held at United States financial institutions. Several commenters supported a principles-guided, outcomes-focused approach that imposes a risk-based standard that requires a defensible estimation methodology and periodic reassessment with no fixed percentage. These commenters argued that a fixed percentage could impose significant cost while bearing little relationship to the actual liquidity risk posed by a particular issuer. One commenter urged that the methodology adopted by the OCC to calculate default reserves should preserve flexibility for Treasury to negotiate reciprocal arrangements under section 18(d) of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5916(d)
). One commenter suggested that a methodology should be calibrated to the issuer's actual or reasonably estimated United States customer exposures with a modest liquidity buffer in the range of 10 to 15 percent above estimated one-month United States customer redemptions. One commenter argued that a fixed percentage would impose a significant and potentially excessive burden on foreign issuers whose United States customer base represents a small or predictable fraction of their total issuance and would be disproportionate relative to the actual liquidity risk the requirement is designed to address. One commenter suggested that objective measures and thresholds should be included for when United States reserve assets are sufficient to meet demands of United States customers. The commenter noted the importance of ensuring standards are objective without prescribing a rigid formula. One commenter suggested that the OCC should not prescribe a single rigid methodology because foreign issuers will not always be able to determine whether a particular holder is a United States customer. One commenter suggested that the OCC should rely on home-jurisdiction frameworks rather than prescribing detailed United States-specific customer identification methodologies for foreign issuers, especially where those issuers are subject to ongoing supervision by a home regulator whose regime has been determined to be comparable under the Act. One commenter suggested that the OCC should confirm that foreign issuers distributing through regulated intermediaries may rely on those intermediaries' customer identification data for purposes of estimating their United States customer base, provided appropriate contractual arrangements are in place requiring the intermediary to share relevant customer data with the issuer for compliance purposes. One commenter discussed on-chain reserves, noting that they could better enable the issuer to meet redemption requirements and that flexible diversification that can be tailored and updated through guidance will provide the OCC maximum flexibility to respond to changing market conditions.
A couple of commenters also requested clarification of which “United States financial institutions” may hold reserves for foreign payment stablecoin issuers, urging the OCC to include United States branches and agencies of foreign banks and, more broadly, any institution located or organized in the United States that is authorized under Federal or State law to provide custodial or safekeeping services for payment stablecoin reserves. One commenter also noted that the proposed definitions appear to exclude foreign custodians from the custody provisions applicable to covered custodians and sub-custodians and asked the OCC to expressly confirm that understanding.
The OCC agrees with commenters that additional guidance is necessary to determine what is sufficient to meet the liquidity demands of United States customers. As discussed above, the final rule defines United States customer as a customer that, at the time of onboarding (1) is an individual and resides in the United States, (2) is incorporated or organized under the laws of the United States or any State, or (3) has its principal place of business in the United States. This revised definition ensures that the customer has a clear nexus to the United States and is administrable.
The final rule clarifies that a United States financial institution is an eligible financial institution that is incorporated or organized under the laws of the United States or of any State. The Act does not define financial institution, and it has been defined broadly in the context of other banking laws. The final rule uses “eligible financial institution” in this context. Eligible financial institutions generally are persons that are eligible to hold reserve assets in custody under section 10 of the GENIUS Act and otherwise comply with section 10 of the Act. As any entity holding reserve assets would be required to comply with section 10, the use of “eligible financial institution” broadly defines the scope of “financial institutions” under section 18(a)(3) of the Act, consistent with the Act's use of the term financial institution and with its structure.
To effect the Act's requirement that the financial institution must be a “United States” financial institution, final § 15.31(a)(3)(i) confirms that the eligible financial institution must be incorporated or organized under the laws of the United States or any State. As the statute makes clear, the financial institution itself—as opposed to a branch, agency, or other office—must be a United States entity.
The OCC also recognizes that there may be difficulties in determining what is sufficient to meet the liquidity demands of United States customers. Accordingly, the final rule includes four different options that clarify how foreign payment stablecoin issuers can demonstrate compliance with the requirement in section 18(a)(3) of the Act (
12 U.S.C. 5916(a)(3)
). Final § 15.31(a)(3)(i) provides that a foreign payment stablecoin issuer must hold reserves in eligible financial institutions incorporated or organized under the laws of the United States or any State that are sufficient to meet the liquidity demands of United States customers, unless otherwise permitted under a reciprocal arrangement created and implemented by the Secretary of the Treasury under section 18(d) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5916(d)
). This largely restates the statutory requirement in section 18(a)(3) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5916(a)(3)
). Paragraph (a)(3)(ii) sets forth the relevant options to achieve compliance with the requirement in section 18(a)(3) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5916(a)(3)
). Under paragraph (a)(3)(ii), reserves are sufficient to meet the liquidity demands of United States customers only if the foreign payment
(
printed page 67119)
stablecoin issuer complies with one of four alternatives. Under one alternative, the foreign payment stablecoin issuer would (1) attest that fewer than 50 percent of the foreign payment stablecoin issuer's outstanding issuance value is held by payment stablecoin holders located in the United States; and (2) hold reserves in eligible financial institutions incorporated or organized under the laws of the United States or any State, the value of which equals or exceeds 50 percent of the foreign payment stablecoin issuer's outstanding issuance value. Under the second alternative, the foreign payment stablecoin issuer would (1) attest that it holds substantially all of its reserves in eligible financial institutions incorporated or organized under the laws of the United States or any State and (2) hold substantially all of its reserves in eligible financial institutions incorporated or organized under the laws of the United States or any State. These first two alternatives are intended to provide simple and clear paths for compliance. Depending on the business model of a foreign issuer, these two alternatives may or may not be viable. Accordingly, the OCC is including two additional means of establishing compliance that, while somewhat more complicated, could accommodate a wider variety of business models than the first two alternatives. Under the third alternative, the foreign payment stablecoin issuer would ensure, on an ongoing basis, that the value and composition of reserves held in eligible financial institutions incorporated or organized under the laws of the United States will be capable of supporting timely redemption requests from United States customers under both normal conditions and adverse economic, liquidity, market, and interest rate conditions, including, to the extent necessary, maintaining a buffer of reserves.

This alternative entails ongoing assessment of liquidity demands and recalibration of amounts held in United States financial institutions. Under the final alternative, the foreign payment stablecoin issuer would submit a detailed proposal to meet the requirements of paragraph (a)(3)(i) for the OCC's approval. The foreign payment stablecoin issuer would need to respond to all OCC requests for additional information regarding the proposal, receive the OCC's written approval of the proposal, and comply, on an ongoing basis, with the proposal approved by the OCC, including any conditions and limitations imposed on such approval by the OCC. This final option is intended to provide flexibility for foreign payment stablecoin issuers that can demonstrate alternative means of complying with paragraph (a)(3)(i) while ensuring that the OCC has the opportunity to opine on whether the method is reasonable.
Paragraph (a)(3)(iii) of § 15.31 imposes a limitation similar to that applicable to permitted payment stablecoin issuers under § 15.11 and provides that a foreign payment stablecoin issuer must only withdraw reserves in excess of the amount required under paragraph (a)(3)(i) after appropriate due diligence and confirmation that the withdrawal would not cause the reserves held in eligible financial institutions incorporated or organized under the laws of the United States or any State to fall below the amount required under paragraph (a)(3)(i), calculated as of the time and date of withdrawal.

Although foreign payment stablecoin issuers will be subject to reporting requirements in their home jurisdiction as well as the United States, it is beyond the scope of this rulemaking to compare all such reporting obligations to the information requirements needed by the OCC to supervise foreign issuers. Moreover, the same reporting obligations across the OCC's supervised entities as a baseline ensures that the OCC will receive the information it needs to monitor its supervised entities and allows for comparability across them. The OCC will conduct full-scope examinations of foreign payment stablecoin issuers registered with the OCC. The OCC will generally focus on the United States activity of foreign issuers in those examinations and only on any foreign activity to the extent that it is relevant to their United States operations and activities.

7. Revocation or Rescission of Approval (§ 15.33)
a. Description of the Proposed Rule
Section 5(i)(3)(A) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5904(i)(3)(A)
) permits the OCC to revoke the approval of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer that does not submit the certification regarding implementation of anti-money laundering and economic sanctions compliance programs required by section 5(i)(1) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5904(i)(1)
). Proposed § 15.14(k) set forth those requirements. Similarly, section 18(c)(3)(A) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5916(c)(3)(A)
) permits the OCC, in consultation with the Secretary of the Treasury, to rescind approval of a registration of a foreign payment stablecoin issuer if the OCC determines that the foreign payment stablecoin issuer is not in compliance with the requirements of the GENIUS Act, including for maintaining insufficient reserves or posing an illicit finance risk or financial stability risk.
Proposed § 15.33(a) would have implemented revocation of approval of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's application. Proposed paragraph (a)(1) stated that the OCC may revoke approval of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's application under proposed § 15.30 if the permitted payment stablecoin issuer does not submit the certification required by proposed § 15.14(k). Proposed paragraph (a)(2)(i) stated that the OCC may issue an order to revoke the application approval after providing notice to the permitted payment stablecoin issuer and after providing an opportunity for a hearing. Proposed paragraph (a)(2)(ii) provided that the OCC would conduct a hearing pursuant to the OCC's Rules of Practice and Procedure in
12 CFR part 19
. Proposed paragraph (a)(2)(iii) provided for expedited OCC action without an opportunity for a hearing if the OCC determines that expeditious action is necessary in order to protect the public interest. In this situation, the OCC could, in its sole discretion, provide the permitted payment stablecoin issuer with notice of the intended revocation, grant the permitted payment stablecoin issuer an opportunity to oppose the revocation in writing, or take any other action designed to provide the permitted payment stablecoin issuer with notice and an opportunity to present its views concerning the revocation of application approval. Proposed paragraph (a)(3) stated that a decision to revoke an application approval would be effective upon provision of notice to the permitted payment stablecoin issuer, unless otherwise specified by the OCC.
Proposed paragraph (b) provided procedures for rescission of approval of a registration of a foreign payment stablecoin issuer. Proposed paragraph (b) was substantially the same as proposed § 15.33(a), except that proposed paragraph (b)(1) referred to the OCC's consultation with the Secretary of the Treasury, consistent with section 18(c)(3)(A) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5916(c)(3)(A)
). Proposed paragraph (b)(3) provided that a decision to rescind approval of a registration is effective upon publication in the
Federal Register
, as required by section 18(c)(3)(A) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5916(c)(3)(A)
), unless otherwise specified by the OCC. The OCC could, for example, specify a later effective date than the date of publication in the
Federal Register
. Under proposed § 15.33(b), except as otherwise provided, the OCC could have issued an order to rescind the foreign payment stablecoin issuer's registration approval under proposed § 15.32 after providing notice to the foreign payment stablecoin issuer and providing an opportunity for a hearing. Proposed paragraph (b)(2)(ii) provided that the OCC would conduct a hearing under this section pursuant to the OCC's Rules of Practice and Procedure in
12 CFR part 19
. Proposed paragraph (b)(2)(iii) provided that the OCC could act without providing an opportunity for a hearing if it determines that expeditious action is necessary in order to protect the public interest. Under the proposed rule, if the OCC found it necessary to act without providing an opportunity for a hearing, the OCC, in its sole discretion, could have: provided the foreign payment stablecoin issuer with notice of the intended rescission of approval registration; granted the foreign payment stablecoin issuer an opportunity to present a written submission opposing rescission of approval registration; or taken any other action designed to provide the foreign payment stablecoin issuer with notice and an opportunity to present its views concerning the rescission of approval registration.
The revocation and rescission procedures in proposed § 15.33 largely parallel those for termination of a Federal branch or agency in
12 CFR 28.24(b)

E. Subpart E—Capital and Operational Backstop
Section 4(a)(4)(A)(i) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(4)(A)(i)
) requires the OCC to establish capital requirements for permitted payment stablecoin issuers. The capital requirements must be tailored to the business model and risk profile of permitted payment stablecoin issuers and not exceed requirements sufficient to ensure the ongoing operations of permitted payment stablecoin issuers. The OCC proposed to address these capital requirements in subpart E of part 15.
1. Overview of Changes From Proposed Rule to Final Rule for Subpart E
The agency is finalizing § 15.40 with changes. The section name and the title for § 15.40(a) have changed from the proposed “Capital elements” to “Capital.” Whereas proposed § 15.40(a) described a minimum capital requirement as common equity tier 1 capital (described in proposed § 15.40(b)) and additional tier 1 capital (described in proposed § 15.40(c)), final § 15.40(a) requires a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to meet the minimum capital requirement in final § 15.41(a) through the total of its equity accounts after deducting the items listed in final § 15.40(b). As described below, both proposed and final § 15.41(a) describe minimum capital requirements. The final § 15.40(b) lists capital deductions, including intangible assets (
e.g.,
goodwill) and operational backstop assets funded by equity. Proposed § 15.40 did not describe the funding of the operational backstop specifically. Final § 15.40(c) describes operational backstop debt and requires that such debt not exceed 50 percent of the operational backstop requirement in final § 15.41(b). As described below, both proposed and final § 15.41(b) describe the operational backstop requirement. Proposed § 15.40(c)(1) described criteria for additional tier 1 capital whereas final § 15.40(c)(1) describes the criteria for operational backstop debt.
In final § 15.41, the section title “Minimum capital and operational backstop” includes “operational” while the title of proposed § 15.41 did not.
