The OCC first would use the existing formula set forth under § 8.2(a) to determine the institution's semiannual assessment attributable to assets other than those reflecting minimum stablecoin reserve assets. The OCC next would apply the same formula to those assets reflecting minimum stablecoin reserve assets, except that it would reduce the resulting amount by 35 percent, or by such other percentage (up to 55 percent) that the OCC may deem appropriate for minimum stablecoin reserves held by national banks and Federal savings associations, based on its experience supervising stablecoin issuers. The OCC would publish the percentage reduction deemed appropriate for minimum stablecoin reserve assets on an annual basis in the Notice of Fees. An institution's semiannual general assessment fee would be the sum of the two figures above.

The OCC considered whether to propose a larger baseline discount for required stablecoin reserve assets and recognizes that it may be appropriate over time for the agency to discount assessments on required stablecoin reserve assets by more than the baseline 35 percent. However, the agency explained that it expected to commit more resources to supervising GENIUS Act-related activities in the first several years following passage of the GENIUS Act as institutions and the OCC adapt to the exercise and supervision of new GENIUS Act powers. Additionally, the OCC anticipated that the new powers granted under the GENIUS Act may result in many new de novo chartered institutions, which typically require heightened supervision in the early years of such institutions. To address potential differences in the OCC's immediate- and longer-term supervisory commitments in connection with GENIUS Act-related activities, the proposed rule provided the OCC with sufficient flexibility to annually adjust the discounted rate to reflect changes in the overall share of the supervisory burden attributable to the GENIUS Act-related activities of national banks and Federal savings associations.

However, the agency determined that it lacked reliable information or evidence to suggest that assessing stablecoin reserve assets above the minimum at undiscounted rates would meaningfully influence an issuer's business judgment on whether and to what extent it should hold on-balance-sheet stablecoin reserves above the minimum. Additionally, while the OCC did not wish to disincentivize holdings above the minimum, the agency expressed initial concern that extending the proposed discount to reserves above the minimum might encourage some institutions to mischaracterize the status of certain on-balance-sheet assets as reserves to minimize their overall assessment. Nevertheless, the OCC sought comment on whether it should extend the reserve asset discount to holdings above the minimum and, if it did, whether to cap the discount at an amount equal to between 1 and 5 percent of required reserves. This range of 1 to 5 percent reflected the agency's understanding that current stablecoin reserve asset holdings above the minimum typically occur within this range.
The OCC received several comments on its proposal to discount assessments on assets attributable to required stablecoin reserves, including on whether it should have a mechanism to account for reserve asset holdings above the minimum.
One commenter stated that reserve assets backing payment stablecoins are fundamentally different from traditional bank assets such that the supervisory complexity is substantially reduced with regard to these reserve assets. The commenter stated that under the GENIUS Act's required 1 to 1 reserve requirement, issuers hold high-quality liquid assets that pose minimal credit risk and do not require loan-loss provisioning, underwriting decisions, or complex valuations. Rather, they are passive, transparent holdings verifiable through automated systems and monthly attestation reports, while traditional bank supervision requires intense examination of credit portfolios, loan classifications, borrower financial conditions, collateral valuations, and complex management frameworks. The commenter stated that the marginal cost to the OCC of supervising an additional billion dollars in passive Treasury holdings is substantially lower than for an equivalent amount of commercial loans or other credit products. The commenter stated that the proposed 35 percent discount implies that supervising stablecoin reserves requires 65 percent of the resources of traditional bank assets, posited that this does not adequately account for the supervisory burden, and urged the OCC to adopt the proposed maximum discount of 55 percent.
Separately, a comment addressed the possibility of an assessment discount in the context of stablecoin issuers holding more reserve assets than are strictly required. In the proposal, the OCC had asked about mechanisms to account for such holdings above the minimum, such as assessment discounts. The comment explained a framework to incentivize reserve asset holdings above the minimum and structure such holdings. Rather than employing assessment discounts that could give entities a reason to mischaracterize balance sheet assets as reserve assets above the minimum, the comment suggested a mechanism that would tie the holding of reserve assets above the minimum to a higher ceiling on the portfolio weighted average maturity. Such a mechanism, the comment argued, would avoid the agency's well-founded concern about mischaracterization.
In the final rule, the OCC is adopting the discount methodology as proposed and as described above (with the below-described removal of the word “minimum”). For the portion of stablecoin issuer assessments that are attributable to the stablecoin reserve assets, the final rule sets a 35 percent discount on the asset-based assessment. Additionally, the final rule describes how the OCC will publish updates to the percentage reduction (up to a 55 percent reduction) annually. Whereas the proposed rule would allow the agency to deem some percentage “other” than 35 percent (up to a 55 percent reduction) as appropriate, the final rule clarifies that 35 percent is the lower limit on potential discounts by allowing the agency to deem some percentage “higher” than 35 percent (up to a 55 percent reduction) as appropriate. As in the proposal, no discount applies to the portion of stablecoin issuer assessments for assets other than stablecoin reserve assets.
As the OCC explained in the proposal, a 35 percent discount for stablecoin reserve assets reflects the OCC's judgment that the cost of supervising non-custodial GENIUS Act-related activities is likely to be meaningfully lower than the cost of supervising more traditional activities conducted by national banks and Federal savings associations. The GENIUS Act limits the stablecoin-related activities in which issuing institutions may engage, and certain of these newly authorized GENIUS Act-related activities may present lower risks to participating institutions and the Federal banking system than certain traditional banking activities. Notably, the GENIUS Act significantly restricts the composition of, and the permissible activities in connection with, required stablecoin reserves. The OCC continues to believe these limitations warrant treating stablecoin reserve assets differently for assessment purposes than existing, on-balance-sheet assets attributable to more traditional banking activities.
However, in the absence of stronger empirical evidence of its supervisory costs, the OCC believes it is premature to conclude that these factors would support providing discounts larger than 35 percent on reserve assets at this time. While the OCC generally agrees with commenters that the cost of supervising certain GENIUS Act-related activities likely will be lower than supervising certain activities of traditional banks and Federal savings associations, the permissible GENIUS Act-related activities of an issuer overall can still present significant operational, organizational and management, and compliance-related complexities and risks (including, for example, liquidity and AML/CFT risk management and monitoring). And, as discussed in further detail below, the OCC anticipates that growth in the scale and scope of permitted payment stablecoin issuers will correspond with increases in their overall complexity and risk profile, in turn increasing the resources the OCC will need to commit to their supervision. Aside from reserve assets, much of this complexity and risk is not directly reflected on the balance sheet of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer.
Taking into account these considerations, while acknowledging limits in the OCC's ability to predict with precision the extent of those complexities, the agency continues to believe that a baseline 35 percent discount is the best approximation of the expected marginal increase in its overall supervisory costs attributable to GENIUS Act-related activities. As described in the proposal, that baseline derives from the median discount currently provided on a per-asset basis to all custodial assets under existing § 8.6(c) relative to the median per-asset assessment charge for non-custodial assets under existing § 8.2(a). In addition, that baseline reflects the OCC's view that certain GENIUS Act-related activities are likely more complex than traditional custodial banking activities, and this complexity will likely impose a greater economic impact on the OCC's overall supervisory burden than supervising traditional custodial banking activities. To account for this reasoning, the final baseline
(

Specifically, subsequent to the effective date of this rule, the OCC will publish the discount as the rule describes. In preparing these publications, the agency anticipates reviewing the costs and complexity of supervising permitted payment stablecoin issuers as a group to determine the appropriate discount on reserve assets within the range finalized. The agency more generally will monitor supervisory cost data as it becomes available to determine whether any additional modifications or revisions to part 8 are needed to account for GENIUS Act-related supervision.

This discussion was tied to the commenter's discussion of a framework for reserve asset holdings above the minimum, and such holdings above the minimum are discussed below. The commenter did not challenge the proposed assessment discount for the minimum stablecoin reserve assets required under the GENIUS Act,

Whatever benefits may exist in the commenter's suggested framework, the commenter did not offer the framework as a comprehensive substitute for all assessment reductions. The above-described assessment reduction in the final rule is appropriate given the anticipated supervisory burden and the need for adaptability over time.
The OCC also received several comments in response to questions on its approach to assessing for reserve asset holdings above the minimum. Most commenters urged the OCC not to penalize holdings above the minimum through unfavorable assessment treatment. One commenter stated that if an issuer chooses to maintain reserve assets above the required minimum, the assessment framework should not create disincentives for that prudent choice. The commenter stated that voluntary excess reserves can serve as an additional buffer and may reflect conservative risk management, and therefore the OCC should be careful not to inadvertently discourage such practices. Another commenter stated that it would be a mistake to penalize the holding of reserve assets above the minimum because additional high-quality liquid assets held above the 1 to 1 requirement would provide extra cushion against redemption stress without adding complexity, so this practice would reduce, rather than increase, the OCC's supervisory risk. The commenter argued that assessing those incremental reserves at the full, undiscounted rate would treat them as if they imposed proportional supervisory burden when in practice the marginal risk is close to flat or negative.
As mentioned above, some commenters raised concerns related to permitted payment stablecoin issuers holding reserve assets above the minimum. The proposed rule acknowledged the possibility that assessment discounts could encourage asset mischaracterization with the goal of lowering total assessments. A few commenters stated that this concern is well-founded and that if the agency extends assessment relief to voluntary excess reserves, relief should only apply to clearly identified and independently verifiable excess reserves. However, these commenters stated that the OCC could institute guardrails to protect against mischaracterization, such as imposing the same segregation, identification, and recordkeeping standards that apply to required reserves. One commenter argued that there is no opportunity for issuers to mischaracterize reserve assets because, given the requirement that issuers must certify and publish reserve asset coverage, once an issuer allocates assets as reserves, those assets are not “mischaracterized” because they will automatically become part of the pool available to support redemptions for the benefit of holders.
Separately, one commenter offered a framework for incentivizing and structuring reserve asset holdings above the minimum without an assessment reduction. In short, this framework would revolve around the percentage of total short-term Treasury securities outstanding as compared to the amount of short-term Treasury securities plus the notional amount of reverse repos in the hands of permitted payment stablecoin issuers. If the concentration percentage crosses predetermined levels, permitted payment stablecoin issuers with reserve assets above their minimums would be permitted to extend their portfolio weighted average maturity or avoid redemption gating (depending on the level the percentage crosses). In response to a related question from the OCC, some commenters also generally supported providing a capped carve-out for a reasonable band of reserve asset holdings in excess of the minimum (
e.g.,
1 to 5 percent above required reserves) so that issuers are not discouraged from conservative risk management or from extending the general discount to all reserve assets.
The final rule extends the assessment reduction to reserve asset holdings above the minimum as well by removing the word “minimum” such that the assessment reduction applies to stablecoin reserve assets held under
12 U.S.C. 5903
. Two factors impact the agency's decision-making in this respect. First, the OCC is persuaded by comments that holdings above the minimum can contribute to a reduction in overall supervisory risk, insofar as holdings above the minimum may reflect an issuer engaging in appropriate and conservative risk management decisions. Holding reserve assets above the minimum, for example, could provide necessary liquidity for certain issuers in the event of market volatility and thereby lower the risk of a loss of value for the payment stablecoin holders. The agency is also persuaded by comments that in fact assessing excess reserves at a higher assessment rate may discourage holding more reserve assets than the minimum requires.
Second, the OCC has concluded that the supervisory process should be able to promptly identify and address any mischaracterization of certain balance sheet assets as excess reserve assets. Examiners will be aided in this respect by the OCC's final rule and information collection, which will require stablecoin issuers to apply the same segregation, identification, and recordkeeping requirements to report assets designated as reserve assets, regardless of whether they are required reserve assets or excess reserve assets. Compared to other approaches for addressing the risk of mischaracterization (
e.g.,
the commenter's framework tracking outstanding short-term Treasury securities), the planned supervisory process is expected to be comparably effective and administratively simpler. Additionally, the OCC anticipates that limiting reserve asset withdrawal as provided in § 15.11(a)(4) further disincentivizes any attempt to misclassify assets as excess reserves
(
printed page 67142)
solely to obtain lower assessment fees. Consequently, the OCC believes the risks associated with an assessment reduction for reserve assets above the minimum are lower than some commenters indicated.
Other commenter suggestions to reduce incentives to mischaracterize assets are not likely more effective and would create undue supervisory burdens on the agency or stablecoin issuers or unnecessarily increase the complexity of the regulatory framework by increasing assessments' interconnectedness with other aspects of GENIUS Act implementation. The agency therefore is finalizing § 8.2(e) without limiting the assessment reduction to minimum stablecoin reserves. The agency is also finalizing the subsection without capping the allowable assessment discount on reserve assets attributable to reserve asset holdings above the minimum. While the OCC understands that current stablecoin reserve holdings above the minimum typically occur within the range of 1 to 5 percent of required reserves, the agency cannot conclude with a high degree of confidence that holdings more than 5 percent above the minimum are or will remain atypical as the market develops. The agency similarly cannot conclude with confidence that the potential benefits of holdings above the minimum cease to continue outside of the range of 1 to 5 percent of required reserves. The OCC therefore concludes that the most prudent course is to extend the assessment reduction for reserve assets to all reserve asset holdings above the minimum and monitor the marketplace and actions by issuers for developments that might support the introduction of a cap at a later date.

c. Additional Requests for Comments Relevant to Subpart A
The OCC requested comment on whether there is a reserve asset threshold above which it would be appropriate to impose either a series of graduated additional discounts or a cap for the purpose of calculating assessments. The OCC had considered, but preliminarily declined, setting a stablecoin reserve asset threshold above which the agency would impose either additional discounts or a cap. The OCC explained that it has occasionally adopted a similar approach (
e.g.,
a cap) when warranted by circumstances. The agency further described that a required stablecoin reserve asset threshold could be appropriate if the OCC were confident that assessment revenues obtained on stablecoin reserve assets above a certain threshold would be disproportionate to the marginal cost of supervising GENIUS Act-related activities attributable to those assets. However, the agency preliminarily concluded that it lacks sufficient certainty of its future supervisory needs to determine with confidence the threshold above which this circumstance would arise.
One stablecoin issuer commented in support of imposing a hard cap on assessment fees for reserve assets at $10 billion. The commenter argued that the OCC's proposed structure of charging basis-point fees on total reserve assets creates a scaling concern such that assessment revenues could become disproportionate to marginal supervisory costs. The commenter argued that the OCC's assessment structure for traditional banks reflects the reality that larger loan portfolios require proportionally more examiner hours to evaluate credit quality, collateral adequacy, and borrower financial condition. However, the commenter argued that logic does not translate to stablecoin reserves because, unlike traditional bank assets where asset growth corresponds to increased lending complexity and supervisory burden, stablecoin reserve assets scale without a corresponding increase in supervisory complexity. The commenter argued that a $50 billion portfolio of segregated Treasury bills is not 50 times more complex to examine than a $1 billion portfolio, and that it would functionally be the same examination repeated against a larger balance. The commenter argued that linear fee scaling above $10 billion would not constitute recovery for supervision, rather it would constitute a tax on scale that penalizes issuers for growth. The commenter stated that without a hard cap, assessment fees would inevitably become grossly disproportionate to marginal supervisory costs at scale, which could make large-scale Federal stablecoin issuance commercially uncompetitive relative to State-chartered or offshore alternatives—directly undermining the GENIUS Act's objective of concentrating stablecoin issuance within the Federal supervisory framework.
However, two commenters—a stablecoin issuer and an industry association—stated that the OCC should not set a hard reserve asset-size threshold above which additional discounts or caps would automatically apply. One commenter argued that setting such a threshold would require confidence that supervisory scale does not continue to scale, directly or indirectly, with an issuer's size or complexity and that such confidence does not yet exist. The commenter argued that international standards increasingly recognize that large issuers require more, not less, attention to redemption, liquidity, cross-border and third-party risk, as well as operational resilience. Both commenters stated that agency should revisit the issue after the agency has observed several supervisory cycles and has greater certainty about the marginal supervisory costs associated with very large reserve asset balances, particularly given the current stage of the stablecoin industry in the United States market.
On the topic of capping or otherwise discounting assessments on assets above a certain threshold, the agency is finalizing the rule as proposed without such an asset threshold. As discussed,
(
printed page 67145)
while the OCC generally agrees with commenters that the cost of supervising certain GENIUS Act-related activities likely will be lower than supervising the activities of traditional banks and Federal savings associations, the permissible activities of an issuer overall can still present significant operational, organizational and management, and compliance-related complexities and risks. In addition, the OCC anticipates, based on its supervisory experience with national banks and Federal savings associations and its expertise in financial markets, that increases in the scale and scope of permitted payment stablecoin issuers will lead to increases in operational, organizational and management, and compliance-related complexity and risk. For example, the OCC would expect the complexity of liquidity risk management, especially monitoring activity and stress testing possible withdrawals, to generally increase with asset size growth. Likewise, as a stablecoin issuer grows, the likelihood increases that it will take steps that tend to increase the operational complexity of its issuances and redemptions, including entering new market segments, connecting with additional platforms or distributed ledgers, and establishing additional third-party relationships. Additionally, increased complexity and risk commonly necessitate more sophisticated AML/CFT risk management and monitoring as transaction volumes and customer base grow, greater demand for sanctions screening as cross-border risk increases, and cybersecurity risk management becomes more challenging as the technology infrastructure evolves and expands. The OCC has experienced similar effects in connection with the growth of OCC-regulated entities engaged in both traditional and nontraditional banking activities.
Thus, even if the issuer's balance sheet composition means that the marginal cost of supervising an issuer's management of reserve assets does not scale fully with the amount of reserve assets under an issuer's management, other GENIUS Act-related activities likely will scale with the size of an issuer's balance sheet. And, in the absence of information or data from which the OCC can with confidence identify a reserve asset threshold above which the marginal cost of supervision meaningfully decreases, it cannot adopt any such threshold at this time without seriously risking under-assessment.
Further weighing against a threshold-based assessment reduction is the regressive nature (
i.e.,
diminishing rate of increase) of the planned assessments. Contrary to the suggestion of some commenters that the OCC's assessment framework inappropriately scales linearly or mechanically, in fact, the amount an entity pays in assessments per dollar of assets declines as total assets increase. The OCC regularly updates a fee schedule that uses asset-size brackets. As asset size increases and an entity passes into higher brackets, the applicable marginal rate declines such that the lowest marginal rates apply to assets in the largest asset-size categories. This structure reflects the OCC's experience that some economies of scale exist in the supervision of larger banks and Federal savings associations. Because the rule integrates stablecoin issuers into this framework, stablecoin issuers will experience the same decreasing marginal rate structure. As a simplified example of how stablecoin issuer assessments are regressive under the final rule, a stablecoin issuer with $1 billion of assets (of which 75 percent are reserve assets that receive a discounted assessment rate) would have an assessment of $38,421 at 2026 rates. An issuer five times larger ($5 billion of total assets with 75 percent as reserve assets) would have an assessment of about four times larger ($151,558), an issuer ten times larger ($10 billion) would have an assessment between seven and eight times larger ($279,446), and an issuer twenty times larger ($20 billion) would have an assessment between thirteen and fourteen times larger. An additional threshold-based reduction would be a reduction on top of this regressive structure, which the agency does not see as appropriate at this time.
Although one commenter argued that the absence of a hard cap would render Federal stablecoin issuers uncompetitive at scale, the OCC does not believe this is a substantial risk that justifies the creation of an assessment cap. The commenter's point touches on a larger potential concern in the assessment context: whether different assessment rates create an opportunity for regulatory arbitrage or a material incentive for stablecoin issuers to pursue State supervision over Federal supervision. A separate comment addressed the risk of regulatory arbitrage directly: it suggested that asset- or issuance-based OCC assessment fees (as opposed to the flat or activities-based fees of certain foreign digital asset regulatory regimes) could be high enough that stablecoin issuers seek State charters or foreign alternatives. Even if assessments are different under different supervisors, stablecoin issuers would have to weigh assessment costs along with other differences between supervisors, such as the extent of supervisors' experience, what guidance and rules supervisors have issued regarding permissible activities, and the compliance standards expected by third parties. In the complete picture, the agency does not expect assessment amounts to be determinative of a stablecoin issuer's competitiveness or a stablecoin issuer's selection of a supervisor.
Furthermore, the agency is not persuaded that OCC assessments without a cap would be higher than State supervisor assessments. In the proposal, the OCC estimated that in total, the assessment schedule under the proposed rule would save permitted payment stablecoin issuers $11.9 million in assessment fee costs in 2026 relative to the baseline scenario without the OCC assessment framework. While OCC-bank-affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuers would pay additional assessment fees as the agency would begin to supervise GENIUS Act-related activities, the agency estimates that non-OCC-bank-affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuers would save money by transitioning from certain State oversight to OCC supervision. The OCC therefore does not see comparisons to State assessment structures as a compelling reason for an assessment cap.
For the various reasons described above, ranging from the limits on the OCC's confidence to the already regressive nature of stablecoin issuer assessments, the OCC is finalizing the rule as proposed without additional assessment reductions or limits above an asset threshold. As the OCC gains experience with the supervision of stablecoin issuers, the OCC may revisit the appropriateness of this conclusion and its underlying reasons.

The OCC proposed to assess these institutions in connection with the agency's supervisory authority under

a. Issues Specific to the Assessment of State Qualified Payment Stablecoin Issuers
Subpart B in general applies the same methodology to State qualified payment stablecoin issuers as it applies to other institutions subject to that subpart, which in turn is generally the same methodology applied to national banks and Federal savings associations under subpart A. As discussed in the proposal, the OCC considered whether it should assess State qualified payment stablecoin issuers differently, including whether the agency should reduce assessments in connection with those GENIUS Act-related activities that would be subject to joint or coordinated review as between the OCC and State payment stablecoin regulators. The agency explained that the appropriateness of assessing one or more classes of institutions subject to subpart B at lower rates would depend on whether the cost of supervising those institutions' GENIUS Act-related activities is in fact shared jointly with another regulator such that the cost to the OCC is meaningfully lower than the cost of supervising national banks and Federal savings associations. Based on the OCC's supervisory experience in similar circumstances involving joint or coordinated supervision, the agency expressed its preliminary view that it is not likely that the costs will be any lower. The OCC nevertheless sought comments or any information that may support adopting alternative assessment methodologies under proposed subpart B for all or a subset of State qualified payment stablecoin issuers, such as applying a discount in the range of 35 to 55 percent of the assessments under subpart B.
The OCC received a range of comments in response to these questions. A State financial regulator and an organization that advocates for State bank regulators both supported assessment credits or some other form of assessment reductions for State qualified payment stablecoin issuers. They argued such a reduction is consistent with effective coordination with State regulators and with giving prospective stablecoin issuers choices. They further indicated that failing to provide a discount would penalize State qualified payment stablecoin issuers that transition to the Federal regulatory framework because such issuers would face higher assessments.
The advocacy organization further suggested that OCC assessments should include a discount for a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer that is eligible for a waiver from OCC supervision such that it would remain solely supervised by a State payment stablecoin regulator. The organization argued this assessment discount should apply regardless of whether the stablecoin issuer seeks a waiver. The commenter supported such a discount because it understands that qualifying for a waiver means that the stablecoin issuer is already subject to a State payment stablecoin regulatory regime that is substantially similar to the Federal regulatory framework.
Other commenters urged the OCC to ground potential discounts in clear and objective criteria that reflect the nature, degree, and effectiveness of the OCC's supervisory coordination with State regulators. One commenter argued that the agency should adopt an assessments framework that would permit and calibrate supervisory fee reductions where, for example, robust home-jurisdiction supervision materially reduces the OCC's supervisory burden or supervisory coordination arrangements demonstrably reduce duplicative supervisory efforts. Another commenter argued that the framework should reflect the OCC's actual supervisory effort and, by avoiding overly burdensome assessments, avoid discouraging operation within State supervisory frameworks.
After considering all relevant comments, the OCC declines to reduce assessments for institutions subject to subpart B whose GENIUS Act-related activities would be subject to joint or coordinated supervision by the OCC and State payment stablecoin regulators. As a threshold matter, the OCC disagrees with the commenters' view that the absence of a discount penalizes State qualified payment stablecoin issuers. The GENIUS Act established the supervisory framework this final rule implements. Absent a waiver, certain State qualified payment stablecoin issuers are subject to OCC supervision.
[

Subpart B describes assessments for certain OCC-supervised payment stablecoin issuers, and no element of those assessments is a penalty. In addition to its obligation to supervise these payment stablecoin issuers, the OCC has a separate obligation to recover the costs of its expenses. The planned assessments as described in the rule appropriately ensure that the agency can fund the activities it must undertake pursuant to the GENIUS Act without imposing undue burdens. The OCC further disagrees with the implication by one commenter that OCC examination of a State payment stablecoin issuer that operates in a certified State regulatory regime would be unnecessarily costly and disruptive.

b. Issues Specific to the Assessments of Foreign Payment Stablecoin Issuers
Subpart B in general applies the same methodology to foreign payment stablecoin issuers as it applies to other institutions subject to that subpart, which in turn is generally the same methodology applied to national banks and Federal savings associations under subpart A. As discussed above, the GENIUS Act prohibits digital asset service providers from offering or selling a payment stablecoin to a person in the United States unless the issuer is a permitted payment stablecoin issuer or the issuer is a foreign payment stablecoin issuer that meets the following statutory requirements: (1) the foreign payment stablecoin issuer is subject to regulation and supervision by a foreign payment stablecoin regulator that has a regulatory and supervisory regime comparable to the GENIUS Act with respect to payment stablecoins, as determined by the Secretary of the Treasury under section 18(b) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5916(b)
); (2) the foreign payment stablecoin issuer is registered with the OCC; (3) the foreign payment stablecoin issuer holds reserves in a United States financial institution sufficient to meet the liquidity demands of United States customers, unless otherwise permitted under a reciprocal arrangement created and implemented by the Secretary of the Treasury under subsection 18(d) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5916(d)
); and (4) the foreign country in which the foreign payment stablecoin issuer is domiciled and regulated is not subject to comprehensive economic sanctions by the United States or in a jurisdiction that the Secretary of the Treasury has determined to be a jurisdiction of primary money laundering concern.
12 U.S.C. 5902
. The OCC will have regulatory authority over foreign payment stablecoin issuers that meet these conditions, and such issuers must register with the OCC. Registered foreign payment stablecoin issuers are subject to ongoing monitoring by the OCC, including reporting, supervision, and examinations, and they will be subject to a full-scope examination at the same frequency as the OCC would examine a permitted payment stablecoin issuer unless the OCC determines to examine at a different frequency.
The OCC considered whether it should assess foreign payment stablecoin issuers differently in the proposed rule but, for reasons similar to those discussed in connection with State qualified payment stablecoin issuers, the OCC preliminarily concluded that it should not. The agency nevertheless sought comments or any information that may support adopting alternative assessment methodologies under proposed subpart B for all or a subset of foreign payment stablecoin issuers, such as applying a discount in the range of 35 to 55 percent of the assessments under subpart B.
The OCC received several comments in response to its request. Several industry commenters, addressing foreign payment stablecoin issuers together with State qualified stablecoin issuers, expressed the views summarized above with respect to the appropriateness of providing discounts to foreign payment stablecoin issuers and the methodology that the OCC should use if it were to adopt such discounts. For example, these commenters indicated that robust home-jurisdiction supervision could materially reduce the OCC's supervisory burden. Some comments raised similar arguments with additional nuances that were specific to foreign payment stablecoin issuers. One stablecoin issuer discussed both State qualified payment stablecoin issuers and foreign payment stablecoin issuers but noted that differences in regulatory pathways and assessments are particularly relevant to foreign payment stablecoin issuers as they reach decisions about market entry and organization. Two other commenters, writing specifically with respect to foreign payment stablecoin issuers, suggested that the OCC could calibrate a sizable discount within a certain range (
e.g.,
the 35 to 55 percent discount described in the proposal, 55 percent or greater) based on the terms of the supervisory coordination agreement or the actual extent of OCC reliance on the foreign regulator. This was consistent with a larger point by a foreign regulator stating that the OCC should structure its regulations in a manner that preserves the flexibility of the Secretary of the Treasury to negotiate reciprocal arrangements with foreign jurisdictions.
Another set of comments highlighted unique elements of OCC supervision over foreign payment stablecoin issuers that commenters viewed as necessitating further calibration or a different approach to assessments. Commenters focused on the OCC's unique role in supervising primarily the United States operations of and the United States-specific requirements governing foreign issuers. They also flagged some uncertainty as to whether the asset-based semiannual assessments under proposed subpart B would apply solely to those assets of a foreign issuer related to their United States operations or to the foreign issuer's non-U.S. assets, observing that in some instances the volume of a foreign issuer's United States holdings and transactions could be only a small fraction of the foreign issuer's overall business.
After considering comments, the OCC concludes that foreign issuers and the agency's supervision of them occupy a unique space within the overall GENIUS Act regulatory framework. It is therefore appropriate to assess foreign issuers under OCC jurisdiction differently than permitted payment stablecoin issuers. Particularly relevant here, as alluded to above, section 18(d) of the GENIUS Act grants the Secretary of the Treasury broad authority to create and implement reciprocal arrangements or other bilateral agreements between the United States and foreign jurisdictions. These reciprocal arrangements or bilateral agreements have the potential to meaningfully impact the extent of foreign issuer participation in the United States market, as well as the nature and scope of OCC supervision over those issuers. The OCC is not able to anticipate the terms of these reciprocal arrangements or bilateral agreements, or how they may impact the OCC's supervision of any foreign payment stablecoin issuer authorized to register with the OCC. Additionally, the OCC has limited experience with institutions like foreign payment stablecoin issuers that are both subject to ongoing reporting, supervision, and examination requirements as determined by the Comptroller (section 18(c)(2)(A) of the GENIUS Act,
12 U.S.C. 5916(c)(2)(A)
) and ongoing regulation and supervision by a foreign payment stablecoin regulator (subsection 18(a)(1)
(
printed page 67148)
of the GENIUS Act,
12 U.S.C. 5916(a)(1)
). To the extent the OCC determines assessment levels based on the extent it relies on foreign regulators, the OCC lacks enough certainty to set the appropriate framework. In turn, this uncertainty about the terms of agreements and actual future reliance complicates the OCC's ability to conclude that the asset-based formulas upon which it would rely to determine semiannual assessments for permitted payment stablecoin activities (whether discounted or not) would accurately or appropriately reflect a level of funding that the OCC would need to supervise registered foreign stablecoin issuers. The OCC therefore concludes that, at least initially, the proposed semiannual assessments under subpart B should not apply to registered foreign stablecoin issuers.
Notwithstanding this conclusion, the OCC intends to assess foreign payment stablecoin issuers at levels sufficient to ensure that the OCC can fund the activities it undertakes with respect to these issuers. Foreign payment stablecoin issuers will remain subject to § 8.12 which, as finalized, authorizes the OCC to charge fees to conduct special examinations or investigations. That authority mirrors the OCC's existing authority under
12 CFR 8.6
, which the agency has similarly used in the past in limited circumstances where it has reason to believe asset-based semiannual assessments might not adequately or appropriately ensure that it can recoup the cost of supervising a small number of institutions engaged in novel or otherwise nontraditional banking activities. While the OCC does not view this assessment methodology as either adequate or appropriate when applied across wide categories of supervised institutions—including as applied to all or even a subset of permitted payment stablecoin issuers—it has enabled the OCC in certain targeted circumstances to satisfy its supervisory mission in the immediate term while providing the agency with sufficient information to better inform longer-term decision-making.
Given the unique uncertainties related to the OCC's supervision of registered foreign payment stablecoin issuers, combined with an expectation that the universe of such issuers will be limited at least initially, the OCC concludes that fee-based assessments under § 8.12 offer the best assessment methodology at this time for these registered foreign issuers. As the United States authorizes more registered foreign payment stablecoin issuers, and the nature and scope of the OCC's supervisory role with respect to these issuers crystallizes, the OCC anticipates that it will be better positioned to evaluate whether foreign issuers should be subject to subpart B's asset-based semiannual assessments and (if so) whether it would be appropriate to discount those assessments to reflect the OCC's shared supervision of these entities with foreign regulators.
Until such time, under § 8.12, the OCC will calculate cost-based assessments for foreign payment stablecoin issuers semiannually by working with the examiners in charge of each foreign issuer to estimate the anticipated supervisory hours for the forthcoming quarters and multiply the estimated hours by the hourly rate that the OCC publishes in its annual Notice of Office of the Comptroller of the Currency Fees and Assessments, which is described in
12 CFR 8.8
. Consistent with prior precedent under existing § 8.6, the assessment will be based on the anticipated direct supervisory hours and a factor to account for indirect hours associated with supervising the foreign issuers. Assessments of foreign payment stablecoin issuers would be due semiannually, on March 31 and September 30.
Finally, the OCC clarifies that it does
not
view the agency as possessing only narrow or otherwise limited supervisory authority over registered foreign issuers. The GENIUS Act states unequivocally that foreign payment stablecoin issuers “shall . . . be subject to reporting, supervision, and examination requirements as determined by the Comptroller.”
[
208
]
While reciprocal arrangements or other bilateral agreements with foreign regulators may impact the precise nature and scope of OCC supervision, creating the uncertainties discussed above that warrant different treatment of foreign issuers for assessment purposes, it remains the case that Congress has equipped the OCC with robust authority to supervise foreign issuers as necessary to ensure their compliance with all applicable laws. For these reasons, as discussed elsewhere, the final rule provides that the OCC will conduct full-scope examinations of a foreign payment stablecoin issuer registered with the OCC at the same frequency as the OCC would examine a permitted payment stablecoin issuer, unless the OCC determines, in its sole discretion, to examine at a different frequency. Nothing herein should be misconstrued to suggest that the agency has a narrow, limited, or “secondary” role in supervising a foreign payment stablecoin issuer registered with the OCC.
c. Section 8.10—Semiannual Assessment for Certain Institutions
Section 8.10, as proposed, established the primary assessment for nonbank Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuers, certain foreign payment stablecoin issuers, and State qualified payment stablecoin issuers subject to
12 U.S.C. 5903(d)
(except to the extent such issuer remains solely supervised by a State payment stablecoin regulator).
[
209
]
Proposed § 8.10(a) in general incorporated the current structure and asset-based formula used to impose assessments on national banks and Federal savings associations under § 8.2(a), and included the same percentage-based assessment reduction for minimum stablecoin reserve assets that the agency proposed under § 8.2(e)(1), discussed above. Consistent with the agency's treatment of national banks and Federal savings associations, proposed § 8.10(a) imposed a semiannual assessment schedule. In addition to ensuring consistency across all categories of supervised institutions, a semiannual assessment schedule may be especially prudent for those institutions subject to proposed § 8.10, given that stablecoin reserve assets—the primary asset for many of the subject institutions—may experience significant fluctuation over the course of a year as issuance and transaction volumes change.
To ensure the annual assessment of an institution subject to proposed § 8.10(a) would be in an amount equal to the annual assessment of a similarly-sized national bank or Federal savings association under § 8.2(a), the OCC proposed to use the same asset tiers (Columns A and B) in Table 1 of
(
printed page 67149)
§ 8.10(a) as used in Table 1 of § 8.2(a),
[
210
]
and to publish in its annual Notices of Fees tier-specific base amounts (Column C) and marginal rates (Column D) that match those published annually in connection with current § 8.2(a).
[
211
]
Proposed § 8.10(a)(6) likewise established the same two-pronged approach to calculating assessments for the on-balance-sheet assets of institutions subject to that section as proposed in § 8.2(e)(1).
Specifically, the OCC proposed to use the existing asset-based formula to first determine the institution's semiannual assessment attributable to its on-balance-sheet assets that do
not
reflect minimum stablecoin reserve assets. As noted, the agency anticipated that institutions subject to proposed § 8.10 will have a limited amount of such assets on balance sheet. The OCC next proposed to apply the same formula to those minimum stablecoin reserve assets,
except
that it would reduce the resulting amount by 35 percent, or by such other percentage (up to 55 percent) that the OCC may deem appropriate for minimum stablecoin reserves held by institutions subject to proposed § 8.10, based on its experience supervising all stablecoin issuers subject to this part. The OCC would publish the percentage reduction deemed appropriate for minimum stablecoin reserve assets on an annual basis in the Notice of Fees. An institution's semiannual assessment would be the sum of the two figures described above.
For the reasons already discussed, the OCC has removed references to foreign payment stablecoin issuers subject to the OCC's jurisdiction. The OCC will calculate assessments for foreign payment stablecoin issuers in the separate manner described above.
Whereas proposed § 8.10 applied an assessment discount only to the minimum stablecoin reserve assets required by the GENIUS Act, the final version of § 8.10 parallels the change in the final version of § 8.2 by removing the minimum amount limitation and applying the assessment discount to all stablecoin reserve assets held by the issuer. Consequently, the assessment discount would apply to reserve asset holdings above the minimum. As described in the above discussion of § 8.2, the agency understands reserve asset holdings above the minimum can contribute to reduced overall supervisory risk when it reflects appropriate and conservative risk management decisions, and the agency sees a benefit in encouraging such decisions. Furthermore, the information the agency has learned and expects to receive from stablecoin issuers mitigates the potential risks associated with reserve asset holdings above the minimum, such as asset mischaracterization.
Separately, the agency is finalizing the assessment reduction on reserve assets as proposed. Like certain activities of institutions subject to subpart A of part 8, certain GENIUS Act-related activities of institutions subject to subpart B (such as reserve management) are likely to present lower risks and supervisory costs than traditional banking activities. However, given the agency's uncertainty about the complexity of other GENIUS Act-related activities, the agency is not finalizing the reduction above the 35 percent in the proposal. As in the proposal, the agency will review the complexity and supervisory costs associated with GENIUS Act-related activities, which may lead the agency to adjust the assessment reduction as high as 55 percent. The final § 8.10(a)(6)(i) replaces the word “other” with “greater” to clarify that 35 percent is the lower bound of the range of assessment discounts.
The above-described finalization of § 8.10 to apply a 35 percent discount to all stablecoin reserve assets aligns § 8.10 with final § 8.2. As mentioned above, the agency is looking to achieve consistency across categories of supervised institutions to the extent other objectives permit, and applying the same discount between § 8.2 and § 8.10 supports such consistency.
Presently, the OCC relies primarily on Call Reports to calculate the total consolidated on-balance-sheet assets of national banks and Federal savings associations for purposes of calculating semiannual assessments under § 8.2(a). Because many institutions subject to proposed § 8.10 do not presently file Call Reports, proposed § 8.10(a)(5) instead provided that the OCC would base semiannual assessments on the total consolidated assets shown on the most recent quarterly report filed by each institution pursuant to proposed § 15.14(i) preceding the payment date. As discussed elsewhere, the OCC proposed to require all institutions subject to proposed § 8.10 to file quarterly reports reflecting the total consolidated assets held on the balance sheet of the institutions. The OCC anticipated that the asset reporting on these quarterly reports will match the asset reporting that would otherwise appear on Call Reports if all institutions subject to proposed § 8.10 were required to file these reports quarterly.
The OCC requested comment on the proposed use of weekly or quarterly reporting under § 15.14 to determine the appropriate semiannual assessment amount due from each supervised institution in connection with its GENIUS Act-related activities, including for those institutions subject to subpart B. In particular, the OCC asked whether the agency should require reserve asset reporting on a rolling daily or weekly basis directly to the agency and whether required reporting should focus on the latest figures, the highest figures, the median, or the mean.
The OCC received several comments related to this request, some of which it separately addresses in connection with the agency's discussion of § 15.14, as finalized, and the remainder of which are addressed here. One commenter argued that the OCC's assessment methodology should be tied to the reporting regime established in proposed § 15.14 and warned against turning assessments into a reporting regime apart from that contemplated under § 15.14. This commenter also suggested that the OCC rely on the existing weekly reporting under § 15.14(h), arguing that requiring rolling or daily reporting directly to the OCC would be burdensome and not provide clear incremental value relative to the weekly and quarterly reporting.
Another commenter opined that the OCC should use the proposed weekly reporting under § 15.14(h) to calculate assessments from a rolling average or other smoothing measure over the assessment period, rather than from only the latest observation. It suggested that while daily reporting should not be mandatory for all issuers, because that would add substantial burden, the OCC should reserve authority to require daily
(
printed page 67150)
data from large, fast-growing, or stressed issuers.
The OCC concludes that quarterly reporting under § 15.14 is adequate and appropriate to calculate assessments. The OCC agrees with commenters that, at least for assessment-related purposes, daily or other reporting directly to the OCC separate and apart from the reporting required under § 15.14 would be unduly burdensome and would not meaningfully impact the OCC's ability to ensure it can fund its activities in connection with the GENIUS Act. The OCC similarly does not believe that rolling averages or other smoothing techniques—either for purposes of calculating the OCC's jurisdictional thresholds or as a basis for assessments—is necessary for the agency to have actionable and appropriate information to calculate assessments that ensure the agency can fund its activities. Reliance on end-of-quarter reporting of reserve assets is consistent with the agency's current approach to calculating existing asset-based assessments for national banks and Federal savings associations, and the OCC does not expect that reliance on quarterly reporting of reserve assets would meaningfully affect assessment amounts.
One commenter requested that the OCC explain further how reporting data will be used to calculate the semiannual assessment base. As noted, unless otherwise indicated, the semiannual assessment of an institution subject to § 8.10(a) will be in an amount equal to the semiannual assessment of a similarly sized national bank or Federal savings association under § 8.2(a). Total balance sheet asset reporting under § 15.14, Schedule B, should provide the OCC with the same or substantially similar balance sheet asset reporting as that provided by similarly situated national banks and Federal savings associations in Call Reports. The OCC will therefore calculate the semiannual assessments under § 8.10(a) using the assets shown on Schedule B of the most recent quarterly report filed by each institution, and relying on the same assessment formula applicable to national banks and Federal savings associations under § 8.2(a), with the reserve asset data provided to the OCC in Schedule B to calculate the reserve asset discount. Section 8.10, as finalized, is revised to better reflect this formula.
Finally, similar to proposed amendments in subpart A, proposed § 8.10(a)(6) included language clarifying that the OCC shall increase the assessment set forth in § 8.10(a) for any institution if the assets reported on that institution's quarterly report for any reason do not reflect the minimum stablecoin reserve assets that a stablecoin issuer must hold under
12 U.S.C. 5903
and these implementing regulations. The proposed increase would reflect the difference between the amount of stablecoin reserve assets reflected on the quarterly report and the minimum required stablecoin reserve assets for the amount of outstanding stablecoin issuances that the institution reports. As discussed above, among other things, this proposed subsection would permit the OCC to address any potential under-assessment resulting from an institution's failure to ensure that it holds sufficient stablecoin reserve assets to meet its obligations under
12 U.S.C. 5903
and these implementing regulations. If a stablecoin issuer's actual reserve amount is less than its required reserve amount, the OCC anticipates that the institution may incur additional fees and charges under proposed § 8.12 associated with (among other things) examinations conducted to understand and address the stablecoin issuer's reserve asset deficiencies.
While the OCC did not receive comment directly on this provision, the final rule makes certain revisions to ensure overall consistency with similar revisions to subpart A (final § 8.7(d)). Specifically, the final rule provides that, if the assets reported by an institution on its most recent quarterly report preceding the payment date for assessments do not reflect the assets that the institution holds under
12 U.S.C. 5903
—or the assets that are otherwise attributable to the institution's custodial and safekeeping activities—the OCC may increase the assessment set forth in subpart B for such institution to fully reflect the appropriate amount of attributable assets. Because the provision would no longer apply solely to reporting inconsistencies in connection with semiannual assessments under § 8.10, the OCC will remove this provision from § 8.10 and add it to proposed § 8.13, “Payment of interest on delinquent assessments and examination and investigation fees.” As discussed in connection with similar revisions in subpart A, by expanding the provision to cover
all
assets attributable to GENIUS Act-related activities subject to assessment—and not simply minimum reserve assets subject to semiannual assessment under § 8.10—the revised provision best ensures that an institution's assessment amount appropriately reflects the GENIUS Act-related activities of permitted payment stablecoin issuers. The OCC does not anticipate this provision would apply to institutions in the ordinary course. Absent reporting errors or non-compliance with the quarterly reporting forms established under § 15.14, the OCC expects to receive all the information that it will need to assess institutions subject to subpart B solely by reference to Schedules B and C of the institution's quarterly reporting. And, except to the extent a reallocation appears to be the result of misreporting on the part of the institution, the OCC does not intend to treat reallocations under this new subsection as delinquent assessments subject to fees unless and until it has informed the institution of the reassessment and the institution has declined to pay the assessment by the date indicated.
Proposed § 8.10(b), modeled after existing § 8.2(d), applied a surcharge to the semiannual assessments for stablecoin issuers that require increased OCC supervisory resources. Similar to the OCC's assessment schedule for national banks and Federal savings associations, the surcharge ensures that fees reflect the increased cost of supervising stablecoin issuers determined to require rehabilitation. As explained above, a condition-based surcharge ensures the OCC has sufficient resources to fund the special supervisory attention that lower-rated entities require without raising general assessments; in the absence of such a charge, healthier entities would in effect subsidize their lower-rated competitors.
[
212
]
The OCC proposed to determine relevant surcharges by multiplying the semiannual assessment computed in accordance with paragraph (a) by 1.5, in the case of any institution that was found to require rehabilitation at its most recent examination; and 2.0 in the case of any institution that was found to have material financial or operational deficiencies that threaten the viability of the institution at its most recent examination prior to December 31 or June 30, as appropriate. This proposed methodology was intended to operate in the same manner, and on the same rationale, as the surcharges tied to UFIRS ratings in § 8.2(d). The OCC generally requested information and comment on its proposed methodology to ensure that assessments for all regulated entities requiring rehabilitation are adequately reflected in the increased cost of supervising those institutions. In § 8.10(b), as finalized, the OCC is changing the language used for purposes of the surcharge to better align with the conditions specified in the surcharges tied to UFIRS ratings in § 8.2(d). Specifically, under the final
(
printed page 67151)
rule, the OCC will determine relevant surcharges by multiplying the semiannual assessment computed in accordance with paragraph (a) by 1.5, in the case of any institution that was found to be in less than satisfactory condition, and by 2.0, in the case of any institution that was found to be in deficient or critically deficient condition, at its most recent examination prior to December 31 or June 30, as appropriate.
Proposed § 8.10(c) clarified that, even if certain State qualified payment stablecoin issuers are not subject to the assessment proposed in that section, these institutions still may be subject to certain other assessments and fees under subpart B. The GENIUS Act requires the OCC to engage in certain supervisory and enforcement activities outside the ordinary course of its operations that are not otherwise accounted for in semiannual assessments contemplated under subpart B, including the OCC's exercise of certain enforcement authorities under
12 U.S.C. 5906(e)(2)(A)
over certain State qualified payment stablecoin issuers with consolidated total outstanding issuances less than $10 billion. Twelve U.S.C. 5903(d)(3)(A) separately requires the OCC to adjudicate waiver requests from certain State qualified payment stablecoin issuers with consolidated total outstanding issuances exceeding $10 billion to remain subject to the sole supervision of their State payment stablecoin regulators. Proposed § 8.10(c) acknowledged these and other similar circumstances by clarifying that, while these issuers may not be subject to the assessments proposed in subpart B, they may still be subject to fees under proposed § 8.12 in connection with the OCC's exercise of these and any other authorities relevant to their operations under the GENIUS Act.
The OCC did not receive comment specifically on § 8.10(c) and finalizes it as proposed.
d. Section 8.11—Fees for Certain Institutions Engaged in the Custodial and Safekeeping Activities Permitted Under the GENIUS Act
Certain institutions subject to assessments under proposed § 8.10 also would have been subject to an additional assessment under proposed § 8.11 in connection with their participation in custodial or safekeeping activities permitted under
12 U.S.C. 5901
et seq.
Specifically, proposed § 8.11 would have applied to those institutions for which 50 percent or more of their income is derived from custodial or safekeeping activities permitted under
12 U.S.C. 5901
et seq.
Proposed § 8.11 is modeled on the existing provisions of § 8.6(c), which addresses additional assessments imposed upon independent trust national banks and independent trust Federal savings associations. Further, as described below, the asset-based assessment formula under proposed § 8.11 would have generally matched the formula under existing § 8.6(c) so that like-sized institutions would be subject to the same assessment amounts for similar activities under § 8.6(c) and proposed § 8.11.
Proposed § 8.11 reflected the OCC's preliminary conclusion that an assessment based solely on an institution's activities covered under § 8.10—
i.e.,
non-custodial assets—would not adequately reflect the supervisory burden on the OCC for supervising institutions for which 50 percent or more of their income is derived from the custodial or safekeeping activities permitted under
12 U.S.C. 5901
et seq.
This preliminary finding is consistent with the agency's longstanding position that chartered institutions should be subject to an assessment under § 8.6(c) in connection with their fiduciary and related assets, in addition to an assessment based on their non-fiduciary activities. As discussed, the OCC adopted existing § 8.6(c) upon finding that—unlike “full-service” institutions that may exercise trust powers but that also engage in sufficient non-custodial activities—the limited balance sheet assets of “independent trusts” result in assessments under § 8.2(a) that do not constitute a fair representation of the complexity of their operations, or the extent of the OCC's supervisory activities related to these institutions.
[
213
]
The OCC preliminarily concluded that a similar risk of under-assessment would likely occur for those institutions subject to proposed § 8.10 that primarily derive their income from custodial and safekeeping activities. The additional assessment proposed under proposed § 8.11 would better ensure that such institutions contribute their fair share of the costs associated with the OCC's supervisory activities.
Consistent with the existing assessment formula under § 8.6(c), assessments for each institution subject to proposed § 8.11 would include a minimum fee associated with the first $1 billion of assets attributable to the custodial and safekeeping activities permitted under the GENIUS Act, and an additional amount associated with assets in excess of $1 billion. To reflect the similar activities of institutions subject to proposed § 8.11 and existing § 8.6(c), the initial fee and the multiplier associated with excess assets would match the amounts used to assess independent trust national banks and independent trust Federal savings associations subject to § 8.6(c).
Additionally, consistent with existing § 8.6(c)(1)(iii), and for the reasons described earlier in connection with proposed § 8.10(b), the OCC proposed to apply a surcharge to the semiannual assessments for permitted payment stablecoin issuers subject to proposed § 8.11(b) determined to require rehabilitation. Specifically, under proposed § 8.11(b), the agency would have adjusted the semiannual assessment computed under § 8.11(a) by applying to it the following multiples: 1.5, in the case of any institution that was found to require rehabilitation at its most recent examination; and 2.0 in the case of any institution that was found to have material financial or operational deficiencies threatening the viability of the institution at its most recent examination prior to December 31 or June 30, as appropriate. As discussed above, this proposed methodology was intended to functionally mirror the distinction made in § 8.6(c)(1)(iii), whether or not assessed using the UFIRS system. The OCC generally requested information and comment on its proposed methodology to ensure that assessments for all regulated entities requiring rehabilitation are adequately reflected in the increased cost of supervising those institutions. As discussed above, in final § 8.11(b), the OCC is changing the language used for purposes of the surcharge to better align with the conditions specified in the surcharges tied to UFIRS ratings in § 8.2(d). Under the final rule, similar to § 8.10(b), the OCC will determine relevant surcharges by multiplying the semiannual assessment computed in accordance with paragraph (a) by 1.5, in the case of any institution that was found to be in less than satisfactory condition, and by 2.0, in the case of any institution that was found to be in deficient or critically deficient condition, at its most recent examination prior to December 31 or June 30, as appropriate.
The OCC received no comments on this provision and is finalizing this section with no other changes from the proposal, except that the final rule includes language clarifying that the agency will rely on the most recent report filed by each institution pursuant to
12 CFR 15.14(i)
preceding the payment date to determine whether an institution is subject to the minimum
(
printed page 67152)
additional assessment under § 8.11(a)(1) and that the OCC will rely on Schedule C: Off Balance Sheet Items, to calculate any additional amount of assessment on custodial and safekeeping assets in excess of $1 billion. The OCC reiterates that, unless otherwise indicated, the assessment of an institution subject to § 8.11 should be in an amount equal to the assessment of a similarly situated national bank or Federal savings association under § 8.6(c).
e. Section 8.12—Fees for Special Examinations and Investigations
Section 8.12 proposed fees for special examinations and investigations the OCC would undertake with respect to certain institutions covered under subpart B. The fees covered by this section would be in addition to any fees and charges assessed in connection with the other sections of subpart B and generally align with the fees and charges currently imposed on national banks and Federal savings associations under existing § 8.6. The OCC intended proposed § 8.12 to apply to any institution subject to the OCC's jurisdiction under
12 U.S.C. 5901
et seq.
For example, as discussed above, the OCC anticipated charging fees in connection with the OCC's resolution of a request for a waiver from a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer with consolidated total outstanding issuances exceeding $10 billion to remain subject to the sole supervision of its State stablecoin regulator pursuant to
12 U.S.C. 5903(d)(3)
. The OCC also anticipated charging fees in connection with any instance in which the OCC must conduct investigations to support its enforcement authority under
12 U.S.C. 5906(e)(2)(A)
.
Other special examinations or investigations under proposed § 8.12 included, but were not limited to, those in connection with (i) supervision- or enforcement-related activities described in
12 U.S.C. 5905
; (ii) activities related to examining affiliates of institutions subject to subpart B; and (iii) activities related to
12 CFR part 5
.
The OCC received no comments on this provision and will finalize it largely as proposed, except that the section as finalized expressly references registered foreign payment stablecoin issuers, consistent with the OCC's decision to rely primarily on § 8.12 to ensure that it can fund the agency's supervisory activities in connection with these registered issuers.
f. Section 8.13—Payment of Interest on Delinquent Assessments and Examination and Investigation Fees
The OCC modeled proposed § 8.13 after and did not differ materially from existing § 8.7. Proposed § 8.13 covered the payment of interest on delinquent assessment and examination and investigation fees by each Federal, Foreign, or State payment stablecoin issuer under OCC jurisdiction for purposes of the GENIUS Act. The OCC preliminarily concluded that provisions covering the payment of interest on delinquent assessment and examination and investigation fees from these institutions should match the existing provisions covering payment of interest on delinquent assessment and examination and investigation fees that currently govern national banks and Federal savings associations, although it sought comment and information on any potential justifications to treat the respective institutions differently.
The OCC received no comments on this provision and is finalizing it as proposed except, as discussed above, the agency will include a new subsection (d) addressing unusual circumstances where the assessable assets attributable to GENIUS Act-related activities do not appear on the institution's most recent quarterly report preceding the payment date. As discussed above, except to the extent a reallocation appears to be the result of misreporting on the part of the institution, the OCC does not intend to treat reallocations under this new subsection as delinquent assessments subject to fees unless and until it has informed the institution of the reassessment and the institution has declined to pay the assessment by the date indicated.
In addition, final § 8.13(a) includes a technical change wherein the word “All” beginning the paragraph in the proposal is changed to “Any” to reflect the singular language used in the remainder of the paragraph. This change is technical in nature and not intended to be substantive.
6. Subpart C—General Provisions
In addition to finalizing subparts A and B of part 8 as described above, the final rule includes subpart C for provisions that are not specific to subpart A or subpart B. At the present time, the only section within this subpart is § 8.14, which the OCC is adding in the final rule as a reservation of authority. Section 8.14 provides that the OCC may waive or modify the requirements of part 8 or adopt different procedures implementing this part, as necessary, to administer and carry out its authorities to collect assessments, fees, and other charges to meet the agency's expenses in carrying out authorized activities. The OCC is adopting this provision in recognition of the nascent nature of the stablecoin industry and the novelty of the GENIUS Act framework. Those circumstances relate to the OCC's ability to adequately and appropriately ensure that the OCC can fund its activities to carry out its statutory obligations under the GENIUS Act. The OCC will only exercise this reservation of authority where consistent with the agency's assessment authorities, the GENIUS Act, and where circumstances justify the use of this reservation. The OCC generally uses reservations sparingly.
