III. Effective Date
The effective date for the final rule is January 18, 2027. The GENIUS Act will be effective on January 18, 2027, and it is important for the implementing regulations to be effective as of the same date. Although the effective date will not be the first day of the next calendar quarter that begins at least 60 days after the final rule is published in the
Federal Register
,
[
215
]
the effective date is in the next calendar quarter that begins at least 60 days after the final rule is published in the
Federal Register
. The final rule cannot be effective until the underlying Act that it is implementing is effective. Congress provided in the GENIUS Act that the Act would take effect the earlier of the date that is 18 months after enactment, which would be January 18, 2027, or the date that is 120 days after the date on which the primary Federal payment stablecoin regulators issue any final regulations. Because this final rule is the first final rule issued by a primary Federal payment stablecoin regulator implementing the Act and 120 days following it would be later than January 18, 2027, January 18, 2027, will be the effective date of the Act.
IV. Expected Effects
The OCC anticipates that the primary effect of the Act and the final rule would be an increase in the aggregate market capitalization of payment stablecoins in response to an increased demand for payment stablecoins due to greater adoption. While the OCC expects that payment stablecoins would still have been issued in the absence of the GENIUS Act, the OCC anticipates that regulatory clarity and regulatory simplification from the final rule will encourage payment stablecoin issuance in the short run beyond the issuance that would have taken place in the absence of the rule.
Consistent with the final rule text, this analysis assumes that permitted payment stablecoin issuers will not pay the holder of a payment stablecoin any form of interest or yield solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of such payment stablecoin. The analysis below focuses on the increased demand for short-term Treasury debt securities that may follow as a result of the reserve requirements in the rule.
Effect on Cost of Short-Term Treasury Debt Financing
The OCC anticipates that the final rule will benefit the U.S. government and taxpayers by increasing the demand for short-term Treasury debt securities. The rule may raise demand for short-term Treasuries because it requires stablecoin issuers to back outstanding stablecoins with highly liquid assets, which include short-term U.S. Treasury bills with a maturity of 93 days or less.
Because research suggests that short-term Treasury securities do not have close substitutes, an increase in demand for these securities would be expected to lower short-term Treasury yields. Azzimonthi and Quadrini (2024) and Ahmed and Aldasoro (2025) similarly estimate that increased demand for short-term Treasuries arising from stablecoin issuance could have a sizeable impact on short-term Treasury yields and other short-term interest rates.
[
216
]
The final rule's effect on short-term Treasury yields may also be moderated by external factors. For example, the U.S. Treasury could respond to lower financing costs by increasing short-term debt issuance or the Federal Reserve could sell short-term Treasury securities from its balance sheet. Either response would increase supply and partially offset downward pressure on yields.
Overall, the final rule has the potential to lower short-term Treasury financing costs. However, this effect would be offset to the extent that stablecoin reserve demand represents a substitution away from other sources of demand for short-term Treasury securities rather than a net increase in demand. Ultimately, the total effect will be driven by the proposal's net effect on the supply and demand for Treasury debt securities.
Finally, these effects should be evaluated relative to the pre-GENIUS Act baseline. Using a post-GENIUS baseline would risk attributing the effects of new stablecoin issuance on Treasury markets to the GENIUS Act rather than the rule.
Effect of Demand for Short-Term Debt on Other Short-Term Debt Markets
The OCC expects that an increase in demand for short-term Treasury securities resulting from the final rule's reserve requirements could benefit borrowers in short-term debt markets by lowering short-term interest rates overall. This could occur if the reserve requirement increases market demand for short-term government debt, which would put downward pressure on overall short-term market debt yields. For example, the increase in demand for short-term Treasury debt from stablecoin reserve assets could benefit corporate debt issuers by lowering yields on short-term corporate debt issues, potentially raising private sector investment in the economy.
The economic reasoning underlying this effect relies on the assumption that debt instruments with different maturities are imperfect substitutes for investors. Under imperfect substitutability, an increase in demand for short-term Treasury securities represents an increase in overall market demand for short-term debt, which lowers the cost of short-term debt financing if other investors bidding for short-term debt do not shift their demand to long-term debt securities in to obtain higher yields.
In particular, a study by Greenwood, Hanson, and Stein (2010) suggest that an increase in the supply of short-term Treasury debt would raise the relative cost of short-term debt financing relative to long-term financing if new short-term Treasury debt issuance exhausts
(
printed page 67154)
additional market demand for short-term debt.
[
217
]
The OCC expects that an offsetting increase in the demand for short-term Treasury debt to fund stablecoin reserves would neutralize the effect of short-term Treasury debt issuance on the market cost of short-term debt financing as described by Greenwood, Hanson, and Stein (2010). This is because an increase in the demand for short-term Treasury debt from stablecoin reserves would consume some fraction of the additional supply of Treasury debt.
Therefore, the OCC expects that, if the rule's reserve requirements increase the demand for short-term Treasury debt, this could increase the overall market demand for short-term debt and lower the cost of short-term debt for other borrowers, such as short-term corporate debt issuers.

Section 15.11(a)(1) requires a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to maintain reserve assets that are identifiable, are segregated from and not commingled with other assets owned or held by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer, at all times have a reserve asset value that equals or exceeds the outstanding issuance value of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer, and are either held directly by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer or within the custody of an eligible financial institution.
Section 15.11(f)(1) requires a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to, each month, have the information disclosed in the previous month-end report required under § 15.11(e) examined by a registered public accounting firm. Section 15.11(f)(2) requires that each month, the Chief Executive Officer and Chief Financial Officer (or the persons performing the equivalent functions) of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer submit to the OCC a certification that the monthly report required under § 15.11(e) is accurate.
Section 15.12(c) requires a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's redemption policy to provide clear and conspicuous procedures for timely redemption of outstanding payment stablecoins. Timely redemption may not exceed two business days following the date of the requested redemption and any discretionary limitations on timely redemptions can only be imposed by the OCC or, in the case of a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer, by the OCC, Board, or the State payment stablecoin regulator, as applicable.
Section 15.13(a)(1) covers internal controls and information systems. A permitted payment stablecoin issuer is required to have internal controls and information systems to support effective risk management that are appropriate for the size and complexity of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer and the nature, scope, and risk of its activities. The internal controls are required to provide for: an organizational structure that establishes clear lines of authority and responsibility for monitoring adherence to established policies, including appropriate segregation of duties and dual controls; effective risk assessment; timely and accurate financial, operational, and regulatory reporting, including with respect to the reports required under
12 CFR part 15
; adequate procedures to monitor, safeguard, manage, control, and monetize assets, including reserve assets; and compliance with applicable laws and regulations.
Section 15.13(a)(2) covers internal audit systems. A permitted payment stablecoin issuer is required to have an internal audit system that is appropriate to the size and complexity of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer and the nature, scope, and risk of its activities. The internal audit system is required to provide for adequate monitoring of the system of internal controls through an internal audit function or if the size, complexity, or scope of operations of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer does not warrant a full-scale internal audit function, a system of independent reviews of key internal controls. Additionally, the internal audit system is required to provide: independence and objectivity; qualified persons responsible for the audit function; and adequate independent testing and review of internal controls and information systems, verification of published information available to customers, calculations for required reserves, and regulatory filings. The internal audit system must also provide for adequate documentation of tests and findings and any corrective actions; verification and review of management actions to address deficiencies; and review by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's audit committee or board of directors of the effectiveness of the internal audit systems.
Section 15.13(a)(5) requires a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to establish and maintain a system that is commensurate with the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's size and complexity and the nature and scope of its operations to evaluate and monitor earnings and ensure that earnings are sufficient to support operations and maintain the capital levels required by subpart E of
12 CFR part 15
.
Section 15.13(a)(6)(i)(D) requires that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer ensure that transactions between the permitted payment stablecoin issuer and insiders or affiliates alone, or in the aggregate, are appropriately documented and reviewed by the board of directors.
Section 15.13(a)(10)(ii)(D) requires a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to have in place policies and procedures that appropriately manage its foreign exchange risk and any attendant risks, including risks related to the posting or collection of margin, foreign exchange counterparties, and basis risk. The policies and procedures must include adherence to §§ 15.13(a)(10)(iii) and (iv).
Section 15.13(b) covers information technology and security programs. Section 15.13(b)(1) requires a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to implement a comprehensive written information security risk and control framework, including a program that assesses and manages information technology and information security risks. Section 15.13(b)(2) requires the board of directors or an appropriate board committee to approve the information technology and security program and oversee the development, implementation, and maintenance of the program, including the appointment of a qualified individual responsible for the program. Such oversight includes assigning specific responsibility for program implementation and review of program-related reports. Section 15.13(b)(3) requires a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's information technology and security program include: an inventory and classification of assets, processes, and sensitivity of data; controls supporting and safeguarding sensitive information and processes; evaluation, validation, and reporting processes to ensure that key information technology systems and controls, including smart contracts, are operating as intended; periodic independent testing; and a comprehensive and effective incident identification and assessment process and incident response program. Section 15.13(b)(4) requires that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's information technology and security program includes administrative, technical, and physical safeguards designed to ensure the security and confidentiality of records containing nonpublic personal
(
printed page 67159)
information about a customer or sensitive customer information. The program must also protect against any anticipated threats or hazards to the security or integrity of such records, protect against unauthorized access to or use of such records that could result in substantial harm or inconvenience to any customer, and to ensure the proper disposal of such records. Section 15.13(b)(6)(i) provides that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer must monitor any relevant changes in technology, the sensitivity of its customer information, internal or external threats, and the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's own changing business arrangements, such as mergers and acquisitions, alliances and joint ventures, third-party arrangements, and changes to applicable information systems. Under § 15.13(b)(6)(ii), a permitted payment stablecoin issuer is required to evaluate and adjust its information technology and security program, as appropriate, based on the monitoring required by § 15.13(b)(6)(i). Finally, § 15.13(b)(8) requires a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's information technology and security program include measures to ensure continuity of operations and recovery of critical functions, including by conducting business impact analyses, testing for vulnerabilities, and testing with critical service providers.
Section 15.13(b)(5) requires a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to develop, implement, and maintain appropriate measures to ensure secure handling of digital assets, including private key management, backup, and recovery incorporating: (i) relevant technical, operational, strategic, market, legal, and compliance considerations relating to each digital asset and its underlying ledger; and (ii) material developments specifically related to supported digital assets and their underlying ledgers.

]
Section 15.14(f) requires all permitted payment stablecoin issuers to maintain a complete set of books and records in English.
Section 15.14(g) requires all permitted payment stablecoin issuers to develop and implement a records retention policy that ensures the permitted payment stablecoin issuer can demonstrate compliance with the GENIUS Act,
12 CFR part 15
, and all applicable laws and regulations.
Section 15.14(l)(1) requires a registered public accounting firm to perform an audit of the financial statements described in § 15.14(l) and sets forth the auditing requirements.
Section 15.15(b) covers the requirements related to a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer that is a nonbank entity transitioning to the OCC's regulatory framework pursuant to section 4 of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903
). Sections 15.15(b)(1)(i) and (ii) require a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer with a total consolidated outstanding issuance value of more than $10 billion to no later than 360 days after reaching such threshold, transition to the Federal regulatory framework under
12 CFR part 15
and comply with the provisions of this part applicable to Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuers or cease issuing, on a net basis, new payment stablecoins until the issuer is under the $10 billion total consolidated outstanding issuance value threshold. Additionally, § 15.15(b)(4)(ii) provides that a State qualified payment stablecoin issuer that does not cease issuing new payment stablecoins in accordance with § 15.15(b)(1)(ii) would be required to transition to the regulatory framework under this part on the earlier of 360 days after reaching the $10 billion outstanding issuance value threshold or the date on which the State qualified payment stablecoin issuer provides written notification under § 15.15(b)(4)(i).
Section 15.21 sets forth covered asset custodial property requirements. Section 15.21(b)(1) provides that a covered custodian is required to take appropriate steps to protect the covered assets of covered customers from the claims of creditors of the covered custodian and any sub-custodian, as applicable, through adopting, implementing, and maintaining written custody agreements and policies, procedures, and internal controls that are adequate to comply with applicable law and that are commensurate with the covered custodian's size, complexity, and risk profile and with the nature of the applicable covered assets for which it provides custodial services or safekeeping services. Section 15.21(b)(2)(i) further provides that a covered custodian may maintain the covered assets of a covered customer through the use of a sub-custodian if consistent with applicable law, provided that the covered custodian maintains adequate safeguards and internal controls reasonably designed to provide the covered custodian with oversight of the sub-custodian's compliance with the requirements of
12 CFR part 15, subpart C
.
Section 15.22 sets forth the use of omnibus accounts. Under § 15.22(c), a sub-custodian may, for convenience, commingle the covered custodian's assets with the covered assets of its covered customers in one or more omnibus accounts of the sub-custodian; provided that the covered custodian maintains adequate safeguards and internal controls reasonably designed to ensure that the sub-custodian segregates all covered assets of the covered custodian's covered customers from, and does not commingle such covered assets with, the assets of the sub-custodian.
Section 15.41(a)(2)(ii) requires a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to have a process for assessing its overall capital adequacy in relation to its business model and risk profile and a comprehensive strategy for sustaining an appropriate level of capital to maintain ongoing operations.
Section 15.41(c)(5) provides that among other criteria, the OCC may permit a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to continue operations while its operational backstop is below the required amount, if the permitted payment stablecoin issuer provides a plan within seven days to regain compliance with the operational backstop requirement within 90 days, and the OCC deems the plan viable.
Disclosure Requirements
Section 15.11(e) sets forth the specific disclosure requirements for composition reports. Section 15.11(e)(1) requires a permitted payment stablecoin issuer by noon on the last day of each month, to publish on the website of the issuer the monthly composition of the issuer's reserves held pursuant to the GENIUS Act as of noon on the last day of the previous month.
Section 15.12(b) requires a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to publicly disclose its redemption policy and include: the timeframe in which the issuer will redeem payment stablecoins and the timeframe under which the issuer is required to redeem payment stablecoins under § 15.12(c)(1)(i); a statement explaining the limitation in § 15.12(c)(1)(ii); a statement explaining the scenarios under which the redemption period may be extended as described in § 15.12(d); a statement with clear instructions on how a payment stablecoin holder can redeem a payment stablecoin, including a link to the
(
printed page 67160)
website(s) where a payment stablecoin holder can redeem the payment stablecoin; and the minimum number of payment stablecoins, if any, that the permitted payment stablecoin issuer will redeem, provided that the issuer must redeem any number greater than or equal to one payment stablecoin, subject to appropriate customer screening and onboarding.
Section 15.12(e) sets forth purchase and redemption disclosures and fee requirements. Section 15.12(e)(1) requires a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to publicly, clearly, and conspicuously disclose in plain language and in a format that is readily noticeable to payment stablecoin holders, and segregated from other information: the name of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer that issues the payment stablecoin; that the permitted payment stablecoin issuer is the entity that is obligated to convert, redeem, or repurchase the payment stablecoin for a fixed amount of monetary value; the website that contains a link to the monthly composition report of the relevant permitted payment stablecoin issuer's reserves required under § 15.11(e); all fees associated with purchasing or redeeming payment stablecoins; that the payment stablecoin is not legal tender, issued by the United States, or guaranteed or approved by the United States; and that payment stablecoins are not deposits, not backed by the full faith and credit of the United States, not subject to deposit insurance by the FDIC, and not subject to share insurance by the National Credit Union Administration. Additionally, § 15.12(e)(2) requires the permitted payment stablecoin issuer to update the disclosures in § 15.12(e)(1)(iv) if there are any changes in fees associated with purchasing or redeeming payment stablecoins and provide payment stablecoin holders at least seven calendar days' prior notice of the change, including by delivering the notice to customers with whom the permitted payment stablecoin issuer has a current relationship. Section 15.12(e)(3) also requires a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to publish the disclosures in § 15.12(e)(1) and any updates made in accordance with § 15.12(e)(2) on the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's website. Section 15.12(e)(4) also requires the permitted payment stablecoin issuer to include the disclosures in § 15.12(e)(1) and any updates made in accordance with § 15.12(e)(2) in any customer agreements.
Section 15.14(l) requires that the described annual financial statement includes the disclosure of any related party transactions, as defined by GAAP.
Section 15.14(l)(2)(i) requires a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to make the audited financial statements under § 15.15(14)(l), publicly available on the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's website.
Section 15.22(b) provides that a covered custodian may, for convenience, commingle the covered assets of multiple covered customers in one or more omnibus accounts to the extent that the steps it has taken pursuant to § 15.21(b) are adequate to maintain safe and sound practices for the use and terms of any omnibus account, and to the extent that the use of omnibus accounts is consistent with applicable law, and is fully disclosed in the applicable custody agreement.
Section 15.32(e) sets forth the conditions of approval for foreign payment stablecoin issuers seeking to be registered with the OCC under section 18(c) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5916(c)
). Sections 15.32(e)(1) and (2) provide that upon request by the OCC, foreign payment stablecoin issuers are required to grant the OCC prompt and complete access to all officers, directors, employees, and agents and to all relevant books, records, or documents of any type, in a form and location accessible to the OCC in the United States. The foreign payment stablecoin issuer is also required to make all information available to the OCC in English.

Regulatory Flexibility Act
In general, the Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA)
[
223
]
requires an agency, in connection with a final rule, to prepare a final regulatory flexibility analysis describing the impact of the rules on small entities (defined by the United States Small Business Administration (SBA) for purposes of the RFA to include commercial banks and savings institutions with total assets of $850 million or less and trust companies with total assets of $47 million or less). Baselines
Prior to passage of the GENIUS Act and drafting of the final rule, there was no comprehensive Federal framework governing payment stablecoin issuance. Rather, payment stablecoin issuance was subject to State stablecoin laws, State crypto-asset regulations, and/or State money transmission laws.
For non-OCC-regulated financial companies that will become permitted payment stablecoin issuers, the OCC used the requirements contained in New York stablecoin laws and the Money Transmission Modernization Act (MTMA) as the baseline based on the assumption that non-OCC-regulated financial companies that issue stablecoins would have complied with New York State laws and regulations given that at least a portion of the issuers' stablecoin activity would occur
(
printed page 67165)
in New York or be covered by state money transmission laws similar to the MTMA standard.
[
233
]
To the extent that an issuer does not need to be in compliance with New York State, but instead to a different state, MTMA would better reflect the baseline.
For OCC-regulated national banks and Federal savings association-affiliated subsidiaries that would be permitted payment stablecoin issuers, in the absence of the final rule, these entities would be subject to existing laws and regulations that do not specifically contemplate stablecoins. The OCC confirmed in interpretive letters that its regulated institutions can issue stablecoins and are allowed to hold deposits that serve as reserves for their stablecoin issuer customers.
[
234
]
While the interpretive letters recognized that OCC-regulated institutions may provide stablecoin services, the interpretive letters did not provide a formal Federal regulatory structure governing OCC-regulated banks' stablecoin issuance. Therefore, the baseline would be treatment under existing applicable Federal law and regulations that did not specifically contemplate stablecoins. Issued stablecoins and stablecoin reserve assets would generally have been treated as standard balance sheet liabilities and assets, and so the OCC estimated costs for OCC-regulated bank-affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuers relative to a baseline where the stablecoins and stablecoin reserve assets would be subject to applicable laws and regulations governing national bank and Federal savings association assets and liabilities.
For the baseline described above, the OCC assumes the most likely regulatory outcome in the absence of the GENIUS Act and its implementing regulations. Specifically, the OCC assumes that OCC-regulated banks would have been allowed to legally issue payment stablecoins and would not have been subject to State stablecoin laws. This baseline assumes some OCC-regulated banks would eventually begin issuing or would increase their issuance of payment stablecoins to compete with nonbank issuers' payment stablecoin activities.
Under this baseline, the OCC concludes that stablecoin issuance by OCC entities would increase, but by an amount that is significantly less than the increase likely to occur after the implementation of the rules required by the GENIUS Act. The OCC expects that OCC-regulated entities would issue relatively fewer payment stablecoins under this baseline because payment stablecoin issuance would be more costly in absence of the final rule's provisions. In addition, the OCC believes that stablecoin issuance would be more limited under the baseline as there would be costs due to a lack of uniform Federal rules. Nevertheless, the OCC believes that the most likely scenario is that OCC entities would still have issued some amount of payment stablecoins under the baseline to meet consumer demand, and this would occur despite the greater costs of issuance than would have occurred without the GENIUS Act and its implementing regulations under the baseline.
Any market practices that an issuer would likely have voluntarily abided by in the absence of the final rule and the GENIUS Act or any other stablecoin regulations would also be included in the baseline. For example, when the OCC refers to these components of the baseline, the OCC means the types of standards with which current unregulated stablecoin issuers would already voluntarily abide by as a result of market conventions market competitive pressures. For instance, the OCC expects that, in the absence of stablecoin-specific regulations, stablecoin issuers would voluntarily disclose details of their redemption policies and comply with any mandates, requirements, or practices that would increase demand for their stablecoins.
This baseline is also relevant for OCC-bank-affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuers operating in States where laws already have mandates similar to the mandates set forth in the rule, and where current bank regulations would not independently enforce similar requirements under the rules. In certain cases, the OCC could use mandates similar to the non-OCC bank-affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuer baseline for the OCC-bank-affiliated baseline based on the argument that OCC bank-affiliated-permitted payment stablecoin issuers would likely have voluntarily complied with various mandates similar to those under the nonbank baseline to compete with the broader permitted payment stablecoin issuer market outside the regulated bank industry.
With regard to capital requirements, the OCC assumes stablecoins issued by OCC entities would have been treated as standard balance sheet assets under the baseline, and hence, all stablecoin reserve assets would have been subject to the minimum tier 1 leverage ratio. The OCC assumes that all stablecoin reserve assets would have counted toward the leverage requirement for all OCC-regulated bank permitted payment stablecoin issuers or permitted payment stablecoin issuers that are subsidiaries of OCC-regulated banks (collectively, OCC-regulated bank-affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuers).
For non-OCC-regulated bank-affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuers, the OCC assumes that such institutions would have complied with the lowest capital requirements across all States in order for stablecoins to transact seamlessly across state lines. The Money Transmission Modernization Act (MTMA) is a set of nationwide standards developed by the Conference of State Bank Supervisors to unify and streamline the licensing and regulation of money service businesses and fintech companies across the United States. The OCC uses New York State stablecoin laws and the MTMA as the baselines. Hence, for non-OCC-regulated bank-affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuers, the OCC uses the MTMA's tangible net worth requirement to estimate tier 1 leverage under the baseline.
Overall, to the extent that any requirements under applicable baselines are substantially the same as the requirements in the final rule, the OCC's analysis considered the effect of these requirements to generally be de minimis. To the extent that there were differences between the mandates in the final rule and the assumed baselines, the OCC's analysis measures costs and benefits by comparing the costs and benefits of the mandates in the final rule and the mandates in the applicable baselines.

Economic Analysis of Requirements and Expected Costs and Cost Savings
For calculations that require an estimate of the total value of expected payment stablecoin issuance, the OCC used forecasts of aggregate stablecoin issuances from private sector forecasts reported in the media. The forecast data indicate upper bounds for payment stablecoin issuance of $378.8 billion in 2027 and $765 billion in 2028.
[
236

The private sector forecast is reduced by Tether's public announcement that its USDT coin will not be for domestic use, and instead the firm will launch its USAT coin, which is intended to comply with the GENIUS Act.
[
237

For purposes of calculating the costs of mandates in the rule, the OCC only accounts for issuers that would have existed in the absence of the rule, under the pre-existing regulatory baseline. The OCC assumes that initially in 2027, the market size of outstanding stablecoins in the absence of the Act would be $272.3 billion. Of this $272.3 billion in issuance, the OCC attributes $222.3 billion to non-OCC-bank-affiliated issuers and $50 billion to OCC-regulated issuers.
The OCC reviewed costs and benefits associated with the final rule according to the following categories: a) reserve requirements; b) redemption requirements; c) capital requirements; d) custody requirements; and e) miscellaneous administrative and compliance requirements. The OCC aggregated the cost estimates to generate a total against the baseline.
Reserve Requirements
The final rule implements section 4(a) of the GENIUS Act and includes requirements governing the management, composition, and reporting of reserves that back payment stablecoin issuance. Under the final rule, a permitted payment stablecoin issuer must maintain and demonstrate the operational capacity to monetize reserve assets, commensurate with the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's risk profile and business model. Because liquidity measurement and management are already integral components of a bank's ongoing operations, the OCC expects many permitted payment stablecoin issuers to already have the internal practices in place to meet this requirement or to be able to demonstrate monetization through the usual course of business. For example, institutions that monetize United States Treasury securities on a regular basis through the ordinary course of business may be able to rely on evidence of sales to meet the monetization requirement. Permitted payment stablecoin issuers may also be able to demonstrate liquidity by establishing that they maintain appropriate repo arrangements through which they can quickly pledge and receive liquid funds. Additionally, large institutions under OCC supervision are already subject to extensive monetization testing and analysis to demonstrate liquidity. In these cases, the OCC does not expect additional compliance costs due to the monetization requirement. To the extent that demonstrating liquidity does not already reflect an institution's current business practices, the requirement to demonstrate monetization could increase operational expenses; however, based on the institutions expected to become permitted payment stablecoin issuers, the OCC expects affected institutions (
i.e.,
both non-OCC-regulated bank-affiliated institutions and OCC-regulated bank-affiliated institutions) would already have internal liquidity practices in place and be able to meet the requirement without additional burden.
The final rule states that for some permitted payment stablecoin issuers—depending on the issuer's size, business model, and operations—it may be necessary to periodically conduct monetization transactions to demonstrate liquidity, which could introduce new costs for some permitted payment stablecoin issuers. For example, institutions that do not monetize certain assets already on a frequent basis may need to conduct specific transactions that go beyond ordinary business activities. In another context, trade associations have pointed out that this could potentially lead to institutions having to recognize a loss for a sale solely for demonstration purposes.
[
238
]
However, based on the experience of OCC banks that currently engage in monetization testing, the OCC expects these instances to be rare.
The final rule also includes requirements on the composition and reporting of reserves. Identifiable reserves must comprise specified highly liquid instrument types, such as cash, demand deposits, and short-term United States Treasury bills, notes, and bonds. Relative to the pre-existing regulatory baseline, the OCC estimates that non-OCC-regulated-bank affiliated issuers would have already managed reserves in a manner consistent with the final rule. New York's Department of Financial Services (NYDFS) imposes restrictions on how reserves can be held by stablecoin issuers and are similar to those in the final rule.
[
239
]
Therefore, the OCC estimates that non-OCC-regulated-bank-affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuers would incur no new costs to acquire and report reserve assets in the instrument types required by the GENIUS Act and the final rule as these institutions would already satisfy these requirements under the baseline.
[
240
]
(
printed page 67167)
For OCC-regulated bank-affiliated issuers, there could be opportunity costs associated with holding reserves in the specified high-quality liquid assets compared to potentially higher-yielding alternatives, given that any prior payment stablecoin issuance may not have been subject to NYDFS regulations. While the OCC does not attempt to quantify this cost, which would fluctuate with current market rates at any given point in time, the OCC anticipates that many permitted payment stablecoin issuers would likely have managed reserves in a manner consistent with the reserve requirements either to conform with market practices and remain competitive with non-OCC-regulated bank-affiliated issuers or to comply with requirements that would be applicable to payment stablecoins if held on banks' balance sheets.
Finally, the final rule mandates publication of a monthly reserve composition report, examination of this report by a registered public accounting firm, and monthly submission of certification of the CEO and CFO (or the persons performing the equivalent functions) to the OCC. These efforts will require various reporting, training, and auditing expenses. The OCC estimates the average burden of the monthly composition report to be two hours per response, or $3,816 (24 hours *$159) per issuer on an annual basis and applies to all permitted payment stablecoin issuers.
[
241
]
Due to an overlap with existing State laws, the OCC does not expect that the examination of these reports by a registered public accounting firm will impose additional burden on non-OCC-regulated institutions relative to the baseline; NYDFS requires reserves to be subject to examination at least once per month by an independent Certified Public Accountant. In contrast, the OCC anticipates that OCC-regulated bank-affiliated institutions would face higher auditing costs from a monthly auditing requirement. OCC-regulated institutions are generally audited quarterly. Moving to monthly audits performed by an independent Certified Public Accountant would result in a threefold increase in auditing frequency. The OCC estimates the incremental cost in moving from quarterly to monthly certification of these reports by a public accounting firm to range from $56,000 to $166,667 per issuer on an annual basis, depending on the size and complexity of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer.
[

]
Overall, the OCC attributes aggregate reporting costs of $83,952 ($3,816 * 22 issuers) and auditing costs of $560,000 to $1,666,667 ($56,000-$166,667 on average*10 issuers) to the statute in 2027, relative to the existing regulatory baseline.
[

The total estimated costs associated with the reserve requirements are therefore $1,197,285 ($1,197,285=$83,952 + $1,113,333).
Redemption Requirements
The final rule would impose several mandates governing payment stablecoin redemption. These include requirements for the issuer to develop and disclose its redemption policy. The OCC expects that non-OCC-regulated-bank-affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuers would have already complied with such mandates under the baseline. Additionally, for OCC-regulated bank-affiliated banks, the OCC expects that such banks would have voluntarily abided by these conditions and therefore generally incur no new costs relative to the baseline.
With respect to the disclosure, including the fee change, mandates required by the final rule, the OCC does not expect that the final rule will cause non-OCC-regulated bank-affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuers to incur significant new costs because current stablecoin regulations and money-transmission laws that govern New York State stablecoin issuance already impose similar mandates. For OCC-regulated bank-affiliated issuers, the OCC expects that such institutions would voluntarily provide such information to compete for customers. Additionally, because OCC-regulated banks already comply with several reporting and disclosure requirements in other business lines, the OCC does not expect that there would be significant fixed costs in complying with the redemption disclosure requirements. Therefore, OCC-regulated banks that would be permitted payment stablecoin issuers would also not incur significant new costs related to these disclosure requirements.
The final rule defines “timely” to mean that the permitted payment stablecoin issuer would generally have to redeem a payment stablecoin no later than two business days from the date of the requested redemption. Redemption is deemed to occur when the permitted payment stablecoin issuer has fully processed and initiated the outgoing transfer of monetary value to the customer or customer's financial institution, or, if requested by the customer, credited monetary value to the customer's account with the permitted payment stablecoin issuer. This is substantially the same as New York State's guideline of two business days and comparable to existing stablecoin procedures. Therefore, non-OCC-regulated-bank-affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuers would incur no new costs relative to the baseline. Additionally, the OCC expects that OCC-regulated bank-affiliated banks would have abided by the two-business-day timeframe in the absence of this timeliness requirement due to market conventions and competitive pressures. Since current technology allows for nearly instantaneous transfers of account funds within financial institutions, the OCC believes that the costs associated with complying with the two-business-day requirement would be de minimis.
A permitted payment stablecoin issuer must provide notice to the OCC through its supervisory office within 24 hours if it receives redemption requests in excess of 10 percent of its outstanding issuance value in a single 24-hour period. A permitted payment stablecoin issuer that experiences redemption requests in excess of 10 percent of its outstanding issuance value in a single 24-hour period may request an extension to the timeframe for timely redemption. The OCC may, in its discretion, grant or deny an extension request under § 15.12(d)(2) or impose discretionary limitations upon timely redemption in accordance with section 4(a)(1)(B)(i) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(1)(B)(i)
). Since all issuers would only benefit from the extended redemption period, the OCC does not believe there would be costs
(
printed page 67168)
associated with this provision for permitted payment stablecoin issuers.
Furthermore, this provision would be beneficial to broader society as the extension strengthens the stablecoin system by establishing a clear, rule-based response to stress and reducing incentives for panic-driven runs. This provision would benefit issuers and society by preventing panic-driven runs on permitted payment stablecoin issuers' stablecoins. The seven-day extension is modest and less disruptive than emergency redemption suspensions. Absent this provision, issuers must rely on broad contractual discretion, which increases legal uncertainty and litigation risk. By codifying a redemption extension tied to objective conditions, the rule sets expectations in advance and reduces the risk of arbitrary or uneven treatment. Clear regulatory authority reduces litigation risk and the need for ad hoc supervisory intervention. In addition, the 24-hour OCC notification requirement ensures timely supervisory awareness and enables prompt regulatory engagement during emerging stress events. Because the communication of stress events to the OCC would occur through direct contact with issuers' existing supervisory contacts, the OCC expects the cost of implementing this mandate to be de minimis.
Capital Requirements
In order to estimate the monetary cost of the capital requirements in the final rule, the OCC assumed an average cost for each payment stablecoin issuer and made assumptions regarding the inputs to the cost calculations. To calculate the cost of equity capital requirements, the OCC assumed that under the final rule, all payment stablecoin issuers will initially be required to maintain the minimum amount of capital which includes the $5 million requirement for de novo banks and the ongoing 12-month-operating-expense backstop. The OCC assumes that the amount of capital a permitted payment stablecoin issuer must maintain, commensurate with the level and nature of all risks, including those arising from off-balance-sheet activities, would be unchanged relative to the baseline under the GENIUS Act. The OCC also assumes that, for any portion of the capital requirement left to a permitted payment stablecoin issuer's discretion, a permitted payment stablecoin issuer would not hold more capital than it would elect to hold absent the rule. In estimating the benefits and costs of the GENIUS Act's capital requirement, the OCC assesses only the effect on the cost of capital for issuance under the baseline rules and does not include any incremental capital costs arising from new issuance induced by the GENIUS Act. The OCC assumes that these incremental capital costs are offset by the consumer and producer surplus generated by that new issuance.
For the cost-of-equity-capital calculation the OCC assumed:
Under the baseline of no GENIUS Act, there would have been 10 OCC-regulated bank-affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuers and 12 non-OCC-regulated bank-affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuers.
The OCC assumes that initially in 2027, the market size entering OCC supervision, measured by the value of outstanding stablecoins, will be $272.3 billion. Of this $272.3 billion in issuance, $222.3 billion of this forecast is attributed to non-OCC-regulated bank-affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuers and $50 billion to OCC-regulated bank-affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuers.
The cost of equity capital is the ongoing yearly required return on equity capital that the OCC expects issuers to pay to obtain equity to satisfy capital requirements. The current estimate of the cost of capital in the banking industry is 7.34 percent. Permitted payment stablecoin issuers incur the cost of equity capital upfront by receiving a discounted payment from investors for equity shares in the permitted payment stablecoin issuers. The rule allows 50 percent of the backstop to be held in subordinate debt which the OCC estimates to be 4.73 percent.
The initial operational backstop amount would be based on reasonable expense projections and adjusted each quarter based on actual amounts for that quarter. The OCC recognizes that operational backstop will not be linear and will vary based on the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's business model and amount of issuance. The OCC has no precise ability to forecast the ongoing operational expense each issuer will incur and therefore the OCC assumes a flat rate for all issuers for the purpose of this analysis. The OCC assumes that the 12-month operating expense amount for each issuer is 0.48 percent of outstanding stablecoins which the OCC believes is a conservative estimate of ongoing operating expense based on money market fund performance and Circle's financial statements.
[
244
]
The OCC calculated the ultimate impact of capital mandates separately for OCC-regulated bank-affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuers and for non-OCC-regulated bank-affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuers due to differences in baselines. The OCC calculated the effect of capital mandates for OCC-regulated bank-affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuers under the bank and bank-affiliated baseline and the OCC calculated the effect of the mandates relative to the MTMA for non-OCC-regulated bank affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuers.
The OCC calculated the total minimum required capital under the final rule for all expected permitted payment stablecoin issuers. The first calculation is for the final rule's fixed capital requirement of $5 million for de novo issuers. The final rule allows for the backstop to be partially funded with up to 50 percent in subordinated debt. Assuming issuers fund 50 percent of their backstop with subordinated debt, the cost of capital will be 6.04 percent (6.04 percent = 7.34 percent * .5 + 4.73 percent * .5). The overall cost of capital could be slightly lower to the extent that permitted payment stablecoin issuers are able to obtain lower cost subordinated debt financing to partially meet capital requirements.
Permitted payment stablecoin issuers would also accrue benefits from tax-deductible interest on any subordinated debt used to fund the capital backstop. However, under the OCC's economic analyses for rulemakings, these tax benefits only count toward any impact estimates as transfers, and not as explicit regulatory cost savings for the purposes of
Executive Order 14192
. The second part of the cost of capital estimate includes the final rule's operational backstop which is a requirement equal to 12 months of operating costs. The OCC estimated the 12-month-operating-expenses to be 0.48% times the expected $272.3 billion in outstanding stablecoin issuance which amounts to $1.3 billion ($272.3 billion * .48%). The cost of this $1.3
(
printed page 67169)
billion of required capital is the amount of capital times the cost of equity capital, which the OCC measures as 6.04% which totals $78.9 million.
[
245
]
Because there is no comparable backstop estimate in the regulatory baseline, the OCC includes the full $78.9 million toward the cost of capital calculation. The total cost of minimum capital requirements under the final rule is $87 million which is the sum of the $8.1 million cost of the de novo permitted payment stablecoin issuer requirement plus the $78.9 million cost of the operational backstop requirement.
For non-OCC-regulated bank-affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuers, to calculate total capital requirements, the OCC subtracted the corresponding expected capital requirement for these permitted payment stablecoin issuers under the MTMA. Under the MTMA, the tangible net worth requirement is 3.0 percent for the first $100 million in assets, 2 percent on assets from $100 million to $1 billion, and 0.5 percent of assets over $1 billion. For the calculation, the OCC assumes that the $222.3 billion of issuance is equal among the 12 nonbank issuers. Therefore, for the 12 non-OCC-regulated bank affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuers, the OCC calculates a minimum capital requirement of $1.3 billion (.03 * 100M * 12 + .02 * $900M * 12 + .005 * ($222.3B-$12B)).
For OCC-regulated bank-affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuers, the OCC assumed that payment stablecoins issued by OCC-regulated banks would have been treated as standard balance-sheet assets and hence, all stablecoin reserve assets would have been subject to the tier 1 leverage ratio, which is set at 4 percent. The OCC projected that OCC-regulated bank-affiliated issuers would be responsible for $50 billion in stablecoin issuance in 2027 and would therefore have needed to hold $2 billion in tier 1 capital ($2 billion = .04 × $50 billion).
Taken together, under the two assumed baselines for the 22 expected permitted payment stablecoin issuers, the OCC calculated that these permitted payment stablecoin issuers would have been required to hold $3.3 billion ($3.3 billion = $2 billion + $1.3 billion) under the assumed baselines. The OCC calculated the cost of equity capital under the baseline to be approximately $242.5 million ($242.5 million = $3.3 billion × 7.34 percent). Therefore, after accounting for the regulatory baseline, the OCC estimated the capital requirements under the final rule to result in a net savings of $155.5 million ($155.5 million = 87 million − $242.5 million) relative to the regulatory baselines.
The last component of the minimum capital requirement is a self-imposed amount of capital to be determined by each permitted payment stablecoin issuer. The OCC estimated the cost of this additional requirement to be zero.
Custody Requirements
The final rule imposes mandates governing certain custodial activities of OCC-supervised institutions (including OCC-supervised permitted payment stablecoin issuers).
[
246
]
For the final rule, the OCC expects that covered custodians for covered assets would likely already be specialized custodial institutions for several asset classes or already provide custodial services for crypto-assets, including stablecoins. The OCC concluded that since New York State has already imposed substantially similar compliance mandates on covered custodians for providing custodial services for covered assets, the final rule will not result in new costs for covered custodial activities for non-OCC supervised entities.
With respect to OCC-supervised bank-affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuers, OCC-regulated banks were previously allowed to provide custody services for crypto-assets, as confirmed in Interpretive Letters 1170, 1183, and 1184. The OCC does not expect that OCC banks would incur new costs as a result of the custody services mandates in the final rule because OCC banks providing custody services for crypto-assets generally followed industry best practices and guidance governing non-fiduciary custody activities. Therefore, the OCC concluded that OCC-regulated bank-affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuers would not incur new compliance costs under the final rule.
Miscellaneous Administrative and Compliance Requirements
The final rule includes other administrative and compliance mandates which include risk management mandates in § 15.13 and compliance mandates in § 15.14. The OCC estimated the cost of all mandates in these sections.
[
247
]
The OCC assessed that for non-OCC-regulated bank-affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuers that miscellaneous administrative and compliance mandates in the final rule effectively overlap with New York State requirements except for the higher frequency confidential weekly reporting requirement and the regular 12- or 18- to 24-month examination requirement in the final rule.
The OCC assessed that for OCC-regulated bank-affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuers, miscellaneous administrative and compliance mandates from the final rule overlap with the requirements under the assumed regulatory baseline and that there would be no material new costs to these issuers under the final rule.
The OCC estimated the weekly reporting requirement will require two hours per week with a cost of $159 per hour. The total weekly reporting cost for 12 non-OCC-regulated bank permitted payment stablecoin issuers annually is therefore $198,432 ($198,432 = 52 * 159 * 12 * 2).
To comply with ongoing OCC exam requirements, the OCC estimated that each of the 12 non-OCC-regulated bank-affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuers will employ 1000 employee hours annually on supervisory exams for a total of $159,000 ($159,000 = 159 * 1,000). Therefore, the OCC expected that these 12 permitted payment
(
printed page 67170)
stablecoin issuers' total expenditures on examinations to total $1,908,000 ($1,908,000 = 159,000 * 12).
In summary, the OCC estimated the ongoing miscellaneous administrative and compliance mandate costs to total $2,106,432 per year ($2,106,432 = $1,908,000 + 198,432).
Assessments
The OCC estimated that in total, the assessment schedule under the final rule will save permitted payment stablecoin issuers a total of $13.6 million in assessment fee costs in 2027. The OCC estimated that the 25 OCC-bank-affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuers would save $1.9 million in assessment fees relative to their baseline. The 12 non-OCC bank affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuers would pay approximately $8.4 million in assessments in 2027 but save approximately $12.5 million relative to the New York State baseline. The increase in savings is primarily attributed to a 35 percent discount on the OCC's general assessment.
The OCC estimated that the assessment mandates in the final rule will cost permitted payment stablecoin issuers and increase the OCC's assessment revenue by $7.2 million in 2027 if the final rule were implemented at the start of 2027. The OCC's projections are based on the January 2026 assessment fee structure for existing OCC-supervised banks applied to the stablecoin market and includes a 35 percent discount for stablecoin issuers. The final rule suggests discounts can be increased to as high as 55 percent if approved by the OCC, based on agency needs.
[
248
]
The projections do not consider future changes in assessment fee structure or changes to fee schedules. The estimates also assume permitted payment stablecoin issuers will not be subject to the cost-plus method that is typically applied to new firms entering OCC supervision. The estimates make the following assumptions:
All payment stablecoins will be issued by OCC-regulated permitted payment stablecoin issuers.
[
249
]
All payment stablecoins equal minimum reserve assets, even though operationally firms can hold assets in excess of outstanding stablecoins to manage market risks.
The market will be occupied by 12 non-OCC-regulated bank-affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuers and 25 OCC-regulated bank-affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuers and two consortia permitted payment stablecoin issuers by 2027.
While assessment revenue will increase for the OCC, the assessment fees under the final rule for existing issuers that would have otherwise been paid to NYDFS by non-OCC-regulated bank permitted payment stablecoin issuers under the baseline would be considered a cost savings to these permitted payment stablecoin issuers. NYDFS budgets $16.3 million in assessment revenue for State fiscal year (SFY) 2026-2027, which ends March 31, 2027. For SFY 2027-2028, the OCC projects NYDFS would collect $20.9 million in fees if the GENIUS Act were not effective.
[
250
]
It is anticipated that large stablecoin issuers under NYDFS oversight, who pay the bulk of NYDFS assessments, will migrate to OCC. Given the discounts in the final rule, and difference in the fee structure, a migration to OCC from NYDFS oversight will be a cost savings to permitted payment stablecoin issuers as NYDFS's assessment fee incorporates transaction volumes and broader custodial volume supervision. The OCC does not currently anticipate transaction volumes to factor into OCC assessment calculations, and the OCC will not supervise custodians outside the Federal banking system other than OCC-regulated permitted payment stablecoin issuers.
For OCC-regulated bank-affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuers, the impact on assessments may be a cost savings relative to the baseline as stablecoin reserve assets would move from bank balance sheets to the balance sheets of the subsidiary permitted payment stablecoin issuer. The cost savings are due to a 35 percent discount on assessments from the standard assessment fee schedule in the final rule. However, the enactment of the final rule would expand the market beyond the baseline, resulting in a net increase in assessment revenue. Under the final rule, the OCC estimated that permitted payment stablecoin issuers affiliated with OCC-regulated-banks would save $1.0 million in 2027 relative to their regulatory baseline. Consortia PPSIs would also see assets shift from the main bank to a joint venture which would benefit from an assessment discount, resulting in savings of $0.1 million in 2027.
Total Impact of Costs and Cost Savings
The OCC estimated that as a result of the final rule, permitted payment stablecoin issuers would save $165.8 million on a net basis in 2027 relative to the baselines assumed, due largely to relief in capital costs and assessments. While the OCC estimated additional costs of $3,303,717 ($3,303,717 = $1,197,285 + $2,106,432) discussed above, from reserve, reporting, and administrative compliance associated with the final rule, the OCC estimated $169.1 million in cost savings ($169.1 million = $13.6 million + $155.5 million). The OCC also expected that ongoing annual savings relative to the regulatory baselines would increase over time as both stablecoin issuance and the number of permitted payment stablecoin issuers increase in the coming years.
Analysis of Regulatory Alternatives
Executive Order 12866
requires the analysis of alternatives to the final regulations. The order says that the OCC should provide: “An assessment, including the underlying analysis, of costs and benefits of potentially effective and reasonably feasible alternatives to the planned regulation, identified by the agencies or the public (including improving the current regulation and reasonably viable nonregulatory actions), and an explanation why the planned regulatory action is preferable to the identified potential alternatives.”
An assessment of two alternatives follows:
Scenario 1
Under the first scenario, the OCC considered replacing the fixed capital requirement of $5 million for de novo issuers with a requirement that issuers instead hold 2 percent of the par value of stablecoins issued. Under the final rule, the OCC estimates that the fixed capital requirement of $5 million would require issuers to hold $110 million in equity capital in 2027 in aggregate. An alternative requirement to hold 2 percent of issuance, would require issuers to hold $5.5 billion in aggregate equity capital (0.02 * $273 billion issuance in 2027), in which case
(
printed page 67171)
permitted payment stablecoin issuers' total minimum required equity capital would increase by about $5.4 billion. Given the cost of equity capital of 7.34 percent, the total cost of equity capital issuances would be $395.6 million higher under this scenario.
However, the OCC notes that while additional capital that scales with issuance may benefit permitted payment stablecoin issuers and society by potentially reducing failure risk of permitted payment stablecoin issuers, this level of capital would be unnecessary relative to the more appropriate level included in the final rule. Because the other requirements in the final rule related to payment stablecoins (
e.g.,
reserve asset and diversification requirements, risk management standards) are designed to manage risk, a fixed minimum de novo requirement is more appropriate than the 2 percent requirement discussed in this scenario.
Scenario 2
Under the second scenario, the OCC considered reducing the requirement to hold funds against operating expenses. The current final rule requires permitted payment stablecoin issuers to hold an operational backstop which is equal to 12 months of operating costs. In this scenario, the OCC decreased this requirement to 6 months of operating expenses.
To estimate the effect of reducing the operational backstop requirement to cover only 6 months of operating expenses, the OCC assumed that the backstop requirement would be 50 percent of the requirement we include in the main analysis.
In the main analysis, the OCC estimated that permitted payment stablecoin issuers would be required to hold $1.3 billion as a backstop and therefore, in this scenario, the OCC estimated that permitted payment stablecoin issuers would only be required to hold $650 million as a backstop. The total cost of this requirement would be $39.3 million ($39.3 million = $650 million * .0604). Because there is no comparable backstop estimate in either of our regulatory baselines, the OCC would include the full $39.3 million toward the cost of capital calculation. Therefore, in this scenario, in total, the 22 permitted payment stablecoin issuers would save $39.3 million in capital costs under this alternative.
This scenario would lower capital costs for permitted payment stablecoin issuers overall. Although a lower operational backstop requirement would decrease capital costs for permitted payment stablecoin issuers, given the calibration of the other final capital and other requirements, the OCC opted to take a more conservative approach related to the operational backstop in the proposal to ensure adequate coverage. Like other components of capital, after considering comments and issuing a final rule, the OCC will revisit these requirements in the future to ensure appropriate calibration.
Executive Order 14192
Executive Order 14192
, titled “Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation,” requires that an agency, unless prohibited by law, identify at least ten existing regulations to be repealed when the agency publicly proposes for notice and comment or otherwise promulgates a new regulation with total costs greater than zero.
Executive Order 14192
further requires that new incremental costs associated with new regulations shall, to the extent permitted by law, be offset by the elimination of existing costs associated with at least ten prior regulations. This final rule is a deregulatory action under
Executive Order 14192
because it would result in potential cost savings related to capital costs and assessment fees for permitted payment stablecoin issuers and OCC-supervised banks.

PART 15—PAYMENT STABLECOINS
Subpart A—Purpose, Scope, Definitions, Severability, and Reservation of Authority
§ 15.1
Purpose and scope.
(a)
Purpose.
This part implements the Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins Act (
12 U.S.C. 5901
et seq.
) (GENIUS Act) with respect to entities for which the OCC is authorized to issue regulations or exercise its enforcement authority under the Act.
(b)
Scope.
This part applies to the following entities' activities related to payment stablecoins and certain custody activities—
(
printed page 67176)
(1) National banks and their subsidiaries;
(2) Federal savings associations and their subsidiaries;
(3) Federal branches and their subsidiaries;
(4) Foreign payment stablecoin issuers;
(5) Nonbank entities that seek to be or are approved as Federal qualified payment stablecoin issuers; and
(6) State qualified payment stablecoin issuers for which the OCC has regulatory or enforcement authority pursuant to § 15.15 or § 15.16.

Affiliate
means a person that controls, is controlled by, or is under common control with another person.

et seq.

Subchapter II of chapter 53 of title 31, United States Code

Subpart B—Permitted Payment Stablecoin Issuers and State Qualified Payment Stablecoin Issuers
§ 15.10
Activities.
(a)
Permitted activities.
A permitted payment stablecoin issuer may not engage in any activity other than the following:
(1) Issue payment stablecoins;
(2) Redeem payment stablecoins;
(3) Manage reserves related to the issuance or redemption of payment stablecoins, including purchasing, selling, and holding reserve assets or providing custodial services for reserve assets, consistent with applicable State and Federal law;
(4) Provide custodial or safekeeping services for payment stablecoins, required reserves, or private keys of payment stablecoins, consistent with subpart C of this part;
(5) Assess fees associated with purchasing or redeeming payment stablecoins;
(6) Act as principal or agent with respect to any payment stablecoin;
(7) Pay fees to facilitate customer transactions;
(8) Hold as principal non-payment stablecoin digital assets as necessary to pay fees, including customer fees and network fees, or to conduct necessary testing on distributed ledger-based platforms, provided that such principal holdings shall not exceed quantities necessary for the reasonably foreseeable conduct of such activities;
(9) Establish a trust arrangement under applicable law for reserve assets, including the granting of a security interest in reserve assets, provided that:
(i) Any security interest in reserve assets granted to the trustee is for the sole benefit of payment stablecoin holders;
(ii) The arrangement with the trustee does not impair the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's ability to timely redeem payment stablecoins in the normal course of business prior to default;
(iii) The arrangement does not introduce claims that would compete with the claims of payment stablecoin holders of payment stablecoins issued by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer in the event of the insolvency of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer; and
(iv) The arrangement with the trustee does not impair the ability of a receiver of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer to direct the prompt transfer or liquidation of the reserve assets in order to pay claims to payment stablecoin holders;
(10) Manage foreign exchange risk, subject to the requirements of § 15.13(a)(10); and
(11) Undertake any other activities, including hiring third parties, that directly support any of the activities described in paragraphs (a)(1) through (4) of this section.
(b)
Rule of construction.
Nothing in paragraph (a) of this section may be construed to limit:
(1) The authority of a depository institution, national bank, or trust company to engage in activities permissible pursuant to applicable State and Federal law; or
(2) The authority of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to engage in an activity authorized consistent with section 4(a)(7)(B) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(7)(B)
).
(c)
Prohibitions.
A permitted payment stablecoin issuer must not:
(1) Use a deceptive name by using any combination of terms relating to the United States Government, including “United States,” “United States Government,” and “USG,” in the name of the payment stablecoin. This prohibition does not apply to abbreviations relating directly to the currency to which the payment stablecoin is pegged, such as “USD”.
(2) Market a payment stablecoin in such a way that a reasonable person would perceive the payment stablecoin to be:
(i) Legal tender as described in
31 U.S.C. 5103
;
(ii) Issued by the United States; or
(iii) Guaranteed or approved by the Government of the United States.
(3) Directly or through implication represent that payment stablecoins are backed by the full faith and credit of the United States, guaranteed by the United States Government, or subject to Federal deposit insurance or Federal share insurance.
(4) Pay a payment stablecoin holder any form of interest or yield (whether in cash, tokens, or other consideration) solely in connection with the holding, use, or retention of such payment stablecoin.
(5) Pledge, rehypothecate, or reuse any reserve assets required under § 15.11 either directly or indirectly (
e.g.,
through a third-party custodian of the reserve assets) except for the purpose of:
(i) Satisfying margin obligations in connection with investments in permitted reserves under § 15.11(b)(4) or (5);
(ii) Satisfying obligations associated with the use, receipt, or provision of standard custodial services; or
(iii) Creating liquidity to meet reasonable expectations of requests to redeem payment stablecoins, such that reserves in the form of Treasury bills with a maturity of 93 days or less may be sold as purchased securities in repurchase agreements, provided that either:
(A) The repurchase agreements are cleared by a clearing agency registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission; or
(B) The permitted payment stablecoin issuer receives prior approval from the OCC by order or pursuant to paragraph (d) of this section.
(6) Engage in any activity that the OCC determines is an evasion of the requirements of section 4 of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903
) or this part.
(d)
Prior approval.
Pursuant to section 4(a)(2)(C)(ii) of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5903(a)(2)(C)(ii)
) and paragraph (c)(5)(iii)(B) of this section, the OCC approves, for all permitted payment stablecoin issuers, repurchase agreements wherein the Treasury bills that are sold as purchased securities have a maturity of 93 days or less.
§ 15.11
Reserve assets.
(a)
Reserve requirements.
A permitted payment stablecoin issuer must:
(1) Maintain reserve assets that:
(i) Are identifiable;
(ii) Are segregated from and not commingled with other assets owned or held by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer;
(iii) At all times have a reserve asset value that equals or exceeds the outstanding issuance value of the permitted payment stablecoin issuer; and
(iv) Are either held directly by the permitted payment stablecoin issuer or within the custody of an eligible financial institution.
(2) Demonstrate the operational capability to access and monetize the identifiable reserve assets to meet redemptions, in both normal and adverse economic, liquidity, market, and interest rate conditions, commensurate with the permitted payment stablecoin issuer's risk profile and business model, taking into account, among other relevant factors, market access, financing channels, haircut assumptions, and operational readiness;
(3) Ensure that reserve asset value will continue to equal or exceed outstanding
