Another commenter recommended utilizing standardized machine-readable fields rather than recurring narrative responses,
As discussed above, the OCC will ensure that the reporting forms are consistent with the FDTA and the agencies' joint rule.
Similarly, another commenter recommended that the Federal stablecoin regulators jointly adopt reporting forms. The commenter stated that this would improve consistency, reduce burden, and align with the statutory mandate of the GENIUS Act.
The OCC has coordinated closely with the other primary Federal payment stablecoin regulators. Further, the OCC has taken seriously its obligation to coordinate with other agencies, as appropriate, and does not believe that it is necessary to do so through a joint rule or joint reporting forms. The OCC will continue to coordinate with other Federal payment stablecoin regulators as appropriate.
Another commenter stated that the OCC should revise Form PS-01 so that Schedules A, D, E, G, and H only require weekly data, rather than requiring end-of-day data for each calendar day in the reporting week. Alternatively, the commenter stated that the OCC could require daily data capture and reporting only upon notice from the OCC. The commenter stated that a weekly snapshot would reduce the reporting burden on permitted payment stablecoin issuers without eliminating supervisory information and would also reduce the time required for the OCC to review Form PS-01 submissions.
As discussed above, the OCC is amending the instructions for Form PS-01 to reduce the weekly reporting burden on smaller issuers to allow those issuers that are not currently subject to a formal enforcement proceeding or order; have an outstanding issuance value, together with any affiliated permitted payment stablecoin issuers, of less than $1 billion; and are in compliance with all of the reserve requirements set forth in section 15.11 and the reporting requirements in section 15.14, to satisfy their obligations for revised Schedules D through G by only submitting the required data for the last day of the reporting period (
i.e.
, each Monday) for each payment stablecoin it issues. The OCC believes this approach serves the goals of reducing the reporting burden for smaller issuers while also ensuring that the OCC receives the information necessary to supervise permitted payment stablecoin issuers. In addition, once reporting has commenced, the OCC will continue to assess the information collection and consider if further revisions are warranted.
Another commenter explained that the daily reporting requirement multiplies extraction, validation, reconciliation, exception management, and data-governance work across each affected schedule. According to the commenter, for Schedules B (Issuance and Redemption), C (Reserve Assets), and F (Reverse Repurchase Agreements), this burden is well justified by the supervisory value of monitoring data that closely correlates with risks to permitted payment stablecoin issuers or individual stablecoins. However, the commenter claimed that several of Form PS-01's schedules are unlikely to have meaningful daily fluctuations. Specifically, proposed Schedule A (General) primarily tracks information on the largest wallets and most active exchanges. The commenter explained that proposed Schedule A's data fields will undoubtedly change daily because of ordinary settlement flows, operational transfers, or short-lived trading activity, but these changes are unlikely to provide insight into sustained concentrations or material trends as compared to weekly snapshots and aggregates. Similarly, the values in proposed Schedule D (Cash Balances) are likely to exhibit daily noise as a result of normal operations without corresponding supervisory value.
The commenter further explained that other Form PS-01 schedules are more appropriate for weekly reporting precisely because they contain numerous fields that will not change significantly from day to day. Specifically, proposed Schedule E (U.S. Treasury Securities), proposed Schedule G (Money Market Mutual Funds), and proposed Schedule H (Other Instruments) are substantially composed of static and slow-changing information. CUSIPs, coupon rates, maturity dates, custodians, and other security-identification fields do not ordinarily change each day, and so will be of little value for daily tracking in Schedule E. The commenter added that the same is true for many of the money market mutual fund fields in proposed Schedule G and the fields in proposed Schedule H. Weekly reporting of fair value and amortized cost of Treasuries, WAM, and ownership concentrations of money market mutual funds, or fair value and WAM of other instruments in proposed Schedule H should provide sufficient information for the OCC to permit effective supervision.
The revisions to Form PS-01 reflect that the OCC considered these comments. For example, the OCC

                         “Wrapping” is a process where a crypto-asset is provided to a wrapped token provider, the provider controls or programmatically locks up the crypto-asset in a way that it cannot be transferred, lent, pledged, rehypothecated, or otherwise used for any reason, then mints a new crypto-asset in the form of a redeemable wrapped token. The redeemable wrapped token confers to the holder the right to “un-lock” the original crypto-asset from the wrapped token provider and is designed so that the number of redeemable wrapped tokens outstanding equals the underlying crypto-assets wrapped. Wrapped tokens are primarily used to enhance interoperability between blockchains by creating a redeemable wrapped token that is issued on a different blockchain than the original crypto-asset, effectively allowing holders to transact crypto-assets on blockchains they are not natively minted on.
“Bridging” is the process of moving a crypto-asset from one blockchain to another or creating a redeemable wrapped token on a different blockchain than the underlying crypto-assets. Crypto-asset issuers that can mint and burn their crypto-asset on multiple blockchains may offer the ability to natively “bridge” crypto-assets. They do this by accepting their crypto-asset issued on one blockchain, burning, or permanently removing it from circulation, and simultaneously minting it on another blockchain. The new crypto-asset has been permanently transferred to the second blockchain while the overall supply of crypto-assets issued by the provider remains the same. In contrast, a wrapped token provider may provide “bridging” services. However, as described above, the resulting crypto-asset is a redeemable wrapped token. It does not burn or alter the original crypto-asset in any way.

Department of the Treasury
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
AGENCY:
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), Treasury.
ACTION:
Notice and request for comment.
SUMMARY:
The OCC, as part of its continuing effort to reduce paperwork and respondent burden, invites comment on a new information collection, as required by the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA). In accordance with the requirements of the PRA, the OCC may not conduct or sponsor, and the respondent is not required to respond to, an information collection unless it displays a currently valid Office of Management and Budget (OMB) control number. The OCC is proposing a new information collection to comply with the Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins Act (GENIUS Act or the Act) requirement for entities seeking to issue payment stablecoins in the United States, titled “Applications for Licensing or Registration to Issue Payment Stablecoins Under the GENIUS Act.” The OCC is seeking a new OMB control number for this information collection and is giving notice that it has sent the collection to OMB for review.
DATES:
Comments must be received by November 23, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Commenters are encouraged to submit comments by email, if possible. You may submit comments by any of the following methods:
Email:
prainfo@occ.treas.gov
.
Mail:
Chief Counsel's Office, Attention: Comment Processing, Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, Attention: 1557-NEW, 400 7th Street SW, Suite 1E-216, Washington, DC 20219.
Hand Delivery/Courier:
400 7th Street SW, Suite 1E-216, Washington, DC 20219.
Fax:
(571) 293-4835.
Instructions:
You must include “OCC” as the agency name and “1557-NEW” in your comment. In general, the OCC will publish comments on
www.reginfo.gov
without change, including any business or personal information provided, such as name and address information, email addresses, or phone numbers. Comments received, including attachments and other supporting materials, are part of the public record and subject to public disclosure. Do not include any information in your comment or supporting materials that you consider confidential or inappropriate for public disclosure.
Written comments and recommendations for the proposed information collection should also be sent within 30 days of publication of this notice to
www.reginfo.gov/​public/​do/​PRAMain
.
You can find this information collection by selecting “Currently under 30-day Review—Open for Public Comments” or by using the search function.
You may review comments and other related materials that pertain to this information collection following the close of the 30-day comment period for this notice by the method set forth in the next bullet.
Viewing Comments Electronically:
Go to
www.reginfo.gov
.
Hover over the “Information Collection Review” tab and click on “Information Collection Review” from the drop-down menu. From the “Currently under Review” drop-down menu, select “Department of the Treasury” and then click “submit.” This information collection can be located by searching OMB control number “1557-NEW” or “Applications for Licensing or Registration to Issue Payment Stablecoins Under the GENIUS Act.” Upon finding the appropriate information collection, click on the related “ICR Reference Number.” On the next screen, select “View Supporting Statement and Other Documents” and then click on the link to any comment listed at the bottom of the screen.
For assistance in navigating
www.reginfo.gov
,
please contact the Regulatory Information Service Center at (202) 482-7340.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Shaquita Merritt, Clearance Officer, (202) 649-5490, Chief Counsel's Office, Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, 400 7th Street SW, Washington, DC 20219. If you are deaf, hard of hearing, or have a speech disability, please dial 7-1-1 to access telecommunications relay services.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Under the PRA (
44 U.S.C. 3501
et seq.
), Federal agencies must obtain approval from the OMB for each collection of information that they conduct or sponsor. “Collection of information” is defined in
44 U.S.C. 3502(3)
and
5 CFR 1320.3(c)
to include agency requests or requirements that members of the public submit reports, keep records, or provide information to a third party. The OCC asks the OMB to approve the collection of information in this notice.
Title:
Applications for Licensing or Registration to Issue Payment Stablecoins Under the GENIUS Act.
OMB Control No.:
1557-NEW.
Type of Review:
Regular.
Affected Public:
Businesses or other for-profit.
Description:
The GENIUS Act
[
1
]
was enacted on July 18, 2025. The Act will be effective on January 18, 2026. The Act establishes a regulatory framework for payment stablecoin activities. On
(
printed page 66940)
March 2, 2026, the OCC issued a proposed rule that would implement requirements of the Act with respect to the issuance of payment stablecoins and certain related activities by entities subject to the OCC's jurisdiction (the proposed rule).
[
2
]
The Act generally prohibits any person other than a permitted payment stablecoin issuer (PPSI) from issuing payment stablecoins in the United States. Further, the Act prohibits a foreign payment stablecoin issuer from offering, selling, or otherwise making available in the United States a payment stablecoin unless, among other conditions, the foreign payment stablecoin issuer is registered with the OCC.
The proposed rule set out the process by which entities may seek OCC approval to become a PPSI or for foreign payment stablecoin issuers to register with the OCC. The final rule related to the proposed rule (final rule) is published elsewhere in this issue of the
Federal Register
.
[
3
]
The OCC is now proposing a new information collection which includes the application forms which these entities will complete and submit to the OCC.
Twelve CFR 15.30(b)(1) of the final rule outlines the information required for approval of PPSIs. Twelve CFR 15.30(d) outlines the factors against which the OCC will evaluate substantially complete applications. These are:
(1) The ability of the applicant (or in the case of an applicant that is an insured national bank, Federal savings association or insured Federal branch, the subsidiary of the applicant), based on financial condition and resources, to meet the requirements for issuing payment stablecoins under subpart B of
12 CFR part 15
;
(2) Whether any officer or director of the applicant has been convicted of a felony offense involving insider trading, embezzlement, cybercrime, money laundering, financing of terrorism, or financial fraud;
(3) The competence, experience, and integrity of the officers, directors, and principal shareholders of the applicant, its subsidiaries, and parent companies, including:
(i) The record of those officers, directors, and principal shareholders of compliance with laws and regulations; and
(ii) The ability of those officers, directors, and principal shareholders to fulfill any commitments or conditions imposed by the OCC in connection with the application filed under this section or any prior application;
(4) Whether the applicant's redemption policy meets the standards under
12 CFR 15.12
; and
(5) The ability of the applicant (or in the case of an applicant that is an insured national bank, Federal savings association, or insured Federal branch, the subsidiary of the applicant) to conduct its proposed activities in a safe and sound manner, including whether the applicant's proposed structure adequately addresses run risks and adequately ensures the ability to redeem payment stablecoins.
The application must include an overview of the applicant, a detailed business plan, and information to assess the above factors, including proposed activities and their permissibility; reserve policy and requirements; redemption policy and requirements; and risk management policy and program, and certification that any filing or supporting material submitted to the OCC contains no material misrepresentations or omissions. In addition, the application must include (or the applicant must ensure each director, executive officer, and principal shareholder also submits the information prescribed in the Interagency Biographical and Financial Report,
[
4
]
available at
www.occ.gov
).
Twelve CFR 15.32(b)(1) of the final rule outlines the information required for approval of foreign payment stablecoin issuers. Twelve CFR 15.32(d) outlines the factors against which the OCC will evaluate applications for registration. These are:
(1) The Secretary of the Treasury's determination that the foreign payment stablecoin issuer is subject to a regulatory and supervisory regime comparable to the GENIUS Act with respect to payment stablecoins under section 18 of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5916
);
(2) The financial and managerial resources of the United States operations of the foreign payment stablecoin issuer;
(3) Whether the foreign payment stablecoin issuer will provide adequate information to the OCC to determine compliance with the GENIUS Act and
12 CFR part 15
;
(4) Whether the foreign payment stablecoin issuer presents a risk to the financial stability of the United States, including risks relating to ensuring timely redemption for United States customers;
(5) Whether the foreign payment stablecoin issuer presents illicit finance risks to the United States; and
(6) The ability of the applicant to conduct its proposed activities in a safe and sound manner, including whether the applicant's proposed structure adequately addresses run risks and adequately ensures the ability to redeem payment stablecoins.
The application must include an overview of the applicant, a detailed business plan, and information to assess the above factors, including evidence that the Secretary of the Treasury has determined that the applicant is subject to regulatory supervisory regime comparable to the GENIUS Act with respect to payment stablecoins, under section 18 of the GENIUS Act (
12 U.S.C. 5916
), a certification that the applicant will make available to the OCC all information that the OCC deems necessary to determine and enforce compliance with the GENIUS Act, the applicant's consent to United States jurisdiction relating to enforcement of the GENIUS Act and
12 CFR part 15
, and certification that any filing or supporting material submitted to the OCC contains no material misrepresentations or omissions.
Estimated Burden
Estimated Frequency of Response:
On occasion.
Estimated Number of Respondents:
40.
[
5
]
Estimated Total Annual Responses:
40.
Estimated Total Annual Burden:
4,915 hours.
Comments:
On July 27, 2026, the OCC published a 60-day notice for this information collection, (
91 FR 47032
). The OCC received two comments. One of these comments reiterated recommendations made in response to the proposed rule. In particular, the comment recommended that the OCC (1) differentiate between insured depository institution (IDI) and non-IDI applicants, (2) publish and solicit comment on permitted payment stablecoin issuer applications, and (3) require foreign payment stablecoin issuers seeking to register with the OCC to be subject to home-country capital requirements consistent with those imposed on permitted payment stablecoin issuers. These
(
printed page 66941)
recommendations are addressed in detail in the OCC's final rule.
The second comment expressed general support for the proposed application process and criteria but included certain recommendations. First, the commenter stated that the OCC should conduct a forward-looking review in light of the short time period between finalization of the OCC's final rule and the effective date of the GENIUS Act. In particular, the commenter stated that the OCC should evaluate whether the application presents a credible and detailed pathway to compliance by the effective date of the Act, rather than requiring an applicant to complete any operational changes necessary to achieve compliance with the Act before evaluating the application. The OCC will consider the applicant's plan for compliance and may include conditions, as appropriate, to ensure that a permitted payment stablecoin issuer does not commence business as a permitted payment stablecoin issuer until it is in compliance with all applicable portions of the GENIUS Act. The OCC will also consider requests for waiver under section 5 of the GENIUS Act, as appropriate.
Relatedly, the commenter recommended distinguishing what constitutes a substantially complete application (
i.e.,
what information is sufficient to evaluate the application under
12 CFR part 15
) from an applicant being demonstrably ready. The OCC will evaluate an application under the factors detailed in
12 CFR part 15
and may impose conditions, as appropriate, to ensure that the applicant is operationally ready before it commences business as a permitted payment stablecoin issuer. The OCC notes that, in certain circumstances, detailed information about the issuer's operational processes may be necessary to ensure the applicant's ability to conduct its proposed activities in a safe and sound manner, consistent with
12 CFR 15.30(d)(5)
.
The commenter also recommended providing transition relief and guidance for applications pending on the Act's effective date. The OCC will consider requests for waiver under section 5(f) of the GENIUS Act.
The commenter recommended that safety and soundness assessments of permitted payment stablecoin issuers should remain consistent with the OCC's final rule concerning unsafe and unsound practices. The commenter also stated that an application should not be held incomplete merely because the OCC seeks additional documentation or process enhancements after receiving information sufficient to evaluate the statutory factors. The GENIUS Act expressly permits the OCC to evaluate, as part of the application process, any other factors established by the OCC necessary to ensure the safety and soundness of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer. The OCC has implemented this provision in § 15.30(d)(5).
The commenter also included several technical recommendations. First, the commenter recommended against relying solely on standardized fields and required fields in favor of using a common evidentiary baseline while allowing narrative space in the application. The questions in the application are not intended to limit the applicant's presentation. Supporting information for all relevant factors, setting forth the basis for applicant's conclusions, should accompany the application.
Next, the commenter recommended that the OCC expressly state that the application process under
12 CFR part 15
is the controlling filing for OCC approval to issue payment stablecoins and conduct directly supporting activities. The OCC confirms that the application process under
12 CFR part 15
is the only application process required to issue payment stablecoins under the GENIUS Act. An issuer may, however, need to apply pursuant to other regulations to engage in certain activities. For example, an applicant that seeks to issue payment stablecoins as an uninsured national bank would need to separately apply for a national bank charter under
12 CFR part 5
and apply to be a permitted payment stablecoin issuer under
12 CFR part 15
.
Next, the commenter stated that an applicant should be able to seek approval to issue more than one payment stablecoin brand through a single entity. An applicant may apply to issue more than one brand of payment stablecoin out of a single entity. The OCC will evaluate whether such a proposal is consistent with the GENIUS Act, including with respect to safety and soundness and the protections afforded to stablecoin holders. Certain issuers may wish to apply to use multiple special purpose vehicle (SPV) issuers to better protect stablecoin holders. The OCC will ensure that the application process for such business models is not unduly burdensome.
Finally, the commenter stated that applicants should be able to incorporate current information held by the OCC by reference. The application form collects information that the OCC needs to evaluate requests for approval as a permitted payment stablecoin issuer. Efforts to reduce burden will be considered.
The commenter also stated that the OCC should use tailored applicant schedules to ensure that applications contain pertinent information and that outcomes are consistent. The proposed forms have been tailored with this goal in mind.
The commenter further stated that the information collection should not establish substantive standards separate from the regulation. It does not do so. The OCC will review applications in accordance with the factors under
12 CFR 15.30
.
The commenter also requested that the OCC condition the required certification that the supporting materials contain no material misrepresentations or omissions on a reasonable inquiry with respect to information that the applicant knows or reasonably should know. Consistent with the final rule an applicant must certify that any filing or supporting material submitted to the OCC contains no material misrepresentations or omissions. This requirement is similar to the certification requirements in other licensing forms that the OCC uses, and the OCC does not believe that it is necessary to further qualify the certification.
The commenter stated that the OCC should preserve the ability of a permitted payment stablecoin issuer to issue multiple payment stablecoin brands and to deploy a brand across multiple networks. In particular, the commenter stated that an application should not be required for each brand or technical deployment. An issuer may issue the same brand across multiple blockchains without a separate application. Similarly, the final rule does not preclude an issuer from issuing multiple separate brands of payment stablecoin. To the extent that a particular business model necessitates the use of multiple SPV issuers, the OCC will endeavor to minimize the burden of seeking out a new license for each SPV.
The commenter also stated that, for multi-affiliate issuance structures, the application should recognize that regulated affiliates may need separate issuance and redemption structures to comply with local law and may need to rebalance reserves so that liquidity is positioned where redemption requests are expected. The OCC will evaluate any proposed multi-affiliate issuance model on its terms to determine compliance with the GENIUS Act. The OCC does not believe that any changes to the application forms are necessary to facilitate such an evaluation.
(
printed page 66942)
The commenter requested that the OCC apply heightened scrutiny to consortium and multi-parent applicants. The OCC will evaluate each application based on the facts particular to that application.
The commenter stated that the OCC should ensure that there is a clear registration process under section 18(c) of the Act. The final rule, in conjunction with this information collection, and ongoing coordination with the Department of the Treasury, will help to provide such a clear pathway.
The commenter also stated that the OCC and other primary Federal payment stablecoin regulators should coordinate on application standards. The agencies have coordinated and will continue to do so.
Finally, the commenter addressed the OCC's burden estimates. The commenter stated that the OCC's estimate of burden materially understated the work necessary to prepare a complete application. The commenter did not provide an alternative estimate. In addition, the commenter noted that existing businesses may face additional burdens and that the OCC should consider using its waiver authority under section 5(f) of the GENIUS Act. The OCC will use its waiver authority, as appropriate.
Comments continue to be invited on:
(a) Whether the collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the OCC, including whether the information has practical utility;
(b) The accuracy of the OCC's estimate of the burden of the collection of information;
(c) Ways to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected;
(d) Ways to minimize the burden of the collection on respondents, including through the use of automated collection techniques or other forms of information technology; and
(e) Estimates of capital or start-up costs and costs of operation, maintenance, and purchase of services to provide information.
Sarah E. Turney,
Assistant Director, Office of the Comptroller of the Currency.

SYSTEM NAME:
“Readjustment Counseling Service (RCS) Vet Center Program-VA” (64VA10)
(
printed page 66948)
SECURITY CLASSIFICATION:
Unclassified.
SYSTEM LOCATION:
(a) Vet Center Record: Starting in Fiscal Year 2010 the location of the Vet Center record was transitioned from paper files maintained at each individual Vet Center to being electronically maintained in the national computerized intra-net database (RCSNet). The RCSNet servers are located in Philadelphia, PA in a secure, protected, and approved VA Office of Information and Technology (OIT) Service Delivery and Engineering (SDE) site maintained by OIT personnel. Full confidentiality for RCS Vet Center information is maintained by limiting access to RCS-qualified personnel with the appropriate authority to administer RCS program data systems.
Records are also located within the Salesforce Government Cloud Plus and the Microsoft Azure Government cloud at participating servers in the United States.
(b) All paper Vet Center records established prior to 2010 have been archived, and scanned copies have been uploaded into the RCSNet electronic record system.
SYSTEM MANAGER(S):
Chief Readjustment Counseling Officer (10RCS), VA Central Office, 810 Vermont Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20420, 202-461-6525.
AUTHORITY FOR MAINTENANCE OF THE SYSTEM:
38 U.S.C. 1712A
;
38 CFR 17.2000(e)
.
PURPOSE(S) OF THE SYSTEM:
38 CFR 17.2000(e)
, requires that Vet Center records be independent from VA or Department of War medical records and not be disclosed without the client or eligible individual's voluntarily signed authorization or under the conditions of a permissive disclosure as outlined below under Routine Uses. Vet Center records may include VCOA records, RCSNet records (Client records and eligible individual's records), Secure Messaging Platform records, and Vet Center Call Center records. The purpose of this system of records is to maintain client confidentiality. The Vet Center records will collect and maintain demographic and clinical information required by Vet Center counselors. These counselors will provide quality readjustment counseling to eligible veterans, service members including National Guard and Reserve components, and their families. The information documented provides an accountable record of the course of Vet Center services provided inclusive of psychosocial assessment, number and type of visits provided, type of readjustment counseling sessions provided and referrals, along with follow-up documentation made to VA partners for other services needed for a successful readjustment. Vet Center records will be used for outreach and analytical purposes and for direct secure communication with eligible veterans, service members including National Guard and Reserve components, and their families. These records are also used to produce various management and follow-up reports in responding to clients and other inquiries. Vet Center Call Center records will be used and recorded for quality assurance purposes.
CATEGORIES OF INDIVIDUALS COVERED BY THE SYSTEM:
Eligibility for readjustment counseling includes veterans or service members who served in a combat theater or an area of armed hostility, inclusive of those who provided direct emergency medical care or mortuary services to the casualties of combat operations, even if such services were provided outside of the combat theater. Eligibility also includes participation in actions against enemy forces by remotely controlling unmanned aerial vehicles from outside the combat theater. Eligibility has been extended to veterans, service members including Reserve, National Guard, and Coast Guard who were activated in response to a national emergency, a State or national civil disturbance, or foreign drug interdiction. Family members of all eligible individuals are eligible for family readjustment counseling as indicated for the successful readjustment of the eligible individual. Family counseling is also available for family members of deployed service members to assist them in adjusting to the deployment. Members of the community include, but are not limited to, Veterans Service Organizations and Congressional liaisons and attorneys. These records will also include information on VA employees/providers.
CATEGORIES OF RECORDS IN THE SYSTEM:
The Vet Center record contains demographic personally identifiable information, such as unique veteran identification number/veteran identification form, name, address, Social Security number (SSN), EDIPI, marital status, gender identity, birth date, military service information, veteran eligibility information (
i.e.
DD-214), referral, and follow-up information, signed General Consent for the receipt of readjustment counseling, and other identifying statistical information. The Vet Center record also contains protected health information such as documentation of the Warwick-Edinberg Mental Well-Being Scale, suicide risk assessment, psychosocial assessment, military history, service plans, and ongoing case clinical notes documenting the course of RCS delivery. Bereavement services and military sexual trauma counseling information are also included in the Vet Center record. Also documented in the Vet Center record are health care power of attorney, court-ordered counseling information, and completed release of information authorizations as needed to promote efficient and expedient sharing of confidential information for referral and case coordination with VA medical center partners.
Vet Center Call Center records will contain the input form, full name of caller, telephone number of caller, comments from the caller, current location of caller, and physical address of caller.
RECORD SOURCE CATEGORIES:
(1) Relevant forms to be filled out by Vet Center team members on first contact and each contact thereafter; counseling sessions with veterans and other eligible counselees; (2) Other VA and Federal agency systems (
i.e.
VADIR and VA Profile), including from the VA electronic health record; (3) Relevant veteran data protocols completed by Vet Center staff to document the course of readjustment counseling provided; (4) veterans, service members and their family; (5) VA employees and VA health care providers; and (6) Vet Center Call Center.
ROUTINE USES OF RECORDS MAINTAINED IN THE SYSTEM, INCLUDING CATEGORIES OF USERS AND THE PURPOSES OF SUCH USES:
To the extent that records contained in the system include information protected by
45 CFR parts 160
and
164
,
i.e.,
individually identifiable health information of VHA or any of its business associates, and
38 U.S.C. 7332
,
i.e.,
medical treatment information related to drug abuse, alcoholism or alcohol abuse, sickle cell anemia, or infection with the human immunodeficiency virus, that information cannot be disclosed under a routine use unless there is also specific statutory authority in both
38 U.S.C. 7332
and CFR parts 160 and 164 permitting disclosure.
1. Congress:
To a Member of Congress or staff acting upon the Member's behalf when the Member or staff requests the information on behalf of, and at the request of, the individual who is the subject of the record.
(
printed page 66949)
2. National Archives and Records Administration:
To the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) in records management inspections conducted under
44 U.S.C. 2904
and
2906
or other functions authorized by laws and policies governing NARA operations and VA records management responsibilities.
3. Department of Justice for Litigation or Administrative Proceeding:
To the Department of Justice (DoJ), or in a proceeding before a court, adjudicative body, or other administrative body before which VA is authorized to appear, when any of the following is a party to such proceedings or has an interest in such proceedings, and VA determines that use of such records is relevant and necessary to the proceedings for:
(a) VA or any component thereof;
(b) Any VA employee in his or her official capacity;
(c) Any VA employee in his or her official capacity where DoJ has agreed to represent the employee; or
(d) The United States, where VA determines that litigation is likely to affect the agency or any of its components.
4. Contractors:
To contractors, grantees, experts, consultants, students, and others performing or working on a contract, service, grant, cooperative agreement, or other assignment for VA, when reasonably necessary to accomplish an agency function related to the records.
5. Law Enforcement Authorities, for Reporting Violations of Law:
To a Federal, State, local, territorial, Tribal, or foreign law enforcement authority or other appropriate entity charged with the responsibility of investigating or prosecuting a violation or potential violation of law, whether civil, criminal, or regulatory in nature, or charged with enforcing or implementing such law, provided that the disclosure is limited to information that, either alone or in conjunction with other information, indicates such a violation or potential violation. A disclosure of information about veterans or their dependents from VA claims files under this routine use must also comply with the requirements of
38 U.S.C. 5701(f)
.
6. Federal Agencies, Fraud and Abuse:
To other Federal agencies, such as Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services or United States Postal Services to assist such agencies in preventing and detecting possible fraud or abuse by individuals in their operations and programs, such as detecting duplicate payments for care, or mail fraud related to delivery of VA medications. This list is not meant to be exhaustive as VA cannot anticipate each specific need in advance of requests by other Federal agencies.
7. Data Breach Response and Remediation, for VA:
To appropriate agencies, entities, and persons when: (a) VA suspects or has confirmed that there has been a breach of the system of records; (b) VA has determined that as a result of the suspected or confirmed breach there is a risk of harm to individuals, VA (including its information systems, programs, and operations), the Federal Government, or national security; and (c) the disclosure made to such agencies, entities, or persons is reasonably necessary to assist in connection with VA's efforts to respond to the suspected or confirmed breach or to prevent, minimize, or remedy such harm.
8. Data Breach Response and Remediation, for Another Federal Agency:
To another Federal agency or Federal entity when VA determines that information from this system of records is reasonably necessary to assist the recipient agency or entity in (a) responding to a suspected or confirmed breach or (b) preventing, minimizing, or remedying the risk of harm to individuals, the recipient agency or entity (including its information systems, programs, and operations), the Federal Government, or national security resulting from a suspected or confirmed breach.
9. State Licensing Boards, for Licensing:
To a Federal agency, a State or local government licensing board, the Federation of State Medical Boards, or a similar non-governmental entity that maintains records concerning individuals' employment histories or concerning the issuance, retention, or revocation of licenses, certifications, or registration necessary to practice an occupation, profession, or specialty to inform such non-governmental entities about the health care practices of a terminated, resigned, or retired health care employee whose professional health care activity so significantly failed to conform to generally accepted standards of professional medical practice as to raise reasonable concern for the health and safety of patients in the private sector or from another Federal agency. These records may also be disclosed as part of an ongoing computer matching program to accomplish these purposes.
10. National Practitioner Data Bank for Hiring, Privileging:
To the National Practitioner Data Bank at the time of hiring or clinical privileging/re-privileging of health care practitioners and other times as deemed necessary by VA in order for VA to obtain information relevant to a Department decision concerning the hiring, privileging/re-privileging, retention, or termination of the applicant or employee.
POLICIES AND PRACTICES FOR STORAGE OF RECORDS:
Vet Center Record Storage: (a) Vet Center Records established during and after 2010 are electronically stored in the national computerized RCSNet servers located in Philadelphia, PA, in a secure, protected, and approved VA OIT SDE environment maintained by OIT personnel; (b) Paper Vet Center Records established prior to 2010 have been archived and scanned copies are uploaded into the RCSNet electronic record system.
POLICIES AND PRACTICES FOR RETRIEVAL OF RECORDS:
The Vet Center Record is indexed by the Vet Center number in conjunction with the veteran's name, SSN, and unique veteran client number.
POLICIES AND PRACTICES FOR RETENTION AND DISPOSAL OF RECORDS:
The Vet Center records in this system are retained and disposed of in accordance with the schedule approved by the Archivist of the United States, Records Control Schedule 10-1 and General Record Schedule. These records are currently unscheduled and should not be destroyed.
ADMINISTRATIVE, TECHNICAL, AND PHYSICAL SAFEGUARDS:
(a) Within RCS, access to the Vet Center record is limited to authorized RCS staff (Vet Center, District Director Office, and/or the Office of the Chief Readjustment Counseling Officer in the VA Central Office (VACO) with a legitimate need to know connected to direct service delivery and/or the quality oversight of services provided. RCS staff access to the electronic Vet Center record is via standalone computers located in locked Vet Centers. RCS program computers are username and password protected. Computer security is in compliance with RCS and VA computer security policy and protocol. (b) Access to a veteran's or service member's counseling records by elements outside of RCS, whether VA or non-VA, is contingent upon the veteran's or service member's signed authorization or one of the routine uses identified above. (c) Authorized RCS staff will have access to the Vet Record via stand-alone RCSNet computers located in locked Vet Centers, District Director Offices, and VACO. (d) VA Enterprise Cloud data storage conforms to security protocols as
(
printed page 66950)
stipulated in VA Directives 6500 and 6517. Access control standards are stipulated in specific agreements with cloud vendors to restrict and monitor access.
RECORD ACCESS PROCEDURE:
Individuals seeking information regarding access to Vet Center records in this system pertaining to them should contact the system manager in writing as indicated above, or may write, call, or visit the last Vet Center where counseling was provided. A request for access to records must contain the requester's full name, address, and telephone number, be signed by the requester, and describe the records sought in sufficient detail to enable VA personnel to locate them with a reasonable amount of effort.
CONTESTING RECORD PROCEDURES:
Individuals seeking information regarding access to Vet Center records in this system pertaining to them should contact the system manager in writing as indicated above, or may write, call, or visit the last Vet Center where counseling was provided. A request for access to records must contain the requester's full name, address, and telephone number, be signed by the requester, and describe the records sought in sufficient detail to enable VA personnel to locate them with a reasonable amount of effort.
NOTIFICATION PROCEDURE:
A veteran who wishes to determine whether a record is being maintained by the RCS Vet Center Program under his or her name or other personal identifier or wishes to determine the contents of such records should submit a written request or apply in person to: (1) the Vet Center Director, (2) the RCS Deputy District Director having supervisory responsibility for the Vet Center with whom he or she had contact, or (3) the Deputy Chief Readjustment Counseling Officer, VA Central Office, 810 Vermont Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20420. Inquiries should include the individual's full name and SSN.
EXEMPTIONS PROMULGATED FOR THE SYSTEM:
None.

AGENCY:

ACTION:
Rescindment of a system of records.
SUMMARY:
Pursuant to the Privacy Act of 1974, notice is hereby given that VA is rescinding an existing system of records titled, “Federal Case Management Tool (FCMT)—VA” (202VA005Q). FCMT is a web-based application that supports VA and the Department of War with the management and tracking of veteran and service member beneficiaries at all levels of the continuum of care.
DATES:
Comments on this rescindment notice must be received no later than November 23, 2026.
This rescindment is effective as of November 23, 2026 unless modified by a subsequent notice incorporating any comments received.
ADDRESSES:
Comments may be submitted through
www.regulations.gov
under docket number VA-2026-VACO-0001 or mailed to VA Privacy Service (005X6F), 810 Vermont Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20420. Comments should indicate that they are submitted in response to “Federal Case Management Tool (FCMT)—VA” (202VA005Q). Comments received will be available at
www.regulations.gov
for public viewing, inspection, or copies.

Freda Perry, Project Manager, Federal Case Management Tool (FCMT), Product Delivery Service (005S), OIT,
Freda.Perry2@va.gov
or Riley Ross, Acting Director, Education Veterans Readiness and Employment Product Line—EVREPL (FCMT), Product Delivery Service (005S), OIT,
Riley.Ross@va.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The FCMT is not being decommissioned; only the system of record notice is being rescinded. Although this system uses information collected by VA, it does not meet the criteria of a Privacy Act System of Records, as defined by the Privacy Act of 1974. All information used by FCMT is covered under various other VA Systems of Records.

(

Overview of This Information Collection
(1)
Type of Information Collection:
Extension, Without Change, of a Currently Approved Collection.

Title of the Form/Collection:
Application to Register Permanent Residence or Adjust Status; Supplement A to Form I-485, Adjustment of Status Under Section 245(i); Supplement J, Confirmation of Bona Fide Offer or Request for Job Portability Under Section 204(j); National Interest Waiver.

Affected public who will be asked or required to respond, as well as a brief abstract: Primary:

The Form I-485 Supplement A is used to adjust status under section 245(i) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (Act). The Form I-485 Supplement J is used if you are an employment-based applicant for adjustment of status who is filing or has previously filed a Form I-485 as the principal beneficiary of a valid Form I-140 in an employment-based immigrant visa category that requires a job offer, and you now seek, in connection with your Form I-485, to (1) confirm that the job offered in your Form I-140 is a bona fide offer you intend to accept or (2) request job portability under INA section 204(j) to a new, full-time permanent job offer that you intent to accept, once your Form I-485 is approved.
