. To begin the search, select “Begin Web-based ADAMS Search.” For problems with ADAMS, please contact the NRC's Public Document Room (PDR) reference staff at 1-800-397-4209, 301-415-4737, or by email to
PDR.Resource@nrc.gov
. The ADAMS accession number for each document referenced (if it is available in ADAMS) is provided the first time that it is mentioned in this document.
NRC's PDR:
The PDR, where you may examine and order copies of publicly available documents, is open by appointment. To make an appointment to visit the PDR, please send an email to
PDR.Resource@nrc.gov
or call 1-800-397-4209 or 301-415-4737, between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m. eastern time, Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays.
B. Submitting Comments
The NRC encourages electronic comment submission through the Federal Rulemaking website (
https://www.regulations.gov
). Please include Docket ID NRC-2026-4456 in your comment submission.
The NRC cautions you not to include identifying or contact information that you do not want to be publicly disclosed in your comment submission. The NRC will post all comment submissions at
https://www.regulations.gov
as well as enter the comment submissions into ADAMS. The NRC does not routinely edit comment submissions to remove identifying or contact information.
If you are requesting or aggregating comments from other persons for submission to the NRC, then you should inform those persons not to include identifying or contact information that they do not want to be publicly disclosed in their comment submission. Your request should state that the NRC does not routinely edit comment submissions to remove such information before making the comment submissions available to the public or entering the comment into ADAMS.
II. The Petitioner and Petition
The PRM was submitted by Howard L. Hall, Ph.D., a nuclear and radiochemist. The petitioner submits this petition in his individual capacity as a member of the technical public, not on behalf of any institution. The PRM requests that the NRC amend
10 CFR part 74
, “Material Control and Accounting of Special Nuclear Material,” of title 10 of the
Code of Federal Regulations
(10 CFR), to remove the exclusion of irradiated fuel reprocessing plants from the material control and accounting (MC&A) requirements in § 74.51(a). The petition proposes applying subpart E of
10 CFR part 74
, “Formula Quantities of Strategic Special Nuclear Material,” requirements to irradiated fuel reprocessing facilities, adding bulk-processing provisions, and restoring proportionate relief for research and pilot-scale operations. The petition may be found in ADAMS at Accession No. ML26257A310.
III. Discussion of the Petition
The petitioner requests that the NRC amend its regulations in § 74.51(a) to remove the exclusion of irradiated fuel reprocessing plants and establish MC&A requirements for the bulk handling of formula quantities of plutonium in a continuous chemical process, either in
(
printed page 66795)
the existing subpart E of
10 CFR part 74
or in a new subpart. The petitioner argues that the current regulatory framework for reprocessing facilities is inadequate and incomplete. Current regulations in
10 CFR part 74
place reprocessing facilities under requirements designated for special nuclear material (SNM) of moderate strategic significance (subpart D of
10 CFR part 74
, “Special nuclear material of moderate strategic significance), even though large-scale reprocessing facilities would handle formula quantities of strategic SNM. The petitioner emphasizes the exclusion in § 74.51(a) was added to the regulations nearly 40 years ago when the NRC believed that commercial reprocessing was unlikely in the near future and that more advanced technology would be needed before new regulations could be written. The petitioner asserts that reprocessing has now become viable due to recent Federal actions, including
Executive Order 14299
, “Deploying Advanced Nuclear Reactor Technologies for National Security” (May 29, 2025;
90 FR 22581
), recent U.S. Department of Energy solicitations, and emerging commercial proposals for privately funded reprocessing facilities.
The petitioner proposes several regulatory updates to
10 CFR part 74
. The proposals fall into four main categories:
1. Primary amendment to § 74.51(a): The petitioner proposes removing “an irradiated fuel reprocessing plant” from the exclusion list in § 74.51(a). This change would place reprocessing facilities under subpart E of
10 CFR part 74
MC&A requirements for licensees possessing formula quantities of strategic SNM. The petitioner also proposes a conforming amendment to § 74.41(a) in subpart D of
10 CFR part 74
to create an upper bound of less than five formula kilograms, to ensure reprocessing facilities are not subject to both subparts simultaneously.
2. Additions to subpart E of
10 CFR part 74
specifically addressing bulk chemical processing: The petitioner proposes adding a new section to subpart E establishing requirements specific to the continuous chemical processes used in reprocessing plants. The proposed requirements include near-real time accountancy for each material balance area for material balance periods of days to weeks; quantitative targets for inventory difference uncertainty; process monitoring aligned to the flowsheets of the continuous reprocessing operations employed; safeguards-by-design at the construction stage; and compatibility with international safeguards.
3. Clarification of requirements for research and development (R&D) and pilot-scale operations: The petitioner proposes the NRC confirm the applicability of existing subpart E of
10 CFR part 74
provisions for R&D reprocessing operations and clarify requirements for pilot-scale reprocessing operations.
4. Alternative approach if subpart E is not amended: If the NRC prefers to preserve the structure of subpart E, the petitioner proposes creating a new subpart in
10 CFR part 74
specifically for reprocessing plants which provides requirements equivalent to subpart E and incorporating the proposed elements for bulk chemical processing and small-scale operations.
The petitioner concludes that rulemaking is the appropriate method to resolve the problem because it is a generic issue affecting all prospective reprocessing licensees, and rulemaking provides clarity and consistency in requirements for this facility class. The petitioner argues that establishing an updated, predictable, MC&A framework for reprocessing facilities will reduce long-term burden on applicants, enhance safeguards effectiveness, and align the regulatory landscape with current national nuclear fuel cycle initiatives.
IV. Request for Comment
The NRC is seeking general comments from the public on the PRM. Additionally, the NRC asks the following specific questions:
1. Should the exclusion for irradiated fuel reprocessing facilities be removed from § 74.51(a)? Please explain the basis for your response.
2. Given the requirements in subpart D of
10 CFR part 74
, can a large-scale reprocessing facility credibly meet the subpart D general performance objectives for timely detection of a significant quantity and the required system capabilities for inventory difference and standard error of inventory difference without implementing some form of process monitoring? Please explain the basis for your response and provide examples as appropriate.
3. Is there a need to clarify the MC&A requirements for R&D and pilot-scale reprocessing operations? Please explain your response.
4. Are there additional changes to the MC&A regulations for reprocessing facilities that the NRC should consider? Please explain the basis for your response and provide specific recommendations to the extent possible.
V. Conclusion
The NRC has determined that the petition meets the sufficiency requirements for docketing a PRM under § 2.803, “Petition for rulemaking-NRC action.” The NRC will examine the issues raised in PRM-74-1 and any comments received in response to this comment request to determine whether these issues should be considered in rulemaking. The public can monitor further action on the rulemaking that will address this petition by searching Docket ID NRC-2026-4456 on the Federal rulemaking website,
https://www.regulations.gov
. The site allows members of the public to receive alerts when changes or additions occur in a docket folder. To subscribe: (1) navigate to the docket folder (NRC-2026-4456); (2) click the “Subscribe” link; and (3) enter an email address and click on the “Subscribe” link. The NRC also tracks the status of all NRC rules and PRMs on its website at
https://www.nrc.gov/​about-nrc/​regulatory/​rulemaking/​rules-petitions.html
.

Secretary of the Commission.

ACTION:
Final rule; correction.
SUMMARY:
The FAA is correcting an airworthiness directive (AD) that was published in the
Federal Register
. That AD applies to certain The Boeing Company Model 787-8, 787-9, and 787-10 airplanes. As published, a paragraph reference specified in the regulatory text is incorrect. This document corrects that error. In all other respects, the original document remains the same.
DATES:
This correction is effective November 12, 2026. The effective date of AD 2026-20-10 remains November 12, 2026.
The Director of the Federal Register approved the incorporation by reference of a certain publication listed in this AD as of November 12, 2026 (
91 FR 64259

The Director of the Federal Register approved the incorporation by reference of a certain other publication listed in this AD as of October 11, 2019 (

You may examine the AD docket at
regulations.gov
by searching for and locating Docket No. FAA-2026-2712; or in person at Docket Operations between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays. The AD docket contains this final rule; correction, any comments received, and other information. The street address for Docket Operations is U.S. Department of Transportation, Docket Operations, M-30, West Building Ground Floor, Room W12-140, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590.

regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-2712.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
AD 2026-20-10, Amendment 39-23483 (
91 FR 64259
, October 8, 2026) (AD 2026-20-10), requires repetitive operational checks of the leading edge (LE) outboard (OB) slats and applicable on-condition actions, revising the airplane flight manual (AFM) to prohibit flap retraction under icing conditions after landing, and revising the existing maintenance or inspection program, as applicable, to incorporate a new operation check. AD 2026-20-10 also requires replacing the LE outboard geared rotary actuator (GRA) with a LE outboard lockout actuator (LEOLA) at leading edge OB slat locations and revising the existing maintenance or inspection program, as applicable, to incorporate a new certification maintenance requirement (CMR). That AD applies to certain The Boeing Company Model 787-8, 787-9, and 787-10 airplanes.
Need for Correction
As published, a paragraph reference specified in the regulatory text of AD 2026-20-10 is incorrect. Paragraph (l) of AD 2026-20-10 inadvertently references paragraph (i) of the AD instead of paragraph (n) of the AD.
Material Incorporated by Reference Under
1 CFR Part 51
The FAA reviewed Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin B787-81205-SB270055-00 RB, Issue 002, dated November 25, 2024. This material specifies procedures for replacing the LE outboard GRA with a LEOLA at leading edge slat 2 and slat 11 outboard locations and revising the operator's maintenance program to incorporate CMR document item 27-CMR-14, “Functionally check the Leading Edge Power Drive Unit Half System Torque Brake.”
This AD also requires Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin B787-81205-SB270051-00 RB, Issue 001, dated July 5, 2019, which the Director of the Federal Register approved for incorporation by reference as of October 11, 2019 (
84 FR 54765
, October 11, 2019).
This material is reasonably available because the interested parties have access to it through their normal course of business or by the means identified in the
ADDRESSES
section.
Correction of Publication
This document corrects an error and correctly adds the AD as an amendment to
14 CFR 39.13
. Although no other part of the preamble or regulatory information has been corrected, the FAA is publishing the entire rule in the
Federal Register
.
The effective date of this AD remains November 12, 2026.
Since this action only corrects a paragraph reference, it has no adverse economic impact and imposes no additional burden on any person. Therefore, the FAA has determined that notice and public comment procedures are unnecessary.

(a) Effective Date
This airworthiness directive (AD) is effective November 12, 2026.
(b) Affected ADs
This AD replaces AD 2019-20-07, Amendment 39-19760 (
84 FR 54765
, October 11, 2019) (AD 2019-20-07).
(c) Applicability
This AD applies to The Boeing Company Model 787-8, 787-9, and 787-10 airplanes, certificated in any category, as identified in Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin B787-81205-SB270055-00 RB, Issue 002, dated November 25, 2024.
(d) Subject
Air Transport Association (ATA) of America Code 27, Flight Controls.
(e) Unsafe Condition
This AD was prompted by a determination that the leading edge (LE) outboard (OB) slat system could be out of position without flight deck annunciation. The FAA is issuing this AD to address a potential condition in which the LE OB slat system could be out of position without flight deck annunciation. The unsafe condition, if not addressed, could result in insufficient lift, resulting in inability to maintain continued safe flight and landing.
(f) Compliance
Comply with this AD within the compliance times specified, unless already done.
(g) Retained Required Actions, With No Changes
This paragraph restates the requirements of paragraph (g) of AD 2019-20-07, with no changes. Except as specified by paragraph (h) of this AD: At the applicable times specified in the “Compliance” paragraph of Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin B787-81205-SB270051-00 RB, Issue 001, dated July 5, 2019, do all applicable actions identified in, and in accordance with, the Accomplishment Instructions of Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin B787-81205-SB270051-00 RB, Issue 001, dated July 5, 2019.
Note 1 to paragraph (g):
Guidance for accomplishing the actions required by this AD can be found in Boeing Alert Service Bulletin B787-81205-SB270051-00, Issue 001, dated July 5, 2019, which is referred to in Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin B787-81205-SB270051-00 RB, Issue 001, dated July 5, 2019.
(h) Retained Exception to Service Information Specifications, With No Changes
This paragraph restates the requirements of paragraph (h) of AD 2019-20-07, with no changes. For purposes of determining compliance with the requirements of this AD: Where Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin B787-81205-SB270051-00 RB, Issue 001, dated July 5, 2019, uses the phrase “the Issue 001 date of Requirements Bulletin B787-81205-SB270051-00 RB,” this AD requires using “October 11, 2019” (the effective date of AD 2019-20-07).
(i) Retained Airplane Flight Manual (AFM) Revision To Prohibit Flap Retraction Under Icing Conditions, With No Changes
This paragraph restates the requirements of paragraph (i) of AD 2019-20-07, with no changes. Within 60 days after October 11, 2019 (the effective date of AD 2019-20-07), revise the Limitations Section of the existing AFM to include the information in figure 1 to paragraph (i) of this AD. This may be done by inserting a copy of figure 1 to paragraph (i) of this AD into the Limitations Section of the existing AFM.
Figure 1 to Paragraph (i): AFM Revision
Flap Operation After Landing (Required by AD 2019-20-07)
In order to prevent failure of the slat drive system after landing, flaps must not be retracted if:
• Operating on the ground with ice, snow, slush, or standing water in icing conditions, or;
• An accumulation of airframe ice is observed or suspected.
Under circumstances where the flight crew deems it necessary to retract the flaps for safety reasons, they must notify maintenance via an approved means.
(j) Retained Maintenance or Inspection Program Revision To Incorporate a New Operation Check, With No Changes
This paragraph restates the requirements of paragraph (j) of AD 2019-20-07, with no changes. Within 60 days after October 11, 2019 (the effective date of AD 2019-20-07), revise the existing maintenance or inspection program, as applicable, to incorporate the information specified in figure 2 to paragraph (j) of this AD. This may be done by inserting a copy of figure 2 to paragraph (j) of this AD into the existing maintenance or inspection program.

(3) After an airplane lands in icing conditions, do the OPERATION CHECKS—SLAT/FLAP INSPECTION in this task before retracting the slats/flaps.
NOTE:

• When visible moisture (clouds, fog with visibility of one statute mile (1600 m) or less, rain, snow, sleet, ice crystals, and so on) is present.
• When ice, snow, slush or standing water is present on the taxiways, or runways.
(a) Do this inspection to make sure that contaminants (ice, snow, slush) are not present which can either obstruct retraction of the LE slats or TE flaps, or freeze the slats to the fixed leading edge after retraction.
(b) The type and area of inspection is as follows:
(1) Do an examination of the entire leading edge slats and trailing edge flaps areas.

(1)
SLAT/FLAP INSPECTION
After any landing in icing conditions, do this inspection with the slats/flaps (flaps 25 detent) fully extended (Figure 2):

(b) Remove the contamination that you find.

(a) Confirm a contaminant-free condition in these areas immediately prior to retraction of the slats/flaps surfaces.
(1) Slats/flaps surfaces
(2) Leading edge contact surfaces

(3) Slat actuation areas, including exposed areas of the slat track cavity, and slat cove

(d) When the inspection is complete, do these steps:
NOTE:
These steps make sure that the leading edge slat system is functional.
NOTE:
Two persons are necessary to do these steps. One person will move the flap control lever in the flight compartment, and the other will confirm slat position from the ground.
(1) Do not use Alternate mode to operate the surfaces.
NOTE:
The Alternate mode only allows extension of slats to the Middle (sealed) position and not to the Extended (gapped) position.
WARNING:
MAKE SURE THAT YOU USE THE NECESSARY PRECAUTIONS IF PERSONNEL ARE NEAR THE FLIGHT CONTROL SURFACES. THE FLIGHT CONTROL SURFACES CAN MOVE QUICKLY. THIS CAN CAUSE INJURIES TO PERSONNEL AND DAMAGE TO EQUIPMENT.
(2) Retract the leading edge slats to the full up position (Flaps UP detent).
(a) Make sure that you visually confirm from the ground that the slats have retracted to the Retracted (up) position.
(3) Extend the leading edge slats to the full extend position (Flaps 25 detent).
(a) Make sure that you visually confirm from the ground that the slats have extended to the Extended (gapped) position.
(4) Retract the leading edge slats to the full up position (Flaps UP detent).
(a) Make sure that you visually confirm from the ground that the slats have retracted to the Retracted (up) position.
(e) When all of the above steps are completed, the OPERATION CHECKS—SLAT/FLAP INSPECTION is complete.

This paragraph restates the requirements of paragraph (k) of AD 2019-20-07, with no changes. After the existing maintenance or inspection program has been revised as required by paragraph (j) of this AD, no alternative actions (

title: Clarification on Department of Justice and Department of Education Guidance Documents Regarding Federal Nondiscrimination Laws
abstract: The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) and U.S. Department of Education (ED) (the Departments) are issuing this document to clarify that seven guidance documents issued jointly by the Departments are not enforceable. In addition, the Departments plan to revisit these guidance documents in light of the Supreme Court's decision in Loper Bright Enters. v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369, 400 (2024), to assess whether they are consistent with the single best meaning of the relevant statutory text. The Departments will not rely upon these guidance documents in their enforcement of federal civil rights laws, including Titles IV and VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (Title IV and Title VI), 42 U.S.C. 2000c et seq. and 2000d et seq., the Equal Educational Opportunities Act of 1974 (EEOA), 20 U.S.C. 1701-1720, the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 (ADA), 42 U.S.C. 12101 et seq., and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 (Section 504), 29 U.S.C. 794.

AGENCY:

ACTION:
Notice; clarification.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) and U.S. Department of Education (ED) (the Departments) are issuing this document to clarify that seven guidance documents issued jointly by the Departments are not enforceable. In addition, the Departments plan to revisit these guidance documents in light of the Supreme Court's decision in
Loper Bright Enters.
v.
Raimondo
, 603 U.S. 369, 400 (2024), to assess whether they are consistent with the single best meaning of the relevant statutory text. The Departments will not rely upon these guidance documents in their enforcement of federal civil rights laws, including Titles IV and VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (Title IV and Title VI),
42 U.S.C. 2000c
et seq.
and 2000d
et seq.
, the Equal Educational Opportunities Act of 1974 (EEOA),
20 U.S.C. 1701-1720
, the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 (ADA),
42 U.S.C. 12101
et seq.
, and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 (Section 504),
29 U.S.C. 794
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
John Mertens, Acting Chief, Educational Opportunities Section, Civil Rights Division, 202-514-4092; Maria Litsakis, Acting Director, Program Legal Group, Office for Civil Rights, 800-421-3481.

v.
Guernsey Mem'l Hosp.
, 514 U.S. 87, 99 (1995)). Regardless, the Departments are concerned about confusion over the non-enforceable nature of the guidance documents and issue this clarification that the guidance documents are not enforceable.
Further, each of the guidance documents was issued prior to the Supreme Court's decision in
Loper Bright
, which held that agency interpretations must be consistent with the “single, best meaning” of the statute authorizing them. 603 U.S. at 400. For these reasons, the Departments plan to revisit the guidance documents listed in this notice in light of
Loper Bright
to determine whether they are consistent with the “single, best meaning” of the relevant federal civil rights laws enforced by the Departments. The Departments will not rely upon the guidance documents listed in this notice in their enforcement of Titles IV and Title VI, the EEOA, the ADA, and Section 504.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Explain the circumstances that make the collection of information necessary.
The collection of information is necessary to support the National Intellectual Property Rights Coordination Center's mission to combat counterfeiting, piracy, and related intellectual property crimes. The IPR Center, led by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Homeland Security Investigations, serves as the U.S. Government's clearinghouse for investigative and enforcement efforts involving intellectual property rights violations that may affect public health and safety, the U.S. economy, and national security interests.
The “Allegation of Counterfeiting and Piracy” electronic form provides a mechanism for members of the public, industry, trade associations, law
(
printed page 66867)
enforcement, and government agencies to report suspected intellectual property violations and submit investigative leads. Information collected through the form is reviewed by HSI officials at the IPR Center and may be shared, as appropriate, with IPR Center partner agencies for investigative response, deconfliction, and tactical use.
This collection enables law enforcement and regulatory agencies to identify suspected perpetrators, assess allegations involving counterfeiting, piracy, and commercial trade fraud, and coordinate enforcement activities more efficiently. It also helps reduce duplicative federal investigative efforts, improve interagency communication, and support protection of the public and affected industries.
The collection is authorized under HSI's enforcement authorities, including
19 U.S.C. 1589a
and
1509
, and DHS's records management authority under
44 U.S.C. 3101
. Information collected may also be subject to applicable privacy, trade secret, and confidential commercial information protections, including the Privacy Act of 1974,
5 U.S.C. 552a
;
18 U.S.C. 1905
; and
19 CFR 103.35
.
Indicate how, by whom, and for what purpose the information is to be used.
The information is collected from members of the public (including industry right-holders and trade associations), as well as federal, state, local and tribal law enforcement, and government agencies. Such information is provided on a voluntary basis and through the use of an electronic form accessible via clicking the “Report IP Theft” button located on multiple websites, including the
WWW.IPRCENTER.GOV
website. Once completed, the Form is electronically transmitted to the IPR Center for review, analysis and deconfliction among the IPR Center partner agencies, as appropriate. If the submitted form contains information relevant to entities outside of the IPR Center, the information is provided to the applicable agency for review and action, as appropriate and in accordance with any applicable laws, regulations, directives, policies, or procedures applicable to information sharing.
Both IPR Center partners and non-partners who receive information from the Form query their respective databases, analyze the results, and respond to the IPR Center as to whether they have a potential matching record to deconflict and/or jurisdictional interest in the matter.
Describe whether, and to what extent, the collection of information involves the use of automated, electronic, mechanical, or other technological collection techniques or other forms of information technology, e.g., permitting electronic submission of responses, and the basis for the decision for adopting this means of collection.
The Form is used as part of an automated allegation and deconfliction program. The Form is completed and submitted electronically. In addition to permitting IPR Center partners to review potential leads involving IP infringement, the Form reduces and minimizes any burden to members of the public and is part of an automated referral process to the IPR Center.
If the collection of information impacts small businesses or other small entities.
The use of the Form does not have a significant economic impact on small businesses or other small entities. The Form is used as part of an automated allegation and deconfliction program and is completed and submitted electronically as part of the IPR Center's automated program.
Describe the consequence to Federal program or policy activities if the collection is not conducted or is conducted less frequently, as well as any technical or legal obstacles to reducing burden.
If the information is not collected, HSI's ability to provide a comprehensive and coordinated response to intellectual property rights crimes would be severely limited.
Describe any assurance of confidentiality provided to respondents and the basis for the assurance in statute, regulation, or agency policy.
The SharePoint site may contain the Sensitive Personally Identifiable Information (SPII) of complainants, victims, witnesses, and alleged violators; as well as the Personally Identifiable Information (PII) of ICE personnel who may access the site, as appropriate. The SharePoint site will comport with the requirements for SharePoint as established by the ICE Office of Chief Information Officer (OCIO). This collection of information will be covered by the National Intellectual Property Rights Coordination Center Privacy Impact Assessment and the existing DHS/ICE-009 External Investigations System of Records Notice.
Explain the reasons for any program changes or adjustments reporting in Items 13 or 14 of the OMB Form 83-I.
There has been an update in the number of collections expected for OMB Form 83-I. The increase in collections has led to an overall increase in burden costs.

50 CFR Part 679
[Docket No. 260305-0067; RTID 0648-XF991]
AGENCY:
National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Commerce.
ACTION:
Temporary rule; closure.
SUMMARY:
NMFS is prohibiting directed fishing for Pacific cod by catcher vessels using trawl gear in the Central Regulatory Area of the Gulf of Alaska (GOA). This action is necessary to prevent exceeding the 2026 total allowable catch (TAC) of Pacific cod allocated to catcher vessels using trawl gear in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA.
DATES:
Effective 1200 hours, Alaska local time (A.l.t.), October 21, 2026, through 2400 hours, A.l.t., December 31, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Abby Jahn, 907-586-7228.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
NMFS manages the groundfish fishery in the GOA exclusive economic zone according to the Fishery Management Plan for Groundfish of the GOA (FMP) prepared and recommended by the North Pacific Fishery Management Council under authority of the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (Magnuson-Stevens Act). Regulations governing fishing by U.S. vessels in accordance with the FMP appear at subpart H of
50 CFR part 600
and
50 CFR part 679
.
The annual 2026 Pacific cod TAC allocated to catcher vessels using trawl gear in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA not participating in the cooperative fishery of the Rockfish Program is 7,782 metric tons (mt) as established by the final 2026 and 2027 harvest specifications for groundfish in the GOA (
91 FR 11902
, March 11, 2026).
The Regional Administrator, Alaska Region, NMFS (Regional Administrator) has determined that the annual 2026 Pacific cod TAC allocated to catcher vessels using trawl gear in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA will be, or has been, reached. Therefore, in accordance with § 679.20(d)(1)(i) and (d)(1)(ii)(B), the Regional Administrator is establishing a directed fishing allowance of 5,782 mt and is setting aside the remaining 2,000 mt as incidental catch to support other anticipated groundfish fisheries. The Regional Administrator finds that this directed fishing allowance will be or has been reached. Consequently, in accordance with § 679.20(d)(1)(iii), NMFS is prohibiting directed fishing for Pacific cod caught by catcher vessels using trawl gear in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA to prevent exceeding this sector's annual allocation of Pacific cod TAC.
While this closure is effective the maximum retainable amounts at § 679.20(e) and (f) apply at any time during a trip. This closure does not apply to fishing by vessels participating in the cooperative fishery of the Rockfish Program in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA.
Classification
NMFS issues this action pursuant to section 305(d) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act. This action is required by
50 CFR part 679
, which was issued pursuant to section 304(b) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act, and is exempt from review under
Executive Order 12866
.
Pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B)
, there is good cause to waive prior notice and an opportunity for public comment on this action, as notice and comment would be impracticable and contrary to the public interest, as it would prevent NMFS from responding to the most recent fisheries data on the catch of Pacific cod in a timely fashion and would delay the closure of Pacific cod by catcher vessels using trawl gear in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA. NMFS was unable to publish a notice providing time for public comment because the most recent, relevant data regarding catch of Pacific cod by catcher vessels using trawl gear in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA only became available as of October 20, 2026.
There is good cause under
5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3)
to establish an effective date less than 30 days after date of publication. This finding is based upon the reasons provided above for waiver of prior notice and opportunity for public comment.

16 U.S.C. 1801
et seq.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
FDA is announcing the availability of a final guidance for industry entitled “Questions and Answers Regarding Mandatory Cosmetics Recalls: Guidance for Industry.” The purpose of this guidance document is to provide guidance to industry on the implementation of the mandatory cosmetics recall provisions of section 611 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, which was added by section 3502 of the Modernization of Cosmetics Regulation Act of 2022. The guidance is in the form of Questions and Answers and provides answers to common questions that might arise about these mandatory recall provisions and FDA's current thinking regarding their implementation.
In the
Federal Register
of December 18, 2025 (
90 FR 59129
), FDA announced the availability of the draft guidance entitled “Questions and Answers Regarding Mandatory Cosmetics Recalls; Draft Guidance for Industry.”
FDA received seven comments on the draft guidance, which were broadly supportive of the guidance, and some of which asked for certain clarifications of issues discussed in the guidance. After considering the comments we received, we are publishing the guidance as drafted with no substantive changes. The guidance announced in this notice finalizes the draft guidance dated December 18, 2025.
This guidance is being issued consistent with FDA's good guidance practices regulation (
21 CFR 10.115
). The guidance represents the current thinking of FDA on mandatory cosmetics recalls. It does not establish any rights for any person and is not binding on FDA or the public. You can use an alternative approach if it satisfies the requirements of the applicable statutes and regulations.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
If the Secretary selects an applicant for verification, the applicant's Institutional Student Information Record (ISIR) includes flags that indicate (1) that the applicant has been selected by the Secretary for verification and (2) the verification tracking group in which the applicant has been placed. The verification tracking group indicates which FAFSA information needs to be verified for the applicant and, if appropriate, for the applicant's parent(s) or spouse. The FAFSA Submission Summary indicates that the applicant's FAFSA information has been selected for verification and directs the applicant to contact the institution for further instructions for completing the verification process.
In accordance with the Fostering Undergraduate Talent by Unlocking Resources for Education (FUTURE) Act, much of the applicant's tax return information, including information from their spouse and/or parents, will come directly from the IRS and will not be viewable by the student and other contributors. Such information that is transferred and not edited will essentially be verified and need no further verification. However, for instances where income and tax information cannot be obtained directly from the IRS, the applicant will have to manually enter the necessary information into the FAFSA form, and that manual entry may be subject to verification.
The following chart lists, for the 2027-2028 award year, the FAFSA information that an institution and an applicant and, if appropriate, the applicant's parent(s) or spouse may be required to verify under
34 CFR 668.56
. The chart also lists the acceptable documentation that must, under § 668.57, be provided to an institution for that information to be verified.

SUMMARY:
NMFS is prohibiting directed fishing for pollock in Statistical Area 620 in the Gulf of Alaska (GOA). This action is necessary to prevent exceeding the annual 2026 total allowable catch (TAC) of pollock in Statistical Area 620 in the GOA.
DATES:
Effective 1200 hours, Alaska local time (A.l.t.), October 21, 2026 through 2400 hours, A.l.t., December 31, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Abby Jahn, 907-586-7228.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
NMFS manages the groundfish fishery in the GOA exclusive economic zone according to the Fishery Management Plan for Groundfish of the Gulf of Alaska (FMP) prepared and recommended by the North Pacific Fishery Management Council under
(
printed page 66793)
authority of the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (Magnuson-Stevens Act). Regulations governing fishing by U.S. vessels in accordance with the FMP appear at subpart H of
50 CFR part 600
and
50 CFR part 679
.
The annual 2026 TAC of pollock in Statistical Area 620 in the GOA is 60,477 metric tons (mt) as established by the final 2026 and 2027 harvest specifications for groundfish in the GOA (
91 FR 11902
, March 11, 2026).
The Regional Administrator, Alaska Region, NMFS (Regional Administrator) has determined that the annual 2026 TAC of pollock in Statistical Area 620 in the GOA will be or has been reached. Therefore, in accordance with § 679.20(d)(1)(i) and 679.20(d)(1)(ii)(B), the Regional Administrator is establishing a directed fishing allowance of 60,277 mt and is setting aside the remaining 200 mt as incidental catch because it is necessary to support other anticipated groundfish fisheries. The Regional Administrator finds that this directed fishing allowance will be or has been reached. Consequently, in accordance with § 679.20(d)(1)(iii), NMFS is prohibiting directed fishing for pollock in Statistical Area 620 in the GOA to prevent exceeding the annual apportionment of pollock TAC for this area.
While this closure is effective, the maximum retainable amounts at § 679.20(e) and (f) apply at any time during a trip.
Classification
NMFS issues this action pursuant to section 305(d) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act. This action is required by
50 CFR part 679
, which was issued pursuant to section 304(b) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act, and is exempt from review under
Executive Order 12866
.
Pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B)
, there is good cause to waive prior notice and an opportunity for public comment on this action, as notice and comment would be impracticable and contrary to the public interest, as it would prevent NMFS from responding to the most recent fisheries data on pollock catch in a timely fashion, and would delay the closure of directed fishing for pollock in Statistical Area 620 in the GOA. NMFS was unable to publish a notice providing time for public comment because the most recent, relevant data on pollock catch in Statistical Area 620 in the GOA only became available as of October 21, 2026.
There is good cause under
5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3)
to establish an effective date less than 30 days after date of publication. This finding is based upon the reasons provided above for waiver of prior notice and opportunity for public comment.

ACTION:

SUMMARY:
The Department of the Treasury (Treasury) is issuing this proposed rule to carry out the purposes of section 1001 of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act (the Act or the ROAD Act). Section 1001 of the ROAD Act prohibits large institutional investors from purchasing single-family homes, subject to certain exceptions.
(
printed page 66800)
The proposed rule would clarify certain terms relevant to those restrictions, including “large institutional investor”; clarify the application of certain exceptions from the statutory prohibition; and clarify the statutory enforcement mechanism. The proposed rule is intended to provide clarity to market participants and other stakeholders on the application of the statute before the effective date of the ROAD Act.
DATES:
Comments on this notice of proposed rulemaking must be received on or before November 23, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Written comments may be submitted through one of two methods:
Electronic Submission:
Comments may be submitted electronically through the Federal Government eRulemaking portal at

.

Send to U.S. Department of the Treasury, Attention: Office of Capital Markets, 1500 Pennsylvania Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20220.
Given potential delays in the receipt of comments by mail, we strongly encourage all comments to be submitted via
https://www.regulations.gov
.
All comments should be captioned “Restrictions on Large Institutional Investor Purchases of Single-Family Homes.” Please include your name, organizational affiliation, address, email address, and telephone number in your comment. In general, all comments received, including attachments and other supporting materials, will be part of the public record and subject to public disclosure. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Introduction and Overview
A. Statutory Background and Authority
Section 1001 of the ROAD Act,
[
1
]
enacted on July 11, 2026, is intended to promote homeownership opportunities for American families by prohibiting purchases of single-family homes by large institutional investors,
[
2
]
subject to specified “excepted purchases.” The statute defines “excepted purchase” to include purchases made pursuant to a build-to-rent program, renovate-to-rent program, homeownership program, or program to boost homeownership, among others.
[
3
]
In appropriate circumstances, these excepted activities can support or increase the nation's housing supply without reducing the availability of single-family homes for families and other owner-occupants.
The ROAD Act authorizes Treasury, in consultation with the Secretary of Housing and Urban Development, the Director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency, and the Chair of the Securities and Exchange Commission, to issue regulations to carry out the purposes of section 1001, including regulations to “(i) minimize market disruptions upon identifying a risk of material negative impact on the housing market, including an impact on the ability of market participants to dispose of single-family homes in an orderly fashion; and (ii) mitigate, to the extent possible, negative impacts on consumers and communities.”
[
4
]
Treasury's regulations may not “amend the definitions” of certain terms that are defined in the statute.
[
5
]
The statute's requirements and prohibitions take effect on the date that is 180 days after the date of enactment of the Act (
i.e.,
on January 7, 2027).
B. Purpose of the Proposed Rule
Treasury is issuing this proposed rule in order to promote clarity for market participants and other stakeholders regarding the restrictions in section 1001 of the ROAD Act. Treasury may subsequently engage in additional rulemakings regarding other aspects of the statute.
This proposed rule is intended to clarify the meaning and application of certain terms that are used but not defined in the Act. Specifically, the proposed rule clarifies terms used in the statutory definitions of “excepted purchase” and “large institutional investor”: “program,” “build-to-rent program,” “renovate-to-rent program,” “homeownership program,” “program to boost homeownership,” “engaged in the business of,” “passive investor,” “purchase price of the single-family home,” and “structural or core system.” Treasury also proposes to clarify the scope of excepted purchases made pursuant to sections 1001(a)(2)(F), (G), and (H) of the Act, which relate to certain purchases in connection with the satisfaction of debts previously contracted; certain purchases for the purpose of loss mitigation or compliance with servicing or investor obligations; and certain purchases from another large institutional investor. Finally, Treasury proposes to clarify the calculation of the maximum civil penalty for a purchase made in violation of the Act by more than one large institutional investor.
The proposed rule is intended to assist market participants and other stakeholders in determining whether particular acquisition structures, contractual arrangements, and purchase programs are consistent with the ROAD Act.
[
6
]
C. Phased Rulemaking Approach
The purchase prohibition in section 1001 of the ROAD Act becomes effective 180 days after enactment.
[
7
]
Given this short implementation period and the need for market participants to make decisions regarding homebuilding, acquisitions, ownership structures, investment arrangements, and compliance systems, Treasury currently intends to take a phased rulemaking approach.
This proposed rule is the first phase, focusing on issues that Treasury believes would be beneficial to address as soon as possible to provide clarity and minimize market disruptions.
Treasury expects to consider engaging in future rulemakings to address other aspects of section 1001 of the ROAD Act, such as other statutory excepted-purchase categories, compliance procedures, reporting and recordkeeping, and enforcement actions.
D. Overview of the Proposed Rule
Following are brief summaries of the provisions of the proposed rule. For further explanation, see the discussion in section II below.
Proposed § 36.1 sets forth the authority, purpose, and scope of Part 36.
Proposed § 36.2 defines certain key terms for use in Part 36. Proposed § 36.2 defines “property control right” to mean a right, including a consent, approval, veto, or other right, that gives an entity the ability to make, direct, or prevent a second entity's decisions, directly or indirectly, related to the purchase, sale, holding, leasing, renovation, or management of a single-family home. As discussed below, this term is relevant within the proposed definition of “passive investor.” Proposed § 36.2 also defines “purchase price of the property”
(
printed page 66801)
and “purchase price of the single-family home.” These definitions are intended to distinguish the total amount paid to purchase a property, including the land on which the single-family home is situated, from the portion of that amount attributable to the structure for purposes of applying the renovate-to-rent exception. Proposed § 36.2 also defines “structural or core system,” based on the Department of Housing and Urban Development's (HUD's) residential building-code comparison framework for identifying systems or areas that affect structural integrity, habitability, life safety, or major building systems.
Proposed § 36.3 would define “program” for purposes of the statutory definition of “excepted purchase,” which refers to four categories of program-based excepted purchases: build-to-rent programs, renovate-to-rent programs, homeownership programs, and programs to boost homeownership. Under the proposal, a program would mean a set of written policies or written procedures that are adopted before the purchase of single-family homes pursuant to such program and are reasonably designed and implemented to ensure that all purchases of single-family homes pursuant to the program satisfy the applicable requirements of the Act, Part 36, and the program.
Proposed § 36.5 would clarify when a build-to-rent program meets the statutory requirements. Under the proposed rule, a build-to-rent program is a program pursuant to which purchased single-family homes have not been occupied by an owner-occupant before being purchased, are purchased within 18 months of the single-family home receiving its certificate of occupancy, and, after the purchase, are first occupied by renters.
Proposed § 36.6 would clarify when a renovate-to-rent program meets the statutory requirements. Under the proposal, a renovate-to-rent program is a program pursuant to which a large institutional investor substantially rehabilitates single-family homes that do not meet structural or core system elements of local building codes at the time of purchase, resolves all material deficiencies, and makes improvements to each single-family home in an aggregate dollar amount of not less than 15 percent of the purchase price of the single-family home. Proposed § 36.6 also would provide a non-exclusive safe harbor for the substantial-rehabilitation requirement, if the large institutional investor makes improvements in an aggregate amount of not less than 10 percent of the purchase price of the single-family home on structural or core system elements and resolves all material deficiencies in such elements.
Proposed § 36.7 would clarify when a homeownership program meets the statutory requirements for that program. Under the proposal, a homeownership program would be a program pursuant to which a large institutional investor enters into contracts with renters to rent single-family homes purchased by the large institutional investor, where those contracts include certain terms relating to rental payments and fees and provide for specified consumer-credit treatment, positive reporting of rental payments, meaningful financial support for the purchase of the single-family home, the renter's right to purchase the single-family home, and the continuation of the homeownership program's terms in the event the home is sold to another large institutional investor. Proposed § 36.7 would also provide a non-exclusive safe harbor for determining whether a large institutional investor has provided meaningful financial support for the purchase of the single-family home.
Proposed § 36.8 would clarify when a program to boost homeownership meets the statutory requirements. Under the proposal, such a program would be a program pursuant to which a large institutional investor enters into contracts with renters to rent single-family homes purchased by the large institutional investor, where those contracts include certain terms relating to positive reporting of rental payments, a right of first refusal and 30-day first-look period, meaningful financial support for the renter's purchase of a single-family home, and the continuation of the program's terms in the event the home is sold to another large institutional investor. Proposed § 36.8 would also provide a non-exclusive safe harbor for determining whether a large institutional investor has provided meaningful financial support, a right of first refusal, and 30-day first-look period.
Proposed § 36.9 would clarify when a large institutional investor purchases a single-family home under the statutory exception for the satisfaction of certain debts previously contracted. Under the proposed rule, this category would include certain direct purchases by a large institutional investor in connection with the satisfaction of debts previously contracted by that large institutional investor, and certain indirect purchases by a large institutional investor from another person or entity that purchased the single-family home in connection with the satisfaction of debts previously contracted.
Proposed § 36.10 would clarify when a large institutional investor purchases a single-family home in accordance with the statutory exception for purchases for the purpose of loss mitigation or compliance with servicing or investor obligations. Under the proposed rule, this category would apply where the purchase is undertaken by a mortgage servicer, lender, or other entity that has a legal right to a single-family home for the purpose of loss mitigation or compliance with servicing or investor obligations, and not as a long-term investment strategy, and is solely as a result of specified default-related events. The proposed rule would also address purchases directly (by such a mortgage servicer, lender, or other entity) or indirectly (from such a mortgage servicer, lender, or other entity).
Proposed § 36.11 would clarify when a large institutional investor purchases a single-family home from another large institutional investor pursuant to section 1001(a)(2)(H) of the Act. Under the proposal, such a purchase would be an excepted purchase if the selling large institutional investor either owned the single-family home on the date of enactment of the Act or purchased the single-family home in compliance with the Act, including in a purchase from another large institutional investor under section 1001(a)(2)(H).
Proposed § 36.15 would clarify when an entity is engaged, in whole or in part, in the business of investing in, owning, renting, managing, or holding single-family homes for purposes of section 1001(a)(3)(A)(i)(I) of the Act. Under the proposal, an entity would fall within this scope if it invests, directly or indirectly, in, owns, rents, manages, or holds single-family homes for the purpose, in whole or in part, of receiving investment gains, rental income, management fees, or any other type of income or financial gain. Proposed § 36.15 would also clarify that an entity is not engaged in that business if the entity, directly or indirectly, invests in, owns, rents, manages, or holds single-family homes solely on a temporary and incidental basis in furtherance of a different bona fide business, only to the extent reasonably necessary for the conduct of such other bona fide business, and not as a regular or continuing investment strategy or portfolio management activity.
Proposed § 36.16 would define “passive investor” for purposes of section 1001(a)(3)(B)(iv) of the Act. Under the proposed rule, an entity would be a passive investor in a second entity only if it satisfies certain conditions relating to director and
(
printed page 66802)
management overlap and property control rights.
Proposed § 36.17 would clarify enforcement of the statutory restrictions under section 1001(d) of the Act, which provides for civil penalties of up to the greater of $1 million or three times the purchase price of the property. Under the proposed rule, a purchase of a single-family home that violates section 1001(b) of the Act with respect to more than one large institutional investor would be deemed a single violation for purposes of calculating the maximum civil penalty under section 1001(d)(1) of the Act. This provision is intended to prevent any single purchase of a single-family home from resulting in total penalties exceeding the statutory limit due to more than one large institutional investor being involved in the purchase.
Finally, proposed § 36.18 includes a severability provision.
II. Section-by-Section Discussion
A. Authority, Purpose, and Scope (Proposed § 36.1)
Proposed § 36.1 sets forth the authority, purpose, and scope of proposed Part 36.
The authority for Part 36 is section 1001 of the Act. Paragraph (b) notes that the Act authorizes Treasury to issue regulations to carry out the purposes of section 1001 of the Act.
B. Definitions (Proposed § 36.2)
1. Act or ROAD Act
The proposed rule defines “Act” or “ROAD Act” to mean the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, as amended from time to time.
2. Property Control Rights
The proposed rule defines “property control right” as “a right, including a consent, approval, veto, or other right, that gives an entity the ability to make, direct, or prevent a second entity's decisions, directly or indirectly, related to the purchase, sale, holding, leasing, renovation, or management of a single-family home.” This term is used in proposed § 36.16, which relates to passive investors for purposes of section 1001(a)(3)(B)(iv) of the Act, as discussed in section II.L below.
The proposed definition is intended to identify rights that provide an investor with an ability to control an entity's decisions regarding single-family homes it owns. An investor may have such authority, and therefore not be a passive investor, even if the investor does not own a majority of the entity's voting interests and does not have formal management authority over the entity.
The proposed formulation is intended to encompass the variety of rights that arise under investment agreements, limited partnership agreements, and other relevant structures. An investor may have the ability to make a decision itself, to direct the second entity or its manager to make or not make a decision, or to prevent a decision through a consent, approval, veto, or other right. Such rights appear to be inconsistent with passive investor status. The proposed definition focuses on rights related to a second entity's decisions to purchase, sell, hold, lease, renovate, or manage a single-family home. These decisions are central to the statutory framework because they affect whether and how a large institutional investor acquires, operates, retains, improves, or disposes of single-family homes.
Under the proposed rule, the definition would focus on rights related to single-family homes; as a result, investor rights unrelated to single-family homes would not generally be considered a property control right. Similarly, an investor's right to reduce or liquidate its investment would not generally be considered a property control right, even if it indirectly results in the sale of single-family homes by the second entity. Commercial contracts include various rights that protect the parties' interests, such as payment rights, default remedies, information rights, audit rights, inspection rights, and standard covenants, that would not generally be considered property control rights under the proposed definition. This approach is intended to avoid disrupting an investor's portfolio-level control of its investments.
The proposed definition focuses on the effect of the right rather than the label assigned to the right. A right may constitute a property control right even if it is described as a consent right, approval right, veto right, consultation right, covenant, restriction, or similar arrangement. The proposed definition does not set forth an exhaustive list of types of relevant rights. Contractual arrangements vary widely, and a fixed list would be both overinclusive and underinclusive.
Treasury is not proposing a safe harbor for minority-investor protective rights, because such arrangements may provide an entity with control over a second entity's purchases, sales, holdings, leases, renovations, or management of single-family homes.
Treasury invites comments on all aspects of the definition of “property control right.” In particular, Treasury seeks comment on the following aspects of the proposed rule:
Question 1: Is the proposed definition appropriate? How could it be modified to better accomplish the statutory purposes while minimizing market disruptions and mitigating negative impacts on consumers and communities? Are there ways in which the definition is either overinclusive or underinclusive?
Question 2: Is it appropriate for the definition of “property control right” to focus on an entity's decisions to purchase, sell, hold, lease, renovate, or manage a single-family home?
Question 3: Are the terms “make,” “direct,” and “prevent” in the proposed definition sufficiently clear?
Question 4: Should the definition include examples of rights that do or do not constitute property control rights? If so, what examples would be appropriate?
Question 5: Should any exclusions be added to the definition? How should such exclusions be framed to avoid creating opportunities for evasion of the statutory requirements?
Question 6: Should rights that become exercisable only after default, or a similar event, be treated differently from rights exercisable in the ordinary course of business?
Question 7: Should rights held by lenders, mortgage servicers, vendors, or similar entities be treated differently from rights held by investors?
3. Purchase Price of the Property
Treasury is proposing to define “purchase price of the property” to mean “the total amount paid by an entity to purchase a single-family home, including the amount paid for the land on which the single-family home is situated.” This definition is used (i) to calculate the “purchase price of the single-family home,” (ii) in the proposed rule's provisions regarding homeownership programs and programs to boost homeownership, and (iii) to calculate the statutory limit on civil penalties in enforcement actions.
Purchases of single-family homes generally include both the residential structure and the land on which the structure is situated. Accordingly, the statutory exception for renovate-to-rent programs requires “improvements in an aggregate dollar amount of not less than 15 percent of the purchase price of the single-family home,”
[
8
]
while the statutory limit on civil penalties is based on “the purchase price of the property involved.”
[
9
]
Treasury believes it is appropriate to distinguish between these statutory terms as contemplated
(
printed page 66803)
by the proposed definition, which distinguishes between the total amount paid in a real estate transaction and the portion of that amount attributable to the single-family home itself. Treasury preliminarily believes the Act's reference to “purchase price of the property” refers to the amount paid for both the single-family-home structure and the associated land.
The proposed definition of “purchase price of the property” refers to the amount paid by the purchaser, which provides an objective and administrable figure.
Treasury invites comments on all aspects of the definition of “purchase price of the property.” In particular, Treasury seeks comment on the following aspects of the proposed rule:
Question 8: Is the proposed definition of “purchase price of the property” appropriate and clear? How could it be modified to better accomplish the statutory purposes while minimizing market disruptions and mitigating negative impacts on consumers and communities? Should the rule distinguish between “purchase price of the property” and “purchase price of the single-family home”?
Question 9: Should the definition be modified to address whether the “total amount paid” includes factors such as non-cash consideration, assumed liabilities, closing costs, transaction costs, seller credits, or other adjustments? If so, how? How should the definition account for the full scope of the definition of “purchase” including “mergers, acquisitions, construction, foreclosures, or bulk purchases, whether or not for cash consideration”?
Question 10: Should the definition be modified to provide different rules for portfolio purchases, bulk purchases, purchases involving multiple structures, or purchases involving a single contract price for multiple single-family homes?
Question 11: Is it practicable to calculate the purchase price of the property, as defined in this proposed rule, in an objective and consistent manner? What modifications to the definition could be made to increase its administrability and consistent application?
4. Purchase Price of the Single-Family Home
Treasury is proposing to define “purchase price of the single-family home” to mean “the portion of the purchase price of the property attributable to the value of the structure, as calculated by subtracting the tax-assessed value of the land at the time of the purchase on which the single-family home is situated from the purchase price of the property.” This term is used in the exception for renovate-to-rent programs.
This definition is intended to provide a clear and simple method for calculating the purchase price of a single-family home. As noted above in the context of the definition of “purchase price of the property,” Treasury believes it is appropriate, in the purchase of a single-family home, to distinguish between the purchase price of the structure and the total amount paid for the structure and land together. Further, the Act's definition of “single-family home” refers to “a structure,” so it is appropriate for the “purchase price of the single-family home” to mean the purchase price of the “structure,” rather than the value of associated land. In addition, the renovate-to-rent exception is focused on substantial rehabilitation of single-family homes that do not meet structural or core system elements of local building codes, and a denominator focused on the value of the structure is better aligned with that statutory construct than a denominator that includes the value of the purchased land.
The proposed definition, which subtracts the tax-assessed value of land at the time of purchase, is intended to provide an administrable method for determining the portion of the purchase price attributable to the structure. Tax-assessed land values generally provide a transaction-specific, location-specific measure that may be more reliable and administrable than other valuation methods, such as appraisals.
Treasury recognizes, however, that tax assessment practices vary across jurisdictions. In some jurisdictions, land and improvement values may be separately assessed. In others, the relevant assessed values may not be current, may be subject to assessment limitations, may be under appeal, or may not be available at the time of purchase. Treasury alternatively considered deducting from the purchase price of the property an amount that is proportionate to the amount of the total tax-assessed value attributable to land, but that approach creates the risk of overly complicating the calculation and creating more uncertainty than the proposed definition.

5. Structural or Core System
a. Overview of Definition
Proposed § 36.2 would define “structural or core system” to mean “systems or areas of a single-family home that substantially affect structural integrity, habitability, life safety, or the functioning of major building systems, which may include fire safety, light and ventilation, structural loads and seismic design, foundation systems, materials standards, construction components, glass, mechanical, plumbing, and electrical.” This definition is intended to clarify the scope of the renovate-to-rent exception in section 1001(a)(2)(C) of the Act, which applies to purchases made pursuant to a renovate-to-rent program that substantially rehabilitates single-family homes “that do not meet structural or core system elements of local building codes” and makes improvements in an aggregate dollar amount of not less than 15 percent of the purchase price of the single-family home.
[
10
]
The proposed definition is intended, for purposes of the Act's renovate-to-rent exception, to clarify the types of building-code deficiencies that qualify as structural or core system elements and distinguish these improvements from cosmetic improvements, ordinary turnover work, routine maintenance, or discretionary upgrades. A deficiency would not qualify merely because the
(
printed page 66804)
home is outdated, requires routine repairs, could benefit from modernization, or fails to satisfy a building-code requirement not related to structural integrity, habitability, life safety, or the functioning of major building systems. For example, ordinary painting, flooring replacement, landscaping, appliance upgrades, cabinet or countertop replacement, or other cosmetic or marketability improvements generally would not involve structural or core systems.
Treasury recognizes that renovation projects may include both qualifying and non-qualifying work under this definition. A project that involves substantial repairs to structural or core systems as well as incidental related demolition, finish work, restoration, or other work necessary to complete the rehabilitation would also qualify. Cosmetic work or other work unrelated to repairs to structural or core systems would not fall within the proposed definition.
A large institutional investor seeking to rely on the renovate-to-rent exception would need to identify deficiencies that result in the single-family home not meeting structural or core system elements (as defined in the proposed rule) of applicable local building codes. Notably, this definition and the related excepted purchase standard do not replace or displace applicable local building codes.
b. Use of HUD Residential Building-Code Comparison Framework
The proposed definition is based on HUD's residential building-code comparison framework under
24 CFR 200.926
and
200.926a
. Treasury believes that incorporating existing standards from HUD will minimize administrative burdens and potential disruptions to existing construction practices. HUD's regulations provide that, when evaluating local building codes, HUD compares those codes to the areas listed in
24 CFR 200.926a
. The listed major areas include fire safety, light and ventilation, structural loads and seismic design, foundation systems, materials standards, construction components, glass, mechanical, plumbing, and electrical.
Treasury is not proposing to incorporate HUD's minimum property standards wholesale or to make eligibility for the renovate-to-rent exception dependent on whether a property satisfies standards applicable to HUD mortgage insurance or other HUD programs. Rather, as reflected in the proposed definition, Treasury proposes to use the categories in HUD's framework as a reference point for identifying the types of local building-code elements that should be treated as structural or core systems for purposes of the renovate-to-rent category of excepted purchases under the Act.
Treasury believes this approach would promote consistency across jurisdictions nationwide. Local codes vary in terminology, organization, and scope. The proposed definition would provide a federal reference for the relevant categories of code requirements.
The proposed definition is intended to exclude single-family homes that have only cosmetic deficiencies or need only routine repairs rather than repairs to structural or core system deficiencies. For example, ordinary painting, flooring replacement, landscaping, appliance upgrades, cabinet replacement, countertop replacement, or other cosmetic or marketability improvements generally would not, standing alone, involve structural or core systems unless the work is necessary to address a covered local building-code deficiency relating to structural integrity, habitability, life safety, or a major building system.
At the same time, Treasury recognizes that renovation projects may include both qualifying and non-qualifying work. A project may involve repairs to structural or core systems as well as related demolition, finish work, restoration, or other work necessary to complete the rehabilitation, which would also qualify. Purely cosmetic work or other work unrelated to repairs to structural or core systems would not be considered within scope for purposes of this definition.

C. Program (Proposed § 36.3)
1. Overview of “Program”
Proposed § 36.3 would define “program” to mean a set of written policies or written procedures that are (i) adopted before the purchase of single-family homes pursuant to such program; and (ii) reasonably designed and implemented to ensure that all purchases of single-family homes pursuant to the program satisfy the applicable requirements of the Act, Part 36, and the program.
The Act uses the term “program” in the context of excepted purchases under build-to-rent programs, renovate-to-rent programs, homeownership programs, and programs to boost homeownership. The proposed definition of “program” would apply to each of these categories and reflects Treasury's view of the best interpretation of the statutory term, given the context in the Act and the need for a clear and objective standard.
Under the proposed definition, the relevant program must be tailored to the excepted-purchase category on which the large institutional investor intends to rely. For example, a build-to-rent program should be reasonably designed and implemented to ensure that all purchases satisfy the new-construction and rental property requirements; a renovate-to-rent program should be reasonably designed to ensure that all purchases satisfy applicable rehabilitation, local building-code deficiency, structural or core system, and improvement requirements; a homeownership program should be reasonably designed to ensure that all purchases satisfy the rental payment, consumer-credit treatment, positive rent reporting, meaningful financial support, purchase-right, and transfer-related requirements; and a program to boost homeownership should be reasonably designed to ensure that all purchases satisfy the positive rent reporting, right of first refusal and first-look, meaningful financial support, and transfer-related requirements. Therefore, the proposed definition of “program” would apply to proposed §§ 36.5, 36.6, 36.7, and 36.8, which address the Act's program-based excepted-purchase categories.
2. Written Policies or Written Procedures
The proposed definition would require a program to be codified in
(
printed page 66805)
“written policies or written procedures.” Treasury believes that documentation of policies and procedures is necessary to distinguish a program from an ad hoc or post hoc characterization of purchases. For the same reason, Treasury proposes to require that a program be “adopted before the purchase of single-family homes pursuant to such program”: a purchase cannot be made “pursuant to” a program, as the statute requires,
[
11
]
if the program does not yet exist at the time of the purchase.
The proposed definition does not prescribe a specific form for a program's written policies and procedures. Large institutional investors vary in size, structure, geography, property type, business model, and acquisition strategy. The proposed definition is intended to provide an appropriate degree of flexibility to avoid undue burdens.
While the proposed definition does not specify in detail the content of the required policies and procedures, Treasury generally expects that such documentation would include a combination of eligibility criteria, purchase criteria, property criteria, renter criteria, rehabilitation criteria, sales criteria, approval standards, compliance standards, review workflows, transaction checklists, approval processes, escalation procedures, certifications, training materials, monitoring procedures, and audit processes.
3. Reasonably Designed and Implemented
The proposed definition would require that the program be reasonably designed and implemented to ensure that all purchases of single-family homes pursuant to the program satisfy the applicable requirements of the Act, Part 36, and the program.
A reasonably designed program should be tailored to the requirements under the Act and part 36 for the relevant category of excepted purchase. The program should include policies and procedures sufficient to identify whether a purchase is eligible, document the basis for eligibility, and prevent purchases that do not satisfy the applicable requirements from being treated and reported as excepted purchases.
Treasury expects that large institutional investors seeking to rely on program-based excepted purchases would maintain records sufficient to demonstrate that the program was implemented and that relevant purchases were made pursuant to the program. The specific records may vary depending on the program and purchase.
This definition is intended to require meaningful compliance controls without disqualifying all purchases made pursuant to a program due to isolated, good-faith failures in the effectiveness of that program with respect to other purchases. This approach is intended to preserve the availability of the statutory exceptions and to avoid unnecessary disruption to housing supply, home building, and capital formation.

D. Build-to-Rent Program (Proposed § 36.5)
1. Overview
Proposed § 36.5 would clarify when a build-to-rent program meets the requirements for an excepted purchase under section 1001(a)(2)(B) of the Act. That statutory provision states that a purchase of a single-family home is an excepted purchase if it is made “pursuant to a build-to-rent program where the large institutional investor purchases, constructs, or constructs and retains newly constructed single-family homes to be managed as a rental property, whether as part of a community made up exclusively of renter-occupied single-family homes or as part of a community made up of single-family homes that are both owner- and renter-occupied.”
As proposed, a build-to-rent program is a program (as defined in proposed § 36.3) pursuant to which purchased single-family homes (i) have not been occupied by an owner-occupant before being purchased, (ii) are purchased within 18 months of the single-family home receiving its certificate of occupancy (or equivalent); and (iii) are, after the purchase, first occupied by renters, whether as part of a community made up exclusively of renter-occupied single-family homes or as part of a community made up of single-family homes that are both owner- and renter-occupied.

12
]
The proposed rule interprets “newly constructed” as excluding homes previously occupied by an owner-occupant and “to be managed as a rental property” as requiring initial rental use, and proposes the 18-month certificate-of-occupancy criterion as an administrable line for applying those statutory standards.
The proposed rule is intended to provide an administrable means for investors to make build-to-rent purchases that maintain liquidity in the build-to-rent market and do not reduce the availability of owner-occupant housing stock.
