If a purchase of a single-family home does not meet the conditions in the proposed rule, the purchase would not be pursuant to a build-to-rent program and would not qualify for that category of excepted purchase.
2. Newly Constructed
The statutory build-to-rent exception applies to “newly constructed”
[
13
]
single-family homes. Proposed § 36.5(a) and (b) would implement this concept by requiring (i) that the home has not previously been occupied by an owner-occupant and (ii) is purchased within 18 months of the home receiving its certificate of occupancy (or equivalent).
A purchase of a home that has previously been occupied by an owner-occupant would not qualify as a purchase pursuant to a build-to-rent program. This distinction is important because the build-to-rent exception is directed at homes that are newly constructed for rental use, rather than homes that have already been part of the existing stock of owner-occupied housing. The proposed requirement would apply to occupancy before the single-family home was purchased.
Treasury preliminarily believes that a certificate of occupancy provides a clear, administrable standard for when a single-family home has been constructed. The 18-month standard in the proposed provision is intended to be an appropriate length of time for a single-family home to have been constructed before it may no longer be considered newly constructed in accordance with the Act.
Treasury has alternatively considered interpreting the statutory term “newly constructed” to be time-bound, such as covering homes constructed after enactment of the ROAD Act or homes that received their certificate of occupancy within a certain number of years. Treasury preliminarily believes that the approach in the proposed rule more appropriately construes the term “newly constructed” and covers the kinds of homes that are intended to be eligible for purchase by large institutional investors under the ROAD Act.
Treasury also considered an alternative under which a purchase of a single-family home could be made pursuant to a build-to-rent program if the single-family home was originally constructed to be rented and has remained rented. In effect, this would include existing build-to-rent properties in the scope of the build-to-rent program excepted purchase. However, interpreting “newly constructed single-family home” to include older homes that have been renter-occupied for potentially decades appears to be inconsistent with the statutory text and purpose. Because “newly constructed” and “originally constructed” are not equivalent, such an interpretation would effectively render “newly constructed” meaningless. In addition, focusing the exemption on single-family homes that are not pre-existing is consistent with the ROAD Act's goal to increase overall housing supply.
3. Managed as a Rental Property
Proposed § 36.5(c) would require that a single-family home is, after the purchase by a large institutional investor, first occupied by renters. This requirement is intended to ensure that purchases pursuant to a build-to-rent program meet the statutory requirement that they be single-family homes purchased “to be managed as a rental property”
[
14
]
—not homes purchased for resale, land banking, speculative appreciation, or other purposes. To effectuate this statutory language, the proposal would require more than a general intention to rent the single-family home. Treasury preliminarily believes that the strongest, most objective evidence that a large institutional investor purchased the single-family home “to be managed as a rental property” is that the large institutional investor actually rents the home. At the same time, proposed § 36.5 would not prohibit the large institutional investor from selling the home.

E. Renovate-to-Rent Program (Proposed § 36.6)
1. Overview
Proposed § 36.6 would clarify when a renovate-to-rent program meets the requirements for an excepted purchase under section 1001(a)(2)(C) of the Act. That statutory provision states that a purchase of a single-family home is an excepted purchase if it is made “pursuant to a renovate-to-rent program that (i) substantially rehabilitates single-family homes that do not meet structural or core system elements of local building codes; and (ii) makes improvements in an aggregate dollar amount of not less than 15 percent of the purchase price of the single-family home.”
As proposed, a renovate-to-rent program is a program (as defined in proposed § 36.3) pursuant to which the large institutional investor (i) substantially rehabilitates (including by resolving all material deficiencies in) single-family homes that do not meet structural or core system elements of local building codes at the time of purchase; and (ii) makes improvements, including those made to resolve such deficiencies, to each single-family home in an aggregate dollar amount of not less than 15 percent of the purchase price of the single-family home.
Proposed § 36.6 largely reflects the text of the Act, with limited clarifications intended to promote the purposes of the statute and provide an administrable framework for applying the renovate-to-rent exception. As specified by the Act, the exception would apply only to purchases of single-family homes that require meaningful rehabilitation of structural or core system elements, not those requiring only cosmetic improvements, ordinary turnover work, routine maintenance, or discretionary upgrades. The exception is intended to be available for purchases that restore deficient single-family homes to a condition in which they may be safely used as rental housing. Therefore, the proposed rule would require the large institutional investor to resolve all material deficiencies in single-family homes under a renovate-to-rent program.
A purchase would not qualify as made pursuant to a renovate-to-rent program merely because it is later described as having involved rehabilitation work. Instead, consistent with the proposed approach for each type of “program” described in the Act, the large institutional investor must have a program that satisfies proposed § 36.3 and must make the purchase pursuant to that program. Appropriate activities for each single-family home purchased under this exception would generally be expected to include identifying, before or at the time of purchase, whether the single-family home does not meet structural or core system elements of local building codes; determining whether those deficiencies are material; resolving all material deficiencies; and ensuring that the 15 percent threshold described above is satisfied.

2. Structural or Core System Deficiencies at the Time of Purchase
Proposed § 36.6(a)(1) would require that the single-family home not meet structural or core system elements of local building codes at the time of purchase. Making this determination as of the time of purchase is intended to comply with the Act, which contemplates the renovate-to-rent exception applying only to the purchase of single-family homes that are materially deficient when acquired. A home would not become eligible for the exception solely because of post-purchase deterioration or damage. Conversely, a single-family home that has no material deficiencies in structural or core system elements of local building codes at the time of purchase could not be substantially rehabilitated for purposes of the proposed rule.
Local building codes vary across jurisdictions, and the manner in which deficiencies are identified, documented, and resolved differs depending on local law and practice. Treasury is not proposing to establish a federal building-code enforcement regime or to displace local building officials. Rather, proposed § 36.6 would use local building codes to determine whether the home has relevant deficiencies, and proposed § 36.2 would identify the categories of local building-code elements that constitute structural or core systems for purposes of the renovate-to-rent exception.

3. Substantial Rehabilitation, Improvements, and Safe Harbor
Proposed § 36.6(a)(1) would require the large institutional investor to substantially rehabilitate the single-family home, including by resolving all material deficiencies in structural or core system elements of local building codes. This requirement is consistent with the text of the Act and is intended to ensure that the purchaser in fact rehabilitates the single-family home. A renovation that leaves material deficiencies in structural integrity, habitability, life safety, or major building systems unresolved would not constitute substantial rehabilitation for purposes of the Act or the proposed rule. The requirement for substantial rehabilitation would not be satisfied by work that merely improves marketability or increases rental value.
Proposed § 36.6(a)(2) would require the large institutional investor to make improvements, including the improvements described in proposed § 36.6(a)(1), to each single-family home in an aggregate dollar amount of not less than 15 percent of the purchase price of the single-family home. This requirement largely reflects the statutory text, with limited additions. First, the proposed rule clarifies the Act by applying this requirement to each relevant single-family home to ensure that the exception only applies as contemplated by the Act. Second, the proposed rule provides that improvements made under proposed § 36.6(a)(1) (regarding substantial rehabilitation) count toward the 15 percent threshold. Under proposed § 36.6(a)(2), all improvements by the large institutional investor, not only the improvements related to the substantial rehabilitation of the single-family home, would count toward the 15 percent threshold.
Proposed § 36.6(b) would provide that a large institutional investor that makes improvements to structural or core system elements of a single-family home that does not meet structural or core system elements of local building codes at the time of purchase in an aggregate dollar amount of not less than 10 percent of the purchase price of the single-family home, and that resolves all material deficiencies in such structural or core system elements, will be deemed to have satisfied proposed § 36.6(a)(1), which sets forth the requirements related to substantial rehabilitation. This non-exclusive safe harbor is intended to provide a clear standard for determining when a large institutional investor has substantially rehabilitated a deficient single-family home. In general, determining whether a large institutional investor has substantially rehabilitated a single-family home may depend on the facts and circumstances. Proposed § 36.6(b) would provide greater certainty in cases where a large institutional investor makes a meaningful level of improvements specifically to structural or core system elements and resolves all material deficiencies in such elements.
The proposed safe harbor provision would not reduce the statutory 15 percent improvement requirement. A large institutional investor that satisfies proposed § 36.6(b) would be deemed to have satisfied proposed § 36.6(a)(1) but would still need to satisfy proposed § 36.6(a)(2). Accordingly, if the investor makes improvements equal to 10 percent of the purchase price of the single-family home to structural or core system elements and resolves all material deficiencies in such elements, the investor would still need to make total improvements to the single-family home in an aggregate dollar amount of not less than 15 percent of the purchase price of the single-family home.
As discussed above in section II.B, proposed § 36.2 would define the term “purchase price of the single-family home,” which proposed § 36.6 would use both for the 15 percent improvement requirement in proposed § 36.6(a)(2) and for the 10 percent safe harbor threshold in proposed § 36.6(b). Using the purchase price of the single-family home, rather than the purchase price of the entire property including land, is intended to focus the renovate-to-rent exception on rehabilitation of the home itself. Land values vary significantly across jurisdictions and may bear little relationship to the cost or extent of rehabilitation needed to resolve structural or core system deficiencies. By using the purchase price of the single-family home, the proposed rule is intended to align the two percentage thresholds with the value of the structure that is being rehabilitated.

F. Homeownership Program (Proposed § 36.7)
1. Overview
Proposed § 36.7 would clarify when a homeownership program meets the requirements for an excepted purchase in section 1001(a)(2)(D) of the Act. That statutory provision states that a purchase of a single-family home is an excepted purchase if it is made pursuant to a homeownership program that (i) requires rental payments and other fees not greater than those on other similarly situated single-family homes not covered by the program; (ii) is subject to a contract between the large institutional investor and renter that is considered a consumer credit transaction secured by a dwelling or real property; (iii) provides for positive reporting of rental payments to consumer reporting agencies; and (iv) requires contribution of meaningful financial support from the large institutional investor, including price concessions, for the purchase of the single-family home by the renter.
As proposed, a homeownership program is a program (as defined in proposed § 36.3) that generally includes the provisions as described in section 1001(a)(2)(D) of the Act. The proposed rule also includes several clarifications, described below, of the statutory requirements in order to provide an administrable framework for determining when a purchase of a single-family home is made pursuant to a homeownership program.

Determining whether single-family homes are similarly situated may require consideration of facts and circumstances. Relevant factors may include location, size, number of bedrooms and bathrooms, property condition, amenities, lease term, market rent, timing of lease execution, and other features that affect rental value. Treasury is not proposing a specific comparison methodology at this time, but expects that a large institutional investor seeking to rely on the homeownership program exception would maintain records sufficient to support its determination that the renter's rental payments and other fees are not greater than those collected on other similarly situated single-family homes not covered by the program.

5. Meaningful Financial Support and Right To Purchase
As set forth in the Act, proposed § 36.7(a)(4) would require contracts under a homeownership program to require the large institutional investor to contribute meaningful financial support for the purchase of the single-family home by the renter. In addition, the proposed rule states that the contract must provide the renter the right, exercisable no later than the termination of the contract, to purchase the single-family home from the large institutional investor at a price no greater than fair market value minus the amount of such meaningful financial support.
The requirement to contribute meaningful financial support is central to distinguishing a homeownership program from an ordinary rental program. A homeownership program should provide the renter with real economic assistance in purchasing the single-family home, rather than merely providing the renter with a right to make an offer at market price. Proposed § 36.7(a)(4) would require that the renter's purchase price be reduced by the amount of meaningful financial support, ensuring that the support is reflected in the economics of the purchase.
The proposed rule would require that the renter have a right to purchase the single-family home and that such right be exercisable no later than the termination of the contract. Treasury preliminarily believes that the renter having a right to purchase the single-family home at a price no greater than fair market value minus the amount of any meaningful financial support is necessary for a homeownership program described in the Act to be meaningful. Absent such a requirement, the provision of meaningful financial support could be obviated by a large institutional investor refusing to accept an offer from a renter. The timing of this requirement is intended to ensure that the renter has a meaningful opportunity to exercise the purchase right before the contractual arrangement ends, regardless of the duration or structure of the contract. Large institutional investors could choose whether to provide the right during the term of the rental contract, at termination of the contract, or a combination thereof.
Relatedly, proposed § 36.7(b) would provide a non-exclusive safe harbor for meaningful financial support. Under the proposal, a large institutional investor would be deemed to contribute meaningful financial support for the purchase of the single-family home by a renter who has rented the single-family home for at least 5 years if, in the event the renter purchases the single-family home from the large institutional investor, the amount of such financial support is at least the lesser of (i) $5,000 or (ii) 2.5 percent if the renter has rented the single-family home for at least five years and at least 3.5 percent if the renter has rented the single-family home for at least seven years. In each case, the applicable percentage would be calculated using the lesser of (a) the purchase price of the property purchased by the renter or (b) the Federal Housing Administration's mortgage limit for a one-unit property that applies to the county where the single-family home is located and that is in effect on the date the renter purchases the single-family home. Thus, the applicable safe-harbor percentage would increase when the renter's rental reaches five and seven years.
This safe harbor is intended to promote clarity and administrability, as the statute does not specify the amount of financial support that should constitute “meaningful financial support” in a homeownership program. The proposed approach would increase with the duration of the renter's rental of the single-family home, up to a maximum of seven years, while using a county-specific reference to account for regional differences in home prices. The use of the lesser of the purchase price of the property and the applicable Federal Housing Administration mortgage limit is intended to promote meaningful financial support while limiting the extent to which the amount of support increases solely because the renter purchases a higher-priced property. This lesser-of approach is intended to provide large institutional investors with greater certainty for long-term financial projections, which may support the use of homeownership programs. The 3.5 percent amount in the proposed rule is based on the Federal Housing Administration's minimum down payment amount, as described below in the context of programs to boost homeownership. Although meaningful financial support provided pursuant to a homeownership program may not be eligible to supplement a renter's down payment under federal mortgage standards, because it may be considered an interested party contribution, Treasury believes that using the same approach for meaningful financial support in each program will simplify the rules and therefore minimize market confusion. For purposes of the safe-harbor calculation, the purchase price of the property would be determined before applying or crediting meaningful financial support. This treatment would avoid a circular calculation in which the amount of support reduces the purchase price used to calculate that same support.
The proposed rule would increase the safe-harbor amount in stages based on the renter's completed rental period. This approach is intended to balance the goal of providing progressively greater assistance to longer-term renters with the goal of encouraging large institutional investors to offer homeownership programs. Making the full 3.5 percent safe harbor amount available at the beginning of the rental relationship could discourage large institutional investors from offering such programs. Conversely, providing no safe-harbor amount until the renter
(
printed page 66811)
has completed seven years of rental could delay the renter's transition to homeownership or reduce the number of renters who ultimately receive meaningful financial support.
Treasury also believes it is appropriate to cap the amount of financial support required to satisfy the safe harbor at $5,000. This amount is intended to ensure that the financial support will be impactful for the renter's purchase of the single-family home, without making the program cost-prohibitive for large institutional investors.
Under proposed § 36.7(b)(2), to qualify for the safe harbor, the large institutional investor must not directly or indirectly recover any portion of the meaningful financial support from the renter, including by increasing the purchase price of the single-family home or imposing any expense, charge, or fee in connection with the financial support. This requirement is intended to ensure that the financial support provides a net economic benefit to the renter, as contemplated by the Act, and is not offset through an increase in the purchase price or through separately imposed costs.
Because proposed § 36.7(b) would provide a non-exclusive safe harbor, a contribution that does not satisfy the safe-harbor formula may nevertheless constitute meaningful financial support based on the facts and circumstances. This could include support provided where a renter purchases the single-family home before completing five years of the rental or where the support is structured differently than contemplated by the safe harbor, provided that the support gives the renter a real economic benefit and is not directly or indirectly recovered from the renter.

6. Termination of Financial Support
Proposed § 36.7(c) would provide that a homeownership program does not fail to satisfy proposed § 36.7(a) solely because the program allows the large institutional investor's obligation to contribute meaningful financial support under proposed § 36.7(a)(4) to terminate in any of three circumstances: (i) if, as of the scheduled date for the renter's purchase of the single-family home, the renter has failed to pay all rent then due and payable to the large institutional investor, other than amounts lawfully withheld; (ii) if the renter breaches the rental contract in a manner that permits the large institutional investor to terminate the contract under applicable law; or (iii) if the renter elects to terminate the rental contract for a purpose other than purchasing the single-family home. Proposed § 36.7(c) would not require or automatically cause the obligation to contribute meaningful financial support to terminate; instead, it would permit a homeownership program to include contractual terms allowing termination of that obligation in the specified circumstances without causing the program to fail to satisfy proposed § 36.7(a).
This approach is intended to avoid situations in which a large institutional investor is required to provide meaningful financial support to a renter who has failed to pay their rent, breached other material contractual obligations, or chosen to end the rental for a purpose other than purchasing the single-family home. The condition would not include future rent that is contemplated by the rental contract but is not yet due and payable. The proposed breach condition would not require that the large institutional investor actually evict the renter. A breach that does not permit termination of the rental contract under applicable law would not satisfy this condition. Treasury believes that the alternative of requiring a large institutional investor to actually terminate the rental contract or evict the renter in order to eliminate the requirement for meaningful financial support would create adverse incentives.

7. Transfer to Another Large Institutional Investor
Proposed § 36.7(a)(5) would require contracts under a homeownership program to provide that, if the large institutional investor sells or otherwise transfers the single-family home to another large institutional investor before termination of the contract, the transferring large institutional investor's obligations under proposed § 36.7(a)(1) through (4) are automatically deemed to be assigned to, and enforceable by the renter against, the transferee large institutional investor. The transferring large institutional investor also would be required to cause the transferee large institutional investor expressly to assume those obligations in writing and effective upon consummation of the transfer.
The relevant provision of the Act does not expressly address the continuation of homeownership program obligations when a large institutional investor sells the single-family home to another large institutional investor. Proposed § 36.7(a)(5) is intended to preserve the renter protections associated with a homeownership program and contemplated by the Act. Without such a requirement, a large institutional investor could transfer the home to another large institutional investor in a manner that eliminates the renter's rights under the program. Such a result would be inconsistent with the purpose of the statutory exception for homeownership programs.
The proposed rule would require both automatic assignment and express written assumption of the large institutional investor's obligations. Automatic assignment is intended to ensure that the renter's rights are not dependent on the parties' actions, while express written assumption would provide additional clarity and mitigate the risk of disputes regarding the transferee's obligations.

G. Program To Boost Homeownership (Proposed § 36.8)
1. Overview
Proposed § 36.8 would clarify when a program to boost homeownership meets the requirements for an excepted purchase under section 1001(a)(2)(E) of the Act. That statutory provision states that a purchase of a single-family home is an excepted purchase if it is pursuant to a program to boost homeownership that (i) provides for positive reporting of rental payments to consumer reporting agencies for any renter, who must be informed of and opts into such reporting; (ii) provides for the right of first refusal and a 30-day “first look” period; and (iii) may entail meaningful financial support from the large institutional investor, including price concessions, for the purchase of a single-family home by the renter (whether it is the home the renter occupies or another home).
As proposed, a program to boost homeownership is a program (as defined in proposed § 36.3) that generally includes the provisions as described in section 1001(a)(2)(E) of the Act. The proposed rule also includes several clarifications, described below, of the statutory requirements intended to provide an administrable framework for determining when a purchase of a single-family home is made pursuant to a program to boost homeownership, while preserving the practical availability of programs that support renters' transition to homeownership.
Under the Act and the proposed rule, a program to boost homeownership differs from a homeownership program in several important respects. Under section 1001(a)(2)(D) of the Act, a homeownership program provides for the renter to purchase “the single-family home” rented by the renter from the large institutional investor; in contrast, section 1001(a)(2)(E) of the Act provides for the renter to purchase “a single-family home,” not necessarily the home occupied by the renter.

As set forth in the Act, proposed § 36.8(a)(1) would require contracts under a program to boost homeownership to require the large institutional investor to inform the renter of the option for positive reporting of rental payments to consumer reporting agencies and to provide for such positive reporting for any renter who opts into such reporting. The proposed rule would require the large institutional investor to provide positive reporting at no charge or expense to the renter, to ensure that the renter actually receives the intended benefit of the program, as contemplated by sections 1001(a)(2)(E) and 1001(b)(4)(A)(ii) of the Act, and that such benefit is not offset by additional charges or expenses.
This requirement serves the same general purpose as the positive-reporting requirement for homeownership programs under proposed § 36.7(a)(3). The positive-reporting requirement may support renters' ability to establish or improve credit histories relevant to mortgage eligibility and a transition to homeownership. Providing that reporting without charge or expense may support homeownership.

3. Meaningful Financial Support
Proposed § 36.8(a)(3) would require contracts under a program to boost homeownership to provide for the large institutional investor to contribute meaningful financial support for the purchase of a single-family home by the renter, whether it is the home the renter occupies or another home.
(

Section 1001(a)(2)(E)(iii) of the Act states that a program to boost homeownership may entail the provision of meaningful financial support. Its reference to such support reflects the relevance of this factor to programs to boost homeownership. The statute does not mandate excepted-purchase treatment for programs that do not provide such support. Proposed § 36.8(a)(3) specifies how Treasury proposes to evaluate meaningful financial support, in order to give effect to the statutory framework for programs to boost homeownership and to promote the purpose of increasing homeownership.
The meaningful financial support provided under a program to boost homeownership, as opposed to a homeownership program, is required regardless of whether the renter purchases the single-family home occupied by the renter or another single-family home. A renter may be interested in purchasing the home the renter occupies but may also prefer or need to purchase a different home. Proposed § 36.8 would permit meaningful financial support to be used for the purchase of another single-family home, thereby focusing on the renter's transition to homeownership rather than on only the disposition of the specific rented property.
Proposed § 36.8(b) would provide a safe harbor for meaningful financial support, similar to the safe harbor for homeownership programs, described above. Under the proposal, a large institutional investor would be deemed to contribute meaningful financial support to a renter who has rented a single-family home for at least 5 years if, in the event the renter purchases a single-family home, the amount of the support is at least the lesser of (i) $5,000 or (ii) 2.5 percent if the renter has rented the single-family home for at least five years and at least 3.5 percent if the renter has rented the single-family home for at least seven years. In each case, the applicable percentage would be calculated using the lesser of (a) the purchase price of the property purchased by the renter or (b) the Federal Housing Administration's mortgage limit for a one-unit property that applies to the county where the single-family home rented by the renter is located and that is in effect on the date the renter purchases a single-family home. As under proposed § 36.7(b), the safe-harbor percentage would change only when the renter reaches the specified five- and seven-year thresholds and would not be prorated between those thresholds.
Treasury preliminarily believes this formula would provide a clear and administrable standard while accounting for both the duration of the renter's rental of the single-family home and regional variation in home prices. Proposed § 36.8(b)(2) would specify how the contribution must be provided. If the seller of the single-family home is not the large institutional investor, the large institutional investor would be required to transmit the amount to the seller of the single-family home for the renter's account at or before the sale. Treasury has proposed financial support of up to 3.5 percent under this formula because, if the purchase price does not exceed the applicable Federal Housing Administration mortgage limit and applicable mortgage requirements permit, a contribution at that level could potentially satisfy the renter's minimum down payment for a Federal Housing Administration-insured mortgage. Treasury does not propose to require a specific account structure for a large institutional investor's contribution of meaningful financial support to a third-party seller. If the seller is the large institutional investor, the large institutional investor would be required to credit the amount toward the purchase price. Because a contribution by a large institutional investor that is selling the home to a renter may be considered an interested party contribution for purposes of Federal mortgage standards, the contribution would not count towards a down payment. As a result, a price concession may be an appropriate alternative in this situation. These payment mechanics are intended to ensure that the financial support is actually available for the renter's purchase and is not merely a post-closing reimbursement or unenforceable promise. For purposes of the safe-harbor calculation, the purchase price of the property would be determined before applying or crediting meaningful financial support. This treatment would avoid a circular calculation in which the amount of support reduces the purchase price used to calculate that same support.
The proposed rule would increase the safe-harbor amount in stages based on the renter's completed period of rental, to encourage large institutional investors to offer programs to boost homeownership while providing progressively greater assistance to longer-term renters. Making the full 3.5 percent safe-harbor amount available at the beginning of the rental relationship could discourage participation by large institutional investors, while further delaying any safe-harbor amount could slow the renter's transition to homeownership or reduce the number of renters who ultimately receive support.
Treasury also believes it is appropriate to cap the amount of financial support required to satisfy the safe harbor at $5,000. This amount is intended to ensure that the financial support will be impactful for the renter's purchase of a single-family home, without making the program cost-prohibitive for large institutional investors.
Proposed § 36.8(b)(3) would require the large institutional investor not, directly or indirectly, to recover any portion of the meaningful financial support from the renter, including by increasing the purchase price of the single-family home or imposing any expense, charge, or fee in connection with the financial support. This requirement is intended to ensure that the economic value of the support is not reduced by offsetting charges.

6. Facts-and-Circumstances Support
Proposed § 36.8(e) would provide that a contribution that does not satisfy the safe harbor may constitute meaningful financial support based on the facts and circumstances, including the economic value of price concessions, down-payment assistance, closing-cost assistance, or other support for the renter's purchase.
Programs to boost homeownership may provide meaningful financial support in forms that are not fully captured by a single formula. For example, a large institutional investor may provide support through a below-market sale price, assistance with closing costs, or similar support. These forms of support may have substantial economic value to the renter even if they do not take the form specified in proposed § 36.8(b)(1) and (2). At the same time, a facts-and-circumstances standard should not undermine the administrability of the proposed rule.

7. Right of First Refusal and 30-Day First-Look Period
As specified in section 1001(a)(2)(E)(ii) of the Act, proposed § 36.8(a)(2) would require contracts under a program to boost homeownership to provide the renter with a right of first refusal and a 30-day first-look period. Proposed § 36.8(f) would provide a non-exclusive safe harbor for this requirement.
Under the proposed safe harbor, a large institutional investor would be deemed to provide the required right of first refusal and 30-day first-look period if, until the earlier of 90 days after the renter's rental contract terminates or the date the single-family home is rented to a person other than such renter, the large institutional investor provides certain rights specified in proposed § 36.8(f)(1), (2), and (3).

The proposed time period for these rights is intended to prevent a large institutional investor from declining to renew a rental agreement with a renter and immediately selling the single-family home, while also not requiring the large institutional investor to offer such rights to multiple individuals at once.
During the applicable period, before the large institutional investor lists, markets, solicits offers for the purchase of, negotiates for the potential sale of, or accepts from any person other than the renter any offer to purchase the single-family home occupied by the renter, the large institutional investor must provide the renter with written notice. The notice must include the large institutional investor's intent to sell the home, the proposed sale or list price, any proposed material sale terms known to the large institutional investor, the amount of any meaningful financial support to which the renter is entitled, and the manner and date by which the renter may submit an offer to purchase the home.
Proposed § 36.8(f)(2) would require that, during the 30-day period beginning on, but not including, the date the notice is provided, the large institutional investor not list, market, solicit offers for the purchase of, negotiate for the potential sale of, or accept from any person other than the renter any offer to purchase the single-family home. This restriction is intended to provide the renter a meaningful first opportunity to consider purchasing the home without competing against other potential purchasers during the first-look period.
Proposed § 36.8(f)(3) would address the right of first refusal. If, after the 30-day first-look period described above, the large institutional investor receives a bona fide offer from any person other than the renter that the large institutional investor is prepared to accept and that is less than or equal to a price offered by the renter during the first-look period, then, before accepting that offer, the large institutional investor must provide the renter with written notice of all material economic terms of the offer and not less than five business days to elect to purchase the home on terms that match the material economic terms of the offer, before giving effect to any meaningful financial support required under proposed § 36.8(a)(3). If the renter timely elects to match such terms, the large institutional investor must sell the home to the renter on such terms, subject to customary closing conditions applicable to an owner-occupant purchaser.
This two-stage structure is intended to give effect to both the 30-day first-look period and the right of first refusal, which are not further described in section 1001 of the Act. The first-look period provides the renter an exclusive initial opportunity to make an offer. The right of first refusal protects the renter if the large institutional investor later receives a bona fide offer that it is prepared to accept and that is less than or equal to the renter's earlier offer. Measuring the renter's ability to match the third-party offer before giving effect to meaningful financial support is intended to ensure that the renter receives the benefit of the required support.
Proposed § 36.8(g) would provide that, for purposes of the safe harbor in proposed § 36.8(f), written notice would be deemed to be provided on the date the notice is delivered personally to the renter, sent by electronic means to an electronic address designated by the renter for notices under the rental agreement, or deposited in the U.S. mail or with a commercial delivery service for delivery to the renter's address for notices under the rental agreement, at the option of the large institutional investor. If notice is provided by mail or commercial delivery service, the applicable response period would begin on the third business day after the notice is deposited.

8. Transfer to Another Large Institutional Investor
Proposed § 36.8(a)(4) would require contracts under a program to boost homeownership to provide that, if the large institutional investor sells or otherwise transfers the single-family home to another large institutional investor before the renter's rights under the program terminate, the transferring large institutional investor's obligations under proposed § 36.8(a)(1) through (3) are automatically deemed to be assigned to, and enforceable by the renter against, the transferee large institutional investor. The transferring large institutional investor also would be required to cause the transferee large institutional investor expressly to assume those obligations in writing and effective upon consummation of the transfer.
The relevant provision of the Act does not expressly address the continuation of program obligations when a large institutional investor sells the single-family home to another large institutional investor. Proposed § 36.8(a)(4) is intended to preserve the renter protections associated with a program to boost homeownership and contemplated by the Act. Without such a requirement, a large institutional investor could transfer the home to another large institutional investor in a manner that eliminates the renter's rights under the program. Such a result would be inconsistent with the purpose of the statutory exception for programs to boost homeownership.
The proposed rule would require both automatic assignment and express written assumption of the large institutional investor's obligations. Automatic assignment is intended to ensure that the renter's rights are not dependent on the parties' actions, while express written assumption would provide additional clarity and mitigate the risk of disputes regarding the transferee's obligations.

H. Satisfaction of Debts Previously Contracted (Proposed § 36.9)
Proposed § 36.9 would clarify the application of section 1001(a)(2)(F) of the Act, which states that a purchase of a single-family home is an excepted purchase if it is in connection with the satisfaction of debts previously contracted in good faith and where the large institutional investor has the right to repossess the single-family home under such contract.
The proposed rule primarily clarifies that a large institutional investor may purchase a single-family home in accordance with this category of excepted purchase either directly or indirectly. Specifically, the proposed rule provides for a large institutional investor to (i) directly purchase the single-family home, by purchasing the single-family home in connection with the satisfaction of debts previously contracted by such large institutional investor in good faith and where such large institutional investor has the right to repossess the single-family home under such contract; or (ii) indirectly purchase the single-family home, by purchasing the single-family home directly or indirectly from another person or entity that purchased the single-family home in connection with the satisfaction of debts previously contracted in good faith by such person or entity and where such person or entity had the right to repossess the single-family home under such contract.
This clarification of the statutory text is intended to ensure that the exception remains available for debt-collection and collateral-related circumstances that are distinct from ordinary investment purchases of single-family homes, while mitigating market disruptions. As set forth in the Act, the proposed rule would require that the debt was previously contracted in good faith and that the relevant person had the right to repossess the single-family home under the contract. This excepted purchase would not apply merely because a purchaser is owed money by a seller or because proceeds of the sale may be used to satisfy a debt; instead, the debt relationship must include a right to repossess the single-family home.
Proposed § 36.9(b), regarding indirect purchases, is intended to address circumstances in which a large institutional investor acquires a single-family home through a chain of transactions following a debt-satisfaction event. For example, an entity with the right to repossess a single-family home may acquire the home in connection with satisfaction of a debt and later sell the home. Prohibiting indirect purchases of such homes may disrupt debt markets in a manner that the Act did not intend. For example, if a bank that has repossessed a single-family home enters receivership, it would not be consistent with the purposes of the Act for this restriction potentially to prevent the sale of that bank or its assets to a large institutional investor. At the same time, the indirect-purchase provision should not permit evasion of the purchase prohibition. A large institutional investor should not be able to rely on the exception solely because a transaction is routed through an intermediary. The proposed rule therefore requires that the person or entity from which the home is purchased acquired the home in connection with the satisfaction of debts previously contracted in good faith and had the right to repossess the home under the contract.

Proposed § 36.10(a) reflects the statutory text. The proposed rule would permit a large institutional investor to purchase the home directly or indirectly from such an entity where the conditions of proposed § 36.10 are satisfied. J. Purchases From Another Large Institutional Investor (Proposed § 36.11)
Proposed § 36.11 would clarify the application of section 1001(a)(2)(H) of the Act, which states that a purchase of a single-family home is an excepted purchase if the home is purchased from another large institutional investor that either owned the single-family home on the date of enactment of the Act or purchased the single-family home in compliance with section 1001 of the Act.
Proposed § 36.11 reflects the statutory text, with a clarification that the Act's reference to purchases of single-family homes in compliance with section 1001 of the Act includes a purchase from a large institutional investor that purchased the home under section 1001(a)(2)(H) of the Act. Treasury preliminarily believes this approach represents the best reading of the text and structure of section 1001(a)(2)(H). The ROAD Act permits a large institutional investor to purchase a single-family home from another large institutional investor where the selling large institutional investor purchased the home in compliance with the Act. With respect to potential means of compliance, the Act does not indicate that certain excepted purchases should be excluded. Therefore, under the proposed rule, a single-family home purchased in compliance with the Act would remain eligible for subsequent purchases by large institutional investors, provided that each transfer satisfies a purchase exemption, including section 1001(a)(2)(H). In addition to consistency with the statute, the proposed rule is intended to provide clarity and reduce market disruption by permitting orderly transfers of existing or compliant inventory among large institutional investors.
Treasury views the statutory phrase “purchased the single-family home in compliance with the Act” to include purchases made before the large institutional investor was subject to the prohibition under the Act, purchases that qualify for any category of excepted purchase, and purchases made under section 1001(b)(2)(B) of the Act (
i.e.,
purchases in connection with a restructuring or other reorganization of ownership of single-family homes that were owned or purchased on or before the date of enactment of the Act). This interpretation gives meaning to the plain text of the statute. Further, a contrary interpretation could impair market liquidity and orderly disposition of single-family homes without materially advancing the purposes of the Act.
At the same time, the proposed rule would not permit a large institutional investor to rely on section 1001(a)(2)(H) of the Act if the selling large institutional investor acquired the single-family home in violation of the Act. If a large institutional investor acquired a single-family home in violation of the Act, a later sale of that single-family home to another large institutional investor would not satisfy proposed § 36.11 merely because the seller is a large institutional investor. The selling large institutional investor must have owned the single-family home on the date of enactment or purchased the single-family home in compliance with the Act.

K. In the Business of (Proposed § 36.15)
1. Overview
Proposed § 36.15 would clarify when an entity is engaged, in whole or in part, in the business of investing in, owning, renting, managing, or holding single-family homes as described in section 1001(a)(3)(A)(i)(I) of the Act. Section 1001(a)(3)(A) of the Act defines “large institutional investor” by reference to, among other things, whether the entity “is engaged, in whole or in part, in the business of investing in, owning, renting, managing, or holding single-family homes.” The Act does not further define “in the business of” for this purpose and proposed § 36.15 would do so.
The proposed rule would interpret “in the business of” in order to enable stakeholders to identify entities that participate in the single-family home market as a business or investment activity in a manner that relates to the purposes of the Act, while excluding entities that hold or manage single-family homes for reasons that are properly outside the scope of the Act's definition of “large institutional investor.”
Under proposed § 36.15(a), an entity would be considered to be engaged, in whole or in part, in the business of investing in, owning, renting, managing, or holding single-family homes if the entity, directly or indirectly, invests in, owns, rents, manages, or holds single-family homes for the purpose, in whole or in part, of receiving investment gains, rental income, management fees, or any other type of income or financial gain.
Proposed § 36.15(b) is intended to clarify the types of entities that are not considered to be large institutional investors. Specifically, that provision states that an entity would not be considered to be engaged, in whole or in part, “in the business” if the entity,
(
printed page 66818)
directly or indirectly, invests in, owns, rents, manages, or holds single-family homes (i) solely on a temporary and incidental basis in furtherance of a different bona fide business; (ii) only to the extent reasonably necessary for the conduct of such other bona fide business; and (iii) not as a regular or continuing investment strategy or portfolio management activity. These limits are narrowly tailored; a broad exclusion could allow entities to hold substantial single-family home portfolios while claiming that the activity is incidental to a broader enterprise.
Proposed § 36.15 would interpret only one element of the statutory definition of “large institutional investor.” It would not determine, by itself, whether an entity is a large institutional investor. An entity “in the business of” activities related to single-family homes under proposed § 36.15 is not a large institutional investor unless it also meets the other criteria under the Act and Part 36, including provisions regarding whether the entity has direct or indirect investment control over the required number of single-family homes and whether the entity is a passive investor.
Importantly, under the Act, purchases of single-family homes that would constitute excepted purchases if the purchaser were a large institutional investor should still be taken into consideration in determining whether an entity is engaged in the business of investing in, owning, renting, managing, or holding single-family homes. For example, an entity engaged in build-to-rent activities may be engaged in the relevant business even if such activities would constitute excepted purchases if the entity were a large institutional investor.

2. For the Purpose of Receiving Income or Financial Gain
As noted above, proposed § 36.15(a) would provide that an entity is engaged, in whole or in part, in the business of investing in, owning, renting, managing, or holding single-family homes if the entity, directly or indirectly, invests in, owns, rents, manages, or holds single-family homes “for the purpose, in whole or in part, of receiving investment gains, rental income, management fees, or any other type of income or financial gain.” This standard is intended to implement the reference in section 1001(a)(3)(A)(i)(I) of the Act to an entity engaged “in the business of investing in, owning, renting, managing, or holding single-family homes.” Each part of that statutory phrase addresses activities that are undertaken by entities for income or financial gain. Investment gains, rental income, and management fees are common forms of economic return from single-family home investment, ownership, rental, management, and holding activity. The proposed rule also would include “any other type of income or financial gain” as a catch-all to prevent opportunities for evasion based on the technical nature of the compensation or economic return, such as entities receiving income or financial gain through appreciation, fees, carried interest, incentive compensation, servicing compensation, management compensation, affiliate arrangements, or another arrangement.
The proposed definition would apply where the relevant purpose exists “in whole or in part.” This language is intended to give effect to the statutory phrase “engaged, in whole or in part, in the business.” That statutory definition includes an entity even if its single-family home investment, ownership, rental, management, or holding activity is merely one part of a broader business. Notably, the statute does not establish any minimum threshold for the extent of an entity's engagement in such business “in part.” Similarly, an entity should not avoid the business element solely because it receives financial gain through appreciation, fees, carried interest, incentive compensation, servicing compensation, management compensation, affiliate arrangements, or another economic arrangement rather than through direct rental income.
Proposed § 36.15(a) focuses on an entity's purpose rather than profit. An entity may be engaged in a business even if its homes, portfolios, or business lines do not generate a profit in a particular period.

3. Covered Activities
Proposed § 36.15(a) incorporates the language in section 1001(a)(3)(A)(i)(I) of the Act regarding entities engaged in the business of “investing in, owning, renting, managing, or holding” single-family homes. Treasury anticipates interpreting this phrase to give independent meaning to each of those listed activities. An entity may be engaged in the relevant business through investment activity, ownership, rental activity, management activity,

Being “in the business of” one of the activities above does not, by itself, mean that an entity is a large institutional investor. To be a large institutional investor, an entity must also meet the other statutory criteria, including having direct or indirect investment control of not less than 350 single-family homes, as provided in section 1001(a)(3)(A)(i)(II) of the Act. For example, a fee-based property management company may be “in the business of” managing single-family homes, but if that entity does not have direct or indirect investment control over those single-family homes as defined in the Act, including that it does not have “primary authority . . . to make material . . . management decisions,”

4. Temporary and Incidental Holdings
Proposed § 36.15(b) would provide that an entity is not engaged, in whole or in part, in the business of investing in, owning, renting, managing, or holding single-family homes if the entity directly or indirectly invests in, owns, rents, manages, or holds single-family homes “solely on a temporary and incidental basis in furtherance of a different bona fide business” and satisfies certain other criteria. As described above, the Act refers to entities that are engaged “in the business of” the relevant activities; an entity that holds or manages single-family homes solely temporarily and incidentally in furtherance of a different bona fide business, in accordance with the terms of proposed § 36.15(b), would not fall within the scope of this definition.
Treasury preliminarily believes that each of these limits is necessary to prevent the exclusion from being used to avoid the statutory definition of large institutional investor. A broad exclusion for entities with another primary business could allow entities to hold substantial single-family home portfolios while claiming that the activity is incidental to a broader enterprise. Proposed § 36.15(b) would therefore require that the activity be both incidental and reasonably necessary to the other bona fide business, and not a regular or continuing investment strategy or portfolio management activity.

5. Reasonably Necessary to the Conduct of Another Bona Fide Business
Proposed § 36.15(b)(2) would provide that an entity is not engaged, in whole or in part, in the business of investing in, owning, renting, managing, or holding single-family homes if the entity directly or indirectly engages in such activities “only to the extent reasonably necessary for the conduct of” the entity's other bona fide business and satisfies certain other criteria. This criterion is intended to help appropriately limit the exclusion to circumstances where the entity's activities related to single-family homes do not indicate the company is “in the business” of conducting such activities. The exclusion would not apply merely because the entity also conducts another bona fide business; instead, under proposed § 36.15(b)(2), the entity's single-family home activities must be limited to activities reasonably necessary for the conduct of that other business.
Treasury recognizes that the determination of whether an activity is reasonably necessary to a business will depend on the facts and circumstances. Relevant considerations may include the nature of the business; the reason the entity acquired, holds, or manages the homes; the length of time the homes are held; whether the entity receives rental income or other financial gain as a result of its activity related to single-family homes; whether the entity markets or manages the homes as part of a continuing portfolio; and whether the entity has policies setting forth its practice of disposing of homes promptly.

L. Passive Investor Definition (Proposed § 36.16)
1. Overview of Passive Investor Treatment
Proposed § 36.16 would clarify when one entity is a “passive investor” in a second entity. The ROAD Act uses the term “passive investor” only in the definition of “large institutional investor.” Specifically, a large institutional investor generally includes an entity that has direct or indirect investment control of not less than 350 single-family homes, and “investment control” is defined to include owning or controlling more than 25 percent of any class of equity interests of the entity that owns the single-family home, “unless such entity is a passive investor.”
[
16
]
In other words, an entity that holds a significant equity interest in another entity that owns single-family homes may avoid being considered a large institutional investor if it is a passive investor. Importantly, an entity that is a passive investor may meet other criteria in the “large institutional investor” definition, in which case the entity could nonetheless be a large institutional investor.
Under the proposal, passive-investor treatment would be available only if each of two conditions is met: (i) no director, officer, employee, or designee of the first entity, or of any entity controlled by the first entity, is a director or officer of the second entity; and (ii) the first entity does not have a property control right (as defined in proposed § 36.2) with respect to single-family homes over which the second entity has direct or indirect investment control. Each of these proposed conditions is explained further below. The proposed rule uses the term “first entity” and “second entity” to refer, respectively, to the potential passive investor and the entity in which it owns or controls equity interests.
These two proposed conditions are intended to provide administrable criteria that reflect common understandings of passivity, and to exclude investors with rights, employees, or designees that provide an ability to make, direct, or prevent decisions related to single-family homes.

2. Director and Officer Interlocks
Under proposed § 36.16(a), for a first entity to qualify as a passive investor in a second entity, no director, officer, employee, or designee of the first entity, or of any entity controlled by the first entity, can be a director or officer of the second entity. This condition is intended to prevent passive-investor treatment where the investor's representatives participate in the governance or management of the entity that owns or controls single-family homes.
Overlapping directors or officers can provide an investor with access, influence, or control inconsistent with passive status. The proposed condition is designed to provide an administrable indicator that the investor is not passive where such overlap exists. The proposed rule uses “designee” to describe persons selected, designated, appointed, or otherwise placed by the first entity or its controlled entities, regardless of whether the person is formally described as a representative.
Treasury invites comments on all aspects of the director and officer interlock condition. In particular, Treasury seeks comment on the following aspects of the proposed rule:

3. No Property Control Right
Under proposed § 36.16(b), for a first entity to qualify as a passive investor in a second entity, the first entity must not have a property control right (as defined in proposed § 36.2) with respect to single-family homes over which the second entity has direct or indirect investment control. This condition is intended to ensure that an investor will not be treated as passive if it has a right to make, direct, or prevent decisions, directly or indirectly, related to the purchase, sale, holding, leasing, renovation, or management of a single-family home. An investor that can require, block, or condition decisions regarding single-family homes would not be passive even if it lacks formal management authority.

M. Enforcement (Proposed § 36.17)
1. Overview
Section 1001(d)(1) of the Act authorizes Treasury, or the Department of Justice at Treasury's request, to bring an action against a large institutional investor that violates the Act's prohibition for a civil penalty up to the greater of $1 million per violation or three times the purchase price of the property involved. Proposed § 36.17 would provide that a purchase of a single-family home that violates the Act's prohibition with respect to more than one large institutional investor is deemed a single violation for purposes of calculating this maximum civil penalty.
More than one large institutional investor may be involved in a transaction in which a single-family home is purchased. For example, an investment fund, an investment manager, and a general partner may each have direct or indirect investment control with respect to the same single-family home. Similarly, a large institutional investor may acquire a single-family home through a subsidiary, and an affiliated large institutional investor may have indirect investment control with respect to the same home. In those circumstances, a prohibited purchase of a single-family home could violate the statutory prohibition with respect to multiple large institutional investors. Treasury believes it is appropriate to treat each purchase as a single violation for purposes of calculating the maximum civil penalty under section 1001(d)(1) of the Act. This approach maintains consistency between the effects of the violation and the resulting penalty, and avoids the potential for an unwarranted increase in the total penalty based merely on the number of large institutional investors involved.
Proposed § 36.17 would apply only to the calculation of the maximum civil penalty under section 1001(d)(1). It would not alter whether a purchase violates section 1001(b) of the Act, whether any particular entity is a large institutional investor, or whether more than one entity may be responsible for a violation.
[
18
]
In addition, the proposed rule would not treat purchases of different single-family homes, or purchases of the same single-family home in separate transactions, as a single violation. It also does not establish procedures for investigating potential violations, which Treasury may address in the future. The proposed rule does not specify how responsibility for a violation should be allocated among large institutional investors, and does not limit Treasury's ability to pursue enforcement actions against all entities whose conduct violates section 1001(b) of the Act. The proposed rule would preserve Treasury's ability to consider the facts and circumstances of any violation, including the role of each large institutional investor, in any enforcement process. Treasury may address such issues in the future.

Proposed § 36.18 provides that the provisions of Part 36 are separate and severable from one another. If any provision, clause, or phrase of Part 36, or the application thereof to any person, entity, or circumstance, is stayed or deemed to be invalid, unlawful, or unenforceable by a court of competent jurisdiction, such determination would not affect the validity, lawfulness, or enforceability of the remaining provisions or applications of this regulation, which would remain in full force and effect to the maximum extent permitted by law.

A. Regulatory Flexibility Act
The Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) requires an agency to consider the impact of its proposed rules on small entities. In connection with a proposed rule, the RFA generally requires an agency to prepare an Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (IRFA) describing the impact of the rule on small entities, unless the head of the agency certifies that the proposed rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities and publishes such certification along with a statement providing the factual basis for such certification in the
Federal Register
.
Section 1001 of the ROAD Act establishes a statutory framework that generally prohibits a large institutional investor from purchasing, or entering into a contract to purchase, a single-family home unless the purchase is an excepted purchase. This proposed rule is intended to provide interpretive and operational clarity for certain statutory terms and conditions. The proposed rule would not create additional categories of excepted purchases, alter the statutory definition of “large institutional investor,” or eliminate any statutory exception. Treasury's rulemaking authority, described further below in section III.E, is limited by a rule of construction providing that no regulation issued by Treasury “may amend the definitions of the [statutorily defined terms], including to” make certain specified categories of changes.
Treasury expects that the economic effect of the proposed rule on small entities would be limited, in part because the statutory prohibition applies only to large institutional investors, although some large institutional investors may be small entities, and the rule as proposed would primarily relate to compliance review, documentation, and transaction planning. Therefore, at this time, Treasury does not expect that the proposed rule would have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities as described under the RFA.
B. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act
Treasury has analyzed the proposed rule under the factors in the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (UMRA). Under this analysis, Treasury considered whether the proposed rule includes a federal mandate that may result in the expenditure by state, local, and tribal governments, in the aggregate, or by the private sector, of $100 million or more in any one year (adjusted annually for inflation). Pursuant to section 202 of the UMRA, if a proposed rule meets this UMRA threshold, Treasury would need to prepare a written statement that includes, among other things, a cost-benefit analysis of the proposal. This requirement does not apply to regulations to the extent they incorporate requirements specifically set forth in law.
Treasury has determined that the proposed rule would not result in a covered unfunded mandate within the meaning of UMRA. The proposed rule would not require state, local, or Tribal governments to administer a program or expend funds. The proposed rule may result in incremental recordkeeping and planning costs for entities that evaluate whether they are large institutional investors or whether particular purchases qualify as excepted purchases, but Treasury does not expect those incremental costs to meet the UMRA threshold.

1. Affected Parties
Parties directly affected by this proposal are large institutional investors and entities that may be part of, or provide capital to, the investment control ownership chain for single-family homes for large institutional investors. Treasury proposes to interpret the definitions in the statute in a manner that accounts for the practical effect of ownership interests, contractual rights, and governance arrangements. Large institutional investment in single-family homes may involve layered ownership structures, special-purpose vehicles, affiliated funds, side letters, contractual consent rights, service agreements, debt covenants, and other arrangements that may make it difficult to understand who has direct or indirect investment control over a single-family home. The proposed rule is intended to account for these variations in form. Reliable data are not currently available regarding how many institutional investors and other entities may be affected.
2. Baseline
Treasury has assessed the benefits and costs of the proposed rules relative to a no-action baseline reflecting the statutory requirements in the absence of the proposed rules. Once the prohibition in the ROAD Act becomes effective, a large institutional investor may not purchase, or enter into a contract to directly or indirectly purchase, any single-family home, unless the home is purchased pursuant to one of several exceptions defined in the ROAD Act. Section 1001 of the Act generally defines a large institutional investor as a for-profit entity engaged, in whole or in part, in the business of investing in, owning, renting, managing, or holding single-family homes that, alone or in concert with one or more other entities, directly or indirectly has investment control of not less than 350 single-family homes, excluding any single-family home purchased in an excepted purchase after enactment of the Act. Section 1001 of the Act also provides several categories of excepted purchases, including purchases pursuant to a build-to-rent program, renovate-to-rent program, homeownership program, and program to boost homeownership.
In the absence of this proposed rule, large institutional investors and other market participants would face significant uncertainty over the application of section 1001 of the Act to their business models, ownership structures, equity interests, governance rights, investment management arrangements, contracts, and other business decisions associated with the ownership of or investment in single-family homes. Investors might forgo otherwise permissible transactions, expend significant resources on transaction-specific legal analysis and structures, or take inconsistent positions across similar investments.
3. Costs
Costs associated with determining whether a purchase of a single-family home is prohibited or excepted will largely be attributable to the ROAD Act itself rather than the proposed rules. Treasury expects that its proposed rulemaking will bring clarity and reduce risk for market participants. Relative to the baseline, Treasury expects that market participants will not need to expend significant time and other resources to ensure that they are in compliance with the proposed rules. The proposed definitions are designed to address potential uncertainty regarding the application of the statutory prohibition. The proposal is intended to reduce, rather than increase, total compliance costs for many affected entities by providing clearer standards for conduct that the ROAD Act already regulates.
Compliance with the proposed rules may impose certain compliance and operational costs on large institutional investors. These market participants would need to evaluate the extent to which their businesses and activities are covered by the terms of this proposal. Treasury also expectsthat anentity seeking to rely on the terms in this rulemaking would maintain records sufficientto demonstrate that each condition is satisfied as outlined in the proposed rule; some of those records may already be created in the ordinary course of business for a large institutional investor.
Some large institutional investors and other market participants may choose not to engage in activities that are subject to the ROAD Act's prohibition. This proposal does not establish any obligations, and will not impose any direct costs, on entities that determine not to engage in such activities.
Question 1: What information and methodology could Treasury use to quantify the total cost of requiring that large institutional investors provide meaningful financial support if they seek to rely on the purchase exception in section 1001(a)(2)(E)?
4. Benefits
As discussed in section II of this preamble, Treasury expects the proposed definitions and clarifications to be beneficial to the housing market. The proposed rules would reduce uncertainty for large institutional investors and other market participants, support more consistent compliance and enforcement, and help prevent circumvention of the law through layered ownership structures, nominally passive arrangements, or contractual rights that confer material control. The proposed rule also would help promote the practical availability of the statutory exceptions while reducing the risk that those exceptions are used in ways inconsistent with the ROAD Act. The clarifications in the proposed rule are expected to reduce inadvertent violations, improve administrability, reduce uncertainty, support more consistent compliance and enforcement outcomes, and avoid unnecessary disruption to housing supply, homebuilding, housing stock rehabilitation activity, and capital formation. Treasury expects that the definitions in this proposed rule will reduce the ability and incentives to evade the statutory prohibition. Treasury also expects that the rulemaking will reduce or eliminate the risk that truly passive capital providers are treated as having direct or indirect investment control, and therefore could potentially be scoped in as large institutional investors that are subject to restrictions and compliance obligations in connection with the ROAD Act.
5. Discretion and Alternatives
In establishing the statutory framework for the large institutional investor ban on purchasing single-family homes, Congress used several terms that are central to the administration and enforcement of the statute. The ROAD Act does not define these terms in detail. However, Treasury believes that these terms would benefit from clarification to support an
(

administrable framework for large institutional investors and other market participants.
Treasury's rulemaking authority is limited by a rule of construction in section 1001(b)(4)(B) of the Act providing that no regulation issued by Treasury “may amend the definitions of [certain statutorily defined terms],” including to make certain specified categories of changes.

The list of specified categories of prohibited changes is illustrative rather than exhaustive. The phrase “including to” indicates that the listed categories are examples of amendments that Treasury may not make, not an affirmative authorization to amend the statutory definitions in other ways. Accordingly, in the proposed rule, Treasury has sought to clarify certain statutory terms, without amending the statutory definitions themselves. Interpreting the statutory terms by regulation is intended to provide greater clarity and certainty, relative to the alternative of addressing interpretive questions through subregulatory guidance.
