§ 36.1
Authority, purpose, and scope.
(a)
Authority.
This part is issued by the U.S. Department of the Treasury (Treasury) pursuant to section 1001 of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing (ROAD) Act (
42 U.S.C. 19521
).
(b)
Purpose and scope.
The ROAD Act authorizes Treasury to issue regulations to carry out the statutory purposes. This part contains those regulations. Nothing in this part limits the authority of the Secretary of Housing and Urban Development to administer Section 1001(c) of the Act.
§ 36.2
Definitions.
“Act” or “ROAD Act” means the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, as amended from time to time.
“Property control right” means a right, including a consent, approval, veto, or other right, that gives an entity the ability to make, direct, or prevent a second entity's decisions, directly or indirectly, related to the purchase, sale, holding, leasing, renovation, or management of a single-family home.
“Purchase price of the property” means the total amount paid by an entity to purchase a single-family home, including the amount paid for the land on which the single-family home is situated.
“Purchase price of the single-family home” means the portion of the purchase price of the property attributable to the value of the structure, as calculated by subtracting the tax-assessed value of the land at the time of the purchase on which the single-family home is situated from the purchase price of the property.
“Structural or core system” means systems or areas of a single-family home that substantially affect structural integrity, habitability, life safety, or the functioning of major building systems, which may include fire safety, light and ventilation, structural loads and seismic design, foundation systems, materials standards, construction components, glass, mechanical, plumbing, and electrical.
§ 36.3
Program.
For purposes of sections 1001(a)(2)(B) to (E) of the Act, a program is a set of written policies or written procedures that are—
(a) adopted before the purchase of single-family homes pursuant to such program; and
(b) reasonably designed and implemented to ensure that all purchases of single-family homes pursuant to the program satisfy the applicable requirements of the Act, this part, and the program.
§ 36.4
[Reserved]
§ 36.5
Build-to-rent program.
A build-to-rent program as described in section 1001(a)(2)(B) of the Act is a program pursuant to which single-family homes—
(a) have not been occupied by an owner-occupant before being purchased;
(b) are purchased within 18 months of the single-family home receiving its certificate of occupancy (or equivalent); and
(c) are, after the purchase, first occupied by renters, whether as part of a community made up exclusively of renter-occupied single-family homes or as part of a community made up of single-family homes that are both owner- and renter-occupied.
§ 36.6
Renovate-to-rent program.
(a) A renovate-to-rent program as described in section 1001(a)(2)(C) of the Act is a program pursuant to which the large institutional investor—
(1) substantially rehabilitates (including by resolving all material deficiencies in) single-family homes that do not meet structural or core system elements of local building codes at the time of purchase; and
(2) makes improvements, including those under paragraph (1), to each single-family home in an aggregate dollar amount of not less than 15 percent of the purchase price of the single-family home.
(b) A large institutional investor that makes improvements to structural or core system elements of a single-family home that does not meet structural or core system elements of local building codes at the time of purchase in an aggregate dollar amount of not less than 10 percent of the purchase price of the single-family home, and that resolves all material deficiencies in such structural or core system elements, shall be deemed to have satisfied paragraph (a)(1).
§ 36.7
Homeownership program.
(a) A homeownership program as described in section 1001(a)(2)(D) of the Act is a program pursuant to which a large institutional investor enters into contracts with renters to rent single-family homes purchased by the large institutional investor, where the contracts—
(1) require rental payments and any other fees that are not greater than those collected by the large institutional investor on other similarly situated single-family homes not covered by the homeownership program;
(2) are considered a consumer credit transaction secured by a dwelling or real property;
(3) require the large institutional investor to inform the renter of the option for positive reporting of rental payments to consumer reporting agencies, and provide for such positive reporting, at no charge or expense to the renter, for any renter who opts into such reporting;
(
printed page 66825)
(4) require the large institutional investor to contribute meaningful financial support for the purchase of the single-family home by the renter and provide the renter the right, exercisable no later than the termination of the contract, to purchase the single-family home from the large institutional investor at a price no greater than fair market value minus the amount of such meaningful financial support; and
(5) provide that, if the large institutional investor sells or otherwise transfers the single-family home to another large institutional investor before the termination of the contract, (i) the transferring large institutional investor's obligations described in paragraphs (1) through (4) shall automatically be deemed to be assigned to, and enforceable by the renter against, the transferee large institutional investor, and (ii) the transferring large institutional investor shall cause the transferee large institutional investor expressly to assume, in writing and effective upon consummation of the transfer, the transferring large institutional investor's obligations described in paragraphs (1) through (4).
(b) For purposes of paragraph (a)(4), a large institutional investor shall be deemed to contribute meaningful financial support for the purchase of the single-family home by a renter who has rented the single-family home for at least 5 years if, in the event the renter purchases the single-family home from the large institutional investor—
(1) The amount of such financial support is at least the lesser of—
(i) $5,000; or
(ii) 2.5 percent if the renter has rented the single-family home for at least 5 years, and 3.5 percent if the renter has rented the single-family home for at least 7 years, in each case calculated as a percentage of the lesser of—
(A) The purchase price of the property purchased by the renter, determined before giving effect to the meaningful financial support provided under this section; or
(B) The Federal Housing Administration's mortgage limit for a one-unit property that applies to the county where the single-family home rented by the renter is located and that is in effect on the date the renter purchases the single-family home; and
(2) The large institutional investor does not, directly or indirectly, recover any portion of the financial support from the renter, including by increasing the purchase price of the single-family home or imposing any expense, charge, or fee in connection with the financial support.
(c) A homeownership program does not fail to satisfy the requirements of paragraph (a) solely because the program allows the large institutional investor's obligation to contribute meaningful financial support under paragraph (a)(4) to terminate if—
(1) As of the scheduled date for the renter's purchase of the single-family home, the renter has failed to pay all rent then due and payable to the large institutional investor, other than any amounts lawfully withheld;
(2) The renter breaches the rental contract in a manner that permits the large institutional investor to terminate the contract under applicable law; or
(3) The renter elects to terminate the rental contract for a purpose other than purchasing the single-family home.
§ 36.8
Program to boost homeownership.
(a) A program to boost homeownership as described in section 1001(a)(2)(E) of the Act is a program pursuant to which a large institutional investor enters into contracts with renters to rent single-family homes purchased by the large institutional investor, where the contracts—
(1) require the large institutional investor to inform the renter of the option for positive reporting of rental payments to consumer reporting agencies, and provide for such positive reporting, at no charge or expense to the renter, for any renter who opts into such reporting;
(2) provide the renter with a right of first refusal and a 30-day first-look period, as described in paragraph (f);
(3) provide for the large institutional investor to contribute meaningful financial support for the purchase of a single-family home by the renter (whether it is the home the renter occupies or another home), in accordance with this section; and
(4) provide that, if the large institutional investor sells or otherwise transfers the single-family home to another large institutional investor before the renter's rights under the program to boost homeownership terminate, (i) the transferring large institutional investor's obligations described in paragraphs (1) through (3) shall automatically be deemed to be assigned to, and enforceable by the renter against, the transferee large institutional investor, and (ii) the transferring large institutional investor shall cause the transferee large institutional investor expressly to assume, in writing and effective upon consummation of the transfer, the transferring large institutional investor's obligations described in paragraphs (1) through (3).
(b) For purposes of paragraph (a)(3), a large institutional investor shall be deemed to contribute meaningful financial support for the purchase of a single-family home by a renter who has rented a single-family home for at least 5 years if, in the event the renter purchases a single-family home—
(1) The amount of such financial support is at least the lesser of—
(i) $5,000; or
(ii) 2.5 percent if the renter has rented the single-family home for at least 5 years and 3.5 percent if the renter has rented the single-family home for at least 7 years, in each case calculated as a percentage of the lesser of—
(A) The purchase price of the property purchased by the renter, determined before giving effect to the meaningful financial support provided under this section; or
(B) The Federal Housing Administration's mortgage limit for a one-unit property that applies to the county where the single-family home rented by the renter is located and that is in effect on the date the renter purchases the single-family home; and
(2) The large institutional investor contributes the amount described in paragraph (1)—
(i) if the seller of the single-family home is not the large institutional investor, by transmitting such amount to the seller of the single-family home for the renter's account at or before the sale of such single-family home; or
(ii) if the seller of the single-family home is the large institutional investor, by crediting such amount toward the purchase price of such single-family home; and
(3) The large institutional investor does not, directly or indirectly, recover any portion of the meaningful financial support from the renter, including by increasing the purchase price of the single-family home or imposing any expense, charge, or fee in connection with the financial support.
(c) A program to boost homeownership does not fail to satisfy the requirements of paragraph (a) solely because the program allows the large institutional investor's obligation to contribute meaningful financial support under paragraph (a)(3) to terminate if—
(1) As of the scheduled date for the renter's purchase of a single-family home, the renter has failed to pay all rent then due and payable to the large institutional investor, other than any amounts lawfully withheld;
(2) The renter has caused material damage to the single-family home occupied by the renter, beyond ordinary wear and tear, excluding any damage caused by the large institutional
(
printed page 66826)
investor's failure to maintain the single-family home, and the large institutional investor has provided the renter with written notice and a reasonable opportunity to cure; or
(3) The renter breaches the rental contract in a manner that permits the large institutional investor to terminate the contract under applicable law.
(d) A large institutional investor's obligation to contribute meaningful financial support to a renter under a program to boost homeownership may terminate beginning 90 days after the renter no longer occupies a single-family home owned by the large institutional investor.
(e) A contribution that does not satisfy the safe harbor in paragraph (b) may constitute meaningful financial support based on the facts and circumstances, including the economic value of price concessions, down-payment assistance, closing-cost assistance, or other support for the renter's purchase.
(f) For purposes of paragraph (a)(2), a large institutional investor shall be deemed to provide the renter with a right of first refusal and a 30-day first-look period if, until the earlier of 90 days after the renter's rental contract terminates and the date the single-family home is rented to a person other than such renter—
(1) before the large institutional investor lists, markets, solicits offers for the purchase of, negotiates for the potential sale of, or accepts from any person other than the renter any offer to purchase the single-family home occupied by such renter, the large institutional investor provides the renter with written notice of the large institutional investor's intent to sell the single-family home, the proposed sale or list price, any proposed material sale terms known to the large institutional investor, the amount of any meaningful financial support to which the renter is entitled under paragraph (a)(3), and the manner and date by which the renter may submit an offer to purchase the single-family home;
(2) during the 30-day period beginning on, but not including, the date the notice described in paragraph (f)(1) is provided, the large institutional investor does not list, market, solicit offers for the purchase of, negotiate for the potential sale of, or accept from any person other than the renter any offer to purchase the single-family home; and
(3) if, after the 30-day period described in paragraph (f)(2), the large institutional investor receives a bona fide offer from any person other than the renter that the large institutional investor is prepared to accept and that is less than or equal to a price offered by the renter during the 30-day period described in paragraph (f)(2), then, before accepting such offer, the large institutional investor provides the renter with written notice of all material economic terms of the offer and not less than five business days to elect to purchase the single-family home on terms that match the material economic terms of such offer (before giving effect to any meaningful financial support required under paragraph (a)(3)), and if the renter timely elects to match such terms, the large institutional investor sells the single-family home to the renter on such terms, subject to customary closing conditions applicable to an owner-occupant purchaser.
(g) For purposes of paragraph (f), written notice is provided on the date the notice is delivered personally to the renter, sent by electronic means to an electronic address designated by the renter for notices under the rental agreement, or deposited in the United States mail or with a commercial delivery service for delivery to the renter's address for notices under the rental agreement, at the option of the large institutional investor. If notice is provided by mail or commercial delivery service, the applicable response period begins on the third business day after the notice is deposited.
§ 36.9
Satisfaction of debts previously contracted.
A large institutional investor purchases a single-family home in accordance with section 1001(a)(2)(F) of the Act if the large institutional investor—
(a) directly purchases the single-family home in connection with the satisfaction of debts previously contracted by such large institutional investor in good faith and where such large institutional investor has the right to repossess the single-family home under such contract; or
(b) indirectly purchases the single-family home, by purchasing the single-family home directly or indirectly from another person or entity that purchased the single-family home in connection with the satisfaction of debts previously contracted in good faith by such person or entity and where such person or entity had the right to repossess the single-family home under such contract.
§ 36.10
Loss mitigation or compliance.
A large institutional investor purchases a single-family home in accordance with section 1001(a)(2)(G) of the Act if—
(a) the purchase is undertaken by a mortgage servicer, lender, or other entity that has a legal right to a single-family home, for the purpose of loss mitigation or compliance with servicing or investor obligations, and not as a long-term investment strategy, and is solely as a result of—
(1) a foreclosure;
(2) a deed-in-lieu of foreclosure;
(3) enforcement of a mortgage, deed of trust, or other security interest; or
(4) operation of law following borrower default; and
(b) the large institutional investor—
(1) is such mortgage servicer, lender, or other entity; or
(2) purchases the single-family home directly or indirectly from such mortgage servicer, lender, or other entity.
§ 36.11
Purchases from another large institutional investor.
A large institutional investor purchases a single-family home from another large institutional investor pursuant to section 1001(a)(2)(H) of the Act if the other large institutional investor either—
(a) owned the single-family home on the date of enactment of the Act; or
(b) purchased the single-family home in compliance with the Act, including in a purchase from a large institutional investor that purchased the home under section 1001(a)(2)(H) of the Act.

§ 36.15
In the business of.
(a) An entity is engaged, in whole or in part, in the business of investing in, owning, renting, managing, or holding single-family homes as described in section 1001(a)(3)(A)(i)(I) of the Act if the entity, directly or indirectly, invests in, owns, rents, manages, or holds single-family homes for the purpose, in whole or in part, of receiving investment gains, rental income, management fees, or any other type of income or financial gain.
(b) An entity is not engaged, in whole or in part, in the business of investing in, owning, renting, managing, or holding single-family homes as described in section 1001(a)(3)(A)(i)(I) of the Act if the entity, directly or indirectly, invests in, owns, rents, manages, or holds single-family homes—
(1) solely on a temporary and incidental basis in furtherance of a different bona fide business;
(2) only to the extent reasonably necessary for the conduct of such other bona fide business; and
(
printed page 66827)
(3) not as a regular or continuing investment strategy or portfolio management activity.
§ 36.16
Passive investor.
An entity is a passive investor in a second entity as described in section 1001(a)(3)(B)(iv) of the Act if—
(a) no director, officer, employee, or designee of the first entity or of any entity controlled by the first entity is a director or officer of the second entity; and
(b) the first entity does not have a property control right with respect to single-family homes over which the second entity has direct or indirect investment control.
§ 36.17
Enforcement.
A purchase of a single-family home that violates section 1001(b) of the Act with respect to more than one large institutional investor shall be deemed a single violation for purposes of calculating the maximum civil penalty under section 1001(d)(1) of the Act.
§ 36.18
Severability.
The provisions of this part are separate and severable from one another. If any provision, clause, or phrase of this part, or the application of any such provision, clause, or phrase to any person, entity, or circumstance, is stayed or determined to be invalid, unlawful, or unenforceable by a court of competent jurisdiction, such determination shall not affect the validity, lawfulness, or enforceability of the remaining provisions or applications of this regulation, which shall remain in full force and effect to the maximum extent permitted by law.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Information Collection Request Title:
Advanced Nursing Education Program Specific Form OMB No. 0906-0089—Revision
Abstract:
HRSA provides advanced nursing education grants to educational institutions to increase the supply, distribution, quality of, and access to advanced education nurses through the Advanced Nursing Education (ANE) Programs. The ANE Programs are authorized by Section 811 of the Public Health Service (PHS) Act (
42 U.S.C. 296j
), as amended. This clearance request is for continued approval of the information collection OMB No. 0906-0089.
The proposed revision to Table 2 of the ANE Program Specific Form outlined in the initial public comment request that was published on July 22, 2026, was to remove the Part-Time column under the Nurse Midwife and Nurse Anesthetist specialty headers, based on the requirement that trainees participating in programs for these two specialty areas must be enrolled full-time. Upon further consideration, HRSA decided to retain the Full-Time and Part-Time columns to provide a consistent, comprehensive format that accommodates the varying enrollment requirements across programs and supports accurate and complete data collection. This is important because the ANE Program Specific Form is used across multiple ANE Programs, the majority of which support both full-time and part-time trainees. Therefore, the proposed revision is retracted and the Part-Time column under the Nurse Midwife and Nurse Anesthetist specialty headers in Table 2 will be retained.
In addition, it is proposed that the ANE Program Specific Form, Table 1: Funding Preference section will be updated to collect the combined number of graduates/program completers employed in funding preference settings (Rural Area, Medically Underserved Community, State or Local Health Department) in one row rather than three separate rows (1a, 1b, 1c). Since the funding preference settings are not mutually exclusive and a graduate must only be counted once, this is to avoid confusion for the applicant on which row to include a graduate/program completer, and for greater administrative efficiency.
A 60-day notice published in the
Federal Register
on July 22, 2026, vol. 91, No. 139; pp. 46126-27. There were no public comments.
Need and Proposed Use of the Information:
Section 811 of the PHS Act provides the Secretary of Health and Human Services with the authority to award grants to and enter into contracts with eligible entities to meet the costs of: (1) projects that support the enhancement of advanced nursing education and practice; and (2) traineeships for individuals in advanced nursing education programs. Under this section, HRSA makes awards to entities who train and support nurses characterized as “advanced education nurses.” Section 805 of the PHS Act (
42 U.S.C. 296d
) requires that in awarding such grants, a statutory funding preference is given to “applicants with projects that will substantially benefit rural or underserved populations, or help meet public health nursing needs in State or local health departments.” For traineeship awards, PHS Act section 811(h)(2) requires special consideration be given to an eligible entity that agrees to expend the award to train advanced education nurses who will practice in designated Health Professional Shortage Areas.
The ANE Program Specific Form allows HRSA to effectively target funding and measure the impact of the ANE Programs in meeting the legislative intent and program goals of supporting the enhancement of advanced nursing education and creating opportunities for individuals in advanced nursing education programs to increase the number of advanced practice nurses, especially in rural and medically underserved areas. Additionally, collecting this data assists HRSA in carrying out the most impactful program and ensuring resources are used responsibly.
Likely Respondents:
Likely respondents will be current ANE Programs awardees and new applicants to ANE Programs.

Information Collection Request Title:
National Practitioner Data Bank for Adverse Information on Physicians and Other Health Care Practitioners—
45 CFR part 60
Regulations and Forms, OMB No. 0906-0081—Revision.
Abstract:
This is a request for a revision of the OMB-approved information collection contained in regulations found in
45 CFR part 60
governing the National Practitioner Data Bank (NPDB) and the forms to be used in registering with, reporting information to, and requesting information from the NPDB. Administrative forms are also included to aid in monitoring compliance with federal reporting and querying requirements. Responsibility for NPDB implementation and operation resides in HRSA's Bureau of Health Workforce.
The intent of the NPDB is to improve the quality of health care by encouraging entities such as hospitals, state licensing boards, professional societies, and other eligible entities
[
1
]
providing health care services to identify and discipline those who engage in unprofessional behavior, and to restrict the ability of incompetent health care practitioners, providers, or suppliers to move from state to state without disclosure or discovery of previous damaging or incompetent performance. It also serves as a fraud and abuse clearinghouse for the reporting and disclosing of certain final adverse actions taken against health care practitioners, providers, or suppliers by health plans, federal agencies, and state agencies (excluding settlements in which no findings of liability have been made). Users of the NPDB include reporters (entities that are required to submit reports) and queriers (entities and individuals that are authorized to request information).
The reporting forms, request for information forms (query forms), and administrative forms (used to monitor compliance) are accessed, completed, and submitted to the NPDB electronically through the NPDB website at
https://www.npdb.hrsa.gov
. All reporting and querying is performed through the secure portal of this website. This revision proposes changes to update burden totals as well as minor text changes. In addition, this revision eliminates the Account Balance Transfer Request form which allowed registered entities to transfer funds between their accounts. The data collected on this form is part of an electronic workflow that falls under a Paperwork Reduction Act exemption for voluntary commercial transactions.
A 60-day notice published in the
Federal Register
on July 17, 2026, vol. 91, No. 136; pp. 44865-67. HRSA received one comment during the 60-day comment period from Highmark Inc. (Highmark), an independent licensee of the Blue Cross Blue Shield Association. Highmark suggested HRSA explore greater patient access to NPDB information, improve the timeliness of reporting and data availability, implement safeguards to avoid creating disincentives for error reporting and organizational learning, and develop additional educational resources to assist the public with understanding practitioner information.
By law, HRSA is unable to make information about specific health care practitioners, entities, providers, or
(
printed page 66857)
suppliers available to the general public. Rather, information available through the NPDB helps eligible entities make informed hiring, credentialing, privileging, and licensing decisions that promote patient safety. As such, HRSA recognizes the importance of information reported to the NPDB being readily available to the entities authorized by law to query the NPDB. Once submitted to the NPDB, reports become immediately available to eligible entities. Eligible entities using the NPDB's Continuous Query monitoring service are notified of new reports for their enrolled subjects within one business day. The NPDB is currently merging its One-Time Query and Continuous Query services into a single query process. Under this approach, eligible entities that query the NPDB will receive an initial query response and will be enrolled in continuous monitoring for the duration of the query period. If new or updated information is reported to the NPDB during that period, the querying entity will be notified, reducing the potential gap between when information is reported to the NPDB and when it becomes available to an eligible entity with an active query.
Health care entities and other entities that are required to submit reports to the NPDB must submit a report to the NPDB within 30 days of taking a reportable action. The NPDB system accepts reports from eligible entities virtually 24/7 via both manual online entry and via an automated machine-to-machine interface. Over the last 18 months, over 75 percent of adverse action reports received were submitted on time with an overall median reporting time of fewer than 14 days.
The NPDB maintains ongoing compliance education and outreach efforts designed to support reporting entities in understanding and meeting their reporting responsibilities. These efforts are continuous and responsive to the needs of reporting entities, which regularly seek NPDB guidance, education, and technical assistance regarding reporting requirements and processes. The NPDB provides outreach and educational resources through a variety of channels, including conference presentations, other professional forums, educational sessions, technical assistance, and direct engagement with reporting entities to address questions, and clarify reporting responsibilities. The NPDB also reviews reporting compliance for state licensing and certification agencies to assess whether required information is being appropriately reported to the NPDB. These efforts complement improvements to the query process by ensuring that information that is required to be reported to the NPDB is available to eligible querying entities and can support health care quality, professional review, and other purposes authorized by law.
Together, these efforts are intended to continue strengthening the timeliness, completeness, and availability of NPDB information, in accordance with the law.
Need and Proposed Use of the Information:
The NPDB acts primarily as a flagging system; its principal purpose is to facilitate comprehensive review of practitioners' professional credentials and background. Information is collected from, and disseminated to, eligible entities (entities that are entitled to query and/or report to the NPDB as authorized in
Title 45 CFR
part 60 of the Code of Federal Regulations) on the following: (1) medical malpractice payments, (2) licensure actions taken by Boards of Medical Examiners, (3) state licensure and certification actions, (4) federal licensure and certification actions, (5) negative actions or findings taken by peer review organizations or private accreditation entities, (6) adverse actions taken against clinical privileges, (7) federal or state criminal convictions related to the delivery of a health care item or service, (8) civil judgments related to the delivery of a health care item or service, (9) exclusions from participation in federal or state health care programs, and (10) other adjudicated actions or decisions. It is intended for NPDB information to be considered with other relevant information in evaluating credentials of health care practitioners, providers, and suppliers.
Likely Respondents:
Eligible entities or individuals that are entitled to query and/or report to the NPDB as authorized in regulations found at
45 CFR part 60
.

Burden in this context means the time expended by persons to generate, maintain, retain, disclose, or provide the information requested. This includes the time needed to review instructions; to develop, acquire, install, and utilize technology and systems for the purpose of collecting, validating, and verifying information, processing and maintaining information, and disclosing and providing information; to train personnel and to be able to respond to a collection of information; to search data sources; to complete and review the collection of information; and to transmit or otherwise disclose the information. AGENCY:
Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
HRSA is publishing this notice of petitions received under the National Vaccine Injury Compensation Program (the Program), as required by the Public Health Service (PHS) Act, as amended. While the Secretary of HHS is named as the respondent in all proceedings brought by the filing of petitions for compensation under the Program, the United States Court of Federal Claims is charged by statute with responsibility for considering and acting upon the petitions.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
For information about requirements for filing petitions, and the Program in general, contact Lisa L. Reyes, Clerk of Court, United States Court of Federal Claims, 717 Madison Place NW, Washington, DC 20005, (202) 357-6400. For information on HRSA's role in the Program, contact the Director, Division of Injury Compensation Programs, 5600 Fishers Lane, Room 14W-17, Rockville, Maryland 20857; 1-800-338-2382, or visit our website at:
https://www.hrsa.gov/​vaccine-compensation
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The Program provides a system of no-fault compensation for certain individuals who have been injured by specified childhood vaccines. Subtitle 2 of Title XXI of the PHS Act,
42 U.S.C. 300aa-10
et seq.,
provides that those seeking compensation are to file a petition with the United States Court of Federal Claims and to serve a copy of the petition to the Secretary of HHS, who is named as the respondent in each proceeding. The Secretary has delegated this responsibility under the Program to HRSA. The Court is directed by statute to appoint special masters who take evidence, conduct hearings as appropriate, and make initial decisions as to eligibility for, and amount of, compensation.
A petition may be filed with respect to injuries, disabilities, illnesses, conditions, and deaths resulting from vaccines described in the Vaccine Injury Table (the Table) set forth at
42 CFR 100.3
. This Table lists for each covered childhood vaccine the conditions that may lead to compensation and, for each condition, the time period for occurrence of the first symptom or manifestation of onset or of significant aggravation after vaccine administration. Compensation may also be awarded for conditions not listed in the Table and for conditions that are manifested outside the time periods specified in the Table, but only if the petitioner shows that the condition was caused by one of the listed vaccines.
Section 2112(b)(2) of the PHS Act,
42 U.S.C. 300aa-12(b)(2)
, requires that “[w]ithin 30 days after the Secretary receives service of any petition filed under section 2111 the Secretary shall publish notice of such petition in the
Federal Register
.” Set forth below is a list of petitions received by HRSA on September 1, 2026, through September 30, 2026. This list provides the name of the petitioner, city, and state of vaccination (if unknown then the city and state of the person or attorney filing the claim), and case number. In cases where the Court has redacted the name of a petitioner and/or the case number, the list reflects such redaction.
Section 2112(b)(2) also provides that the special master “shall afford all interested persons an opportunity to submit relevant, written information” relating to the following:
1. The existence of evidence “that there is not a preponderance of the evidence that the illness, disability, injury, condition, or death described in the petition is due to factors unrelated to the administration of the vaccine described in the petition,” and
2. Any allegation in a petition that the petitioner either:
a. “[S]ustained, or had significantly aggravated, any illness, disability, injury, or condition not set forth in the Vaccine Injury Table but which was caused by” one of the vaccines referred to in the Table, or
b. “[S]ustained, or had significantly aggravated, any illness, disability, injury, or condition set forth in the Vaccine Injury Table the first symptom or manifestation of the onset or significant aggravation of which did not occur within the time period set forth in the Table but which was caused by a vaccine” referred to in the Table.
In accordance with Section 2112(b)(2), all interested persons may submit written information relevant to the issues described above in the case of the petitions listed below. Any person choosing to do so should file an original and three copies of the information with the Clerk of the United States Court of Federal Claims at the address listed above (under the heading
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
), with a copy to HRSA addressed to Director, Division of Injury Compensation Programs, Health Systems Bureau, 5600 Fishers Lane, 14W-17, Rockville, Maryland 20857. The Court's caption (
Petitioner's Name
v.
Secretary of HHS
) and the docket number assigned to the petition should be used as the caption for the written submission.
Chapter 35 of Title 44, United States Code
, related to paperwork reduction, does not apply to information required for purposes of carrying out the Program.
Thomas J. Engels,
Administrator.

AGENCY:
Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).
ACTION:
Notice.
SUMMARY:
This notice publishes a list of HHS approved Medical Review Officers (MROs) certification entities. The most recent HHS Mandatory Guidelines for Federal Workplace Drug Testing Programs (Mandatory Guidelines), effective on October 10, 2023, (Oral Fluid) and February 1, 2024, (Urine), address the role and qualifications of MROs and HHS approval of entities that certify MROs.
DATES:
HHS approval is effective October 23, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Joshua Hunt, Pharm.D., MPH, LCDR, United States Public Health Service, Area/Regional Pharmacy Consultant, Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, 5600 Fishers Lane, Rockville, Maryland 20857; Telephone: (301) 642-9354; Email:
Joshua.hunt@samhsa.hhs.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Subpart M—Medical Review Officer (MRO), Section 13.2 of the Mandatory Guidelines, “How are nationally recognized entities or subspecialty boards that certify MROs approved?” states as follows: “All nationally recognized entities or subspecialty boards which seek approval by the Secretary to certify physicians as MROs for federal workplace drug testing programs must submit their qualifications, a sample examination, and other necessary supporting examination materials (
e.g.,
answers, previous examination statistics or other background examination information, if requested). Approval will be based on an objective review of qualifications that include a copy of the MRO applicant application form, documentation that the continuing education courses are accredited by a professional organization, and the delivery method and content of the examination. Each approved MRO certification entity must resubmit their qualifications for approval every 2 years. The Secretary shall publish at least every 2 years a notice in the
Federal Register
listing those entities and subspecialty boards that have been approved.”
HHS has completed its review of entities that certify MROs, in accordance with requests submitted by such entities to HHS.
The HHS Secretary approves the following MRO certifying entities that offer MRO certification through examination:

.

SUMMARY:
The Food and Drug Administration (FDA, the Agency, or we) is announcing the availability of a draft guidance for industry entitled “Action Levels for Cadmium in Processed Food Intended for Babies and Young Children.” The draft guidance, when finalized, will establish action levels for cadmium in certain processed foods intended for babies and young children less than 2 years old. The draft guidance is intended to set achievable action levels that will help further reduce cadmium in the food supply.
DATES:
Submit either electronic or written comments on the draft guidance by December 22, 2026 to ensure that the Agency considers your comments on the draft guidance before it begins work on the final version of the guidance.

.

https://www.regulations.gov

Please note that if you include your name, contact information, or other information that identifies you in the body of your comments, that information will be posted on

I. Background
We are announcing the availability of a draft guidance for industry entitled “Action Levels for Cadmium in Processed Food Intended for Babies and Young Children.” We are issuing the draft guidance consistent with our good guidance practices regulation (
21 CFR 10.115
). The draft guidance, when finalized, will represent the current thinking of FDA on this topic. It does not establish any rights for any person and is not binding on FDA or the public. You can use an alternate approach if it satisfies the requirements of the applicable statutes and regulations.
This draft guidance, when finalized, would, in accordance with § 109.6 (
21 CFR 109.6
), establish the following action levels for cadmium in processed food intended for babies and young children less than 2 years old: 10 parts per billion (ppb) for fruits, vegetables (excluding single-ingredient carrots), and mixtures (including grain- and meat-based mixtures); 25 ppb for single-ingredient carrots; 45 ppb for dry infant cereals; 20 ppb for yogurts, puddings, and custards; and 25 ppb for single-ingredient meats. Consistent with § 109.6(d), these action levels would reflect levels of cadmium at which FDA may regard the food as adulterated within the meaning of section 402(a)(1) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (
21 U.S.C. 342(a)(1)
). We intend to consider these action levels, in addition to other factors, when considering whether to bring enforcement action in a particular case.
We request comments on these proposed action levels in general, including on whether there may be sufficient data or information that would support different levels for these categories of foods.

We are announcing the availability of one additional draft chapter of a multichapter draft guidance for industry entitled “Hazard Analysis and Risk-Based Preventive Controls for Human Food.” The newly available draft chapter is entitled “Chapter 12: Control of Chemical Hazards.” We are issuing the draft guidance consistent with our good guidance practices regulation (

The FDA Food Safety Modernization Act (FSMA) (
Pub. L. 111-353
) enables FDA to better protect public health by helping to ensure the safety and security of the food supply. FSMA enables FDA to focus more on preventing food safety problems rather than relying primarily on reacting to problems after they occur. FSMA recognizes the important role industry plays in ensuring the safety of the food supply, including the adoption of modern systems of preventive controls in food production.
Section 103 of FSMA amended the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) by adding section 418 (
21 U.S.C. 350g
) with requirements for hazard analysis and risk-based preventive controls for establishments that are required to register as food facilities under our regulations in
21 CFR part 1, subpart H
, in accordance with section 415 of the FD&C Act (
21 U.S.C. 350d
). We have established regulations to implement these requirements within part 117 (
21 CFR part 117
).
The multichapter draft guidance for industry is intended to explain our current thinking on how to comply with the requirements for hazard analysis and risk-based preventive controls under part 117, principally in subparts C and G. This draft chapter addresses controls for known or reasonably foreseeable (“potential”) chemical hazards. On February 13, 2025, the Trump Administration issued
Executive Order 14212
“Establishing the President's Make American Healthy Again Commission” (
90 FR 9833
). The goal of this Commission is to address the health crisis in America and lower chronic disease and, in furtherance of this goal, advance efforts to improve food quality and safety. This guidance seeks to help “Make America Healthy Again” by improving understanding of the regulations regarding controlling chemical hazards in foods, including radiological hazards, pesticide and drug residues, natural toxins, decomposition, and unapproved food or color additives, as specified in
21 CFR 117.130(b)(1)(ii)
, as well as environmental contaminants (
e.g.,
toxic elements (
e.g.,
lead, cadmium, arsenic), dioxin, and per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS)), and hazardous chemicals that can form during food production (process-related contaminants). Controlling chemical hazards in foods helps ensure the safety and quality of the food supply and protect U.S. consumers.
We intend to announce the availability for public comment of additional chapters of the draft guidance as we complete them. The titles of the additional chapters that we expect to make available for public comment are included in the table of contents for the complete multichapter guidance.
As we develop final guidance on this topic, FDA will consider comments on costs or cost savings the guidance may generate, relevant for
Executive Order 14192
.

The previously approved collections of information are subject to review by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA) (
44 U.S.C. 3501-3521
). The collections of information in part 117 have been approved under OMB control number 0910-0751.

AGENCY:
Agricultural Marketing Service, USDA.
ACTION:
Request for information.
SUMMARY:
The Agricultural Marketing Service (AMS) is seeking input from the public, including dairy industry stakeholders, on market conditions related to monthly route sales limits within the exempt plant definition in its regulations. AMS is requesting input on whether and how marketing conditions have changed since the definition was implemented in 1999.
DATES:
Comments must be received by November 23, 2026 to be considered.
ADDRESSES:
Interested persons are invited to submit comments concerning this notice. Comments may be submitted through the Federal e-rulemaking portal at
https://www.regulations.gov
and should reference the document number, date, and page number of this issue of the
Federal Register
. Written comments may be submitted via mail to USDA/AMS/Dairy Programs, Stop 0225—Room 2530, 1400 Independence Avenue SW, Washington, DC 20250-0225. All comments submitted in response to this notice, including the identity of the individuals or entities submitting the comments, will be included in the record and made available to the public, and can be viewed at
https://www.regulations.gov
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Erin Taylor, USDA/AMS/Dairy Programs, Order Formulation and Enforcement Division, STOP 0225—Room 2530, 1400 Independence Avenue SW, Washington, DC 20250-0225; telephone: (202) 720-4392; email address:
OFEB@usda.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
A nonpool plant is defined within the Federal milk marketing order (FMMO) regulations in
7 CFR 1000.8
, which includes the definition for an exempt plant in § 1000.8(e), and specifically a definition for a
de minimis
plant exemption in § 1000.8(e)(4). The regulations were implemented in the Federal Milk Marketing Order Reform (Order Reform) final rule published on September 1, 1999 (
64 FR 47898
), and the definition of a nonpool plant has not been amended since.
To determine the monthly pounds threshold that would qualify a plant for an exemption under the
de minimis
definition being established during the Order Reform process, AMS reviewed the route sales limits of all FMMOs that had a
de minimis
exempt plant provision in place at the time. In an effort not to impose a pool obligation on any plant that was exempt for size at the time, AMS selected the highest plant exemption level allowed in any FMMO, which was 150,000 pounds or less of monthly route disposition.
In considering whether marketing conditions have changed since the definition was implemented in 1999, AMS seeks input from impacted dairy stakeholders on relevant market conditions, route disposition levels, and other related factors.
Request for Information
In this Request for Information (RFI), AMS will consider how fluid milk market conditions have changed since the
de minimis
route disposition limit in the exempt plant definition was implemented, as well as current fluid milk marketing conditions. Through this RFI, AMS is soliciting comments on the market effects for handlers currently operating an exempt plant, as well as the effects of the disposition limit on regulated handlers who are not exempt. All interested parties are encouraged to provide input during the comment period. AMS will review and consider all information submitted in response to this RFI.
Respondents may provide information for one or more of the questions or topics listed below, as desired.
1. What market conditions or other factors should AMS consider in evaluating the current
de minimis
exempt plant route disposition limit?
2. Has the dairy market changed in such a way that the 150,000 pound per month route disposition limit may no longer be appropriate? If so, how?
3. What plant data or other data should AMS consider in its evaluation of the
de minimis
exempt plant definition relative to the current marketing of fluid milk?
4. What impact on the industry—including on producers, handlers, and consumers—would a change in the
de minimis
exempt plant route disposition have, including any increasing or decreasing costs for producers, handlers, or consumers?
5. What effects does the
de minimis
exempt plant route disposition limit have on small businesses? Currently, the Small Business Administration defines a small fluid milk processing plant as a plant, or larger company operating multiple plants, with 1,150 or fewer employees collectively.

Administrator, Agricultural Marketing Service.

on July 1, 2026 (
91 FR 39903
). The NPRM was prompted by a report that couplings having part number (P/N) 369H5660 were found with mechanical damage to the root fillets, spline faces, and the major diameter. It was also reported that a new vendor improperly manufactured certain couplings having P/N 369H5660, with a total of 148 shipped to customers between June 3, 2020, and May 1, 2022. The manufacturer reported that 86 affected couplings have been recovered, with the remaining 62 affected couplings at unknown locations.
In the NPRM, the FAA proposed to require a one-time visual inspection of the couplings for cracks of the splines and, depending on the results, replacement of the couplings. The FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.
Discussion of Final Airworthiness Directive
Comments
The FAA received one comment from an anonymous commenter. The following presents the comment received on the NPRM and the FAA's response to the comment.
Request for Clarification of the Determination for the One-Time Visual Inspection
An anonymous commenter requested that the FAA clarify the determination for a one-time visual inspection. The commenter stated that the NPRM proposed to require a one-time visual inspection for spline cracking. The commenter specified that if spline cracking is caused by fatigue, alignment wear, or operational vibration, then a single inspection only catches existing cracks but fails to protect against future fatigue failures occurring hundreds of flight hours later. The commenter asked what data or modeling was evaluated in making the determination that a one-time visual inspection is safer than a recurring inspection interval or a time-in-service replacement requirement. In addition, the commenter asked whether data was gathered from different agencies or incident logs to further back up the analysis and could be used to monitor the unsafe condition for recurrence.
The FAA agrees to clarify. This AD addresses a manufacturing defect that could lead to fatigue cracking during normal helicopter operation. The one-time visual inspection is to determine whether a crack is present in the defective part and require immediate replacement if cracked. If the defective part is not cracked, the compliance time for replacement is set significantly earlier than the calculated critical crack propagation threshold, which ensures that all defective parts are replaced before any fatigue crack reaches a critical failure point. Therefore, recurring inspections are unnecessary. The FAA did not change this AD as a result of this comment.
Additional Changes to This AD
In the NPRM, the FAA inadvertently included multiple references related to material incorporated by reference (IBR). However, no IBR material was necessary for the NPRM or this AD. Therefore, the FAA has removed all IBR references from this AD. In addition, paragraph (j) “Material Incorporated by Reference” of this AD has been changed to state “None.”
Conclusion
The FAA reviewed the relevant data, considered any comments received, and determined that air safety requires adopting this AD as proposed. Accordingly, the FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products. Except for minor editorial changes, this AD is adopted as proposed in the NPRM. None of the changes will increase the economic burden on any operator.

Authority for This Rulemaking
Title 49 of the United States Code specifies the FAA's authority to issue rules on aviation safety. Subtitle I, section 106, describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII: Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the Agency's authority.
The FAA is issuing this rulemaking under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart III, Section 44701: General requirements. Under that section, Congress charges the FAA with promoting safe flight of civil aircraft in air commerce by prescribing regulations for practices, methods, and procedures the Administrator finds necessary for safety in air commerce. This regulation is within the scope of that authority because it addresses an unsafe condition that is likely to exist or develop on products identified in this rulemaking action.

This AD applies to MD Helicopters, LLC (MDHI) Model 369D, 369E, 369F, 369FF, 369H, and 500N helicopters, certificated in any category, with an installed main transmission drive shaft coupling (coupling) part number 369H5660 with serial numbers 8564-0001 through 8564-0308.
(d) Subject

(e) Unsafe Condition
This AD was prompted by a report of mechanical damage to the coupling. The FAA is issuing this AD to detect and address couplings with damage to the root fillets, spline faces, and major diameter. The unsafe condition, if not addressed, could result in fatigue cracks that grow from the damaged root fillets and spline faces, which could lead to failure of the coupling with consequent loss of power to the main rotor blades and possible emergency autorotational landing.

Abstract:
This information collection and these recordkeeping requirements are necessary to conduct the Federal Seed Act (FSA) (
7 U.S.C. 1551
et seq.
) program with respect to certain testing, labeling, and recordkeeping requirements for agricultural and vegetable seeds in interstate commerce. Regulations under the FSA are contained in
7 CFR part 201
.
The FSA, title II, is a truth-in-labeling law that regulates agricultural and vegetable planting seed in interstate commerce. Seed subject to the FSA must be labeled with certain quality information and title II requires that information to be truthful. The FSA prohibits the interstate shipment of falsely advertised seed and seed containing noxious-weed seeds that are prohibited from sale in the State into which the seed is being shipped.
No unique forms are required for this information collection. The FSA requires seed in interstate commerce to be tested and labeled. Once seed enters a State, it must comply with the testing and labeling requirements of that State's seed law. The testing and labeling required by FSA nearly always satisfies the State's testing and labeling requirements. The receiving sales, cleaning, testing, and labeling records required by FSA are also records that the shipper would normally keep in good business practice.
The information in this collection is the minimum information necessary to effectively carry out the enforcement of FSA. With the exception of the requirements for entering a new variety into a State seed certification program (set forth separately below), the information collection is entirely recordkeeping rather than reporting.
While the number of applicants has slightly increased, the number of requests has decreased due to expanded program outreach and better understanding of the FSA requirements by shippers. This has resulted in a decrease in burden hours over the previous submission.

Abstract of Proposed Collection
1405-0011, DS-2029,
Application for Consular Report of Birth Abroad of a Citizen of the United States of America:
The form is used to apply for a Consular Report of Birth Abroad of a U.S. citizen. The information collected on this form will be used to certify the acquisition of U.S. citizenship at birth of a person born abroad.
8 U.S.C. 1104
and
22 CFR 50.5-50.7
are among the important legal authorities pertaining to the Department's use of this form.
1405-0187, DS-5507,
Affidavit of Physical Presence or Residence, Parentage, and Support:
The form is used to determine whether a U.S. national parent has met the statutory physical presence or residence requirements to transmit U.S. nationality to his/her child born abroad or in a United States territory for U.S. noncitizen nationality; to establish parentage of the child; and to fulfill the requirements of
8 U.S.C. 1409(a)
, which permits acknowledgment of paternity under oath and requires the U.S. citizen father's written agreement to provide financial support for a child born abroad out of wedlock to a U.S. citizen father.
Methodology
Parents normally apply for a Consular Report of Birth Abroad at a U.S. embassy or consulate in the consular district in which the birth occurred. A consular officer will interview the parent(s)/guardian, examine the application and supporting documentation, and enter the information provided into the Department of State American Citizen Services (ACS) electronic database. The DS-2029 application is also available in an online format known as eCRBA. eCRBA allows applicants to enter their data, upload required documents, pay fees, and schedule an appointment to appear at the adjudicating post for an interview. Additionally, the applicant may check the status of their application.
Parent(s) may complete and submit the Affidavit of Physical Presence or Residence, Parentage, and Support in person or by mail. The form may be accessed online, completed electronically, printed, and signed; or it may be downloaded, printed, and completed manually.

This is a request for an extension of an approved information collection. As part of its fishery management responsibilities, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) collects information to determine the amount and type of groundfish caught by fishing vessels. Electronic fish tickets are submissions of landings data from the first receiver to the Pacific States Marine Fisheries Commission (PSMFC) and NMFS. This collection supports requirements for participants of the Pacific Coast shorebased commercial groundfish fisheries (including the shorebased Individual Fishing Quota (IFQ) program, the limited entry fixed gear fishery, and the open access fixed gear fishery) to account for all landed catch and to send electronic catch data used to manage the catch allocations and limits. Analysis of Agreement Containing Consent Orders To Aid Public Comment
I. Introduction
The Federal Trade Commission (“Commission”) has accepted, subject to final approval, an Agreement Containing Consent Orders (“Consent
(
printed page 66843)
Agreement”) designed to remedy the anticompetitive effects resulting from Publicis Groupe S.A.'s (“Publicis”) proposed acquisition of LiveRamp Holdings, Inc. (“LiveRamp”). Pursuant to an Agreement and Plan of Merger dated May 16, 2026, Publicis will acquire LiveRamp in an all-cash transaction for a total enterprise value of approximately $2.2 billion (the “Acquisition”).
The Commission's Complaint alleges that the Acquisition, if consummated, would violate section 7 of the Clayton Act, as amended,
15 U.S.C. 18
, and section 5 of the FTC Act, as amended,
15 U.S.C. 45
, by substantially lessening competition in: (1) the U.S. market for media agency services; and (2) the U.S. market for audience data services. In the relevant market for media agency services, the Acquisition would likely result in Publicis having the ability and incentive to pull customers away from competing media agency service providers by using or misusing competitively sensitive data for its clients' benefit. In the relevant market for audience data services, the Acquisition would likely also result in Publicis having the ability and incentive to use or misuse the competitively sensitive data of its competitors, thereby raising its rivals' costs or otherwise undermining their ability to compete.
The proposed Decision and Order (“Order”) will remedy the Acquisition's likely anticompetitive effects in each relevant market by requiring, for a period of five years, Publicis and LiveRamp (collectively, the “Respondents”) to (1) act as a non-discriminatory supplier of LiveRamp's data connectivity services to both current and future customers of LiveRamp and (2) protect competitors' competitively sensitive information from improper use or disclosure.
The Consent Agreement has been placed on the public record for 30 days for receipt of comments from interested persons. Comments received during this period will become part of the public record. After 30 days, the Commission will again evaluate the Consent Agreement, along with the comments received, to make a final decision as to whether it should withdraw from the Consent Agreement, modify it, or make final the Order.
II. The Respondents
Publicis is a French corporation with its principal place of business in Paris, France. Publicis is a leading global advertising agency that provides creative advertising (
i.e.,
developing brand identities, messaging, visual designs, and advertisements themselves) and media agency services (
i.e.,
planning, executing, and measuring digital advertisement campaigns) for its clients. Relevant here, Publicis provides media agency services for digital advertising across an array of business sectors in the United States. Publicis also provides audience data services, through its subsidiary Epsilon, which include providing advertisers with third-party data that may help in identifying an appropriate audience.
LiveRamp is a Delaware corporation with its principal place of business in San Francisco, California. LiveRamp is a global data collaboration technology company that provides technological services that facilitate the planning, execution, and measurement of digital advertising campaigns. These services include providing technological infrastructure that allows for the movement of data between service providers in the advertisement technology workflow, for example between media agency service providers and websites when executing a campaign or between media agency service providers and audience data service providers.
III. The Products and Structure of the Markets
Publicis is one of five major global advertising holding companies that provide media agency services, along with WPP, Omnicom, Dentsu, and Havas. Media agency services generally cover the following components of an advertising campaign: planning an ad campaign, which includes identifying an audience; executing an ad campaign, which includes placing ads on search engines, social media, digital video, and streaming services; and measuring an ad campaign to determine if the ads reached the intended audience. Several smaller advertising agencies exist and primarily compete for smaller customers or portions of larger advertisers' work but generally do not compete for the same types of business as the major agencies. In the United States, Publicis's share of the media agency services market has been growing, and it leads the five major advertising agencies in terms of media billings. On a worldwide basis, since 2020, Publicis's net new business has substantially exceeded the net new business of other major media agencies.
Audience data services involve the provision of third-party audience data and related services to assist in identifying and/or constructing an appropriate audience for an advertising campaign. Marketers generally design ad campaigns to target potential customers based on relevant attributes. The audience construction process frequently begins with a marketer's own first-party data. In many cases, however, marketers will supplement their first-party data with third-party data to expand the reach of a campaign or refine audience attributes. For example, a sunscreen producer might want to target their advertisement to individuals who have recently rented hotel rooms in Florida beach destinations. The producer is unlikely to possess that information in its first-party data but could purchase that information from third-party sources. There are numerous providers of audience data services, including Publicis's Epsilon. These audience data service providers use data connectivity service providers to share data with marketers in a privacy-compliant manner.
LiveRamp is the leading data connectivity provider in the U.S. media marketing ecosystem. It has the largest scale and is the only provider with a full spectrum of data connectivity services. Data connectivity services can include data onboarding, identity graphs, identity resolution, clean rooms, and an array of other services. Other competitors exist in the data connectivity space, but they may provide only some of the possible suite of data connectivity services, lack in scale compared to LiveRamp, or both. Of particular value in this market are the number of connections, also referred to as integrations, that a data connectivity provider has to facilitate the flow of data between partners in the advertising ecosystem. Currently, LiveRamp has more integrations than any other data connectivity service provider.
IV. Entry
Entry into the relevant markets would not be timely, likely, or sufficient in magnitude, character, and scope to deter or counteract the likely anticompetitive effects of the Acquisition. There are significant barriers to entry into the development, sale, and provision of data connectivity services. It would be difficult, costly, and time consuming for a new entrant to establish the technological scale necessary to compete successfully in the market for data connectivity services.
V. Effects of the Acquisition
The Acquisition would likely result in Publicis having the ability and incentive to misuse the competitively sensitive information, including pricing and other ad campaign data, that it would gain access to when audience data service providers use LiveRamp. Publicis could utilize such information to undermine
(
printed page 66844)
audience data service competitors of Epsilon, thereby making it harder for them to compete or even pushing them out of the market completely. The Acquisition would also likely result in Publicis having the ability and incentive to deny or degrade access to LiveRamp's services for audience data service providers that compete with Epsilon. This type of foreclosure could raise Epsilon's competitors' costs by forcing them to turn to less preferred data connectivity providers with smaller scale and reach and/or spend resources on building out additional data connections.
In addition, the Acquisition would likely result in Publicis having the ability and incentive to appropriate competitively sensitive LiveRamp client data for the benefit of Publicis's media agency services and its own clients. As a result, clients that otherwise prefer the media agency services of competing ad agencies may be pressured to switch to Publicis in order to avoid the competitive harm of data appropriation. This may substantially lessen competition in the market for U.S. media agency services considering Publicis's already large share of net new business awarded over the past few years.
Absent the protections of the Consent Agreement, after the Acquisition, Publicis would likely have the ability and incentive to foreclose by denying or degrading access to LiveRamp's services or by otherwise making decisions to undermine and disadvantage their competitors in the markets for audience data services and media agency services. Publicis would also gain access to competitively sensitive information relating to its competitors and exploit it to its own advantage.
VI. The Order and the Order To Maintain Assets
The Order and the Order to Maintain Assets effectively remedy the Acquisition's likely anticompetitive effects in both the market for audience data services and the market for media agency services by requiring that LiveRamp continue to operate as a neutral platform for all current and future customers by: (1) providing non-discriminatory access to and support for LiveRamp's standalone products and services; (2) preserving access to and support for LiveRamp's standalone products and services, including any access or support required from Publicis; and (3) supporting non-discriminatory interoperability between LiveRamp's standalone products and services and non-Publicis third-party platforms. The non-discrimination prohibitions of the Order apply to any potential discriminatory conduct affecting access, customer and technical support, price, product functionality, technology, and product and platform choice.
The Order requires Publicis to establish firewalls to ensure that Publicis does not access or use LiveRamp customer data and confidential business information that it receives from a customer's use of LiveRamp's standalone products and services, and that Publicis does not transfer or commingle such data for the benefit or development of Publicis products and services. The Order also requires that certain employees who receive any LiveRamp customer confidential business information receive training regarding the restrictions on the use and dissemination of such information.
The Order provides that Publicis shall appoint an independent industry-standard auditor to audit Publicis's compliance with the Order every six months for the first two years after the date of Acquisition, and then once a year thereafter. Copies of the audit will be provided to the Commission. LiveRamp customers may also request an audit, up to once a year, and the Order requires Publicis to conduct an audit of its compliance with the Order's obligations for that customer. The Order also provides for third-party mediation in the event of any disputes arising or relating to noncompliance with the Order.
Finally, the Order specifies that it will terminate five years from the date it is issued.
The purpose of this analysis is to facilitate public comment on the proposed Consent Agreement, and it is not intended to constitute an official interpretation of the proposed Consent Agreement or to modify its terms in any way.
By direction of the Commission.

Acting Secretary.

SUMMARY:
