SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Acronyms, Abbreviations, and Definitions
CSC—Card Security Code. A numeric code printed on a payment card by the issuer used to verify possession of the physical card. May also be known as a Card Verification Value (CVV), Card Validation Code (CVC), Card Authentication Value (CAV), or by other similar terms.
EBT—Electronic Benefit(s) Transfer. An electronic system allowing the issuance of benefits via payment cards.
EBT Host Processor—The vendor contracted by a State to operate the State's central EBT database.
EMV—Europay, Mastercard, and VISA. A payment standard in the consumer payment industry for payment cards with an integrated electronic circuit chip and the terminals which accept them.
FNA/the Agency—Food and Nutrition Administration. The Federal agency with oversight over the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program.
IVR—Interactive Voice Response. A technology allowing automated customer service interactions to take place over a telephone call.
NFC—Near Field Communication. Protocols which enable wireless communication over short distances for payment cards and their terminals, also known as `tap-to-pay' or contactless payment.
PAN—Primary Account Number, commonly found on payment cards.
PII—Personally Identifiable Information. Any representation of information that permits the identity of an individual to whom the information applies to be reasonably inferred by either direct or indirect means.
PIN—Personal Identification Number. In SNAP, a user-selected numeric passcode used for authentication purposes.
POS—Point-of-Sale—the point where a retail transaction is processed and payments from customers are accepted.
SNAP—Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program
The Act—The Food and Nutrition Act of 2008, as amended.
TPP—Third-party Processor—within the context of SNAP, a business entity serving as host processor that facilitates enabling a retailer to accept EBT payments
USDA/the Department—The United States Department of Agriculture
WIC—Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children
Background
SNAP is the largest domestic nutrition assistance program in the United States. In fiscal year 2025, around 42 million low-income individuals received SNAP benefits in an average month to help meet their food needs.
Since 2004, all States have exclusively used EBT cards, which operate similarly to a debit card, to deliver SNAP benefits to households. Most States completed the transition from the paper coupons previously used to EBT cards in the 1990s. At the time of transition, payment cards with magnetic stripes were the predominant form of electronic payment technology in the consumer payment industry. Accordingly, as States transitioned to EBT, payment cards with magnetic stripes were the standard used for EBT as well.
As payment technology has evolved in the years since the universal implementation of EBT, EBT cards utilizing magnetic stripes have fallen behind newer consumer payment methods in terms of security, placing household SNAP benefits at risk. Most EBT systems currently lack security elements common in the consumer payment industry and lag behind in terms of customer experience features as well. The Department employed commercial standards that were in place when EBT was initially rolled out. However, due to evolving consumer payment methods and increased security risks and the Congressional directive to issue proposed rulemaking, the Department must update and modernize those standards to maintain ongoing alignment with the current commercial marketplace.
Through this rule, the Department proposes changes to SNAP with the goal of improving EBT card security, as well as aligning the SNAP client experience to consumer payment processing industry standards, improving both Program integrity and convenience for SNAP clients who depend on the benefits provided to feed their families.
Authority
Section 11 of the Food and Nutrition Act of 2008, as amended (`the Act'), establishes the responsibility of State agencies for issuing benefits via EBT. Section 7(h)(2) of the Act authorizes the USDA to establish and revise standards for EBT issuance.
Section 501(a) Title IV within Division HH of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023,
Public Law 117-328
, requires that the Secretary promulgate regulations through notice-and-comment rulemaking to require
(
printed page 66959)
State SNAP agencies to take security measures in detecting and preventing the theft of benefits, including through card skimming, card cloning, and other similar fraudulent methods.
Summary of EBT Technology
Federal regulations at
7 CFR part 271.2
currently define EBT cards as a method for SNAP households to access the EBT system and their SNAP benefits, including via an online magnetic stripe card (requiring connectivity to a central EBT database), an offline smart card (where benefit balances are tracked individually on the EBT cards themselves), a chip card, a contactless digital wallet with a stored card, or any other similar benefit access technology approved by FNA.
However, all agencies operating SNAP have continued to issue benefits via the same payment method used since the transition from paper coupons: EBT cards with magnetic stripes, secured using Personal Identification Numbers (PINs).
Regulations require that households who participate in SNAP be able to use their cards at any FNA-approved SNAP retailer throughout the United States. Each SNAP transaction involves a series of steps and partners that exchange data.
When EBT cards with magnetic stripes are used, the point-of-sale (POS) terminals operated by SNAP retailers read the data stored on the magnetic stripe and send the transaction information, frequently routed by a third-party processor (TPP) via an EBT gateway, to the card-issuing State's EBT host processor, who is responsible for the operation of the central EBT database and tracking SNAP benefit balances for the State. The EBT host processor responsible for the central EBT database containing the benefits subsequently determines if the transaction is approved or denied and routes the response back to the POS terminal.
In addition to SNAP, several other benefit programs including Summer EBT and Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) are issued on EBT cards. State agencies may provide these benefits on the same EBT card as SNAP or separate EBT cards. In cases where States issue other benefits on the same EBT card as SNAP, those benefits would also be protected by the security improvements proposed in this rule. Although separately issued EBT cards are subject to the same security weaknesses that affect SNAP, they would not be required to comply with the standards proposed in this rule. Regulations for other EBT programs are distinct from SNAP regulations, and changes to requirements for those programs would be promulgated in a separate rulemaking process.
Benefit Theft and Card Security
SNAP benefit theft is a direct threat to the health and well-being of SNAP participants, denying them access to food that they may not otherwise have the financial means to purchase. Ensuring the integrity of SNAP benefits is necessary so that clients can shop for food with confidence in the EBT system and to ensure that benefits are reserved only for eligible SNAP households. Further, fraudulent EBT schemes also constitute the theft of hard-earned, American tax dollars. Under its oversight of SNAP, the Department is responsible for ensuring EBT systems prevent fraud, waste, and abuse of funds.
Historically, it was preferable for bad actors to pursue the cash obtained from credit/debit cards versus the SNAP benefits obtained from EBT cards. Over the last decade, the changing technology used by the consumer payment industry has strengthened protections against credit/debit card theft, yet SNAP continues to rely on magnetic stripes secured only by PINs as the primary means of conducting transactions. Now that credit/debit cards have significantly increased protections and primarily rely on chip and NFC transactions, experienced criminals have turned their attention to EBT cards and implemented the same techniques previously used against credit/debit cardholders. This leaves SNAP participants increasingly vulnerable to benefit theft, potentially forcing them to spend money already budgeted for other necessities on food.
Magnetic stripes as a technology for conducting transactions are inherently vulnerable, as many techniques have been developed that exploit known vulnerabilities. Bad actors may attach devices to POS terminals that can intercept card data to easily access information that is encoded on the magnetic stripe of the EBT card (“card skimming”), such as the Primary Account Number (PAN). PINs can be obtained or guessed by a variety of methods including interception methods, hidden cameras, algorithmic attacks, customer service interactive voice response (IVR) vulnerabilities, and phishing attacks where SNAP clients are deceived into unwittingly divulging PIN information.
In the past, when complete card information was obtained, bad actors still had challenges obtaining equipment that could then write the stolen card information onto a new card (“card cloning”). Due to the cost of complex electronics decreasing over time, card cloning equipment is now more affordable and easily accessible. This has minimized the barrier for bad actors to clone cards and use benefits stolen from the original SNAP benefit account involved.
Additionally, bad actors exploited the expansion of SNAP online shopping as another route to spend fraudulently obtained EBT card information. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the USDA expedited nationwide participation in the previously existing SNAP Online Purchasing Pilot. To help SNAP clients make purchases of food while remaining safely isolated, clients in all States could enter their EBT card number and PIN to make online purchases from authorized SNAP retailers offering pick-up or delivery of SNAP-eligible products. Post-pandemic, SNAP online purchasing continues to be available nationwide. If proper security measures are not implemented in these online purchasing systems, algorithmic attacks can be used by bad actors to attempt large numbers of transactions with varying inputs until they succeed. For example, there is often significant vulnerability to `soft' PINs that may be easily guessed, such as common number sequences (“1234”), or repeating numbers (“1111”).
With this proposed rule, the Department looks to address some of the common vulnerabilities inherent to the transaction technologies currently used in EBT systems by bringing EBT in alignment with the consumer credit/debit industry. The Department intends to take advantage of existing strategies and technologies known to be effective in detecting and preventing theft of SNAP benefits through card skimming, card cloning, and other similar electronic fraudulent methods, with the goal of ensuring the integrity of SNAP benefit issuances.
Availability of Data
Although EBT fraud and benefit theft has attracted national attention in recent years, the Department does not have data that can conclusively and accurately track long-term historical levels of EBT benefit theft perpetrated via electronic methods such as card skimming and card cloning, as historically there were no requirements for States to provide data on EBT fraud.
The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023 included time-limited requirements for States to provide FNA with statistical reports on such theft and implement plans to replace stolen SNAP benefits with Federal funds. The data provided by States pursuant to this requirement (starting in Federal Fiscal
(
printed page 66960)
Year 2023) on the volume of stolen SNAP benefits replaced can be viewed online at:
https://www.fna.usda.gov/​data-research/​data-visualization/​snap-replacement-stolen-benefits-dashboard
,
and provides FNA and the public with limited insight into the scale and patterns of EBT benefit theft. However, the authority provided by the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023 for replacement of stolen SNAP benefits with Federal funds expired on December 20, 2024, so States are once again no longer required to report EBT fraud statistics to the Department. As of the second quarter of Federal Fiscal Year 2025, 753,929 claims for replacement of stolen SNAP benefits have been approved across the nation, with a total replacement value of $360,441,561. A limited number of retroactive claims and associated replacements are expected as States sunset their replacement process. Further, these data only reflect fraudulent transactions for which SNAP households filed claims to replace their benefits during this period and may not capture the full scope of benefit theft during this period.
While the lack of retrospective data makes it difficult to assess historical rates of EBT benefit theft, analysis of publicly available reporting on the topic points strongly to a significant increase in reports of benefit theft to State agencies starting in recent years.
Information Access for Benefit Integrity
Beyond the deficiencies with the transaction method itself, SNAP EBT also frequently lags the consumer payment industry in features available to clients to monitor and secure their benefits. Some existing EBT systems do not make available comprehensive transaction information including the name of the retailer involved. The availability of user-selectable account security options (such as benefit account freezing or blocking of purchases of specific types or in specific locations) also varies widely from State to State.
Ensuring all SNAP clients in every State are fully aware of the details of purchases being made with their account helps to strengthen benefit integrity and enhance the customer experience. Giving SNAP clients access to enhanced account features, many of which are common in the consumer payment industry, will enable them to control how their benefits can be spent and help avoid EBT fraud. SNAP clients must be able to activate and deactivate these accounts freely via online cardholder portal systems, or mobile account information applications, as well as by contacting their local State office via telephone or visiting in person. Offering multiple customer service channels is critical for all services offered to ensure that the disparate needs of SNAP clients are met, including disabled clients or clients with limited internet or mobile phone access.
With these changes, this proposed rule intends to improve the general customer experience of SNAP clients as they purchase food via EBT by giving them greater control and understanding of their benefit account.
Listening Sessions
In 2023, the Department prepared for this proposed rule by conducting 16 listening sessions focused on the migration to EBT cards with electronic chip and NFC payment technology with partners from the SNAP industry, such as: EBT host processors, third-party processors, retailers and retailer associations, anti-hunger advocates, equipment manufacturers, and State agencies. The Department continues to engage with these partners with additional listening sessions facilitated through the USDA EBT Card Industry Forum hosted by the Accredited Standards Committee X9. The Accredited Standards Committee X9 is the American National Standards Institute (ANSI)-accredited standards developing organization that sets standards for exchanging EBT financial transaction messages. Beginning in June 2023, the X9 EBT Card Industry Forum was created, consisting of FNA, State agencies, EBT host processors, third-party payment processors, retailers, point-of-sale providers, the branded card networks, and mobile payment processors. All partners involved in the Forum agreed on the establishment of national standards for mobile payment and electronic chip card technologies to be used in EBT. After an extensive public notice and comment process, the updated EBT standard was officially ratified and published
[
1
]
by ANSI in August 2024.
Guidance
In October 2022, the Department issued guidance titled “Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) and Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) Electronic Benefit Transfer (EBT) Card Skimming Prevention—Tools and Resources” with the intent to educate State SNAP agencies on known forms of benefit theft and recommended prevention tactics.
[
2
]
The Department issued this guidance in response to increasing reports of benefit theft from State SNAP agencies. In March 2023, the Department issued guidance titled “Addressing Stolen SNAP Benefits” to SNAP participants, State SNAP agencies, and SNAP retailers additional regarding best practices to combat benefit theft.
[
3
]
In the creation of this rule, the Department has considered effectiveness against benefit theft and consistency with consumer payment industry standards, as well as the cost of the requirements to be imposed on parties involved with implementing the EBT changes.
With this proposed rule, the Department seeks comments from the public regarding the potential changes to EBT. The Department will discuss each of the proposed regulatory changes in more detail below.
Discussion of Proposed Rule
SNAP EBT Operating Standards
The Department currently does not utilize any type of operating standards for SNAP EBT-related purposes. As a result, when payment technology that enhances security evolves in the consumer payment industry, the Department is unable to enforce integration of such technology into EBT due to the time constraints of the regulatory process. Financial pressures and lack of updated Federal standards may also cause State SNAP agencies to delay or avoid EBT system enhancements.
The Department proposes the creation and adoption of a set of SNAP EBT Operating Standards into regulation to address these issues. These standards will be found at Appendix A to Part 274—Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program Electronic Benefit Transfer Operating Standards. This document establishes technical operating standards to be utilized by State agencies (and the contracted vendors acting on their behalf) in their operation of SNAP and EBT payment methods and supplement the regulatory requirements found in
7 CFR 274
. The SNAP EBT Operating Standards define a variety of mandatory and optional features for State agencies to implement within their EBT systems and payment methods. Some of the elements covered within the SNAP EBT Operating Standards include transaction
(
printed page 66961)
processing, documentation, reporting, and system requirements.
The SNAP EBT Operating Standards, in conjunction with the proposed regulatory changes, have the following key objectives:
—Aligning SNAP closer to consumer payment (credit and debit) industry practices
—Ensuring responsiveness to future industry developments
—Reduction of benefit theft targeting SNAP clients
—Increased informational awareness and confidence for clients regarding their SNAP benefit accounts
—Improved SNAP customer experience
—Improved FNA oversight of new EBT implementation projects, database conversions, and system testing
—Enhanced data availability and accuracy for key Program metrics
Along with these key objectives, the SNAP EBT Operating Standards will specifically provide guidance on requirements and standards for: SNAP-authorized retailers; EBT host processors; what is required to perform and process an EBT transaction; how parties to a transaction share and store transaction data; security measures related to EBT transaction fraud and benefit theft; State EBT system implementation; the design, security, and functions of EBT cards; SNAP Online and card-not-present transaction requirements for internet retailers; SNAP EBT mobile payments; and household EBT training.
The Department proposes to create and then subsequently revise the Operating Standards on a regular, ongoing basis. The Department seeks feedback regarding the format and frequency of future revisions.
The SNAP EBT Operating Standards are available within Appendix A of Part 274.
EBT Cards With Chip and NFC Technology
While the regulatory definition at
7 CFR 271.2
for “Electronic Benefit Transfer (EBT) card” includes chip cards within the definition, at the time of this writing there are a limited number of States actively working to transition their EBT payment system to payment cards with electronic chip and near-field communication (NFC) technology, commonly known as EMV (Europay, Mastercard and Visa) technology from the commercial industry's security standard with that name. EBT cards with chip and NFC technology have enhanced security features that mitigate skimming and cloning attacks when compared to EBT cards with only magnetic stripe technology.
Information available to FNA suggests a significant portion of EBT benefit theft is due to skimming of EBT card data facilitated by magnetic stripes. The Department believes that EBT cards utilizing chip and NFC technology are likely to significantly reduce incidences of benefit theft based on information available regarding the transition to chip and NFC technology in the consumer payment industry. In the early stages of chip and NFC adoption, Mastercard fraud data showed a 54 percent decrease in counterfeit fraud costs at US retailers completing chip and NFC adoption from April 2015 to April 2016.
[
4
]
Visa fraud data showed in 2019
[
5
]
that merchants who accepted chip and NFC cards “witnessed a 76 percent dip in card present counterfeit payment fraud since the U.S. payments industry began the shift to EMV chip.” The shift to universal adoption of chip technology starting in 2015 (when liability was moved onto retailers for non-chip transactions), and the increasing prevalence of NFC technology in the consumer payment industry, together mean that many SNAP households will likely already be familiar with the use of a payment card with chip and NFC technology. The Department is also hopeful that the experience gained from years of established use of chip and NFC technology in the consumer payment industry will help expedite payment method transitions for all parties as well as reducing costs involved when compared to earlier transitions.
While mobile wallet payment systems may benefit from even greater security due to the use of tokenization, a process that adds an additional layer of authentication to the purchasing process by replacing traditional card data with unique electronic tokens tied to specific devices, the technology is newer and potentially requires significant additional costs to provide token services. The Agricultural Act of 2018 (
Pub. L. 115-334
) authorizes the use of mobile technologies for the purpose of accessing SNAP benefits for payment at the point-of-sale following up to five initial demonstration projects. The Department will continue the Mobile Payment Pilot and evaluate its results to determine if mobile payment technology should be authorized or required nationwide in the future. At this time, the Department is prioritizing chip and NFC technologies within the existing EBT systems infrastructure to expedite more secure payment methods for all SNAP households.
The Department is proposing a two-year timeframe after the date of publication of a final rule for implementing requirements regarding the issuance of SNAP benefits via EBT cards utilizing chip and NFC technology. This timeframe will allow for sufficient testing of systems with State agencies, third-party processors, EBT vendors, and retailers both large and small, to ensure that no complications arise from the switch in payment technology that could hinder SNAP clients from making the same regular purchases that they rely on. However, the Department encourages and continues to support States moving towards more secure EBT cards before the proposed implementation date. As of August 2026, seven States have issued EBT chip cards to participants with additional States in progress.
[
6
]
Aligned with this timeframe will be the requirement that States adequately notify households and retailers in advance regarding any such transition in payment method. In conjunction with this, the Department proposes updating the definition of an EBT card, defined at
7 CFR 271.2
“Electronic Benefit Transfer (EBT) card,” to explicitly include cards with integrated electronic chips capable of conducting transactions either by being inserted into a card reader or via wireless NFC protocols. The Department welcomes public comment on the proposed chip and NFC technology implementation timeframe of two years from the date of publication of the final rule and whether that timeframe is both sufficient for compliance and effective at combating electronic benefit theft.
As noted, a limited number of States are now actively working to transition their EBT payment system to EBT cards with chip and NFC technology. It is clear that transition to payment processing via chip and NFC transactions will require significant system changes for all parties involved, along with replacement of EBT cards for all participants, as well as cooperation by retailers upgrading their equipment to comply with the requirements needed to accept payments via EBT cards with chip and NFC technology. The Department believes that the best approach would be an expedited nationwide transition to EBT cards with chip and NFC technology, as opposed to a limited pilot program. This expedited
(
printed page 66962)
approach would be best due to the scale of the existing nationwide threat of SNAP benefit theft through the skimming of EBT cards with magnetic stripes, demonstrated clearly with at least $360 million in stolen benefits that have been replaced through the second quarter of Federal fiscal year 2025. Furthermore, an expedited transition would streamline interoperability concerns and transition communications for SNAP households.
The Department acknowledges that a transition to EBT cards with chip and NFC technology will come at a financial cost to the State agencies administering SNAP and to other entities involved in the operation of EBT systems. However, the Department believes that it is critical for SNAP clients to have reliable and secure access to the benefits that they use to purchase food for their families, and that the transition to chip and NFC cards in the credit/debit industry has proven the effectiveness of the technology involved in reducing incidents of fraud. Letting the consumer payment industry lead in transitioning payment technology has positioned EBT to benefit from experiences gained there and will help avoid costs that would otherwise be encountered in developing untested payment technology. Further, as stewards of taxpayer dollars, the Department considers these administrative costs as a necessary investment to deter the loss of Federally-funded SNAP benefits.
The Department also encourages State SNAP agencies to work with retailers and retailer associations to ensure that as many SNAP retailers as possible complete preparations for the acceptance of EBT transactions via chip and NFC before State SNAP agencies begin the process of replacing existing SNAP cards, to simplify the transition from the perspective of SNAP households who might otherwise face confusion over which transaction methods should be used at individual retailers. Furthermore, the Department encourages State SNAP agencies to educate SNAP households regarding the security benefits of chip and NFC technologies to conduct transactions.
Given the current prevalence of issues with the timely delivery of benefits in accordance with
7 CFR 274.2(b)
, the Department is specifically interested in comments from State SNAP agencies on the impact that migrating to EBT cards with chip and NFC technology would have on over-the-counter issuance of EBT cards and for State operations.
With the goal of a smooth transition to EBT cards with chip and NFC technology, there will be a need for retailers to continue to accept transactions via EBT card with magnetic stripe, for the time being (although fallback rules would enforce the requirement of inserting/tapping a card with a chip to attempt the transaction in that manner before the magnetic stripe could be used). As such, the Department is also interested in understanding the costs that will be borne by State agencies, third-party processors of EBT transactions, and retailers to ensure that point-of-sale machines can properly fall back to accepting magnetic stripe transactions if chip/NFC-based transactions fail or are otherwise unavailable (such as during a period of transition, or due to shopping across State borders in a State that has not yet transitioned to EBT cards with chip and NFC technology).
One consideration for moving to EBT cards with chip and NFC technology is the limited lifespan of chip technology. As a result of this, EBT cards with chip and NFC technologies will have expiration dates. The Department proposes to update regulations at
7 CFR 274.6(b)(3)
,
274.6(b)(5)
, and
274.6(b)(6)
to clarify that EBT cards replaced as a result of their expiration date, or replaced as a result of a change in benefit delivery method, must not be counted towards the threshold for the number of card replacements considered excessive in
7 CFR 274.6(b)(5)
.
In conjunction with the move to EBT cards with chip and NFC technology, the Department is proposing to update regulations at
7 CFR 274.8(b)(5)(vi)
to specify that the PAN on each EBT card shall be printed on the back of the card. This will enhance security measures by making it more difficult to capture account information visually from EBT cards and is aligned with the consumer credit/debit industry.
Magnetic Stripe
EBT's current reliance on magnetic stripes for payment cards is a major enabler of benefit theft, as the account information stored on the magnetic stripe can be easily read in plain text by skimming devices that intercept card data during a transaction. This creates an incentive for thieves who may have targeted credit/debit transactions in the past, when they were conducted mainly via magnetic stripe, to now focus their efforts on EBT cards made more vulnerable as one of the last remaining payment methods conducted almost exclusively via magnetic stripe.
The consumer payment card industry has begun preparations to phase out magnetic stripes, with Mastercard stating in 2023 that “by 2033, no Mastercard cards will have magnetic stripes.”
[
7
]
With this in mind, the Department is seeking public comment specifically related to the eventual removal of magnetic stripes from EBT cards, particularly regarding:
—Barriers to the removal of magnetic stripes
—Alternative methods of conducting transactions if chip and NFC technology fails at the point-of-sale
—Interoperability issues
—Timeframe for removal
The Department proposes revising the existing regulation at
7 CFR 274.8(b)(3)(ii)(C)
to remove the reference to EBT cards specifically containing magnetic stripes in advance of any transition away from their use, as well as revising references at
7 CFR 274.6(b)
to clarify that the card replacement methods within that section of regulations apply specifically to physical card replacements. This will enable a transition away from magnetic stripe technology in the future and ensure clarity if SNAP benefits are to be delivered via EBT cards in non-physical form such as virtual cards in mobile wallets.
End of Manual Voucher Transactions
SNAP regulations in the past allowed SNAP retailers to redeem benefits using manual vouchers if they did not have, or were unable to use, a POS device to process SNAP transactions at the time of the purchase. This was designed to help ensure that SNAP clients would not be denied the ability to use their benefits as the result of unreliable EBT system connectivity.
Since these manual voucher transactions do not require the use of a secure PIN, they have been shown to be susceptible to fraud. The Agricultural Act of 2014 (2014 Farm Bill) amended Section 7(f) of the Act to prohibit the use of manual vouchers for benefit redemption, except in the specific cases where the Secretary determines they are necessary such as due to an EBT system outage or a disaster. The 2014 Farm Bill also provided the Department with the option to exempt certain retailer categories from this prohibition based on established criteria established by the Secretary if the Department determined it appropriate.
The March 21, 2014, implementing memorandum for the 2014 Farm Bill
[
8
]
stipulated that this manual voucher restriction would be effective immediately for any newly authorized
(
printed page 66963)
retailer. However, the memorandum also noted that until regulations were promulgated, the Secretary was exempting those existing retailers that were already using manual vouchers for ongoing business. At the same time, the implementing memorandum stated that it was “the intent of the Secretary to largely eliminate manual vouchers as a means to conduct ongoing business through regulations, but [that FNA would] use the regulatory process to fully define the extent continued usage will be permitted.” Consistent with that stated intent, this rule proposes to codify elimination of the usage of manual vouchers except in disasters or in the event of an EBT system failure, with other exceptions being limited.
Proposed language revising
7 CFR 274.3(a)(1)(i)
would stipulate manual vouchers be authorized only when there is a significant EBT connectivity problem. This could occur as the result of either system issues, or other outage issues, including those resulting from a natural disaster. The Department's expectation is that State SNAP agencies would require of their EBT vendors that the processing of manual vouchers be disabled by default. Manual vouchers would then be enabled by EBT vendors upon request by their State SNAP agency, restricted to certain geographic areas as appropriate. FNA would monitor for manual voucher use that would be considered excessive on an ongoing basis, and work with States to resolve any issues encountered. In situations where manual voucher use is not being appropriately restricted and sufficient levels of fraud are being encountered as a direct result, FNA may seek disallowance of administrative funding under
7 CFR 276.4(a)(2)
and
276.4(a)(3)
regarding State agency responsibilities for preventing losses of Federal funds.
It is important to note that manual voucher transactions are an extremely small minority of SNAP transactions in total.
[
9
]
The proposed changes to manual vouchers would primarily impact retailers that conduct business via delivery routes as well as some retailers operating in remote areas; both have been known to rely on manual vouchers historically as their principal method of benefit redemption. Those retailers would be expected to utilize some form of mobile POS device or mobile POS phone/tablet application to conduct their business, with both approaches becoming even more commonplace in the consumer payment industry since the implementing memorandum for the 2014 Farm Bill. Since the passing of that legislation, general internet connectivity nationwide has improved significantly. A June 2020 Government Accountability Office report
[
10
]
indicated that, based on FCC data, broadband internet availability in rural areas of the US increased from 45.7% to 77.7% from 2012 to 2018.
The Department will consider allowing limited exceptions on a case-by-case basis in specific scenarios, and seeks public comment regarding the need for these exceptions:
First, the Department will consider an exception for retailers that regularly process transactions via manual vouchers in rural areas that do not have internet connectivity, such as some areas of Alaska, making it impossible to utilize mobile POS devices or mobile POS phone/tablet applications.
Second, the Department will consider exempting retailers who are eligible for free State-provided EBT equipment due to the nature of their organization.
Third, the Department will consider exempting retailers in designated Tribal areas from requirements regarding manual vouchers. During consultation with Tribal leaders on March 15, 2024, a summary of this proposed rule was presented and there were no concerns expressed.
EBT Equipment Costs
To better align SNAP with current industry practices, the 2014 Farm Bill amended Section 7(f) of the Food and Nutrition Act to require that all non-exempt retailers be financially responsible for any EBT equipment, supplies, and related services needed to participate in EBT. As a result, most retailers are no longer eligible to receive free EBT equipment, supplies, and related services to participate in SNAP which they may previously have been eligible for.
This legislative change recognized that credit and debit card usage is more prevalent today than it was when EBT was first implemented, and the equipment needed for card acceptance has become nearly ubiquitous. The statute provided exemptions for farmers markets, direct marketing farmers, military commissaries, non-profit food buying cooperatives, and establishments, organizations, programs or group living arrangements described in clauses (3), (4), (5), (7), (8), and (9) of section 3(k) of the Act. While this change was put in place by the March 21, 2014, FNA implementing memorandum,
[
11
]
it must still be codified in regulations.
This proposed rule would codify the statutory provision by making changes accordingly at
7 CFR 274.3(a)(2)
. The Department also proposes changing regulations in this area at
7 CFR 274.3(b)
to remove outdated requirements regarding EBT terminal deployment, to properly reflect that FNA currently only requires States to provide no-cost, EBT-only POS equipment to retailers exempted by the Agricultural Act of 2014 from the requirement that SNAP retailers pay for their own EBT equipment. All other retailers must source their own equipment to be able to process EBT transactions.
SNAP Transaction and Account Information Access
Informational awareness is a critical element in benefit theft prevention and early detection of signs of potential fraud.
7 CFR 274.7(d)
requires that SNAP households be able to access their account balances, and that EBT systems be “. . . capable of providing a transaction history for a period of up to 2 calendar months to households . . .” but the existing regulation does not specify the information regarding each transaction which should be included in that transaction history, nor how quickly the systems which display this information to SNAP clients be updated with new transaction data.
As a result, existing online account management systems and mobile account information applications accessed by SNAP participants in some States do not currently display detailed information such as retailer names and locations of prior purchases made, and do not offer participants the ability to review certain activity on their account such as balance inquiries. The lack of a requirement for immediate updates to this information also means that some EBT systems only make SNAP transaction information available after a delay. Both of these shortcomings hinder the abilities of SNAP households to review and confirm the activity on their own account to ensure purchases made and other actions taken are legitimate.
The Department intends to create new provisions in SNAP regulations at
7 CFR 274.8(b)(4)(i)(H)
and
274.8(b)(4)(i)(I)
to specify information which must be made available to SNAP participants when they review their benefit account through an online account management
(
printed page 66964)
system or mobile account information system, including:
—Transaction dates, times, and amounts
—Type of transaction (card-not-present or card present. Card-not-present transactions would be encountered when making purchases from internet retailers)
—Identifying information for retailer, excluding FNA retailer numbers
—History of balance inquiries made
—History of PIN changes
—History of other personal account information changes including address, email address, and telephone number
The Department also intends to revise SNAP regulations at
7 CFR 274.7(d)(2)
to require EBT systems to provide 12 months of transaction history instead of the current requirement of 2 months. This will align SNAP with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's Regulation E requirements for electronic fund transfers at
12 CFR 1005.15(d)(1)(ii)
.
These regulatory updates will also require that the required information be made available to SNAP clients immediately after SNAP purchases are made. With these changes in place, the Department believes SNAP households will have greater informational awareness regarding the integrity of their account and will be able to monitor their benefit account for potentially fraudulent transactions.
One concern regarding this information being made available involves victims of domestic violence. There is the possibility that a household member who has fled a domestic violence situation could be tracked using a SNAP online cardholder portal or cardholder mobile application by another household member with access, who would be able to review the location of purchases made with the SNAP benefits. The Department is considering requiring that State agencies accept verified requests via telephone or in-person contact to disable all location-based account information (including masking transaction locations) in their online cardholder portal and mobile application for a specific account, and requests comment from the public in this area specifically.
Balance Inquiries
At this time, there are no requirements regarding verification of minimum information for a balance inquiry to be conducted via IVR. As a result, it is possible for bad actors to conduct bulk balance inquiries via the EBT customer service phone number. These bulk balance inquiries facilitate benefit theft by making it significantly easier for bad actors to determine which card data can potentially be exploited.
To prevent benefit theft, the Department proposes creating regulations at
7 CFR 274.7(d)(4)
and using the SNAP EBT Operating Standards document (see Appendix A to Part 274) to require that SNAP balance inquiries conducted via IVR shall require verification. This will help reduce incidents of bad actors using IVR as a method of enabling and expediting benefit theft—a pattern that has been noted across the country by State SNAP agencies reporting to FNA trends in EBT benefit theft. The verification must involve secured information (such as additional card security features) but should not involve PII, as a SNAP household may include multiple persons shopping with the benefits of the SNAP account.
As an additional measure to ensure the integrity of balance inquiries, the Department intends to revise existing regulations at
7 CFR 274.7(d)(1)
to permit internet retailers to conduct business without offering a method of balance inquiry. Online balance inquiry methods can be vulnerable due to security flaws, and FNA regularly grants waivers in this area currently as a matter of business. The Agency has not received any complaints regarding balance inquiry availability after 5 years of the pilot program for SNAP online purchasing. Though the Department considers it a safe assumption that households who are making SNAP purchases online can conduct a balance inquiry online in a secure manner by logging into their State's SNAP cardholder portal or mobile application, public comments regarding the accessibility and security of balance inquiries are welcomed.
In addition, the introduction of internet retailers has brought awareness to the outdated requirements in
7 CFR 274.7(d)(3)
and
274.8(b)(7)
that mention printed receipts. Since many internet retailers (and some brick-and-mortar retailers) now take advantage of electronic receipts, the Department proposes revising these regulations to remove the word “printed” to clarify that retailers may also provide receipts via electronic means.
Household Training Updates
Current regulations at
7 CFR 274.2(e)
on household training requirements for SNAP households do not specify that the households be trained on best practices to avoid EBT benefit theft, although FNA does offer a Tips and Resources website
[
12
]
with suggestions for SNAP clients to follow to reduce incidents of SNAP fraud.
Household training should empower SNAP households not only with the knowledge needed to use their SNAP benefits, familiarity with program requirements, and awareness of time limits for using SNAP benefits before they are expunged, but also with knowledge of security best practices that will reduce their chances of being a victim of benefit theft. The training requirements' message and format should also balance not overwhelming participants with information that prevents them from absorbing the most important knowledge.
The Department proposes updating the household training requirements accordingly. The Department does not intend to change or specify to State agencies the method in which each element of household training should be delivered, as long as all clients can be assured to receive all elements of the required household training.
The Department proposes revising training requirements to include familiarizing participants specifically with:
—Timeframes within which households are to be given the opportunity to participate (also known as timeliness requirements);
—The issuance schedule and availability date for households to access their benefits;
—The appropriate utilization and security of the EBT card's PIN including a number of important steps to take in fraud prevention;
—Responsibilities in reporting theft of or damage to a physical EBT card, and responsibilities in reporting suspected fraud;
—Information regarding EBT card replacement, including any applicable fees;
—Requirements regarding availability of information in languages other than English, for households with disabilities, and the inclusion of civil rights statements;
—Information needed to recognize retailers where EBT benefits can be used;
—Information regarding retailer-initiated debit adjustments and a household's right to notice, fair hearings, and provisional credits, as well as how to dispute such adjustments by requesting a hearing and the timeframes involved;
(
printed page 66965)
—The right to request an adjustment in case of an error transaction and the timeframes involved;
—Timeframes involving benefit expungement;
—Information regarding replacement of food destroyed in a household misfortune including the timeframe for a timely report;
—Food that is eligible for purchase with SNAP benefits;
—The prior payment prohibition described in
7 CFR 274.7(b)
;
—Information on transaction limits as described in
7 CFR 274.7(c)
;
—Information regarding container deposit fees;
—Common methods of EBT theft and how to avoid them;
—Where information regarding rights and responsibilities as a SNAP client can be found;
—Information regarding expiration dates on physical EBT cards and the resulting replacement, in order to avoid client confusion with misinterpreting expiration dates as reflecting either benefit expungement or certification period end dates.
Codifying Common Waivers
FNA routinely receives EBT waiver requests regarding client-initiated credit adjustments and retailer-initiated debit adjustments that replace the timeliness standard of 10 business days with an extended time period of 15 calendar days and that allow State SNAP agencies to act on retailer-initiated debit adjustment requests without placing a hold on the adjustment balance in the household's account. The Department proposes revisions to regulations at
7 CFR 274.2(g)(2)
to bring the procedures for client-initiated credit adjustments and retailer-initiated debit adjustments in line with these waivers, which are commonly approved, to simplify SNAP operations and ensure that State agencies will not need to potentially revise training material contingent on waiver approval or denial.
The Department also proposes revisions to
7 CFR 274.2(f)(2)(i)
regarding the ability of clients to select PINs for their EBT cards via IVR telephone system. Current regulations state that PINs provided to or selected by SNAP clients for use in accessing benefits in the household's EBT account must be encrypted, at a minimum, from the point of entry, in accordance with the current requirement at
7 CFR 274.8(b)(3)(ii)(C)
. This protects the client's PIN both when the client is initially selecting it at the local office and afterwards when using it to make a purchase at a POS device. Because of this encryption, the PIN cannot be viewed or obtained by someone else with access to the system, whether authorized or not. However, due to these regulations, States have needed to obtain a waiver from this requirement to allow clients to select their own PINs over a telephone or cellular line through an IVR system, a process in which the PIN is not encrypted when the client first enters a PIN of his/her own choosing. FNA has approved this waiver to allow States to provide this enhanced customer service. However, in doing so, the Agency has also reminded States that they would have liability for any losses resulting from this procedure.
In response to State waiver requests, the proposed rule would allow States the option to give clients the ability to select their own PIN at their convenience without having to visit the local certification office. While this procedure is consistent with the PIN selection process used by commercial bank customers, it does pose inherent risks when compared to the encrypted capture and transmission of a PIN from the point-of-entry utilizing PIN select devices. As a partial safeguard, the Department would also require the process to be completely automated, with no involvement of a customer service representative, and that clients using this process would need to enter two elements of their personally identifiable information (PII) to confirm their identity. Consistent with Section 7(e)of the Act, and FNA regulations at
7 CFR 274.1(d)(1)
. FNA would also continue to require States to accept liability for any losses resulting from this procedure, such as the replacement of the lost benefits due to an unauthorized transaction, compromise in security, or incorrect identification of the person requesting a PIN via the telephone.
Implementation of Specific Anti-Fraud Measures in EBT Systems
EBT vendors offer to State SNAP agencies a variety of optional card security services focused on combating EBT fraud. Many of these services involve household-selected options to restrict usage of their account in some form, while other services can affect how households manage use of their benefits. However, States are not required to elect any of the most common card security services designed to reduce levels of EBT fraud.
Section 501(a) of Title IV within Division HH of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023 required that the Department issue guidance to State SNAP agencies to protect and replace SNAP benefits stolen via card skimming, card cloning, and other similar fraudulent methods. In response to this, the Department published Tips and Resources
[
13
]
regarding fraud mitigation best practices for SNAP participants, State SNAP agencies, and SNAP retailers. One of the recommendations for State SNAP agencies was to “Let SNAP households know how to opt into card security services that proactively protect their cards and PINs.” However, SNAP clients are unable to opt into card security services when they live in a State that has not worked with their EBT vendor to make some or all of these card security services available. Different State SNAP agencies have elected to implement different optional card security services, leaving households with different treatment and protections depending on their location.
The Department proposes adding a new regulation at
7 CFR 274.7(k)
to require that all State SNAP agencies offer a minimum list of specific card security services, referred to as participant-selected account options. The regulation will refer to the SNAP EBT Operating Standards (see Appendix A to Part 274), which will contain the list of specific card security services required, many of which are designed to reduce incidents of benefit theft.
The Department also proposes updating
7 CFR 274.7(d)
to require that States establish standards covering client access to platforms such as client websites, EBT cardholder portals, or mobile applications that clearly inform clients of balances, features, security options, and other services available for their EBT account.
First, regulations at 274.2(f)(2)(i) and the SNAP EBT Operating Standards document (see Appendix A to Part 274) will require that States disallow the use of common PINs, including PINs with:
—Entirely sequential digits (with zero considered sequential to both one and nine);
—Entirely reverse sequential digits (with zero considered sequential to both one and nine);
—One digit repeated for the entire length of the PIN;
—The last digits of the associated EBT card's PAN;
—Entirely alternating digits (
e.g.,
1212, 8989, or 5454);
—The first two digits 19 (potential birth year vulnerability);
—The first two digits 20 (potential birth year vulnerability);
—The sequential digits 2580, 8520, 0852, or 0258 (these sequences are
(
printed page 66966)
common as they reflect the vertical digits of a numeric keypad in order).
Second, the SNAP EBT Operating Standards document will require that States offer SNAP households the self-service ability to elect or remove all of the following specific account options at a minimum:
—An account block on out-of-State transactions;
—An account block on card-not-present (online) transactions;
—An account block on all transactions;
—Alerts delivered via email or text message for purchases on the account, including rejected purchases, out-of-State purchases, and purchases over a user-selected limit;
—Alerts delivered via email and/or text message for specific account activity such as PIN changes, balance inquiries, and changes to personal account information such as address, email address, or telephone number;
—A user-selected maximum transaction limit, over which all transactions are to be blocked.
There are some States which, working with their EBT host processors, have already opted to provide transaction blocking account options to SNAP households. In States where these options are available, a particular type of blocking (for example, an account block on out-of-State transactions) may be enabled by default for SNAP households as long as States adhere to statute and regulations regarding interoperability and ease-of-use for EBT transactions. The Department seeks comments on concerns or benefits related to blocking transactions by default.
Clients must be able to opt-in to these account options via all of the following methods, and clients should not be restricted in making such a selection in any way by disability or speaking a primary language other than English:
—EBT cardholder portal
—Mobile application or equivalent mobile-first web interface
—Telephone request
—In-person request
Fourth, newly proposed regulations at 274.2(f)(3) and the SNAP EBT Operating Standards document will require that States issue EBT cards that are not active until the recipient takes actions to enable the card.
Vendor Monitoring of EBT Terminals
Current regulations require State SNAP agencies to ensure that only authorized retailers can access the EBT system. This is important to the integrity of the EBT system, as unauthorized EBT terminal usage by bad actors can facilitate the commission of EBT fraud in several ways.
First, bad actors can use EBT terminals to verify skimmed card data by attempting to make purchases or balance inquiries to determine which benefit accounts they are able to access.
Second, bad actors can utilize fraudulent balance inquiries to facilitate algorithmic attacks where large quantities of transactions are attempted using computer automation to find access to new benefit accounts.
Third, bad actors can input fraudulent transactions to drain funds from SNAP benefit accounts. These events have been encountered in greater numbers in recent years, as witnessed by State agencies monitoring terminal usage and receiving reports of fraud. Illegitimate access is made possible by third-party processors or their contracted independent sales organizations (
e.g.,
sub-vendors), who facilitate payment for EBT transactions via the EBT gateway. When third-party processors and independent sales organizations fail to verify that retailers they transact with are authorized by FNA to participate in the program before they process any transactions from a given retailer, they make it possible for bad actors to access the EBT system. The Department is exploring various ways to address this issue, in alignment with the priorities of the Task Force to Eliminate Fraud established in
Executive Order 14395
.
[
14
]
The Department proposes revising
7 CFR 274.3(e)(4)
and
274.8(b)(3)(v)(F)
to clarify that State SNAP agencies, and by extension their contracted EBT vendors, both play a critical role in denying access to bad actors and must perform adequate due diligence. EBT terminal usage must be actively monitored by the EBT vendors contracted by State SNAP agencies to remove unauthorized terminal access to the EBT system, in accordance with existing regulations at
7 CFR 274.8(b)(3)(ii)(A)
which require controls to “ensure acceptance of data from authorized terminals only.”
FNA is improving fraud prevention efforts with support from third party vendors by providing ways in which FNA can block miscoded payment terminals from accessing the EBT network. FNA expects that State agencies and their contracted EBT vendors will investigate and consider such terminals for deactivation. Additionally, FNA is working with State agencies and providing technical support to help identify and block miscoded terminals. New retailers participating in the EBT system with addresses that do not match the address registered for their FNA retailer account number must also be investigated where possible.
In the event of unchecked fraudulent activity, clear signs of unauthorized access, or other similar negligence with no response or action taken to address an ongoing issue, FNA may seek disallowance of administrative funding under
7 CFR 276.4(a)(2)
and
276.4(a)(3)
regarding State agency responsibilities for preventing losses of Federal funds.
Requiring Timely Updates to EBT Systems in Accordance With the X9.58 Technical Specifications
Current regulations require that State SNAP agencies ensure their EBT systems comply with technical specifications established by the American National Standards Institute (ANSI) and International Organization for Standardization (ISO) where applicable, but do not explicitly cover technical specifications established by the Accredited Standards Committee (ASC) X9. ASC is responsible for the development of their technical specification X9.58
Financial transaction messages—Electronic benefits transfer (EBT)—Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP)
to accommodate the use of EBT cards with chip and NFC technology, as well as specifying all aspects of EBT financial transaction data transmission. The latest revision to the ASC X9.58 technical specification was released in 2024,
[
15
]
but the Department also assumes that ASC X9 will implement additional revisions in the future, as payment technology continues to grow and evolve. The ASC X9.58 technical specification has previously been updated in 2022, 2013, and 2007. When updates are made to the ISO 8583 or ANSI X9.58 specification, or other applicable specifications, the Department proposes that State agencies ensure EBT systems comply with the new version of the specification within 180 days from the publication of the updated specification.
The Department welcomes public comment on the 180-day timeframe for compliance, with the understanding that deploying upgrades to EBT systems can require significant financial resources in addition to the time and staffing requirements needed to ensure successful deployment.
The Department also proposes revising regulations at
7 CFR 274.8(b)(3)(iv)(B)
to require that State
(
printed page 66967)
EBT systems and data processing centers utilize multifactor authentication as a method of enhancing internal security. Multifactor authentication is commonly used in the consumer payment industry and requires at least two forms of verification to protect online accounts, such as password, a one-time pin sent to a verified email or phone, and user selected challenge question.
Delete References to Offline EBT Systems
Regulations at
7 CFR 274.1(b)
currently require SNAP benefits to be issued via either an online EBT system involving a central computer database accessed electronically by EBT cards at the point of sale, or an offline EBT system with benefit allotments stored on EBT cards.
7 CFR 274.1(b)(2)
currently permits State agencies to issue SNAP benefits through an offline EBT system in which “. . . benefit allotments can be stored on a card or in a card access device and used to purchase authorized items.”
No States currently use an offline EBT system, and none are expected to in the future. Given that all States now utilize an approach to managing accounts in which benefits are issued from and stored in an online central databank, as well as the existence of new initiatives such as online purchasing and mobile payments, each relying significantly on online EBT systems, the Department does not believe an offline EBT system would be a viable alternative to online EBT systems going forward. Only two States have ever used an offline EBT system for SNAP. The last State to use an offline EBT system was Wyoming, which moved to an online EBT system in May 2007.
In addition to these developments away from offline EBT systems,
7 CFR 271.2
currently defines EBT as a system where benefits are “. . . issued from and stored in a central databank.” This also points away from an offline system where benefits are primarily stored on the cards. As a result of these factors, the Department is proposing to update the regulations by removing
7 CFR 274.1(b)
and adding `online' to the definition of an EBT system in
7 CFR 271.2
“Electronic Benefit Transfer (EBT) system”. As noted, no States would be impacted by this change.
Related to this change, the Department proposes modifying regulations at
7 CFR 274.1(c)
to note that when the Secretary, in consultation with the Office of Inspector General, determines that program integrity would be improved by changing the issuance system of a State, the alternative method would no longer be limited to one of the methods currently described in 274.1(b). This will allow States to utilize methods of payment issuance in the future that may not exist currently, as consumer payment technology continues to develop.
Implementation of Card Security Code (CSC) and Expiration Date
SNAP's existing Online Purchasing Pilot began in 2019 and quickly expanded to all States as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic. While much of the online shopping experience is consistent with online purchasing using credit/debit cards, a significant difference is the lack of printed card security codes, or CSCs, and expiration dates on EBT cards. The type of CSC that will be most familiar to users of debit and credit cards is the 3 or 4-digit code printed on the payment card, which is commonly entered by the customer when conducting card-not-present transactions with internet retailers (along with other information such as zip code and expiration date of the card).
Since the CSC and expiration date are not encoded in the data on the card but merely printed on the surface of the card and entered at the time of purchase, this information cannot be obtained by traditional electronic skimming methods that take data from a payment card's magnetic stripe. The addition of the CSC and expiration date significantly enhances security for card-not-present (online) transactions by requiring customers to enter these additional values which are not encoded in the data on the card and are not stored at any time by retailers.
The Department intends to revise regulations at
7 CFR 274.8(a)(2)(ii)
and use the SNAP EBT Operating Standards document to require specific security measures for card-not-present (online) transactions, including primarily the use of a CSC and expiration date as part of these transactions. This will mirror best practices already established in the consumer payment industry.
While this will add an additional step to card-not-present (online) transactions, the Department considers this additional step worth the value provided in terms of reducing benefit theft. Many households will already be familiar with the entry of a CSC and expiration date while making online purchases, due to the prevalence of the requirement when using credit/debit cards, so this additional step is unlikely to cause confusion when encountered.
Interoperability and Interchange Fees
Existing regulations regarding interoperability including
7 CFR 274.8(b)(10)
apply to all aspects of any changes resulting from implementation of the requirements of this rule. Benefits issued via EBT by any one State must continue to be able to be redeemed for food purchases in any other State. Therefore, no State should take actions in response to this rule which would prevent benefits issued from being redeemed in another State.
The Department also proposes adding a new section in the regulations at
7 CFR 274.3(a)(4)
to clarify that interchange fees shall not apply to any EBT transaction, even if the retailer uses commercial equipment provided by an independent third-party processor to accept SNAP benefits. These changes will align regulations with the prohibition of interchange fees in Section 7(h)(13)(A) of the Food and Nutrition Act.
Mobile Purchasing Virtual EBT Card Provisioning
The SNAP Mobile Purchasing pilot remains in progress at this time. The Department looks forward to recommendations that will be made in the future resulting from the resolution of the pilot with regard to provisioning of virtual EBT cards on mobile devices for making SNAP payments. Outcomes from the pilot will be used to inform future rule making or updates to the SNAP EBT Operating Standards. Therefore, this rule does not propose any regulatory changes regarding virtual EBT cards on mobile devices at this time.
