Title:
Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program: Electronic Benefits Transfer Card Security Measures.
OMB Number:
0584-NEW.
Forms:
None.
Expiration Date:
Not Yet Determined.
Type of Request:
New.
Abstract:
The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023, requires the Department to issue regulations establishing security measures to identify and prevent SNAP benefit theft. The measures must be consistent with industry standards for detecting, identifying, and preventing debit and credit card skimming, card cloning, and other fraudulent methods and must consider implementation feasibility for the States. This proposed rule modernizes Electronic Benefit Transfer (EBT) technology and brings EBT into alignment with consumer payment processing industry standards, improving the experiences of SNAP participants. FNA is requesting a new OMB Control Number for the requirements in this proposed rule.
The proposed rule includes numerous proposals to enhance EBT card security and account usability. Several of these proposals will result in an increase in reporting burdens for State SNAP agencies, Individuals/Households, Business-for-profit such as EBT host processors, and some SNAP retailers. There is no recordkeeping or third-party disclosure associated with this rulemaking.
First, the rule proposes creating SNAP EBT Operating Standards, which would be revised on a regular, ongoing basis. SNAP EBT Operating Standards would allow the Department to revise EBT requirements more dynamically in response to rapidly evolving payment technology and best practices in the consumer payment industry. Some of the SNAP EBT Operating Standards will create an information collection burden, as discussed below.
In this proposed rule, the Department will require State SNAP agencies to upgrade to EBT cards utilizing chip and NFC technology, as well as require that SNAP retailers accept EBT transactions via chip and NFC technology, within a certain time frame. Based on the experience of the consumer payment industry, the Department believes EBT cards utilizing chip and NFC technology will significantly reduce SNAP benefit theft due to the enhanced security features that mitigate skimming and cloning attacks. Households will be required to activate these new chip cards upon receipt, and households experiencing homelessness may need to travel to a local office to obtain their new card.
The proposal will also update the regulations at
7 CFR 274.2(e)
on EBT household training requirements for SNAP participants. Under the proposed regulations, the EBT household training will inform households about security best practices that will reduce their chances of being affected by benefit theft, in addition to their rights and responsibilities and how to use their benefits.
The proposal will create new regulations at
7 CFR 274.8(b)(4)(i)(H)
and
274.8(b)(4)(i)(I)
to specify information that must be made available to all SNAP participants, including transaction dates, times, and amounts; retailer name and location; balance inquiry history; PIN change history; and history of other account management changes including address, email address, and telephone number. These changes will better equip SNAP households to review their account activity and detect potentially fraudulent activity.
The proposal makes two changes regarding balance inquiries. The SNAP EBT Operating Standards (see Appendix A to Part 274) will require verification for all SNAP balance inquiries, and the proposal will update
7 CFR 274.7(d)(1)
to permit internet retailers to conduct business without offering balance inquiry, codifying a standard waiver the Department currently issues. Related to this, the Department proposes revising
7 CFR 274.7(d)(3)
and
274.8(b)(7)
to confirm that transaction receipts may be delivered via electronic means. As transaction receipts are required to be provided, eCommerce providers and internet retailers that do not use an eCommerce provider will need to modify their website purchasing pages accordingly.
The proposed rule revises
7 CFR 274.3(e)(4)
and
274.8(b)(3)(v)(F)
, to clarify that State SNAP agencies, and by extension their contracted EBT vendors, both play a critical role in denying access to bad actors.
The proposed rule also revises regulations at
7 CFR 274.8(b)
and
274.8(b)(10)(ii)
to require all participants in the EBT system to update their systems in accordance with the X9.58 technical specification to ensure proper functioning of the system.
Finally, the proposed rule would revise
7 CFR 274.7(d)(3)
and
274.8(b)(7)
to confirm that transaction receipts for online purchases may be delivered via online cardholder accounts, confirmation invoices, other electronic communications such as email or text messages, or printed invoices upon delivery.
In addition to the changes discussed above, the proposed rule also includes changes that do not have an information collection burden. These include: updates to
7 CFR 274.8(b)(5)(vi)
to specify that the primary account number shall be printed on the back of each EBT card; updates to
7 CFR 274.6(b)(3)
,
274.6(b)(5)
, and
274.6(b)(6)
clarifying that EBT cards replaced as a result of their expiration date must not be counted towards the excessive card replacement threshold; updates at
7 CFR 274.6(b)
,
274.6(b)(2)
, and
274.8(b)(3)(ii)(C)
to remove references to
(
printed page 66970)
magnetic stripes and to clarify that card replacement does not apply only to physical cards; updates to
7 CFR 274.3(a)(1)(i)
ending the use of manual vouchers as a means to conduct ongoing business, except in certain limited circumstances; updates to
7 CFR 274.3(a)(2)
to codify the 2014 Farm Bill amendment regarding non-exempt retailers' financial responsibility for EBT equipment, supplies, and related services; updates to
7 CFR 274.3(b)
to remove outdated requirements regarding EBT terminal deployment; removal of
7 CFR 274.1(b)
and updates to
7 CFR 271.2
“Electronic Benefit Transfer (EBT) system” to remove the option of offline EBT systems; updates to
7 CFR 274.3(a)(4)
to clarify that interchange fees shall not apply to any EBT transaction; the creation of
7 CFR 274.2(f)(3)
to require that EBT cards are issued in an inactive state; and updates to
7 CFR 274.8(b)(5)(vii)
to require EBT cards to contain card security codes (CSCs). The proposed SNAP EBT Operating Standards and regulations at 274.7(k) will also require that all State SNAP agencies offer certain specific card security services provided by EBT vendors. States will be required to prohibit use of common PINs and offer participant-selected account options to manage and monitor their own account usage. Relatedly, the proposal creates new regulations at
7 CFR 274.8(a)(1)(ii)
and modifies regulations at
7 CFR 274.3(f)(2)(i)
to require PINs to comply with the specifications of the SNAP EBT Operating Standards.
First Year (One-Time) Burden
State SNAP Agencies
State SNAP agencies will have a one-time reporting burden of communicating to SNAP households about the implementation of EBT cards with chip and NFC technology. This burden comprises 53 responses totaling 424 hours. FNA expects that this communication will, at a minimum, take the form of a notice to each SNAP household. FNA estimates that each State Agency will need to draft a notice and set up an automated process to send communications out to each household. FNA estimates that it will take a State Agency 8.00 hours to draft a notice and set up the automated process for a total one-time burden of 424.00 hours (53 State Agencies * 8.00 = 424.00 total hours).
State SNAP agencies will also have a one-time reporting burden of revising household training materials to reflect the additional information required by the rule. FNA estimates that these revisions would take the equivalent of 80.00 hours per State SNAP agency, for a total one-time burden of 4,240.00 hours (80.00 hours per State SNAP agency * 53 State SNAP agencies = 4,240.00 hours).
State SNAP agencies will have a one-time reporting burden to revise all documentation and training materials to include information regarding chip card technology and anti-fraud measures that will be available to households. FNA estimates that these revisions would take the equivalent of 80.00 hours per State SNAP agency, for a total one-time burden of 4,240.00 hours (80.00 hours per State SNAP agency * 53 State SNAP agencies = 4,240.00 hours).
Finally, State SNAP agencies will have a one-time reporting burden related to conducting staff training on the various changes in the proposed rule and FNA estimates there will be 2,650 responses, with approximately 50 State SNAP agency staff receiving training per agency. FNA estimates that training would take approximately 4.00 hours per staff member, for a total of 10,600.00 hours (4.00 hours * 50 staff * 53 State SNAP agencies = 10,600.00 hours).
In total, the one-time reporting burden for State SNAP agencies would be 19,504.00 hours (424 chip card communications hours + 4,240.00 household training update hours + 4,240 anti-fraud documentation update hours + 10,600.00 staff training hours = 19,504.00 total hours).
EBT Host Processors
Although four EBT host processors are currently operating, FNA has been informed that one processor plans to end its EBT work soon, so we are only including the three EBT host processors that will remain in the market. Therefore, there will be 3 responses for this reporting burden.
EBT host processors will have a one-time reporting burden for making EBT system updates to provide detailed SNAP transaction history and account activity history, provide balance inquiry validation, comply with upcoming updates to the X9.58 technical specification for chip and NFC support, and monitor unauthorized EBT terminal usage.
FNA estimates that adding this functionality and implementing the updates would take approximately 160.00 hours per EBT host processor, for a total start-up reporting cost of 480.00 hours (160.00 hours per processor * 3 EBT host processors = 480.00 hours). Once the EBT host processors add the functionality to their systems, the reporting activities would be automated and would not impose an ongoing burden on processors.
EBT host processors will also incur a one-time reporting burden for developing a process to monitor and block potential unauthorized terminal usage. This will require 3 responses, one for each of the EBT host processors. FNA expects that developing a process to monitor terminals that exhibit certain patterns indicative of trafficking will take the equivalent of a three-week sprint for each EBT host processor, for a total of 360.00 reporting hours (40.00 hours * 3 weeks = 120.00 hours; 120.00 hours * 3 EBT host processors = 360.00 total one-time reporting burden hours).
Households
SNAP households will have a one-time reporting burden related to the activation of chip-enabled cards. FNA estimates that it will take households 5 minutes to activate a chip card, for a total reporting burden of 2,249,365.40 hours (22,493,654 households * 0.10 hours = 2,249,365.40 hours.)
FNA estimates that households will have a burden to review the State agency notice regarding chip card implementation. FNA estimates that 80 percent of households (22,493,654 households * 0.8 = 17,994,923) will review this notice. FNA estimates that it will take households 5 minutes to review. In total, FNA estimates this burden to be 1,799,492.32 hours (17,813,637 households * 0.10 hours = 1,799,492.324 hours.)
FNA estimates that there will be a burden for households experiencing homelessness to travel to a local office and to wait to obtain a new chip card. SNAP Quality Control data for FY 2022 estimated that 5.6% of the SNAP caseload experiences homelessness. FNA also estimates that not all households, approximately 50 percent, experiencing homelessness will not need to visit a local office to obtain a new chip card. As there are 22,493,654 households, 5.6% equals 1,259,644. Half of 1,259,6441 households equals approximately 629,822 households that may need to travel to a local office to obtain a chip card. FNA estimates the travel and wait burden for these households to be one hour, which would bring the total burden hours to households experiencing homelessness to 629,822 hours.
In total, FNA estimates that the total one-time household burden will be 4,704,463.72 hours (4,453,409.20 hours to review household training materials that now include chip card activation and anti-fraud measures + 2,249,365.40 hours to activate a chip cards and 629,822 hours for households experiencing homelessness to travel to a local office for a new card.).
(
printed page 66971)
Retailers
Finally, online SNAP retailers will have a one-time reporting burden of removing capabilities for balance inquiry and receipts with account balances displayed from their online purchasing interfaces. To implement the change, internet retailers will need to update their ordering web page to remove the balance inquiry functionality and adjust the method of receipt. Currently, 116 SNAP retailers are, or are in the process to become, online SNAP retailers as direct integrators, operating their own online purchasing platform. There are currently 29 eCommerce providers total, including those that do not have a retailer who has gone live with SNAP Online Purchasing yet. FNA estimates that this one-time update to online purchasing will take both the direct integrators and eCommerce providers approximately 40.00 hours each, for a total of 5,920.00 hours ((116 direct integrators + 29 eCommerce providers) * 40.00 hours = 5,920.00 hours).
In total, the one-time startup burden of the proposed rule will be an estimated 41,121,359.20 responses for a total of 4,704,463.72 hours.
Ongoing Burden
EBT Host Processors
EBT host processors will also have an ongoing burden of monitoring EBT terminal usage and blocking unauthorized terminals to ensure that only authorized retailers can access the EBT system. Once the monitoring process is set up, the EBT host processors will need to monitor terminals on an ongoing basis and block unauthorized terminals that they discover throughout the course of the monitoring. The monitoring itself will be largely automated and not result in an ongoing burden for EBT host processors. FNA estimates that blocking terminals will take approximately one hour per month per EBT host processor, for a total of 12.00 hours per processor per year, or 36.00 hours total per year for all EBT host processors.
State Agencies
This rule includes a burden to account for the ongoing distribution of EBT related household training materials by each State agency. Per regulations at 274.2(e), household training includes content that will familiarize households with benefit issuance, benefit redemption, and rights and responsibilities. FNA did not previously account for this burden for the distribution of training to households and is including it in this new information collection. FNA estimates that each year, each household may receive some form of EBT training materials, which are most often provided as a pamphlet or brochure that accompanies their EBT card. FNA estimates that it would take a State three minutes to hand out information in an office or send via mail. FNA also estimates that this effort would take the equivalent of 626,862.90 total hours for State agencies (0.05 hours per State agency to distribute materials to a household * 12,537,250 newly certified households per year = 626,862.90 hours).
Households
FNA previously did not account for the ongoing annual burden on households to review EBT-related household training materials which are required to be provided by State SNAP agencies in regulations at
7 CFR 274.2(e)
. Per State-provided data, 12,537,250 households joined the program in Fiscal Year 2025. Based on that number, FNA estimates that each year eighty percent of households that join the program (10,029,806) will spend five minutes reviewing EBT household training notices in a year for a total ongoing reporting burden of 1,799,492 hours (10,029,806 * 0.10 hours = 1,799,492).
In total, the ongoing burden of the proposed rule will be an estimated 22,567,100.40 annual responses and 1,629,879.54 hours. Together, the one-time startup burden and ongoing burden are 63,688,459.60 responses and 6,334,343.26 hours.

(g)
Adjustments.
(1) The State agency may make adjustments to benefits posted to household accounts after the posting process is complete but prior to the availability date for household access in the event benefits are erroneously posted.
(2) A State agency shall make adjustments to an account to correct an auditable, out-of-balance settlement condition that occurs during the redemption process as a result of a system error. A system error is defined as an error resulting from a malfunction at any point in the redemption process: from the system host computer, to the switch, to the third party processors, to a store's host computer or POS device. These adjustments may occur after the availability date and may result in either a debit or credit to the household. The household shall have 90 days from the date of the notice of a denied credit adjustment to request a fair hearing.
(i)
Credit adjustments.
The State agency must act on all requests for credit adjustments made by client households within 90 calendar days of the error transaction. The State agency has 15 calendar days from the date the household notifies it of the error to investigate and reach a decision on an adjustment and move funds into the client account. This timeframe also applies if the State agency or entity other than the household discovers a system error that requires a credit adjustment to the household. The household shall have 90 days from the date of the notice of a denied credit adjustment to request a fair hearing.
(ii)
Debit adjustments.
Upon receiving a timely debit adjustment request, the State must validate the adjustment within 15 calendar days.
(A)
Standard procedure.
Upon receiving a timely debit adjustment request, the State shall place a hold on the household's account. If there are insufficient benefits to cover the entire adjustment, a hold shall be placed on any remaining balance that exists, with the difference being subject to availability only in the next future month. The household shall be given, at a minimum, adequate notice in accordance with § 273.13 of this chapter. The notice must be sent after the adjustment request is validated, at the time the initial hold is attempted on the household's current month's remaining balance, clearly state the full adjustment amount, and advise the household that any amount still owed is subject to collection from the household's next future month's benefits. The household shall have 90 days from the date of the notice to request a fair hearing. Should the household dispute the adjustment and request a hearing within 15 calendar days of the notice, a provisional credit must be made to the household's account by releasing the hold on the adjustment balance within 48 hours of the request by the household, pending resolution of the fair hearing. If no request for a hearing is made within 15
(

calendar days of the notice, the hold is released on the adjustment balance, and this amount is credited to the retailer's account. If there are insufficient funds available in the current month to cover the full adjustment amount, the hold may be maintained and settled at one time after the next month's benefits become available. If the State agency does not have the capability of placing a hold on benefits, the State may choose to wait until the household has had 15 calendar days from the date of the notice to debit the household's account. If the State cannot verify the error within 15 days of the initial debit request, the request must be denied.
(B)
Alternative no-hold procedure.
As an alternative procedure, the State agency may instead choose to act on all requests for debit adjustments to a household's account which are initiated within 15 calendar days from the date of the transaction involved, without placing a hold on the household's account for the amount of the debit adjustment. If so, the State agency must send a concurrent notice to households upon receipt of the debit adjustment request after validating the request, and provide them with 15 calendar days to request a fair hearing before any action is taken to debit the household's account. If a household disputes the requested adjustment and requests a fair hearing within 15 calendar days, no further action shall be taken to debit the household's account until the fair hearing decision is rendered.

(b)
Performance and technical standards.
The State agency shall ensure that EBT systems comply with the X9.58 technical specification, the ISO 8583 technical specification, the ISO 7812 technical specification, and the SNAP EBT Operating Standards (see Appendix A to section 274) in the areas of system processing speeds, system availability and reliability, system security, system ease-of-use, minimum card and terminal requirements, performance bonding, and a minimum transaction set.
(1)
System processing speeds.
(i) For leased line systems, 98 percent of EBT transactions shall be processed within 10 seconds or less and all EBT transactions shall be processed within 15 seconds. Leased line systems rent telecommunications carriers specifically to connect to the central authorizing computer. For dial-up systems, 95 percent of the EBT transactions shall be processed within 15 seconds or less and all EBT transactions shall be processed within 20 seconds or less. Dial-up systems utilize existing telecommunications lines to dial up and connect to the central computer at the time of the transaction. Processing response time shall be measured at the POS terminal from the time the `enter' or `send' key is pressed to the receipt and display of authorization or disapproval information. Third party processors, as defined in paragraph (h)(5) of this section, shall be required by the State agency to comply with the same processing response times required of the primary processor.
(ii) The EBT system shall provide re-ports, as determined by the State agency, that document transaction processing response time and the number and type of problematic transactions that could not be processed within the standard response time.
(2)
System availability and reliability.
(i) The EBT system central computer shall be available 99.9 percent of scheduled up-time, 24 hours a day, 7 days per week. Scheduled up-time shall mean the time the database is available for transactions excluding scheduled downtime for routine maintenance. The total system, including the system's central computer, any network or intermediate processing facilities and cardholder authorization processors, shall be available 98 percent of scheduled up-time, 24 hours per day, 7 days per week. Scheduled downtime for routine maintenance shall occur during non-peak transaction periods. State certification procedures shall determine whether intermediate processing facilities and cardholder authorization processors are capable of complying with system availability standards prescribed herein prior to permitting the interface with the central computer system.
(ii) Reconciliation reports and other information regarding problematic transactions shall be made available to the State agency by the system operator, individual retailers, households or financial institutions as appropriate. Reports on problematic transactions, including inaccurate transactions shall be delineated by the source of the problem such as card failure, POS terminal failure, interruption of telecommunications, or other component failure. Errors shall be resolved in a timely manner.
(3)
System security.
As an addition to or component of the Security Program required of Automated Data Processing systems prescribed under § 277.18(m) of this chapter, the State agency shall ensure that the following EBT security requirements are established:
(i) Storage and control measures to control blank unissued EBT cards and PINs, and unused or spare POS devices;
(ii) Measures to ensure communication access control. Communication controls shall include the transmission of transaction data and issuance information from POS terminals to work-stations and terminals at the data processing center. The following specific security measures shall be included, as appropriate, in the system design documentation, operating procedures or the State agency Security Program:
(A) Computer hardware controls that ensure acceptance of data from authorized terminals only. These controls shall include the use of mechanisms such as retailer identification codes, terminal identifiers and user identification codes, and/or other mechanisms and procedures recognized by the industry;
(B) Software controls, placed at either the terminal or central computer or both, that establish separate control files containing lists of authorized retailers, terminal identifying codes, and user access and identification codes. EBT system software controls shall include separate checks against the control files in order to validate each transaction prior to authorization and limiting the number of unsuccessful PIN attempts that can be made utilizing standard industry practices before the card is deactivated;
(C) Communications network security that utilizes the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) algorithm to encrypt the PIN, at a minimum, from the point of entry. Other security may include authentication codes and check-sum digits, in combination with data encoded on the EBT card such as the PIN and/or PIN offset, to ensure data security during electronic transmission. Any of the network security measures may be utilized together or separately and may be applied at the terminal or central computer as indicated in the approved system design to ensure communications control, and other levels of equivalent security may be permitted subject to FNA waiver request and approval;
(D) Manual procedures that provide for secure access to the system with minimal risk to household or retailer accounts. Manual procedures may include the utilization of manager identification codes in obtaining telephonic authorization from the central computer system; requirements for separate entry with audio response unit verification and authorization number; and/or the utilization of 24 hour hotline telephone numbers to authorize transactions.
(iii) Message validation shall include but shall not be limited to:
(A) Message format checks for completeness of the message, correct order of data, existence of control characters, number and size of data fields and appropriate format standards as specified in the approved system design;
(B) Range checks for acceptable date fields, number and valid account numbers, purchase and refund upper limitations in order to prevent and control damage to the system accounts;
(C) Reversal of messages that are not fully processed and recorded.

At a minimum, the State agency shall ensure that the EBT system, including third party processors and retailers driving their own terminals, is capable of providing for authorizing or rejecting purchases, refunds or customer credits, voids or cancellations, key entered transactions, balance inquiries and settlement or close-out transactions. The system must be capable of completing this transaction set across State borders nationwide in accordance with standards specified in paragraph (b)(10) of this section.
(10)
Interoperability.
State agencies must adopt uniform standards to facilitate interoperability and portability nationwide. The term “interoperability” means the EBT system must enable benefits issued in the form of an EBT card to be redeemed in any State. The term “portability” means the EBT system must enable benefits issued in the form of an EBT card to be used in any State by a household to purchase food at a participating authorized retailer. The standards must include the following:
(i)
EBT system connectivity.
State agencies are responsible for establishing telecommunications links, transaction switching facilities and any other arrangements with other State agencies necessary for the routing of interoperable transactions to such other State EBT authorization systems. State agencies are also responsible for facilitating the settlement of such interoperable transactions and the handling of adjustments. These connections need not be direct connections between State authorization systems but may be facilitated through agreements and linkages with other designated agents or third party processors. All State agencies must agree to the timing and disposition of disputes, error resolution, and adjustments in accordance with Department regulations at § 273.13(a) and § 273.15(k) of this chapter and paragraph (f) of this section. State agencies or their designated agents must draw funds from State SNAP accounts for SNAP benefits transacted by that State's SNAP recipients, regardless of where benefits were transacted.
(ii)
Message format.
Each authorization system must use the message format required by the ASC X9.58 and ISO 8583 technical specifications, in a version mutually agreed to between the authorization agent and the party connected for all transactions. Each authorization system must process each financial transaction as a single message financial transaction, except for pre-authorized transactions and reversals, processed as paired transactions.
(iii)
Card Primary Account Number (PAN) Requirements.
Track 2 on each card shall contain the PAN. Each Government entity must obtain an Issuer Identification Number (IIN) from the American Banker's Association (ABA). The IIN should be included as the first six digits of the PAN. The PAN must comply with the ISO 7812 technical specification Each State agency must be responsible for generating, updating, and distributing IIN files of all States to each retailer, processor, or acquirer that is directly connected to the State's authorization system. Each terminal operator that uses a routing table for routing acquired transactions must, within 7 calendar days of receiving an IIN routing table update, modify its routing tables to reflect the updated routing information.
(iv)
Third Party Processor requirements.
Each Third Party Processor or terminal operator must have primary responsibility and liability for operating the telecommunications and processing system (including software and hardware) through which transactions initiated at POS terminals it owns, operates, controls or for which it has signed an agreement to accept EBT transactions, are processed and routed, directly or indirectly, to the appropriate State authorization system. Each terminal operator must maintain the necessary computer hardware and software to interface either directly with a State authorization system or with a third party service provider to obtain access to one or more State authorization systems. Each terminal operator must also establish a direct or indirect telecommunications connection for the routing of transactions to the State authorization system or to a processor directly or indirectly connected to the State authorization system.
(v)
REDE File.
The State agency must ensure that their EBT system verifies FNA retailer numbers for all interstate transactions against the National REDE file of all FNA EBT retailers to validate these transactions.

Add the Appendix A to part 274 Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program Electronic Benefit Transfer Operating Standards to read as follows:
Appendix A to Part 274: Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program Electronic Benefit Transfer Operating Standards
(a) Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) Overview
(1) The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) is the largest nutrition assistance program in the United States.
(2) SNAP is a means-tested program, which means low-income households must apply to participate and will only be accepted if they meet the Program's income and asset requirements. If they meet those requirements, their application is approved, and they become a SNAP household (a SNAP household can include one or more people).
7 CFR 273.1
,
7 CFR 273.8-273.11
.
(3) SNAP households receive a monthly benefit, which can (1) only be used to buy SNAP-eligible foods, and (2) only be used at SNAP-authorized retailers.
7 CFR 274.7(a)
,
7 CFR 278.2(a)
.
(4) SNAP benefits are provided to SNAP households via an Electronic Benefits Transfer (EBT) card. The EBT card is a method to access benefits issued to a household member or authorized representative (the SNAP household) through the EBT system by a benefit issuer (the SNAP State agency, through its EBT host processor). This EBT card may be a magnetic stripe card; a card with an integrated electronic chip capable of conducting contact or contactless payments, by either being inserted into a card reader or via wireless Near Field Communication (NFC) protocols; a digital wallet with a stored virtual EBT card; or any other similar benefit access technology approved by FNA.
(5) An EBT system is an electronic payment system that allows SNAP households to pay for food using their SNAP benefits via an EBT card when shopping at a SNAP-authorized retail store. When a
(
printed page 66981)
participant makes such purchases, their SNAP EBT account is debited to reimburse the store for the food they bought. SNAP benefits are issued from, and stored in, a central database, which is maintained and managed by a State or its contractor EBT processor. Such EBT systems use electronic funds transfer technology for the delivery and control of SNAP benefits and other public assistance benefits.
(6) EBT is used in all 50 States, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, the Virgin Islands, and Guam. EBT has been the sole method of SNAP issuance in all States since June of 2004.
(b) Operating Standards Purpose
(1) The purpose of this document is to provide Operating Standards for SNAP EBT systems. These standards have been published as an appendix to Part 274 of the Code of Federal Regulations.
(2) The SNAP EBT operating standards are the rules that govern SNAP EBT systems and EBT transaction processing methods. This includes establishing system requirements, establishing the systems themselves, maintenance, operation, and interaction with such systems, transaction processing, documentation, and reporting. The Operating Standards define the technical environment of EBT systems, define the responsibilities of each entity that interacts with a SNAP EBT system, and help to ensure those systems operate consistently, successfully, and securely; and provide a framework for mitigating errors and assigning liabilities.
(3) The SNAP EBT Operating Standards are modeled on operating rules used by debit, ATM, and credit card payment networks. Ultimately, the standards will ensure consistency in program experiences for all SNAP households and SNAP-authorized retailers, reflect ongoing advancements made in the consumer payment industry, and safeguard SNAP program integrity.
(4) Legislative and Regulatory Authorities for SNAP EBT Operating Standards
(i) All State Agencies and SNAP EBT systems must comply with all applicable SNAP legislation, regulations, policies, and guidelines, including this document.
(ii) This Operating Standards document is created under the rulemaking authority authorized in the Food and Nutrition Act of 2008, as amended (
7 U.S.C. 2011-2036
), and the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023 (
Pub. L. 117-328
).
(iii) SNAP legislative requirements can be found in the United States Code (U.S.C.), at
7 U.S.C. 2011-2036d
(the Food and Nutrition Act of 2008, as amended).
(iv) SNAP regulations can be found in the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR), at
7 CFR 271-283
(Title 7, Subtitle B, Chapter II, Subchapter C). These Operating Standards focus primarily on EBT issuance regulations that can be found at
7 CFR 274
.
(v) Additionally, Regulation E, at
12 CFR 1005
plays a role in governing SNAP EBT Operating Standards (Title 12, Chapter X, Part 1005 Electronic Fund Transfers).
(vi) FNA also issues SNAP policy memoranda, technical assistance, and other guidance on an ongoing basis on the FNA Documents & Resources page of the FNA website.
(vii) EBT transaction message specifications follow the X9.58 standard. That standard is established by ANSI's Accredited Standards Committee X9. ANSI is the American National Standards Institute, the accredited organization responsible for developing technical standards, including exchanging EBT financial transaction messages. The published standard is available on the American National Standards Institute (ANSI) website.
(c) SNAP EBT Processing Overview
(1) SNAP EBT Systems Roles and Responsibilities
(i) This section describes entities that operate or interact with SNAP EBT systems, including those involved in processing SNAP transactions. Relevant entities in this environment include:
(A) SNAP Households: The person(s) who apply and are approved to participate in SNAP, receive SNAP benefits, and use a SNAP EBT card to purchase SNAP-eligible food. A SNAP household may authorize people who are not part of the household to use its SNAP EBT card to purchase food on its behalf.
7 CFR 273.1
,
7 CFR 274.8(f)(10)
.
(B) SNAP-Authorized Retailers: A merchant that applies and is authorized to accept SNAP benefits from SNAP households in exchange for SNAP-eligible foods. SNAP-authorized retailers (“retailers”) are the only places where SNAP households can use their benefits.
(C) The United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) Food and Nutrition Administration (FNA): The government agency that administers SNAP at the Federal/national level, in partnership with SNAP State agencies, EBT host processors, SNAP-authorized retailers, and other entities.
(D) SNAP State agencies: The governmental agency that administers SNAP at the State and local level. SNAP State agencies (State agencies or States) in all 50 States, the District of Columbia, the Virgin Islands, and Guam operate statewide EBT systems to issue SNAP benefits.
(E) EBT host processors: A contractor that builds and operates SNAP EBT systems on behalf of States. This includes:
(1)
Initial creation, maintenance, upgrading of EBT systems.
(2)
Processing EBT transactions, managing individual SNAP benefit accounts.
(3)
Reporting and data management.
(4)
Enabling and disabling retailers.
(5)
End-of-day processing, settlement, reconciliation, and (in some cases) providing Point-of-Sale (POS) devices to SNAP-authorized retailers.
(6)
Certification of Third-Party Processors.
(F) Gateway: An entity that routes EBT transactions from Third-Party Processors to an EBT host processor based on the BIN of the EBT card.
(G) Third-Party Processor (TPP): Financial institution that receives EBT transactions from SNAP-authorized retailers and acquirers and subsequently transmits those transactions to an EBT gateway for further routing or directly to an EBT host processor for transaction approval. SNAP State agencies and their contracted EBT host processors must allow retailers to use EBT services provided by TPPs and acquirers, and must provide interface specifications and certification standards, in order for the TPPs to participate in the EBT system per
7 CFR 274.3 (d)
.
(1)
The TPPs have contractual agreements to connect to all existing EBT processor systems, either directly or via gateways, in order to facilitate the approval/denial transactions anywhere SNAP is operated. TPPs typically provide EBT services and POS equipment directly to larger retailers (such as those with many locations) who may utilize other non-EBT services that the TPPs offer. Smaller retailers who are unable to contract directly with a TPP instead may rely on an acquirer to provide EBT services and POS equipment.
(H) Acquirer: A financial institution (or the agent of a financial institution) that facilitates the authorization of SNAP transactions by acquiring transaction-related data from SNAP-authorized retailers and transmitting that data to a Third-Party Processor for further routing. An acquirer may only need to contract with a single TPP, as the TPP would handle subsequent routing to gateways and EBT host processors.
(I) POS Service Provider: A financial institution (or its agent) that provides retailers with the equipment and technology needed to process SNAP benefits.
(2) SNAP EBT Transaction Flow
(i) This section describes how a SNAP EBT transaction flows through the EBT system and related financial systems.
(ii) See Figure 1 for a visual representation of the SNAP EBT transaction flow as of FY 2026. Please note that this figure is not comprehensive, as there may be other participants not represented in this figure, or participants who go by other names.
(iii) The left half of Figure 1 illustrates the flow of an EBT transaction:
(A) After being approved to participate in the Program, a SNAP household wants to buy SNAP-eligible food at a SNAP-authorized retailer. To pay for the food, the SNAP household swipes, inserts, or taps their EBT card—or uses another payment method, such as a mobile wallet—at the retailer's POS device. This generates an EBT transaction message, that is sent to the retailer's contracted TPP. The EBT transaction message is electronic data that contains information needed to process a transaction. The information contained in the transaction message is defined by the ANSI X9.58 specification.
(B) The TPP receives the transaction message from the retailer's POS device and forwards it to either a Gateway or directly to the EBT host processor, depending on the capabilities of the TPP. If the transaction message goes to a Gateway, the Gateway forwards it to the correct EBT host processor, based on the BIN of the card.
(C) Upon receipt, the EBT host processor reviews the information contained in the transaction message to ensure the transaction is valid, as defined in the processor's Business Rules (which are approved by the State and FNA). This includes:
(1)
The SNAP household's Primary Account Number (PAN), to ensure the card number is valid;
(2)
The PIN;
(
printed page 66982)
(3)
Whether there are sufficient benefits in the household's account to cover the purchase;
(4)
Whether the EBT card is statused/inactive;
(5)
The retailer's FNA number, to ensure the retailer is authorized to participate in SNAP); and
(D) The retailer's store type, to determine whether it is a store type that has additional limitations/requirements (internet retailers, restaurants, etc.). The processor will impose such requirements as appropriate.
(E) The processor will then generate a transaction message response to send back to the retailer's POS device, approving or denying the transaction providing SNAP account balance information and, if applicable, the denial reason). The processor sends FNA the transaction data, per
7 CFR 274.4(b)(2)
and the requirements outlined in their contract with the State.
(F) To get to the retailer's POS device, the transaction message response will follow the same path that was used to send the original transaction message (
i.e.,
through the TPP and then to the retailer; or through a Gateway, then a TPP, and then to the retailer).
(G) Once the transaction message response reaches the retailer's POS device, the retailer provides approval/denial information and a receipt to the SNAP household with the remaining account balance.
(iv) The right half of Figure 1 describes the settlement flow (
i.e.,
the transfer of funds which reimburses a SNAP-authorized retailer for a SNAP transaction):
(A) TPPs request reimbursement from either the Gateway or the EBT host processor (depending on how a particular transaction message was routed).
(B) If a transaction message was routed through a Gateway, the Gateway then requests reimbursement from the EBT host processor.
(C) Upon receipt of reimbursement requests from TPPs or Gateways, the EBT host processor sends its own reimbursement request to the Federal Reserve Bank (FRB), which authorizes reimbursement to the EBT host processor from the appropriate SNAP State agency's Letter of Credit.
(D) FRB then transfers the funds to the EBT host processor, and the reimbursement funds flow down the chain and are settled—from the host processor to the Gateway/TPP, and finally to the retailer.
