(d) SNAP-Authorized Retailer Requirements
(1) SNAP-Authorized Retailers: EBT Card Acceptance
(i) The following are rules for SNAP-authorized retailers regarding EBT card acceptance.
(A) SNAP EBT cards must be interoperable. This means that all SNAP-authorized retailers must be able to accept SNAP EBT cards from any of the 53 States and Territories that operate SNAP, in accordance with interoperability standards specified in
7 CFR 274.8(b)(10)
.
(B) SNAP EBT cards must be presented at the time of purchase, except for purchases from internet retailers.
(C) The SNAP household member (or their authorized representative) must enter the Personal Identification Number (PIN) associated with the card at the POS device.
(D) For SNAP online purchasing, the SNAP household member (or their authorized representative) must key-enter the card number and PIN. Once chip card technology is implemented, it will be a best practice for each retailer or eCommerce provider to update their online payment platform (website, app, etc.) to collect the card expiration date and Card Verification Value (CVV)/Card Security Code (CSC). PIN solution providers or others in the transaction flow may also need to update their systems. Ecommerce refers to an online sales platform that allows customers to make online purchases, such as a website or mobile app.
(E) SNAP-authorized retailers must never store (
i.e.,
maintain a record of) a SNAP household's card number (unless tokenized), PIN, expiration date, or CVV/CSC.
(2) SNAP-Authorized Retailers: EBT Training
(i) The following are the rules for SNAP-authorized retailers regarding effective EBT training for employees (
7 CFR 278.6(i)(2)
):
(
printed page 66983)
(A) SNAP-authorized retailers must ensure that all managers and employees whose work brings them into contact with SNAP benefits—or who are assigned to a location where SNAP benefits are accepted, handled, or processed—are effectively trained on the correct acceptance and use of SNAP benefits.
(B) Such training must be designed to establish a level of competence that ensures compliance with federal requirements.
(C) Training must include written, program-specific material, such as SNAP regulations, relevant guidance issued pursuant to those regulations (policy memoranda, fact sheets, training presentations, etc.), and correct use of POS devices and related equipment.
(D) Training materials must clearly state that trafficking is prohibited, as it violates the Food and Nutrition Act of 2008 and SNAP regulations. Trafficking is the exchange or attempted exchange of SNAP benefits for anything other than SNAP-eligible food.
(E) Employees at previously authorized SNAP retailers must be trained within 30 days of being hired.
(F) After their initial EBT training, employees must periodically have refresher training.
(ii) SNAP State agencies are required to provide training that meets these requirements, including the provision of appropriate written and program-specific materials. However, retailers have the option to waive the State-provided training. In cases where a retailer waives the State-provided training, the SNAP State agency must direct retailers to confirm their waiver in writing (
7 CFR 274.3(e)(7)
).
(e) EBT Host Processor Requirements
(1) EBT host processors are contractors that build and operate SNAP EBT systems on behalf of States. Processors are also sometimes referred to as “card issuers” since they issue EBT cards to SNAP households on behalf of SNAP State agencies.
(2) EBT Host Processors: Processing Standards
(i) Card processing standards create and enforce a level of service for the SNAP EBT processing environment, ensuring that users receive a consistent level of service, regardless of the technology used or the entities involved. FNA establishes card processing standards, in cooperation with entities that operate in the SNAP EBT environment.
(ii) The following are card processing standards that all processors must adhere to, and which must be incorporated into contractual agreements with processors (or their agents) (
7 CFR 274.8(b)
):
(A) Processors must maintain computer hardware and software necessary to interface directly with data processing facilities required to accommodate transaction and file processing.
(B) Processors must establish direct or indirect telecommunications connections to route transactions and to retrieve and deliver files to/from other processors and TPPs.
(C) System uptime is required 99.9% of the time, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. States may negotiate more rigorous uptime requirements in their contracts with processors.
(D) Processors may schedule downtime for system maintenance, repairs, upgrades, etc., provided the processor provides prior notice to all network participants, including FNA.
(1)
Outages must be scheduled to occur during non-peak transaction periods.
(2)
Scheduled outages must not be included when calculating whether the monthly 99.9% system uptime requirement has been met.
(3)
In the instance of emergency downtime, the processor must promptly inform all network participants.
(E) Processors must initiate a response to a SNAP EBT transaction request within two seconds from the time such a request is received by the processor's system, 98% of the time, per month.
(1)
Data transmission times between the processor and the acquirer must not be included when calculating whether the monthly 98% transaction request response requirement has been met.
(F) No more than two in every 10,000 transactions processed by a processor's system shall lead to an adjustment resulting from processor error.
(G) Processors must ensure that SNAP transactions originate from a SNAP-authorized retailer by validating the retailers against the Retailer EBT Data Exchange (REDE) file.
(H) Processors must ensure their International Organization for Standardization (ISO) message specifications are aligned with the most recent version of the ANSI X9.58 standards.
(I) Processors must provide all required data, such as redemption and transaction data, to FNA in accordance with the most up-to-date file specifications.
(J) When updates are made to the ISO 8583 or ANSI X9.58 specification, or other applicable specifications, State agencies shall ensure that EBT systems comply with the new version of the specification within 180 days from the publication of the updated specification.
(3) Issuer Identification Number (IIN)/Bank Identification Number (BIN)
(i) Issuer Identification Numbers (IIN), formerly called Bank Identification Numbers (BIN), are six-digit to eight-digit numbers that identify the bank, financial institution, or other entity that issued a card. IINs are issued by American Bank Association (ABA), and are placed on credit, debit, and other types of payment cards worldwide, including SNAP EBT cards. The ABA no longer issues six-digit IINs and is moving towards adopting eight-digit IINs.
(ii) The first digit in an IIN is the Major Industry Identifier (MII), which is determined according to the numbering scheme specified in the ISO 7812—Part 1 standard.
(iii) Each SNAP State agency via their EBT host processor must apply for and maintain its own IIN. The IIN is registered to the SNAP State agency rather than their EBT host processor.
(f) TPP and Acquirer Responsibilities
(1) Each acquirer or TPP shall enter into an agreement with an EBT Host Processor, gateway, or other relevant party, stating it will comply with FNA Regulations and EBT technical specifications, as outlined in ANSI X9.58. These EBT Operating Standards do not negate any terms or conditions of TPP or acquirer agreements, as long as the conditions of said agreement do not conflict with FNA regulations. A TPP or acquirer may enter into agreements with more than one EBT Host Processor, Gateway, or other connection point.
(2) Each acquirer must ensure that the POS terminals it owns, operates, controls, or for which it has signed an agreement to accept EBT transactions, must do so in accordance with FNA regulations.
(3) Each TPP and acquirer must settle all authorized transactions in accordance with FNA regulations and EBT Host Processor standards.
(4) Only a retailer that has received authorization from FNA to participate in SNAP may accept EBT cards for SNAP transactions. Each acquirer for a retailer that seeks such participation must make efforts to ensure EBT fraud is not occurring under their platform. Each acquirer must promptly ensure that it does not process SNAP transactions for a retailer following receipt of notice that authorization for that retailer has been revoked, rescinded or otherwise eliminated.
(g) Required EBT Transactions
(1) Minimum Transaction Set
(i) At minimum, every entity that interacts with the SNAP EBT system is capable of processing the following SNAP EBT transactions:
(A) Authorizations and denials,
(B) Refunds,
(C) Voids or cancellations,
(D) Key-entered transactions,
(E) Settlement or close-out transactions, and
(F) Balance inquiries (does not apply to SNAP-authorized internet retailers).
(ii) Each of these required transaction types is explained in more detail below. State agencies must ensure that their EBT systems are capable of completing this transaction set and be able to do so in every State nationwide, in accordance with interoperability standards specified in
7 CFR 274.8(b)(10)
.
(iii) Lastly, all SNAP EBT transactions are electronically processed and recorded. FNA has access to all SNAP EBT transaction records including the date, time, and dollar amount.
(iv) Authorization or Denial of SNAP Purchases: A SNAP household selects SNAP-eligible food at a SNAP-authorized retailer and goes to check out. The cost of the food items is totaled, and the purchase price is displayed by the POS device. The EBT card is presented to the POS device (inserted, tapped, swiped etc.), and the household must enter their PIN. The POS device then processes the transaction.
(A) If the purchase is approved, the retailer must provide the household with a receipt that shows the purchase and remaining SNAP balance. The purchase amount is deducted from the household's SNAP account and credited to the retailer's bank account generally within two banking days.
(v) Refunds: Refund transactions are when SNAP benefits are returned to a household's
(
printed page 66984)
account. Refunded SNAP benefits must only be returned to the household's SNAP card/account. Refunding SNAP benefits in any other form (cash, gift cards, etc.) constitutes trafficking and would subject both the retailer and household to sanctions.
(A) In-Person Refunds:
(1)
In-person refund transactions are conducted on a retailer's POS device.
(2)
The SNAP households must enter their PIN to authorize the refund.
(B) Internet Refunds:
(1)
Internet refund transactions do not require SNAP households to enter their PIN.
(2)
Whole or partial refunds may occur automatically for internet refunds. This may occur if an item is no longer in stock, if the order is cancelled, if the SNAP household does not receive all the items they ordered, or if an item is priced by weight and the final weight (and therefore the price) is different from the weight estimated at the time of purchase.
(3)
If the original payment was a split tender transaction, the refund will be issued to the card that was used to pay for the refunded items.
(4)
Refunds cannot occur after 90 days of the original transaction.
(C) Refund transactions differ from reversals because they are generally customer-initiated (except for automatic internet refunds) rather than retailer-initiated.
(vi) Void Or Cancellation: Void or cancellation transactions are used when an incorrect purchase amount is processed through a retailer's POS device. The void/cancellation must be done immediately after the purchase transaction and on the same POS device.
(vii) Key-Entered Transactions: If a POS device cannot read an EBT card, the SNAP household and retailer may conduct a key-entered transaction. To do so, the retailer must manually enter the EBT PAN into the POS device. Thereafter, the household must enter its PIN into the POS device, to authorize and process the transaction. Key-entered transactions must only be used as a last resort, when the POS device cannot read the EBT card.
(A) States may request a temporary waiver from FNA to prohibit some key-entered transactions as an EBT theft prevention measure.
(viii) Settlement: For SNAP-authorized retailers, this is the transaction where they are paid for the SNAP benefits redeemed at their store in exchange for food. Generally, SNAP-authorized retailers must receive payment for approved SNAP transactions within two business days of the transaction.
(ix) Balance Inquiries: Balance inquiries are used when a household wants to check the amount of benefits currently in its SNAP account.
(A) In-Person Balance Inquiries: In-person (or “brick-and-mortar”) SNAP-authorized retailers must provide SNAP households the ability to conduct balance inquiries. The SNAP household must present its EBT card to the POS device, enter their PIN, and follow the prompts to obtain the account balance.
(B) Online Balance Inquiries: SNAP-authorized internet retailers are not required to provide the ability to conduct balance inquiries, and FNA strongly recommends they do not do so (
7 CFR 274.7(d)(1)
).
(1)
However, internet retailers are allowed to provide balance inquiries. If an internet retailer allows balance inquiries, FNA requires them to do the following to mitigate fraudulent inquiries:
(i)
Remove the “guest checkout” option from its online sales platform (website, app, etc.).
(ii)
Limit the number of times a SNAP household can change the EBT card they are using to make purchases within a specific time period.
(iii)
Limit the number of balance inquiries a SNAP household can conduct within a specific time period. FNA recommends a maximum of two balance inquiries per hour.
(C) Balance Inquiries in Cardholder Portal/Mobile Apps: All SNAP households have the ability to log into their State's online SNAP cardholder portal to conduct balance inquiries. Processors in some States also offer households the ability to conduct balance inquiries in their mobile application. These platforms are protected with a User ID and password functionality.
(D) Interactive Voice Response (IVR) SNAP Balance Inquiry Requirements: Households can conduct balance inquiries by calling the EBT host processer's IVR number. Previously, households were able to conduct IVR balance inquiries by entering only their PAN. However, that practice has proven highly susceptible to fraud.
(1)
To prevent fraudulent balance inquiries by unauthorized users, States must work with their processor to ensure that all telephonic methods for conducting balance inquiries utilize an approved form of verification (
7 CFR 274.7(d)(4)
). Verification methods must use information only available to the household, such as a CVV/CSC printed on the card, and must not use personally identifiable information (PII).
(2) Reversals
(i) A reversal, sent to an EBT host processor by a retailer, acquirer, or TPP, is a partial or complete nullification of the effects of a previous transaction which cannot be processed as intended,
i.e.,
is undeliverable, is cancelled, or the previous transaction has timed out waiting for a response. The voiding of a transaction at the point of sale, when initiated by a retailer, is processed using a reversal message. Reversals should be processed per the ANSI X9.58 standards.
(ii) Reversals are a valid transaction type for internet transactions and must be processed according to the standard reversal specifications. Reversals must only be used in cases as described above, with one exception for internet transactions: in the event that a SNAP internet transaction occurs with mixed tender, and the additional payment type (cash/credit/debit) was rejected, the original SNAP transaction can be reversed so that the transaction can be attempted again. PINs are not required in reversal messages.
(iii) If the customer is unable to find a payment method with sufficient funds to cover the balance, and the website needs to cancel the original SNAP transaction, the retailer must submit a reversal to their processor.
(3) Adjustments
(i) An adjustment is a change to the balance of a household's SNAP benefit account, implemented by a State SNAP agency (and/or by their contracted EBT host processor) in response to an incorrect account balance caused by a system error during the redemption process (
7 CFR 274.2(g)
). Adjustments may increase the balance of a SNAP account (“credit adjustment”) or decrease the balance of an account (“debit adjustment”).
(ii) A system error is an error resulting from a malfunction at any point in the SNAP benefit redemption process, such as an error made by a retailer's host computer or POS device, a TPP, the Gateway, or processor. System errors should be rare. Adjustments must only be used to correct system errors and must never be used to correct a human error. Examples of system errors include:
(A) A State agency review of documentation shows that a household's benefit account was charged a different amount than the amount submitted by the retailer, or
(B) A charge submitted by a retailer to the EBT processor is erroneously deducted from the wrong household's benefit account.
(iii) When investigating a potential adjustment, the State should not rely solely on a retailer disputing a proposed credit adjustment as the sole evidence to for rejecting that proposal. The State must investigate the transaction(s) involved thoroughly, and determine if a valid system error occurred, regardless of the retailer's response to an inquiry.
(iv) Adjustments should not be utilized in response to household reports of retailer errors. Adjustments can only be used to correct system errors. Households must seek corrections to retailer errors (via refund and returns, for example) with the retailers themselves. Some examples of retailer errors (which are not true system errors) follow:
(A) Retailer Errors (must be done as returns, NOT as adjustments):
(1)
A retailer clerk erroneously scans a single item multiple times,
(2)
A clerk erroneously charges a household for one type of food item when a different type was purchased,
(3)
A retailer charges a different amount for a SNAP item at the register than was advertised,
(4)
A retailer attempts to input a refund to a household's benefit account, but erroneously charges a household a second time for the same amount,
(5)
A SNAP internet retailer delivers SNAP items that a household has already paid for, but they arrive damaged or with items missing,
(6)
A client returns items accidentally purchased with SNAP benefits, and/or
(7)
A client is unhappy with the quality of the product they received.
(B) Additionally, adjustments should not be used to replace stolen SNAP benefits.
(v) SNAP Household-Initiated Adjustments
(A) In order to be timely, SNAP households must request adjustments to their benefit account within 90 calendar days of an alleged system error transaction (
7 CFR 274.2(g)(2)(i)
). Households most often request
(
printed page 66985)
credit (
i.e.,
upward) adjustments but may request debit (
i.e.,
downward) adjustments. Household-initiated adjustment requests that are made over 90 days from the date of an alleged error transaction must be denied as untimely.
(B) If a household-initiated adjustment request is timely, the SNAP State agency has 15 calendar days from the date the household reports the alleged error to investigate the transaction(s) involved, reach a decision, and either move funds into the household's account or issue a written denial of the request to the household (
7 CFR 274.2(g)(2)(i)
).
(C) Approvals:
(1)
To approve a household-initiated adjustment request, the State agency must determine that a system error occurred and document that the system error was reviewed and verified. The State agency must make this determination prior to notifying the SNAP-authorized retailer involved and prior to adjusting the household's benefit account.
(2)
For credit adjustments, States must not give a provisional credit to the household while the State is determining whether their claim should be approved or denied.
(D) Denials:
(1)
If the State cannot verify the household's claim that a system error occurred, the State must deny the adjustment request.
(2)
If the State denies a household-initiated adjustment request, they must send the household a denial notice. This notice explains the action being taken, the reason for the action, and fair hearing rights, so the household can appeal the determination. The denial notice must be sent by the 15th calendar day after the adjustment was requested by the household.
(3)
Households must be granted a fair hearing if the request for hearing is submitted within 90 calendar days from the date of the denial notice. If the 90-day adverse notice period ends on a weekend or holiday, and a request for a fair hearing is submitted the next business day after the weekend or holiday, the State agency must consider the request timely.
(4)
For credit adjustments, States must not give a provisional credit to the household pending a fair hearing for a denied adjustment request.
(vi) Retailer-Initiated Adjustments
(A) In order to be timely, SNAP-authorized retailers must submit adjustment requests no later than 15 calendar days after an alleged system error occurred (
7 CFR 274.2(g)(2)(ii)
). Retailers typically submit debit (
i.e.,
downward) adjustment requests to household benefit accounts, seeking additional payment (which they would receive upon settlement) related to an alleged system error, but it is possible they may request credit (
i.e.,
upward) adjustments as well.
(B) To proceed with a debit adjustment request, the State must first review relevant data/documents, maintain documentation of its investigation, and validate that a system error did occur.
(C) The State has 15 calendar days from the date the retailer reports the alleged error to investigate the transaction(s) involved and reach a decision. If the State cannot validate that a system error (not a retailer error) occurred, the State must deny the request. In addition, if the State cannot validate the requested debit adjustment within 15 calendar days of the request, the request must be denied. The State (or their EBT processor) is not required to notify households of adjustment requests that were initiated by the retailer and subsequently denied if no hold was placed on the household's account.
(D) States can choose between following the standard procedure for debit adjustments (274.2(g)(2)(ii)(A)) or an alternative no-hold procedure (274.2(g)(2)(ii)(B)):
(1)
Standard procedure: If the State determines there is a timely and valid request for a debit adjustment, the State may choose to place a hold on the household's account in the amount of the requested adjustment. If the State validates the adjustment request and places such a hold, it must immediately notify the household that it has done so.
(i)
If there are insufficient benefits in the account to cover the entire proposed adjustment, the State may also place a hold on all or part of the next month's issuance, to make up the difference (but only the next month's issuance).
(ii)
If the household appeals the adjustment by requesting a fair hearing within 15 calendar days of being notified, the State must—within 48 hours—make a provisional credit to the household's account (by releasing the hold on the adjustment balance), pending resolution of the fair hearing. If no request for a hearing is made within 15 calendar days of the notice, the hold is released on the adjustment balance, and this amount is credited to the retailer's account.
(2)
Alternative No-Hold Procedure: Alternatively, the State agency may instead choose to act on requests for debit adjustments without placing a hold on the household's account. Under this procedure, the State must first notify the household of the proposed adjustment and then allow the household 15 calendar days to appeal by requesting a fair hearing before implementing the adjustment. In such cases, the State must not take any further action until the 15-day window for appeal expires. If the household does timely request a fair hearing, the State should not adjust the household's account until the fair hearing decision is rendered.
(E) Household Notice: Household adjustment notices must:
(1)
Clearly state the proposed full adjustment amount,
(2)
The reason for the action, including documentation of the system error,
(3)
If the State places a hold, it must give the household adequate notice regarding the details of the hold, and advise the household that any amount owed, above and beyond the hold amount, is subject to collection from the household's next month's benefits.
(4)
Inform households that they have the right to request a fair hearing within 90 days of the date of the notice.
(vii) State-Initiated Adjustments
(A) In cases where the State agency identifies a possible system error, the State has 15 calendar days to investigate and, if appropriate, adjust the household's account (
7 CFR 274.2(g)(2)(i)
). If the State cannot validate that a system error occurred, they do not need to notify the household or the retailer because the adjustment was initiated by the State.
(B) If the State validates that a system error occurred and the adjustment results in a debit (
i.e.,
reduction) to a household's account, the State must notify the household and allow them to request a fair hearing.
(C) In cases where SNAP benefits are erroneously issued to a household, the State agency may adjust benefits issued to household accounts after the issuance process is complete, but prior to the availability date for household access (
7 CFR 274.2(g)(1)
).
(h) Clearing, Settlement, and Reconciliation
(1) In general, clearing, settlement, and reconciliation describe the processes through which different entities interact with each other to pay amounts owed to each other for conducting and processing EBT transactions.
(2) Clearing is when retailers send transaction information to the SNAP State agency or the EBT host processor to request payment. This can be done directly by the retailer or through their contracted TPP or acquirer.
(3) Settlement processing is when a State or processor creates and transmits a payment to a retailer's bank for approved, cleared SNAP transactions.
(4) Reconciliation is the process States must follow to account for all SNAP issuance and transaction activity. This is done to ensure accuracy and consistency, and to identify and rectify any discrepancies.
(5) Clearing EBT Transactions
(i) Retailers clear transactions by submitting SNAP claim files containing transaction information. The standards for SNAP claim file processing are as follows:
(A) Retailers must submit SNAP claim files each business day no later than 48 hours after the date and time of the oldest transaction in the file.
(B) Retailers may submit a single claim file for multiple store locations. The retailer must identify the specific store where each transaction occurred in the SNAP claim file using the numeric identifier assigned by FNA.
(C) If the State or processor approves a retailer to submit a corrected claim file or corrected transactions, the retailer must submit the correction within 60 days of the date of the original file submission, unless the State approves a longer timeframe.
(6) Settlement Processing
(i) The standards for settlement processing are as follows:
(A) The State must set a standard daily cut-off time for transaction processing and inform retailers and TPPs about this cut-off time.
(B) The State must ensure that retailers receive payment at their financial institution for approved, cleared EBT transactions, within two business days of the settlement day of the transaction. The State, processor, TPP, or acquirer must pay retailers as soon as payments are ready to be transmitted.
(C) The processor must request payment from the Federal Reserve Bank. Then, the Federal Reserve Bank verifies the request and
(
printed page 66986)
sends an Automated Clearinghouse (ACH) payment file to the State's bank account (which is managed by the processor) directing the bank to pay the processor for all settled transactions.
(1)
On behalf of the State, the processor directs its bank to pay the first authorized downstream entity in the EBT system for all authorized transactions that were processed by the entity on first authorized downstream will be a processor. Downstream entities might include TPPs and acquirers, who then pay further downstream entities. The final downstream entity is the retailer.
(D) The processor is responsible for meeting the settlement cutoff timeframe established by the State. When submitting transactions for settlement to a TPP, the processor must provide a standard settlement cutoff timeframe to the TPP. Any differences in these settlement cutoff timeframes are the responsibility of the processor.
(7) Reconciliation
(i) SNAP State agencies must account for all SNAP benefit issuances and transactions through a reconciliation process. Reconciliation must be conducted and records kept as follows:
(A) Reconciliation of SNAP benefits issued to household accounts against benefits on the Issuance Authorization File;
(B) Reconciliation of individual household account balances against account activities on a daily basis;
(C) Reconciliation of each retail store's SNAP transactions, per POS terminal and in total to deposits on a daily basis;
(D) Verification of retailer's credits against deposit information entered into the ACH network;
(E) Reconciliation of total funds entered into, exiting from, and remaining in the system each day;
(F) Maintenance of audit trails that document the full cycle of issuance, from benefit allotment posting to the State issuance authorization file, through posting to POS transactions at retailers, through settlement of retailer credits.
(i) End of Day Cut-Off and Processing
(1) The following are the rules for SNAP State agencies, EBT host processors, retailers, and TPPs regarding end-of-day cut-off and processing:
(i) Each SNAP State agency must designate a standard daily cut-off time for SNAP EBT transaction processing by TPPs interacting with the State's EBT system.
(ii) That cut-off time must not be earlier than 12:00 p.m. (noon) local time at any POS device accepting SNAP EBT transactions for the TPP.
(iii) Transactions conducted during a business day must be settled on the next business day after the next cut-off time.
(iv) Most cut-off times are at 2:00 p.m. Central Time. For example, transactions that occur before 2:00 p.m. on a Wednesday will be settled on Thursday (the next business day). Transactions that occur after 2:00 p.m. on a Wednesday will be settled on Friday (the business day after the next cut-off time).
(2) If retailers, TPPs, and/or acquirers establish their own cut-off times, which are different from the State's, they must maintain appropriate suspense accounts for such purposes.
(j) Manual Vouchers
(1) Manual vouchers are paper forms completed by the retailer with information about the cardholder and the transaction. Manual vouchers should only be used when the POS system is down or cannot connect to the EBT processor (
e.g.,
no connection can be established, transactions are not processing; or when the POS device displays messages such as “No MSG from Host,” “Host Sent NAK,”: “Lost Carrier,” “No Answer,” etc.), or in certain situations where a POS terminal cannot be used (
e.g.,
remote delivery).
(2) Because manual vouchers do not require a PIN, they are highly susceptible to fraud. In addition, the Agricultural Act of 2014 (2014 Farm Bill) amended Section 7(f) of the Food and Nutrition Act to prohibit the use of manual vouchers for benefit redemption, except in specific cases where FNA determines they are necessary. For this reason, FNA prohibits the use of manual vouchers as a common day-to-day practice in SNAP (
7 CFR 274.3(a)(1)(i)
). FNA only grants exemptions/waivers to allow the use of manual vouchers as a regular business practice in the following situations:
(i) In rural areas where retailers do not have internet connectivity,
(ii) For retailers eligible for free State-provided EBT equipment (direct-marketing farmers and farmers' markets),
(iii) In designated Tribal areas.
(3) Retailers that wish to seek an exemption/waiver to conduct manual voucher transactions as a regular business practice must contact their TPP to confirm they have the capability to accept and clear vouchers and will be able to provide the retailer with the paper forms used for the voucher process. Once approved to accept manual vouchers, retailers must request a supply of paper forms to keep on hand.
(4) Retailers must adhere to the following procedure for processing manual vouchers:
(i) Manual vouchers require a customer signature. The clerk or manager must then call the State's retailer customer service line and enter the following data: the store's FNA authorization number, the card number, transaction type (purchase/refund), dollar amount and the pre-printed voucher number.
(ii) If approved, the EBT system places the funds on hold so that the customer cannot use them elsewhere and gives the retailer a six-digit authorization number to record on the form.
(iii) Retailers must clear vouchers using the method required by their TPP within ten calendar days. Some TPPs require the retailer to mail the original copy of the paper voucher to the TPP, and the TPP converts it to an electronic transaction themselves.
(iv) If the retailer fails to clear the voucher on time, they are not paid, and the system releases the held funds back to SNAP client.
(5) EBT host processors should process manual voucher transactions as follows:
(i) A voucher authorization is required when the retailer calls to validate that the amount of the transaction is available.
(ii) If the household account has the amount required for the transaction, the retailer will receive an approval code and confirmation.
(iii) For a purchase, the amount of the voucher will be placed on hold in the household's account.
(iv) The retailer must later call to clear the voucher.
(v) Once the voucher is cleared, the benefits will be removed from the household account.
(vi) In the case of a voucher return, the amount of funds to be returned to the household will not be credited to the household's account until the voucher is cleared.
(6) If a voucher authorization remains open without an associated voucher clear, the voucher authorization will be reversed no later than 30 days after the authorization.
(k) Store-and-Forward Processing
(1) Store-and-forward transactions are a very limited exception to the rule that retailers cannot store EBT card numbers and PINs, described in
7 CFR 274.8(e)(1)
. In cases where an EBT system is not functioning or is otherwise inaccessible (
i.e.,
during a power outage, natural disaster, etc.), SNAP-authorized retailers are allowed to temporarily store SNAP EBT transaction data (including EBT card numbers and PINs) and forward them for processing later, when EBT system functionality has been restored.
(2) Per
7 CFR 274.8(e)(1)
, only the SNAP State agency has the authority to allow retailers to accept store-and-forward transactions. The decision to accept store-and-forward is entirely the retailer's, and retailers assume 100% of the liability for such transactions.
(3) The standards for store-and-forward transactions are as follows:
(i) The retailer may choose to set a maximum amount that they will accept on a store-and-forward.
(ii) Store-and-forward transactions, when processed, must comply with regular rules for processing SNAP EBT transactions, including:
(A) Validation of card number,
(B) Validation of PIN,
(C) Validation of retailer, and
(D) Benefit balance availability.
(iii) The card acceptor is responsible for securely storing the transaction information with the encrypted PIN. The stored purchase information is later forwarded to the Card issuer for approval as a Financial Presentment transaction.
(iv) The retailer must forward such transactions for processing within 24 hours of the EBT system becoming accessible; and may only forward those transactions for processing one time.
(v) After the retailer forwards those transactions for processing, the retailer must delete all data regarding EBT card numbers and PINs.
(vi) A store-and-forward transaction may be partially approved, if the SNAP household's benefit account balances are insufficient to cover the purchase.
(vii) The retailer is liable for any portion of a store-and-forward transaction that does not comply with these rules.
(l) Transaction Data Retention
(1) The following are the rules for SNAP State agencies, EBT host processors, and SNAP-authorized retailers regarding
(
printed page 66987)
retention of data on SNAP EBT transactions. SNAP-authorized retailers must be able to comply with the requirements of this section at the time they become authorized.
(i) States must retain data on SNAP EBT transactions for at least three years.
(ii) SNAP-authorized retailers must maintain records of all SNAP EBT transactions for a minimum of seven calendar days.
(iii) Upon request from the State's SNAP agency or EBT host processor, retailers must provide records of such transactions within seven business days.
(2) Transaction Response Codes and Declined Transactions
(i) The EBT transaction response code is a sequence of letters and numbers that indicate whether a transaction was approved or denied. EBT transaction response codes display on a retailer's POS device after they attempt to conduct an EBT transaction. All transactions must be date- and time-stamped (using the retailer's location) and must be settled in U.S. dollars currency.
(ii) EBT transaction message specifications follow the X9.58 standard. That standard is established by ANSI's Accredited Standards Committee X9. ANSI is the American National Standards Institute, the accredited organization responsible for developing technical standards, including exchanging EBT financial transaction messages. .
