(m) SNAP Data Security Requirements
(1) SNAP Data: For purposes of this document, SNAP data means any data generated as a result of a household's or retailers' participation in SNAP and application to participate in SNAP. This includes:
(i) Information in household and retailer applications, including personally identifiable information, such as name, address, Social Security number, etc.
(ii) Information regarding individual SNAP transactions,
(iii) SNAP card/account numbers,
(iv) Retailers' FNA numbers,
(v) Retailer SNAP redemption data.
(2) The following are the data security rules for SNAP State agencies, EBT host processors, SNAP-authorized retailers, TPPs, acquirers, Gateways, and any other entity that handles SNAP data:
(i) Such entities may exchange data other than the PIN for the purposes of processing transactions if they enter agreements to do so and if they follow transaction processing specifications and requirements.
(ii) SNAP EBT transactions must generally conform to the Payment Card Industry (PCI) Data Security Standard. The only exception is that processors must comply with federal requirements for sharing PAN data.
(n) Electronic SNAP Benefit Theft
(1) Electronic SNAP benefit theft occurs when criminals use electronic methods to steal a SNAP household's benefits and/or take control of their benefit account.
(2) To provide context for FNA requirements regarding EBT card security, this section summarizes the most common electronic SNAP theft and/or EBT fraud schemes currently in use by criminals.
(i)
Card skimming:
Card skimming is when a criminal places a card reading device on a retailer's POS equipment. The reader collects key card information—such as the PAN and PIN—when a client swipes or inserts their card during a transaction. Criminals then use this card information to steal a household's benefits.
(ii)
Algorithmic attacks:
Criminals can use bots or artificial intelligence (AI) to exploit internet vulnerabilities, by conducting a high number of rapid and repeated inquiries to steal key card information. For example, criminals have used this technology to exploit balance inquiry features of SNAP internet retailers and Interactive Voice Response (IVR) systems, to identify valid PANs and PINs and determine whether accounts have positive balances.
(iii)
Phishing scams:
Criminals use scams on text, email, phone, and social media to deceive households into providing key EBT card information. For example, in some States, scammers have spoofed, or imitated, the phone number of a government agency or the EBT processor customer service number to obtain key card information from households.
(iv)
Card cloning:
After key card information has been stolen through methods like skimming or phishing, criminals can use equipment to encode stolen card information onto blank magnetic stripe cards. Criminals then use cloned cards to steal SNAP benefits, after the SNAP State agency reloads benefits to the household accounts.
(A) While some cloned cards are physical cards, criminals can also use stolen information to complete transactions without an actual physical card (such as internet purchases, also known as “card-not-present” transactions).
(3) Required EBT Theft Prevention Options
(i) This section summarizes the EBT theft prevention account options that State agencies must offer to SNAP households, in order to protect their SNAP benefits from electronic theft and fraud.
(ii) States are required to educate SNAP households about how these options work (
7 CFR 274.2(e)(15)
, must ensure all households have the ability to use these options, and are not excluded from using these options based on a disability or because they speak a primary language other than English (
7 CFR 274.8(b)(4)
).
(iii) Households must be able to opt in or opt out of using these options through each of the following interfaces (
7 CFR 274.7(k)
):
(A) EBT cardholder internet portal
(B) Mobile application
(C) Telephone request
(D) In-person request
(iv) EBT Card Blocking
(A) States must provide households with the ability to block and unblock (
i.e.,
freeze/unfreeze, lock/unlock) their EBT card from processing transactions, which protects benefits while the card is not in use. Households must be able to turn these options off and on instantaneously, as needed. For example, households should be able to unblock their card while they are checking out at a cash register and re-block it immediately afterwards.
(B) Currently, there are three types of blocks: card freeze, out-of-State transactions block, and internet transaction block. When any of these three blocking types are activated, purchases and balance inquiries will be blocked, but benefits can still be loaded onto the card and returns/refunds must still be processed.
(C) States must offer households the option to use each of the following types of blocking:
(1) Card Freeze:
Households must have the option to “freeze” their EBT card, which prevents it from being used for purchases (either online or at brick-and-mortar retailers) or balance inquiries.
(2) Out-of-State Transactions Block/Freeze/Lock:
When criminals obtain EBT card information, they often make unauthorized transactions outside of the household's home State. Households must have the option to block some or all out-of-State transactions (
e.g.,
blocking all transactions that do not occur in the household's home State, blocking transactions in certain States with high rates of theft).
(i)
When implementing out-of-State blocking, States should be aware that internet transactions may appear to be out-of-State transactions, if the internet retailer is located or headquartered outside of the household's home State. For example, when out-of-State blocking is activated, a SNAP household who lives in one State should not be blocked from buying food on a large retailer's website, even though that retailer's headquarters is in another State, as long as the purchase is delivered or picked up in the household's home State.
(ii)
States may choose to consider internet purchases that are delivered or picked up out-of-State to be “out-of-State transactions”
(
printed page 66989)
for the purposes of this card block. For example, when out-of-State blocking is activated, a State agency may choose to block a household's transaction on a large retailer's website if they set the purchase or delivery address to one within a neighboring State.
(3)
Internet Transactions Block/Freeze/Lock: Households must have the option to block their EBT card from being used for internet (“card-not-present”) transactions. Specifically, households must be able to unblock their card before making an internet purchase and re-block it afterwards.
(i)
Note:
This option should block all internet purchase transactions and balance inquiries, regardless of where the internet retailer is located or where the delivery/pickup address is located.
(D) Currently, States are not allowed to completely freeze EBT cards by default, due to interoperability requirements at
7 CFR 274.8(b)(10)
.
(E) States are allowed to implement a default block on out-of-State transactions and/or internet transactions. States are only permitted to implement these default blocks if they comply with relevant statute and regulations and provide a way for households to unblock transactions. States that implement default transaction blocking must ensure that all SNAP clients maintain access to their benefits, including those clients with disabilities.
(v) Maximum Amount Per Transaction Limit
(A) States must provide households with the option to set a maximum purchase amount per transaction limit, so that transactions over that limit are automatically blocked.
(vi) Limits on Returns
(A) States may choose to provide households with the option to set a limit on the number of returns that can be conducted within a period of time (
e.g.,
no more than five returns per day) or a maximum dollar amount per return.
(B) States may choose to enable this option as the default setting for all SNAP households for brick-and-mortar purchases only. States should not enable this option for internet purchases. States do not have to allow households to remove returns limits.
(vii) Alerts
(A) States must provide households with the capability to receive transaction alerts, similar to alerts that are standard in the commercial banking industry. Households must be able to opt into these alerts, which will be delivered via email and/or text message. The required alerts are the following:
(1)
Purchases on the account, including rejected purchases (
e.g.,
insufficient funds purchases, blocked purchases due to card restrictions). These alerts should include information on the purchase method (
e.g.,
point-of-sale transaction, internet transaction) and date and time of the purchase.
(2)
Specific account activity, including PIN changes and balance inquiries. These alerts should include information on the activity method (
e.g.,
point-of-sale transaction, internet transaction, IVR) and date and time of the activity.
(3)
Changes to personal account information such as address, email address, and telephone number.
(B) States may choose to enable this option as a default setting for all SNAP households. States must allow households to turn off the alerts if desired.
(viii) Transaction History
(A) For purposes of preventing EBT benefit theft, households must have up-to-date information on their account activity. To that end, States must provide SNAP households with access to 12 months of transaction history for their EBT account through an online account management system and mobile account information system (
7 CFR 274.7(d)(2)
,
7 CFR 274.8(b)(4)(i)(H)
,
274.8(b)(4)(i)(I)
). This must include the following information:
(1) EBT transaction dates, times, and amounts. This must include information on whether the transaction was approved or rejected, and why (
e.g.,
insufficient funds purchases, blocked purchases due to card restrictions).
(2)
Type of transaction (card-not-present or card present).
(3)
Identifying information for retailer, excluding FNA numbers.
(4)
History of balance inquiries made.
(5)
Dates and times of PIN changes.
(6)
History of other personal account information changes including address, email address, and telephone number.
(7)
Other account changes such as enabling or disabling specific account options.
(B) This information must be made available to SNAP households in real time.
(ix) CAV Validation
(A) States must work with their processors to require Cardholder Authentication Value (CAV) validation (
7 CFR 274.8(5)(vii)
.
(B) CAVs are encoded in the magnetic stripe of EBT cards and are not printed on the card. Criminals can obtain CAVs through card skimming, but not through other methods (
e.g.,
phishing, algorithmic attacks). Thus, CAV validation can prevent benefit theft from cards that are cloned via methods other than skimming, since they will not be encoded with the correct CAV information.
(4) PIN Security
(i) The Personal Identification Number (PIN) is a number that is connected to a particular SNAP EBT card and is assigned to or chosen by a SNAP household. The PIN is used as a password, to verify a household's identity, granting them authorization to conduct SNAP transactions and otherwise access the SNAP account.
(ii) This section describes the requirements for PINs used with SNAP EBT cards/accounts. SNAP State agencies—working through their EBT host processor—must ensure these requirements are met.
(iii) Blocking Easy-to-Guess PINs
(A) States must prohibit SNAP households from having PINs that are easy for criminals to guess (
7 CFR 274.2(f)(2)
). Specifically, States must prohibit PINs that are comprised:
(1)
Entirely of sequential digits (with zero considered sequential to both one and nine),
(2)
Entirely of reverse sequential digits (with zero considered sequential to both one and nine),
(3)
Entirely of one repeated digit,
(4)
Of the last four digits of the associated EBT card's PAN,
(5)
Entirely of alternating digits (
e.g.,
1212, 8989, or 5454),
(6)
Of a number that has 19 or 20 as the first two digits,
(7)
Of the sequential digits 2580, 8520, 0852, or 0258 (these sequences are commonly chosen for PINs because they reflect the vertical digits of a numeric keypad in order).
(iv) Activation of Newly Issued EBT Cards
(A) States must ensure that new and replacement EBT cards are issued to households in inactive status (
7 CFR 274.2(f)(3)
). This means the EBT card is not functional until the SNAP household activates the card (
e.g.,
by calling into the IVR). After activation, households can select their own PIN.
(v) PIN Security Requirements
(A) The following standards apply to PIN security:
(1)
PIN security and management must conform to the most current version of technical standards at ANSI X9.8 and ISO 9564.
(2)
When selecting or changing their PINs, SNAP households must do so at the State agency office or via a secure electronic process approved by FNA and the State agency (
e.g.,
an online cardholder portal, a mobile application, a phone or interactive voice response [IVR] process),
(3)
EBT cards must not contain any data which could be used to identify PINs.
(4)
POS devices used for SNAP must:
(i)
Accept and securely encrypt a PIN of at least four digits,
(ii)
Not display PIN in plain text,
(iii)
Not print, electronically record, or otherwise create or maintain a record of PINs.
(5)
PINs must be encrypted at minimum from the point of entry, in accordance with requirements at
7 CFR 274.8(b)(3)(ii)(C)
. This protects PINs, both when the household is initially selecting a PIN, and afterwards, when using it to make a purchase at a retailer's POS device.
(i)
PIN data must be encrypted and represented as packed binary data, (
i.e.,
eight binary bits shall be represented as 16 hexadecimal characters). The PIN must be formatted into a PIN block consistent with the most current version of standards at ANSI X9.8/ISO 9564-1 before encryption.
(6)
SNAP households commonly choose their PIN by calling into an Interactive Voice Response (IVR) telephone system. The IVR PIN-selection process is not as secure as an encrypted in-office PIN selection device, but aligns with common practice in the commercial banking industry (
7 CFR 274.2(f)(2)
). States and their processors must adhere to the following requirements, to ensure the IVR PIN-selection process is as secure as possible:
(i)
The IVR PIN-selection process must be completely automated, without involving any customer service representatives,
(ii)
When households select their PIN via IVR, they must enter two elements of their personally identifiable information (PII), such as birth date, last four of the social security number, zip code, case number, etc., to confirm their identity,
(iii)
States are 100% liable for losses resulting from the IVR PIN-selection process,
(
printed page 66990)
including the replacement of the stolen SNAP benefits due to unauthorized transactions, security breaches, or incorrect identification of the person setting a PIN via IVR.
(7)
States may request exemptions to these PIN encryption methods by proposing an alternative that is at least as effective, which FNA may consider and grant on a case-by-case basis.
(vi) Online PIN Entry Method
(A) SNAP regulations at
7 CFR 274.8(b)
require that PINs be entered only through ANSI-compliant POS devices.
7 CFR 274.8(b)(3)(ii)(C)
and
274.8(b)(6)(iii)
require that PINs must be encrypted, at a minimum, from the point of entry.
(B) FNA has waived those requirements for internet retailers, instead, they must comply with the following requirements:
(1)
Secure, implement, and enforce a contract for secure PIN-entry services to be used on their SNAP online purchasing website.
(2)
Online SNAP transactions must go through a secure PIN-entry TPP. Currently, the only approved TPPs for SNAP online are Fiserv, WorldPay, and Forage. FNA is willing to work with any TPP an applicant chooses to partner with, assuming they meet the technical requirements for securely processing EBT payments online.
(3)
Retailer's website and mobile application must conform to all PIN-entry requirements and standards required by FNA regulations and applicable industry standards.
(4)
The website, mobile application, and/or any other intermediary service provider(s) responsible for use of SNAP EBT card numbers must continue to maintain PCI certification.
(5)
Retailers must maintain a secure system that ensures the security and privacy of EBT customer data.
(vii) Transactions that do not require a PIN
(A) Manual Voucher Clear (previously known as “Voice-Authorized Manual Voucher”): This is a request to clear a previously voice-authorized manual voucher, where a voucher clear, voucher number, and a voice approval code were assigned, and the SNAP household is no longer present. To clear a voucher, the retailer must use the same voucher number and card number that was used on the voucher authorization, and the approval number that was given for the voucher authorization.
(B) PIN-less Refunds for SNAP-Authorized Online Retailers: Because SNAP households—and therefore their PINs—will typically not be present when a SNAP-authorized online retailer processes a refund, such retailers have a blanket waiver from the
7 CFR 274.8(a)(2)
requirement that PINs be present for refunds. The following conditions apply:
(1)
All PIN-less refund transactions must be processed by a secure PIN-entry TPP.
(2)
Retailers must maintain a secure method for entering and authorizing PIN-less refunds.
(3)
While a PIN is not required for an internet return, if the household does enter a PIN it must match the card PIN.
(4)
PIN-less refunds for internet transactions must return the funds to the household's account, even if the card has been “statused” (
e.g.,
cancelled, de-activated, or reported as lost).
(5)
Retailers must use the PIN-less refund process when items are out of stock or to refund an amount that was overestimated for weighted items.
(6)
Due to the PIN-less refund functionality, internet retailers must not use manual adjustments for this purpose.
(o) SNAP EBT Chip Cards
(1) EBT Chip Card Requirements
(i) EBT chip cards are payment cards that have a computer chip embedded in them, providing security features that are superior to payment cards which only utilize a magnetic stripe. An EBT chip card can be insert-only or dual interface. A dual-interface card can be inserted (a.k.a., “contact” payment) or “tapped” (a.k.a., contactless payment) at a point-of-sale device. The contactless payment technology in an EBT chip card utilizes Near Field Communication (NFC). NFC is a protocol that enables wireless communication over short distances (a few inches) between payment cards and POS devices. Chip cards that are capable of conducting NFC contactless transactions are generally considered more secure than chip cards that must be inserted into POS devices.
(ii) All States must issue SNAP benefits via NFC-enabled chip cards (
7 CFR 274.1(a)
). Generally, States will begin implementation by piloting chip cards in limited geographic areas. States must provide adequate notification to households and retailers before making this transition. States must ensure that chip cards continue to include a magnetic stripe to ensure that SNAP households have a fallback payment option in case the chip card does not work at a certain retailer.
(iii) FNA recommends that States issue new EBT chip cards in phases, in order to minimize disruption for SNAP households, and to provide an opportunity to troubleshoot any issues that arise. Retailers, processers, TPPs, and Gateways must work with their SNAP State agencies to conduct testing as soon as possible, to ensure the new chip cards work as intended. If retailer POS systems have not yet been programmed to accept EBT chip cards, retailers (or their acquirer or TPP) must conduct testing to confirm the card will “fallback” to use the magnetic stripe on the card until the retailer's POS system can process chip card payments. Retailers should contact their POS service provider or TPP for help conducting the fallback testing.
(2) Retailer Upgrades to Support SNAP EBT Chip Cards
(i) The following are the requirements for SNAP-authorized retailers to support NFC-enabled SNAP chip cards.
(A) SNAP chip cards will include a new service code (220), informing the POS terminal that the card has a chip.
(B) The payment application on the chip will use a new Application ID (AID): A0000000044542. POS providers, acquirers, and TPPs must assist retailers in updating their POS devices and systems accordingly.
(C) The application identifier (AID) encoded in the chip indicates to the POS terminal what type of card is being used. POS terminals are also coded to accept specific AIDs. For a chip card transaction to be successful, the card and the terminal need matching AIDs, meaning that all POS terminals must be updated with the new EBT chip AID in order to process EBT chip card transactions.
(D) The AID is composed of two parts, the registered application provider identifier (RID) and the proprietary application identifier extension (PIX). EBT chip cards will include the unique AID A0000000044542. The unique AID will allow POS terminals to support SNAP processing rules (
e.g.,
PIN entry required, fallback rules) via standard terminal action codes (TACs).
(3) Empty Candidate List Fallback Process
(i) Most retailers currently accept other NFC-enabled chip cards (
e.g.,
credit and debit cards issued by a bank or credit union), but their POS devices do not yet support the new AID for SNAP EBT. In such cases, when a SNAP household tries to use a SNAP chip card at the POS device, the device will recognize that the card has a chip but will not recognize the SNAP AID. When this occurs, the POS device must allow the card to proceed with a magnetic stripe transaction. The technical name for this process is Empty Candidate List (ECL) fallback. The specific steps for an ECL fallback transaction are as follows:
(A) If a household with an NFC-enabled SNAP chip card attempts a magnetic stripe transaction before attempting a chip transaction, the POS device will direct the household to insert or tap the card instead.
(B) If the retailer's POS device has been updated with the new chip card AID, the chip transaction will process successfully.
(C) If the POS device has not been updated, attempts to conduct EBT chip card transaction will fail. The POS device will then prompt the client to swipe their card.
(D) It is important that retailers train all employees working at checkout on this new ECL fallback process.
(ii) Magnetic stripe EBT cards that do not contain a chip have a service code (120) in the magnetic stripe indicating that they are magnetic stripe only and should continue to function as usual.
(iii) SNAP households should follow the same process to select the tender type (
e.g.,
SNAP or cash) and enter their PIN, regardless of whether they process the transaction by swiping, inserting, or tapping their EBT card.
(4) Household Notification for Changes in Payment Technology
(i) States must notify SNAP households before they implement a new payment method, including integrating electronic chips into EBT cards. This may include notifications about an upcoming transition issued via press releases; updates to their websites, apps, or client portals; posters in certification and issuance offices; through outreach partners; and/or notices mailed to households in advance of a payment technology transition. States must also send households detailed individual notifications containing the information necessary to make the transition without suffering loss of access to their benefits (
e.g.,
directing households to activate their new EBT card).
(ii) FNA also expects States to notify and work with SNAP-authorized retailers and
(
printed page 66991)
retailer associations to ensure that as many SNAP retailers as possible prepare to accept EBT transactions via new methods before States begin the process of replacing existing SNAP cards. This will simplify the transition for SNAP households, who might otherwise face confusion over which transaction methods they should use at individual retailers. States should also educate households about the security benefits of new transaction methods, so that households understand the benefits of selecting retailers who have made the necessary upgrades to accept more secure payment systems.
(5) Key Management
(i) State master keys utilized for EBT chip card personalization and transaction processing must be transferable in the event of a state conversion to another EBT processor. EBT processor contracts for EBT chip card services must include a transition plan detailing how master keys for EBT chip card personalization and transaction processing will be transferred to an incoming EBT processor in the event that services from the incumbent EBT processor are discontinued. Impacts to and preservation of EBT chip card stock for over-the-counter issuance should also be considered and detailed in the transition plan.
(p) SNAP EBT Card Design and Requirements
(1) SNAP EBT cards issued by States must comply with the requirements of this section, which reflect the requirements in
7 CFR 274.8(b)(5)
.
(i) Required (printed on the card):
(A) Address of the office where the card can be returned if it is lost or no longer in use.
(B) Text that says “[a]ny user with valid PIN can use SNAP benefits on this card and need not be pictured . . .” or similar text approved by FNA.
(ii) Prohibited:
(A) EBT cards—as well as their sleeves, jackets, buck slips, and the like—must not contain the name of any State or local official.
(B) EBT informational materials must not indicate any political affiliation (with a party or otherwise).
(iii) Allowed: State agencies may require that EBT cards include photographs of household members. However, if the State agency does so, it must establish procedures to ensure that all appropriate household members and authorized representatives are able to access benefits from the account.
(iv) FNA reserves the right to require State agencies to place a Department logo on the EBT card, sleeves, jackets, buck slips, and the like.
(2) SNAP regulations at
7 CFR 271.2
define the various types of EBT cards:
(i) Magnetic stripe,
(ii) Integrated electronic chip capable of conducting transactions by either being inserted into a card reader or via wireless Near Field Communication (NFC) protocols,
(iii) Contactless digital wallet with a stored virtual card, and
(iv) Any other similar benefit access technology approved by FNA.
(3) Newly issued EBT cards can no longer rely solely on a magnetic stripe as a method to conduct transactions (
7 CFR 274.1(a)
). The primary method of conducting EBT transactions must be a physical card with an integrated electronic chip that is capable of conducting transactions both by being inserted into a card reader and via wireless NFC protocols.
(4) EBT cards may continue containing magnetic stripes to conduct transactions as a fallback method and must not permit a transaction to be conducted via magnetic stripe until there has been at least one failed attempt to conduct the transaction via electronic chip.
(5) Card Verification Value/Card Security Code
(i) Validation of a Card Verification Value (CVV)/Card Security Code (CSC) is a method used to confirm that an internet transaction is being conducted by a SNAP household in possession of their physical/actual SNAP EBT card. For the purposes of this document, we will refer to these as CSC. All EBT cards must have a three-digit number for the CSC, printed or stamped onto the back of physical SNAP EBT cards, which must not be electronically stored on the card itself in any form (
7 CFR 274.8(b)(5)
).
(ii) The CSC must be input by the SNAP household when they conduct an internet SNAP transaction, thereby proving that the person conducting the transaction has possession of the actual/physical card.
(iii) SNAP internet retailers must ensure that their EBT systems are capable of requiring input of a card's CSC and verifying the content of the input along with verification of other transaction details. Retailers must not store the CSC in any form.
(6) Card Expiration Date
(i) EBT cards must utilize an expiration date (
7 CFR 274.8(b)(5)
). The card expiration date is specifically related to the physical card and does not refer to the expiration of client benefits. The expiration date must be set for a length of time that ensures the card must be replaced before degradation of electronic components in the EBT card which would affect the use of the card begins. The card expiration date is also an important fraud prevention strategy, as it relates to internet purchases, as it is another data point that households must input when making a purchase.
(ii) State SNAP agencies must establish an effective replacement procedure for expiring EBT cards in order to ensure that SNAP clients do not experience interruption to the continued use of their EBT cards.
(iii) States must not charge a fee for an EBT card that is being replaced due to expiration, or an EBT card being replaced due to a change in benefit delivery method (
e.g.,
a move to chip cards). States also must not count these card replacements toward the excessive replacements threshold as described in
7 CFR 274.6(b)(6)
.
(iv) See Section (t) on household training requirements regarding the card expiration date.
(q) SNAP Online EBT Processing
(1)
The Agricultural Act of 2014
directed FNA to implement a pilot to allow the use of SNAP benefits to purchase SNAP-eligible food from SNAP-authorized internet retailers. Today, SNAP online purchasing is available in every State. For households to make online purchases, the SNAP online shopping and payment process must be secure, private, easy to use, and provide similar support to that found for SNAP transactions in a physical “brick-and-mortar” retail store.
(2) EBT Processing Requirements for Internet Retailers
(i) Retailers that want to accept SNAP benefits for online purchases must apply to become a SNAP-authorized internet retailer. Such authorizations are separate from the authorization that brick-and-mortar stores must submit.
(ii) To be approved, retailers must already have an existing online eCommerce presence. In other words, they must have an online sales platform that allows customers to make online purchases. Retailers' online sales platform (
e.g.,
website, mobile app, etc.) must meet the requirements for SNAP online purchasing, including functionality for:
(A) Securely integrating online PIN-entry through a TPP's Application Programming Interface (API).
(B) Handling errors with appropriate codes.
(C) Processing SNAP payments and refunds.
(D) Processing variable and estimated item pricing (
e.g.,
buying items that are priced by weight, meaning that the final weight and cost may vary).
(E) Allowing only one SNAP EBT card to be saved to a household account.
(F) Ensuring only SNAP-eligible foods can be purchased with SNAP benefits.
(G) Allowing split-tender transactions.
(H) Collecting and transmitting the EBT card's CVV/CSC and expiration date when conducting an internet transaction.
(I) Preventing fraud either by not allowing balance inquiries or doing all of the following:
(1)
Remove the “guest checkout” option from its eCommerce platform.
(2)
Limit the number of balance inquiries a SNAP household can conduct within a specific time period. FNA recommends a maximum of two balance inquiries per hour.
(3)
Limit the number of times a SNAP household can change the EBT card they are using to make purchases within a specific time period.
(J) Ensuring that API information is secure and protected from unauthorized access. If a retailer has blocked balance inquiries from its website and balance inquiries are still occurring, it could mean that the retailer-side API connection to its secure online PIN solution may have been hacked.
(iii) SNAP-authorized internet retailers must be capable of conducting many of the same EBT transactions as other SNAP-authorized retailers: authorizations/denials, refunds, cancellations, and settlement.
(3) Internet Shopping Customer Fees
(i) The 2014 Farm Bill prohibits the use of SNAP benefits to pay for any fees for delivery, pickup, shipping, ordering, convenience, handling, or other charges related to a SNAP online purchase. When households conduct a SNAP internet purchase, retailers must provide clear notification that these fees cannot be paid with SNAP benefits. The notice must display as soon as the household selects SNAP EBT
(
printed page 66992)
as the payment method. The household must also be given the opportunity to terminate the purchase or select a different form of payment before the sale is finalized.
(4) Internet Purchases
(i) Purchases from SNAP-authorized internet retailers do not generate a printed receipt at the time of sale. However, internet retailers must still comply with regulations on receipts per
7 CFR 274.8(b)(7)
.
(ii) For all approved purchases, internet retailers must:
(A) Display a confirmation screen that appears immediately after the purchase, which the household can print, screenshot, or download, and
(B) Email or text an order confirmation within 24 hours of the purchase time.
(iii) In addition to the receipt requirements applicable to all SNAP-authorized retailers, internet retailers must also include the following items in the purchase confirmation screen and email/text confirmation:
(A) Retailer phone number (or other contact information),
(B) Pickup location or delivery address, and
(C) Actual or estimated delivery/pickup date (and time, if known)
(iv) Alternatively, instead of the emailed or text message order confirmation, the retailer may maintain a secure online order history for customers to easily see their orders.
(5) Internet Refunds
(i) Internet refund policies differ by retailer. Internet retailers can only process returns/refunds up to 90 days after an internet purchase. FNA does not require that PINs be present for SNAP internet refund. Retailers must have the capability of initiating a refund without a direct request or input from the SNAP household being refunded.
(ii) For internet refunds, retailers must issue an electronic notice to the customer within 24 hours, containing, at a minimum, the transaction date and time, retailer name, retailer phone number (or other contact information), pickup location or delivery address, actual or estimated delivery/pickup date (and time, if known), EBT program type (
e.g.,
SNAP, Summer EBT, or cash EBT), SNAP purchase amount, remaining EBT balance(s), and the truncated PAN (last four digits).
(iii) Instead of an electronic receipt for refunds processed after the initial purchase (
e.g.,
refunds for out-of-stock items), the retailer may choose to provide a paper refund receipt containing the above information with the order (
e.g.,
in the box with the delivered items). This may be combined with the final itemized order listing or on a separate paper receipt.
(iv) Shipping costs, including fees for returns, may not be paid for using SNAP benefits. The full value of any returned item purchased with SNAP benefits must be refunded back to the household's SNAP account. Internet retailers must cover return shipment costs themselves or ask the household to pay those costs with an alternate form of tender (
e.g.,
EBT cash, credit/debit card).
(v) Internet retailers must ensure that refunds for internet purchases are returned to the account associated with the internet retailer's FNA number rather than the brick-and-mortar retailer's FNA number, even if the return physically takes place at the brick-and mortar location.
(vi) Refunds for returned items or other customer-initiated events must be processed within two company business days.
(6) Denied Internet Transactions
(i) EBT host processors must ensure that internet transactions are properly received, processed, transmitted, and settled. Processors must ensure that internet transactions are denied in the following situations:
(A) Internet purchases from any internet retailer not authorized by FNA,
(B) PINless refunds from any internet retailer not authorized by FNA, and
(C) Purchases from an internet retailer that are being made from a POS device.
(ii) If an internet transaction is denied, the internet retailer must provide a reason for the denial (
i.e.,
a denial code). Specifically, the platform (website, app, etc.) must immediately provide the household with an onscreen explanation of the denial reason, so they have a chance to correct the issue. The most common reasons for denial are invalid card number, invalid PIN, and insufficient funds.
(iii) The customer must be offered the opportunity to perform the transaction again, select a different payment method, or opt out of the sale.
(iv) If a transaction is denied for insufficient funds, the household should be given the opportunity to perform the transaction for a lesser amount or select different tender. The website may opt to:
(A) Provide a message indicating to the client that they do not have sufficient funds to complete the transaction, but the balance does not need to be included in this error message display.
(B) Use the remaining SNAP account balance to pre-fill the amount entered for the new transaction attempt.
(C) Require the household to delete individual items from their purchase cart or move items to a non-SNAP cart for payment with another tender (
e.g.,
cash), until they reach a subtotal less than or equal to the remaining SNAP balance.
(7) Prepayment and Deliveries
(i) FNA regulations at
7 CFR 274.7(b)
prohibit retailers from accepting SNAP “prepayment” (
e.g.,
payment before an EBT card is presented to the retailer). This regulation is waived for internet retailers. However, internet retailers must comply with the following prepayment and delivery timeframe standards:
(A) Internet retailers must not allow households to use multiple delivery addresses for a single SNAP EBT transaction.
(B) Internet retailers are required to deliver and/or prepare all orders for pickup within seven calendar days, unless the household specifically selects a later delivery or pickup date.
(C) If a retailer allows split orders (
e.g.,
multiple separate deliveries for a single SNAP EBT purchase), all portions of the order must be received by the household within the mandatory timeframe.
(D) Prior to submitting the transaction for authorization, internet retailers must clearly explain the delivery process and timeframe to the household.
(E) Internet retailers that do not allow households to select their own delivery or pickup time must provide the estimated delivery/pickup date and allow the household to cancel the transaction before the sale is finalized.
(F) Retailers must not allow the use of EBT cards for standing-subscription orders (
e.g.,
automatic monthly food deliveries).
(G) If, by the fifth day after the transaction, it is clear the seven-day delivery/pickup limit will be exceeded, the retailer must notify the household of the new expected delivery/pickup date—by email, text, or phone—and offer the opportunity for an immediate and full refund instead.
(H) Refunds that result from overestimated weighed products, substitutions, or out-of-stock items must be made to the client immediately after fulfillment of the order.
(8) Payment Card Industry Compliance
(i) All SNAP-authorized internet retailers must be compliant with the Payment Card Industry (PCI) Data Security Standards. PCI standards address the secure encryption and handling of sensitive data, such as card numbers and PINs while “at rest” (
i.e.,
being stored temporarily or permanently). Before a retailer can be authorized to accept debit or credit transactions, they must be certified as PCI-compliant by their acquiring institution. This certification is performed annually and covers a wide spectrum of security and privacy issues. FNA requires that every SNAP-authorized internet retailer be PCI-certified and maintain that certification on an ongoing basis.
(ii) Because there is no single way to become PCI compliant, the payment security industry uses several best practices to safeguard sensitive data and customer privacy. The PCI Security Standards Council offers a variety of standards which can be used to achieve PCI compliance. Ultimately, the specific methods used by any given organization to achieve compliance will vary. Each organization must identify and document the methods they will use to achieve PCI compliance, and must continually upgrade and improve their methods.
(iii) Generally, best practices to achieve PCI compliance include:
(A) Tokenization (replacing sensitive data like card numbers with unique, random strings of digits to protect against data breaches during transactions).
(B) Device fingerprinting (comparing current hardware/software characteristics to a user's previous usage, including comparing their physical device, browser version, internet Protocol [IP]) address, app vs. browser usage, etc.).
(C) Use of secure sockets layer (SSL) technology or other strong firewall configurations.
(D) Minimum browser standards (requiring certain browser versions, 128-binary digit (bit) encryption, etc.).
(E) Required use of login IDs and passwords for internal and external access to website.
(
printed page 66993)
(F) Strong policies for ID and password format and handling of forgotten IDs and passwords.
(G) Establishing system user roles that restrict users from updating or extracting PII and card data, based on whether they legitimately need to access such information.
(H) Use of sitekeys or other customer site authentication (a security system that verifies both the user and the website itself, and displays a unique image or phrase when users attempt to log in).
(I) Use of commercial security and encryption products for both data in transit and at rest.
(J) Trust seal certification (a visual stamp or badge displayed on a website or data repository to indicate that it has undergone security and verification checks by a trusted third party, demonstrating a commitment to data protection and compliance).
(K) Stringent information security policies for all company and contractor personnel.
(L) Regular use and update of anti-virus software or programs.
(M) Restricted physical access to personal data stored on the system.
(9) Card Must Be Present
(i) In regular brick-and-mortar transactions, the EBT card must always be present when a household performs a transaction, whether the card is swiped, tapped, inserted, key-entered, or processed by manual voucher. However, it is not possible for internet retailers to determine if households have their EBT card in hand when they enter the card number to make an internet purchase. Therefore, FNA automatically waives the “card must be present” requirement for all approved internet retailers. The following conditions apply:
(A) Internet retailer payment systems must always code internet transaction messages as “card not present” transactions.
(B) The internet retailer must notify FNA whenever significant changes are made to its online shopping/payment platform policies and practices regarding refunds, customer complaints, privacy, or security. Retailers must provide FNA with a copy of or link to the revised information.
(10) Equal Treatment
(i) FNA regulations at
7 CFR 274.7(f)
and
278.2(b)
require that SNAP-authorized retailers treat SNAP households equally to other customers. This is generally referred to as the equal treatment rule. In other words, retailers may generally not treat SNAP households differently (either positively or negatively), in any way.
(ii) There are some exceptions to the equal treatment rule: First, retailers must never charge sales tax on eligible foods purchased with SNAP benefits. There are some additional exceptions that automatically apply to SNAP-authorized internet retailers:
(A) Internet retailers may offer to waive or discount delivery and in-store pickup fees for SNAP households.
(B) Internet retailers may offer to waive or discount fees in their membership or discount clubs for SNAP households.
(r) Mobile Payments
(1) A digital wallet (or electronic wallet) is a software-based system or an application that runs on any connected device. It stores your payment information and passwords of numerous payment methods and websites. Digital wallets run primarily on smartphones, but may be accessible from a computer—mobile wallets, which are a subset, are primarily used on mobile devices.
(2) Mobile payments require the use of a Token Service Provider (TSP) that manages and issues payment tokens, which are unique identifiers that replace the PAN with a Device Primary Account number (DPAN) which is a token that is stored on the device after the card is provisioned (
i.e.,
added, saved, or stored) to the wallet.
(3) Mobile payments work using similar technology as “contactless” or “tap” cards (
i.e.,
NFC-enabled chip cards). The same AID will be used for chip cards and mobile payments.
(4) Adding a Card
(i) When a card is added to Wallet, a digital representation (token) of that card is created and linked to a single device. Tokenization masks the underlying card number, helping to protect the cardholder from data breaches and criminals trying to steal benefits.
(ii) The wallet provider performs cardholder verification in conjunction with the EBT host processor, allowing the card issuer to verify that the individual provisioning the card matches the identity of cardholder/household before a card can be added to the wallet. This may be through the use of the processor's client portal or other means.
(s) EBT System Project Implementation
(1) The implementation of new State EBT systems and updates/modifications to existing EBT systems require thorough testing by States prior to implementation (
i.e.,
“go-live”). As part of this testing, each State must successfully pass a Federal Acceptance Test with FNA prior to implementation, in accordance with FNA policy. Federal Acceptance Testing is required for changes caused by updates to the X9.58 standards; implementation of new programs, projects, or pilots; and the addition of significant new features or tools for the State or households. FNA will decide the level of its involvement in system testing based by conducting a risk assessment. When there is minimal risk—for example, there is no host processor or platform change and no major changes in functionality—FNA oversight of testing is likely not required.
(2) User Acceptance Testing (UAT) is the testing performed by the State (
i.e.,
the system user). Testing may take several weeks. Typically, States require the EBT contractor to provide them with test equipment (POS terminals) and software (access to a test environment for the administrative terminal and POS simulator), sufficient for performing preliminary testing prior to a UAT. This section discusses UAT specifically as it relates to SNAP EBT.
(3) System changes that require User Acceptance Testing (UAT) include:
(i) State's initial implementation of EBT
(ii) Change in a State's contracted EBT host processor (database conversions)
(iii) Transition to EBT chip cards
(iv) Nutrition incentive program implementation
(v) Mobile Payment Pilot implementation
(vi) Any modifications to the system due to updates to the X9.58 standards; implementation of new programs, projects, or pilots; and the addition of new features or tools for the State or households.
(4) UAT must include end-to-end testing, conducted by the SNAP State Agency, in conjunction with their EBT host processor and FNA, in order to ensure that system changes work as expected throughout every component of the EBT system.
(i) The processor is responsible for conducting preliminary performance testing to simulate large transaction volumes, to determine how the system responds to various conditions, to gauge response time, and identify processing errors.
(ii) The remaining functional areas are tested by the State, processor, and FNA during the UAT.
(iii) UAT can be hosted by the State or the processor.
(iv) FNA must be involved with UAT planning and attend all testing, either in person or virtually. Additionally, FNA may have a technical assistance contractor participate in the UAT as well.
(v) Before the UAT:
(A) The State should provide the test plan and test scripts for review and comment before finalized. These documents should be made available to FNA at least 60 days before testing begins.
(B) FNA will also provide suggested “what-if” tests to the State before the UAT.
(5) Conversion is the movement of data from an old EBT system to a new EBT system. Most typically, it is necessary when a State awards an EBT contract to a processor that is not their incumbent. If the State selects a new EBT contractor, the transition process is very complex, because it usually involves both database and retailer conversion. Database conversion involves the movement of data from one system or platform to another and implementation of a new administrative terminal system. Retailer conversion involves the State's new EBT host processor issuing new EBT-only POS equipment to retailers who previously received EBT-only POS equipment from the State's outgoing EBT host processor, since that existing equipment connects directly to the outgoing EBT host processor.
(i) The incumbent processor must cooperate fully with the State and the new processor.
(ii) During conversions (which generally take months to complete), States must continue using their outgoing processors' system while the incoming processor is building a new EBT system.
(A) As discussed in the sub-section above, the State, new processor, and FNA will conduct UAT prior to implementing the new EBT system.
(iii) States are responsible for communication regarding EBT Database Conversion to households and retailers. FNA will often assist the State in sending out retailer notifications.
(iv) The final steps in a conversion are typically conducted during a weekend (conversion weekend).
(v) During conversion weekend (and in the days leading up to that weekend),
(
printed page 66994)
participants follow an hour-by-hour schedule of events.
(A) The incoming processor is responsible for creating that schedule, with input from the State, incumbent contractor, and FNA. Preparation of this schedule typically takes several weeks, so incoming processors must plan accordingly.
(B) The completion of tasks in the hour-by-hour schedule typically begins several days before conversion weekend and runs through the Monday after conversion weekend.
(C) The conversion weekend schedule must include all tasks required for the conversion and their estimated timeframes that were based on the mock runs. The schedule must also include all conversion conference call and the required attendees for those calls. The status of each task on the schedules is updated as conversion weekend progresses, which informs participants about next steps to be taken.
(t) Household Training on EBT
(1) States are required to educate SNAP households on SNAP participation including use of the EBT system (including all elements listed in
7 CFR 274.2(e)
). Household training must be incorporated into the SNAP household certification process. States may choose various methods to convey this required information, as long as households receive training on all required. States should design their household education to ensure that SNAP households are not overwhelmed with information that prevents them from absorbing the most important knowledge.
(2) States may use a variety of training materials including:
(i) EBT card brochure
(ii) SNAP policy manual
(iii) Information available on the State agency's web portal
(iv) Information available through the State agency's mobile application
(v) Training videos posted online or displayed in State field offices
(vi) Verbal information provided during initial interview or re-certification
(A) If this method is used as a household training method, it should be documented in the State agency's eligibility system.
(3) The following sub-sections provide more detailed information on two important topic for elements household training.
(4) Household Training: EBT Theft Prevention
(i) States must provide household training that informs SNAP households about EBT card security best practices that will reduce their chances of being a victim of benefit theft.
(ii) FNA recommends that household training include the following elements:
(A) The appropriate utilization and security of the EBT card's PIN. Specifically:
(1)
Households should change their PIN frequently (at least monthly), ahead of benefit issuance dates.
(2)
Households should be informed that they are not allowed to choose simple or easy-to-guess PINS (
e.g.,
1111, 1234).
(3)
Households should not share their PIN or card number with anyone outside your household.
(4)
Households should cover the keypad when they enter their PIN on a machine.
(5)
Cardholders should avoid writing their PIN on their card or anywhere that could easily be found.
(B) Common methods of EBT theft and how to avoid them. States should keep this training material up to date as fraud methods change.
(1)
This training should include education on card skimming and phishing schemes. States should inform households that neither the State nor EBT processors will ever call or text to ask for their PIN or card number.
(C) Households should check their EBT account regularly for unauthorized charges.
(D) States must educate households on how to report unauthorized use of their EBT card or unauthorized use on their EBT account, including suspected fraudulent activity.
(1)
If a household suspects that their account has been compromised by EBT theft, they should change their PIN, contact the State, and request a replacement card.
(E) States must inform households about all EBT theft prevention tools available to them. This includes options to freeze their account, block out-of-State or internet transactions, set up purchase and PIN change alerts, or set up transaction limits.
(F) States must educate households on the benefit of freezing and unfreezing their EBT card to prevent benefit theft, and inform them that benefits can still be loaded to an account that is frozen.
(G) States must inform households about any EBT theft prevention features that the State has enabled by default (
e.g.,
default block on out-of-State or internet transactions).
(H) States should educate households about transaction and return limits. This should include training on any limits the State puts in place by default and any options for the household to enable or disable for themselves.
(I) If a household's EBT card includes a chip, the household should always attempt to tap or insert their card and should only swipe their card if the retailer's POS device is not capable of conducting a chip transaction. Households should minimize their risk of EBT theft by choosing retailers that can process more secure payment methods.
(J) Household should inspect ATMs, POS terminals, and other card readers before using. Look for anything loose, crooked, damaged, or scratched. Do not use any card reader if you notice anything unusual.
(1)
Pull at the edges of the keypad before entering your PIN. Then, cover the keypad as fully as possible when you enter your PIN to prevent cameras from recording your entry. Keep in mind that a pinhole camera may be present anywhere on or around the terminal.
(2)
Households that access TANF benefits via ATM should use ATMs in a well-lit, indoor location whenever possible. These may still be compromised but are less vulnerable targets.
(3)
Be especially alert for skimming devices in tourist areas, since these are popular targets.
(5) Household Training: Expiration Dates on EBT Cards
(i) As States implement chip card technology, they must add an expiration date to the new EBT cards. States must educate household on the difference between the expiration date on the card, timelines for benefit expungement, and certification or recertification end dates.
(ii) States must ensure that household training includes the following elements:
(A) The expiration date on the new EBT cards is a new feature, indicating when the card will need to be replaced.
(B) Card expiration date has no relation to benefit expungement.
(C) Card expiration date has no relation to certification or recertification end date.
(1)
When a household receives an EBT chip card, this does not mean they do not have to certify or recertify for benefits upon receipt of the card.
(D) State agencies should work with their EBT host processor to update the card sleeve mailed with the EBT card. The new card sleeve should explain:
(1)
The expiration date on the card and where it is located.
(2)
The CVV/CSC digits on the card and where it is located.
(3)
Any additional new items listed on the card.
Definitions
For the purposes of this appendix, the following additional terms and definitions apply.
Acquirer:
A financial institution (or the agent of a financial institution) that facilitates the authorization of SNAP transactions by acquiring transaction-related data from SNAP-authorized retailers and transmitting that data to a Third-Party Processor for further routing. An acquirer may only need to contract with a single TPP, as the TPP would handle subsequent routing to gateways and EBT host processors.
Adjustment:
A change to the balance of a household's SNAP benefit account, implemented by a SNAP State agency and/or by their contracted EBT host processor in response to an incorrect account balance caused by a system error during the redemption process. Adjustments may increase the balance of a SNAP account (“credit adjustment”) or decrease the balance of an account (“debit adjustment”).
Algorithmic Attacks:
Attacks that use bots, artificial intelligence (AI), or similar automated electronic means to exploit internet and IVR vulnerabilities. For example, some criminals use algorithmic attacks to conduct a high number of rapid and repeated balance inquiries to steal key card information.
Application ID (AID):
The application identifier (AID) encoded in the chip indicates to the POS device what type of card is being used. POS devices are also coded to accept specific AIDs. For a chip card transaction to be successful, the card and the device need matching AIDs, meaning that all POS devices must be updated with the new EBT chip AID in order to process EBT chip card transactions.
The AID is composed of two parts, the registered application provider identifier (RID) and the proprietary application identifier extension (PIX). EBT chip cards will include the unique AID
(
printed page 66995)
A0000000044542. The unique AID will allow POS terminals to support SNAP processing rules (
e.g.,
PIN entry required, fallback rules) via standard terminal action codes (TACs).
Application Programming Interface (API):
A set of rules or protocols that enable software applications to communicate with each other to exchange data, features, and functionality.
Automated Clearinghouse (ACH):
A financial network that is part of the Federal Reserve banking system and is used to process electronic funds transfers. Funds are credited to the receiving financial institution on the morning of the next business day after submission of the ACH file; the ACH does not operate on weekends or Federal holidays. The ACH network is used by the EBT processor to disburse credits for both food and cash programs from their own bank accounts to the various financial institutions holding the retailer and TPP bank accounts. The EBT processor/State may also request that funds be transferred between ASAP and their disbursement account through the ACH network. The EBT processor may hold its disbursement accounts at different banks for different States. Only financial institutions may submit ACH files to the FRM. Therefore, EBT processors must contract with a concentrator bank for this service. The concentrator bank may or may not be the same bank which holds the EBT processor's disbursement account.
Balance Inquiries:
When a household checks the amount of benefits in its SNAP account. There are four types: In-person, via brick-and-mortar retailers; internet, via internet retailers; internet, via each State's cardholder portal/mobile app, and; Phone, via EBT host processors' IVR systems.
Brick-and-Mortar:
In the context of SNAP retailers, this means a physical retailer (as opposed to an internet retailer).
Card Cloning:
After key card information has been stolen through methods like skimming or phishing, criminals can use equipment to copy stolen card information onto blank magnetic stripe cards. Criminals then use cloned cards to steal SNAP benefits.
Card Issuer:
Financial institution or agency (or their agent) that issues the card to the cardholder.
Card Skimming:
A method of electronically stealing SNAP EBT benefits. Card skimming occurs when a criminal places a card reading device on a retailer's POS equipment. The reader collects key card information—such as the PAN and PIN—when a client swipes or inserts their card during a transaction. Criminals then use this card information to steal a household's benefits.
Card Verification Value
(CVV)/Card Security Code (CSC): A three-digit number that is printed or stamped onto the back of all SNAP EBT cards, and is not electronically stored on the card, and is a method of mitigating the electronic theft of SNAP EBT benefits. Specifically, when a SNAP household is conducting an internet transaction, they are required to enter the CVV/CSC to complete their transaction, thereby confirming that they are in possession of the physical/actual SNAP card.
Cash Benefit/Cash Benefit Program:
A Federal or State government benefit program that provides households with benefits on an EBT card in the form of cash. Unlike SNAP benefits, cash benefits can be used to purchase items other than SNAP eligible food. Examples of cash benefit programs include Temporary Assistance for Needy Families and Aid for the Aged, Blind, and Disabled.
CAV (Card Authentication Value):
A security component used by card associations to authenticate the validity of cards during transactions. It is embedded in the magnetic stripe of the card.
Chip Cards:
Payment cards that have a computer chip embedded in them. Such chips provide security features that are superior to payment cards which only utilize a magnetic stripe. A chip card can be insert-only or dual interface. A dual interface card can be inserted (a.k.a., “contact” payment) or “tapped” (a.k.a., contactless payment) at a POS device. The contactless payment technology in an EBT chip card utilizes Near Field Communication (NFC). NFC is a protocol that enables wireless communication over short distances (a few inches) between payment cards and POS devices. Chip cards that are capable of conducting NFC contactless transactions are generally considered more secure than chip cards which must be inserted into POS devices.
Clearing:
Clearing is when retailers send information to the SNAP State agency or the EBT host processor to request payment. This can be done directly by the retailer or through their contracted TPP or acquirer.
Database Conversion:
The movement of data from an old EBT system or platform to a new EBT system or platform, and implementation of a new administrative terminal system.
Electronic Benefit Theft:
This occurs when criminals use electronic methods to steal a SNAP household's benefits.
EBT Transaction Message:
EBT transaction messages are comprised of the electronic data needed to process a transaction as defined by the ANSI X9.58 specification. Transaction messages flow from the retailer's POS to a TPP, (possibly) to a Gateway, and finally to the EBT host processor.
EBT Transaction Response Code:
A sequence of letters and numbers that indicate whether a transaction was approved or denied. EBT transaction response codes display on a retailer's POS device after an attempted EBT transaction.
Empty Candidate List (ECL) Fallback:
Most retailers currently accept other NFC-enabled chip cards (
e.g.,
credit and debit cards issued by a bank or credit union), but do not yet support the new AID for SNAP EBT chip cards. In such cases, a SNAP household will try to use a SNAP chip card in the POS device, and the device will recognize that the card has a chip but will not recognize the SNAP AID. When this occurs, the POS device must allow the card to proceed with a magnetic stripe transaction. The technical name for this process is Empty Candidate List (ECL) fallback.
End-to-End Testing:
A part of the UAT process, conducted by the SNAP State Agency, in conjunction with their EBT host processor and FNA, in order to ensure that system changes work as expected throughout every component of the EBT system.
Equal Treatment:
FNA regulations at
7 CFR 274.7(f)
and
278.2(b)
require that SNAP-authorized retailers treat SNAP households equally to other customers. This is generally referred to as the equal treatment rule. In other words, retailers may generally not treat SNAP households differently (either positively or negatively), in any way.
Federal Acceptance Test:
The implementation of new State EBT systems and updates/modifications to existing EBT systems requires thorough testing by States prior to implementation (
i.e.,
“go-live”). As part of this testing, each State must successfully pass a Federal Acceptance Test with FNA prior to implementation, in accordance with FNA policy.
Federal Reserve Bank (FRB
): The central bank of the United States, responsible for implementing and adjusting monetary policy, overseeing the largest U.S. banks, and providing financial services to the U.S. government. In the context of SNAP, FRB operates the ACH, which is a crucial component in reimbursing SNAP-authorized retailers, EBT processors, and TPPs for redeemed SNAP benefits.
Gateway:
An entity that routes EBT transactions from TPPs to an EBT host processor based on the BIN of the EBT card. A Gateway is a combination of hardware and software which allows transactions to be supported between and among network switches, TPPs, EBT processors, and/or retailers driving their own terminals.
Inactive Status:
An EBT card that is not functional upon receipt. To be made functional, the household has to take additional steps. Most often, those steps involve interacting with the State's processor IVR, and inputting a password, PIN, etc.
Interactive Voice Response (IVR):
An automated phone system—operated by a State's EBT processor or their contracted entity—that allows SNAP households to navigate a menu of options using their voice or by pressing numbers to access information, complete tasks (
e.g.,
change their PIN), or be routed to other phone numbers.
Issuer Identification Number:
A 6-8 digit number that identifies the bank, financial institution, or other entity that issued a card.
Key-Entered Transaction:
A transaction when the card number is manually entered into a POS device, as opposed to tapping, inserting, or swiping an EBT card. Typically, key-entered transactions occur when a POS device cannot read an EBT card.
Letter of Credit:
The document by which an official of FNA authorizes a State agency to draw funds from the United States Treasury to reimburse SNAP-authorized retailers for SNAP benefits they redeem (through their TPPs, EBT processors, etc.).
Near Field Communication (NFC):
Protocols that enable wireless communication over short distances (a few inches) between payment cards and POS devices, which allows the use of contactless payments (also called “tap-to-pay”).
(
printed page 66996)
Packed Binary Data:
PIN data must be encrypted and represented as packed binary data, (
i.e.,
eight binary bits shall be represented as 16 hexadecimal characters). The PIN must be formatted into a PIN block consistent with the most current version of standards at ANSI X9.8/ISO 9564-1 before encryption.
Payment Card Industry (PCI) Data Security Standards:
Security standards that address the secure encryption and handling of sensitive data, such as card numbers and PINs while “at rest” (
i.e.,
being stored temporarily or permanently). Before a retailer can be authorized to accept debit or credit transactions, they must be certified as PCI-compliant by their acquiring institution.
Phishing Scams:
Scams on text, email, phone, and social media to deceive households into providing key EBT card information.
Point-of-Sale Service Provider:
A financial institution (or its agent) that provides retailers with the equipment and technology needed to process SNAP benefits.
Processing Code:
A series of digits used to describe the effect of a transaction on the SNAP household's account and identify the accounts affected (
e.g.,
SNAP benefits, cash benefits, or regular cash).
Reconciliation:
The process States must follow to account for all SNAP issuance and transaction activity, in accordance with
7 CFR 274.4(a)
. This is done to ensure accuracy and consistency, and to identify and rectify any discrepancies.
Refund/Return:
In this context, a transaction where SNAP benefits are returned to a household's account. Most often (but not always), these are the result of an error at the POS device being corrected on-the-spot or the customer returning a purchased item to the store.
Service Code:
A code encoded in EBT cards that communicates information to the POS terminal (including informing the POS terminal whether the card has a magnetic stripe or a chip).
Settlement:
When a State or processor creates and transmits a payment to a retailer's bank for approved, cleared SNAP transactions.
Settlement Day:
The day when a SNAP-authorized retailer gets reimbursed for an approved, cleared SNAP transaction.
Settlement Flow:
The transfer of funds through different accounts held by different parties involved in processing SNAP transactions that ultimately reimburse a SNAP-authorized retailer for a SNAP transaction.
SNAP Online Purchasing:
The Agricultural Act of 2014 directed FNA to implement a pilot to allow the use of SNAP benefits to purchase SNAP-eligible food from SNAP-authorized internet retailers. SNAP online shopping and payment processes must be secure, private, easy-to-use, and provide similar support to that found for SNAP transactions in a physical “brick-and-mortar” retail store.
SNAP-Authorized Internet Retailer (also referred to as “internet retailer”):
A store that accepts SNAP benefits in exchange for SNAP-eligible foods on their website. A separate FNA authorization is required in order to participate in SNAP online purchasing.
SNAP Data:
Any data generated as a result of a household's or retailers' participation in SNAP and application to participate in SNAP.
SNAP Household:
The person(s) who apply and are approved to participate in SNAP, receive SNAP benefits, and use a SNAP EBT card to purchase SNAP-eligible food.
SNAP State Agency:
The governmental agency that administers SNAP at the State and local level.
Split Tender Transaction:
When a household chooses to pay for its purchase of SNAP-eligible food partly with SNAP benefits and partly through some other means (cash, credit card, etc.).
Statused:
An EBT card is referred to as “statused” if it is not active (
e.g.,
it has been cancelled, de-activated, or reported as lost, stolen, or damaged).
Store-and-Forward:
The process where a retailer electronically stores a SNAP EBT transaction with an encrypted PIN when an EBT system is not functioning or is otherwise inaccessible (
i.e.,
during a power outage, natural disaster, etc.). The retailer then forwards the transaction for processing later, when EBT system functionality has been restored.
System Error:
An error resulting from a malfunction at any point in the SNAP benefit redemption process, such as an error made by a retailer's host computer or POS device, a TPP, the Gateway, or processor.
Third-Party Processors (TPPs):
Financial institution that receives EBT transactions from SNAP-authorized retailers and acquirers and subsequently transmits those transactions to an EBT gateway for further routing or directly to an EBT host processor for transaction approval. SNAP State agencies and their contracted EBT host processors must allow retailers to use EBT services provided by TPPs and acquirers, and must provide interface specifications and certification standards, in order for the TPPs to participate in the EBT system per
7 CFR 274.3(d)
. The TPPs have contractual agreements to connect to all existing EBT processor systems, either directly or via gateways, in order to facilitate the approval/denial transactions anywhere SNAP is operated.
TPPs typically provide EBT services and POS equipment directly to larger retailers (such as those with many locations) who may utilize other non-EBT services that the TPPs offer. Smaller retailers who are unable to contract directly with a TPP instead may rely on an acquirer to provide EBT services and POS equipment.
Token:
A digital representation of sensitive data (such as a PAN on an EBT card), most often created and linked to a specific device. Tokens replace sensitive data with unique, random strings of digits to protect against data breaches during transactions.
Token Service Provider (TSP):
Entity that manages and issues payment tokens.
Transaction Message Response:
Upon receipt of an EBT transaction message, the processor reviews the information contained in the message to ensure the transaction is valid. The processor will then generate a transaction message response to send back to the retailer's POS device, approving or denying the transaction and (if applicable) providing the denial reason and SNAP account balance information. The processor sends FNA the transaction data, per
7 CFR 274.4(b)(2)
and the specifications as outlined in the State's contract.
User Acceptance Testing (UAT):
Testing of new State EBT systems and updates/modifications to existing EBT systems performed by the State (
i.e.,
the system user).
Voucher Clear:
The process where a POS transaction is completed by obtaining a voice authorization and manually processing a pre-numbered voucher that is later forwarded to the card issuer electronically.
Void:
Void or cancellation transactions are used when an incorrect purchase amount is processed through a retailer's POS device. The void/cancellation must be done immediately after the purchase transaction and on the same POS device.
(
printed page 66997)

AGENCY:
Securities and Exchange Commission.
ACTION:
Publication of list of rules scheduled for review.
SUMMARY:
The Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission”) is publishing a list of rules to be reviewed pursuant to section 610 of the Regulatory Flexibility Act. The list is published to provide the public with notice that these rules are scheduled for review by the agency and to invite public comment on whether the rules should be continued without change, or should be amended or rescinded to minimize any significant economic impact of the rules upon a substantial number of small entities.
DATES:
This release was published in the
Federal Register
on October 23, 2026. Comments should be submitted by November 23, 2026.
(
printed page 66796)
ADDRESSES:
Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
https://www.sec.gov/​comments/​s7-2026-37/​list-rules-be-reviewed-pursuant-regulatory-flexibility-act
); or
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
.
Please include File Number S7-2026-37 on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments to Vanessa A. Countryman, Secretary, U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
All submissions should refer to File Number S7-2026-37. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method of submission. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules-regulations/​public-comments/​s7-2026-37
). Do not include personally identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. The Commission may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Sandra Sojka, General Attorney, Office of the General Counsel, 202-551-4928.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The Regulatory Flexibility Act (“RFA”), codified at
5 U.S.C. 601
through
612
, requires an agency to review its rules that have a significant economic impact upon a substantial number of small entities within 10 years of the publication of such rules as final rules.
5 U.S.C. 610(a)
. The purpose of the review is “to determine whether such rules should be continued without change, or should be amended or rescinded . . . to minimize any significant economic impact of the rules upon a substantial number of such small entities.”
5 U.S.C. 610(a)
. The RFA sets forth specific considerations that must be addressed in the review of each rule:
The continued need for the rule;
The nature of complaints or comments received concerning the rule from the public;
The complexity of the rule;
The extent to which the rule overlaps, duplicates or conflicts with other Federal rules, and, to the extent feasible, with state and local governmental rules; and
The length of time since the rule has been evaluated or the degree to which technology, economic conditions, or other factors have changed in the area affected by the rule.
5 U.S.C. 610(b)
.
The list below includes rules adopted in 2017 that may have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities (but excludes rules that have been substantially changed since adoption, rules that are minor amendments to previously adopted rules, and rules that are ministerial, procedural, or technical in nature). Where the Commission has previously made a determination of a rule's impact on small businesses, the determination is noted on the list.
The Commission particularly solicits public comment on whether the rules in the release listed below affect small businesses in new or different ways than when first adopted. The release listed below is scheduled for review by staff of the Commission.
