AGENCY:
United States Department of Agriculture (USDA).
ACTION:
Notice to solicit nominations for membership.
SUMMARY:
Through this notice, the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) is soliciting nominations for eight (8) vacancies on the USDA Tribal Advisory Committee (“the Committee”).
DATES:
Nominations must be submitted via email December 8, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Please submit nominations and resumes for recognition and appointment by the Chair or Ranking Member of the House Committee on Agriculture, the Senate Committee on Indian Affairs, and the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry (official Appointors) through Josiah Griffin, Designated Federal Officer, at
Tribal.Relations@usda.gov
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Inquiries may be sent to, Josiah Griffin, Designated Federal Officer, USDA, Office of Tribal Relations, at
Tribal.Relations@usda.gov
or by phone at (202) 205-2249.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Committee consists of eleven (11) members serving staggered terms. The balance of these appointments by the Chair and Ranking Members of the House Committee on Agriculture, the Senate Committee on Indian Affairs, and the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry will be managed according to the
(
printed page 66831)
Committee's statutory authority (7 U.S. Code § 6921(b)(3)(a)). Members may only serve on one USDA advisory committee at a time. Pursuant to the Committee's statutory authorization, only Indian tribes as defined by
25 U.S.C. 5304
, Tribal organizations as defined by
25 U.S.C. 5304
, or national or regional organizations with expertise in issues relating to the Committee may nominate candidates for consideration.
Candidates and alternates selected for potential appointments will undergo a USDA background check. Complete nomination packages will include a nomination letter signed by a representative authorized to make decisions on behalf of the nominating entity, the nominee's resume, and a USDA Advisory Committee Membership Background Information form completed by the nominee (available online at
https://www.usda.gov/​sites/​default/​files/​documents/​ad-755-advisory-committee-commodity-board-background-information.pdf
). Resumes or curriculum vitae must be limited to five one-sided pages and should include a summary of the following information: current and past organization affiliations; areas of expertise; education; career positions held; any other notable positions held; and geographic locations and regions served. Additional letters of endorsement are optional.
About the Committee:
The Tribal Advisory Committee is established pursuant to section 12303 of the Agriculture Improvement Act of 2018 (
Pub. L. 115-334
) to advise the Secretary of Agriculture on matters relating to Tribal and Indian Affairs. the TAC defines “Indian affairs” similarly to the SCIA jurisdiction (as defined in Section 25 of S. Res. 71, 103rd Congress, 1st Session), which includes but is not limited to all matters pertaining to American Indian, Native Hawaiian, and Alaska Native peoples. The Committee Chairperson and Vice Chairperson shall be elected by the Committee from among its members.
Eligible Nominators:
Nominations may only be submitted by signatories authorized to represent an Indian tribe as defined by
25 U.S.C. 5304
, a Tribal organization as defined by
25 U.S.C. 5304
, or a national or regional organization with expertise in issues relating to the above duties of the Committee. These organizations include but are not limited to intertribal consortia, national or regional tribal serving organizations, land-grant institutions, and credit institutions such as Native Community Development Financial Institutions. Nominees are not required to represent the nominating entity.
Nomination Packages:
Nominating entities must submit a complete nomination package for full consideration. Documents should be typed and must include the below elements. Additional letters of endorsement are optional.
1. Nomination letters. Nomination letters must include a brief summary, no more than two pages, explaining the nominee's qualifications to serve on the Tribal Advisory Committee and addressing the membership composition and criteria described above. The signatory of these letters must be authorized to represent the nominating entity.
2. Resume. A resume providing the nominee's background, experience, and educational qualifications.
3. Background Information Form. A completed Advisory Committee or Research and Promotion Background Information form (AD-755) signed by the nominee available online at
https://www.usda.gov/​sites/​default/​files/​documents/​ad-755.pdf
.
Meeting Frequency:
The Committee is required by law to meet at least twice in-person per year and is expected to convene quarterly, with meetings hosted virtually in between in-person meetings. All Committee meetings will be announced in the
Federal Register
.
Appointment Terms and Process:
All eligible nominating entities must submit a new nomination package to be considered for appointment. Official Appointors will each have access to this same
Federal Register
nomination process and pool of nominations. Pursuant to the Federal Advisory Committee Act (
5 U.S.C. 10
), notice is hereby given that the Chair and Ranking Member of the House Committee on Agriculture will each appoint two (2) members respectively; the Chair and Ranking Member of the Senate Committee on Indian Affairs will each appoint one (1) member respectively; and the Chair and Ranking Member of the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry will each appoint one (1) member respectively. These members will serve for three (3) years starting their date of appointment.
Membership Balance:
USDA encourages nominees reflect the broad slate of what makes American agriculture great including but not limited to farmers/ranchers, food businesses, subsistence foragers, foresters, agriculture educators and land-grant faculty/staff, extension and technical assistance specialists, agriculture financiers (banks and credit institutions), Tribal leaders and Tribal government officials, and agriculture/forestry law experts.
Equal opportunity practices, in accordance with USDA policies, will be followed in all membership appointments to the Committee.
In accordance with Federal civil rights law and U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) civil rights regulations and policies, the USDA, its Agencies, offices, and employees, and institutions participating in or administering USDA programs are prohibited from discriminating based on race, color, national origin, religion, sex, disability, age, marital status, family/parental status, income derived from a public assistance program, political beliefs, or reprisal or retaliation for prior civil rights activity, in any program or activity conducted or funded by USDA (not all bases apply to all programs). Remedies and complaint filing deadlines vary by program or incident.
Persons with disabilities who require alternative means for communication of program information (Braille, large print, audiotape, etc.) should contact USDA's TARGET center at (202) 720-2600 (voice and TDD) or the State or local Agency that administers the program.

Forest Service
AGENCY:
Forest Service, Agriculture.
ACTION:
Notice of opportunity to object.
SUMMARY:
The Forest Service, U.S. Department of Agriculture, is amending the 1989 Okanogan National Forest Land Management Plan and 1990 Wenatchee National Forest Land Management Plan (forest plans). The Forest Service has prepared a Final Environmental Impact Statement (FEIS) for the Planning and Management of Domestic Sheep and Goat Grazing Within the Range of Bighorn Sheep Project and a draft Record of Decision that includes a programmatic plan amendment to both forest plans. The plan amendment would add two standards for domestic sheep and goat grazing activities on the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest to both
(
printed page 66832)
forest plans. This notice is to inform the public that the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest is initiating a 60-day period where individuals or entities with specific concerns about the amendments to the forest plans may file objections for Forest Service review prior to the approval of the amendments.
DATES:
The publication date of the legal notice in the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest newspaper of record,
The Wenatchee World,
initiates the 60-day objection filing period and is the exclusive means for calculating the time to file an objection (
36 CFR 219.52(c)(5)
). An electronic copy of the legal notice with the publication date, as well as the FEIS, draft record of decision (ROD), and supporting documentation, will be posted at
https://www.fs.usda.gov/​r06/​okanogan-wenatchee/​projects/​301825
.
ADDRESSES:
Written objections, including attachments, may be submitted via regular mail, private carrier, or hand delivery to: USDA Forest Service, Pacific Northwest Region, Attn: Objection Reviewing Officer/1570 Objections, 1220 SW 3rd Ave., Portland, OR 97204. The office business hours for those submitting hand-delivered objections are: 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Monday through Friday, excluding federal holidays. Objections may also be submitted electronically by 11:59 p.m. Pacific Daylight Time on December 22, 2026 at
https://cara.fs2c.usda.gov/​Public/​CommentInput?​project=​NP-4727
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
David Topolewski, Forest Wildlife Program Manager,
SM.FS.OKW_SheepEIS@usda.gov
,
509-664-9376. Individuals who use telecommunication devices for the hearing-impaired may call 711 to reach the Telecommunications Relay Service, 24 hours a day, every day of the year, including holidays.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The Enterprise Land Management System identification number for the project and the associated amendments is 301825.
The amendments would add standards BHS 1 and 2 to both the Okanogan and Wenatchee Forest Plans. BHS 1 requires maintaining effective separation of domestic sheep and bighorn sheep on active grazing allotments to reduce the likelihood and risk of disease transmission. BHS 2 requires utilizing a risk assessment to inform whether and how domestic sheep and goat allotments are stocked or not, according to risk of disease transmission between domestic livestock, primarily domestic sheep and goats, and bighorn sheep.
The decision to approve the programmatic amendments to the 1989 Okanogan National Forest Land Management Plan and 1990 Wenatchee National Forest Land Management Plan in association with the Planning and Management of Domestic Sheep and Goat Grazing Within the Range of Bighorn Sheep Project will be subject to the objection process identified in
36 CFR part 219, subpart B
(§§  219.50 through 219.62). Per
36 CFR 219.53
, only individuals and entities who have submitted substantive formal comments related to the plan amendment during the opportunities for public comment may file an objection. Objections must be based on previously submitted substantive formal comments attributed to the objector unless the objection concerns an issue that arose after the opportunities for formal comment.
A legal notice will be published in the newspaper of record starting the 45-day objection period for the project-specific amendments per
36 CFR 218.26
. Both the 45-day objection period for the project-specific amendments and the 60-day objection period for the programmatic plan amendments will run concurrently beginning with the date of publication of the legal notice and the NOO respectively.
How To File an Objection
Objections must be submitted to the Reviewing Officer at the address shown in the
ADDRESSES
section of this notice. An objection must include the following (
36 CFR 219.54(c)
):
(1) The objector's name and address along with a telephone number or email address if available. In cases where no identifiable name is attached to an objection, the Forest Service will attempt to verify the identity of the objector to confirm objection eligibility;
(2) Signature or other verification of authorship upon request (a scanned signature for electronic mail may be filed with the objection);
(3) Identification of the lead objector when multiple names are listed on an objection. The Forest Service will communicate to all parties to an objection through the lead objector. Verification of the identity of the lead objector must also be provided if requested;
(4) The name of the plan amendment being objected to, and the name and title of the responsible official;
(5) A statement of the issues and/or parts of the plan amendment to which the objection applies;
(6) A concise statement explaining the objection and suggesting how the draft plan decision may be improved. If the objector believes that the plan amendment is inconsistent with law, regulation, or policy, an explanation should be included;
(7) A statement that demonstrates the link between the objector's prior substantive formal comments and the content of the objection, unless the objection concerns an issue that arose after the opportunities for formal comment; and
(8) All documents referenced in the objection (a bibliography is not sufficient), except the following need not be provided:
a. All or any part of a Federal law or regulation,
b. Forest Service Directive System documents and land management plans or other published Forest Service documents,
c. Documents referenced by the Forest Service in the planning documentation related to the proposal subject to objection, and
d. Formal comments previously provided to the Forest Service by the objector during the proposed plan amendment comment period.
Additionally, objections should be identified as pertaining to the “Amendments to the Okanogan and Wenatchee National Forest Land Management Plans”, as these are subject to separate processes from objections to project activities in the Planning and Management of Domestic Sheep and Goat Grazing Within the Range of Bighorn Sheep Project. See the legal notice for instructions on how to object to project activities. Objectors filing objections on both topics should submit these as separate objection letters.
It is the responsibility of the objector to ensure that the Reviewing Officer receives the objection in a timely manner. The regulations generally prohibit extending the length of the objection filing period (
36 CFR 219.56(d)
). However, when the time period expires on a Saturday, Sunday, or a Federal holiday, the time is extended to the end of the next Federal working day (11:59 p.m. for objections filed by electronic means such as email) (
36 CFR 219.56
).
Responsible Official
The responsible official who will approve the record of decision and the amendments to the forest plans is Forest Supervisor Tara Umphries, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, 215 Melody Lane, Wenatchee, WA 98801, (509) 664-9200.
The Regional Forester is the reviewing officer for the amendments to the forest plans because the Forest Supervisor is
(
printed page 66833)
the responsible official (
36 CFR 219.56(e)
).

Associate Deputy Chief, National Forest System.

October 20, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1)
[
1

of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”)

[

notice is hereby given that on October 6, 2026, New York Stock Exchange LLC (“NYSE” or the “Exchange”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the “Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I and II below, which Items have been prepared by the self-regulatory organization. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
The Exchange proposes to restore former Rule 123D to its rulebook and mark it “Reserved.” The proposed rule change is available on the Exchange's website at
www.nyse.com
and at the principal office of the Exchange.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the self-regulatory organization included statements concerning the purpose of, and basis for, the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of those statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant parts of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and the Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
New York Stock Exchange LLC (“NYSE” or the “Exchange”) proposes restore former Rule 123D to its rulebook and mark it “Reserved.”
In July 2025, the Exchange proposed to reorganize its trading halt rules into Rule 7.18 and to delete Rule 123D, where some trading halt rules had been located.
[
4
]
That filing proposed to delete Rule 123D in its entirety, completely removing any reference to it from the Exchange's rulebook. The Commission noticed the proposed rule change for immediate effectiveness, and the change became operative in August 2026 in a coordinated roll-out of trading halt changes with other equities exchanges.
For the sake of posterity, the Exchange now wishes to add former Rule 123D back into its rulebook and note that the rule is “Reserved.” In so doing, the Exchange would also add back the adoption and amendment history of Rule 123D, so that the history and legacy of the rule and its development is preserved in the rulebook.
The proposed change is non-substantive. The content of former Rule 123D would remain deleted; this filing
(
printed page 66904)
would only restore its title, the word “Reserved,” and its adoption and amendment history.
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes that its proposal is consistent with the requirements of the Act and the rules and regulations thereunder that are applicable to a national securities exchange, and, in particular, with the requirements of Section 6(b) of the Act.
[
5
]
Specifically, the proposal is consistent with Section 6(b)(5) of the Act
[
6
]
because it would promote just and equitable principles of trade, remove impediments to, and perfect the mechanism of, a free and open market and a national market system, and, in general, protect investors and the public interest.
The Exchange believes the proposed rule change would protect investors and the public interest and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system. Adding reference to former Rule 123D back into the rulebook as “Reserved” and restoring its adoption and amendment history would preserve the legacy of the rule and its development, thereby providing clarity and transparency for the Exchange and for market participants about the rule's history and evolution.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange believes the proposal is consistent with Section 6(b)(8) of the Act
[
7
]
in that it does not impose any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act as explained below. Rather than impacting competition, the proposed change would simply add back into the Exchange's rulebook the title “Rule 123D,” the word “Reserved,” and the former rule's adoption and amendment history.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
No written comments were solicited or received with respect to the proposed rule change.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
The Exchange has filed the proposed rule change pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A)(iii) of the Act
[
8
]
and Rule 19b-4(f)(6) thereunder.
[
9
]
Because the proposed rule change does not: (i) significantly affect the protection of investors or the public interest; (ii) impose any significant burden on competition; and (iii) become operative prior to 30 days from the date on which it was filed, or such shorter time as the Commission may designate, if consistent with the protection of investors and the public interest, the proposed rule change has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A) of the Act and Rule 19b-4(f)(6)(iii) thereunder.
A proposed rule change filed under Rule 19b-4(f)(6)
[
10
]
normally does not become operative prior to 30 days after the date of the filing. However, pursuant to Rule 19b-4(f)(6)(iii),
[
11
]
the Commission may designate a shorter time if such action is consistent with the protection of investors and the public interest. The Exchange has asked the Commission to waive the 30-day operative delay so that the proposal may become operative immediately upon filing with the Commission pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A) of the Act
[
12
]
and paragraph (f)(6) of Rule 19b-4 thereunder.
[
13
]
The Commission believes that it is consistent with the protection of investors and the public interest to waive the operative date of the proposal so that it becomes operative upon filing.
[
14
]
The Commission believes that the waiver would provide member organizations greater clarity about the recent changes to the Exchange's trading halt rules. In addition, the proposal does not present any unique or novel regulatory issues because it simply adds back into the Exchange's rulebook the title “Rule 123D,” the word “reserved,” and the “former rule's adoption and amendment history.” For this reason, the Commission hereby waives the 30-day operative period and designates the proposal operative upon filing.
At any time within 60 days of the filing of such proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, for the protection of investors, or otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission shall institute proceedings under Section 19(b)(2)(B)
[
15
]
of the Act to determine whether the proposed rule change should be approved or disapproved.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
); or
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
.
Please include file number SR-NYSE-2026-49 on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
All submissions should refer to file number SR-NYSE-2026-49. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
). Copies of the filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of the Exchange. Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection. All submissions should refer to file number SR-NYSE-2026-49 and should be submitted on or before November 13, 2026.
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.

Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”),
[
1

[
2
]
notice is hereby given that on October 7, 2026, Texas Stock Exchange LLC (the “Exchange” or “TXSE”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I, II, and III below, which Items have been prepared by the Exchange. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
The Exchange is filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission”) a proposal to adopt annual fees applicable to corporate listings on the Exchange. The text of the proposed rule change is available on the Commission's website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
) at the Exchange's website (
https://www.txse.com/​regulations/​rules-filings
), and at the principal office of the Exchange.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the Exchange included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in Sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant parts of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The Exchange proposes to add Section G to its Fee Schedule to establish an initial corporate listing fee framework for securities listed pursuant to Chapter 16 of the TXSE Rules.
[
3
]
The proposed section would establish an Entry Fee, an Initial Application Fee, and All-Inclusive Annual Listing Fees, including a separate annual fee for Companies with Dually-Listed Securities. The proposal also specifies the timing of assessments, transfer exemptions, fee-credit mechanics, proration, and limited circumstances in which fees may be deferred or waived.
Entry Fee
A Company would pay a one-time Entry Fee of $325,000 the first time it lists any class of securities on the Exchange. The fee would be assessed on the date of listing.
[
4
]
A Company whose business plan is to complete one or more acquisitions (an “Acquisition Company” or “SPAC”) would instead pay a flat $80,000 Entry Fee. That fee would cover the SPAC's primary equity securities and any units, warrants, or rights issued in connection with the listing. The lower SPAC Entry Fee recognizes that a SPAC generally lists a package of related securities at the same time and has not yet completed a Business Combination.
A Company transferring the listing of any class of equity securities from another national securities exchange would not pay an Entry Fee. The transfer exemption is designed to reduce duplicative costs for an issuer that has already completed an exchange listing process and to support competition among listing markets.
The Exchange Board or its designee may, in its discretion, defer or waive all or any portion of an Entry Fee. Any exercise of that authority would be administered in a manner consistent with the Exchange Act, including the requirements that exchange fees be equitably allocated and not unfairly discriminatory.
Initial Application Fee
A Company, including a SPAC, would pay a non-refundable Initial Application Fee of $25,000 in connection with its first application to list an equity security on the Exchange. The Exchange would not grant eligibility clearance until it receives the Initial Application Fee. If the Company lists, the Initial Application Fee would be credited in full toward the applicable Entry Fee, so the fee would not increase the total Entry Fee paid by a successful first-time applicant.
A Company transferring the listing of any class of equity securities from another national securities exchange would be exempt from the Initial Application Fee. In addition, a Company that pays the Initial Application Fee but does not immediately list would not pay a second Initial Application Fee upon a later listing if it continues to have a registration statement regarding the security on file with the Commission or, after withdrawing the registration statement, refiles it within 24 months. These provisions avoid duplicative charges where the Exchange can continue to rely on the application work associated with the earlier submission.
All-Inclusive Annual Listing Fees
A Company would pay All-Inclusive Annual Fees for the continued listing of its securities. In the first year of listing, the Exchange would assess a prorated fee covering the period from the listing date through the end of the calendar year. For each later year, the Exchange would invoice the applicable annual fee at the beginning of the year.
A Company transferring its primary class of shares or units from another national securities exchange would not pay the All-Inclusive Annual Fee for that primary class for the transfer year. The exemption recognizes that a transferring Company may already have paid an annual listing fee to its prior exchange. Except as expressly provided in the Fee Schedule, an annual fee that is due and payable would not be waived or refunded if a class is later delisted or otherwise removed. The Exchange Board or its designee may defer or waive all or any portion of an All-Inclusive
(
printed page 66877)
Annual Fee, subject to the Exchange Act requirements described above.
Primary Listed Securities
For primary listed securities, the All-Inclusive Annual Fee for each class would equal the greater of the applicable minimum fee or the number of shares outstanding as of December 31 of the preceding year multiplied by $0.001250 per share, subject to a $250,000 maximum. The applicable minimum would be $70,000 for common shares and for a primary class of preferred stock where no common shares are listed, and $15,000 for each other class of preferred stock and each class of warrants, units, or rights. Additional common-share and preferred-stock issuances during the year of issuance would not generate an additional fee.
The per-share design, minimum fees, and maximum fee are intended to allocate annual fees in relation to the scale of the listed class while providing Companies with a predictable floor and ceiling. This structure is similar to the per-share annual fee schedules used by other national securities exchanges.
[
5
]
As an example, a Company with 40 million common shares outstanding would pay the $70,000 minimum because 40 million multiplied by $0.001250 equals $50,000. A Company with 100 million common shares outstanding would pay $125,000. A Company with 300 million common shares outstanding would pay the $250,000 maximum because the calculated amount would otherwise equal $375,000.
The proposed Fee Schedule includes rules addressing multiple common classes, foreign private issuers, and transaction-related listings. The Exchange would aggregate all listed classes of common shares or equivalent common equity securities when calculating the annual fee. For a foreign private issuer, the calculation would include only equity securities issued and outstanding in the United States if the Company timely provides the required information. Additional common share issuances will not be charged an additional per share fee during the year of issuance.
[
6
]
A newly listed Company resulting from a transaction involving an existing TXSE-listed Company would not pay annual fees for the calendar year in which it lists.
Dually-Listed Securities
A Company with one or more Dually-Listed Securities listed on the Exchange would pay a Company-wide All-Inclusive Annual Fee of $600,000. “Dually-Listed Securities” refers to securities listed on TXSE and another national securities exchange under TXSE Rule 16.205 and Supplementary Material .01 thereto.
[
7
]
The Exchange would assess the fee on the first day of the calendar month following the date on which the dual listing becomes effective and prorate it for the remaining calendar months in that year. At the beginning of each later calendar year, the Exchange would invoice the full annual fee. If the Company ceases to maintain its dual listing on the Exchange, fees already paid for the remainder of the applicable period would not be refunded.
For example, if a dual listing becomes effective on April 15, the fee would be assessed on May 1 for the eight remaining calendar months in that year, resulting in a prorated fee of $400,000. A Company with more than one Dually-Listed Security would remain subject to the same Company-wide fee rather than a separate $600,000 fee for each security.
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change is consistent with Section 6(b) of the Act,
[
8
]
in general, and furthers the objectives of Sections 6(b)(4) and 6(b)(5) of the Act,
[
9
]
in particular, because it provides for the equitable allocation of reasonable dues, fees, and other charges among issuers and other persons using the Exchange's facilities and is not designed to permit unfair discrimination among issuers.
TXSE notes that the Exchange operates in a highly competitive marketplace for the listing of companies.
[
10
]
The Commission has repeatedly expressed its preference for competition over regulatory intervention in determining prices, products, and services in the securities markets. The Exchange believes that the ever-shifting market share among exchanges with respect to new listings and the transfer of existing listings between competitor exchanges demonstrates that issuers can choose different listing markets in response to fee changes. Moreover, new competitors, such as the Exchange, can enter the space, as well as existing exchanges currently without listing programs. Accordingly, competitive forces constrain the Exchange's listing fees and changes to the listing fees can have a direct effect on the ability of TXSE to compete for new listings and retain existing listings.
The Exchange believes that the proposed fees are reasonable because they are designed to support the costs and value associated with reviewing applications, onboarding new listings, conducting ongoing regulatory oversight, administering corporate actions and issuer submissions, maintaining systems that support listed securities, and providing issuer services. The Exchange also considered fees charged by competing listing markets. In particular, the proposed $325,000 Entry Fee is the same as the current initial listing fee for specified primary equity listings on both Nasdaq and NYSE, and the proposed primary-listing annual fee uses a per-share structure, minimums, and a maximum that are familiar in the market for exchange listing services.
The Exchange believes that the $25,000 Initial Application Fee is reasonable because it applies only to a Company's first application, is credited in full toward the Entry Fee if the Company lists, and compensates the Exchange for application review where the applicant does not proceed immediately to listing. The proposed fee also limits duplicative charges where the application remains active or is renewed within the specified period.
The Exchange believes that the primary-listing annual fees are reasonable because the minimum and per-share components scale the fee to the listed class, while the maximum provides predictability for issuers with a large number of shares outstanding. Free treatment for additional issuances during the year avoids repeated charges for changes in shares outstanding before the next annual measurement date.
The Exchange also notes that the proposed fee for Dually-Listed Securities is subject to significant competitive constraints. A Company is not required to obtain a dual listing on the Exchange (or any exchange) and may decline to do so without affecting its existing primary listing or the ability of its securities to trade on other
(
printed page 66878)
national securities exchanges pursuant to unlisted trading privileges. Companies may therefore evaluate whether the benefits of an additional listing relationship with the Exchange justify the proposed fee.
The Exchange also believes that the proposal equitably allocates fees because each fee applies on objective terms to all Companies in the same category. The Entry Fee differentiates between an operating Company and a SPAC based on the nature and scope of the initial listing. The transfer exemptions apply to all eligible transfers from another national securities exchange. The Initial Application Fee applies only to a first application and is credited against the Entry Fee. The primary annual fee is determined using the same minimum, per-share rate, and maximum for each security category specified in the schedule.
The proposed annual-fee differences among common stock, preferred stock, warrants, units, and rights are not unfairly discriminatory because the categories reflect the role of the security in the Company's listing relationship and the scope of the Exchange's ongoing services. The lower minimum for additional preferred classes and for warrants, units, and rights recognizes that those securities generally accompany or supplement a primary equity listing, while the common-share and primary preferred-share minimum applies to the principal class supporting the listing relationship.
The proposal is not unfairly discriminatory with respect to Companies with Dually-Listed Securities because each such Company would pay the same Company-wide fee under the same proration and no-refund rules. The Company-wide approach also avoids charging a larger fee solely because the Company has more than one Dually-Listed Security on TXSE.
The Exchange believes that the $600,000 annual fee for a Company with Dually-Listed Securities is reasonable in light of the economic relationship with dually-listed companies, specifically the Exchange's ongoing regulatory oversight responsibilities with respect to the Company and its listed securities and the fact that the Exchange does not receive the economic benefit associated with a primary listing. Exchanges that have a primary listing draw the vast majority of auction volume in a security, volume which is particularly profitable for an exchange. Further, primary listing venues also generally attract an outsize portion of intraday trading volume in their primary listings. While this additional economic value to a primary listing exchange varies by company, the Exchange believes that the proposed across the board $600,000 annual dual-listing fee is reasonable given the reduced economic opportunity that comes with a dual-listing while requiring generally similar regulatory costs. The flat Company-wide structure also allows a Company to maintain more than one Dually-Listed Security without multiplying the fee by the number of securities. As noted above, the proposed fee for Dually-Listed Securities is subject to significant competitive constraints. A Company is not required to obtain a dual listing on the Exchange (or any exchange) and may decline to do so without affecting its existing primary listing or the ability of its securities to trade on other national securities exchanges pursuant to unlisted trading privileges. Companies may therefore evaluate whether the benefits of an additional listing relationship with the Exchange justify the proposed fee.
The limited waiver authority is consistent with the Act because any waiver or deferral must be administered on an equitable and not unfairly discriminatory basis. The Exchange would retain records explaining the basis for any waiver or deferral and would apply substantially similar treatment to similarly situated Companies.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act.
[
11
]
The market for corporate listing services is competitive. Companies may choose among national securities exchanges based on listing standards, market quality, services, fees, and other factors, and may transfer listings subject to applicable requirements. The proposed fee framework is designed to permit the Exchange to compete for new, transfer, and dual listings while supporting the costs of operating its corporate listing program.
The Exchange does not believe that the proposal will impose an inappropriate burden on intermarket competition because the fees apply only to Companies that voluntarily choose to list on TXSE. Competing exchanges may respond through their own fees, services, or listing programs. The transfer exemptions reduce the cost of moving a listing to TXSE and therefore may promote competition among listing markets.
The Exchange also does not believe that the proposal will impose an inappropriate burden on intramarket competition. The same fee calculation would apply to all similarly situated Companies, and the distinctions among operating Companies, SPACs, transfer listings, primary listed securities, and Dually-Listed Securities are based on objective characteristics of the listing and the associated Exchange relationship.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
The Exchange neither solicited nor received written comments on the proposed rule change.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
The foregoing rule change has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A) of the Act
[
12
]
and Rule 19b-4(f)(2)
[
13
]
thereunder. At any time within 60 days of the filing of the proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, for the protection of investors, or otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission will institute proceedings to determine whether the proposed rule change should be approved or disapproved.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposal is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
); or
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
.
Please include File No. SR-TXSE-2026-040 on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
(
printed page 66879)
All submissions should refer to File No. SR-TXSE-2026-040. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
). Copies of the filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of the Exchange. Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection. All submissions should refer to file number SR-TXSE-2026-040 and should be submitted on or before November 13, 2026.
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.
[
14
]
Sherry R. Haywood,
Assistant Secretary.

Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106705; File No. SR-NYSE-2026-50]
October 20, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1)
[
1
]
of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”)
[
2
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
3
]
notice is hereby given that on October 8, 2026, New York Stock Exchange LLC (“NYSE” or the “Exchange”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the “Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I, II, and III below, which Items have been prepared by the self-regulatory organization. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
The Exchange proposes to amend Rule 7.10 (Clearly Erroneous Executions). The proposed rule change is available on the Exchange's website at
www.nyse.com
and at the principal office of the Exchange.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the self-regulatory organization included statements concerning the purpose of, and basis for, the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of those statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant parts of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and the Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The purpose of the proposed rule change is to amend Rule 7.10 (Clearly Erroneous Executions). Specifically, the Exchange proposes to: (1) reorganize the Rule to enhance its clarity; (2) specify the impact of missing or erroneous LULD Price Bands
[
4
]
on the availability of Clearly Erroneous review during the Core Trading Session or Overnight Protected Hours;
[
5
]
(3) amend provisions on “multi-stock events”; (4) remove references to “multi-day events”; (5) add a provision on reasonable cross-market coordination; and (6) eliminate redundancies in the Rule.
Background
Following a severe disruption in the U.S. equities markets on May 6, 2010 (known as the Flash Crash), the Commission approved, on a pilot basis, the clearly erroneous rule to “provide greater transparency and certainty to the process of breaking trades.”
[
6
]
Largely,
(
printed page 66893)
the pilot reduced the discretion of the Exchange, other national securities exchanges, and Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (“FINRA”) to deviate from the objective standards in their respective rules when dealing with potentially erroneous transactions. After revisions in 2013 and 2014,
[
7
]
the clearly erroneous pilot was extended in six-month increments numerous times until 2022.
In April 2019, the Commission approved an amendment to the LULD Plan to make that Plan permanent.
[
8
]
Following that change, in 2022, the Commission approved a proposal to amend the clearly erroneous rule (the “2022 Amendment” to Rule 7.10).
[
9
]
The 2022 Amendment made the clearly erroneous rule permanent and aimed to harmonize it with the LULD Plan by making explicit that, with limited exceptions, the LULD mechanism was the primary means of preventing clearly erroneous trades during the Core Trading Session.
In 2026, in conjunction with the industry's plans for the introduction of 23/5 Trading, the Operating Committee of the LULD Plan filed proposed Amendment 27 to the LULD Plan, which proposed to establish price band protections during overnight trading hours (“Overnight Price Bands”).
[
10
]
On August 5, 2026, the Commission approved the proposal.
[
11
]
On September 14, 2026, in light of the addition of Overnight Price Bands to the LULD Plan, the Exchange filed an amendment to Rule 7.10 that extended the restrictions on clearly erroneous review that apply in the Core Trading Session to the Overnight Protected Hours when Overnight Price Bands are in place.
[
12
]
Proposed Amendment
Following the 2022 Amendment, market disruptions on January 24, 2023 and June 3, 2024
[
13
]
further highlighted the close interplay of the LULD Plan and the clearly erroneous rule. Following those events, the Exchange, in consultation with other equities exchanges, closely reviewed the current text of Rule 7.10 and identified areas where the Exchange believes the Rule's clarity can be enhanced, its organization can be improved, and duplicate and obsolete sections can be eliminated. In sum, the proposed rule text is not substantively new, but rather a reorganization and further specification of existing Exchange authority.
Accordingly, the Exchange proposes to reorganize Rule 7.10 into three clear paragraphs: (a) Definitions, (b) Availability of Clearly Erroneous Review, and (c) Procedures. In the current Rule, definitions are spread across paragraphs (a), (c), and (d); rules on the availability of clearly erroneous review are split between paragraphs (c), (g), (h), and (i); and procedures are split across paragraphs (b), (c), (e), and (f). By reorganizing the Rule and gathering similar provisions together, the Exchange believes the proposed rule text will be easier for market participants to navigate, understand, and use.
(a) Definitions
The Exchange proposes to amend paragraph (a) of Rule 7.10 to include the definitions of terms used in the current version of the Rule, as well as new terms that would be added as a result of this proposal, as follows:
Proposed paragraph (a) would be titled “Definitions” and would provide that “[f]or purposes of this Rule, the terms below have the following meanings.”
Proposed subparagraph (a)(1) would define “CEE Reference Price” as the consolidated last sale immediately prior to the execution(s) under review, or, in cases where there are no prior trades, the previous day's official closing price, unless an Officer determines to utilize a Revised CEE Reference Price
[
14
]
as provided in this Rule. The first part of this definition is based on the current definition of “Reference Price” in paragraph (d) of Rule 7.10. The second part of this definition is based on the Exchange's definition of “Official Closing Price” in Rule 1.1(u)(1)(D), which states that when there have been no consolidated last-sale eligible trades during the Core Trading Hours on that trading day, the Exchange's Official Closing Price will be the previous day's Official Closing Price. As such, the proposed definition of “CEE Reference Price” in subparagraph (a)(1) is not novel.
Proposed subparagraph (a)(2), the definition of “Clearly erroneous,” would encompass the text of current paragraph (a), without substantive change.
Proposed subparagraph (a)(3) would define “LULD Plan” to mean the Plan to Address Extraordinary Market Volatility Pursuant to Rule 608 of Regulation NMS under the Act. This term is currently defined in paragraph (c)(1) of Rule 7.10.
Proposed subparagraph (a)(4) would define “LULD Price Bands” or “Price Bands” as the Price Bands defined in Section V of the LULD Plan and Overnight Price Bands as defined in Section VIII of the LULD Plan. These terms are currently defined in paragraph (c)(1) of Rule 7.10.
Proposed subparagraph (a)(5) would define “LULD Protected Hours” to include the Core Trading Session and Overnight Protected Hours. This term is currently defined in paragraph (c)(1) of Rule 7.10.
Proposed subparagraph (a)(6) would define “LULD Reference Price” as the Reference Price or Overnight Reference Prices defined in the LULD Plan. This definition does not appear in the current text of Rule 7.10 and is being added for clarity to facilitate the proposed reorganization of the Rule.
Proposed subparagraph (a)(7) would define “LULD Tier” as Tier 1 or Tier 2 as defined in Appendix A to the LULD Plan. This definition does not appear in the current text of Rule 7.10 and is being added for clarity to facilitate the proposed reorganization of the Rule.
Proposed subparagraph (a)(8) would define “Multi-Stock Event” as an event involving 50 or more securities whose executions occurred within 5 minutes. As discussed below, this is a proposed
(
printed page 66894)
increase to 50 securities from 20 securities in the current Rule.
Proposed subparagraph (a)(9) would define “Numerical Guidelines” as the percentage difference from the CEE Reference Price specified in Case 5A
[
15
]
below for transactions executed during LULD Protected Hours in NMS stocks that are not subject to the LULD Plan and transactions executed outside of LULD Protected Hours. This term is currently defined in paragraph (c)(2)(A) of Rule 7.10.
Proposed subparagraph (a)(10) would define “Officer” as an Officer of the Exchange or such other employee designee of the Exchange. This term is currently defined in paragraph (b) of Rule 7.10.
Proposed subparagraph (a)(11) would define “Overnight Protected Hours” as the Overnight Protected Hours defined in Section VIII of the LULD Plan. This term is not defined in the current text of Rule 7.10 and is being added for clarity to facilitate the proposed reorganization of the Rule.
Proposed subparagraph (a)(12) would define “Percentage Parameter” as the Percentage Parameter defined in Appendix A to the LULD Plan or Overnight Percentage Parameter defined in Section VIII of the LULD Plan. These terms are currently defined in paragraph (c)(1)(B) of Rule 7.10.
Proposed subparagraph (a)(13) would define “SRO” as a national securities exchange and/or a national securities association, as those terms are defined in Regulation NMS. This definition does not appear in the current text of Rule 7.10.
(b) Availability of Clearly Erroneous Review
Next, the Exchange proposes to reorganize all rule text about the availability of clearly erroneous review into a revised paragraph (b). In the current Rule, this content is spread across paragraph (c)(1), which addresses the availability of clearly erroneous review during the Core Trading Session; paragraph (c)(2), which addresses the availability of clearly erroneous review outside of the Core Trading Session and for stocks not subject to the LULD Plan; paragraph (g), which addresses transactions occurring outside of LULD Price Bands; paragraph (h), which addresses Multi-Day Events; and paragraph (i), which addresses transactions occurring during trading halts.
The Exchange proposes to reorganize all of these provisions into proposed paragraph (b). Further, instead of separating the rules for clearly erroneous review during the Core Trading Session vs. other times (
i.e.,
current paragraphs (c)(1) vs. (c)(2)) as in the current Rule, the Exchange proposes to assign a “Case” number to each circumstance where clearly erroneous review is available, and to include within the Case description all of the rules relevant to that particular Case. In addition, to the extent that the rules in current paragraphs (c)(1) and (c)(2) address the same issues as current paragraphs (g) and (i), the Exchange proposes to combine and streamline such rules within the relevant Case.
Specifically, the Exchange proposes to replace paragraph (b) of Rule 7.10 as follows:
The Exchange proposes to title the revised paragraph (b) as “Availability of Clearly Erroneous Review.” Proposed paragraph (b) would specify that “transactions are reviewable as clearly erroneous only in the enumerated cases below.”
Proposed subparagraph (b)(1) would be titled “Case 1—Transactions Erroneously Executed During a Trading Halt, Suspension, or Pause.”
Proposed subparagraph (b)(2) would be titled “Case 2—Transactions Executed Outside LULD Price Bands.”
Proposed subparagraph (b)(3) would be titled “Case 3—Unavailable or Missing LULD Price Bands.”
Proposed subparagraph (b)(4) would be titled “Case 4—Erroneous LULD Price Bands.”
Proposed subparagraph (b)(5) would be titled “Case 5—Transactions Executed During LULD Protected Hours in NMS Stocks Not Subject to the LULD Plan, and Transactions Executed Outside of LULD Protected Hours.”
Each of the Cases is discussed further below.
Case 1—Transactions Erroneously Executed During a Trading Halt, Suspension, or Pause
Proposed Case 1 (proposed subparagraph (b)(1)) is based on current paragraph (i) of Rule 7.10, with certain changes identified below. Proposed Case 1 would apply when a “transaction was executed after implementation of a regulatory trading halt, suspension, or pause that has been declared by the primary listing market or imposed by the Commission
[
16
]
and before such regulatory halt, suspension, or pause officially ended according to the primary listing market.” The current text of paragraph (i) expresses the same concept, but includes additional unnecessary detail about the event where a trading halt, suspension or pause is “prematurely lifted in error and then re-instituted,” which the Exchange believes is encompassed in the more general language above. The Exchange believes that removing such unnecessary detail will streamline the rule text and enhance comprehension of the Rule.
In addition, the current text of paragraph (i) includes language limiting the application of the Rule to “the event of any disruption, or malfunction in the operation of the electronic communications and trading facilities of the Exchange, another market center or responsible single plan processor in connection with the transmittal or receipt of a regulatory trading halt, suspension or pause . . . .” The Exchange believes that such limitation is unnecessary, because transactions erroneously executed during a trading halt, suspension, or pause should be nullified in all cases, whether the cause was one of the conditions listed in current paragraph (i) or some other issue that has not yet been imagined. The inclusion of such limiting language has the potential to cause confusion and add delay to the process of addressing such trades.
Proposed Case 1 would further provide:
“A Case 1 transaction shall be nullified by an Officer acting on his or her own motion or at the request of a third party without regard to the Percentage Parameters or Numerical Guidelines set forth in this Rule, and without regard to the trading session during which the transaction was executed.” The provisions providing that an Officer shall nullify such transactions acting on his or her own motion and that such action will be taken without regard to the Percentage Parameters or Numerical Guidelines are taken directly from current paragraph (i), without substantive change. The Exchange proposes to add the further language “without regard to the trading session during which the transaction was executed” to make explicit that Case 1 applies both during LULD Protected Hours and outside of them. The Exchange also proposes to add that an Officer may nullify such a
(
printed page 66895)
transaction “acting on his or her own motion
or at the request of a third party.”
Current paragraph (g), regarding transactions executed outside of LULD Price Bands, currently contains such language, and so it is not novel. The Exchange believes it is reasonable to also include such language in proposed Case 1, to make explicit that a third party market participant may inform the Exchange when such third party becomes aware of transactions erroneously executed during a trading halt, suspension, or pause.
Current paragraph (i) contains additional language regarding the timing of the Officer's review, the notification of parties involved in the subject transaction, and the appeal rights of aggrieved parties. This language is substantively identical to the procedural language contained in current paragraph (f). In light of the Exchange's proposal to reorganize all such procedural language into one location (
i.e.,
paragraph (c) of the proposed Rule), the Exchange proposes not to include such procedural language within Case 1 itself, but instead to include it in the “Procedures” section of the proposed Rule at paragraph (c)(1)(B).
The Exchange notes that current paragraph (c)(1)(B) includes a provision that indicates that a transaction that “is executed after the primary listing market for the security declares a regulatory trading halt, suspension, or pause pursuant to paragraph (i)” will be “subject to review . . . and found to be clearly erroneous if the price of the transaction to buy (sell) that is subject of the complaint is greater than (less than) the Reference Price, described in paragraph (d) below, by an amount that equals or exceeds the applicable Percentage Parameter . . . .” This provision was added as part of the 2022 Amendment and appears to be inconsistent with paragraph (i), which requires the Exchange to nullify such transactions without regard to Percentage Parameters. Case 2—Transactions Executed Outside LULD Price Bands
Proposed Case 2 (proposed subparagraph (b)(2)) is based on current paragraph (g) of Rule 7.10, with certain changes identified below.
Proposed Case 2 would apply when a “transaction was executed during LULD Protected Hours outside the LULD Price Bands at a time when the Price Bands were available and correct, as determined by an Officer, using his or her own discretion.” Current paragraph (g) contains this concept, but with the limitation that the execution of such a transaction outside the LULD Price Bands must be “as a result of an Exchange technology or systems issue.” The Exchange believes that such limitation is unnecessary, because transactions erroneously executed outside of available and correct Price Bands during LULD Protected Hours should be nullified in all cases, whether the cause was an Exchange technology or systems issue or some other issue that has not yet been imagined. The inclusion of such limiting language has the potential to cause confusion and add delay to the process of addressing such trades.
As noted above, proposed Case 2 would apply “when Price Bands were available and correct, as determined by an Officer, using his or her own discretion.” The Exchange proposes to add this condition to distinguish Case 2 from other potential scenarios where transactions should be evaluated when the LULD Price Bands were erroneous or missing, as described below in proposed Cases 3 and 4. The Exchange believes it is appropriate for an Officer, using his or her own discretion, to determine whether the Price Bands were available and correct such that Case 2 applies.
Proposed Case 2 would provide:
“A Case 2 transaction shall be nullified by an Officer acting on his or her own motion or at the request of a third party, without regard to the Percentage Parameters or Numerical Guidelines set forth in this Rule.” The provision providing that an Officer shall nullify such transactions acting on his or her own motion is taken directly from current paragraph (g), without substantive change. The Exchange proposes to add “without regard to the Percentage Parameters or Numerical Guidelines set forth in this Rule” to make clear that such nullification by the Officer is not discretionary, nor is it based on computations described elsewhere in the Rule.
Current paragraph (g) contains additional language regarding the timing of the Officer's review, the notification of parties involved in the subject transaction, and the appeal rights of aggrieved parties. This language is substantively identical to the procedural language contained in current paragraph (f). As with Case 1 above, the Exchange proposes not to include the procedural language within Case 2 itself, but to include it instead in the “Procedures” section of the proposed Rule at paragraph (c)(1)(B).
The Exchange notes that current paragraph (c)(1)(B) includes a provision that indicates that a transaction that “is the result of an Exchange technology or systems issue that results in the transaction occurring outside of the applicable LULD Price Bands pursuant to paragraph (g)” will be “subject to review . . . and found to be clearly erroneous if the price of the transaction to buy (sell) that is subject of the complaint is greater than (less than) the Reference Price, described in paragraph (d) below, by an amount that equals or exceeds the applicable Percentage Parameter . . . .” This provision was added as part of the 2022 Amendment and appears to be inconsistent with paragraph (g), which requires the Exchange simply to nullify such transactions. The Exchange believes that the paragraph (g) approach—which has been part of the clearly erroneous rule since 2013
[
18
]
—is the more reasonable approach, and that transactions executed outside LULD Price Bands should be nullified without further analysis. For that reason, the Exchange proposes to eliminate the inconsistent provisions of paragraph (c)(1)(B) and adopt the paragraph (g) approach, as described and revised above, in Case 2.
Finally, current paragraph (g) includes the caveat that “[i]n the event that a single plan processor experiences a technology or systems issue that prevents the dissemination of Price Bands, the Exchange will make the determination of whether to nullify transactions based on paragraph (c)(1)(B) above.” Because the Exchange proposes to address such processor issues in Cases 3 and 4 below, the Exchange proposes not to include this sentence in Case 2.

Proposed Case 3 (proposed subparagraph (b)(3)) would apply when

This proposed language is a clarification of the portion of current paragraph (c)(1)(B), added in the 2022 Amendment, that provides that clearly erroneous review is available if the transaction “was executed at a time when Price Bands under the LULD Plan were not available.” The Exchange's Rule 19b-4 filing in support of the 2022 Amendment noted that in certain circumstances during the Core Trading Session, clearly erroneous review should act as a “backstop” to the LULD Plan:
[T]here are instances, such as the opening auction on the primary listing market, or circumstances where a transaction that ordinarily would have been subject to the LULD Plan is not—due, for example, to some issue with processing the Price Bands. These transactions would continue to be eligible for clearly erroneous review [under the 2022 Amendment], effectively ensuring that such review remains available as a backstop when the LULD Plan would not prevent executions from occurring at erroneous prices in the first instance.

i.e.,
clause (a) of proposed paragraph (b)(3)). This provision is intended to capture the first circumstance identified in the quoted passage above: the case of an opening (or reopening) auction, when LULD Price Bands are not yet in effect. Because the protection of the Price Bands is not available at that time, transactions executed during that interval should be entitled to clearly erroneous review.
Proposed Case 3 would also make explicit that clearly erroneous review is available in the case of missing Price Bands during LULD Protected Hours (
i.e.,

The Exchange believes that Case 3 should cover all cases where Price Bands are missing during LULD Protected Hours, regardless of whether the missing Price Bands are caused by the processor's failure to disseminate them, the Exchange's failure to receive or implement them, or some other reason that has not yet been imagined. As such, the Exchange does not propose to include limiting language such as the language in current paragraph (g) (
i.e.,
“[i]n the event that a single plan processor experiences a technology or systems issue that prevents the dissemination of Price Bands”), because the Exchange believes that clearly erroneous review should be available in all instances during LULD Protected Hours where Price Bands are unavailable or missing, regardless of the cause.

Case 4—Erroneous LULD Price Bands
Proposed Case 4 (proposed subparagraph (b)(4)) would apply when a “transaction was executed during LULD Protected Hours at a time when Price Bands under the LULD Plan were available but erroneous, as determined by an Officer using his or her own discretion.”
Similar to Case 3 above, the Exchange's Rule 19b-4 filing in support of the 2022 Amendment contemplated that clearly erroneous review would be available in such situations. The Exchange intended for erroneous Price Bands to be among the “issue[s] with processing the Price Bands” where the clearly erroneous rules would act as “a backstop.”
[
21
]
Proposed Case 4 would make explicit that clearly erroneous review is available when a transaction was executed during LULD Protected Hours at a time when Price Bands under the LULD Plan were available but those Price Bands were erroneous, as determined by an Officer using his or her own discretion.
Current Rule 7.10(c)(1)(C) already includes two specific examples in which clearly erroneous review is available during LULD Protected Hours due to erroneous LULD Price Bands: in cases involving “(1) a corporate action or new issue or (2) a security that enters a Trading Pause pursuant to the LULD Plan and resumes trading without an auction” where the Reference Price “is determined to be erroneous by an Officer of the Exchange because it clearly deviated from the theoretical value of the security.” The Exchange now proposes to bring those two examples under Case 4, and to also specify several additional, non-exclusive factors contemplated by the “issue[s] with processing the Price Bands” language from the Exchange's Rule 19b-4 filing in support of the 2022 Amendment, where clearly erroneous review should be available due to erroneous LULD Price Bands, as determined by an Officer using his or her own discretion. The proposed Rule would provide that an Officer “may consider factors including, but not limited to,” the following.
Proposed subparagraph (A)(1) would describe one such factor: “whether the LULD Reference Price that was used to calculate the Price Bands was based on a price that equaled or exceeded the Numerical Guidelines.” This factor illustrates the fact that if the LULD Reference Price deviates from the theoretical value of the security by an amount that equals or exceeds the Numerical Guidelines, it is a telltale sign that the LULD Price Bands are erroneous. Such an instance would be an “issue with processing the Price Bands” within the language that the Exchange included in its Rule 19b-4 filing in support of the 2022 Amendment and is therefore not novel.
Proposed subparagraph (A)(2) would describe a second factor: “whether there was an issue that impacted the processor's calculation of the Price Bands.” This factor would include cases such as the processor experiencing a software or hardware issue, as well as the instances described in footnote 12 [sic] above. This factor is a clear example of the “issue with processing the Price Bands” language that the Exchange included in its Rule 19b-4 filing in support of the 2022 Amendment and is therefore not novel.
Proposed subparagraph (A)(3) would describe a third factor: “whether the security at issue was included in the correct LULD Tier under the LULD Plan.” This factor refers to the LULD Plan's requirement that a security must
(
printed page 66897)
be categorized into either “Tier 1” or “Tier 2,” with Percentage Parameters of either 5% (for Tier 1) or 10% (for Tier 2) for NMS securities with an LULD Reference Price of more than $3.00.
[
22
]
A security incorrectly classified into the wrong LULD Tier would have the wrong Percentage Parameters applied to its LULD Reference Price, meaning that the resulting LULD Price Bands would be erroneous. This factor is another clear example of the “issue with processing the Price Bands” language that the Exchange included in its Rule 19b-4 filing in support of the 2022 Amendment and is therefore not novel.
Proposed subparagraph (A)(4) would describe a fourth factor: “whether the transaction involved a corporate action or new issue where the LULD Reference Price clearly deviated from the theoretical value of the security due to conflicting or incorrect information in the market about the security, or an objective error like a processing or technical error.” This factor is based on paragraph (c)(1)(C)(1) of the current rule, but replaces the term “Reference Price” with “LULD Reference Price” as defined in proposed Rule 7.10(a)(4) (
i.e.,
an erroneous reference price was used for calculating the LULD Price Bands), since it is clear from context that is the meaning contemplated by the current rule text. The Exchange proposes to supplement the current rule text by adding “due to conflicting or incorrect information in the market about the security, or an objective error like a processing or technical error,” as illustrative examples of the types of errors that could result in a corporate action or new issue having an erroneous LULD Reference Price.

The Exchange believes this addition is not material and will enhance comprehension of the Rule.
Proposed subparagraph (A)(5) would describe a fifth factor: “whether the transaction involved a security that entered a Trading Pause pursuant to the LULD Plan and resumed trading without an auction, where the LULD Reference Price clearly deviated from the theoretical value of the security.” This factor is based on paragraph (c)(1)(C)(2) of the current Rule, but, as in proposed subparagraph (A)(4) above, replaces the term “Reference Price” with “LULD Reference Price” as defined in proposed Rule 7.10(a)(4) (
i.e.,
an erroneous reference price was used for calculating the LULD Price Bands), since it is clear from context that is the meaning contemplated by the current rule text.
In sum, proposed subparagraph (A) under Case 4 provides illustrative examples of the types of factors that might lead to LULD Price Bands being erroneous, but as mentioned above, the list is intended to be non-exclusive and subject to Officer discretion.
In proposed subparagraph (B) under Case 4, the first sentence would provide that if the Officer determines that the LULD Price Bands are erroneous, the Officer may use a different CEE Reference Price that is based on the theoretical value of the security (the “Revised CEE Reference Price”) for the purpose of clearly erroneous review. The Exchange believes that this provision is necessary because erroneous LULD Price Bands may be the byproduct of the security trading at prices that deviate from the theoretical value of the security. In such a case, it is likely that the CEE Reference Price that would ordinarily be used for clearly erroneous review
[
24
]
may also deviate from the theoretical value of the security. In such a case, the impact of such error can be corrected by using a Revised CEE Reference Price that is based on the theoretical value of the security. This proposed text is based on paragraph (c)(1)(C) of the current Rule, without substantive change, and is consistent with paragraph (d)(3) of the current Rule, which permits using a Revised CEE Reference Price when “necessary for the maintenance of a fair and orderly market and the protection of investors and the public interest.”
The second sentence of proposed subparagraph (B) under Case 4 would incorporate rule text from current Rule 7.10(c)(1)(C) about how the Exchange would determine the Revised CEE Reference Price in the instances described in subparagraph (A)(4) above. It would provide that: “With respect to transactions that involved a corporate action or new issue, the Exchange would consider a number of factors to determine a Revised CEE Reference Price that is based on the theoretical value of the security, including but not limited to, the offering price of the new issue, the ratio of the stock split applied to the prior day's closing price, the theoretical price derived from the numerical terms of the corporate action transaction such as the exchange ratio and spin-off terms, and for an OTC up-listing, the price of the security as provided in the prior day's FINRA Trade Dissemination Service final closing report.” This language is based on paragraph (c)(1)(C) and the first two sentences of paragraph (d)(2) of the current Rule, without substantive alteration.
The third sentence of proposed subparagraph (B) under Case 4 would incorporate rule text from current Rule 7.10(c)(1)(C) and (d)(2) about how the Exchange would determine the Revised CEE Reference Price in the instances described in subparagraph (A)(5) above. It would provide that: “With respect to transactions that involved a security that entered a Trading Pause pursuant to the LULD Plan and resumed trading without an auction, the Exchange may use the last effective upper or lower Price Band that triggered the limit state before the Trading Pause or another appropriate Revised CEE Reference Price.” This language is based on the last sentence of paragraph (d)(2) of the current Rule, but substitutes the phrase “the last effective upper or lower Price Band that triggered the limit state before the Trading Pause” for the current text (“the last effective Price Band that was in a limit state before the Trading Pause”). The Exchange believes that the addition of the words “upper,” “lower,” and “triggered” adds further specification to the situation described in the current Rule. In addition, the Exchange proposes to add the language “or another appropriate Revised CEE Reference Price” because although the Price Band that triggered the LULD Trading Pause may be a reasonable indicator of the theoretical value of the security at the time of the LULD Trading Pause, trading following the LULD Trading Pause (albeit without a re-opening auction) may suggest that another price may be more appropriate.
Proposed subparagraph (C) under Case 4 would specify that a “Case 4 transaction shall be found to be clearly erroneous if the price of the transaction to buy (sell) is greater than (less than) the Revised CEE Reference Price by an amount that equals or exceeds the Percentage Parameters.” This language is based on paragraph (c)(1)(C) of the current Rule with two alterations.
