Case 5A—Numerical Guideline Requirement
Proposed Case 5A (subparagraph (b)(6)(A)) would describe the first of the two situations in which the transaction under Case 5 shall be found to be clearly erroneous, namely, when, “[s]ubject to the additional factors described below in this Case 5A, the price of the transaction to buy (sell) that is the subject of the complaint is greater than (less than) the Reference Price by an amount that equals or exceeds the Numerical Guidelines set forth below.” This language is based on paragraph (c)(2)(A) of the current Rule, without substantive change.
The “Additional Factors” included in Case 5A is substantively identical to paragraph (c)(2)(C) of the current Rule, and would provide that “an Officer may also consider additional factors to determine whether an execution is clearly erroneous, provided the execution occurred during the Early Trading Session or during LULD Protected Hours in NMS Stocks not subject to the LULD Plan. Such additional factors include, but are not limited to, system malfunctions or disruptions, volume and volatility for the security, derivative securities products that correspond to greater than 100% in the direction of a tracking index, news released for the security, whether trading in the security was recently halted/resumed, whether the security is an IPO, whether the security was subject to a stock-split, reorganization, or other corporate action, overall market conditions, executions outside of the Core Trading Session, validity of the consolidated tapes trades and quotes, consideration of primary market indications, and executions inconsistent with the trading pattern in the stock. Each additional factor will be considered with a view toward maintaining a fair and orderly market and the protection of investors and the public interest.”
Consistent with current practice, when the Exchange considers these additional factors, it typically looks for a representation in the clearly erroneous filing indicating the existence of an error. Such errors may include, for example, a system malfunction or disruption (such as at the Exchange, trade reporting facility, data processor, or market participant), which resulted in incorrect market data or executions, incorrect processing of a corporate action, or a typographical error in the material terms of an order.
Proposed subparagraph (A) under Case 5A would also incorporate the table from current paragraph (c)(2)(A), with the following alteration. The two rows in the current table concerning Multi Stock Events (

Case 5B—Multi-Stock Events
Proposed Case 5B (subparagraph (b)(6)(B)) would describe the second of the two situations in which the transaction under Case 5 may be found to be clearly erroneous, namely, Multi-Stock Events.
As an initial matter, the current version of Rule 7.10 contains two scenarios involving “Multi Stock Events”: (1) “filings involving five or more, but less than twenty, securities whose executions occurred within a period of five minutes or less,” and (2) filings involving twenty or more securities whose executions occurred within a period of five minutes or less.” The Exchange believes that the numbers of affected securities referenced in those scenarios are now too low to justify special treatment, and that events of such size are more properly analyzed on a security-by-security basis by applying the Case 1 through Case 5A as discussed above.
The Exchange proposes instead that an event should be treated as a “Multi-Stock Event” only if it involves 50 or more securities whose executions occurred within 5 minutes. The Exchange believes that 50 securities is a more appropriate trigger for the application of the Multi-Stock Event rule. The 20-security threshold in the current Rule has not been updated since 2010,
[
26

(c) Procedures
Finally, the Exchange proposes to reorganize all rule text about the procedures under the clearly erroneous rule in to a revised paragraph (c). In the current Rule, such procedures are split across paragraphs (b), (c), (e), and (f). The Exchange believes that reorganizing all of the procedures into one area of the Rule will enhance the clarity and comprehension of the Rule.
The Exchange proposes to organize the procedures into two categories: “Review Procedures” in subparagraph (1) and “Appeals” in subparagraph (2).
(c)(1)—Review Procedures
Proposed subparagraph (c)(1) would set out all the procedures for the review of potentially clearly erroneous transactions.
Request for Review by Member Organization
Proposed subparagraph (c)(1)(A), titled “Request for Review by Member Organization,” would set forth the procedures for reviewing a transaction when a member organization requests such review.
Proposed subparagraph (c)(1)(A)(1) would be titled “General.” The first sentence would provide: “A member organization may request that the Exchange review a transaction for its own account or for its customer's account under the Rule.” This language is based on the first sentence of paragraph (b) of the current Rule, except that it omits the phrase “
submitted erroneously
” as used in the current Rule. This change would clarify that a member organization may request review of any transaction. Whether the transaction is “erroneous” would be determined by the review process, and a belief that it was “submitted erroneously” should not be a precursor to requesting review.
The second sentence of proposed subparagraph (c)(1)(A)(1) would provide: “Member organizations are responsible for submitting valid requests for review to the Exchange within the timeframes set out below.” This language does not appear in the current version of the Rule, but the Exchange proposes to include it in the revised version to add specificity to the review procedure.
The third and fourth sentences of proposed subparagraph (c)(1)(A)(1) would provide: “An Officer will review the transaction under dispute and determine whether it is clearly erroneous, with a view toward maintaining a fair and orderly market and the protection of investors and the public interest. Such request for review will be made in writing via email or other electronic means specified from time to time by the Exchange in a circular distributed to member organizations.” This language is based on the second and third sentences of paragraph (b) of the current Rule, without substantive change.
Proposed subparagraph (c)(1)(A)(2) would be titled “Timing of Requests for Review.” Proposed subparagraph (c)(1)(A)(2)(a) would be titled “General” and would provide: “Requests for review must be received by the Exchange within 30 minutes of execution time and will include information concerning the time of the transaction(s), security symbol(s), number of shares, price(s), side (bought or sold), and the factual basis for believing that the trade is clearly erroneous. Upon receipt of a timely filed request, the counterparty to the trade will be notified by the Exchange as soon as practicable, but generally within 30 minutes. An Officer may request additional supporting written information to aid in the resolution of the matter. If requested, each party to the transaction will provide, within 30 minutes of the request, any supporting written information. Either party to the disputed trade may request supporting written information provided by the other party on the matter.” This language is identical to the paragraph (b)(1) of the current Rule, except for the following differences. The current Rule is limited to “receipt of a timely filed request
that satisfies the numerical guidelines set forth in Section (c)(1) of this Rule
,” but in the proposed Rule, the Numerical Guidelines would apply only to Case 5A. The Exchange believes that the clarity of the Rule would be enhanced by removing the limitation, making clear that proposed subparagraph (c)(1)(A)(2)(a) applies to all requests for review under any Case.

A determination will be made generally within 30 minutes of receipt of the complaint, but in no case later than 8:30 a.m. Eastern Time on the following trading day. The parties will be promptly notified of the determination.” This language is based on the third, fourth, and fifth sentences of current paragraph (e)(1) (and similar language in current paragraphs (g) and (i)), without substantive change, except the Exchange proposes the 8:30 a.m. Eastern Time deadline instead of “the start of Core Trading” (as paragraph (e)(1) currently provides) in light of T+1 settlement.
Officer Acting On Own Motion
Proposed subparagraph (c)(1)(B), titled “Officer Acting On Own Motion,” would be substantively identical to paragraph (f) of the current Rule, with updated cross-references. Specifically, in the first sentence, the Exchange proposes to replace the current text's reference to “during the Early Trading Session or during LULD Protected Hours in NMS Stocks not subject to the LULD Plan” with “pursuant to paragraph (b) above.” In the second sentence, the Exchange proposes to replace the current text's reference to “paragraphs (c)(1) and (c)(2)” with an updated reference to “paragraph (b).” In the fourth sentence, the Exchange proposes to replace the current text's reference to “the start of Core Trading” to “no later than 8:30 Eastern Time” in light of T+1 settlement. In the last sentence, the Exchange proposes to delete the phrase “[w]hen such action is taken independently” from the current text as extraneous, and proposes to replace the current cross-reference to the appeal provisions in “subsection (e)(2)-(4) above” with a cross reference to “paragraph (c)(2) below.” None of these changes is substantive.
Cross-Market Coordination
The Exchange proposes to add a new provision as paragraph (c)(1)(C), titled “Cross-Market Coordination.”
The Exchange proposes that subparagraph (c)(1)(C)(1) would provide: “Regarding events involving trading activity on multiple SROs, the Exchange will use reasonable efforts as appropriate to coordinate with other SROs regarding the Exchange's determinations, if any, about (a) whether transactions occurred outside of available and correct Price Bands, (b) whether the LULD Price Bands or LULD Reference Price are erroneous, (c) what CEE Reference Price or Revised CEE Reference Price to use, and (d) issues related to Multi-Stock Events.” The proposed language reflects the Exchange's existing practice of coordinating with other SROs on such topics whenever a market event involving trading activity on multiple SROs raises questions about the availability of clearly erroneous review. Cross-exchange coordination is already reflected in the current rule text applicable to Multi-Stock Events and Multi-Day Events, and in practice, the exchanges currently coordinate with each other about additional aspects of market-wide events. The proposed rule text synthesizes the existing rule text and the Exchange's current practices, making explicit the Exchange's practice of using reasonable efforts as appropriate to coordinate with other markets on such issues.
The Exchange proposes that subparagraph (c)(1)(C)(2) would provide: “Regarding events involving trading activity on multiple SROs, if another SRO receives a valid request to review a transaction(s) as clearly erroneous and coordinates with the Exchange about such request, an Officer may declare transactions on the Exchange that meet the same criteria to be clearly erroneous on his or her own motion, pursuant to paragraph (c)(1)(B) above.” The proposed language reflects the Exchange's existing practice of acting on its Officer's own motion to declare transactions clearly erroneous based on criteria agreed upon as a result of coordination with other affected exchanges.
[
28
]
In light of these proposed provisions about cross-market coordination, the Exchange proposes to delete current paragraph (b)(2), which is titled “Routed Executions.” That provision currently provides that “[o]ther market centers will generally have an additional 30 minutes from receipt of their participant's timely filing, but no longer than 60 minutes from the time of the execution at issue, to file with the Exchange for review of transactions routed to the Exchange from that market center and executed on the Exchange.” This provision predates the Exchange's current practice of coordinating with other SROs whenever a market event involving trading activity on multiple SROs raises questions about the availability of clearly erroneous review,
(
printed page 66901)
regardless of whether particular orders had been routed to particular exchanges. As such, the Exchange believes that the language in current paragraph (b)(2) setting a particular time limit to consider routed orders is unnecessarily limiting, and proposes instead to replace current paragraph (b)(2) with the procedures regarding cross-market collaboration in proposed subparagraph (c)(1)(C).
(c)(2)—Appeals
Proposed subparagraph (c)(2) would set out the appeal procedures for clearly erroneous review. This proposed subparagraph would be identical to current paragraph (e)(2)-(6), with the following alterations.
First, the Exchange proposes to renumber the several subparagraphs of the Rule. Current subparagraph (e)(3), (e)(4), (e)(5), and (e)(6) would become proposed subparagraphs (c)(2)(C), (c)(2)(D), (c)(2)(E), and (c)(2)(F), respectively.
Second, the reference in current paragraph (e)(2) to decisions “under paragraph (g)” would be updated to refer to “Case 2,” and the current reference to “applicable Price Bands” would be updated to refer to “available and correct Price Bands,” which is the language used in proposed Case 2.
Third, the Exchange proposes to reduce the number of member organization representatives that must be designated to serve on the CEE Panel to 5 (in proposed subparagraph (c)(2)(B)), from 10 (in current paragraph (e)(2)(B). The Exchange notes that in practice, appeals from clearly erroneous determination are quite rare and the CEE Panel meets infrequently. The requirement to have 10 member organization representatives at the ready for such a small number of appeals has become excessive, and accordingly, the Exchange proposes to recalibrate that number to better reflect the actual need for CEE Panel members currently.
Fourth, the Exchange proposes to change the time for the CEE Panel to render a decision from “no later than the trading day following the date of the execution under review” (in current paragraph (e)(3)) to “no later than 8:30 a.m. Eastern Time on the trading day following the date of the execution under review.” The Exchange proposes this 8:30 a.m. Eastern Time deadline in light of T+1 settlement.
Fifth, the cross-reference to “Rule 7.10(E)(1)” in current subparagraph (e)(5) would be updated in proposed subparagraph (c)(2)(E) to refer instead to “paragraph (c)(1)(A) or (B).”
Implementation
The Exchange will publish a trader notice before implementing the proposed changes.
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the requirements of Section 6(b) of the Act,
[
29
]
in general, and Section 6(b)(5) of the Act,
[
30
]
in particular, in that it is designed to remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system, to promote just and equitable principles of trade, and, in general, to protect investors and the public interest and not to permit unfair discrimination between customers, issuers, brokers, or dealers.
Reorganization.
The Exchange believes that it is consistent with just and equitable principles of trade to reorganize Rule 7.10 into three clear subsections addressing (a) Definitions, (b) Availability of Clearly Erroneous Review, and (c) Procedures, as proposed here. The current Rule is an amalgam of rule text originating in 2010, 2013, 2014, 2022, and 2026, and has not been comprehensively reorganized since its inception. The Exchange believes that the clarity of the Rule can be enhanced and improved by the reorganizing the Rule and gathering similar provisions together. In addition, the Exchange believes that identifying each situation in which clearly erroneous review is available and assigning such situations with easy-to-identify Case numbers will make it easier for market participants to navigate, understand, and use the Rule.
Definitions.
The Exchange believes that it is consistent with just and equitable principles of trade to include in proposed paragraph (a), “Definitions,” definitions of all terms used within the Rule, and to move definitions that previously existed elsewhere in the Rule to the “Definitions” section in paragraph (a). The Exchange believes that gathering definitions in one paragraph at the start of the Rule will enhance the ability of market participants to navigate, understand, and use the Rule, and minimize the amount of cross-referencing that market participants must do in order to comprehend and apply the Rule text.
Cases 1 and 2 and the Elimination of Inconsistent and Duplicative Provisions.
The Exchange believes it is consistent with just and equitable principles of trade and with the protection of investors and the public interest to delete from the Rule the provisions of current paragraph (c)(1)(B) that direct the Exchange to perform an analysis using Percentage Parameters in cases where a transaction occurred outside of LULD Price bands pursuant current to paragraph (g) or during a regulatory halt, suspension, or pause pursuant to current paragraph (i). As noted above, the reference to Percentage Parameters in such cases was added to the Rule as part of the 2022 Amendment, and appears to be inconsistent with preexisting requirements of paragraphs (g) and (i), which require the Exchange to nullify such transactions without regard to Percentage Parameters. The Exchange believes that the approach in paragraphs (g) and (i)—which have been part of the clearly erroneous rule since 2013 and 2014 respectively
[
31
]
—should be maintained and thus proposes in Cases 1 and 2 that transactions executed outside of LULD Bands or during a trading halt, suspension, or pause should be nullified without further analysis.
Cases 3 and 4 Covering Unavailable, Missing, and Erroneous LULD Price Bands.
The Exchange believes that it is consistent with just and equitable principles of trade and with the protection of investors and the public interest to add rule text making explicit that clearly erroneous review is available in the cases of unavailable or missing LULD Price Bands (proposed Case 3) and erroneous LULD Price Bands (proposed Case 4). As explained above, current paragraph (c)(1)(B) provides that clearly erroneous review is available if the transaction “was executed at a time when Price Bands under the LULD Plan were not available,” and the Exchange's Rule 19b-4 filing in support of the 2022 Amendment explained that clearly erroneous review should be available to act as a “backstop” to the LULD Plan during the Core Trading Session in situations where there is “some issue with processing the Price Bands.”
[
32
]
The proposed addition of Cases 3 and 4 would make explicit that the “issue[s] with processing the Price Bands” referred to in the Exchange's Rule 19b-4 filing include cases where the Price Bands are unavailable because the first Price Bands had not yet been received after a security's opening or reopening, the Price Bands are missing, or the Price Bands were available but erroneous. As such, this proposed change is not substantive, but would be a clarification of the existing rule text and rationale.
(
printed page 66902)
Case 5B—Multi-Stock Events.
The Exchange believes that it is consistent with just and equitable principles of trade to combine the two Multi-Stock Events currently codified in Rule 7.10 into proposed Case 5B, which sets forth a single standard of review for erroneous transactions involving at least 50 securities occurring outside of the Core Trading Session over a five-minute period. Rather than having two separate criteria for reviewing Multi-Stock Events, which occur infrequently, the Exchange believes that moving to one set of criteria would provide a more uniform application of the Rule and enable the Exchange to respond more efficiently during situations where a large number of transactions across multiple securities are under review.
Procedures.
The Exchange believes that it is consistent with equitable principles of trade and with the protection of investors and the public interest to make the proposed clarifying changes to the procedures for clearly erroneous review, as described above. In particular, the Exchange believes that referring in the proposed Rule to its existing procedures regarding cross-market coordination on events involving trading activity on multiple SROs would provide greater certainty and clarity to market participants about the clearly erroneous review process.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change would impose any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. The proposal would ensure the continued, uninterrupted operation of harmonized clearly erroneous execution rules across the U.S. equities markets while also amending those rules to provide greater certainty to SROs, member organizations, and investors regarding the particular Cases where clearly erroneous review is available. The Exchange understands that the other national securities exchanges and FINRA will also file similar proposals, the substance of which are identical to this proposal. Thus, the proposed rule change will help to ensure consistency across SROs without implicating any competitive issues.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
No written comments were solicited or received with respect to the proposed rule change.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
Within 45 days of the date of publication of this notice in the
Federal Register
or within such longer period up to 90 days (i) as the Commission may designate if it finds such longer period to be appropriate and publishes its reasons for so finding or (ii) as to which the self-regulatory organization consents, the Commission will:
(A) by order approve or disapprove the proposed rule change, or
(B) institute proceedings to determine whether the proposed rule change should be disapproved.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
); or
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
.
Please include file number SR-NYSE-2026-50 on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
All submissions should refer to file number SR-NYSE-2026-50. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
). Copies of the filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of the Exchange. Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection. All submissions should refer to file number SR-NYSE-2026-50 and should be submitted on or before November 13, 2026.
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.
[
33
]
Sherry R. Haywood,
Assistant Secretary.

full_text:

Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106703; File No. SR-OCC-2026-010]
October 20, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Exchange Act” or “Act”),
[
1
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
2
]
notice is hereby given that on October 8, 2026, The Options Clearing Corporation (“OCC” or “Corporation”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I, II, and III below, which Items have been prepared primarily by OCC. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Clearing Agency's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
This proposed rule change would amend OCC Rule 213—Cybersecurity Obligations (“Rule 213”) to further enhance OCC's security protocols and promote resiliency in OCC's approach to assessing and managing cybersecurity risks. OCC's proposed changes to Rule 213 would, among other things, (i) establish the concept of a “Major Clearing Member System Event,” in which OCC would be authorized to take certain action, including disconnection of a Clearing Member, or its Third-Party Service Provider, connected to OCC's Systems (as defined below); (ii) enhance the requirements of a Clearing Member to notify OCC in the event of a Security Incident (which would be redefined as a “Clearing Member System Event”); (iii) remove language that invites a Clearing Member to assess potential impact of a Clearing Member System Event on OCC's Systems and clarify OCC's authority to assess such incident and determine impact; (iv) provide OCC with the authority to inform, or require the Clearing Member to inform, the Clearing Member's Third-Party Service Provider (as defined below) of the Clearing Member System Event; (v) update and add defined terms used throughout Rule 213; and (vi) incorporate other reporting, testing and approval requirements, process, obligations, and governance necessary for reconnection.
The proposed changes to OCC Rule 213 are contained in Exhibit 5 to File No. SR-OCC-2026-010. Material proposed to be added is marked by underlining and material proposed to be deleted is marked with strikethrough text. All terms with initial capitalization that are not otherwise defined herein have the same meaning as set forth in the OCC By-Laws and Rules.
[
3
]
II. Clearing Agency's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, OCC included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. OCC has prepared summaries, set forth in sections (A), (B), and (C) below, of the most significant aspects of these statements.
(A) Clearing Agency's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
Background
OCC is the sole clearing agency for standardized equity options listed on national securities exchanges registered with the Commission. OCC provides clearing services for options on equities, indices, Exchange Traded Funds (“ETFs”), for certain transactions in futures and options on futures, and for certain stock loan transactions. Organizations become OCC Clearing Members to facilitate the clearing and settlement of their customer transactions or proprietary transactions through OCC. More specifically, in its role as a clearing agency, OCC guarantees the performance of its Clearing Members for all transactions cleared by OCC by becoming the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer (or the lender to every borrower and the borrower to every lender, in the case of stock loan transactions). In 2012, OCC was designated as a systemically important financial market utility (“SIFMU”) by the Financial Stability Oversight Council pursuant to Title VIII of the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act of 2010 (“Dodd-Frank Act”).
[
4
]
Such designation highlights the critical role that OCC plays in ensuring the stability and integrity of the financial markets.
Based on OCC's interconnections with its Clearing Members and with its Clearing Member's Third-Party Service Provider connected to OCC's Systems, OCC is exposed to various cybersecurity risks. Such cybersecurity risks have the potential to impact OCC, as well as market participants, as a cybersecurity attack on OCC may lead to the loss of data or system integrity, unauthorized disclosure of sensitive information, or an inability to conduct essential clearance and settlement functions. Moreover, as a SIFMU, a failure or disruption to OCC could threaten the stability of the financial system in the United States. Therefore, OCC believes it is prudent to enhance the cybersecurity notification obligations of its Clearing Members and strengthen OCC's ability to protect against and respond to such events to safeguard OCC's Systems and information against cyberattacks.
(
printed page 66880)
In November 2023, OCC received approval
[
5
]
from the Commission to amend certain provisions in OCC's Rules relating to a Clearing Member's obligation to address a “Security Incident” (currently defined as the occurrence of a cyber-related disruption or intrusion of a Clearing Member's systems that is reasonably likely to pose an imminent risk or threat to OCC's operations). The amended provisions became OCC's existing Rule 213, which established, among other things: (i) notification requirements of a Clearing Member in the event of a Security Incident and (ii) OCC's security requirements for the reconnection process of a Clearing Member following a Security Incident that results in a Clearing Member's disconnection.
In recent years, OCC has received Rule 213 notifications, however, none have impacted OCC. OCC monitors the threat landscape on an ongoing basis, maintaining a dedicated threat intelligence team responsible for monitoring the activities of threat actors targeting the financial services industry. Through this monitoring, OCC has observed an increase in the frequency and elevated risk of cyber events targeting the industry and the broader marketplace. Considering OCC's experience receiving Rule 213 notifications, together with the increasing frequency and elevated risk of cyber events in the financial services industry at large, OCC has identified opportunities for additional enhancements to Rule 213. Though no specific triggering event necessitated these enhancements, OCC's actions are proactive, taken in light of the elevated risk environment across the industry.
1. Purpose
OCC's proposed amendments to Rule 213 are intended to further promote resiliency, strengthen OCC's cybersecurity protocols, and maintain consistency with industry standards, including by aligning OCC's Rules with recent rule amendments
[
6
]
of similarly situated self-regulatory organizations (“SROs”) with overlapping membership with OCC. Among other things, OCC's proposed enhancements to Rule 213 would:
Add a defined terms section to Rule 213, including defining OCC's “Systems” to include not only direct connections, but also established communication channels (
e.g.,
access to File Transfer Protocols (“FTPs”) for transmitting data or instructions that may be compromised by a systems intrusion to a Clearing Member's back-office systems);
Require the Cybersecurity Confirmation to be signed by a senior executive of the Clearing Member or applicant who is authorized to attest to such matters;
Remove language that invites a Clearing Member to assess the potential impact of a Clearing Member System Event on OCC's Systems and operations when determining whether such incident is reportable, specify the timeframe in which OCC requires a Clearing Member System Event to be reported, and identify the specific information a Clearing Member must include in such notice;
Establish the concept of a “Major Clearing Member System Event,” including a declaration requiring the approval of two or more Designated Officers and prompt notification to the Chairman of the Board of Directors;
Reorganize and clarify OCC's authority to take action in response to a Clearing Member System Event, including specifying the actions that constitute a “disconnect,” and clarify a Clearing Member's related cooperation obligations;
Add provisions incorporating the reporting, testing, and approval requirements, process, obligations, and governance necessary for reconnection, including the ability for OCC to require an audit report from a Third-Party Cybersecurity Firm; and
Provide OCC with the authority to inform, or require the Clearing Member to inform, the Clearing Member's Third-Party Service Provider of the Clearing Member System Event if OCC determines, in its discretion, that such action is necessary for the protection of OCC and other Clearing Members.
As described in more detail below, OCC believes its proposed changes will strengthen OCC's security protocols by enhancing Rule 213 to be more efficient, effective and clear in its cybersecurity obligations of Clearing Members so that OCC may better address cybersecurity risks to protect OCC and its Clearing Members. Furthermore, OCC believes its proposed changes will enable OCC's Clearing Members to better understand and prepare for their obligations to OCC as it relates to a cybersecurity event.
Proposed Changes
Proposed Rule 213(a)

—Defined Terms
First, OCC proposes to introduce new section (a) titled “Defined Terms.” To strengthen the provisions of proposed Rule 213 and further clarify OCC's requirements related to the cybersecurity obligations of a Clearing Member, OCC proposes to define several terms specifically for the purposes of Rule 213.
[

OCC's proposed changes would:
Define “Best Practices” to mean policies, procedures, practices or similar standards and guidelines that are reasonably designed and consistent with then current financial-sector cybersecurity standards issued by an authoritative body that is a U.S. governmental entity or agency, an association of a U.S. governmental entity or agency, or a widely recognized industry organization. The purpose of defining “Best Practices” is to clarify the standards that OCC would require a Third-Party Cybersecurity Firm to employ when such firm is engaged, as would be required by OCC Rule 213 as discussed further below. OCC's proposed definition of “Best Practices” aligns with Section 1001(a)(4) of the Commission's Regulation Systems Compliance and Integrity (“Reg SCI”).
[

]
Delete OCC's existing definition of a “Security Incident” and replace it with “Clearing Member System Event.” OCC proposes to define a “Clearing Member System Event” to mean an incident resulting from the unintended or unauthorized access to, or the malfunction or corruption (whether partial or total) of one or more systems, of a Clearing Member or its Third-Party Service Provider, connected to OCC's Systems. The purpose of re-defining the concept of a “Security Incident” to a “Clearing Member System Event” is to capture only those disruptions to systems connected to OCC's Systems, whether via an established communication channel from a Clearing Member, or through the Clearing Member's Third-Party Service Provider; it is not intended to capture every disruption to every system of the Clearing Member or its Third-Party Service Provider. In addition, as described in further detail in section (d) of proposed Rule 213, OCC proposes to eliminate the existing definition of a
(
printed page 66881)
“Security Incident” to remove language that invites Clearing Members to assess the potential impact of such incident on OCC's Systems and operations when determining whether an incident is reportable. OCC's existing definition of a “Security Incident,” is defined, in part, as an incident, or an incident that is occurring, involving a cyber-related disruption or intrusion of the Clearing Member's systems that is reasonably likely to pose an imminent risk or threat to OCC's operations. OCC believes the language in the existing definition invites Clearing Members to assess whether such incident to their systems would impact OCC, and therefore OCC proposes to eliminate the definition of “Security Incident” and replace the definition with “Clearing Member System Event” in proposed Rule 213.
Define “OCC's Systems” to mean the systems, equipment and technology networks of OCC, whether owned, leased, or licensed, and including software, hardware, applications, devices, IP addresses, or other addresses or accounts used in an established communication channel with such systems, equipment and technology networks, to provide the services set forth in these Rules, or otherwise used to transact business or connect with OCC. OCC proposes to introduce the definition of “OCC's Systems” for the purposes of Rule 213 to articulate OCC's potentially impacted connections and any means of connectivity in the event of a Clearing Member System Event. OCC's proposed definition incorporates not only direct connections but also references “established communication channels,” which OCC believes may include access to File Transfer Protocol (“FTPs”) for transmitting data or instructions that may be compromised by a systems intrusion to a Clearing Member's back-office systems.
Define a “Major Clearing Member System Event” to mean a Clearing Member System Event that has or is reasonably anticipated to, for example, disrupt, degrade, cause a delay in, interrupt or otherwise alter the normal operation of OCC's Systems; result in unauthorized access to OCC's Systems; result in the loss of control of, disclosure of, or loss of OCC's Confidential Information; or cause a strain on, loss of, or overall threat to the OCC's resources, functions, security or operations. The purpose of establishing the concept of a “Major Clearing Member System Event,” is to tie the disruption at issue to its effect on the normal operations of OCC. This concept introduces a threshold level in which OCC would be authorized to take action, including disconnection, in the event OCC determines that a Clearing Member System Event rises to the level of a Major Clearing Member System Event.
[

OCC believes the concept of a “Major Clearing Member System Event” will strengthen OCC's security protocols by establishing a baseline by which OCC can measure the disruption at issue against its impact on OCC and, as described in further detail below, take action to mitigate risks presented.
Define “Third-Party Cybersecurity Firm” to mean a firm that, in OCC's reasonable judgement, (A) (i) is well-known and reputable; (ii) is not the subject Clearing Member, or an affiliate or a Third-Party Service Provider of the subject Clearing Member; (iii) is experienced in financial-sector cybersecurity; and (iv) employs Best Practices; or (B) is otherwise determined to be a Third-Party Cybersecurity Firm by OCC. OCC proposes to include this definition to clearly describe the type of firm that OCC would require the subject Clearing Member to engage under proposed Rule 213(g)(3).
Define “Third-Party Service Provider” to mean an affiliate of any Clearing Member, service bureau or other similar entity, that connects to OCC's Systems on behalf of or for the benefit of a Clearing Member. This proposed definition would help clarify that OCC Rule 213 applies to a Clearing Member's Third-Party Service Provider's connections to OCC's Systems.
Proposed Rule 213(b)—Cybersecurity Confirmation Submission
Proposed Rule 213(b) incorporates the provision from existing Rule 213(a)(ii) into proposed Rule 213(b)(1) to promote clarification and efficiency. Proposed Rule 213(b) also makes other conforming and non-substantive changes, including reorganizing provisions into a hierarchical structure, and updating language to promote clarity and efficiency.
Existing Rule 213(a) requires Clearing Members and clearing membership applicants to periodically submit a form, provided by OCC, confirming, in part, that they have a cybersecurity program in place (“Cybersecurity Confirmation”). Sections (i) and (ii) of existing Rule 213(a) require that applicants must submit it with their application, and existing Clearing Members must resubmit it at least every two years, within 180 days of the OCC's notice requiring attestation. OCC's proposed changes streamline existing Rule 213(a) into proposed Rule 213(b)(1) by combining the general description of the Cybersecurity Confirmation requirement with the specific timing obligation applicable to Clearing Members into a single paragraph. Specifically, OCC's proposed Rule 213(b)(1) would provide, in part, that each Clearing Member must complete and submit “an attestation at least every two years, and not later than 180 calendar days from the date that OCC notifies the Clearing Member that the attestation is required.” In addition, proposed Rule 213(b)(1) would remove the reference to the phrase “applicant for clearing membership” as OCC believes such language is duplicative since it is included in the subsequent provision in proposed Rule 213(b)(2). OCC's proposed changes replace the term “shall” with “must” in proposed Rule 213(b)(1) and proposed Rule 213(b)(2) to promote stronger cadence and readability. OCC's proposed changes also eliminate the specific reference to the word “form” after “attestation.” The concept of a “form” and an “attestation” may introduce different meanings, so this proposed change is intended to eliminate ambiguity and maintain consistency with OCC's referenced term, “Cybersecurity Confirmation.” OCC also proposes to eliminate the reference that the attestation is “provided by the Corporation” because OCC believes this is unnecessary to specify. Finally, OCC proposes to remove the word “materials” in proposed Rule 213(b)(2) to promote efficiency.

Proposed Rule 213(d)—Occurrence of a Clearing Member System Event
OCC's proposed Rule 213(d) would introduce enhanced notification requirements for a Clearing Member in the event of a Clearing Member System Event. More specifically, OCC's proposed changes would introduce a particular timeframe required for Clearing Members to report such incident and specify the information that must be included in the notification.
First, as referenced above in the proposed “Defined Terms” section, OCC proposes to re-define and broaden the definition of “Security Incident” to “Clearing Member System Event.” In alignment with this proposed change, OCC would also eliminate the existing definition of a “Security Incident” in proposed Rule 213(d), which states in part, that such incident is one that is occurring involving a cyber related disruption or intrusion of the Clearing Member's systems that is reasonably likely to pose an imminent risk or threat to OCC's operations.
Second, OCC's proposed changes would require that a Clearing Member experiencing a Clearing Member System Event must notify OCC immediately “in writing, but no later than two hours” after the Clearing Member becomes aware or should be aware that there has been a Clearing Member System Event. The purpose of including a specific timeframe of two hours for which a Clearing Member System Event must be reported is to clarify OCC's existing standard of “immediate” in order to help mitigate the risk presented by a Clearing Member or its Third-Party Service Provider that is experiencing such incident.
[
12
]
OCC believes that the term “immediately,” standing alone, may be interpreted differently and therefore could create uncertainty and inconsistent compliance. By pairing “immediately” with a definite, objective two-hour limit, OCC's Clearing Members will have a clear, unambiguous benchmark for timely notification. By receiving notification of a Clearing Member System Event within two hours of its occurrence, OCC believes it will be able to address and respond to such event in a timely manner and take proactive steps to reduce any future risk presented to OCC and its Clearing Members. If a Clearing Member does not report a Clearing Member System Event within the notification timeframe set forth in section (d), OCC will evaluate the facts and circumstances of the delay in notification to determine whether a rule violation has occurred that is subject to OCC's disciplinary process under Chapter XII of OCC's Rules.
Third, OCC's proposed changes require that notification of proposed section 213(d) must, at a minimum include the following information (as described below), and any such information unconfirmed or otherwise unknown may be identified by the Clearing Member as “Unknown.” OCC's existing Rule 213 does not expressly set out requirements for what to include in a notification of a Clearing Member System Event. While OCC already obtains the required information outlined out in proposed Rule 213(d) through its existing practice, the required information is not memorialized in OCC's Rules, policies, or procedures. This practice has historically included, among other things, requests regarding the legal entity name of the Clearing Member, contact information of individuals authorized to act on its behalf, and key details of the incident such as its nature, status, systems or data affected, and remediation steps taken. OCC typically obtains this information from the Clearing Member via phone or email, depending on the circumstances. This information is generally gathered over the course of OCC's engagement with the Clearing Member as the incident develops and the Clearing Member's own understanding of the incident evolves, rather than all at once at the onset of the incident. As such, the purpose of proposed section 213(d) is to codify what OCC already expects in practice, so that all Clearing Members are aware, in advance, of the information required to be included when reporting a Rule 213 incident.
OCC's proposed changes provide that the information required to be in the notice, if known, include: (i) the legal entity name of the Clearing Member or its Third-Party Service Provider affected by the Clearing Member System Event, (ii) contact information of individuals who are authorized to act on behalf of the subject Clearing Member regarding the Clearing Member System Event, and (iii) key details of the Clearing Member System Event such as event type, event effect, start date, end date, discovery date, scope, and any other notices given that would help to provide additional context of the Clearing Member System Event. As discussed above, OCC's existing Rule 213 does not expressly set out requirements for what information must be included in a notification of a Clearing Member System Event. In practice, OCC would obtain the same details identified in proposed section 213(d), but not all at once and not in the formal manner that proposed section 213(d) establishes.
OCC's proposed changes to Rule 213(d) would provide that the information required in the notice related to “Legal Entities” would include a complete list of the legal entity names of the Clearing Member and any Third-Party Service Providers experiencing or otherwise affected or potentially affected by the Clearing Member System Event. In addition, OCC's proposed changes would require that information required in the notice related to “Contact Information” would include list of persons—with their corresponding titles, primary email addresses and phone numbers, and if those primary email addresses and phone numbers are associated with the systems that are the subject of the Clearing Member System Event, alternate email addresses and phone numbers—who are authorized to act on behalf of the subject Clearing Member regarding the Clearing Member System

(A) Event Type—the type of Clearing Member System Event, for example an insider threat, phishing attack, Man-in-the-Middle (“MITM”)

attack, privilege escalation, denial of service, external threat, malware, unauthorized access, ransomware, compromised user account, SQL injections, brute force attack, system compromise, supply chain attacks (as each term is commonly understood by cybersecurity professionals in the financial sector), or other with a provided explanation;
(B) Event Effect—perceived, anticipated, or known effect of the Clearing Member System Event, for example, loss of communication, data corruption, security breach, or other with a provided explanation;
(C) Start Date—date and time when the Clearing Member System Event began;
(D) End Date—date and time when the Clearing Member System Event ended, if applicable;
(E) Discovery Date—date and time when the Clearing Member System Event was first identified;
(F) Scope—scope of the Clearing Member System Event, including, but not limited to, a list of each affected or likely affected system or data, including OCC's Systems and data, the degree of such affect, and any supporting evidence of such; and
(G) Notices—whether any formal or informal notices or information regarding the Clearing Member System Event was made public and, if so, provide a copy of such notices or information.
The purpose of these proposed changes is to codify OCC's expectations to increase transparency around OCC's existing process. More specifically, OCC's proposed changes codify, within Rule 213(d), the information that OCC has historically requested from Clearing Members during a Rule 213 event. Currently, OCC receives this information from Clearing Members upon request during a Rule 213 event as an incident unfolds, rather than receiving a standardized set of information upfront. By codifying OCC's expectations directly in this Rule, OCC intends to increase transparency and ensure that all Clearing Members know, in advance, precisely what information they must provide when reporting a Rule 213 incident, as well as the types of information OCC may request as its investigation proceeds. OCC believes this advance clarity will enable Clearing Members to prepare more effectively and will allow OCC to more promptly and effectively review and mitigate any risk associated with the incident.
OCC believes that the requested information in the proposed sections (A) through (G), including Legal Entities, Contact Information, and details of the Clearing Member System Event are essential pieces of information that would help OCC to efficiently and effectively review and take action to mitigate risk presented. OCC also believes the proposed changes will allow Clearing Members and their Third-Party Service Providers to better understand and prepare for their obligations to OCC in the event they experience a Clearing Member System Event.
Proposed Rule 213(e)
[
14
]
—Declaration of a Major Clearing Member System Event
OCC proposes to introduce new Rule 213(e) sections (1) through (3), which would focus on the declaration of a Major Clearing Member System Event, including the details surrounding who is authorized to declare such event and notification requirements associated with such event.
First, proposed Rule 213(e)(1) would provide that upon becoming aware of a Clearing Member System Event, OCC will consider whether such Clearing Member System Event meets the definition of a Major Clearing Member System Event. The proposed change would also provide that the existence of a Major Clearing Member System Event must be declared by two or more Designated Officers of OCC, in their reasonable judgement.
Second, proposed Rule 213(e)(2) would provide that upon declaration of a Major Clearing Member System Event, OCC may act (or refrain from acting) pursuant to this Rule to help address, correct, mitigate or alleviate any and all risks presented to OCC by or related to the Major Clearing Member System Event. The proposed change would also provide that action taken will be in consideration of the risks presented to OCC, including but not limited to, information provided pursuant to this Rule.
The purpose of OCC's Proposed Rule 213(e)(1) through (2) is to clarify that OCC will assess the potential impact of a Clearing Member System Event on OCC's Systems and operations, and OCC will determine to act, or refrain from acting, depending on the details of the Clearing Member System Event. The proposed rule removes any ambiguity that may exist in present language that invites the Clearing Member to assess potential impact of the Clearing Member System Event on OCC's Systems or operations. The purpose of the proposed change is also to clearly define who is authorized to declare a Major Clearing Member System event, specifically, that such a declaration must be made by two or more Designated Officers of OCC. OCC believes it is appropriate that such declaration be made by two or more Designated Officers of OCC to ensure that information regarding the Clearing Member System Event has been escalated to and considered at the highest management level. OCC believes the proposed rule change also provides transparency to Clearing Members and other stakeholders as to who is authorized to declare a Major Clearing Member System Event.
Lastly, OCC's proposed changes introduce a new requirement that OCC notify the Chairman of the Board of Directors following a declaration of a Major Clearing Member System Event. Specifically, proposed Rule 213(e)(3) provides that following declaration of a Major Clearing Member System Event, OCC will promptly notify the Chairman of the Board of Directors of such declaration. Because a Major Clearing Member System Event reflects OCC's determination that a Clearing Member System Event may have a significant impact on OCC's Systems or operations, OCC believes it is appropriate that this information be escalated to the Chairman of the Board of Directors without delay. OCC believes that notifying the Chairman is appropriate because it allows the Chairman to determine, based on the nature and severity of the specific Major Clearing Member System Event, the extent to which the full Board or any relevant Board Committee should be further notified or involved.
Proposed Rule 213(f)—Authority To Take Action and Required Cooperation
Proposed Rule 213(f) would expand upon OCC's existing authority to take action in the event of a Clearing Member System Event and associated Major Clearing Member System Event. More specifically, proposed Rule 213(f)
(
printed page 66884)
introduces requirements surrounding: (i) OCC's ability to act, or refrain from acting, in the event of a Major Clearing Member System Event, (ii) OCC's responsibility to notify the Clearing Member of any disconnect or material action taken, and (iii) the Clearing Member's responsibility to cooperate fully and to the reasonable satisfaction of OCC in the event of a Major Clearing Member System Event. Proposed Rule 213(f) also makes other conforming and non-substantive changes, including reorganizing provisions into a hierarchical structure, and updating language to promote clarity and efficiency.
OCC's proposed changes would organize Rule 213(f) into subsections (1) through (4). Proposed Rule 213(f)(1) details, in part, OCC's ability to, in the event of a Clearing Member System Event, take actions reasonably necessary to mitigate any impact to its operations, including actions described in proposed Rule 213(f)(1)(A) through Rule 213(f)(1)(C).
[

]
OCC's changes to proposed Rule 213(f)(1)(A) make conforming and non-substantive changes to the text, including removing the phrase “the right to.” To maintain consistency and align with OCC's proposed definition of OCC's Systems, OCC proposes to eliminate the term “data” before systems in proposed Rule 213(f)(1)(A). Proposed Rule 213(f)(1)(B) is new and provides that OCC may take actions reasonably necessary to mitigate any effects to its operations, including to suspend any and all transmissions, communications, or access between OCC's Systems (together with actions taken under Rule 213(f)(1)(A), “disconnect”). The purpose of this change is to broaden OCC's authority to take action that OCC believes may be necessary to mitigate risk presented by a Clearing Member System Event and associated Major Clearing Member System Event. In addition to OCC's existing authority to disconnect access of a Clearing Member, as described in proposed Rule 213(f)(1)(A), OCC believes the proposed change to expand OCC's authority to suspend any and all transmission, communication or access of a Clearing Member will help to ensure that OCC can adequately address all potential connectivity and communication types of a Clearing Member. OCC also proposes to adopt new Rule 213(f)(1)(C) to provide OCC the authority to act in the event OCC determines that a Major Clearing Member System Event has occurred. Proposed Rule 213(f)(1)(C) provides that OCC may take, or refrain from taking, or require the subject Clearing Member to take or refrain from taking, any and all action that OCC considers appropriate to help address, correct, mitigate or alleviate the Major Clearing Member System Event and, as appropriate and practical, facilitate the continuation of services, which may include issuing instructions to the subject Clearing Member and requiring such Clearing Member to act on such instructions. Examples of actions that OCC considers appropriate may include, but are not limited to, disconnection from OCC's Systems, forced password resets, and requiring the Clearing Member to use alternative communication and file transfer methods (
e.g.,
secure file transport instead of email). The purpose of this proposed change is to provide OCC with the authority to evaluate and address a Major Clearing Member System Event and adequately respond to such event in effort to mitigate impact to OCC and its Clearing Members. Additionally, in the event OCC determines a Major Clearing Member System Event has occurred, by adding the provision that allows OCC to issue instructions and requires the subject Clearing Member to follow those instructions, OCC believes this requirement will help to help facilitate the continuation of services for the subject Clearing Member and alleviate future impact that may otherwise result from the disruption. Specifically, the issuance of instructions allows OCC to direct a more tailored response that is specific to the nature and severity of the Major Clearing Member System Event. This flexibility enables OCC to address the risk presented by a specific Major Clearing Member System Event while, where practicable, preserving the Clearing Member's ability to continue some or all of its services during remediation.
OCC proposes to adopt Rule 213(f)(3), which addresses OCC's notification requirements to the Clearing Member, as well as the subject Clearing Member's obligations to comply with OCC's statutory rules. More specifically, proposed Rule 213(f)(3) would provide that OCC will promptly notify the Clearing Member of any disconnect or other material action that OCC takes with respect to such Clearing Member pursuant to Rule 213. In addition, proposed Rule 213(f)(3) would provide that, notwithstanding any action taken pursuant to Rule 213, the Clearing Member must continue to meet its obligations to OCC and comply with OCC's statutory rules, as defined in its By-Laws. Under OCC's existing Rule 213, if OCC determines that disconnection of a Clearing Member from OCC's Systems is necessary, the Clearing Member must continue to meet its obligations to OCC notwithstanding that disconnection. OCC's existing Rule 213(d) focuses solely on the Clearing Member's continuing obligations following a disconnection and it does not address whether OCC will notify the Clearing Member that a disconnection (or any other action) has occurred. Proposed Rule 213(f)(3) expands the current provision in two respects: (i) it adds a notification obligation on OCC's part, and (ii) it broadens both the scope of triggering actions (from disconnection alone to any material action under the Rule) and the scope of the Clearing Member's continuing obligations to also include compliance with OCC's statutory rules, as the term is defined in OCC's By-Laws.
These proposed changes serve several purposes. First, the purpose of requiring OCC to promptly notify a Clearing Member of any disconnection or other material action taken under this Rule is to provide enhanced transparency to Clearing Members regarding actions that OCC takes that impact them. OCC believes it is prudent to notify the Clearing Member promptly in such event to allow the Clearing Member to better prepare for and understand their obligations to OCC. Second, the proposed change expands the scope of that notification obligation from disconnection alone to “any material action” taken pursuant to the Rule. This may include, for example, modifying the scope and specifications of access of the Clearing Member to OCC's Systems. The purpose of this proposed change is to ensure that Clearing Members receive notice of any material action OCC may take, not solely the most severe action of disconnection. Third, the proposed change broadens the Clearing Member's continuing obligations to apply “notwithstanding any action taken pursuant to this Rule,” rather than only “notwithstanding disconnection,” removing any ambiguity as to whether a Clearing Member's obligations to OCC continue in the event OCC takes a material action, outside of disconnection. Finally, the proposed change also specifies what obligations the Clearing Member must continue to meet, by adding an express requirement that the Clearing Member comply with the statutory rules of OCC, as defined in OCC's By-Laws. OCC's current Rule 213 refers only generally to the Clearing Member's “obligations to OCC” without
(
printed page 66885)
specifying what those obligations include. OCC believes the addition of “comply with the statutory rules of OCC, as defined in its By-Laws” clarifies what those obligations encompass. OCC's proposed changes to proposed Rule 213(f)(3) also make other conforming, non-substantive changes.
Lastly, OCC proposes to adopt new Rule 213(f)(4), which requires that the Clearing Member must cooperate fully and completely with, and to the reasonable satisfaction of, OCC in all matters relating to the Major Clearing Member System Event, including, but not limited: (i) conducting timely investigations and inquiries, as OCC believes reasonably necessary, with respect to any known or unknown information relating to the Clearing Member System Event; (ii) promptly notifying OCC of any material changes, updates, or new information learned regarding the Clearing Member System Event; and (iii) promptly providing any documentation or information requested by OCC, unless not legally permitted to do so, regarding or related to the Clearing Member System Event.

The purpose of this proposed change is to provide enhanced transparency to Clearing Members on their obligations to comply with the proposed requirements. OCC believes that cooperation from Clearing Members on matters relating to a Major Clearing Member System Event will help OCC to efficiently and effectively manage and respond to a Major Clearing Member System Event in effort to mitigate risk presented.

Procedures for Reconnection
OCC proposes to update existing Rule 213(e) titled “Procedures for Connecting Following a Security Incident that Results in Disconnection” to Proposed Rule 213(g) titled “Procedures for Reconnection.” OCC believes that such change in title is necessary to more accurately encompass the obligations of a Clearing Member pursuant to OCC's authority to act in the event of a Clearing Member System Event, as described in proposed Rule 213(f)(1). The retitled rule sets forth the information that the subject Clearing Member would be required to provide OCC in the event OCC takes action pursuant to proposed Rule 213(f)(1) and includes both substantive and non-substantive changes as described below. Proposed Rule 213(g) also reorganizes existing Rule 213(e) into proposed Rule 213(g)(1) through 213(g)(2), and incorporates new section (3) in proposed Rule 213(g)(3) titled “Report from Third-Party Cybersecurity Firm.”
Proposed Rule 213(g)(1) Reconnection Attestation
OCC's proposed Rule 213(g)(1) would be titled “Reconnection Attestation.” Proposed Rule 213(g)(1) would include the current requirement that a subject Clearing Member must complete and submit a Reconnection Attestation prior to OCC reestablishing connectivity to OCC's Systems. More specifically, proposed Rule 213(g)(1) would provide that if OCC takes action pursuant to Rule 213(f)(1), the Clearing Member must complete and submit a form as provided by OCC that describes the Clearing Member System Event and includes required representations (“Reconnection Attestation”). OCC proposes to add language to clarify that such requirement must be met prior to OCC reestablishing connectivity to OCC's Systems (“Reconnection”). OCC proposes to relocate the existing provision that states “The Clearing Member also will be required to complete an associated checklist provided by OCC that describes remediation efforts (“Reconnection Checklist”),” because OCC believes such text is more appropriately located in proposed Rule 213(g)(2), which outlines the requirements in the Reconnection Checklist. In addition, OCC's proposed changes collapse and consolidate Rule 213(e)(1) into Rule 213(e), which becomes proposed Rule 213(g), such that the signature requirement is now reflected in proposed Rule 213(g)(1). Specifically, OCC's proposed changes reflect that the provision in current Rule 213(e)(1) on the requirement for the Reconnection Attestation to be signed by a designated senior executive becomes included in proposed Rule 213(g)(1). This change is intended to make Rule 213 easier to navigate by grouping related requirements together; it does not alter the Clearing Member's underlying obligation to obtain a signature from an individual who maintains the authorization to sign the Reconnection Attestation. OCC's proposed changes also eliminate the term “designated” when describing the senior executive of the Clearing Member that must sign the Reconnection Attestation. OCC believes the term “designated” creates ambiguity. By removing this term, OCC believes it improves operational flexibility by allowing any senior executive of the Clearing Member

OCC believes the proposed change preserves the integrity and reliability of the attestation, since the signatory must still be a senior executive with the requisite authorization to attest to these matters.
In addition, proposed Rule 213(g)(1)(A) through 213(g)(1)(E) incorporates the requirements in current Rule 213(e)(1)(A) though Rule 213(e)(1)(E) and makes other non-substantive changes including renaming the term “Security Incident” to “Clearing Member System Event,” as described in proposed Rule 213(a).

OCC's ability to require an audit report from a Third-Party Cybersecurity Firm provides OCC with essential information that will help OCC to fully evaluate the Clearing Member System Event and take steps to mitigate risks presented by such incident.
Proposed Rule 213(h) Reconnection Testing and Approval
OCC's proposed changes would adopt Rule 213(h) titled “Reconnection Testing and Approval, ” which would require, prior to any Reconnection, that the subject Clearing Member must demonstrate, as applicable, to OCC's reasonable satisfaction, that it: (i) can operate in a test environment, including, but not limited to, sending and receiving messages and transactions; (ii) can replay or resubmit previously submitted messages or transactions; (iii) can reverse or void previously submitted messages or transactions; (iv) can confirm the integrity of messages and transactions; (v) has alternative communication methods with OCC to facilitate the exchange of messages, transactions, and reports; and (vi) can complete any other such requirements as are reasonably requested by OCC. Furthermore, proposed Rule 213(h)(2) would authorize two or more Designated Officers of OCC to, in their reasonable judgment, approve the Reconnection of a Clearing Member that was the subject of action taken pursuant to proposed Rule 213, after OCC has received all required information pursuant to this Rule, in a form and a substance satisfactory OCC, and that all information necessary for a safe Reconnection and certain testing has occurred, pursuant to proposed Rule 213(h)(1).
The purpose of proposed Rule 213(h) is to ensure that the approval for a Reconnection is not made until OCC has received, to its satisfaction, all necessary information from the Clearing Member, and that OCC confirmed the subject Clearing Member can safely perform the capabilities necessary for submitting, receiving, and correcting information appropriately and in a manner unaffected by the Clearing Member System Event, so as to help mitigate the risk presented by the Reconnection. In addition, OCC believes it is appropriate that the approval of a Reconnection be made by at least two members of OCC's management committee to help ensure that information regarding the Reconnection has been escalated to the highest management level.
Proposed Rule 213(i) Certain Miscellaneous Matters
OCC proposes to adopt Rule 213(i), titled “Certain Miscellaneous Matters,” which would address various provisions including, but not limited to, (i) OCC's limited liability to a Clearing Member pursuant to proposed Rule 213; (ii) OCC's authority to inform the subject Clearing Member's Third-Party Service Provider, or require the Clearing Member to inform its Third-Party Service Provider, of a Clearing Member System Event; and (iii) the failure of a Clearing Member to comply with proposed Rule 213.
First, in an effort to promote enhanced transparency to Clearing Members, proposed Rule 213(i)(1) would address, in part, OCC's limited liability to any Clearing Member as it relates to losses arising out of OCC's action or inaction pursuant to proposed Rule 213. More specifically, proposed Rule 213(i)(1) would provide that without limiting any other provisions in these Rules concerning limitations on liability, neither OCC nor its directors, officers, employees, agents, or contractors shall be liable to any Clearing Member or any customer or client thereof for: (i) any failure, hindrance, interruption or delay in performance in whole or in part of the obligations of OCC under these Rules, if that failure, hindrance, interruption or delay arises out of or relates to a Clearing Member System Event, Major Clearing Member System Event, or any action or inaction pursuant to this Rule 213; or (ii) any loss, liability, damage, cost or expense arising from or relating in any way to any advice, request, requirement, instruction, action or inaction pursuant to this Rule 213.

Third, proposed Rule 213(i)(3) would provide that the powers of OCC pursuant to this Rule 213 are in addition to, and not in limitation of, any authority granted elsewhere in these Rules to act as specified therein. 2. Statutory Basis
OCC believes the proposed rule change is consistent with Section 17A of the Exchange Act

[
23

requires, among other things, that the rules of a clearing agency be designed to promote the prompt and accurate clearance and settlement of securities transactions, and to assure the safeguarding of securities and funds which are in the custody or control of the clearing agency or for which it is responsible. OCC's proposed amendments to Rule 213 are designed to help OCC assess and take appropriate action to manage the cybersecurity risks that may be introduced to OCC's Systems and information due to a Clearing Member System Event. The proposed changes to Rule 213 enhance OCC's processes to help mitigate risk and better protect OCC and its Clearing Members.
As described above, the proposed rule change would, in part: (i) introduce a defined terms section to Rule 213 that broadens the definition of OCC Systems to include established communication channels, such as FTPs, in addition to direct connections; (ii) require that the Cybersecurity Confirmation be signed by a senior executive of the Clearing Member or applicant who is authorized to attest to such matters; (iii) remove language inviting a Clearing Member to assess the potential impact of a Clearing Member System Event on OCC's systems and operations when determining whether the event is reportable, and instead specify the timeframe for reporting such an event and the specific information that must be included in the notice; (iv) establish the concept of a “Major Clearing Member System Event,” including a declaration process requiring approval by two or more Designated Officers and prompt notification to the Chairman of the Board; (v) reorganize and clarify OCC's authority to take action in response to a Clearing Member System Event, including specifying the actions that constitute a “disconnect” and clarifying a Clearing Member's related obligations; (vi) add provisions establishing the reporting, testing, approval, and governance requirements necessary for reconnection, including OCC's ability to require an audit report from a Third-Party Cybersecurity Firm; and (vii) provide OCC with the authority to inform, or to require a Clearing Member to inform, the Clearing Member's Third-Party Service Provider of a Clearing Member System Event if OCC determines, in its discretion, that such action is necessary to protect OCC and other Clearing Members. OCC believes that these proposed changes will enhance Rule 213 to be more efficient, effective and clear in the cybersecurity obligations of its Clearing Members so that OCC may better address cybersecurity risks to protect OCC and its Clearing Members. Among the amendments discussed above, OCC believes the following amendments to Rule 213 are particularly consistent with the requirements of Section 17A(b)(3)(F) of the Act, as discussed in further detail below: (i) expanded notification requirements applicable to a Clearing Member System Event; (ii) the establishment of the Major Clearing Member System Event and its related governance; and (iii) the process for Reconnection of a Clearing Member.
First, proposed Rule 213(d) codifies within OCC's rules the specific content and timeframe requirements for notification of a Clearing Member System Event, which OCC believes is consistent with the requirements of Section 17A(b)(3)(F) of the Act.
[
24
]
Under proposed Rule 213(d), a Clearing Member would be required to provide OCC with specified information at the onset of a Clearing Member System Event, including but not limited to the event type, effect, scope, start date, end date, discovery date, and any public notices related to the event. OCC believes this requirement will allow OCC to receive consistent, timely information from Clearing Members, which in turn, will help to minimize the risk that delayed or incomplete information impacts OCC's ability to respond promptly and effectively to such events. As such, OCC believes this proposed change supports the prompt and accurate clearance and settlement of securities transactions and assures the safeguarding of securities and funds that are in the custody or control of OCC, consistent with Section 17A(b)(3)(F) of the Act.
[
25
]
Second, proposed Rule 213(e) establishes the concept of a “Major Clearing Member System Event,” which OCC believes is also consistent with the requirements of Section 17A(b)(3)(F) of the Act.
[
26
]
Under proposed Rule 213(e), OCC would assess the potential impact of a Clearing Member System Event on OCC's Systems and operations, and would determine to act, or refrain from acting, depending on the specific details of the event. This removes the ambiguity that may exist in the current rule text, which instead invites the Clearing Member to assess potential impact of its own Clearing Member System Event on OCC's Systems or operations. Furthermore, under proposed Rule 213(e), the existence of a Major Clearing Member System Event must be declared by two or more Designated Officers of OCC, in their reasonable judgement. Following such a declaration, OCC will promptly notify the Chairman of the Board. OCC believes this process ensures that the most severe threats to OCC's Systems and operations are escalated to the highest levels of OCC's governance. OCC believes the establishment of a Major Clearing Member System Event and the governance outlined in proposed Rule 213(e) is consistent with Section 17A(b)(3)(F) of the Act because OCC, not the reporting Clearing Member, is best positioned to determine the severity of a threat to OCC's own Systems and operations. Additionally, OCC believes that escalation to the highest levels of OCC's governance helps to ensure events with the greatest potential impact to OCC receive attention and oversight proportionate to their severity. As such, OCC believes the proposed rule change is designed to

Under proposed Rule 213(h)(1), prior to Reconnection, a Clearing Member must demonstrate, to OCC's reasonable satisfaction, that it can, in part, operate in a test environment, send and receive messages and transactions, replay or resubmit previously submitted messages or transactions, reverse or void previously submitted messages or transactions, confirm the integrity of messages and transactions, and maintain alternative communication methods with OCC. These requirements test the Clearing Member's operational capability to interact accurately and reliably with OCC's Systems, rather than relying on the Clearing Member's representation that it is prepared to reconnect. OCC believes this proposed change is designed to safeguard securities and funds in the custody or control of OCC by verifying, before Reconnection occurs, that a Clearing Member's systems will not transmit corrupted or otherwise unreliable messages or transactions into OCC's Systems and operations. Therefore, by enhancing OCC's processes to mitigate these risks, including but not limited to: expanding the notification requirements, establishing the concept of a Major Clearing Member System Event, and enhancing its process for Reconnection, OCC believes the proposed changes would promote the prompt and accurate clearance and settlement of securities transactions and assure the safeguarding of securities and funds that are in the custody or control of the clearing agency or for which it is responsible, consistent with the requirements of Section 17A(b)(3)(F) of the Act.

OCC believes the proposed changes to Rule 213 are consistent with Rule 17ad-22(e)(2)(i) and (v), which require, in part, that each covered clearing agency establish, implement, maintain and enforce written policies and procedures reasonably designed to provide for governance arrangements that (i) are clear and transparent and (ii) specify clear and direct lines of responsibility.
